WORKED EXAMPLE — "If it rains, I bring an umbrella"

Contrapositive¬q → ¬pYES — logically equivalent
⚠️ THE CONVERSE TRAP

🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK

  1. ¬q → ¬p
  2. q → p

Show answer + steps

📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)

Implication (p → q)

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

This is the single most confusing thing in logic — once it clicks, the rest gets easier. “If p then q” is a promise. The only way to BREAK a promise is to have the condition happen (p true) but the result fail (q false). If the condition never happens (p false), you never broke the promise — so it counts as kept (true).

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Think “If it rains, I bring an umbrella.” When did I lie? Only if it rained AND I had no umbrella. If it didn't rain, I told no lie no matter what I carried. So p→q is false in exactly one case — p true, q false — and true in the other three.

Truth table for p→q: TT→T, TF→F, FT→T, FF→T. That lone F is the whole concept.

Key rewrite: p → q is logically the same as ¬p ∨ q (“not-p or q”). This identity unlocks tons of simplification problems.

📝 EXAM WORDING

For p → q: the converse is q → p; the inverse is ¬p → ¬q; the contrapositive is ¬q → ¬p. The contrapositive is logically equivalent to the original; converse and inverse are NOT (they equal each other).

⚠️ WATCH OUT

A statement and its converse are not the same — “if rain then umbrella” does not mean “if umbrella then rain.” The exam loves offering the converse as a wrong “equivalent.” Only the contrapositive is equivalent.

🔎 Converse

Swap the two sides: the converse of p → q is q → p. NOT equivalent to the original!

Example: "If it’s a dog, it’s a mammal" is true; the converse "if it’s a mammal, it’s a dog" is false.
📊 FIGURE — The conditional p → q and its three relatives
p → q is false ONLY when a true hypothesis leads to a false conclusion (row 2). The contrapositive ¬q → ¬p always has the SAME truth values as the original (diagonal, green); the converse and inverse are each other’s contrapositives but are NOT equivalent to the original.

NEGATION — flip and move inward
¬∀x P(x) = ∃x ¬P(x) · ¬∃x P(x) = ∀x ¬P(x)
English: the negation of "all passed" is "at least one did not pass" — NOT "none passed."
⚠️ TWO TRAPS
(1) Swapping ∀ and ∃ usually CHANGES the truth value — never assume you can reorder. (2) Negating "all are X" gives "some are not X"; negating "some are X" gives "none are X / all are not X."

📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)

Quantifiers ∀ and ∃

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

∀ means “for all / every”; ∃ means “there exists / at least one.” The hard part is when they're stacked, because order changes the meaning. “Everyone has a mother” (each person gets their own) is very different from “there is one person who is everyone's mother” (a single mother for all).

📊 FIGURE — ∀ "for all" vs. ∃ "there exists"
Top row: every element satisfies P, so both ∀x P(x) and ∃x P(x) hold. Bottom row: only one does — ∃x P(x) is still true, but ∀x P(x) fails. To DISPROVE a ∀ claim you need just one counterexample; to disprove ∃ you must rule out every element.
⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

∀x ∃y P(x,y) = for every x there is SOME y (the y can depend on x). ∃y ∀x P(x,y) = there's ONE y that works for ALL x at once — a much stronger claim.

Over the integers, ∀x ∃y (y > x) is TRUE (for any number there's a bigger one), but ∃y ∀x (y > x) is FALSE (no single number beats every number). Same symbols, opposite truth — order is everything.

Negation flips and moves inward: push ¬ through, turning ∀ into ∃ and ∃ into ∀, and negate the inside. ¬∀x P(x) = ∃x ¬P(x) and ¬∃x P(x) = ∀x ¬P(x).

📝 EXAM WORDING

∀ is the universal quantifier; ∃ is the existential quantifier. “The negation of ∀x∃y P is ∃x∀y ¬P” is a standard item. The English negation of “all passed” is “at least one did not pass” — NOT “none passed.”

⚠️ WATCH OUT

Two traps: (1) swapping ∀ and ∃ usually changes the truth value — never assume you can reorder. (2) Negating “all are X” gives “some are not X”; negating “some are X” gives “none are X / all are not X.”

🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK

  1. ¬p ∧ ¬q
  2. ¬p ∨ ¬q
  3. p ∧ q

📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)

Logical equivalences & De Morgan

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Some logical statements look different but are secretly the same — like 2+3 and 3+2. Knowing the common equivalences lets you simplify a scary expression into an obvious one. De Morgan's laws are the two you'll use most: how to distribute a NOT across an AND or an OR.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

De Morgan: ¬(p ∧ q) = ¬p ∨ ¬q and ¬(p ∨ q) = ¬p ∧ ¬q. In words: “not (both)” = “at least one is not”; “not (either)” = “both are not.” The NOT flips the connective (AND↔OR) as it moves in.

Other high-value ones: p → q = ¬p ∨ q (implication as or); double negation ¬¬p = p; plus distribution, commutation, association — same shapes as ordinary algebra.

📝 EXAM WORDING

A tautology is always true; a contradiction always false; a contingency depends on inputs. Two statements are logically equivalent (≡) when they have identical truth tables. Expect “which expression is equivalent to…” items — apply De Morgan or the implication rewrite.

⚠️ WATCH OUT

De Morgan flips the operator: people negate each part but forget to switch AND↔OR. ¬(p ∧ q) is ¬p ∨ ¬q, not ¬p ∧ ¬q.

POWER SET & INCLUSION–EXCLUSION

|A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B| — subtract the overlap so you don't double-count.
SymbolReads

∈"is an ELEMENT of" — a thing in a set
⊆"is a SUBSET of" — a set inside a set
📊 FIGURE — Subset, membership, and the universal set
The rectangle is the universal set U — everything under discussion. A ⊆ B means A sits entirely inside B. The dot x ∈ A is an ELEMENT (belongs with ∈); A itself relates to B with ⊆. Confusing ∈ with ⊆ is a classic exam trap.
⚠️ ∈ vs ⊆
Don't confuse element-of with subset-of. The empty set is a SUBSET of every set — but an ELEMENT only if explicitly listed.
🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
A set with 5 elements has how many subsets?
  1. 32
  2. 25
  3. 10

Show answer + steps

📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)

Sets, power sets & cardinality

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A set is just a collection of distinct things — no duplicates, no order. Most set operations are common sense once you picture two overlapping circles (a Venn diagram): the overlap, everything combined, what's in one but not the other.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Union (A ∪ B) = everything in either. Intersection (A ∩ B) = only what's in both. Difference (A − B) = in A but not B. Complement (A′) = everything not in A.

🔎 Intersection (∩)

Only what the sets SHARE — the overlap.

Example: {1,2} ∩ {2,3} = {2}.
🔎 Union (∪)

Everything in EITHER set (or both) — the sets merged.

Example: {1,2} ∪ {2,3} = {1,2,3}.

Cardinality |A| = how many elements. The power set P(A) is the set of ALL subsets (including ∅ and A itself). If |A| = n, then P(A) has 2ⁿ subsets — each element is in or out, 2 choices, n times.

🔎 Cardinality |A|

The number of elements in a set.

Example: |{a, b, c}| = 3; |∅| = 0.

Inclusion–exclusion: |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B| — subtract the overlap so you don't double-count.

📝 EXAM WORDING

∅ is the empty set (0 elements). ∈ means “is an element of”; ⊆ means “is a subset of.” A set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets — a guaranteed exam fact.

⚠️ WATCH OUT

Don't confuse ∈ (element of — a thing in a set) with ⊆ (subset — a set inside a set). The empty set is a subset of every set, but an element only if explicitly listed.

🎯 Functions: 1-to-1, Onto, Bijective

PropertyFormal nameMeans
One-to-oneInjectiveDifferent inputs → different outputs; no two arrows land on the same target
OntoSurjectiveEVERY element of the codomain is reached — no target left out
BothBijectiveA perfect one-to-one pairing — the ONLY functions with an inverse
TermDefinition
DomainAllowed inputs
CodomainDECLARED possible outputs
RangeOutputs ACTUALLY produced
THE INVERTIBILITY RULE
A function is invertible if and only if it is bijective.
⚠️ ONTO IS ABOUT THE CODOMAIN
A function is onto only if its range fills the ENTIRE declared codomain — not just "produces outputs." The horizontal-line test checks one-to-one; the vertical-line test just checks whether it's a function at all.
🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
A function has an inverse if and only if it is:
  1. Bijective
  2. Injective only
  3. Surjective only
  4. Any function
Show answer + steps
A. It needs BOTH: no collisions (injective) and every target hit (surjective) for the reverse mapping to be a function.
📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)

Functions: 1-to-1, onto, bijective

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A function is a machine: put in an input, get exactly one output. The three properties describe how inputs map to outputs. One-to-one = no two inputs share an output (no collisions). Onto = every possible output gets hit. Bijective = both at once (a perfect pairing).

🔎 Bijective

Injective AND surjective — a perfect one-to-one pairing. Exactly these functions have inverses.

Example: f(x) = x + 3 pairs every real with exactly one real.
🔎 Surjective (onto)

Every codomain element gets hit by at least one arrow — nothing in the target is missed.

Example: f: ℝ→ℝ, f(x) = x³ is onto; x² is not (misses negatives).
🔎 Injective (one-to-one)

No two inputs share an output — arrows never merge. Different in ⟹ different out.

Example: f(x) = 2x is injective; f(x) = x² is not (f(2) = f(−2)).
⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Injective (one-to-one): different inputs → different outputs. No two arrows land on the same target.

Surjective (onto): every element of the codomain is reached — no target is left out.

Bijective: injective AND surjective — a perfect one-to-one pairing. Only bijections have an inverse function that undoes them.

🔎 Inverse function f⁻¹

The function that UNDOES f: f⁻¹(f(x)) = x. Exists only when f is bijective. Found by swapping input and output.

Example: f(x) = 3x − 2 ⟹ f⁻¹(y) = (y + 2)/3.
📝 EXAM WORDING

“One-to-one” = injective; “onto” = surjective; both = bijective. Domain = allowed inputs; codomain = declared possible outputs; range = outputs actually produced. A function is invertible if and only if it is bijective.

🔎 Inverse matrix A⁻¹

The matrix that undoes A: A·A⁻¹ = I. Exists only when det ≠ 0. Solves Ax = b as x = A⁻¹b.

Example: 2×2 recipe: swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal, divide by det.
⚠️ WATCH OUT

“Onto” is about the codomain, not the range — a function is onto only if its range fills the entire declared codomain. The horizontal-line test checks one-to-one; the vertical-line test just checks whether it's a function at all.

📊 FIGURE — One-to-one vs. onto vs. bijection
Injective (one-to-one): no output is hit twice — arrows never merge. Surjective (onto): every codomain element is hit at least once — nothing left out. Bijective: both at once, giving a perfect pairing (and an inverse function).

🎰 Counting: Permutations vs Combinations

THE ONLY QUESTION
Does ORDER count? Rearranging makes a different result (podium: gold–silver–bronze) → permutation. Same people, same group (committee) → combination.
WORKED EXAMPLE — 3 from 8, both ways
QuestionFormulaComputeAnswer
3 winners, 1st/2nd/3rd differP(n,r) = n!/(n−r)!8×7×6336
3 people for a teamC(n,r) = n!/(r!(n−r)!)336 / 3!56
You divide out the r! orderings you no longer care about. n! = n×(n−1)×…×1, and 0! = 1. Always C(n,r) ≤ P(n,r).
⚠️ GIVE-AWAY WORDS
"Arrange, order, rank, sequence, password, podium" → permutation. "Choose, select, group, committee, team, subset" → combination. Misreading this is the #1 counting mistake. C(n,r) is also written nCr or "n choose r."
🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
How many 3-person teams from 8 people?
  1. 56
  2. 336
  3. 24
  4. 512
Show answer + steps
A — 56. Team = order doesn't matter: C(8,3) = 336/6 = 56. (336 is the podium/permutation answer.)
📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)

Counting: permutations vs combinations

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

The only question that matters: does order count? If rearranging the same items makes a DIFFERENT result (a race podium: gold–silver–bronze), it's a permutation. If order doesn't matter (picking a committee — same people, same group), it's a combination.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Permutations (order matters): P(n,r) = n! / (n−r)!. Choosing 3 winners from 8 where 1st/2nd/3rd differ: 8×7×6 = 336.

Combinations (order doesn't): C(n,r) = n! / (r!(n−r)!). Choosing 3 people from 8 for a team: 336 / 3! = 56. You divide out the r! orderings you no longer care about.

The factorial n! = n×(n−1)×…×1 counts arrangements of n distinct items in a row. And 0! = 1.

📊 FIGURE — Permutation slots — then divide out order for combinations
Choosing 3 of 5 people IN ORDER fills slots 5 · 4 · 3 = 60 ways: P(5,3). If order does not matter, each group of 3 was counted 3! = 6 times, so divide: C(5,3) = 60 / 6 = 10. "Does order matter?" is the entire decision.
📝 EXAM WORDING

Permutation = arrangement (order matters); combination = selection (order doesn't). C(n,r) is also written nCr or “n choose r.” Always C(n,r) ≤ P(n,r) because combinations collapse the orderings.

⚠️ WATCH OUT

Give-away words: “arrange, order, rank, sequence, password, podium” → permutation. “choose, select, group, committee, team, subset” → combination. Misreading this is the #1 counting mistake.

🕐 Modular Arithmetic ("clock math")

THE IDEA
On a 12-hour clock, 4 hours after 10 is 2, not 14 — you WRAP AROUND. "a mod n" = the remainder after dividing by n, always in the range 0 to n−1.
WORKED EXAMPLES
ExpressionWhyResult
17 mod 517 = 3×5 + 22
20 mod 5divides evenly0 (not 5!)
Congruence: a ≡ b (mod n) means a and b leave the SAME remainder — equivalently, n divides (a−b). E.g. 17 ≡ 2 (mod 5). This is the backbone of hashing, cryptography (RSA), and check digits.
⚠️ NEVER NEGATIVE, ALWAYS < n
The remainder is never negative and always LESS than n. 20 mod 5 = 0, not 5 — don't stop one step early.
🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
Compute 23 mod 6.
  1. 5
  2. 6
  3. 3
  4. 4
Show answer + steps
A — 5. 23 = 3×6 + 5.
📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)
📊 FIGURE — Modular arithmetic as a clock
Mod 12 wraps numbers around a circle: counting to 14 lands on 2, so 14 ≡ 2 (mod 12). "a mod n" is simply where a lands after wrapping — which is why mod is perfect for time, cyclic schedules, and hash tables.

Modular arithmetic (“clock math”)

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Modular arithmetic is clock math. On a 12-hour clock, 4 hours after 10 o'clock is 2, not 14 — you wrap around. “mod n” just means “the remainder after dividing by n,” wrapping values into the range 0 to n−1.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

a mod n = the remainder when a is divided by n. 17 mod 5 = 2 (17 = 3×5 + 2). The result is always between 0 and n−1.

“Congruent mod n” (a ≡ b (mod n)) means a and b leave the same remainder — equivalently, n divides (a−b). E.g. 17 ≡ 2 (mod 5). This is the backbone of hashing, cryptography (RSA), and check digits.

📝 EXAM WORDING

“a mod n” gives the remainder; “a ≡ b (mod n)” is read “a is congruent to b modulo n.” Expect “compute x mod n” items and “which values are congruent mod n” groupings.

⚠️ WATCH OUT

The remainder is never negative here and is always less than n. 20 mod 5 = 0 (it divides evenly), not 5. Don't stop one step early.

📐 Proof Techniques — pick the right template

TechniqueThe moveBest when
DirectAssume the hypothesis, march to the conclusionThe path is clear
ContrapositiveInstead of p→q, prove ¬q→¬p (logically identical)The reversed direction is easier
ContradictionAssume the statement is FALSE, derive an impossibilityThe classic √2-is-irrational proof
InductionBase case (n=1) + "if it holds for n=k, it holds for n=k+1"Statements about ALL positive integers
THE DOMINO PICTURE FOR INDUCTION
Knock the first domino (base case), and each domino knocks the next (inductive step, using the inductive hypothesis). Both parts are required.
🔎 Induction

Prove P(1) (base case), then prove P(k) ⟹ P(k+1) (inductive step, using the inductive hypothesis). Dominoes: first falls, each knocks the next — all fall.

Example: 1+2+…+n = n(n+1)/2 for every n.
📊 FIGURE — Induction is a chain of dominoes
The base case tips the first domino (verify P(1) directly). The inductive step proves each domino knocks over the next (P(k) ⟹ P(k+1)). Together they topple every domino — the statement holds for all n. On the exam, always state both parts explicitly.
COUNTEREXAMPLES
A counterexample DISPROVES a universal ("for all") claim.
⚠️ EXAMPLES DON'T PROVE
One counterexample disproves a "for all" statement — but NO number of examples PROVES one; you need a general argument. And induction needs BOTH parts: base case alone or step alone proves nothing.
🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
Assuming a statement is false and deriving an impossibility is proof by:
  1. Contradiction
  2. Induction
  3. Direct proof
  4. Counterexample
Show answer + steps
A. If falsity leads to absurdity, the statement can't be false.
📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)

Proof techniques

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A proof is just an airtight argument that something is always true. There are a few standard “attack patterns,” and half the battle is recognizing which one fits. You rarely invent a new style — you pick the right template.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Direct: assume the hypothesis, march straight to the conclusion. Best when the path is clear.

Contrapositive: instead of proving p→q, prove ¬q→¬p (logically identical, often easier).

Contradiction: assume the statement is FALSE, then derive an impossibility — so it can't be false. The classic √2-is-irrational proof works this way.

Induction: prove a base case (n=1), then “if it holds for n=k it holds for n=k+1.” Like dominoes: knock the first, and each knocks the next. Used for statements about all positive integers.

📝 EXAM WORDING

Match name to method: proof by contrapositive proves ¬q→¬p; proof by contradiction assumes the negation and finds an absurdity; mathematical induction uses a base case plus an inductive step (with the inductive hypothesis). A counterexample disproves a universal claim.

⚠️ WATCH OUT

One counterexample DISPROVES a “for all” statement, but no number of examples PROVES one — you need a general argument. Induction always needs BOTH parts; base case alone or step alone proves nothing.

RuleGivenConcludeExample
Modus ponensp → q, pqIf rain then wet; it rained → wet

THE FALLACIES TO REJECT
FallacyShapeWhy invalid
Affirming the consequentp → q, q ⊬ p"q happened, so p must have" — the converse trap in disguise
Denying the antecedentp → q, ¬p ⊬ ¬qThe condition failing doesn't kill the result
⚠️ TOLLENS vs THE FALLACY
Modus tollens uses ¬q to get ¬p — VALID. Denying the antecedent uses ¬p to claim ¬q — INVALID. Watch which piece is negated.
🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
Given p → q and ¬q, what follows validly?
  1. ¬p (modus tollens)
  2. p
  3. q
  4. Nothing
Show answer + steps
A. If the promise holds but the result failed, the condition can't have happened.
📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)

Rules of inference

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

An argument is a set of premises leading to a conclusion. Rules of inference are the “legal moves” — argument shapes that are always valid. If your argument matches one of these shapes, the conclusion truly follows; if it matches a known fallacy, it doesn't.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Modus ponens: given p → q and p, conclude q. (If it rains, the ground is wet; it rained; so the ground is wet.)

🔎 Modus ponens / tollens

Ponens: from p → q and p, conclude q. Tollens: from p → q and ¬q, conclude ¬p. The two core valid inference rules.

Example: Rain → wet ground. It rained ⟹ ground is wet (ponens). Ground dry ⟹ no rain (tollens).

Modus tollens: given p → q and ¬q, conclude ¬p. (Ground isn't wet, so it didn't rain.)

Hypothetical syllogism: p → q and q → r give p → r (chaining). Disjunctive syllogism: p ∨ q and ¬p give q.

📝 EXAM WORDING

Modus ponens: p→q, p ⊢ q. Modus tollens: p→q, ¬q ⊢ ¬p. Hypothetical syllogism chains implications; disjunctive syllogism eliminates an option. The fallacies to reject: affirming the consequent (p→q, q, so p) and denying the antecedent (p→q, ¬p, so ¬q).

📊 FIGURE — Modus ponens and modus tollens
The two workhorse inference rules. Ponens: from the implication and its hypothesis, conclude the conclusion. Tollens: from the implication and the NEGATED conclusion, conclude the negated hypothesis. (Affirming the consequent — "q, therefore p" — is the classic invalid impostor.)
⚠️ WATCH OUT

Affirming the consequent (“q happened, so p must have”) is INVALID — it's the converse trap in disguise. Modus tollens uses ¬q to get ¬p; don't confuse it with the fallacy of denying the antecedent.

🔗 Relations & Their Properties

Relations & their properties

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A relation just says how elements of a set are connected — “is equal to,” “is less than,” “is a sibling of.” The exam tests whether a relation has certain properties. Picture arrows between dots: the properties describe the arrow patterns.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Reflexive: every element relates to itself (a loop on every dot) — e.g. “=”. Symmetric: if a relates to b, then b relates to a (arrows go both ways) — e.g. “is a sibling of.” Transitive: if a→b and b→c, then a→c — e.g. “≤”.

🔎 Transitive

Chains close: a→b and b→c forces the shortcut a→c.

Example: "Taller than": if Ana > Ben and Ben > Kim, then Ana > Kim.

A relation that is reflexive, symmetric, AND transitive is an equivalence relation (it partitions the set into groups). Reflexive + antisymmetric + transitive gives a partial order (like “≤”).

📝 EXAM WORDING

Reflexive: aRa for all a. Symmetric: aRb → bRa. Transitive: aRb ∧ bRc → aRc. An equivalence relation is reflexive + symmetric + transitive and creates equivalence classes. Expect “which properties does this relation have?” items.

⚠️ WATCH OUT

Check each property against the DEFINITION, not intuition. “Less than” (<) is transitive but NOT reflexive (a is not < a). Antisymmetric is not the same as “not symmetric.”

Sequences, series & summation

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A sequence is an ordered list of numbers following a rule; a series is their sum. The scary-looking Σ (sigma) symbol is just shorthand for “add these up.” Most of it is pattern-spotting: is each term a fixed step apart, or a fixed multiple apart?

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Arithmetic sequence: add a constant each step (2, 5, 8, 11… common difference 3). Geometric sequence: multiply by a constant each step (3, 6, 12, 24… common ratio 2).

🔎 Geometric sequence

Each term MULTIPLIES by the same ratio r. aₙ = a₁·rⁿ⁻¹. Sums: a(1−rⁿ)/(1−r), and a/(1−r) forever when |r| < 1.

Example: 2, 6, 18, 54 … (r = 3).
🔎 Arithmetic sequence

Each term ADDS the same amount d (the common difference). aₙ = a₁ + (n−1)d.

Example: 5, 9, 13, 17 … (d = 4). a₁₂ = 5 + 11·4 = 49.

Summation: Σ from i=1 to n of aᵢ means add up the terms. Handy closed forms: 1+2+…+n = n(n+1)/2; the sum of a geometric series has its own formula. The index below Σ is the start, the number above is the end.

🔎 Sigma notation Σ

Compact "add these up": the index runs from the lower to the upper bound, feeding the formula. A for-loop that sums.

Example: Σᵢ₌₁⁵ 2i = 2+4+6+8+10 = 30.
📝 EXAM WORDING

Arithmetic = common difference (add); geometric = common ratio (multiply). Summation Σ notation: bottom = start index, top = end. Know 1+2+…+n = n(n+1)/2. A series is the sum of a sequence's terms.

⚠️ WATCH OUT

Arithmetic ADDS a common difference; geometric MULTIPLIES by a common ratio — don't mix them. In Σ notation, the bounds are inclusive: Σ from 1 to n includes both 1 and n.

Recursion & recurrence relations

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Recursion is when something is defined using a smaller version of itself, plus a stopping point. Think of Russian nesting dolls, or the factorial: n! = n × (n−1)!. A recurrence relation is a formula that defines each term from earlier terms.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

A recursive definition needs two parts: a base case (the stopping point, e.g. 0! = 1) and a recursive case (the self-reference, e.g. n! = n × (n−1)!). Without a base case it never stops (infinite recursion).

A recurrence relation defines a sequence from prior terms — e.g. Fibonacci: F(n) = F(n−1) + F(n−2), with F(0)=0, F(1)=1. You compute later terms by building on earlier ones.

📝 EXAM WORDING

Recursion = defined in terms of itself, needing a base case + a recursive case. A recurrence relation defines each term from previous ones (Fibonacci is the classic). The base case prevents infinite recursion.

⚠️ WATCH OUT

Every recursion MUST have a base case, or it runs forever (stack overflow). Fibonacci needs TWO base cases (F(0) and F(1)) because each term depends on the two before it.

Matrices & operations

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A matrix is just a rectangular grid of numbers, described by its size (rows × columns). They're used for transformations, systems of equations, and graphs. The two operations people trip on are multiplication (which has strict size rules) and knowing that order matters.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Addition: add matching cells — only works if both matrices are the same size. Scalar multiply: multiply every cell by a number.

🔎 Scalar multiplication

Multiply EVERY entry by one number.

Example: 2·1234 = 2468.

Matrix multiplication: the tricky one. To multiply A×B, A's columns must equal B's rows. The result is “row of A dotted with column of B.” Size: (m×n)×(n×p) = (m×p). Order matters: A×B ≠ B×A in general.

📝 EXAM WORDING

A matrix is rows × columns. Add/subtract requires identical dimensions. For matrix multiplication, the inner dimensions must match: (m×n)(n×p) = (m×p). Matrix multiplication is not commutative (A×B ≠ B×A). The identity matrix acts like 1.

⚠️ WATCH OUT

For multiplication, check the INNER dimensions match (n = n) before you start — otherwise it's undefined. And A×B is generally not equal to B×A, so order matters.

Graphs & trees

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A graph is just dots (vertices) connected by lines (edges) — a model for networks, maps, social connections, anything with relationships. A tree is a special graph shaped like a family tree: one root, branches, no loops. These show up everywhere in CS.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Vertex (node) = a dot; edge = a connection. The degree of a vertex is how many edges touch it. Edges can be directed (one-way arrows) or undirected. A path is a route along edges; a cycle is a path back to the start.

🔎 Degree

How many edge-ends touch a vertex. A loop adds 2.

Example: A vertex with 3 edges attached has degree 3.
🔎 Edge

A line joining two vertices — one connection.

Example: "Ana and Ben are friends" = one edge between their dots.
🔎 Vertex (node)

A dot in a graph — one of the objects being connected.

Example: In a friendship graph, each PERSON is a vertex.

A tree is a connected graph with no cycles. It has a root, parent/child nodes, and leaves (no children). A tree with n nodes has exactly n−1 edges.

📝 EXAM WORDING

A graph = vertices + edges; degree = edges at a vertex; edges are directed or undirected. A tree is a connected, acyclic graph with a root, and n nodes means n−1 edges. A cycle returns to its start; a path does not repeat.

⚠️ WATCH OUT

A tree is a graph with NO cycles and exactly n−1 edges — if it has a cycle, it's not a tree. Degree counts edges at a vertex; in a directed graph, in-degree and out-degree are counted separately.

💡 Boolean Algebra & Logic Circuits

THE NOTATION
AND = · (like multiply) · OR = + (like add) · NOT = a bar/′. This is how hardware designers shrink circuits: simplify the expression → fewer gates, same result.
LawAND formOR form
IdentityA·1 = AA+0 = A
NullA·0 = 0A+1 = 1
IdempotentA·A = AA+A = A
ComplementA·A′ = 0A+A′ = 1
De Morgan's(A·B)′ = A′+B′(A+B)′ = A′·B′
CIRCUITS & TRUTH TABLES
A logic circuit implements a Boolean expression with AND/OR/NOT gates. A truth table lists EVERY input combination and its output — 2ⁿ rows for n inputs.
📊 FIGURE — The three basic logic gates
AND outputs 1 only when both inputs are 1; OR outputs 1 unless both are 0; NOT inverts (the small bubble means inversion). Any truth table can be wired from combinations of these — chapter circuits are just these shapes composed.
⚠️ + IS OR, NOT ADDITION
A + A = A (idempotent), not 2A. The symbols look arithmetic but follow Boolean laws.

  1. 16

  4. 32

Boolean algebra & logic circuits

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Boolean algebra is the algebra of true/false (1/0). It lets you simplify complicated logic expressions the way you'd simplify a math expression — fewer terms, same result. This is exactly how hardware designers shrink circuits.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Operations: AND (·, like multiply), OR (+, like add), NOT (a bar/′). Key laws: identity (A·1=A, A+0=A), null (A·0=0, A+1=1), idempotent (A·A=A), complement (A·A′=0, A+A′=1), and De Morgan's ((A·B)′ = A′+B′).

You use these to reduce an expression to fewer gates. A logic circuit implements a Boolean expression with AND/OR/NOT gates; a truth table lists every input combination and its output.

📝 EXAM WORDING

Boolean algebra uses AND (·), OR (+), NOT (′) with laws (identity, null, idempotent, complement, De Morgan's). Simplify to fewer terms/gates. A logic gate implements an operation; a truth table enumerates all input/output rows. 2ⁿ rows for n inputs.

⚠️ WATCH OUT

In Boolean algebra, + means OR (not arithmetic addition) and · means AND — so A + A = A (idempotent), not 2A. A truth table for n inputs always has 2ⁿ rows.

📖 Final-exam extras — quick hits that appear on tests

A handful of famous results show up in final-style questions. Each with the one-line answer and a worked check:

THE QUICK-HIT LIST
• √2 is irrational — proved by contradiction: assume √2 = a/b in lowest terms, square to get a² = 2b², so a is even (a = 2k), then b² = 2k² makes b even too — contradicting “lowest terms.”
• Infinitely many primes — contradiction again: if p₁…pₙ were all of them, then p₁·…·pₙ + 1 is divisible by none of them, so some prime is missing from the list.
• Euclidean algorithm — gcd via remainders: gcd(48, 18): 48 = 2·18 + 12; 18 = 1·12 + 6; 12 = 2·6 + 0 → gcd = 6 (last nonzero remainder).
• Tower of Hanoi — minimum moves for n disks = 2ⁿ − 1. For 4 disks: 2⁴ − 1 = 15.
• Mergesort recurrence — T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) solves to O(n log n).
• Pigeonhole — 13 people → two share a birth month (13 > 12). Generalized: 25 items in 6 boxes → some box holds ⌈25/6⌉ = 5.
• Floyd–Warshall — computes shortest paths between ALL pairs of vertices (not just from one source — that’s Dijkstra).
• Chromatic number of Kₙ — every vertex touches every other, so Kₙ needs n colors: χ(K₅) = 5.
• Karnaugh map — a grid method for simplifying Boolean expressions by eye (group the 1s in powers of 2).
WORKED EXAMPLE — generalized pigeonhole, start to finish
Place 25 items into 6 boxes. Could every box hold ≤ 4? Then the total would be at most 6 × 4 = 24 < 25 — impossible. So some box holds at least ⌈25/6⌉ = 5. That ceiling formula ⌈items/boxes⌉ is the whole trick.

The Discrete Math (C959) OA is a multiple-choice objective assessment, and you only need to reach "Competent" to pass — roughly 70% of the questions. It is pass/fail (no letter grade), you can retake it if needed, and you can flag questions and come back. Knowing how the exam works, and studying the way memory actually works, removes most of the fear.

How the objective assessment works

  • Format: a set of multiple-choice questions in a proctored, locked-down browser. Each has one best answer (a few may say "select all that apply" — read carefully).
  • To pass: reach the "Competent" cut (about 70%+). Aim higher in practice so test-day nerves still leave you a cushion.

  • You can flag & return: if a question is eating time, mark it, move on, and circle back with a fresh head.
  • Retakes exist: if you don’t pass, you get feedback on weak areas and can retake after a short waiting period. One exam is not your only shot.

The five study techniques that actually work

Decades of learning research keep pointing to the same handful of methods. They feel harder than rereading — and that "desirable difficulty" is exactly why they work.

TechniqueWhat to do

Exam-day tactics for multiple choice

  • Read every word. Watch for NOT, EXCEPT, ALWAYS, NEVER — they flip the meaning of a question.
  • Eliminate first. Cross out the obviously wrong options; even cutting two turns a hard question into a coin flip in your favor.
  • Predict before you peek. Try to answer in your head before reading the choices, so a tempting-but-wrong option can’t anchor you.
  • Trust your first instinct unless you find a concrete reason to change it — second-guessing flips more right answers to wrong than the reverse.
  • Watch the clock. Budget about a minute per question; flag anything slower and return to it.
  • Answer everything. With no penalty for wrong answers, an educated guess always beats a blank.

Calm nerves, clear head

Some adrenaline is normal and even helpful. If it tips into panic, slow your breathing — in for four counts, hold four, out for four — for a few cycles to reset your body. Reframe the moment: this is a checkpoint, not a verdict on you, and you can retake it. Sleep the night before matters more than one more hour of cramming; a rested brain recalls far better than a tired one. Eat something, arrive early, and remember how much you’ve already prepared.

Discrete mathematics starts with logic because every later topic is built on it: a set is defined by a condition, a proof is a chain of implications, and a Boolean circuit is a truth table in hardware. A proposition is the atom of all that — a declarative statement with a definite truth value, true or false, but not both.

The test is whether it can be judged. "7 is prime" is a proposition, and so is "7 is even" — false propositions are still propositions. "What time is it?" is a question, "Close the door" is a command, and "x > 5" contains a free variable, so none of the three is a proposition until the variable is pinned down.

The five operators

OperatorSymbolRead asTrue when
Negation¬pnot pp is false
Conjunctionp ∧ qp and qboth are true
Disjunctionp ∨ qp or qat least one is true — false only when both are false
Exclusive orp ⊕ qp xor qexactly one is true — they differ
Conditionalp → qif p then qalways, except when p is true and q is false

The one that trips people is ∨. In everyday speech "or" usually means one or the other but not both — "you can have soup or salad". In logic ∨ is inclusive: it is true when both are true. The exclusive version has its own symbol, ⊕, and it is the one that means "exactly one".

Truth tables

A truth table lists every combination of truth values for the variables and the resulting value of the expression. With n variables it has 2n rows — two variables give four, three give eight — and that count is asked directly.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — building the table for p ∧ ¬q
  p     q  |  ¬q  |  p ∧ ¬q
--------+------+---------
  T     T  |  F   |    F
  T     F  |  T   |    T     <- the only true row
  F     T  |  F   |    F
  F     F  |  T   |    F

Fill the variable columns in a fixed pattern so you never miss a row: the first column alternates in blocks of half the rows, the next in blocks of a quarter, and so on. Then build the expression up one operator at a time, innermost first.

Order of evaluation matters as much as it does in arithmetic. Work through parentheses first, then ¬, then ∧, then ∨, and finally → and ↔. So ¬p ∨ q means (¬p) ∨ q, not ¬(p ∨ q) — and those two are genuinely different statements.

Three names for whole expressions

Once a table is built, the last column has one of three characters. A tautology is true in every row — p ∨ ¬p. A contradiction is false in every row — p ∧ ¬p. A contingency is anything else, true in some rows and false in others. Most expressions are contingencies; the exam asks about the other two.

📘 DEFINITION

Proposition: a declarative statement with exactly one truth value, true or false

Negation (¬): reverses the truth value

Conjunction (∧): true only when both operands are true

Disjunction (∨): inclusive or — true when at least one operand is true

Exclusive or (⊕): true when exactly one operand is true

Truth table: a table of every truth-value combination and the resulting value; 2ⁿ rows for n variables

Tautology: an expression true under every assignment

Contradiction: an expression false under every assignment

Contingency: an expression that is true in some rows and false in others

Compound proposition: propositions joined by one or more operators

★ ON THE OA

A proposition is a declarative statement with a definite truth value — a question or a command is not one. Operators: ¬ NOT, ∧ AND (true only when both are true), ∨ OR (inclusive — false only when both are false), ⊕ XOR (true when they differ). A table with n variables has 2ⁿ rows.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Do not read ∨ as everyday "or". T ∨ T is true. If a question wants exactly one, it will use ⊕ — and if it says "or" in English, check which one it means before answering.

The six connectives at a glance

Everything in this unit is built from these. The one that costs marks is the conditional: p → q is FALSE in exactly one row — when the promise is made and broken, p true and q false. In every other row, including both rows where p is false, it is true.

📊 FIGURE — every connective, with the rows that define it
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

"p → q is true when p is false" feels wrong the first ten times you meet it. The reading that fixes it: a conditional is a promise. "If it rains, I bring an umbrella." On a dry day you have broken no promise whatever you carry, so the statement stands. It is only falsified by rain plus no umbrella.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — is (p ∧ ¬q) → p a tautology?

Build every row. Two variables means 2² = 4 rows.

pq¬qp ∧ ¬q(p ∧ ¬q) → p
TTFFT
TFTTT
FTFFT
FFTFT

The last column is T in every row, so yes — it is a tautology. A column of all Fs would make it a contradiction; a mixture makes it a contingency. Those three words are the vocabulary the question will use.

A support desk writes its escalation rule in English: a ticket is escalated when it is marked urgent and is not yet assigned, or when it has been open for more than five days. Three conditions carry the whole rule, so give each one a letter: u = marked urgent, a = already assigned, d = open more than five days. The rule is then E = (u ∧ ¬a) ∨ d.

A truth table is built one column at a time, never in one leap. The figure shows the four stages: fill the input columns in the fixed pattern, then the innermost negation, then the AND, then the OR.

📊 FIGURE — a truth-table walk — one column per stage

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Two things go wrong in the same place. First, ∨ is inclusive — p ∨ q is true when both are true, so "at least one" is the right reading, never "exactly one". Second, precedence: ¬p ∨ q means (¬p) ∨ q. Reading it as ¬(p ∨ q) changes the answer in two of the four rows. Negation binds tightest, then ∧, then ∨, then → and ↔.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Three facts pay for themselves. A table over n variables has 2ⁿ rows — 3 sensors give 8, 5 give 32. Fill the inputs in the canonical pattern (leftmost column: T for the top half, F for the bottom half; each column after that alternates twice as fast) so a question about "row 5" means the same row for you as for the examiner. And learn the shortcut rows: ∧ is true in one row only, ∨ is false in one row only, ⊕ is true when the two differ.

Two things these questions expect

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Counting bit strings with fixed positions

How many bit strings of length 5 begin with 1 and end with 0?

  1. Position 1 is forced to 1 — one choice.
  2. Position 5 is forced to 0 — one choice.
  3. The middle three positions are free: 2 × 2 × 2.
  4. Total = 2³ = 8.

Fixing a position multiplies by 1; each free position multiplies by 2.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Translating a policy into a formula

"Unlocks when the badge is valid AND the time is within office hours, OR when the fire panel signals evacuation." Let b, h, e be those three.

  1. "badge valid AND within office hours" → (b ∧ h).
  2. "OR when evacuation" attaches to that whole condition → (b ∧ h) ∨ e.
  3. The brackets carry the meaning: b ∧ (h ∨ e) would wrongly require a badge during an evacuation.

Translate the comma. It marks where the OR splits the sentence.

The conditional p → q is the operator the whole course runs on — every theorem, every proof and every definition is an implication — and it is also the one whose truth table looks wrong the first time you see it.

Read p → q as a promise: "if p happens, I guarantee q". The only way to break a promise is for p to happen and q not to. That is the single false row.

  p     q  |  p → q
--------+---------
  T     T  |    T
  T     F  |    F     <- the ONLY false case
  F     T  |    T     \  promise never tested,
  F     F  |    T     /  so it was not broken

The two bottom rows are called vacuously true. "If I win the lottery I will buy you a car" — if I do not win, I have not lied, whatever happens next. A false hypothesis makes the whole conditional true, and exam questions exploit that constantly.

The four related conditionals

From any p → q you can build three relatives, and knowing which are equivalent is worth several marks.

NameFormEquivalent to the original?
Conditionalp → q—
Converseq → pNo
Inverse¬p → ¬qNo
Contrapositive¬q → ¬pYes — always

Test it with a real sentence. "If it is a dog, it is a mammal" is true. Its converse — "if it is a mammal, it is a dog" — is false. Its inverse — "if it is not a dog, it is not a mammal" — is also false. Its contrapositive — "if it is not a mammal, it is not a dog" — is true, and always will be. The converse and inverse are equivalent to each other, and neither is equivalent to the original.

The contrapositive being equivalent is not a curiosity: it is the engine of contrapositive proof in 7.2, where proving ¬q → ¬p is often far easier than proving p → q directly.

The biconditional

p ↔ q, read "p if and only if q", is true exactly when p and q have the same truth value. It is equivalent to (p → q) ∧ (q → p) — both directions — which is why proving an "if and only if" theorem means proving two separate implications.

📐 Equivalences worth memorising
Conditional as ∨
p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q
Contrapositive
p → q ≡ ¬q → ¬p
Negated conditional
¬(p → q) ≡ p ∧ ¬q
Biconditional
p ↔ q ≡ (p → q) ∧ (q → p)
Double negation
¬(¬p) ≡ p

The third line is the one people get wrong. The negation of "if p then q" is not another conditional — it is the single case that breaks the promise: p is true and q is false.

📘 DEFINITION

Conditional (p → q): false only when p is true and q is false

Hypothesis / antecedent: the p in p → q

Conclusion / consequent: the q in p → q

Vacuously true: a conditional made true by a false hypothesis

Converse: q → p — not equivalent to the original

Inverse: ¬p → ¬q — not equivalent to the original

Contrapositive: ¬q → ¬p — always equivalent to the original

Biconditional (p ↔ q): true when p and q have the same truth value

Logically equivalent (≡): two expressions with identical truth tables

★ ON THE OA

p → q is FALSE in exactly one case: p true, q false. Everything else, including a false premise, is true. The key equivalences are p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q ≡ ¬q → ¬p. The converse and inverse are equivalent to each other and not to the original.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Two expressions are logically equivalent when their truth tables match column for column. If you are unsure whether a claimed equivalence holds, build both tables — four rows settles it and no reasoning can talk you out of it.

Converse, inverse, contrapositive

From one conditional you can form three others, and the exam tests whether you know which of them you are allowed to use.

📊 FIGURE — the conditional square
NameFormEquivalent to the original?
Originalp → q—
Converseq → pNo
Inverse¬p → ¬qNo
Contrapositive¬q → ¬pYes — always
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the sentence that makes it obvious

Original: "If it is a dog, then it is a mammal." True.

Converse — "If it is a mammal, then it is a dog." False: a cat is a counterexample.
Inverse — "If it is not a dog, then it is not a mammal." False: the same cat.
Contrapositive — "If it is not a mammal, then it is not a dog." True, and it has to be — it says exactly what the original says.

Notice the converse and the inverse are false together. That is not a coincidence: they are each other's contrapositive.

📘 DEFINITION

p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q. Rewriting a conditional as a disjunction is the single most useful move in this unit — it lets you push a negation in with De Morgan, and it turns "prove the implication" into "prove the OR".

Consequently ¬(p → q) ≡ p ∧ ¬q: the negation of an implication is not another implication, it is an AND.

An SLA says: if an outage runs past four hours, the customer receives a service credit. That is a conditional, and reading it as a promise makes its odd truth table obvious. The only way to break the promise is for the outage to run long and no credit to appear. Every other combination leaves the promise intact — including the two rows where the outage never ran long, which are the vacuously true ones.

📊 FIGURE — one table settles which relatives of p → q are equivalent
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a prerequisite rule and its three relatives
1.
The catalogue states: if a student is enrolled in Discrete Math II, then they have passed Discrete Math I. Let p = enrolled in II, q = passed I. The rule is p → q, and it is true.
2.
Converse (q → p): if a student has passed Discrete Math I, then they are enrolled in II. False — plenty of students pass I and stop there.
3.
Inverse (¬p → ¬q): if a student is not enrolled in II, then they have not passed I. False, for the same reason, and notice it says the same thing as the converse.
4.
Contrapositive (¬q → ¬p): if a student has not passed Discrete Math I, then they are not enrolled in II. True — and it must be, because it is equivalent to the rule itself.
5.
So of the four sentences, two are true (the rule and its contrapositive) and two are false (converse and inverse). That pairing is the whole examinable point.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — what it takes to break the promise — negating a conditional
1.
A vendor promises: if the device fails within 12 months, we replace it. Symbolically p → q.
2.
A customer wants to claim the promise was broken. That claim is ¬(p → q).
3.
Rewrite the conditional first: p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q.
4.
Negate with De Morgan: ¬(¬p ∨ q) ≡ ¬(¬p) ∧ ¬q ≡ p ∧ ¬q.
5.
In English: the device failed within 12 months AND it was not replaced. The negation of a conditional is not another conditional — it is the single row that breaks it.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
The converse feels like a restatement and is not one. "If it is a dog, it is a mammal" is true; "if it is a mammal, it is a dog" is false. Swapping the two halves is converse; negating both halves is inverse; doing both — swap and negate — is the contrapositive, and only that one is safe to substitute for the original.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Two lines close most conditional questions. p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q turns any conditional into a disjunction you can evaluate at a glance, and ¬(p → q) ≡ p ∧ ¬q handles every "when is this promise broken" item. Remember also that a false hypothesis makes the whole conditional true: "if 2 + 2 = 5 then the sky is green" is a true statement.

Apply the three related forms to "if a number is divisible by 4, then it is even": only the contrapositive ("if it is not even, it is not divisible by 4") is guaranteed true along with the original. The converse ("if even, then divisible by 4") is false — 6 is even and not divisible by 4 — and the inverse is false for the same reason. When a question offers converse, inverse and contrapositive, the contrapositive is the only one that must hold.

📘 DEFINITION
Necessary vs sufficient. In p → q, the hypothesis p is sufficient for q (p happening guarantees q), and q is necessary for p (without q, p cannot have happened — that is the contrapositive speaking). "Scoring 90+ is sufficient for an A; an A is necessary for having scored 90+."

Negation is easy for a single proposition and needs a rule once operators are involved. De Morgan's Laws are that rule, and they are the most reused identities in the course — they reappear for sets in Unit 2 and for circuits in Unit 3, in exactly the same shape.

📐 De Morgan's Laws
Negated AND
¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q
Negated OR
¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q
For sets
(A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′ and (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′

The rule of thumb is break the bar, flip the connective: distribute the negation onto both parts and swap ∧ for ∨. In English: the opposite of "both" is "at least one is not", and the opposite of "at least one" is "neither".

Checking it against a sentence makes it stick. The negation of "it is raining and cold" is not "it is not raining and not cold" — it is "either it is not raining, or it is not cold". Only one of them has to fail for the conjunction to fail.

Predicates and quantifiers

A predicate is a statement containing a variable, like P(x): x > 5. It is not a proposition, because it has no truth value until x is supplied. Quantifiers are what turn one into a proposition by saying how much of the domain it must hold for.

QuantifierSymbolReadsTrue whenFalse when
Universal∀x P(x)for all x, P(x)P(x) holds for every xone counterexample exists
Existential∃x P(x)there exists an x with P(x)at least one x worksno x works at all

The asymmetry in the last two columns is the point. To prove ∀ you must cover the whole domain; to disprove it you need a single counterexample. To prove ∃ one example is enough; to disprove it you must rule out everything.

Negating a quantifier

Negation swaps the quantifier and negates the inside — the same "flip it" pattern as De Morgan, which is not a coincidence, since ∀ is a long conjunction and ∃ is a long disjunction.

📐 Quantifier negation
Negated universal
¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x)
Negated existential
¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x)
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — negate "every student passed"
1.
Write it symbolically: ∀x P(x), where P(x) is "student x passed".
2.
Apply the rule: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x).
3.
Read it back: some student did not pass — not "every student failed", which is a much stronger claim.

With two quantifiers, order matters. ∀x ∃y (y > x) says every number has something bigger, which is true. Swap them and ∃y ∀x (y > x) says one number is bigger than everything, which is false. Same symbols, different claim.

📘 DEFINITION

De Morgan's Laws: negating a conjunction gives a disjunction of negations, and vice versa

Predicate: a statement containing a variable, with no truth value until the variable is supplied

Domain (universe of discourse): the set of values a quantified variable ranges over

Universal quantifier (∀): asserts the predicate holds for every element of the domain

Existential quantifier (∃): asserts the predicate holds for at least one element

Counterexample: a single case that makes a universal statement false

Free vs bound variable: a variable not governed by a quantifier, versus one that is

★ ON THE OA

De Morgan: ¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q and ¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q — break the bar, flip the connective. The same shape works for sets: (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′. Negating a quantifier swaps ∀ and ∃ and negates the predicate.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

The negation of "all birds fly" is "some bird does not fly", not "no bird flies". Flipping ∀ to ∃ is the whole rule; do not over-negate into the opposite extreme.

Negating a quantifier

Two rules, and they are the same shape as De Morgan's laws for ∧ and ∨ — because "for all" is a long AND and "there exists" is a long OR.

📘 DEFINITION

¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x) — "not everything is P" means "something is not P".
¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x) — "nothing is P" means "everything is not P".

📊 FIGURE — what the quantifiers claim about a five-element domain

Read the middle row carefully. One failure — one object that is not P — is enough to kill a ∀ claim. That is why a single counterexample disproves a universal statement, and why no number of examples proves one.

StatementProved byDisproved by
∀x P(x)A general argument covering every xOne counterexample
∃x P(x)One exampleA general argument that no x works
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — negate "every student passed every exam"

Symbolically: ∀s ∀e Passed(s, e). Negate it by walking left to right, flipping each quantifier and carrying the ¬ inward:

¬∀s ∀e Passed(s,e) ≡ ∃s ¬∀e Passed(s,e) ≡ ∃s ∃e ¬Passed(s,e)

In English: "some student failed some exam." Not "no student passed any exam" — that is a much stronger claim, and it is the distractor.

Negation is the operation policies are written around: a rule says what is accepted, and the system has to work out what is rejected. De Morgan is how that is done safely.

📊 FIGURE — negating a policy, and negating a quantifier — the same move
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — negating an access policy with three clauses
1.
The policy: access is granted when the account is active AND the device is enrolled AND the request comes from a managed network. Write it as a ∧ e ∧ m.
2.
Access is denied exactly when the policy fails: ¬(a ∧ e ∧ m).
3.
Apply De Morgan across all three: ¬(a ∧ e ∧ m) ≡ ¬a ∨ ¬e ∨ ¬m.
4.
Read it back: the account is inactive, or the device is not enrolled, or the network is unmanaged. Any one of the three is enough to deny.
5.
Sanity-check with a case. An active account on an enrolled device over a coffee-shop network: a = T, e = T, m = F. The original is T ∧ T ∧ F = F (denied), and the expanded form is F ∨ F ∨ T = T (denied). They agree. ✓
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — negating a nested quantified claim about a course catalogue
1.
The claim: every student has at least one course they are eligible to enrol in. With S(x) the students and E(x, y) "student x is eligible for course y", that is ∀x ∃y E(x, y).
2.
Negate the whole thing: ¬∀x ∃y E(x, y).
3.
Push the negation past the first quantifier — ∀ becomes ∃: ∃x ¬∃y E(x, y).
4.
Push it past the second — ∃ becomes ∀: ∃x ∀y ¬E(x, y).
5.
Read it back: there is a student who is eligible for no course at all. Each quantifier flips as the negation moves inward, and the predicate ends up negated.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
"Not all servers are patched" does not mean "no server is patched". ¬∀x P(x) is ∃x ¬P(x) — at least one fails — whereas "none are patched" is ∀x ¬P(x), a far stronger claim. The same error in De Morgan form is negating a conjunction into a conjunction: ¬(a ∧ e) is ¬a ∨ ¬e, never ¬a ∧ ¬e.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Negation is mechanical if you work outside in: every ∧ becomes ∨, every ∨ becomes ∧, every ∀ becomes ∃, every ∃ becomes ∀, and the innermost predicate is negated last. Order matters too: ∀x ∃y lets y depend on x ("every ticket has some agent"), while ∃y ∀x demands one y that works for all x ("one agent handles every ticket") and is the stronger claim.
📘 DEFINITION
The logical equivalence asked for most often is p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q. A conditional is false only when p is true and q is false, and "not p, or q" fails in exactly that one case. Every implication can be rewritten as a disjunction this way, which is how conditionals are removed before converting a formula to CNF.

A set is an unordered collection of distinct objects. Both adjectives are load-bearing: order carries no information, so {1, 2, 3} and {3, 1, 2} are the same set, and repetition carries none either, so {1, 1, 2} is just {1, 2}. Every counting question in this unit depends on remembering both.

NotationMeansExample
a ∈ Aa is an element of A3 ∈ {1, 2, 3}
a ∉ Aa is not an element of A5 ∉ {1, 2, 3}
A ⊆ BA is a subset of B — every element of A is in B{1, 2} ⊆ {1, 2, 3}
A ⊂ BA is a proper subset — a subset, and not equal{1, 2} ⊂ {1, 2, 3}
|A|cardinality — how many elements A has|{1, 2, 3}| = 3
∅the empty set, with no elements|∅| = 0

Sets are described in two ways. Roster notation lists the members: A = {2, 4, 6, 8}. Set-builder notation states the rule: A = {x | x is even and 0 < x < 10}, read "the set of all x such that…". Set-builder is what makes infinite sets writable.

The empty set behaves in a way that reliably catches people. It is a subset of every set, including itself — vacuously, since there is no element of ∅ that could fail to be in the other set. And ∅ is not the same object as {∅}: the first has no elements, the second has one element which happens to be the empty set, so |∅| = 0 and |{∅}| = 1.

The power set

The power set P(A) is the set of all subsets of A, and its size is the single most examined counting fact in the unit.

|P(A)| = 2|A|

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — list the power set of {a, b}
1.
Start with the empty set: ∅.
2.
All one-element subsets: {a}, {b}.
3.
All two-element subsets: {a, b}.
4.
So P({a, b}) = { ∅, {a}, {b}, {a, b} } — four subsets, and 2² = 4. ✓

The reason it is 2n is worth knowing rather than memorising: building a subset means making one independent yes/no decision per element — in or out — so n elements give 2 × 2 × … × 2 choices. That is the product rule, which returns in the counting unit.

Careful with cardinality when sets are nested. |{a, b, {c, d}}| = 3, because the third element is a single object that happens to be a set. Count the commas at the top level, not the letters.

📘 DEFINITION

Set: an unordered collection of distinct objects

Element (∈): a member of a set

Subset (⊆): every element of the first set is in the second

Proper subset (⊂): a subset that is not equal to the whole set

Cardinality (|A|): the number of elements in a set

Empty set (∅): the set with no elements; a subset of every set

Universal set (U): the set of everything under discussion in a given problem

Power set P(A): the set of all subsets of A; |P(A)| = 2^|A|

Roster notation: describing a set by listing its elements

Set-builder notation: describing a set by the condition its elements satisfy

★ ON THE OA

Know the symbols cold: ∈ element of, ⊆ subset, ∅ empty set (a subset of every set), |S| cardinality. A set of n elements has 2ⁿ subsets — that is its power set, and it is asked in almost every attempt.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

∈ and ⊆ are not interchangeable. 1 ∈ {1, 2} is true and 1 ⊆ {1, 2} is meaningless — 1 is an element, not a set. But {1} ⊆ {1, 2} is true.

Membership, subsets and the power set

Two symbols that look similar and are constantly swapped in the answer options:

SymbolReadsLeft-hand side isExample
∈is an element ofan element2 ∈ {1, 2, 3}
⊆is a subset ofa set{2} ⊆ {1, 2, 3}

So 2 ⊆ {1,2,3} is malformed and {2} ∈ {1,2,3} is false — the set {2} is not one of the three elements. Both appear as distractors.

📊 FIGURE — A ⊆ B drawn — A sits entirely inside B
📘 DEFINITION

The power set P(A) is the set of all subsets of A, including ∅ and A itself. If |A| = n then |P(A)| = 2ⁿ, because building a subset is n independent yes/no choices.

📊 FIGURE — the power set of {a, b}, drawn as a lattice
|A|P(A)|P(A)|
0{∅}1
1{∅, {a}}2
2{∅, {a}, {b}, {a,b}}4
3…8
n…2ⁿ
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

P(∅) is not empty — it is {∅}, a set with one element, so |P(∅)| = 1 = 2⁰. And ∅ ⊆ A for every set A, including A = ∅.

The formula |P(A)| = 2^|A| is usually memorised, and it does not need to be. Building a subset means walking the elements and answering one question about each: in or out? Independent binary choices multiply, so n elements give 2 × 2 × … × 2 outcomes.

📊 FIGURE — why the power set has 2ⁿ members
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — counting a nested equipment catalogue
1.
A field kit is recorded as K = { laptop, charger, {hdmi cable, vga cable}, badge }.
2.
Count the top-level commas, not the words. The members are: laptop, charger, the pair {hdmi cable, vga cable}, and badge.
3.
The third member is a single object that happens to itself be a set — it counts once, not twice.
4.
So |K| = 4, and |P(K)| = 2⁴ = 16.
5.
Notice the difference the braces make: {hdmi cable, vga cable} ∈ K, but hdmi cable ∉ K. The cable is inside a member of K, not a member of K.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — how many tool kits include the multimeter?
1.
A technician chooses any subset of six tools: multimeter, pliers, torch, tester, crimper, driver. There are 2⁶ = 64 possible kits.
2.
Constraint: the multimeter must be in the kit. That decision is now fixed — it is no longer a free choice.
3.
Five free decisions remain, one per remaining tool: in or out.
4.
So the count is 2⁵ = 32 kits.
5.
Sanity-check the ratio: exactly half of all 64 kits contain any given tool, and 64 / 2 = 32. ✓
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Three collisions, all about the difference between a thing and a box containing it. ∅ is not {∅}: |∅| = 0, but |{∅}| = 1, because that set has one member which happens to be empty. ∈ is not ⊆: for A = {1, 2, 3}, 2 ∈ A is true and {2} ∈ A is false, while {2} ⊆ A is true. And repeats do not count: {1, 1, 2} is the set {1, 2}, of size 2.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Learn three counts and most set questions fall out. |P(A)| = 2ⁿ subsets; 2ⁿ − 1 proper subsets (all of them except A itself); and 2ⁿ⁻¹ subsets containing one specified element. Also remember ∅ ⊆ A for every A — vacuously, because there is no element of ∅ that could fail the test.

Set operations are the ∧, ∨ and ¬ of the previous unit wearing different symbols, and noticing that is the fastest way to learn them: intersection is AND, union is OR, and complement is NOT. Every set identity you will meet is a logical equivalence in disguise.

OperationSymbolContainsLogic twin
UnionA ∪ Beverything in A or B (or both)∨
IntersectionA ∩ Beverything in both A and B∧
DifferenceA − Bin A but not in Bp ∧ ¬q
ComplementA′ or Āeverything in U that is not in A¬
Symmetric differenceA ⊕ Bin one or the other but not both⊕
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — computing all five
U = {1,…,8}     A = {1, 2, 3, 5}     B = {1, 2, 4, 6}

A ∪ B  =  {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}     everything in either
A ∩ B  =  {1, 2}                  in both
A − B  =  {3, 5}                  in A, not in B
B − A  =  {4, 6}                  note: NOT the same as A − B
A′     =  {4, 6, 7, 8}            everything in U outside A
A ⊕ B  =  {3, 4, 5, 6}            the union minus the intersection

Two things in that example are worth pausing on. Difference is not symmetric — A − B and B − A are different sets, exactly as subtraction is not commutative. And complement needs a universal set: "everything not in A" is meaningless until you say what "everything" is, which is why U must be stated.

Counting the union

When counting rather than listing, shared elements must not be counted twice. That gives the two-set version of the inclusion–exclusion principle.

|A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|

Adding |A| and |B| counts everything in the overlap once from each side, so subtracting the intersection once restores the correct total. Two sets are disjoint when A ∩ B = ∅, and then the correction is zero and the sizes simply add.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — 30 students take maths, 25 take physics, 12 take both — how many take at least one?
1.
Identify the sets: |M| = 30, |P| = 25, |M ∩ P| = 12.
2.
Apply inclusion–exclusion: |M ∪ P| = 30 + 25 − 12.
3.
43 students. Answering 55 means the overlap was counted twice.

Venn diagrams are the reliable tool for problems like this. Fill the innermost region first — the 12 in both — then work outward, subtracting what is already placed, so each region shows only the students in that region and nowhere else.

📘 DEFINITION

Union (∪): elements in either set or both

Intersection (∩): elements in both sets

Difference (A − B): elements of A that are not in B; not symmetric

Complement (A′): elements of the universal set not in A

Symmetric difference (⊕): elements in exactly one of the two sets

Disjoint sets: sets whose intersection is empty

Inclusion–exclusion: |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|

Venn diagram: overlapping regions showing set relationships

★ ON THE OA

∪ union (in either), ∩ intersection (in both), A − B difference (in A but not B), A′ complement (not in A). Shared elements are counted once — hence |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|.

🎯 EXAM TIP

For a word problem with two or three overlapping groups, draw the Venn diagram and fill from the centre outward. Working the formula in your head is where the double-counting creeps in.

The five operations, shaded

Every set-operation question can be answered by shading. Draw the two circles, shade what the expression asks for, and compare with the options — it is faster and far more reliable than reasoning in words.

📊 FIGURE — the five operations you have to shade on sight
OperationNotationDefinitionFor A = {1,2,3}, B = {3,4}
UnionA ∪ Bx ∈ A or x ∈ B{1, 2, 3, 4}
IntersectionA ∩ Bx ∈ A and x ∈ B{3}
DifferenceA − Bx ∈ A and x ∉ B{1, 2}
Symmetric differenceA △ Bin exactly one of them{1, 2, 4}
ComplementA′x ∈ U and x ∉ Aeverything in U but 1, 2, 3

Note that A − B and B − A are different — difference is not symmetric. Here A − B = {1,2} but B − A = {4}. Union and intersection are symmetric.

📘 DEFINITION

|A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|. Adding the two sizes counts the overlap twice, so you subtract it once. This is inclusion–exclusion for two sets, and it is on the exam in both directions — sometimes you are given the union and asked for the overlap.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — 35 take maths, 28 take physics, 12 take both — how many take at least one?

|M ∪ P| = |M| + |P| − |M ∩ P| = 35 + 28 − 12 = 51.

Sanity-check by filling the Venn regions instead: maths only = 35 − 12 = 23, physics only = 28 − 12 = 16, both = 12. Total 23 + 16 + 12 = 51 ✓. The three-region breakdown is worth writing down whenever numbers are involved — it makes "maths only" questions immediate.

Counting questions about overlapping groups go wrong in one specific way: shared members get counted twice. The fix is to fill a Venn diagram from the middle outwards, so that every number you write is the count of that region alone.

📊 FIGURE — a three-set survey, filled inside-out
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — two sets — a streaming service audits its subscriber base
1.
340 accounts stream music, 215 stream video, and 90 accounts do both.
2.
Do not add 340 + 215. The 90 dual-service accounts sit inside both totals, so that sum counts them twice.
3.
Inclusion–exclusion: |M ∪ V| = |M| + |V| − |M ∩ V| = 340 + 215 − 90 = 465 accounts use at least one service.
4.
Music only is the difference M − V = 340 − 90 = 250. Video only is 215 − 90 = 125.
5.
Check the parts against the whole: 250 + 125 + 90 = 465. ✓ The wrong answer 555 is exactly 465 + 90 — the overlap counted twice.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — three sets — the survey in the figure, region by region
1.
Given: Python 65, SQL 50, Java 40; Python∩SQL 28, Python∩Java 22, SQL∩Java 18; all three 12. 120 students were surveyed.
2.
Centre first. All three = 12. Write it in the middle region.
3.
Pairs next, minus the centre. Python and SQL but not Java = 28 − 12 = 16. Python and Java only = 22 − 12 = 10. SQL and Java only = 18 − 12 = 6.
4.
Singles last, minus everything already placed. Python only = 65 − 16 − 10 − 12 = 27. SQL only = 50 − 16 − 6 − 12 = 16. Java only = 40 − 10 − 6 − 12 = 12.
5.
Union: 27 + 16 + 12 + 16 + 10 + 6 + 12 = 99 use at least one. The formula agrees: 65 + 50 + 40 − 28 − 22 − 18 + 12 = 99. ✓
6.
Outside all three: 120 − 99 = 21 students use none of them.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Difference is not symmetric. "Customers who bought hardware but not support" is H − S; swap the letters and you have described a completely different group. And when a problem says "28 use Python and SQL", that almost always means 28 in total across that overlap, including the ones who also use Java — which is why the centre is subtracted out before the pair region is written down.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Translate the words before you compute: "both" → ∩, "either / at least one" → ∪, "only / but not" → −, "neither" → complement of the union, and "exactly one of the two" → symmetric difference A ⊕ B, which is (A ∪ B) − (A ∩ B). For two sets the whole toolkit is one line — |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B| — and disjoint sets are the special case where the correction term is 0.
📘 DEFINITION
Two consequences of A being a subset of B (A ⊆ B) come up repeatedly: A ∩ B = A (everything in A is already in B, so the overlap is all of A) and A ∪ B = B (A adds nothing B did not have). Drawing the Venn diagram with A entirely inside B makes both immediate.

Everything so far treated sets as unordered. The Cartesian product introduces order and, with it, the structure that relations, functions and graphs are all built from.

A × B is the set of every ordered pair (a, b) with a ∈ A and b ∈ B. Unlike a set, an ordered pair is sensitive to position: (1, 2) ≠ (2, 1).

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A × B versus B × A
A = {1, 2}      B = {x, y}

A × B = { (1,x), (1,y), (2,x), (2,y) }
B × A = { (x,1), (x,2), (y,1), (y,2) }

Same size, different sets — the products are NOT equal.

|A × B| = |A| · |B|

The size rule is the product rule again: each of the |A| first components can be paired with any of the |B| second components. And A × A, often written A², is where relations live — a relation on A is simply a subset of it, which is the definition the next chapter opens with.

The set laws

The identities below are the logical equivalences of Unit 1 rewritten with set symbols. They are worth recognising rather than memorising in isolation, because the pattern transfers.

📐 Set identities
Commutative
A ∪ B = B ∪ A A ∩ B = B ∩ A
Associative
(A ∪ B) ∪ C = A ∪ (B ∪ C)
Distributive
A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C)
De Morgan
(A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′
Identity
A ∪ ∅ = A A ∩ U = A
Domination
A ∪ U = U A ∩ ∅ = ∅
Idempotent
A ∪ A = A A ∩ A = A
Complement
A ∪ A′ = U A ∩ A′ = ∅
Double complement
(A′)′ = A

De Morgan is the one that appears most, and it is exactly the rule from 1.3: the complement of a union is the intersection of complements. Break the bar, flip the operator. In English — "not (in A or B)" means "not in A and not in B".

Note what difference reduces to: A − B = A ∩ B′. Rewriting a difference as an intersection with a complement is often what lets you apply the identities above to an expression that looked like it did not fit them.

Two sets are equal when each is a subset of the other, and that is the standard method for proving a set identity: show A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A. Take an arbitrary element of the left side, argue it must be in the right, then reverse.

📘 DEFINITION

Ordered pair: a pair (a, b) in which position matters

Cartesian product (A × B): the set of all ordered pairs with first component from A and second from B

|A × B|: equals |A| · |B|

A²: A × A — the set relations on A are drawn from

De Morgan for sets: (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ and (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′

Set equality: A = B exactly when A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A

★ ON THE OA

The Cartesian product A × B is the set of ordered pairs, and |A × B| = |A|·|B|. Set laws mirror logic: distributive, and De Morgan (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′. Ordered pairs are not sets — order matters and repetition is allowed.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

Every structure in the rest of the course is a subset of a Cartesian product. A relation is a subset of A × B, a function is a relation with a restriction, and a graph's edge set is a subset of V × V.

The Cartesian product

📘 DEFINITION

A × B is the set of all ordered pairs (a, b) with a ∈ A and b ∈ B. Its size is |A| × |B|.

📊 FIGURE — A × B as a grid — one dot per pair

Because the pairs are ordered, A × B ≠ B × A unless A = B (or one of them is empty). The two sets have the same size but different elements.

The same two laws as in logic, with ∪ for ∨ and ∩ for ∧:

📘 DEFINITION

(A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′
(A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′

Complement each set and flip the operation.

A function from A to B assigns to each element of A exactly one element of B. Both halves of that are conditions a candidate can fail, and most function questions are checking one of them.

The distinction between codomain and range is examined directly and is easy to blur. For f: ℝ → ℝ with f(x) = x², the codomain is all real numbers because that is how the function was declared, but the range is only the non-negative reals, because no square is negative. The codomain is a promise about where outputs live; the range is where they actually land.

Deciding whether something is a function

Two failures disqualify a candidate mapping, and it helps to name them separately.

A = {1, 2, 3}

{(1,a), (2,b), (3,c)}          function ✓
{(1,a), (2,a), (3,a)}          function ✓ — repeats in the OUTPUT are fine
{(1,a), (1,b), (2,c)}          NOT a function — input 1 has two outputs
{(1,a), (2,b)}                 NOT a function on A — input 3 is unmapped

So the rule to apply is: look at the inputs. Every element of the domain must appear exactly once as a first component. Outputs may repeat freely — several inputs sharing an output is completely legal, and only becomes relevant when we ask about injectivity in the next lesson.

The graphical version is the vertical line test: if any vertical line meets the graph more than once, some input has two outputs, so it is not a function.

Functions as a special case of relations

Placing functions inside the relations chapter is deliberate. A relation is any set of pairs; a function is a relation with a restriction imposed on the first components. So every function is a relation, and the question "is this a function" is always the question "does this relation satisfy the restriction".

Stating the restriction precisely: for every element a of the domain there is exactly one pair whose first component is a. "At least one" would allow unmapped inputs; "at most one" would allow gaps. Both halves are needed, which is why two distinct failures exist.

This also explains a piece of notation. We write f(a) = b rather than a f b precisely because the uniqueness guarantee makes "the output of f at a" a well-defined single object. For a general relation there may be no such object, or several, so the function notation would be meaningless.

📘 DEFINITION

Function: a mapping assigning exactly one output to each input

Domain: the set of inputs

Codomain: the declared set of allowed outputs

Range / image: the set of outputs actually produced; a subset of the codomain

Preimage: the set of inputs mapping to a given output

Vertical line test: a graph is a function if no vertical line meets it twice

Identity function: f(x) = x, mapping every element to itself

Constant function: a function whose range has exactly one element

★ ON THE OA

A function maps each input to exactly one output. Domain = inputs, codomain = allowed outputs, range = outputs actually produced. A relation that gives one input two outputs is not a function — the vertical line test is the graphical form of that rule.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Repeated outputs never disqualify a function. {(1,a), (2,a)} is a perfectly good function; only repeated inputs break the definition.

What makes something a function

📘 DEFINITION

A function f: A → B assigns to every element of A exactly one element of B. Two conditions — every input used, and no input used twice.

📊 FIGURE — one arrow out of every left-hand dot, and never two

Codomainthe declared set of possible outputsℝ, as declared

Preimage of yevery x that maps to ypreimage of 4 is {−2, 2}

Range ⊆ codomain always, and they are equal exactly when the function is onto. That is the sentence the next section is built on.

📊 FIGURE — what makes a rule a function: exactly one output per input

A function f : A → B is a rule that assigns to every element of A exactly one element of B. Two words carry all the weight: every (nothing in the domain is left unassigned) and exactly one (nothing gets two answers). Missing arrows and doubled arrows are the only two ways a rule can fail.

TermWhat it meansIn the left-hand diagram

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a shipping cost function, forwards and backwards

A courier charges a $4.50 handling fee plus $1.20 per kilogram, so c(w) = 4.50 + 1.20w for a parcel of w kg. (a) What does a 6 kg parcel cost? (b) A customer is charged $20.10 — how heavy was the parcel?

  1. (a) Substitute the input: c(6) = 4.50 + 1.20(6).
  2. 1.20 × 6 = 7.20, so c(6) = 4.50 + 7.20 = $11.70.
  3. (b) Now the output is known and the input is not, so solve: 20.10 = 4.50 + 1.20w.
  4. Subtract the fixed fee: 15.60 = 1.20w.
  5. Divide: w = 15.60 / 1.20 = 13 kg.

Part (b) is evaluating the inverse function, c⁻¹(20.10) = 13. An inverse only exists because each weight produces its own distinct price — no two weights share a cost.

Answer: (a) $11.70. (b) 13 kg.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — composition — applying two rules in order

A workshop charges f(h) = 2h + 5 in labour units for an h-hour job, and the billing system converts labour units to a tax charge with g(u) = 0.08u dollars. Find (g ∘ f)(40) and say what it means.

  1. (g ∘ f)(40) means "do f first, then feed the result into g". Read composition right to left.
  2. Inner first: f(40) = 2(40) + 5 = 85 labour units.
  3. Now apply g to that: g(85) = 0.08 × 85.
  4. (g ∘ f)(40) = $6.80 of tax on a 40-hour job.
  5. For contrast, (f ∘ g)(40) = f(3.2) = 2(3.2) + 5 = 11.4 — a different number, and in this context a meaningless one.
Answer: $6.80; and composition is not commutative.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Codomain is not range. The codomain is whatever set you declared the outputs live in; the range is the part of it actually used. In the diagram, Marketing sits in the codomain but not in the range — and that single fact is what makes the function fail to be onto. Second trap: (g ∘ f)(x) means g(f(x)), so the function written second is applied first.

🎯 EXAM TIP

To decide whether a rule is a function, ask one question of every element of the domain: how many arrows leave it? Zero arrows → not a function (undefined somewhere). Two or more arrows → not a function (ambiguous). Exactly one arrow every time → function. Nothing about the arrows arriving matters for this question — that is a different property.

📘 DEFINITION
A surjectivity proof (onto) has a fixed shape: take an arbitrary element y of the codomain, and exhibit an x in the domain with f(x) = y. Solving the equation for x is the proof — provided the x you produce genuinely lies in the domain. For f(x) = 3x − 2 on the reals, x = (y + 2)/3 is real for every real y, so f is onto.

TypeConditionPlain EnglishFails when
Injective (one-to-one)f(a₁) = f(a₂) ⟹ a₁ = a₂distinct inputs give distinct outputstwo inputs share an output

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — classifying three functions
f: {1,2,3} -> {a,b,c},  f = {(1,a),(2,b),(3,c)}

   1 and 3 both -> a, so NOT injective;  every output used, so surjective

   distinct outputs, so injective;  c is never produced, so NOT surjective

A counting consequence follows immediately and is worth carrying: an injective function needs |A| ≤ |B| (there must be room for distinct outputs), a surjective one needs |A| ≥ |B| (there must be enough inputs to cover the codomain), and a bijection between finite sets forces |A| = |B|.

Bijectivity is exactly the condition for an inverse to exist. f⁻¹ undoes f by sending each output back to the input it came from — which requires that every output was produced (surjective) and produced only once (injective). A function that is not bijective has no true inverse.

Composition

(g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)), read "g of f of x", applies f first. The order in the notation is the reverse of the order of operation, which is the trap, and composition is not commutative — g ∘ f and f ∘ g are generally different functions.

1.

2.
(f ∘ g)(4): apply g first → 3 × 4 = 12, then f → 12 + 2 = 14.
3.
Different answers, which is the point — read the inner function first.

Two functions appear throughout discrete maths because so much of it deals in whole things.

Negative values are where marks are lost. "Round down" means toward negative infinity, not toward zero, so ⌊−2.3⌋ is −3. And for an integer both agree: ⌊5⌋ = ⌈5⌉ = 5.
