Direct proof handles one statement. Mathematical induction proves infinitely many at once — every statement of the form "for all integers n ≥ 1, P(n)". It is the right tool whenever a claim is indexed by n: a summation formula, a divisibility claim, an inequality.

The image that makes it work is a line of dominoes. Knock over the first one, and guarantee that each domino knocks over the next, and every domino falls — however many there are. The proof has exactly those two parts, and both are required.

PartWhat you doDomino
Base caseverify P(1) directlypush the first domino
Inductive stepassume P(k), prove P(k + 1)each one topples the next

The assumption in the second part has a name — the inductive hypothesis — and it is not circular reasoning, which is the objection everyone raises first. You are not assuming what you want to prove. You are proving a conditional: if it holds at k, then it holds at k + 1. Combined with the base case, that chains upward through every integer.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — prove: 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2
1.
Base case, n = 1. Left side = 1. Right side = 1(2)/2 = 1. They match. ✓
2.
Inductive hypothesis. Assume it holds at n = k: 1 + 2 + … + k = k(k + 1)/2.
3.
Goal. Show it holds at k + 1, i.e. that the sum equals (k + 1)(k + 2)/2.
4.
Build from the hypothesis. The sum to k + 1 is [sum to k] + (k + 1) = k(k + 1)/2 + (k + 1).
5.
Algebra. Factor out (k + 1): (k + 1)[k/2 + 1] = (k + 1)(k + 2)/2.
6.
That is exactly the goal, so P(k) → P(k + 1). With the base case, the formula holds for all n ≥ 1. ∎

Step 4 is where every induction proof is won or lost: you must use the inductive hypothesis, substituting it in rather than re-deriving the sum. If your proof never mentions the assumption, it is not an induction proof.

The base case is not a formality either. The claim "n² + n + 41 is prime for all n ≥ 0" survives an inductive-step argument that looks plausible and fails at n = 41. Both halves have to hold.

Strong induction

Strong induction changes the hypothesis: instead of assuming only P(k), you assume P(1) through P(k) all hold, and prove P(k + 1) from any of them. It is the version needed when the case you are proving depends on a much earlier case rather than the immediately previous one — proving every integer above 1 has a prime factorisation, for instance, where n = a·b sends you to two smaller factors.

📘 DEFINITION

Mathematical induction: proving P(n) for all n ≥ base by proving P(base) and P(k) → P(k+1)

Base case: the smallest value, verified directly

Inductive step: the proof that P(k) implies P(k + 1)

Inductive hypothesis: the assumption that P(k) holds

Strong induction: assuming P(1) through P(k) rather than P(k) alone

Well-ordering principle: every non-empty set of positive integers has a least element — the principle induction rests on

★ ON THE OA

Induction has exactly two required parts: (1) the base case P(1), and (2) the inductive step — assume P(k), prove P(k + 1). A question showing a proof with one part missing is asking you to spot which. The assumption is called the inductive hypothesis.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Write the k + 1 target on the page before doing any algebra. Induction is a matter of steering the expression toward a form you already wrote down, and it is far harder without the destination in front of you.

Why induction works

📊 FIGURE — the two things you must prove, and why they are enough

You never check infinitely many cases. You check one case and one implication, and the implication does the rest of the work forever.

PartWhat you proveWhat it buys you
Base caseThe statement holds for n = 1 (or whatever the smallest n is)The first domino falls
Inductive hypothesisASSUME it holds for some n = kNot a proof — an assumption you are allowed to make
Inductive stepUsing that assumption, prove it holds for n = k + 1Every domino knocks over the next
ConclusionTherefore it holds for all n ≥ 1They all fall
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — prove 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n+1)/2

Base case, n = 1. Left side = 1. Right side = 1(2)/2 = 1. They match. ✓

Inductive hypothesis. Assume 1 + 2 + … + k = k(k+1)/2 for some k ≥ 1.

Inductive step. Show it for k + 1. Start from the left side and split off the last term — this is the move that makes the assumption usable:

1 + 2 + … + k + (k+1)
  = [k(k+1)/2] + (k+1)   ← the bracket is the hypothesis
  = (k+1)[k/2 + 1]
  = (k+1)(k+2)/2

And (k+1)(k+2)/2 is exactly the formula with n replaced by k+1. ✓

Conclusion. By induction the formula holds for all n ≥ 1.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

The inductive step must use the hypothesis. A "proof" that reaches the k+1 case without ever substituting the assumed k case has proved nothing — that is the most common way an induction answer is marked wrong. In the worked example the substitution happens on the second line; if you cannot point at that line in your own work, you have not done induction.

Induction proves infinitely many statements at once, and the place it is won or lost is a single line: the point where the inductive hypothesis is substituted in rather than re-derived. Everything else is bookkeeping.

📊 FIGURE — the inductive step, with the substitution marked
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a lecture hall — row i has 2i seats; prove the first n rows hold n(n + 1) seats
1.
Base case, n = 1. Row 1 has 2 seats. The formula gives 1(1 + 1) = 2. They match. ✓
2.
Inductive hypothesis. Assume that for some k ≥ 1 the first k rows hold k(k + 1) seats.
3.
Goal. Show the first k + 1 rows hold (k + 1)(k + 2) seats.
4.
Build from the hypothesis. Seats in the first k + 1 rows = (seats in the first k rows) + (seats in row k + 1) = k(k + 1) + 2(k + 1).
5.
Factor: (k + 1)[k + 2] = (k + 1)(k + 2). That is exactly the goal.
6.
Base case plus inductive step, so the formula holds for every n ≥ 1. ∎ Spot-check n = 4: 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 = 20 and 4 × 5 = 20. ✓
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a divisibility claim — prove 3 divides 4ⁿ − 1 for every n ≥ 1
1.
Base case, n = 1. 4¹ − 1 = 3, and 3 | 3. ✓
2.
Inductive hypothesis. Assume 3 | (4ᵏ − 1), i.e. 4ᵏ − 1 = 3m for some integer m.
3.
Goal. Show 3 | (4ᵏ⁺¹ − 1).
4.
Rewrite so the hypothesis appears: 4ᵏ⁺¹ − 1 = 4 · 4ᵏ − 1 = 4(4ᵏ − 1) + 3.
5.
Substitute: = 4(3m) + 3 = 3(4m + 1), and 4m + 1 is an integer.
6.
So 3 divides 4ᵏ⁺¹ − 1, and the claim holds for all n ≥ 1. ∎ Check n = 3: 4³ − 1 = 63 = 3 × 21. ✓
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Two failures, both fatal. Not using the hypothesis: if you compute the k + 1 case from scratch, you have proved one more case, not the theorem — the tell-tale sign is that the assumed formula never appears in your algebra. And skipping the base case: "n² + n + 41 is prime" survives a plausible-sounding step and fails outright at n = 41. Both halves are required, and the base case is not always n = 1 — "n! > 2ⁿ" starts at n = 4.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Write the goal for k + 1 before doing any algebra: substitute k + 1 into the formula and simplify it, so you know the target expression you are steering towards. Then start from the k-case, add the next term, and drive it to that target. If a claim at n depends on a much earlier case rather than the previous one — coin or postage problems, for instance — use strong induction, assuming everything from the base up to k.

Inverting a matrix works for 2×2 and becomes unpleasant beyond it. Gaussian elimination is the general method, and it solves systems of any size by systematically clearing entries to zero.

It rests on three elementary row operations, and the reason it is valid is that each one produces a system with the same solutions as the one before.

OperationNotationWhy it is safe
Swap two rowsRi ↔ Rjthe order of equations never mattered
Multiply a row by a non-zero constantkRiscaling an equation does not change its solutions
Add a multiple of one row to anotherRi + kRjadding equal quantities to both sides

The constant in the second operation must be non-zero. Multiplying a row by 0 destroys the equation, and that restriction is examined directly.

The augmented matrix

A system is written as an augmented matrix — the coefficients, a vertical bar, then the constants — so that row operations act on everything at once.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — setting it up

Each row is one equation; each column is one unknown; the bar separates the coefficients from the constants.

  a +   s +  t =  240    (tickets sold)
22a + 14s + 9t = 3920    (takings, £)
       s +  t =  120    (non-adult tickets)

becomesR₁R₂R₃111│24022149│3920011│120columns: a   s   t  │  constants

A missing term is a 0, never a blank — the third equation has no a in it, so its first entry is 0. Losing that zero is how columns get misaligned.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — solve it by elimination
1.
Swap rows so the leading entry is 1: [1 −1 | 1], [2 1 | 5].
2.
Clear below the leading 1: R₂ − 2R₁ gives [0 3 | 3].
3.
Scale: (1/3)R₂ gives [0 1 | 1], so y = 1.
4.
Back-substitute into row 1: x − 1 = 1, so x = 2.
5.
Check both original equations: 2(2) + 1 = 5 ✓ and 2 − 1 = 1 ✓.

Echelon form and reading the answer

The target is row-echelon form: each leading entry (the pivot) is to the right of the one above it, and everything below a pivot is zero. Continue to reduced row-echelon form — pivots equal to 1 with zeros above as well as below — and the solution can be read straight off with no back-substitution.

The final shape also tells you how many solutions there are, which is the question exams most often ask.

Final row looks likeMeans
a pivot in every variable columnexactly one solution
a row of all zerosa redundant equation — infinitely many solutions (a free variable)
[0 0 | c] with c ≠ 0no solution — the system is inconsistent

That last row says 0 = c, which is false, so nothing can satisfy the system. Recognising it immediately saves you from hunting for a solution that does not exist.

📘 DEFINITION

Elementary row operations: swap, scale by a non-zero constant, add a multiple of another row

Augmented matrix: coefficients and constants written together, separated by a bar

Pivot: the leading non-zero entry of a row

Row-echelon form: pivots stepping right, zeros below each pivot

Reduced row-echelon form: pivots equal to 1 with zeros above and below

Back-substitution: working upward from the last equation to find the remaining unknowns

Inconsistent system: a system with no solution

Free variable: a variable with no pivot; its presence gives infinitely many solutions

★ ON THE OA

Gaussian elimination uses exactly three row operations — swap rows, multiply a row by a non-zero constant, and add a multiple of one row to another — to reach row-echelon form. A row [0 0 | c] with c ≠ 0 means no solution; a row of all zeros means infinitely many.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Work one column at a time, top to bottom, and never move on until every entry below the current pivot is zero. Skipping ahead is what turns a mechanical procedure into an unrecoverable mess.

Row reduction, one column at a time

Gaussian elimination drives the augmented matrix to row echelon form — a staircase of leading entries with zeros beneath — then back-substitutes.

📊 FIGURE — three steps of elimination on a 3×3 system
Elementary row operationEffect on the solution set
Swap two rowsNone
Multiply a row by a non-zero scalarNone
Add a multiple of one row to anotherNone

All three are reversible, which is exactly why the solution set never changes. The "non-zero" in the second one matters: multiplying a row by 0 destroys information and is not allowed.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — finish the system above

The last row reads −4z = −12, so z = 3.

The middle row reads y + z = 2, so y = 2 − 3 = −1.

The top row reads x + 2y + 3z = 9, so x = 9 − 2(−1) − 3(3) = 9 + 2 − 9 = 2.

Solution (2, −1, 3). Substituting into the original second equation checks it: 2(2) − (−1) + 3 = 4 + 1 + 3 = 8 ✓.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

A row that reduces to 0 0 0 | 5 says 0 = 5, so the system is inconsistent — no solution. A row of 0 0 0 | 0 is a redundant equation, leaving a free variable and infinitely many solutions. Reading those two rows the wrong way round is the standard error.

Row operations, and why they are safe

Every row of an augmented matrix is an equation. That is the idea the whole method rests on. Anything you are allowed to do to a system of equations, you are allowed to do to the rows — and there are exactly three such moves.

Row operationWrittenThe equation-level reason it is safe
Swap two rowsRᵢ ↔ Rⱼthe order you list equations in never mattered
Multiply a row by a non-zero constantkRᵢdoubling both sides of an equation does not change its solutions
Add a multiple of one row to anotherRᵢ + kRⱼadding equal quantities to both sides of an equation is always valid

The word non-zero in the second one is examined directly. Multiplying a row by 0 turns an equation into 0 = 0, destroying information you cannot get back — so it is not an elementary row operation. All three legal moves are reversible, and that reversibility is precisely why the solution set never changes.

📊 FIGURE — row echelon form: the staircase of pivots

A full elimination, one operation per line

A school fundraiser sold adult tickets at £22, senior tickets at £14 and student tickets at £9. Three facts were recorded:

240 tickets were sold altogether  →  a + s + t = 240
takings were £3,920               →  22a + 14s + 9t = 3920
seniors and students together: 120  →  s + t = 120

Write the coefficients on the left of the bar and the constants on the right. Each column belongs to one unknown: column 1 is a, column 2 is s, column 3 is t.

augmented matrix:R₁R₂R₃111│24022149│3920011│120columns: a   s   t  │  constants
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Gauss–Jordan: every step, every matrix
startR₁R₂R₃111│24022149│3920011│120the system as written
R₂ − 22R₁R₁R₂R₃111│2400−8−13│−1360011│120clears the 22 under the first pivot

Each row operation from the previous lesson can itself be written as a matrix. An elementary matrix is what you get by applying one row operation to the identity matrix — and multiplying by it on the left performs that same operation on any matrix.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — three elementary matrices (3×3)

Each one is the identity matrix with a single row operation applied to it. Multiply on the left and it performs that operation on whatever it multiplies:

OperationElementary matrixWhere the change sits
R₁ ↔ R₂ — swap rows 1 and 2010100001rows 1 and 2 of I have traded places
5R₂ — multiply row 2 by 5100050001the 1 in position (2,2) has become a 5
R₃ + 2R₁ — add 2 × row 1 to row 3100010201a 2 sits in position (3,1): row 3 borrows from row 1

Compare each with the identity 100010001 — exactly one thing has changed in each.

Every elementary matrix is invertible, and its inverse is the matrix of the reversing operation: swapping twice returns you to the start, multiplying by 5 is undone by multiplying by 1/5, and adding 2R₁ is undone by subtracting it. That fact is what makes the next result work.

The Invertible Matrix Theorem

Because Gaussian elimination is a sequence of elementary matrices, a square matrix reduces to the identity exactly when it is invertible. That links every idea in this chapter into one theorem, and the exam treats the statements as interchangeable.

For a square matrix A, these all say the same thing
A is invertible — A−1 exists
det(A) ≠ 0
A row-reduces to the identity matrix
A·x = b has exactly one solution for every b
A·x = 0 has only the trivial solution x = 0
The rows of A are linearly independent
The columns of A are linearly independent
A has a pivot in every row and every column

The practical value is that you may check whichever condition is cheapest. For a 2×2, computing ad − bc is fastest. For a larger matrix, row-reducing and looking for a zero row is usually quicker than computing a determinant by hand.

And the negations are equally interchangeable: if any one fails, all of them fail. A singular matrix has determinant zero, does not reduce to the identity, has dependent rows, and gives a system with either no solution or infinitely many.

Finding an inverse by row reduction

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the augmented method
1.
Write [A | I] — the matrix beside an identity of the same size.
2.
Row-reduce until the left half becomes the identity.
3.
Whatever the right half has become is A⁻¹.
4.
If the left half cannot reach the identity — a zero row appears — then A is singular and has no inverse.

The reason this works is the elementary-matrix view: the operations that turn A into I are exactly the operations that turn I into A−1, because they encode the same sequence of steps.

📘 DEFINITION

Elementary matrix: the identity with one row operation applied

Invertible Matrix Theorem: a list of equivalent conditions for a square matrix to be invertible

Linearly independent: no row (or column) is a combination of the others

Trivial solution: the all-zero solution to A·x = 0

[A | I] method: row-reducing A to I while the attached identity becomes A⁻¹

Rank: the number of pivots; a square matrix is invertible exactly when its rank equals its size

★ ON THE OA

A matrix is invertible ⇔ det ≠ 0 ⇔ it row-reduces to the identity ⇔ A·x = b has a unique solution. For a 2×2, A⁻¹ = (1/det)·d−b−ca. Any one of those statements failing means all of them fail.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

This theorem is why the chapter hangs together. Determinants, row reduction and solving systems are three routes to the same question — does this matrix undo itself — and recognising them as one question is what makes the exam items fast.

For a square matrix these conditions are all equivalent — establish any one and you have all of them. That is what makes the theorem useful: you get to pick whichever is easiest to check.

The practical value is that you may check whichever condition is cheapest. For a 2 × 2, ad − bc takes five seconds. For a 4 × 4, row-reducing and watching for a zero row is far quicker than expanding a determinant by hand. And the negations are equally interchangeable — if any one condition fails, every one of them fails.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — using the theorem instead of computing

“The 3 × 3 matrix M row-reduces to a form whose bottom row is all zeros. What is det M, and how many solutions does M·x = b have?”

No arithmetic is needed. A zero row means M does not reduce to I, so M is singular; therefore det M = 0, and M·x = b has either no solution or infinitely many — never exactly one. Which of the two it is depends on b, and only further reduction of the augmented matrix will say.

“A·x = 0 has a non-zero solution. Is A invertible?” No. A homogeneous system always has the trivial solution x = 0; having a second one puts you in the singular column of the table above.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Multiplying on the wrong side. E·A performs a row operation. A·E performs a column operation, which is a different thing entirely. Row operations always come from multiplying on the left — the same side the inverse goes on when you solve A·x = b.

Assuming the theorem covers non-square matrices. Every statement in it begins “for a square matrix”. A 3 × 4 matrix has no determinant and no inverse, whatever its entries are, so none of the equivalences apply to it.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Learn the theorem as two columns, not nine facts. Given any one statement, you can supply the other eight. Exam items nearly always hand you one condition and ask for another: “det = 0, so how many solutions?”, “reduces to I, so is it invertible?”, “A·x = 0 has only the trivial solution, so what is the rank?”

Remember the one asymmetry: A·x = 0 can never be inconsistent, because x = 0 always works. So for a homogeneous system the only question is whether that trivial solution is the only one — and the answer is yes exactly when A is invertible.

What an elementary matrix actually does

📘 DEFINITION
An elementary matrix E is what you get by performing one row operation on the identity matrix I. Its whole point is this: multiplying on the left, the effect of EA is to perform that same row operation on A. A row operation and a matrix multiplication are the same act.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Building E for "add 2 × row 1 to row 2"
  1. Start from the identity: I₂ = [[1, 0], [0, 1]].
  2. Carry out the operation on the identity: row 2 becomes row 2 + 2 × row 1, so [0, 1] becomes [2, 1].
  3. That gives E = [[1, 0], [2, 1]].
  4. Now EA does that operation to any A. The 2 sits at position (2,1) — row 2 borrowing from row 1.

The same recipe covers the other two kinds. For scaling — multiply row 2 by 5 — scale row 2 of I: [[1, 0], [0, 5]]. To swap rows 1 and 2, swap them in I: [[0, 1], [1, 0]]. Read the operation, do it to I, and you have E.

The Invertible Matrix Theorem, in the form it is asked

If A is invertible……then
its RREF isthe identity Iₙ
its determinant isnon-zero
its rows/columns arelinearly independent
Ax = b hasexactly one solution for every b

Every line is an "if and only if", so each one read backwards is also true — which is how the contrapositive version gets asked: if row-reducing A produces a row of zeros, the RREF cannot be the identity, so A is singular — not invertible. A zero row means one row was a combination of the others, carrying no independent information.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Why row-reducing [A | I] hands you the inverse
  1. Reducing A to I is a chain of row operations, so it is a chain of elementary matrices: Eₖ…E₂E₁A = I.
  2. By the definition of an inverse, that product Eₖ…E₂E₁ is A⁻¹.
  3. So applying the very same steps to the identity gives Eₖ…E₂E₁I = A⁻¹.
  4. Which is why you write [A | I], reduce until the left side is I, and read A⁻¹ off the right.

The augmented-matrix trick is not a coincidence to memorise — it is this identity.

🎯 EXAM TIP
"EA does what?" → performs that row operation on A. "How do I build E?" → do the operation to the identity. "Row of zeros?" → singular.

A graph is a set of vertices together with a set of edges joining pairs of them — written G = (V, E). It is the most general structure in this course, and everything from road networks to social networks to the relations of Unit 6 is one.

In fact a graph is a relation: the edge set is a subset of V × V, which is the definition from 3.3. An undirected graph corresponds to a symmetric relation, and a digraph to any relation at all.

TypeMeaning
Undirectededges have no direction — {a, b} is the same edge as {b, a}
Directed (digraph)edges have a direction — (a, b) is not (b, a)
Weightedeach edge carries a number: distance, cost, capacity
Simpleno loops and no repeated edges
Multigraphrepeated edges between the same pair are allowed
Complete (Kn)every pair of vertices is joined
Bipartitevertices split into two groups, edges only between groups

Degree and the handshaking lemma

The degree of a vertex is the number of edges meeting it, with a loop counting twice. Summing the degrees over the whole graph counts every edge exactly twice — once from each end — which gives the result the exam asks for by name.

Handshaking lemma: Σ deg(v) = 2 · |E|

Two consequences follow, and both are examined. The sum of all degrees is always even. And the number of vertices with odd degree is always even — because the odd degrees must pair up to keep the total even.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a graph has 5 vertices with degrees 3, 3, 2, 2, 2 — how many edges?
1.
Sum the degrees: 3 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 12.
2.
Apply the lemma: 2|E| = 12.
3.
|E| = 6 edges. Note the two odd degrees — an even count, as required.

The lemma also rules things out instantly. A graph with degrees 3, 3, 3 is impossible, because three odd degrees cannot sum to an even number — so a question offering that degree sequence is testing whether you checked.

Complete graphs and edge counts

In a complete graph Kn every pair of vertices is joined, so the number of edges is the number of ways to choose two vertices from n.

|E(Kn)| = n(n − 1)/2

K₄ has 4(3)/2 = 6 edges and every vertex has degree 3. That formula is also the counting result "n choose 2", which is where it comes from.

📘 DEFINITION

Graph G = (V, E): a set of vertices and a set of edges joining pairs of them

Vertex (node): a point of the graph

Edge: a connection between two vertices

Degree deg(v): the number of edges meeting a vertex; a loop counts twice

Handshaking lemma: the degrees sum to twice the number of edges

Adjacent: two vertices joined by an edge

Complete graph Kₙ: every pair joined; n(n − 1)/2 edges

Bipartite graph: vertices split into two sets with edges only between them

Simple graph: no loops, no repeated edges

★ ON THE OA

A graph is vertices plus edges, and the degree of a vertex is its edge count. The handshaking lemma says the degrees sum to 2 × |E|, so the number of odd-degree vertices is always even. A complete graph Kₙ has n(n − 1)/2 edges.

🎯 EXAM TIP

When a question gives a degree sequence, add it up first. An odd total is impossible, and an odd number of odd degrees is impossible — either check can eliminate options before any real work.

Degree and the handshake theorem

The degree of a vertex is the number of edge-ends touching it. Summing every degree counts each edge twice, so Σ deg(v) = 2|E|. Here the degrees 2+3+2+2+1 = 10 = 2 · 5 edges — a quick sanity check you can run on any exam graph.
📘 DEFINITION

Handshake theorem: the sum of all degrees equals twice the number of edges, because every edge contributes 1 to each of its two endpoints.

Σ deg(v) = 2|E|

Two consequences the exam leans on. First, the number of odd-degree vertices is always even — an odd count is impossible, so a question offering one is offering an impossible graph. Second, given the degree sum you get the edge count for free by halving it.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a graph has degree sequence 3, 3, 2, 2, 2 — how many edges?

Sum = 3 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 12. Edges = 12 / 2 = 6.

Check the parity rule: two vertices have odd degree, which is an even count ✓. Had the sequence been 3, 2, 2, 2, 2 the sum would be 11 — odd, so no such graph exists, and that is the answer to "which of these degree sequences is impossible".

📊 FIGURE — the handshake theorem, counted on a route map

The degree of a vertex is the number of edge-ends meeting it. Add up all the degrees and every edge gets counted twice — once at each endpoint — which is the whole content of the handshake theorem: Σ deg(v) = 2|E|. Two consequences fall straight out of it, and both are exam favourites.

📘 DEFINITION

Handshake Theorem. In any undirected graph, the sum of the degrees equals twice the number of edges. Corollary 1: the degree sum is always even. Corollary 2: the number of vertices of odd degree is always even — odd degrees can only occur in pairs.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — how many routes does the network have?

A regional airline serves six airports whose degrees are 4, 3, 3, 2, 2 and 2. How many routes are in the network?

  1. Add the degrees: 4 + 3 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 16.
  2. By the handshake theorem this equals 2|E|, so 2|E| = 16.
  3. |E| = 16 / 2 = 8 routes.
  4. Sanity check: 16 is even, as it must be, and exactly two airports (the two of degree 3) have odd degree — an even count, as required.
Answer: 8 routes.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a network that cannot exist

A planner claims to have built a six-site fibre network with degrees 5, 4, 3, 2, 2 and 1. Is that possible?

  1. Add the degrees: 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 17.
  2. The handshake theorem says the sum must equal 2|E|, which is even for every graph.
  3. 17 is odd, so no graph has this degree sequence.
  4. The second corollary confirms it independently: the odd degrees here are 5, 3 and 1 — three of them, and the count of odd-degree vertices must be even.
  5. Verdict: impossible, and no amount of redrawing will fix it.

Also worth knowing: a simple graph on n vertices has a maximum degree of n − 1, since a vertex can join each of the others at most once. A claimed degree of 6 among six sites would be impossible for that separate reason.

Answer: Impossible — the degree sum is odd.
🎯 EXAM TIP

For the complete graph Kn, every one of the n vertices joins all n − 1 others, so |E| = n(n − 1)/2 = C(n, 2). A nine-city network where every pair has a direct route has 9(8)/2 = 36 routes, and every city has degree 8. Expect this to be asked as "if every pair of offices needs a dedicated line, how many lines?"

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

A loop adds 2 to a vertex's degree, not 1, because both of its ends attach to the same vertex. Second trap: degree counts edge-ends, not neighbours. In a multigraph with two parallel routes between the same pair of cities, each city gains 2 degree from that pair although it has only one neighbour there.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Solving for n from an edge count

The complete graph Kₙ has 15 edges. What is n?

  1. Kₙ has n(n − 1)/2 edges — every pair joined once.
  2. Set n(n − 1)/2 = 15, so n(n − 1) = 30.
  3. Consecutive integers multiplying to 30: 6 × 5.
  4. n = 6.

The hypercube Qₖ has 2k vertices, one for each k-bit string, and joins two whenever they differ in exactly one bit. Each vertex therefore has k neighbours — one per bit you could flip — so Qₖ is k-regular. Q₄ is 4-regular.

A drawing is fine for six vertices and useless for six thousand, so graphs are stored in one of two standard forms. The choice is a genuine trade-off, and the exam asks which suits a given situation.

The adjacency matrix

An adjacency matrix is a |V| × |V| grid with a 1 at position (i, j) when an edge joins vertex i to vertex j, and 0 otherwise.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a small undirected graph
Edges: A–B, A–C, B–C, C–D
ABCDABCD0110101011010010
Symmetric across the diagonal, because the graph is undirected.
Row sums are the degrees: A=2, B=2, C=3, D=1.

Three properties fall out of that example and each is a question in its own right. For an undirected graph the matrix is symmetric. The row sum gives the degree of that vertex. And the main diagonal is all zeros unless the graph has loops.

For a directed graph the symmetry disappears: entry (i, j) records an edge from i to j only. Row sums then give out-degree and column sums give in-degree.

The adjacency list

An adjacency list stores, for each vertex, only the vertices it is joined to.

A: B, C
B: A, C
C: A, B, D
D: C

It records exactly the same graph in far less space when edges are scarce. That is the trade.

A graph is dense when it has close to the maximum n(n − 1)/2 edges and sparse when it has far fewer. A social network is sparse — you know a few hundred people, not a few billion — which is why real systems use adjacency lists.

One further use of the matrix carries over from 3.5: the k-th power of an adjacency matrix counts walks of length exactly k between each pair of vertices, which is how reachability questions are answered computationally.

In an undirected graph, one edge appears twice in the matrix — at (i, j) and (j, i). Counting the 1s and reporting that as the edge count doubles the answer; divide by two.

Two graphs drawn differently can be the same graph. Isomorphic graphs have identical structure and differ only in how their vertices are labelled or positioned — formally, there is a bijection between the vertex sets that preserves adjacency.

"Preserves adjacency" is the load-bearing phrase: if two vertices are joined in the first graph, their partners must be joined in the second, and if they are not joined, their partners must not be.

The necessary conditions

Checking every possible relabelling is impractical, so the practical method is to look for a reason the graphs cannot match. Three properties must agree.

InvariantMust matchIf it differs
Number of vertices|V₁| = |V₂|not isomorphic — done
Number of edges|E₁| = |E₂|not isomorphic — done
Degree sequencethe sorted list of degrees is identicalnot isomorphic — done
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — eliminating a pair quickly
G1: degrees 3, 3, 2, 2       sorted: [3, 3, 2, 2]
G2: degrees 3, 2, 2, 2       sorted: [3, 2, 2, 2]

Different degree sequences  ->  NOT isomorphic.
No further work needed.

The critical qualification is that these conditions are necessary but not sufficient. Two graphs can agree on all three and still fail to be isomorphic, because the degrees can be arranged differently — one graph might join its two degree-3 vertices to each other while the other does not.

So matching invariants never proves isomorphism. To prove it you must exhibit the actual mapping and verify every edge; to disprove it, a single mismatched invariant is enough. That asymmetry is the same one as ∀ and counterexamples in 1.3.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — exhibit an isomorphism
1.
Confirm the invariants agree: same vertex count, edge count and degree sequence.
2.
Match vertices by degree — a degree-3 vertex can only map to a degree-3 vertex.
3.
Write the proposed bijection explicitly, e.g. A→1, B→2, C→3, D→4.
4.
Check every edge: for each edge in the first graph, confirm the mapped pair is an edge in the second.
5.
Check no extra edges exist in the second graph. Both directions must hold.

Other invariants can settle harder cases: the number of cycles of each length, whether the graph is connected, and the number of components. Any structural property that does not depend on labels is fair game.

What isomorphism is actually asserting

Two isomorphic graphs are the same graph drawn differently — same structure, different labels or positions. This matters because a drawing carries information the graph does not: where vertices sit on the page, whether edges cross, how long they look. None of that is part of the graph, which is only a set of vertices and a set of pairs.

So a question showing two very different-looking pictures may well be showing one graph twice. Straightening the edges or moving a vertex changes nothing, and the invariants are exactly the properties that survive such redrawing — which is why they are the right tool.

A practical checking order

Compare vertex counts, then edge counts, then degree sequences, and stop at the first mismatch. If all three agree, look at how the high-degree vertices connect to each other — whether the two degree-3 vertices are adjacent is a structural fact that a degree sequence cannot capture, and it settles most of the remaining cases.

Writing a degree sequence

A degree sequence is conventionally written in non-increasing order — largest first — so that two graphs can be compared term by term. A graph with degrees 2, 3, 1, 3 has degree sequence (3, 3, 2, 1). Sorting is what makes the comparison meaningful, since the labels are arbitrary.

📘 DEFINITION

Isomorphic graphs: graphs related by an adjacency-preserving bijection of their vertices

Graph invariant: a property unchanged by relabelling

Degree sequence: the sorted list of all vertex degrees

Necessary condition: must hold, but does not by itself guarantee the result

Sufficient condition: guarantees the result

Bijection: a one-to-one and onto mapping — from 3.2

★ ON THE OA

Two graphs are isomorphic if a vertex bijection preserves adjacency — same structure, relabelled. The necessary conditions are the same vertex count, edge count and degree sequence — but these can all match and the graphs still not be isomorphic.

🎯 EXAM TIP

To disprove isomorphism, find one differing invariant and stop. To prove it, you must give the mapping and check every edge — there is no shortcut in that direction.

  2. Both are single cycles, so write each one as a cycle in order. G: A–B–C–D–E–F–A. H: P–R–T–Q–S–U–P.

  2. Connectivity: G is connected — you can walk from A to any other vertex. K is not: there is no path from V to Y.
  3. Connectivity is preserved by isomorphism (a relabelling cannot create or destroy a path), so G ≇ K.
  4. A second independent argument: the shortest cycle in K has length 3, while the shortest cycle in G has length 6. Cycle lengths are preserved too.

One invariant that differs is enough. You never need to check all of them, and you certainly never need to try all 720 possible relabellings.

Answer: Not isomorphic — K is disconnected and contains 3-cycles.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Matching degree sequences do not prove isomorphism. This is the single most common wrong answer in the topic, and the two-triangles example is the standard counterexample. Degree sequences are a screening tool: if they differ, stop, the graphs are not isomorphic; if they agree, you have learned nothing and must look at structure.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Work in this order and you will be fast and correct: (1) compare |V|, (2) compare |E|, (3) compare sorted degree sequences, (4) compare number of components, (5) compare shortest cycle length. If any differ, you are done — not isomorphic. Only if all agree do you go hunting for an explicit bijection, and start by matching up the highest-degree vertices.

Moving through a graph has three names, and the exam distinguishes them precisely by what is allowed to repeat.

So a walk is the loosest notion — wander anywhere, revisit anything. A path is the strictest for an open route: no vertex twice. A cycle is a closed path, returning to where it began without repeating anything else. The length of any of these is its number of edges, not vertices.

Connectivity

A graph is connected when there is a path between every pair of vertices. When it is not, it falls into connected components — maximal pieces that are internally connected and joined to nothing outside.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — components
Vertices: A B C D E
Edges:   A–B, B–C, D–E

A–B–C is one component;  D–E is another.
The graph is DISCONNECTED with 2 components.
There is no path from A to D.

For directed graphs the idea splits in two. A digraph is strongly connected when a directed path runs between every ordered pair, and weakly connected when it would be connected if you ignored the directions. A one-way street system can easily be weakly but not strongly connected.

Euler and Hamilton

Two classical questions ask for a route that covers everything, and the difference between them is what "everything" means.

EulerHamilton
Must use everyedge exactly oncevertex exactly once
Path exists whenexactly 0 or 2 vertices have odd degreeno simple criterion known
Circuit exists whenevery vertex has even degreeno simple criterion known
Also requiresthe graph is connectedthe graph is connected

The Euler condition is one of the most quotable results in the course, and it comes straight from the handshaking argument: every time a route passes through a vertex it uses two edges, one in and one out, so an odd-degree vertex can only be a start or an end. With two odd vertices you must start at one and finish at the other; with none you can return to where you began.

The contrast is instructive. Euler routes are decided by a two-second degree count. Hamilton routes have no such test — deciding whether one exists is NP-complete, which is why the exam asks for the Euler criterion and only asks you to find a Hamilton path by inspection on tiny graphs.

Two more terms the questions use

A trail sits between a walk and a path: edges may not repeat, but vertices may. That is what makes a circuit a closed trail rather than a closed path — an Euler circuit revisits vertices freely while using each edge once.

An isolated vertex is one with degree 0 — no edges at all. It forms a connected component by itself, so a graph containing one cannot be connected unless it is the only vertex.

Trail: a walk with no repeated edge

Path: a walk with no repeated vertex

Cycle / circuit: a closed path returning to its start

Connected graph: a path exists between every pair of vertices

Connected component: a maximal connected piece of a graph

Euler path / circuit: uses every edge exactly once; open or closed

Hamilton path / circuit: visits every vertex exactly once

Strongly connected: in a digraph, a directed path exists between every ordered pair

A walk allows repeats; a path repeats no vertex; a cycle is a closed path. A graph is connected when a path joins every pair. An Euler path exists exactly when 0 or 2 vertices have odd degree — and an Euler circuit when all degrees are even.

A delivery network joins depots N–O, O–P, P–N (a triangle) and O–Q, with Q attached only to O. Which vertices and edges are critical?

A tree is a connected graph with no cycles. That one sentence forces a surprising number of consequences, and the exam tests them as separate facts even though they all follow from the definition.

📐 Properties of a tree with n vertices
Edge count
exactly n − 1 edges
Uniqueness
exactly one path between any two vertices
Fragility
removing any edge disconnects it
Saturation
adding any edge creates a cycle
Equivalence
connected + acyclic ⇔ connected with n − 1 edges ⇔ acyclic with n − 1 edges

The last line is worth reading carefully: any two of connected, acyclic and n − 1 edges imply the third. So a question giving you two of them has already told you it is a tree.

The n − 1 count is the fact most often asked. A tree with 10 vertices has 9 edges — no more, no fewer — which also means a graph with 10 vertices and 12 edges cannot possibly be a tree.

Rooted trees

Designating one vertex as the root imposes a hierarchy and brings a family vocabulary that questions use directly.

TermMeans
Rootthe designated top vertex; the only one with no parent
Parentthe vertex immediately above
Childa vertex immediately below
Leafa vertex with no children
Internal vertexany vertex that is not a leaf
Depth / levelthe distance from the root; the root is at level 0
Heightthe depth of the deepest leaf
Subtreea vertex together with all its descendants

Binary trees

A binary tree allows each vertex at most two children, conventionally left and right. Two counting facts about them are examined.

A binary tree of height h has at most 2h+1 − 1 vertices and at most 2h leaves.

A tree achieving those maxima is full at every level. The reason to care is efficiency: n items stored in a balanced binary tree give a height of about log₂n, so a search that descends from the root touches about 20 vertices for a million items — the same logarithmic behaviour as binary search.

A binary search tree adds an ordering rule: everything in the left subtree is smaller than the vertex, everything in the right subtree is larger. That rule is what makes the inorder traversal in the next lesson produce sorted output.

The equivalent definitions, and why they are equivalent

A tree can be characterised in several ways that sound different and describe the same object. Connected and acyclic. Connected with n − 1 edges. Acyclic with n − 1 edges. Exactly one path between every pair. Minimally connected — remove any edge and it breaks. Maximally acyclic — add any edge and a cycle appears.

The reason they coincide is a counting argument. A connected graph needs at least n − 1 edges to reach every vertex, and any graph with more than n − 1 edges must contain a cycle. So n − 1 is exactly the boundary where connectivity is achieved and cycles have not yet appeared — which is what a tree is.

For exam purposes that means any two of the three properties give you the third for free, and a question stating two of them has already told you the answer without saying "tree".

The rest of the family vocabulary

Two vertices with the same parent are siblings. Everything reachable downward from a vertex is its set of descendants, and everything on the path back up to the root is its ancestors. A vertex's subtree is that vertex together with all of its descendants.

Forest: a graph with no cycles that may be disconnected — a set of trees

Leaf: a vertex with no children

Internal vertex: a vertex with at least one child

Depth / level: distance from the root

Height: the greatest depth in the tree

Binary tree: each vertex has at most two children

Binary search tree: a binary tree ordered so left < vertex < right

A tree is connected and acyclic. A tree with n vertices has exactly n − 1 edges and a unique path between any two vertices. Adding any edge creates a cycle; removing any edge disconnects it.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — why is inorder sorted here?

Because a BST stores everything smaller than a node in its left subtree and everything larger in its right. The output A B C D E F G H I is alphabetical, which is the check.

📘 DEFINITION

A tree is a connected graph with no cycles. Four statements about a graph on n vertices are equivalent, and any one of them can be used as the definition: (1) it is connected and acyclic; (2) it is connected with exactly n − 1 edges; (3) it is acyclic with exactly n − 1 edges; (4) there is exactly one path between every pair of vertices.

That last one is the most useful in practice. In an org chart there is exactly one chain of command between any two people; in a road network with a cycle there would be a detour, and a tree has no detours anywhere. Two immediate consequences: adding any edge to a tree creates exactly one cycle, and removing any edge disconnects it — so every edge of a tree is a bridge.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — counting edges, leaves and reporting lines

A company has 10 staff arranged in the org chart above. (a) How many reporting lines are there? (b) How many people are leaves? (c) What is the height of the tree, and what does it mean?

  1. (a) A tree on n vertices has n − 1 edges, so 10 people give 9 reporting lines. No counting of the picture is required.
  2. (b) A leaf is a vertex with no children: Warehouse, Audit, Rider and UI. That is 4 leaves — the staff with nobody reporting to them.
  3. (c) The height is the number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path. CEO → Ops → Delivery → Rider is 3 edges, and nothing is longer, so the height is 3.
  4. In organisational terms the height is the number of management layers between the CEO and the most distant employee.
Answer: (a) 9. (b) 4 leaves. (c) Height 3.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — sizing a full m-ary tree

A decision system is a full binary tree (every internal node has exactly 2 children) with 25 internal nodes. (a) How many nodes in total? (b) How many leaves? (c) Repeat for a full 3-ary tree with 17 internal nodes.

  1. The formula for a full m-ary tree with i internal nodes is n = m·i + 1. The "+ 1" is the root, which is nobody's child.
  2. (a) m = 2, i = 25: n = 2(25) + 1 = 51 nodes.
  3. (b) Leaves are the nodes that are not internal: l = n − i = 51 − 25 = 26 leaves.
  4. (c) m = 3, i = 17: n = 3(17) + 1 = 52 nodes, and l = 52 − 17 = 35 leaves.
  5. Check with the direct leaf formula l = (m − 1)i + 1: for (c) that is 2(17) + 1 = 35 ✓.

The reasoning behind n = m·i + 1: every node except the root is somebody's child, and the i internal nodes contribute m children each, so the number of non-root nodes is m·i.

Answer: (a) 51. (b) 26. (c) 52 nodes and 35 leaves.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Height is measured in edges, not in nodes. A root-to-leaf chain of 4 boxes has height 3. Some sources count levels instead, so read the question — but the standard convention here is edges, and level numbering starts the root at level 0. Second trap: "n − 1 edges" only characterises a tree together with connectivity or acyclicity. A graph with 10 vertices and 9 edges made of a triangle plus a separate 7-vertex tree has the right edge count and is not a tree.

🎯 EXAM TIP

If a question gives you a number of vertices and asks for edges in a tree, the answer is n − 1 with no work required. Going the other way: a connected graph with more than n − 1 edges must contain a cycle, and the number of edges you would have to remove to reach a spanning tree is exactly |E| − (n − 1).

A traversal visits every vertex of a tree in a defined order. For binary trees there are three, and they differ only in when the root is visited relative to its subtrees — which is exactly what their names encode.

TraversalOrderRoot is visited
PreorderRoot, Left, Rightfirst — "pre"
InorderLeft, Root, Rightin the middle — "in"
PostorderLeft, Right, Rootlast — "post"

The prefix names the position of Root in the sequence, and Left always comes before Right in all three. Once you have that, the three orders need no separate memorisation.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — all three on one tree
            F
          /   \
         B     G
        / \     \
       A   D     I
          / \   /
         C   E H

Preorder  (Root,Left,Right):  F B A D C E G I H
Inorder   (Left,Root,Right):  A B C D E F G H I    <- sorted!
Postorder (Left,Right,Root):  A C E D B H I G F

The inorder line is not a coincidence. This is a binary search tree, and the ordering rule — left subtree smaller, right subtree larger — means visiting left, then root, then right produces the values in ascending order. That is the standard exam use of inorder traversal, and it is worth recognising on sight.

How to trace one by hand

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the reliable method for preorder
1.
Start at the root. Write it down (preorder visits Root first).
2.
Move to the entire left subtree and apply the same rule to it, recursively.
3.
When the left subtree is exhausted, do the same for the right subtree.
4.
The recursion is the method — treat each subtree as a smaller tree of the same kind.

Under exam pressure the reliable technique is to work one subtree at a time and write the partial sequence, rather than trying to hold the whole traversal in your head. The recursive structure means a mistake in one subtree does not corrupt the others.

Where each one is used

TraversalTypical use
Preordercopying a tree; producing prefix notation from an expression tree
Inorderreading a BST in sorted order; producing infix notation
Postorderdeleting a tree safely — children before parent; producing postfix notation

Postorder's use for deletion is a good illustration of why the order matters: you cannot free a parent before its children, or you lose the pointers to them. Applied to an expression tree, the same three traversals produce prefix, infix and postfix notation — which is how a compiler converts an expression into a form a stack machine can evaluate.

Descendants, and one classic application

The three traversals can be restated in terms of descendants, which is how questions often word them: preorder visits a vertex before its descendants, postorder visits it after its descendants, and inorder visits it between the left and right ones. Preorder is the natural choice for printing an outline or copying a structure, because the parent must exist before its children are placed.

The classic application of binary trees is Huffman coding, the compression scheme where frequent characters get short codes. Its codes are built by walking the tree, which gives them the prefix-free property: no code is a prefix of another, so a stream of bits can be decoded unambiguously with no separators.

📘 DEFINITION

Traversal: visiting every vertex of a tree in a defined order

Preorder: Root, Left, Right

Inorder: Left, Root, Right — gives sorted output for a BST

Postorder: Left, Right, Root

Expression tree: a tree with operators at internal vertices and operands at leaves

Prefix / infix / postfix: the notations produced by pre-, in- and postorder traversal

Breadth-first traversal: visiting level by level, using a queue

★ ON THE OA

The three binary-tree traversals are preorder (Root, Left, Right), inorder (Left, Root, Right — yields sorted order for a BST) and postorder (Left, Right, Root). The position of "Root" in the name tells you the order.

🎯 EXAM TIP

If a question gives a traversal sequence and asks which type it is, check whether it is sorted — sorted output on a search tree means inorder, and that single observation answers it.

Traversals are notations

The three traversal orders are not arbitrary — each one is a way of writing the expression a tree stores. Operators sit at internal nodes, operands at leaves.

📊 FIGURE — (3 × 4) + (9 − 2) as a tree, read three ways
TraversalOrderProducesUsed by
Preordernode, left, rightprefix (Polish)Lisp; copying a tree
Inorderleft, node, rightinfix — how humans write itprinting a BST in sorted order
Postorderleft, right, nodepostfix (reverse Polish)stack machines; freeing a tree
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — evaluate the postfix 3 4 × 9 2 − +

Push operands; when an operator arrives, pop two, apply, push the result.

3 → [3]. 4 → [3, 4]. × → pop 4 and 3, push 12 → [12].
9 → [12, 9]. 2 → [12, 9, 2]. − → pop 2 and 9, push 7 → [12, 7].
+ → pop 7 and 12, push 19 → [19].

No brackets were needed anywhere. That is the whole reason postfix exists.

📊 FIGURE — the three depth-first traversal orders on one tree

All three depth-first traversals visit the left subtree before the right one. The only thing that changes is when the node itself is recorded: before its subtrees (pre), between them (in), or after both (post). Say the word out loud — "pre-order records the node pre-viously" — and the ordering follows.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — all three traversals of a score tree

Exam scores are inserted into a binary search tree in the order 58, 34, 71, 26, 47, 65, 89 (smaller goes left, larger goes right). List the preorder, inorder and postorder traversals.

  1. First build the tree. 58 is the root. 34 < 58 so it goes left; 71 > 58 so it goes right. 26 < 58 and < 34 so it is 34's left child; 47 < 58 but > 34 so it is 34's right child. 65 > 58 but < 71 so it is 71's left child; 89 > 71 so it is 71's right child.
  2. Preorder (node, left, right): record 58, then do the whole left subtree — 34, then 26, then 47 — then the right subtree — 71, then 65, then 89.
  3. → 58, 34, 26, 47, 71, 65, 89.
  4. Inorder (left, node, right): finish 34's left subtree first (26), then 34, then 47, then the root 58, then 65, then 71, then 89.
  5. → 26, 34, 47, 58, 65, 71, 89.
  6. Postorder (left, right, node): 26 and 47 before 34; then 65 and 89 before 71; then the root last.
  7. → 26, 47, 34, 65, 89, 71, 58.

Two structural checks you get for free: preorder always starts with the root, postorder always ends with the root, and inorder on a BST is sorted. If any of those fails, the traversal is wrong.

Answer: Listed above; the inorder output 26, 34, 47, 58, 65, 71, 89 is sorted, confirming the tree.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — an expression tree and postfix notation

An invoicing formula (12 + 5) × (30 − 18) is stored as an expression tree: the root is ×, its left child is + with children 12 and 5, and its right child is − with children 30 and 18. Give the postorder traversal, evaluate it, and give the preorder traversal.

  1. Postorder visits both children before the operator: 12, 5, +, then 30, 18, −, then the root ×.
  2. → 12 5 + 30 18 − ×, which is exactly postfix (reverse Polish) notation.
  3. Evaluate it with a stack: push 12, push 5; the + pops both and pushes 17.
  4. Push 30, push 18; the − pops both and pushes 30 − 18 = 12.
  5. The × pops 17 and 12 and pushes 17 × 12 = 204.
  6. Preorder puts each operator first: × + 12 5 − 30 18, which is prefix (Polish) notation.

This is why the traversals matter outside the exam: postorder is how a compiler emits stack-machine code, and inorder (with brackets) is how the expression is printed back for a human.

Answer: Postorder 12 5 + 30 18 − × evaluates to 204; preorder is × + 12 5 − 30 18.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Inorder does not mean "the order they were inserted". It means the node is recorded in between its two subtrees, and on a BST that produces sorted output — which is usually nothing like the insertion order. Second trap: subtraction and division are not commutative, so in postfix the operands must stay in order: 30 18 − is 12, while 18 30 − is −12.

🎯 EXAM TIP

For a fast, reliable traversal by hand, draw a loop around the whole tree starting at the root and travelling anticlockwise, hugging the outline. Each node is passed three times: record it on the left pass for preorder, the bottom pass for inorder, and the right pass for postorder. One drawing then gives all three answers.

Variable-length codes. To compress text, give the frequent characters the shorter codes and the rare ones the longer ones — that is the entire idea behind Huffman coding, and it is why the total shrinks even though some characters cost more than before.

🎯 EXAM TIP
The giveaway distinguishing the traversals is the position of the root: pre-order visits it first (root, left, right), in-order in the middle (left, root, right), post-order last (left, right, root). Find the root in the output and you have identified the traversal.

A spanning tree of a connected graph is a subgraph that touches every vertex, is connected, and contains no cycle. In other words, it keeps all the vertices and just enough edges to hold them together — exactly n − 1 of them, by the tree property from 5.

The practical reading is that a spanning tree is the cheapest possible connection: remove any of its edges and the network splits. A graph normally has many different spanning trees, and choosing between them is what makes the problem interesting.

The minimum spanning tree

When edges carry weights — distance, cost, cable length — the minimum spanning tree is the spanning tree whose total weight is smallest. Two algorithms build one, and the exam asks you to trace either.

Kruskal's algorithmPrim's algorithm
Works onedges, globallya growing tree
Each stepadd the cheapest remaining edge that does not create a cycleadd the cheapest edge with exactly one endpoint already in the tree
Start fromthe whole sorted edge listany single vertex
Intermediate statea forest of fragments that eventually mergealways one connected tree
Stop whenn − 1 edges have been addedevery vertex is included

The rule for Prim's is the one worth stating exactly, because it is where traces go wrong: the next edge must have one endpoint inside the tree and one outside. An edge with both endpoints already inside would create a cycle; an edge with neither inside would disconnect the fragment.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — trace Kruskal's on a small graph
1.
Edges with weights: A–B 1, B–C 2, A–C 3, C–D 4, B–D 5.
2.
Sort by weight: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
3.
Take A–B (1). No cycle. ✓
4.
Take B–C (2). No cycle. ✓
5.
Take A–C (3). This would close the triangle A–B–C — skip it.
6.
Take C–D (4). No cycle. ✓ That is 3 edges for 4 vertices, so stop.
7.
MST = {A–B, B–C, C–D}, total weight 7.

Both algorithms are greedy — they take the best available option at each step and never reconsider. Greedy strategies usually fail to find a global optimum, and the minimum spanning tree is one of the cases where the greedy answer is provably correct, which is why these two algorithms are the standard examples of the technique.

One more detail the exam checks: if several edges tie for cheapest, either may be chosen, and different choices can give different spanning trees with the same total weight. The MST is not necessarily unique; its weight is.

📘 DEFINITION

Spanning tree: a subgraph that is a tree and includes every vertex

Minimum spanning tree (MST): the spanning tree of least total weight

Kruskal's algorithm: repeatedly add the cheapest edge that creates no cycle

Prim's algorithm: grow one tree by adding the cheapest edge with exactly one endpoint inside

Greedy algorithm: one that takes the locally best option at each step

Weighted graph: a graph whose edges carry numeric values

Cycle detection: the check that stops Kruskal adding a redundant edge

★ ON THE OA

A spanning tree touches all vertices with n − 1 edges and no cycle. A minimum spanning tree minimises total weight. Kruskal: add the cheapest edge that avoids a cycle. Prim: add the cheapest edge with exactly one endpoint already in the tree.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

This is where the whole graphs unit converges. The MST is a tree (5), found by walking edges (4), stored as a weighted graph (2), and its correctness rests on the acyclic property that defines a tree in the first place.

Spanning trees and the minimum one

📘 DEFINITION

A spanning tree of a connected graph touches every vertex, uses only existing edges, and contains no cycle — so on n vertices it has exactly n − 1 edges. A minimum spanning tree is the spanning tree whose edge weights sum to the least possible total.

📊 FIGURE — a weighted graph with its MST picked out
AlgorithmHow it choosesGrowsNeeds
Kruskalcheapest remaining edge that does not create a cyclea forest that merges into one treeedges sorted by weight; cycle detection
Primcheapest edge leaving the tree built so farone connected tree from a start vertexa priority queue of frontier edges
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Kruskal on the graph above

Sort the weights: 1, 2, 3(B–C), 3(D–E), 4, 5, 6, 7.

Take A–D (1) ✓. Take A–B (2) ✓. Take B–C (3) ✓. Take D–E (3) ✓. Next is B–E (4) — but A–B, A–D and D–E already connect B to E, so it would close a cycle: reject. Take E–G (5) ✓. That is 5 edges on 6 vertices, so stop.

Total = 1 + 2 + 3 + 3 + 5 = 14.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Both algorithms are greedy and both are provably optimal, so they always reach the same total weight — but they can produce different edge sets when weights tie. A question asking "which edges does Prim pick" is not asking the same thing as "what is the minimum total".

📊 FIGURE — a minimum spanning tree, drawn on the network it came from

A spanning tree of a connected graph is a subgraph that reaches every vertex and contains no cycle — so it always has exactly n − 1 edges. A minimum spanning tree is the cheapest such subgraph by total edge weight. It is the answer to "connect every site for the least total cable", and it is worth noticing what it is not: it does not guarantee the cheapest route between any particular pair.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Kruskal's algorithm, edge by edge

Six depots must be joined by fibre. The costs in $1,000s are AB 14, AC 9, BC 6, BD 21, CD 17, CE 12, DE 8, DF 19, EF 15. Find the cheapest network that connects all six.

  1. Kruskal: sort every edge by weight, then take them cheapest-first, skipping any edge that would close a cycle. Stop at n − 1 = 5 edges.
  2. Sorted: BC 6, DE 8, AC 9, CE 12, AB 14, EF 15, CD 17, DF 19, BD 21.
  3. BC 6 — take it. Groups: {B, C}.
  4. DE 8 — take it, it joins two fresh depots. Groups: {B, C}, {D, E}.
  5. AC 9 — take it, A joins the B–C group. Groups: {A, B, C}, {D, E}.
  6. CE 12 — take it, this merges the two groups. Groups: {A, B, C, D, E}.
  7. AB 14 — reject: A and B are already in the same group, so this would close a cycle A–C–B–A.
  8. EF 15 — take it, F joins. All six depots are now in one group and we have 5 edges. Stop.
  9. Total cost: 6 + 8 + 9 + 12 + 15 = 50, that is $50,000.
Answer: Edges BC, DE, AC, CE, EF for a total of $50,000.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Prim's algorithm on the same network

Run Prim from depot A and confirm you get the same total.

  1. Prim: grow one tree from a starting vertex, each step adding the cheapest edge that leaves the tree so far.
  2. Tree = {A}. Edges leaving it: AB 14, AC 9. Cheapest is AC 9. Tree = {A, C}.
  3. Edges leaving {A, C}: AB 14, CB 6, CD 17, CE 12. Cheapest is CB 6. Tree = {A, B, C}.
  4. Edges leaving {A, B, C}: BD 21, CD 17, CE 12. Cheapest is CE 12. Tree = {A, B, C, E}.
  5. Edges leaving: ED 8, EF 15, CD 17, BD 21. Cheapest is ED 8. Tree = {A, B, C, D, E}.
  6. Edges leaving: EF 15, DF 19. Cheapest is EF 15. Tree is now all six depots.
  7. Total: 9 + 6 + 12 + 8 + 15 = 50 — the same tree and the same cost.

The two algorithms differ only in how they keep track of progress: Kruskal manages a collection of growing groups, Prim manages one growing group. On a graph with distinct edge weights they always end at the same tree.

Answer: $50,000, the identical spanning tree.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Kruskal takes the cheapest edge available anywhere, not the cheapest edge next to the tree you have. Mixing the two rules is the usual source of a wrong tree. The other frequent error is forgetting the cycle check: in the run above, AB 14 is cheaper than EF 15 but must be rejected, and a student who takes it ends up with six edges and a cycle. Always stop at exactly n − 1 edges.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Two facts that answer questions on their own. A spanning tree of a graph with n vertices has exactly n − 1 edges, regardless of how many edges the original graph had. And the number of spanning trees of the complete graph Kn is nn−2 (Cayley's formula), so K₄ has 4² = 16 and K₅ has 5³ = 125.

Searching a graph: breadth-first and depth-first

Both traversals visit every reachable vertex exactly once. They differ only in which vertex they take next, and that single choice is what every exam question here turns on.

📊 FIGURE — the same graph, two orders of discovery
BFS — breadth-firstDFS — depth-first
Orderlevel by level: all neighbours of a vertex before any of theirsas deep as possible along one path, then backtracks
Data structurea queue (first in, first out)a stack (last in, first out) — or recursion, which uses the call stack
Good forthe shortest path in an unweighted graphcycle detection, topological order, maze-style exhaustive search
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Mixing up the two data structures. The queue is what makes BFS fair — it hands out turns in the order vertices were discovered, so the search spreads evenly outwards. Swap it for a stack and the newest discovery is always taken next, which is exactly what makes DFS plunge.

Can a graph have more than one MST?

Yes. A minimum spanning tree is minimum by total weight, and nothing says only one set of edges can reach that total. Whenever two edges of equal weight are interchangeable — the clearest case being a graph where every edge has the same weight — several different trees tie for the minimum.

The total weight is unique. The set of edges achieving it need not be. If all edge weights are distinct, the MST is unique.

🎯 EXAM TIP
Read the verb in the question. "Level by level", "all neighbours first", "shortest path in an unweighted graph" → BFS, queue. "As deep as possible", "backtracks" → DFS, stack.

Numbers have reciprocals: 5 × 1/5 = 1. Matrices have inverses: A · A−1 = A−1 · A = I. Only square matrices can have one, and not all of them do — which is the whole content of the determinant.

The determinant

For a 2×2 matrix the determinant is a single number that decides invertibility.

det abcd = ad − bc

If det ≠ 0 the matrix is invertible (also called non-singular). If det = 0 it is singular and has no inverse at all — the analogue of dividing by zero.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — two determinants

A print shop’s machine-time matrix — press and cutter minutes per poster and per banner:

det8532= 8·2 − 5·3 = 16 − 15 =1→ invertible

A second shop whose two machines use time in the same proportion:

det1525915= 15·15 − 25·9 = 225 − 225 =0→ SINGULAR

Row 2 is 0.6 × row 1, so the second row carries no new information and the matrix cannot be undone.

The second case is not a coincidence: a determinant of zero always means the rows are linearly dependent — one is a multiple or combination of the others — so the matrix squashes space flat and cannot be undone.

The 2×2 inverse

A−1 = (1/det) · d−b−ca

The pattern is worth saying in words because that is how it is remembered: swap the diagonal entries, negate the other two, divide by the determinant.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — invert 4726
1.
Determinant: 4·6 − 7·2 = 24 − 14 = 10. Non-zero, so an inverse exists.
2.
Swap a and d: 6724.
3.
Negate b and c: 6−7−24.
4.
Divide by 10: A⁻¹ = 0.6−0.7−0.20.4.
5.
Check: A · A⁻¹ should give 1001. ✓

Solving a linear system

This is what inverses are for. A system of linear equations can be written as A·x = b, with A the coefficient matrix, x the unknowns and b the constants. Multiplying both sides on the left by A−1 isolates x.

A·x = b ⟹ x = A−1·b

The side matters — you must multiply on the left in both cases, because multiplication is not commutative. And the determinant answers the solvability question before any work is done: det ≠ 0 means exactly one solution, while det = 0 means either no solution or infinitely many, and further work is needed to tell which.

📘 DEFINITION

Inverse (A⁻¹): the matrix satisfying A·A⁻¹ = A⁻¹·A = I; only square matrices can have one

Determinant: a scalar deciding invertibility; ad − bc for a 2×2

Singular: determinant zero — no inverse exists

Non-singular / invertible: determinant non-zero — an inverse exists

Coefficient matrix: the matrix A in A·x = b

Unique solution: guaranteed when det ≠ 0

★ ON THE OA

For a 2×2 matrix abcd, the determinant is ad − bc. If det = 0 the matrix is singular and has no inverse; det ≠ 0 means invertible. The inverse is (1/det)·d−b−ca.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

The inverse formula swaps a and d and negates b and c — not the other way round. Swapping the wrong pair produces a matrix that fails the A·A⁻¹ = I check, which is why that check is worth the ten seconds.

The inverse, and when there is not one

📘 DEFINITION

A⁻¹ is the matrix with A·A⁻¹ = A⁻¹·A = I. Only square matrices can have one, and a square matrix has one exactly when its determinant is non-zero.

📊 FIGURE — a 2×2 inverse, verified
For a 2×2 abcdValue
Determinantad − bc
Inverse(1/(ad − bc)) × d−b−ca
Invertible whenad − bc ≠ 0
Called singular whenad − bc = 0 — no inverse exists

The pattern is worth saying aloud: swap a and d, negate b and c, divide by the determinant. Forgetting to divide is the most common slip, and the resulting matrix fails the A·A⁻¹ = I check immediately — which is why you should always run that check.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — solve Ax = b with A = 3423 and b = [10, 7]

det A = 1, so A⁻¹ = 3−4−23.

x = A⁻¹b = [3(10) + (−4)(7), (−2)(10) + 3(7)] = [30 − 28, −20 + 21] = [2, 1].

Check in the original: 3(2) + 4(1) = 10 ✓ and 2(2) + 3(1) = 7 ✓.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

x = A⁻¹b, not bA⁻¹ — the inverse goes on the left, because that is the side you multiplied from to cancel A. Matrix multiplication does not commute, so the sides are not interchangeable.

The determinant is a crossing

For a 2 × 2 matrix the determinant is one number that answers one question: can this matrix be undone? You get it by multiplying along the two diagonals and subtracting. The diagonal that runs down to the right is added; the one that runs down to the left is subtracted.

📊 FIGURE — det = ad − bc, drawn as two crossing diagonals
📘 DEFINITION

For A = abcd    det A = ad − bc.

det A ≠ 0 → A is invertible (also called non-singular): A⁻¹ exists and is unique.

det A = 0 → A is singular: no inverse exists at all. This is the matrix version of dividing by zero.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — two determinants from a real setting

A print shop makes posters and banners. Each poster needs 8 minutes on the press and 3 on the cutter; each banner needs 5 minutes on the press and 2 on the cutter. That is the machine-time matrix:

A =C₁C₂R₁R₂8532R₁ = press, R₂ = cutter · C₁ = poster, C₂ = banner

det A = 8·2 − 5·3 = 16 − 15 = 1

Non-zero, so the machine hours can be worked backwards into a production count — which is exactly the question solved further down.

Now a second shop whose two products use time in the same proportion:

The second machine tells you nothing the first did not, so no total of machine hours can pin down how many of each product were made. A zero determinant always means one row is a multiple or a combination of the others.

A⁻¹ = (1 / det A) · d−b−ca  — swap the two main-diagonal entries a and d, negate the other two, then divide everything by the determinant.

(2,1) = 3·2 + 2·(−3) = 6 − 6   = 0

A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers, described by its dimensions: an m × n matrix has m rows and n columns, always stated in that order. The entry in row i and column j is written aij, and the row index always comes first.

Addition and subtraction

Both are done entry by entry, and both require the two matrices to have identical dimensions. If the sizes differ, the sum is not merely awkward — it is undefined, and that is a favourite exam trap.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — addition

Both matrices are 2 × 3 (two branches, three products), so they add entry by entry:

12894478613062+143885110211758=27118298188247120

But a 2 × 3 and a 3 × 2 cannot be added at all — no entry has a partner in the same position:

128944786130622 × 3+128869413047623 × 2=UNDEFINED

Scalar multiplication

Multiplying by a single number multiplies every entry by it, and it has no dimension restriction at all.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — scalar multiplication

Hours worked, multiplied by an £18 hourly rate — the scalar reaches every entry:

18 ·34274122=612486738396

And it reaches negative entries too: −4 · 25−13−817 = −1005232−68

The transpose

The transpose AT swaps rows and columns: row 1 becomes column 1. An m × n matrix transposes to an n × m matrix, so a 2×3 becomes a 3×2. A matrix equal to its own transpose is symmetric, which requires it to be square.

Addition obeys the rules you would expect — it is commutative and associative, the zero matrix is the identity, and (A + B)T = AT + BT. Multiplication, in the next lesson, is where the surprises are.

Why dimensions dominate this chapter

Almost every matrix question begins with a dimension check, and a surprising number end there. Addition requires identical dimensions; multiplication requires the inner dimensions to match; only square matrices can have a determinant or an inverse; and the transpose swaps the dimensions round. Writing the dimensions above each matrix before starting is the single most effective habit in this chapter.

The habit also catches questions designed to be answered "undefined". An exam that offers a numeric answer for (2×3) + (3×2) is testing whether you checked, and the numbers in the options exist only to look plausible.

Where matrices come from

A matrix is a compact way of writing a table of related numbers, and the three uses in this course are worth naming. As a system of equations — the coefficients of several linear equations, which is 4. As a relation or graph — the adjacency matrices of Units 6 and 7, where entries are 0 or 1. And as a transformation — a rule mapping vectors to vectors, which is what makes the inverse meaningful as "undo".

The main diagonal

The main diagonal of a matrix runs from the top-left to the bottom-right — the entries where the row index equals the column index. It is the diagonal every other definition in this chapter refers to: the identity matrix has 1s on it, a diagonal matrix has non-zeros only on it, a symmetric matrix mirrors across it, and triangular matrices are defined by which side of it is zero.

Dimensions (m × n): rows by columns, always in that order

Entry aᵢⱼ: the value in row i, column j

Square matrix: equal numbers of rows and columns

Zero matrix: every entry zero

Transpose (Aᵀ): rows and columns interchanged

Symmetric matrix: equal to its own transpose

Scalar multiplication: multiplying every entry by a single number

Matrix addition requires identical dimensions and is done entry by entry. If the sizes differ the sum is undefined — that is the trap. Scalar multiplication has no such restriction and touches every entry.

Dimensions are always rows × columns. A 2×3 matrix has two rows and three columns, and reading it the other way makes every subsequent multiplication check come out wrong.

A matrix is just a table with the words stripped off. Keep the words in your head while you learn to read one. The Riverside and Hillcrest branches of a bakery each sold sourdough loaves, bagels and croissants on Monday:

Upper triangularall zeros below the main diagonalthe shape row-reduction drives a system into

The main diagonal runs top-left to bottom-right: the entries a₁₁, a₂₂, a₃₃ … where the row number and the column number are the same. It is the only place a row index and a column index agree, which is why so many definitions are phrased around it.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Rows are horizontal; columns are vertical. Dimensions are rows × columns. A 2 × 3 matrix has 2 rows and 3 columns — it is wider than it is tall. Reading it as “2 columns, 3 rows” makes every later dimension check come out backwards, so a multiplication that is genuinely undefined will look fine to you and one that works will look impossible.

The second half of the same mistake is aᵢⱼ. The row index always comes first: a₃₂ is row 3, column 2 — not column 3, row 2. If a question offers you both numbers as options, it is testing exactly this.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Before doing any arithmetic, write the dimensions above each matrix — “2×3” and “2×3”. For addition and subtraction they must match exactly; if they do not, the answer is “undefined” and you are already finished. Several exam items are pure dimension checks with plausible numeric options attached purely to tempt you into computing something.

Scalar multiplication has no such restriction and never changes the shape, so 5 · (a 2 × 7 matrix) is a 2 × 7 matrix. Transposing does change the shape: m × n becomes n × m.

📘 DEFINITION
Equality of matrices is stricter than it looks: A = B requires the same dimensions and every corresponding entry equal. Two matrices holding the same numbers in a different shape — 2×3 against 3×2 — are not equal, and are not even comparable.
