◆ READ THIS FIRST

Relations questions reward slow, literal checking: take the definition one word at a time and test it against the actual pairs. Every example below does exactly that.

Eight relation problems, fully worked

Example 1 — Test a relation for the three properties
Problem. On A = {1, 2, 3}, let R = {(1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (1,2), (2,1)}. Is R reflexive, symmetric, transitive?
1
Reflexive means every element relates to itself: (1,1), (2,2) and (3,3) must ALL be present. Check the list — all three are there. ✓
2
Symmetric means whenever (a,b) is in R, so is (b,a). The only non-loop pairs are (1,2) and (2,1), and each is matched by the other. ✓
3
Transitive means whenever (a,b) and (b,c) are in R, so is (a,c). Test the chains that actually exist.
4
Chain (1,2) then (2,1) needs (1,1) — present ✓. Chain (2,1) then (1,2) needs (2,2) — present ✓. Chains through loops give back pairs already listed ✓.
5
All three properties hold, so R is an equivalence relation.
6
Its equivalence classes are {1, 2} (which relate to each other) and {3} (which relates only to itself), and those two classes partition A.
Answer. R is reflexive, symmetric and transitive — an equivalence relation, with classes {1,2} and {3}.
◆ WHERE PEOPLE SLIP

Transitivity is only violated by an actual chain. If no (a,b),(b,c) pair exists, the relation is transitive by default — "vacuously true", a favourite exam subtlety.

Example 2 — Injective, surjective, bijective?
Problem. For f: ℝ → ℝ defined by f(x) = 2x + 3, decide whether f is one-to-one, onto, and/or a bijection.
1
One-to-one (injective) asks: can two different inputs give the same output? Assume f(a) = f(b) and see what follows.
2
2a + 3 = 2b + 3 → subtract 3 → 2a = 2b → divide by 2 → a = b. Since equal outputs force equal inputs, f is injective. ✓
3
Onto (surjective) asks: does every real y get produced by some x? Solve y = 2x + 3 for x.
4
x = (y − 3)/2, which is a real number for EVERY real y. So every output is achieved, and f is surjective. ✓
5
Both properties hold, so f is a bijection, and it therefore has an inverse: f⁻¹(y) = (y − 3)/2.
6
Graphical intuition: a non-horizontal straight line passes the horizontal-line test exactly once at every height — one-to-one and onto at the same time.
Answer. f is injective, surjective, and therefore bijective, with f⁻¹(y) = (y − 3)/2.
◆ WHERE PEOPLE SLIP

The domain and codomain matter. The same rule f(x) = 2x + 3 from ℤ to ℤ is injective but NOT surjective — no integer maps to 4, since (4 − 3)/2 = 0.5.

Example 3 — Floor and ceiling, including negatives
Problem. Evaluate ⌊7.8⌋, ⌈7.2⌉, ⌊−2.3⌋ and ⌈−2.3⌉.
1
Floor ⌊x⌋ is the greatest integer LESS THAN OR EQUAL TO x — round DOWN, meaning toward negative infinity.
2
Ceiling ⌈x⌉ is the least integer GREATER THAN OR EQUAL TO x — round UP, toward positive infinity.
3
⌊7.8⌋: the integers at or below 7.8 are 7, 6, 5, …; the greatest is 7.
4
⌈7.2⌉: the integers at or above 7.2 are 8, 9, …; the least is 8.
5
⌊−2.3⌋: careful here. Down from −2.3 means MORE negative, so the answer is −3, not −2.
6
⌈−2.3⌉: up from −2.3 means toward zero, giving −2.
Answer. ⌊7.8⌋ = 7, ⌈7.2⌉ = 8, ⌊−2.3⌋ = −3, ⌈−2.3⌉ = −2.
◆ WHERE PEOPLE SLIP

Negatives are where these questions are decided. Floor is not "chop off the decimal": truncating −2.3 gives −2, but the floor is −3. Picture the number line and move in the named direction.

Example 4 — Adjacency matrix and paths of length 2
Problem. A digraph on {1,2,3} has edges 1→2, 1→3, 2→3, 3→1. Write its adjacency matrix and use it to count walks of length 2.
1
Build the matrix M where entry (i, j) is 1 when there is an edge from i to j. Row 1 has edges to 2 and 3, so row 1 is (0, 1, 1).
2
Row 2 has only 2→3, giving (0, 0, 1). Row 3 has only 3→1, giving (1, 0, 0). So M =
011
001
100
3
Key fact: entry (i, j) of M² counts the walks of length exactly 2 from i to j — because the dot product sums, over every middle vertex k, the product of "i→k exists" and "k→j exists".
4
Compute M² = M · M =
101
100
011
5
Read an entry to check the meaning: entry (1,1) is 1, so there is exactly one walk 1 → ? → 1. Indeed 1→3→1.
6
Entry (1,3) is 1: the walk 1→2→3. Entry (2,1) is 1: the walk 2→3→1. All confirmed against the picture.
Answer. M =
011
001
100
and M² =
101
100
011
, whose entries count length-2 walks.
◆ WHERE PEOPLE SLIP

In a DIRECTED graph the matrix is usually not symmetric — 1→2 does not put a 1 at (2,1). For an undirected graph it always is symmetric.

Example 5 — Equivalence classes and partitions
Problem. On the integers, define a R b when a and b leave the same remainder on division by 3. Describe the equivalence classes.
1
First confirm it IS an equivalence relation. Reflexive: a has the same remainder as itself ✓.
2
Symmetric: if a matches b, then b matches a ✓. Transitive: if a matches b and b matches c, all three share a remainder ✓.
3
Now group by the possible remainders. Division by 3 can only leave 0, 1 or 2 — so there are exactly three classes.
4
Class [0] = {…, −3, 0, 3, 6, 9, …} — the multiples of 3.
5
Class [1] = {…, −2, 1, 4, 7, 10, …} and class [2] = {…, −1, 2, 5, 8, 11, …}.
6
These three classes are disjoint and together contain every integer — that is precisely what it means to PARTITION the set.
Answer. Three classes: [0], [1] and [2] (the remainders mod 3), which partition ℤ.
◆ WHERE PEOPLE SLIP

Every equivalence relation induces a partition, and every partition comes from an equivalence relation — they are two views of the same idea. The number of classes equals the number of possible remainders, so mod n gives n classes.

Example 6 — Partial order and its Hasse diagram
Problem. Let R be “a divides b” on the set {1, 2, 3, 6, 12}. Show R is a partial order, draw its Hasse diagram, and name the minimal and maximal elements.
1
Reflexive? Every number divides itself (a = a·1), so yes.
2
Antisymmetric? If a | b and b | a for positive integers, then a = b — you cannot have two DIFFERENT numbers each dividing the other. Yes.
3
Transitive? If a | b and b | c, then c = a·(something), so a | c. Yes. All three hold: R is a partial order.
4
To draw the Hasse diagram, keep only the COVER relations: drop every loop (reflexivity is implied) and every edge you could rebuild by climbing through a middle element. 1→6 goes, because 1→2→6 already carries it; 1→12, 2→12 and 3→12 go the same way.
5
What survives: 1—2, 1—3, 2—6, 3—6, 6—12. Draw larger elements higher: 
   12
    |
    6
   / \
  2   3
   \ /
    1
6
Minimal element: 1 (nothing below it). Maximal: 12 (nothing above it). Is the order TOTAL? No — 2 and 3 are incomparable: neither divides the other, and the diagram shows them side by side with no path between them.
Answer. R is a partial order; covers are 1—2, 1—3, 2—6, 3—6, 6—12; minimal = 1, maximal = 12; not a total order (2 and 3 are incomparable).
◆ WHERE PEOPLE SLIP

A Hasse diagram NEVER shows loops or transitive edges — drawing 1—6 or 1—12 is the give-away error. If you can walk up through a middle vertex, that edge must not be drawn.

Example 7 — Strict order: < on {1, 2, 3}
Problem. Let R = {(a, b) : a < b} on {1, 2, 3}, so R = {(1,2), (1,3), (2,3)}. Show R is a strict order. Is it a strict TOTAL order?
1
Irreflexive? A strict order must contain NO (a, a) pairs. No number is less than itself — (1,1), (2,2), (3,3) are all absent. Yes.
2
Asymmetric? If (a, b) is in R then (b, a) must not be. 1 < 2 and 2 < 1 cannot both hold. Check all pairs: never both directions. Yes.
3
Transitive? (1,2) and (2,3) are in R — is (1,3)? Yes, it is. No other chains exist to check. Yes.
4
Irreflexive + transitive (asymmetry then follows automatically) = a STRICT order. Compare: ≤ keeps the loops and is antisymmetric instead — that is the whole difference between ≤ and <.
5
Total? For every pair of DIFFERENT elements, one direction must be present: 1,2 ✓ · 1,3 ✓ · 2,3 ✓. Every pair is comparable, so this is a strict total order — that property is called trichotomy: exactly one of a < b, a = b, b < a holds.
Answer. R is a strict order (irreflexive, asymmetric, transitive), and because every pair is comparable it is a strict total order.
◆ WHERE PEOPLE SLIP

Strict orders are IRREFLEXIVE, partial orders (≤) are REFLEXIVE — swapping those two definitions is the standard exam trap. If you see loops in the relation, it cannot be strict.

Example 8 — An n-ary relation as a database table
Problem. The relation Enrolled(Student, Course, Grade) holds these tuples: (S1, C959, B), (S1, D286, A), (S2, C959, A), (S3, D197, A). Find its degree and cardinality, apply the selection Grade = A, project onto (Student, Course), and decide whether Student alone can be a primary key.
1
Degree = how many ATTRIBUTES (columns) each tuple has. Every tuple is a triple, so the degree is 3 — this is a ternary (3-ary) relation.
2
Cardinality = how many TUPLES (rows) the relation currently holds: count them — 4.
3
Selection keeps whole rows passing a condition. σGrade=A keeps (S1, D286, A), (S2, C959, A), (S3, D197, A) — 3 rows, still with all 3 columns.
4
Projection keeps whole COLUMNS: πStudent,Course gives (S1, C959), (S1, D286), (S2, C959), (S3, D197). Duplicates would collapse; here all 4 stay distinct.
5
Primary key test: a key must identify a row UNIQUELY. Student = S1 appears in two rows, so Student alone fails. The pair (Student, Course) never repeats — a composite key that works.
Answer. Degree 3, cardinality 4; the selection returns 3 tuples; the projection returns 4 pairs; Student is not a key, but (Student, Course) is.
◆ WHERE PEOPLE SLIP

Degree and cardinality get swapped constantly: degree counts columns, cardinality counts rows. And selection picks ROWS while projection picks COLUMNS — the σ/π pair is the other classic swap.

"}, "C959/worked/w8": {"body": "
◆ READ THIS FIRST

Graph questions are mostly counting arguments with a picture attached. Draw the graph before doing anything else — most errors here are reading errors, not reasoning errors.

Eight graph problems, fully worked

Example 1 — The handshake theorem
Problem. A graph has 5 vertices with degrees 3, 3, 2, 2, 2. How many edges does it have?
1
The handshake theorem: the sum of all degrees equals TWICE the number of edges, because each edge contributes 1 to the degree at each of its two endpoints.
2
Add the degrees: 3 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 12.
3
So 2|E| = 12, which gives |E| = 6 edges.
4
Sanity check the theorem itself: the degree sum must always be EVEN, and 12 is even ✓.
5
This also proves a classic exam fact: no graph can have an odd number of odd-degree vertices, since the total must come out even.
Answer. The graph has 6 edges.
◆ WHERE PEOPLE SLIP

Answering 12 means you forgot to halve. If a question hands you a degree list summing to an ODD number, the graph is impossible — that is the intended answer.

Example 2 — Counting edges in a tree
Problem. A tree has 12 vertices. How many edges does it have? How many edges would a spanning tree of a connected 12-vertex graph have?
1
A tree is a connected graph with NO cycles. That forces a very rigid count.
2
Build it up: start with 1 vertex and 0 edges. Every new vertex must attach with exactly one new edge — more would create a cycle, fewer would disconnect it.
3
So after n vertices you have used n − 1 edges: a tree on 12 vertices has 11 edges.
4
A spanning tree touches every vertex of the graph and is itself a tree, so it has the same count: 11 edges, however many edges the original graph had.
5
That is why adding ANY extra edge to a tree creates exactly one cycle, and removing any edge disconnects it.
Answer. Both are 11 edges — a tree (or spanning tree) on n vertices always has n − 1 edges.
◆ WHERE PEOPLE SLIP

This "n − 1" is one of the most-tested facts in the unit. It works in reverse too: a connected graph with n vertices and n − 1 edges must be a tree.

Example 3 — Tree traversals
Problem. For a binary tree with root A, left child B (children D and E) and right child C, give the preorder, inorder and postorder traversals.
1
Draw it first: A at the top; B on the left with children D and E; C on the right with no children.
2
The three names describe WHEN the root is visited relative to its subtrees. Left is always visited before right.
3
Preorder = root, left, right. Visit A, then the left subtree (B, then D, then E), then C: A B D E C.
4
Inorder = left, root, right. In the left subtree: D, then B, then E. Then the root A, then C: D B A E C.
5
Postorder = left, right, root. Left subtree first (D, E, then B), then C, then finally A: D E B C A.
6
Check: each traversal must list all five nodes exactly once ✓.
Answer. Preorder A B D E C, inorder D B A E C, postorder D E B C A.
◆ WHERE PEOPLE SLIP

The prefix tells you where the ROOT goes: pre = first, in = middle, post = last. On a binary search tree, inorder always comes out in sorted order — a fact exams lean on.

Example 4 — Minimum spanning tree (Kruskal)
Problem. A weighted graph on {A,B,C,D} has edges AB = 1, BC = 2, AC = 3, CD = 4, BD = 5. Find a minimum spanning tree and its total weight.
1
Kruskal: sort every edge by weight, then add them cheapest-first, SKIPPING any edge that would close a cycle. Stop at n − 1 edges.
2
With 4 vertices we need exactly 4 − 1 = 3 edges.
3
Sorted: AB(1), BC(2), AC(3), CD(4), BD(5).
4
Take AB(1) — no cycle, keep it. Take BC(2) — connects a new vertex C, keep it. Running total 3.
5
Next AC(3): A and C are ALREADY connected through B, so this would close a cycle. Skip it.
6
Next CD(4): D is still unconnected, so keep it. That is our third edge — stop. Total = 1 + 2 + 4 = 7.
Answer. MST = {AB, BC, CD} with total weight 7.
◆ WHERE PEOPLE SLIP

The greedy choice is only rejected when it would form a cycle — that cycle check is the whole algorithm. Taking AC just because it is cheaper than CD gives a wrong, cyclic answer.

Example 5 — Are two graphs isomorphic?
Problem. Graph G has 5 vertices with degrees 2, 2, 2, 3, 3. Graph H has 5 vertices with degrees 1, 2, 2, 3, 4. Can they be isomorphic?
1
Isomorphic means the same structure under a renaming of vertices, so every structural quantity must match.
2
Check the cheap invariants first: both have 5 vertices ✓.
3
Edge counts, via handshake: G has (2+2+2+3+3)/2 = 12/2 = 6 edges. H has (1+2+2+3+4)/2 = 12/2 = 6 edges ✓ — still no contradiction.
4
Now compare the degree SEQUENCES, sorted: G gives (2,2,2,3,3) and H gives (1,2,2,3,4).
5
These differ — H contains a degree-4 vertex and G has none. No renaming can change a vertex degree.
6
So the graphs are not isomorphic.
Answer. Not isomorphic — their degree sequences differ.
◆ WHERE PEOPLE SLIP

Matching degree sequences do NOT prove isomorphism; they only fail to disprove it. The test is one-directional: different sequences settle the question, identical ones mean keep looking.

Example 6 — Walk, trail, path, circuit or cycle?
Problem. G has vertices {a, b, c, d} and edges ab, bc, cd, da, ac. Classify each sequence: (i) a–b–c–a–d (ii) a–b–c–a (iii) a–c–b.
1
Definitions in one line each: a WALK allows any repeats; a TRAIL repeats no EDGE; a PATH repeats no VERTEX; a CIRCUIT is a closed trail; a CYCLE is a closed walk repeating no vertex except the endpoints.
2
(i) a–b–c–a–d uses edges ab, bc, ca, ad — all exist, so it is a walk; all four edges are distinct, so it is a trail. But vertex a appears twice, so NOT a path, and it starts at a while ending at d, so it is not closed — not a circuit.
3
(ii) a–b–c–a uses ab, bc, ca, all distinct — a trail; it is closed (starts and ends at a), so a circuit; and no vertex repeats except the endpoint pair, so it is also a cycle of length 3.
4
(iii) a–c–b uses ac, cb — both exist, no repeated vertex, not closed: a path of length 2.
Answer. (i) walk and trail only · (ii) circuit AND cycle (length 3) · (iii) path.
◆ WHERE PEOPLE SLIP

Trail vs path is the money distinction: trails forbid repeated EDGES, paths forbid repeated VERTICES. Sequence (i) is the exam’s favourite — a legitimate trail that fails to be a path.

Example 7 — Counting walks with A²
Problem. Same graph G (edges ab, bc, cd, da, ac). Using the adjacency matrix, count the walks of length 2 from a to c, and explain the diagonal of A².
1
Order the vertices a, b, c, d and write the adjacency matrix:
abcd
a0111
b1010
c1101
d1010
2
The rule: entry (i, j) of Ak counts the walks of length k from i to j. For length 2, compute the (a, c) entry of A² — that is row a of A dotted with column c: (0)(1) + (1)(1) + (1)(0) + (1)(1) = 2.
3
Name the two walks to see it is right: a–b–c and a–d–c. (a–c alone has length 1, so it does not count here.)
4
The diagonal: the (a, a) entry of A² is (0)² + 1² + 1² + 1² = 3 — each length-2 walk a→x→a is just “out along an edge and straight back”, one per neighbour. So the diagonal of A² lists each vertex’s DEGREE: deg(a) = 3 ✓.
Answer. (A²)a,c = 2 — the walks a–b–c and a–d–c. The diagonal of A² gives vertex degrees.
◆ WHERE PEOPLE SLIP

A² counts WALKS, not paths: for longer powers, walks may re-use vertices freely. And expecting the diagonal to be 0 (“you can’t go a to a in 2 steps”) forgets out-and-back walks.

Example 8 — Components, isolated vertices and bridges
Problem. H has vertices {1, …, 7} and edges 12, 23, 13, 45, 56. Find the connected components, identify every bridge, and give the minimum number of NEW edges that would make H connected.
1
March through the vertices, growing each component: from 1 you can reach 2 and 3 (and 13 closes the triangle) → component {1, 2, 3}. From 4: 4–5–6 → component {4, 5, 6}. Vertex 7 touches no edge → component {7}, all by itself.
2
Three components: {1,2,3}, {4,5,6}, {7}. An isolated vertex IS a component — it counts.
3
Bridges are edges whose removal splits a component. In the triangle {1,2,3}, remove any one edge and the other two still connect everything — no bridges there. In the path 4–5–6, removing 45 strands vertex 4, removing 56 strands vertex 6 — BOTH are bridges.
4
To connect k components you need at least k − 1 new edges (each new edge can merge at most two components). Here k = 3, so 2 edges suffice — for example 3–4 and 6–7.
Answer. Components: {1,2,3}, {4,5,6}, {7} — three of them. Bridges: 45 and 56 (the triangle has none). Minimum new edges to connect H: 2.
◆ WHERE PEOPLE SLIP

The isolated vertex is the mark-loser: it has no edges, so it is easy to skip when counting components. Count components off the VERTEX list, not the edge list.

🏗️ Class vs Object

THE BLUEPRINT MODEL
A class is a blueprint — describes what something is and can do, but isn't a real thing yet. An object is an actual thing built from it. One "House" blueprint; many actual houses. One Car class; many car objects, each with its own color and mileage.
TermDefinition
FieldsThe data each object holds (instance variables / attributes)
MethodsThe actions / behaviors
InstantiationCar myCar = new Car(); — the new keyword builds one object
ConstructorSpecial method named like the class — sets a new object's starting values
EACH OBJECT IS SEPARATE
Each object is its own instance with its own copy of the fields — changing myCar's color doesn't touch yourCar.
⚠️ THE CLASS ISN'T AN OBJECT
The class is written ONCE; objects are made MANY times at runtime. The class is the recipe, not the dish.
🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK

  1. An instance of a class
  2. A blueprint
  3. A method
  4. A data type keyword
Show answer + steps

📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)

Class vs object

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

This is the mental leap that makes all of OOP click. A class is a blueprint — it describes what something is and can do, but isn't a real thing yet. An object is an actual thing built from that blueprint. One “House” blueprint; many actual houses. One Car class; many individual car objects, each with its own color and mileage.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

A class defines fields (the data each object holds — color, speed) and methods (the actions — accelerate). Writing Car myCar = new Car(); uses the new keyword to build (“instantiate”) one object.

Each object is a separate instance with its own copy of the fields. Changing myCar's color doesn't touch yourCar. The constructor (a special method named like the class) sets a new object's starting values.

📝 EXAM WORDING

A class is a blueprint/template; an object is an instance of a class. Creating one is instantiation (via new). Fields = instance variables / attributes; methods = the behaviors. The constructor initializes a new object.

⚠️ WATCH OUT

The class is written once; objects are made many times at runtime. Don't say a class “is” an object — it's the recipe for objects.

The four pillars of OOP

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

OOP rests on four big ideas. In one breath: Encapsulation = keep data private and control access. Inheritance = build new classes on existing ones. Polymorphism = one interface, many behaviors. Abstraction = expose the what, hide the how.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Encapsulation: make fields private and expose public getters/setters. The object guards its own data. It's the “capsule” bundling data with the methods that protect it.

Inheritance: a Dog class extends an Animal class, reusing its members and adding its own. “Is-a”: a Dog IS AN Animal.

Polymorphism: the same call behaves differently by object — animal.makeSound() barks for a Dog, meows for a Cat.

Abstraction: hide complex internals behind a simple interface (call .start() without knowing the engine). Done with abstract classes and interfaces.

📝 EXAM WORDING

Memorize by definition: Encapsulation = data hiding / bundling data with methods; Inheritance = a subclass acquiring a superclass's members (“is-a”); Polymorphism = one interface / many implementations; Abstraction = hiding implementation, showing essentials.

⚠️ WATCH OUT

Encapsulation vs abstraction trips people up: encapsulation is “hide the data” (access control), abstraction is “hide the complexity” (simplified interface). Inheritance is “is-a”; a field you simply contain is “has-a” (composition).

📮 Pass-by-Value

THE RULE
Java ALWAYS passes a COPY — never the original variable. Java is strictly pass-by-value; for objects, "the value of the reference is passed."
Passing…What's copiedCan the method change your original?
A primitive (int, double, boolean, char)The VALUENO — changes inside do nothing to the caller
An objectThe REFERENCE (the arrow)The method points at the SAME object, so mutating its contents IS visible
THE TWO OUTCOMES, SIDE BY SIDE
list.add(x) inside a method → visible outside (same object). list = new ArrayList() inside → only repoints the COPY; the caller's list is unchanged. References point to objects on the heap; primitives live on the stack; null is a reference pointing to nothing.
⚠️ THE EXAM TRAP
Java is NEVER pass-by-reference, even for objects. Reassigning a parameter (=) inside a method never affects the caller — only MUTATING the object's contents does.
🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
Java passes method arguments:
  1. Always by value (copies, including reference copies)
  2. By reference for objects
  3. By reference always
  4. It depends on a keyword
Show answer + steps
A. Strictly pass-by-value — the classic trap says otherwise.
📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)

Pass-by-value

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Java always passes a copy to a method — never the original variable. For a plain number, it copies the number, so the method can't change your original. For an object, it copies the reference (the arrow pointing to the object) — so the method points at the SAME object and CAN change its contents. That subtle difference explains a lot of “why did/didn't my value change?” moments.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

For primitives (int, double, boolean, char): the method gets a copy of the value. Changing it inside does nothing to the caller.

For objects: the method gets a copy of the reference — both arrows point to the same object. So list.add(x) inside a method IS visible outside (same object). But list = new ArrayList() inside only repoints the copy — the caller's list is unchanged.

📝 EXAM WORDING

Java is strictly pass-by-value — for objects, “the value of the reference is passed.” A reference points to an object on the heap; primitives live on the stack. null is a reference pointing to nothing.

⚠️ WATCH OUT

Java is never pass-by-reference, even for objects — a common exam trap says it is. Reassigning a parameter (=) inside a method never affects the caller; only mutating the object's contents does.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Things go wrong at runtime — a file's missing, a divide-by-zero, a user types letters where you wanted digits. Exceptions are Java's way to handle those without crashing. You “try” risky code, “catch” the problem if it happens, and optionally “finally” run cleanup no matter what.

📦 Arrays & Zero-Based Indexing

THE RULE THAT CAUSES HALF OF ALL ARRAY BUGS
Arrays are numbered starting at 0. Five items → valid indices 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — there is NO box 5. Last valid index = length − 1.
THE ESSENTIALS
CodeMeans
int[] a = new int[5];5 slots (indices 0–4), auto-filled with 0
a[0]Access by index
a.lengthSize — a FIELD, no parentheses
for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++)The standard loop (or for-each: for (int x : a))
Arrays are FIXED size and one type. Need to grow? Use an ArrayList, which resizes automatically. Out of range throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
⚠️ TWO EXAM FAVORITES
a[n] on a length-n array is the classic off-by-one crash. And it's a.length for arrays (field) but s.length() for Strings (method) — mixed on purpose.

  2. 8

Arrays & zero-based indexing

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

An array is a fixed-size row of boxes, all the same type, numbered starting at 0. If it has 5 items, the valid box numbers are 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — there is no box 5. Half of all array bugs come from forgetting it starts at 0 and ends at length−1.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

int[] a = new int[5]; makes 5 slots (indices 0–4), auto-filled with 0. Access with a[0]; the size is a.length (a field, no parentheses — unlike String's .length() method).

Arrays are fixed size once created. Need to grow? Use an ArrayList, which resizes automatically. Loop with for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) or a for-each for (int x : a).

📝 EXAM WORDING

Arrays are zero-indexed; the last valid index is length − 1. array.length is a field; string.length() is a method. Out of range throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. Arrays hold one type and a fixed size.

⚠️ WATCH OUT

An array of length n has indices 0 to n−1 — accessing a[n] is the classic “off-by-one” crash. And it's a.length for arrays but s.length() for Strings — the exam mixes these on purpose.

Control flow: if, switch & loops

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

By default code runs top to bottom. Control flow lets it branch (do this OR that) and repeat (do this many times). Master the handful of structures and you can express any logic. The bugs live in the boundaries — off-by-one loops and missing breaks.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

if / else if / else: run a block when a condition is true. switch: pick a branch by a value's cases — each case usually needs a break or execution “falls through” to the next.

📝 EXAM WORDING

if/else branches on conditions; switch branches on a value (cases need break or they fall through). for = counted loops, while/do-while = condition loops (do-while runs ≥ once). break exits; continue skips to next iteration.

⚠️ WATCH OUT

A missing break in a switch causes fall-through to the next case — a classic bug the exam tests. And a while may run zero times, but a do-while always runs at least once.

Interfaces vs abstract classes

Both let you define “what a class must be able to do” without fully building it. An interface is a pure contract — a list of method promises. Strings & immutability

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Strings are everywhere, and they have one surprising rule: they're immutable — once created, a String's contents can't change. Every operation that seems to “change” a String actually makes a NEW String. That explains a lot of subtle bugs.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

s.toUpperCase(), s.replace(...), s + "x" all return NEW Strings; the original is untouched. So s.toUpperCase(); alone does nothing unless you assign it: s = s.toUpperCase();.

Strings are immutable — methods return NEW Strings, they don't modify in place. Compare content with .equals(); == compares references (identity), not text. StringBuilder is the mutable alternative for efficient concatenation. Strings are zero-indexed like arrays.

s.trim() or s.toUpperCase() on its own does nothing — you must assign the result. And use .equals() for text comparison; == can be false for two Strings with identical characters.

📖 Learn it step by step — JVM, JRE, JDK (three nested boxes)

WHO IS WHO
• JVM (Java Virtual Machine) — RUNS bytecode. The reason Java is “write once, run anywhere.”
• JRE (Runtime Environment) — JVM + core libraries. Enough to RUN Java programs.
• JDK (Development Kit) — JRE + compiler (javac) + tools. Needed to WRITE Java.
Nesting: JDK ⊃ JRE ⊃ JVM.
WORKED EXAMPLE — follow Hello.java to the screen
javac Hello.java   →  Hello.class   (compiler produces BYTECODE)
java Hello         →  JVM loads Hello.class and executes it
Bytecode is not machine code for your CPU — it’s a universal format any JVM understands, so the same .class runs on Windows, Mac, Linux. Users installing your app need the JRE; you developing it need the JDK.
⚠️ COMPILED *AND* INTERPRETED
Java compiles source → bytecode (compile step), then the JVM executes bytecode (with JIT compiling hot code as it runs). If asked “what does javac produce?” — bytecode (.class), never machine code.
🎯 QUICK CHECK
Which do you need to COMPILE Java source code?
  1. JDK
  2. JRE only
  3. JVM only
Show answer
A — the JDK; it contains javac. JRE/JVM can only run already-compiled bytecode.
📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

"Write once, run anywhere" is Java's promise — made possible by compiling to bytecode that the JVM executes on any platform. Understanding JVM/JRE/JDK determines what you install, what you ship, and why Java can run on billions of devices from smartphones to servers.

Why bytecode = portability

C++ compiles to machine code for ONE cpu/OS. Java compiles to bytecode — a universal intermediate language. Each platform has its own JVM that translates bytecode to local machine code (with JIT compiling hot paths for speed). Same .class file runs on Windows, Mac, Linux, Android. That's "write once, run anywhere."

The JDK contains the JRE, which contains the JVM. You need the JDK to write Java and the JRE to run it.

🔬 GOING DEEPER — how Java actually runs — and why it is portable

The two-step translation

Most languages compile straight to machine code for one processor. Java does something different, and every "write once, run anywhere" question depends on it. javac compiles your .java source into bytecode (a .class file) — instructions for an imaginary machine, not for any real CPU. At run time the JVM reads that bytecode and executes it on the actual hardware.

So the bytecode is portable and the JVM is platform-specific. You ship one .class file; Windows, macOS and Linux each supply their own JVM. Java is therefore both compiled and interpreted — a statement that sounds contradictory until you see the two stages.

JDK ⊃ JRE ⊃ JVM

These nest, which is the whole exam question:

  • JVM — executes bytecode. Nothing else.
  • JRE = JVM + the standard class libraries. Enough to run a Java program.
  • JDK = JRE + development tools (javac, debugger, docs). Enough to write one.

Practical test: a user only running an app needs the JRE; you, writing code, need the JDK. If javac is missing, you have a JRE, not a JDK.

What the JVM does while running

It does not merely interpret. The JIT compiler notices hot code paths and compiles them to native machine code on the fly, which is why long-running Java approaches native speed. The JVM also performs garbage collection — reclaiming objects nothing references any more — so you never free memory manually. You cannot force collection; System.gc() is only a suggestion.

Decoding the main method

public static void main(String[] args) — every word is required and each is asked about:

  • public — the JVM, outside your class, must be able to call it.
  • static — it runs before any object exists, so it cannot belong to an instance.
  • void — nothing is returned to the JVM.
  • String[] args — command-line arguments.

How this connects

The compile-vs-interpret distinction is the same one from Intro to CS, applied concretely. static here previews static members in Unit 3, and garbage collection explains why Java has no destructors and why memory leaks take the form of forgotten references.

Identifiers & Scientific Notation (zyBooks 2.3, 2.8)

Identifier rules: a legal Java identifier starts with a letter, underscore _, or dollar sign $ — never a digit — and may then contain letters, digits, _ and $. 💡 Exam power-ups: types & casting

Mnemonic: “Small fits in big for free” — widening (int→double) is automatic; narrowing (double→int) needs an explicit cast and TRUNCATES (no rounding): (int)9.99 is 9. int/int stays int: 5/2 is 2, but 5/2.0 is 2.5. Strategy: on every output question, first scan for integer division and mixed types — they are the two most-planted traps.

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Integer division truncates (drops the fraction): 7 / 2 is 3, not 3.5. Mixing an int with a double promotes the result to double. Widening (int→double) is automatic; narrowing (double→int) needs an explicit cast and truncates. A char is a numeric (Unicode) type, so (int)'A' is 65.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
int x = 5, y = 2;
System.out.println(x / y);              // int / int
System.out.println((double) x / y);     // promoted

Output: 2 2.5

x / y is int division → 2. Casting one operand to double forces floating-point division → 2.5. The cast binds to x before the division.

Eight primitives, and why the size matters

TypeSizeHolds
byte / short / int / long1 / 2 / 4 / 8 bytesWhole numbers, exact

int spans about ±2.1 billion; exceed it and the value wraps silently rather than erroring. long literals need an L suffix (10000000000L) and float literals an f, because Java defaults whole numbers to int and decimals to double.

Widening vs narrowing

Widening (int → long → float → double) happens automatically: the target holds everything the source could. Narrowing loses information, so the compiler refuses unless you write an explicit cast — and the cast truncates toward zero rather than rounding: (int) 9.99 is 9. That cast is you telling the compiler "I accept the loss."

The two arithmetic traps

Integer division: if both operands are integers the result is an integer — 5 / 2 is 2, not 2.5. Fix by making one side floating point: 5 / 2.0 or (double) a / b. This silently ruins averages and percentages and appears on nearly every Java exam.

Floating-point precision: 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3, because those fractions have no exact binary form. Never compare doubles with ==, and never store money in a double — use BigDecimal or whole cents in an int.

char is a number in disguise

char c = 'A' stores 65. So c + 1 is 66, and (char)(c + 1) is 'B'. This is what lets you loop through the alphabet or convert case by arithmetic.

Primitives vs wrappers

Each primitive has an object wrapper (int → Integer). Collections hold objects only, so Java autoboxes between them. Two consequences: an uninitialized Integer is null (unboxing it throws a NullPointerException), and == on wrappers compares references — use .equals().

Precedence and the compound-assignment shortcut

Multiplication and division bind before addition and subtraction; parentheses override. One genuinely useful oddity: compound assignment performs an implicit cast. byte b = 10; b += 5; compiles, but b = b + 5; does not — because b + 5 promotes to int, and assigning an int to a byte is narrowing. += quietly inserts the cast for you.

Why String immutability matters

A String can never be changed after creation. Every operation that appears to modify one actually creates a new object: s.concat("!") and s.toUpperCase() return new Strings and leave s untouched. If you write s.concat("!"); without assigning the result, nothing happens — a classic trick question.

Consequences worth knowing: string literals are cached in the string pool and reused, which is why == sometimes appears to work; and building a string in a loop with + creates a new object every iteration, so use StringBuilder (which IS mutable) for that.

== versus .equals() — the single most-tested Java trap

== compares references (are these the same object?). .equals() compares contents. Two Strings built at run time can hold identical text yet fail ==. Always compare Strings with .equals() (or .equalsIgnoreCase()).

String methods, with their gotchas

  • length() — a method on String, but length is a field on arrays. Both appear on exams.
  • charAt(i) — zero-based; charAt(length()) throws.
  • substring(begin, end) — end is exclusive, so "Hello".substring(1,3) is "el".
  • indexOf(x) — returns −1 when not found, not 0.

The Scanner newline problem

nextInt() consumes the number but leaves the newline in the buffer, so the following nextLine() returns an empty string instead of waiting for input. The fix is an extra nextLine() to swallow the leftover newline. This is the most common Scanner bug and a favourite exam scenario.

🔬 GOING DEEPER — branching — conditions, switch and the fall-through rule

Conditions must be boolean

Java will not accept a number where a boolean belongs — if (x) is a compile error unless x is a boolean. This deliberately blocks the C-style bug where if (x = 5) assigns instead of comparing. In Java that mistake only compiles when the variable is boolean, so the language catches most of it for you.

if / else-if chains

Conditions are tested top to bottom and the first true branch wins; everything after it is skipped. Grade-boundary questions rely on this: with score = 85, testing >= 90 then >= 80 prints the second branch and never evaluates the rest. Order your conditions from most to least restrictive, or a broad condition will swallow the narrow ones.

Without braces, an else binds to the nearest unmatched if — which is why the "dangling else" produces behavior that contradicts the indentation. Always use braces.

switch and the break you must not forget

switch compares one variable against discrete constant values. It works with int, char, String and enums — not with ranges or boolean expressions, so case x > 5: is invalid.

The defining behavior is fall-through: once a case matches, execution continues into the following cases until it hits a break. Omit the break and you run several cases — usually a bug, but occasionally deliberate when several values share an action (stacked cases with one body).

Short-circuit evaluation as a tool

&& stops at the first false, || at the first true. Use this to guard: if (s != null && s.length() > 0) can never throw a NullPointerException, because the right side is skipped when the left is false. Reversing the order breaks it. Order is a correctness concern here, not style.

The ternary

result = condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse; is an expression, so it produces a value — unlike an if statement. Good for a single simple choice, unreadable when nested.

📘 Deep dive: while vs do-while, traced

The difference that matters: while checks BEFORE running (may run zero times); do-while checks AFTER (always runs at least once). Mnemonic: do it first, ask later.

Worked trace: int n = 0; while (n > 0) { n--; } — the body never runs, n stays 0. But int n = 0; do { n--; } while (n > 0); runs once — n becomes −1, then the check fails.

Sentinel loop: keep reading until a special value: while (!input.equals("quit")) { … } — the classic event-controlled pattern.

Infinite-loop traps the OA plants: never updating the loop variable in the body, or moving it the wrong direction. If nothing pushes the condition toward false, the loop never ends.

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

A while checks the condition before the body (may run 0 times); a do-while checks after, so it always runs at least once. If the condition never becomes false you get an infinite loop. The loop variable's scope is limited to the loop when declared in it.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
int i = 5;
while (i < 5) { System.out.print("W"); }
do   { System.out.print("D"); } while (i < 5);

Output: D

The while body never runs (5 < 5 is false). The do-while runs once before testing, printing one "D".

🔬 GOING DEEPER — while and do-while — loops that run an unknown number of times

The distinction that decides which to use

while tests before the body, so it can run zero times. do-while tests after, so it always runs at least once. Match this to the scenario: validating input you already have → while; showing a menu then asking whether to repeat → do-while. Note the syntax detail — a do-while ends with a semicolon after the condition.

Sentinel-controlled loops

When you cannot know the iteration count up front you loop until a signal value arrives: read until the user types quit or a reader returns null. The pattern is: read once before the loop, test, then read again at the end of the body. Getting that order wrong either skips the first value or processes the sentinel itself.

Why loops hang

An infinite loop almost always means the condition variable is never updated inside the body, or is updated in a way that can never satisfy the exit test (decrementing when the condition waits for an increase). When tracing, always ask: what changes each pass, and does it move toward the exit?

break and continue

break leaves the loop entirely; continue skips the rest of this pass and jumps to the next test. A frequent bug: using continue in a while loop before the update statement, which skips the update and hangs the program. In a for loop the update still runs, so continue is safer there.

Loop variable scope

A variable declared inside the loop body is destroyed each pass and cannot be read afterwards. Any accumulator — a running total, a counter, a best-so-far — must be declared before the loop, or it resets every iteration.

📖 Learn it step by step — for Loops, break & continue

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — the for anatomy, traced
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    System.out.print(i + " ");
}   // output: 0 1 2
Order of events: init (i=0) → test (0<3 ✓) → body → update (i++) → test → … Runs while the test holds: prints 0 1 2 and stops when i reaches 3. “i <= 3” would print 0 1 2 3 — off-by-one lives in that one character.
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — break vs continue
for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
    if (i == 3) continue;   // skip JUST this pass
    if (i == 5) break;      // exit the loop entirely
    System.out.print(i + " ");
}
i=1 → 1; i=2 → 2; i=3 → continue (nothing); i=4 → 4; i=5 → break. Output: 1 2 4. continue skips one iteration; break abandons the loop.

A loop of n passes inside a loop of m passes runs the inner body m·n times: two nested 1-to-10 loops → 100 executions. break only exits the INNER loop it lives in.

📘 Deep dive: nested loop tracing

Count the prints: for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) for (int j = 1; j <= 4; j++) print("*"); → the inner loop runs fully for EACH outer pass: 3 × 4 = 12 stars. Multiply the trip counts.

Dependent bounds: for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) for (int j = 1; j <= i; j++) print(i); → prints 1 once, 2 twice, 3 three times: 122333 (1+2+3 = 6 outputs).

break vs continue: break exits the ENTIRE current loop; continue skips to the next iteration check. In nested loops each affects only the INNERMOST loop containing it.

OA strategy: write the (i, j) pairs as a small grid before answering — 30 seconds of grid beats a guess.

Exam focus: for-loop mechanics Java tests

When a loop terminates: for(int i=10; i>=1; i--) runs while the condition is true and terminates when the condition becomes false — here when i reaches 0. Loop-variable scope: a variable declared in the header, like int i, is local to the loop; it does not exist after the loop ends. Off-by-one: for(int i=0; i<=arr.length; i++) arr[i] uses <=, so the last access is arr[arr.length] — one past the end — which throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException at runtime (it compiles fine). The safe condition is i < arr.length.

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

for (init; condition; update) — count the iterations carefully. break exits the whole loop; continue skips the rest of the current iteration and jumps to the update. The enhanced for (for (int x : arr)) reads elements but can’t modify the array’s structure.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE

  if (i == 3) break;

}

🔬 GOING DEEPER — for loops, for-each and nesting

The four parts, and their scope

for (init; condition; update) packages the three loop controls on one line, which is why it fits any counted repetition. A variable declared in the init section exists only inside the loop — if you need the final value afterwards, declare it outside.

The standard array traversal is for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++). Note <, not <=: valid indexes stop at length − 1, so <= throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException on the last pass. Note also length with no parentheses — arrays expose a field, Strings a method.

The enhanced for (for-each)

for (String name : names) reads far better when you simply need every element. Its limits are exactly what exams probe:

  • There is no index — if you need the position, use a classic for loop.
  • The loop variable is a copy of the element for primitives, so assigning to it does not change the array.
  • You cannot iterate backwards or skip elements.
  • Structurally modifying a collection while for-eaching it (adding or removing) throws ConcurrentModificationException. Use an explicit iterator, or collect changes and apply them afterwards.

Nested loops

Nesting multiplies: an outer loop of 3 around an inner loop of 4 executes the inner body 12 times. This is how you walk a 2D array (outer = rows, inner = columns) and it is where O(n²) comes from — the practical reason a routine that is fine with 100 items crawls with 10,000.

A plain break exits only the innermost loop. To leave both you need a labeled break or a flag variable — another favourite trace question.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Classes and objects are the fundamental units of Java programs. Every Spring controller, JPA entity, and Android activity is a class. Understanding constructors, the this keyword, and object creation with new is the foundation for every OOP course that follows D286.

Class and Object

public class Car {
    // Fields (instance variables)
    private String make;
    private int year;

    // Constructor
    public Car(String make, int year) {
        this.make = make;    // 'this.make' = field; 'make' = parameter
        this.year = year;
    }

    // Instance method
    public String describe() {
        return year + " " + make;
    }
}

// Creating objects:
Car c1 = new Car("Toyota", 2022);  // new calls the constructor
System.out.println(c1.describe()); // "2022 Toyota"

The this Keyword

this refers to the current object. Required when a constructor/method parameter has the same name as a field:

// Without this: BOTH refer to the parameter (field never set!)
name = name;           // BUG: assigns parameter to itself
// With this: unambiguous
this.name = name;      // CORRECT: field = parameter

Constructor Chaining

public Car() {
    this("Unknown", 2000);  // calls Car(String, int) — must be first line
}
✓ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Class = blueprint. Object = instance created with new.
  • Constructor: same name as class, no return type
  • this = current object; use to disambiguate fields from parameters
  • this() calls another constructor in same class (must be first line)

Objects are references — the mental model that fixes everything

Dog d1 = new Dog("Rex");
Dog d2 = d1;                 // copies the REFERENCE, not the dog!
d2.name = "Buddy";
System.out.println(d1.name); // Buddy — both variables point at ONE object

Dog d3 = null;               // reference to nothing
d3.bark();                   // NullPointerException at runtime

Primitives copy VALUES; objects copy REFERENCES (arrows to the same heap object). Half of all OA object questions reduce to "how many actual objects exist, and who points where?" — draw arrows on scratch paper.

Constructors — the rules that get tested

public class Student {
    String name;
    int age;

    public Student() {                 // no-arg constructor
        this("Unknown", 0);             // constructor chaining — MUST be line 1
    }
    public Student(String name, int age) {
        this.name = name;               // this.name = field, name = parameter
        this.age = age;
    }
}

Student s = new Student("Natasha", 30);

Rule 2Write NO constructor → Java gives a free default no-arg one
Rule 3Write ANY constructor → the free default DISAPPEARS (new Student() breaks unless you add it back)

Methods: pass-by-value, always

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance created with new. A constructor has the same name as the class and no return type (not even void). If you write no constructor, Java supplies a default no-arg one — but adding any constructor removes that default. this refers to the current object.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
class Dog {
  String name;
  Dog(String n) { this.name = n; }
}
Dog d = new Dog("Rex");
System.out.println(d.name);

Output: Rex

new Dog("Rex") calls the constructor, which assigns the parameter to the object’s field via this.name.

🔬 GOING DEEPER — classes, objects and the rules of constructors

Reference variables and the heap

Dog d = new Dog(); does three things: new allocates the object on the heap, the constructor initializes it, and d stores a reference to it — not the object itself. That distinction explains the rest of Java:

  • Two variables can reference one object, so a change through either is visible to both.
  • == on objects compares references, not contents.
  • An uninitialized reference is null, and calling a method on it throws a NullPointerException.

Constructor rules

A constructor has the same name as the class and no return type — not even void. Writing void Dog() silently creates an ordinary method, and the compiler then supplies a default constructor; code that looked fine fails mysteriously.

The critical rule: Java gives you a no-argument default constructor only if you define no constructor at all. The moment you write Dog(String name), the free default disappears and new Dog() stops compiling. If you need both, declare both.

Overloading and this()

Several constructors may differ by parameter list. To avoid duplicating setup, one can call another with this(...) — which must be the first statement in the constructor. Inside an instance method or constructor, this refers to the current object, which is what disambiguates this.name = name when a parameter shadows a field. Without this., that line assigns the parameter to itself and the field stays null — a classic silent bug.

Initialization order

Fields receive their default values first (0, 0.0, false, null), then explicit initializers run, then the constructor body. This is why an object is never in a garbage state, and why forgetting to set a field leaves it null rather than undefined.

📖 Learn it step by step — Encapsulation & Access Modifiers

THE MODIFIERS
• private — visible only inside the class (the default choice for fields).
• public — visible everywhere (the usual choice for methods).
• protected — class + subclasses + same package.
• (no modifier) — package-private: same package only.
WORKED EXAMPLE — a getter/setter that actually protects
public class Account {
    private double balance;                 // hidden from outside

    public double getBalance() { return balance; }

    public void deposit(double amt) {
        if (amt > 0) balance += amt;      // the setter can VALIDATE
    }
}
Outside code cannot write account.balance = -1000; — it doesn’t compile (private). It must go through deposit(), which refuses bad amounts. THAT is the point of encapsulation: the class guards its own data.
⚠️ “WHY PRIVATE FIELDS?” — THE EXPECTED ANSWER
Not secrecy for its own sake: private fields + public methods let the class enforce rules, change internals without breaking callers, and keep invalid states impossible. If an option says “control access / protect data integrity,” that’s the one.
🎯 QUICK CHECK

  1. private, with public getters/setters as needed
  2. public, for convenience
  3. protected, always
Show answer

The encapsulation pattern — private fields, public methods

public class BankAccount {
    private double balance;                  // hidden from outside

    public double getBalance() {            // read access — controlled
        return balance;
    }
    public void deposit(double amount) {     // write access — WITH RULES
        if (amount > 0) balance += amount;   // validation lives here
    }
    public void withdraw(double amount) {
        if (amount > 0 && amount <= balance) balance -= amount;
    }

acct.deposit(-50);          // silently rejected by validation ✓

Why bother? Without encapsulation, every part of a program can corrupt every field — a negative balance, an age of -5. With it, the class GUARDS its own data: one place to validate, one place to change later (switch balance to cents? only this class changes). This "data hiding" is the first pillar of OOP and a guaranteed OA topic.

💡 Exam power-ups: encapsulation

Mnemonic: “private fields, public gates” — data private, access through getters/setters. Access order from open to closed: public → protected → (default/package) → private. Real world: an ATM shows buttons, not the vault — that interface/implementation split is encapsulation. Strategy: if an answer choice exposes a public field, it is almost never the “best practice” answer.

🧠 MEMORY AID

Access modifiers, widest → narrowest: public (everywhere) > protected (package + subclasses) > default/package-private (same package) > private (same class only). Encapsulation = keep fields private and expose them through public getters/setters.

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Encapsulation = private fields + public getters/setters. Access, widest→narrowest: public → protected → default/package → private. A private member is visible only inside its own class; setters let you validate before assigning.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
class Account {
  private double balance;
  public double getBalance() { return balance; }
  public void deposit(double a) { if (a > 0) balance += a; }
}

Output: balance is protected from invalid writes

The field is private, so outside code must go through deposit/getBalance; deposit rejects non-positive amounts, protecting the invariant.

🔬 GOING DEEPER — encapsulation and what each access modifier actually allows

The four levels

Two details that get tested: default has no keyword — you get it by writing nothing — and protected also grants package access, so it is broader than "subclasses only."

What encapsulation actually buys

Private fields plus public methods is not ceremony. A setter is a gate: setAge() can reject a negative value, so the object can never hold an impossible state. A public field accepts anything, and every caller becomes a place the invariant can break.

The second payoff is freedom to change. If a class stores a full name internally but exposes getFirstName(), the team can later split it into two fields and no calling code changes. Public fields would have frozen the internal design permanently.

Encapsulation vs abstraction

Constantly confused, so hold the distinction: abstraction is deciding what to expose (the public interface); encapsulation is the enforcement — private fields and accessor methods — that keeps the rest hidden. Abstraction is the design decision; encapsulation is the mechanism that makes it stick.

A subtle leak

Returning a mutable object from a getter hands the caller a reference to your internals, so they can modify your state without going through your setter. Returning a copy is the defensive fix — a favourite "why is this still broken?" question.

📖 Learn it step by step — static Members & Method Overloading

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — static = shared by the CLASS
public class Counter {
    static int total = 0;    // ONE copy for the whole class
    int mine = 0;            // one copy PER OBJECT

    Counter() { total++; mine++; }
}
new Counter(); new Counter(); new Counter();
System.out.println(Counter.total);   // 3  (shared count)
Each new object bumped the SAME total. Meanwhile every object’s mine is just 1. static belongs to the class (access via Counter.total); instance fields belong to each object.
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — overloading = same name, different parameters
int    max(int a, int b)       { ... }
double max(double a, double b) { ... }
int    max(int a, int b, int c){ ... }
Three methods named max, distinguished by their parameter lists. The compiler picks by the arguments: max(2, 9) → the int version. Return type ALONE cannot distinguish overloads.

main() is static — it runs with NO object existing, so it cannot directly use instance variables (“non-static variable referenced from static context”). That compiler error is quoted verbatim on exams.

public class Demo {

void show(int x)    { System.out.println("int"); }

public class App {

Unit Testing Your Methods (zyBooks 6.x)

Unit testing means verifying one method at a time with test cases: call the method with known inputs, compare the actual returned value against the expected value, and report a failure when they differ. A simple test harness is a main() that runs several assertions. Choose normal cases plus border cases (0, negative numbers, empty strings, the largest value) — border cases are where bugs hide. Testing methods in isolation catches errors before they spread into the larger program.

Exam focus: scope of a variable declared inside a loop body

A variable declared inside a for-loop body is accessible only within that loop body, and it is re-created on every iteration. It is not visible after the loop, in the enclosing method, or anywhere else. Java scope rule: a local variable lives only inside the innermost braces { } where it is declared.

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

static members belong to the class, not an instance — call them via the class name and note they cannot directly access instance (non-static) fields. Overloading = same method name, different parameter lists, resolved at compile time by the argument types.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
static void f(int x)    { System.out.print("int"); }
static void f(double x) { System.out.print("double"); }
f(5);
f(5.0);

Output: intdouble

f(5) matches the int overload exactly; f(5.0) matches double. The compiler picks the best match from the literal’s type.

🔬 GOING DEEPER — static members and overloading resolution

static means "belongs to the class"

A static field exists once, shared by every instance and even when no instance exists. An instance field exists once per object. So a static counter incremented in a constructor counts how many objects were ever created — the standard demonstration.

Static members are accessed through the class: Math.max(), ClassName.method(). This is why main is static — the JVM must call it before any object exists.

The rule that causes the compile error

A static method cannot use this, nor call instance methods or read instance fields directly — there is no particular object for them to belong to. The reverse is fine: an instance method may freely use static members. "Non-static variable cannot be referenced from a static context" always means you tried to use instance state from a static method.

Constants

static final is the idiom for a constant: one shared copy (static) that cannot be reassigned (final), conventionally named in capitals. It documents intent and centralizes change.

Overloading — and how Java picks

Overloaded methods share a name but differ in parameter list (count, types or order). The return type alone is not enough — two methods differing only in return type will not compile, because a call like doThing(5) would be ambiguous.

Resolution happens at compile time from the declared argument types. Contrast this with overriding, resolved at run time from the object's actual type. That single sentence separates the two concepts the exam most likes to confuse:

  • Overloading — same class, same name, different parameters, compile-time.
  • Overriding — subclass, same name, same parameters, run-time.

What an array actually is

An array is a fixed-size, contiguous block of same-typed slots. Two consequences follow from "contiguous": access by index is instant (the machine computes base + index × size), and the size can never change after creation. "Resizing" an array really means allocating a new one and copying — which is exactly what ArrayList does for you internally.

Declaration and defaults

int[] nums = new int[5]; creates five slots already initialized to the type default — 0 for numbers, false for boolean, null for objects. That last one matters: String[] names = new String[3]; holds three nulls, so calling a method on names[0] throws a NullPointerException even though the array itself exists.

The index rules that generate exam questions

  • Indexes run 0 to length − 1. An array of length 5 has no index 5 — arr[5] throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
  • arr.length is a field, no parentheses; str.length() is a method. Mixing them is a compile error and a deliberate exam trap.
  • The last element is always arr[arr.length - 1].
  • Loop with i < arr.length, never <=.

Arrays are objects

An array variable holds a reference. So passing an array to a method passes a copy of the reference — both names point at the same array, and changes made inside the method are visible to the caller. This is the clearest illustration of Java's pass-by-value-of-a-reference rule: mutating the contents is visible, but reassigning the parameter to a new array is not.

Likewise arr2 = arr1 does not copy the array — it creates a second reference to the same one. Use Arrays.copyOf() or clone() for a real copy, and compare contents with Arrays.equals(), since == only compares references.

A try with multiple catch blocks is checked top-down; the first matching block runs and the rest are skipped. Order matters: a subclass exception (like FileNotFoundException) must appear before its superclass (IOException) — putting the superclass first makes the later block unreachable, which is a compile error.

🧠 MEMORY AID

Checked vs Unchecked exceptions: Checked = the Compiler forces you to handle or declare it (IOException, SQLException). Unchecked = RuntimeException subclasses (NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException). Flow: try → catch → finally, and finally runs whether or not an exception was thrown.

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Checked exceptions are compiler-enforced (you must catch or declare them): IOException, SQLException, FileNotFoundException. Unchecked = RuntimeException subclasses: NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, ArithmeticException. Order matters: catch specific before general. finally always runs.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE

  int x = 1 / 0;
} catch (ArithmeticException e) {
  System.out.print("caught");
} finally {
  System.out.print("done");
}

1/0 throws ArithmeticException → the catch prints "caught"; then finally runs no matter what, printing "done".

🔬 GOING DEEPER — exceptions — checked, unchecked and the order of catch blocks

What an exception is

An exception is an object describing a failure. When one is thrown, normal flow stops and the JVM unwinds the call stack looking for a matching catch; if none exists the program terminates and prints a stack trace. The stack trace is a debugging gift: it names the exception, the message, and the exact line and call chain.

Checked vs unchecked — the distinction that decides your code

  • Checked (IOException, FileNotFoundException, SQLException) — conditions outside your control. The compiler forces you to either catch them or declare throws. Refusing is a compile error.
  • Unchecked (NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, ArithmeticException, NumberFormatException) — programming bugs, subclasses of RuntimeException. The compiler does not force handling, because the right fix is usually to correct the logic, not to catch it.

Scenario test: "the compiler will not let this compile until the exception is handled" ⟹ checked.

try / catch / finally

try holds the risky code; catch handles a matching type; finally runs whether or not an exception occurred — even after a return — which makes it the place for cleanup such as closing resources. (Better still, try-with-resources closes them automatically.)

Catch order is a compile-time rule

Catch blocks are tested top to bottom, so they must run most specific first. Putting catch (Exception e) above catch (IOException e) makes the second unreachable, and Java rejects it as a compile error rather than a warning. This ordering question appears on nearly every Java exam.

throw vs throws

throw is a statement that raises an exception right now (throw new IllegalArgumentException("...")). throws is a clause in a method signature declaring what that method might raise, passing responsibility to the caller. One letter, entirely different jobs.

What not to do

An empty catch block swallows the failure and leaves the program running on bad state — the hardest kind of bug to trace. Catch what you can genuinely handle; otherwise let it propagate to someone who can.

UML (Unified Modeling Language) draws each class as a box with three parts: the class name, the fields, and the methods. A + marks public members and a - marks private members. ★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

A subclass uses extends to inherit (Java has single class inheritance). A subclass constructor implicitly calls the parent’s no-arg constructor (super()) first; use super(args) to pick a specific parent constructor and super.method() to call the parent’s version.

🔬 GOING DEEPER — inheritance — what is inherited, and constructor chaining

IS-A, and what actually gets inherited

class Dog extends Animal declares Dog IS-A Animal. Dog inherits Animal's accessible fields and methods and may add its own. It does not inherit constructors, and it cannot see Animal's private members directly — that is what protected or a public getter is for.

Java has single inheritance for classes: one direct superclass, no more. Multiple inheritance of type comes from interfaces, which sidesteps the ambiguity of inheriting two competing implementations. Every class ultimately extends Object, which is where toString(), equals() and hashCode() come from.

Constructor chaining — the rule behind confusing errors

A subclass constructor always runs its superclass constructor first, so the inherited part is initialized before the subclass touches it. If you do not call super(...) explicitly, Java silently inserts super() — the no-argument version.

That implicit call is the source of a classic compile error: if the parent defines only Animal(String name) and no no-arg constructor, the invisible super() has nothing to call and compilation fails. The fix is an explicit super(name) — which, like this(...), must be the first statement in the constructor.

super as a keyword

Beyond constructors, super.method() calls the parent's version — used when an override wants to extend rather than replace behavior: do the parent's work, then add your own. super.field reaches a shadowed parent field.

When NOT to inherit

Inheritance is for IS-A. A Car has an Engine, so Engine belongs as a field (composition), not a superclass. Deep hierarchies are brittle: a change near the top ripples through every descendant, and subclasses depend on parent internals. Modern practice favors composition unless the IS-A relationship is genuine and stable.

📖 Learn it step by step — Overriding & Polymorphism

WORKED EXAMPLE — dynamic dispatch, the whole idea in 10 lines
class Animal { public void speak() { System.out.println("..."); } }
class Dog extends Animal {
    @Override public void speak() { System.out.println("Woof"); }

🧠 MEMORY AID

Overload vs Override: Overload = same method name, different parameter list, decided at compile time (same class). Override = same signature, a subclass replaces the parent’s version, decided at run time (polymorphism). Memory hook: overLOAD changes the LOAD (the parameters); overRIDE rides over the parent.

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Overriding = a subclass redefines a method with the same signature; the version that runs is chosen at run time by the object’s actual type (dynamic dispatch / polymorphism), even through a superclass reference. ▸ WORKED EXAMPLE

class B extends A { @Override String m() { return "B"; } }

The rules of a valid override

An override must have the same name, same parameter list and compatible return type as the parent method. Change the parameters and you have overloaded, not overridden — the parent version still runs for the original signature, which is a silent and very common bug. Add @Override and the compiler will catch that mistake for you; that is its entire purpose.

Additional constraints: you may not reduce visibility (a public method cannot become protected), and static, final and private methods cannot be overridden — final exists precisely to forbid it.

Polymorphism, and the two types in play

Animal a = new Dog(); is legal because Dog IS-A Animal. Now two types matter:

  • The reference type (Animal) decides which methods you may call — checked at compile time. Calling a Dog-only method through an Animal reference will not compile without a cast.
  • The object type (Dog) decides which version actually runs — chosen at run time. This is dynamic dispatch, and it is what polymorphism means.

So a.speak() compiles because Animal declares speak(), but executes Dog's override. Trace questions hinge on exactly this split.

Why it matters practically

A list of Animal can hold Dogs, Cats and Birds, and one loop calling speak() produces the right behavior for each. Adding a new subclass requires no change to that loop — the extensibility argument for OOP in one sentence.

Casting and instanceof

Upcasting (Dog → Animal) is always safe and implicit. Downcasting (Animal → Dog) is checked at run time and throws ClassCastException if the object is not really a Dog — guard it with instanceof first.

The summary line worth memorizing

Overloading is compile-time and depends on the declared argument types; overriding is run-time and depends on the actual object.

📖 Learn it step by step — Abstract Classes & Interfaces

THE TWO CONTRACTS
• Abstract class — a partial class: may mix implemented methods, fields, constructors, and abstract methods (no body). Cannot be instantiated. One per child (extends).
• Interface — a pure contract: method signatures (+ default methods). A class can implement many. No instance state.
Choose: shared code + is-a hierarchy → abstract class. Capability that cuts across unrelated classes (Comparable, Runnable) → interface.
WORKED EXAMPLE — one of each

    abstract double area();                 // children MUST provide
    void describe() {                        // shared, already written
        System.out.println("Area: " + area());
    }
}
class Circle extends Shape {
    double r;
    Circle(double r) { this.r = r; }
    double area() { return Math.PI * r * r; }   // fulfills the contract
}

interface Printable { void print(); }
class Report implements Printable {
    public void print() { System.out.println("report"); }
}
new Shape() is a compile error (abstract). new Circle(2).describe() works — the shared describe() calls the child’s area(). Report implements Printable and could ALSO implement more interfaces at once.

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

An abstract class cannot be instantiated and may mix abstract (unimplemented) and concrete methods; a subclass must implement the abstract ones. An interface is implemented with implements, a class can implement many interfaces, and interfaces hold constants and (modern Java) default methods — but no instance state.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
abstract class Shape { abstract double area(); }
// Shape s = new Shape();   // COMPILE ERROR
class Circle extends Shape { double area() { return 3.14; } }
Shape s = new Circle();

Output: Circle works; new Shape() is illegal

You cannot write new Shape() — abstract classes have no instances. You instantiate a concrete subclass (Circle) that implements the abstract area().

🔬 GOING DEEPER — abstract classes vs interfaces — how to choose

What each one is

An abstract class is a partially built class: it may hold fields, constructors, implemented methods and abstract methods with no body. It cannot be instantiated — new Shape() fails — because it is incomplete. A subclass must implement every abstract method or itself be declared abstract.

An interface is a contract of behavior. Its methods are implicitly public and abstract, its fields implicitly public static final. Modern Java also allows default methods with a body, so an interface can supply shared behavior without breaking existing implementers.

The decision

Use an abstract class when…Use an interface when…
Classes share state (fields) and codeUnrelated classes share a capability
There is a genuine IS-A hierarchyYou need multiple, independent contracts
You want a constructor and protected helpersYou want maximum flexibility for implementers

The decisive constraint: a class may extend one class but implement many interfaces. That is why capabilities such as Comparable, Serializable or Flyable are interfaces — a Bird can extend Animal and implement Flyable, which single inheritance alone could never express.

Programming to the interface

Declaring List<String> items = new ArrayList<>(); rather than ArrayList<String> items means you can swap in a LinkedList later without touching the rest of the code. Depending on the contract instead of the implementation is the practical payoff of abstraction — and the reason interfaces dominate professional Java.

Traps

An abstract class may contain zero abstract methods and still be uninstantiable. A class implementing an interface must implement every method or be abstract itself. And an abstract method has no body — writing {} makes it concrete and empty, which is a different thing entirely.
