◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The D286 OA is NOT multiple choice — you write real Java code in a browser-based environment, and an automated grader runs it. Knowing the format and having a task strategy is worth as much as knowing Java.

What the assessment looks like

You'll face a series of coding tasks (typically around 8-12) in a locked-down browser IDE. Each task gives you a prompt — usually "write a program/method that reads X and outputs Y" — starter code in some cases, and you write Java that must compile and produce exactly the expected output. Partial credit exists per task, but output formatting matters: an extra space or missing newline can fail a test case.

The golden rules of coding OAs

  1. Read the whole prompt twice before typing — half of lost marks are answering a different question.
  2. Trace with a concrete value. Pick a small input and walk the code line by line on paper.
  3. Check boundaries first: 0, 1, empty, the last index — loops live or die at the edges (< vs <=).
  4. Mind integer division and types: 7 / 2 is 3 in int land; == on Strings compares references.
  5. Eliminate before you choose: two options usually die fast; decide between the survivors by tracing.
  6. Never leave blanks. No penalty for guessing — an eliminated-to-two guess is a coin you should always flip.

The complete topic checklist

Go into the OA only when you can code each of these cold:

  • Input/Output: Scanner (nextInt, nextDouble, nextLine, next), System.out.print/println/printf
  • Types: int, double, boolean, char, String; casting; integer division and modulo
  • Strings: length(), charAt(), substring(), equals(), equalsIgnoreCase(), compareTo(), indexOf(), toUpperCase/LowerCase(), trim(), contains()
  • Conditionals: if/else-if/else, switch, ternary, logical operators &&, ||, !
  • Loops: for, while, do-while, for-each, break, continue, nested loops
  • Arrays: declare, initialize, traverse, find max/min/sum/average, search
  • ArrayList: add, get, set, remove, size, contains, traversal
  • Methods: signatures, parameters, return types, overloading, static vs instance
  • Classes: fields, constructors, getters/setters, toString(), creating and using objects
  • Exceptions: try/catch, multiple catches, finally, throwing exceptions

The Scanner trap that fails more students than any Java concept

Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);
int age = sc.nextInt();      // reads the NUMBER but leaves "\n" in the buffer
String name = sc.nextLine(); // reads that leftover "\n" → name is EMPTY!

// THE FIX: consume the leftover newline
int age2 = sc.nextInt();
sc.nextLine();               // eat the newline
String name2 = sc.nextLine(); // now reads the actual next line ✓

Point-losing mistakes catalog

// 1. == on Strings (compares references, not contents)
if (word == "yes")          // ✗ unreliable
if (word.equals("yes"))     // ✓

// 2. Integer division surprise
double avg = sum / count;            // ✗ if both int → truncates BEFORE assigning
double avg2 = (double) sum / count;  // ✓ cast first

// 3. Off-by-one in loops
for (int i = 0; i <= arr.length; i++)  // ✗ ArrayIndexOutOfBounds at i = length
for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++)   // ✓

// 4. println when they asked for print (or vice versa)
// "output the numbers separated by spaces on one line" → print(x + " "), not println

// 5. Forgetting to close/handle the last case in switch (missing break = fall-through)

Your exam-day pacing plan

1. Minutes 0-5: skim every task; mark each Easy / Medium / Hard.
2. First pass: all Easy tasks — compile and verify each before moving on.
3. Second pass: Mediums. If stuck 10+ minutes, write the partial solution (read input, set up structure) and move on.
4. Final pass: Hards + return to stuck tasks with fresh eyes.
5. Last 10 minutes: verify every task at least compiles and prints something — a compile error scores zero even if the logic is 95% there.

✓ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • It's a coding exam — practice WRITING programs, not just reading them
  • Exact output format; compile early; never leave blanks
  • The nextInt-then-nextLine Scanner trap and == on Strings are the classic killers
  • Bank easy tasks first; a compiling partial beats an ambitious blank

Good OA habits: during the exam, flag hard questions and move on rather than fixing every doubt immediately — never ignore the timer. Read compiler-error questions carefully: identify what kind of errors the code produces before choosing. Return to flagged items with your remaining time.

💡 Sure-fire OA strategies

1. Trace every code question on your scratch space — write the variable table; never eyeball increments. 2. Bank the traps: integer division, x++ vs ++x, == vs .equals, fall-through switch, off-by-one at arr.length, subclass-catch-first. 3. Two passes: answer sure ones first, flag the rest — momentum beats perfection. 4. If two answers look identical, re-read the TYPES in the question; the difference is usually a type. 5. The night before: redo only your flagged/weak questions, then stop — rested beats crammed.

Exam focus: edge cases — the testing habit that catches bugs

Good tests go beyond one “happy path” sample. Always check boundary and unusual inputs: 0, negative numbers, the empty string or empty array, the largest/smallest allowed value, and duplicates. Most real bugs — and most exam answers — live at these edges, not in the middle of the range.

🔬 GOING DEEPER — reading the D286 OA like an examiner

What the exam is testing

The OA is not a vocabulary quiz. Most questions show you code and ask what it outputs, whether it compiles, or which construct you should choose. So your preparation should be: trace code on paper, and be able to say why each wrong option is wrong.

The highest-yield trap list

  • == vs .equals() on Strings and wrappers.
  • Integer division: 5 / 2 is 2.
  • arr.length (field) vs str.length() (method) vs list.size().
  • Index bounds: last index is length − 1; loop with <.
  • substring(a, b) — b is exclusive; indexOf returns −1 when absent.
  • Missing break in a switch causes fall-through.
  • Defining any constructor removes the free default one.
  • Overloading (compile-time, different parameters) vs overriding (run-time, same parameters).
  • Catch blocks must be ordered most-specific first, or it will not compile.
  • Checked exceptions must be caught or declared; unchecked need not be.
  • Strings are immutable — methods return a new String, they do not modify.
  • Overriding equals without hashCode breaks HashMap and HashSet.

A method for code questions

1) Scan for a compile error first — wrong catch order, missing constructor, calling an instance member from static, mismatched types. If it will not compile, that is the answer. 2) Otherwise trace with a variable table, writing each value as it changes. 3) Watch the boundaries — first and last iteration are where the errors are planted. 4) Eliminate options you can disprove rather than hunting for the one that feels right.

Treat the output format as part of the problem, not as presentation. WORKED EXAMPLE — count the vowels (full solution, explained)
String s = "banana";
int count = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
    char c = s.charAt(i);
    if (c == 'a' || c == 'e' || c == 'i' || c == 'o' || c == 'u') {
        count++;
    }
}
System.out.println(count);   // 3
The pattern stack: loop over indices (0 to length()−1) → charAt to inspect → condition → accumulate. b-a-n-a-n-a has a at indices 1, 3, 5 → 3. Most drill problems are this same skeleton with a different condition — recognize the skeleton and the problem writes itself.
⚠️ chars USE SINGLE QUOTES
'a' is a char; "a" is a String — c == "a" doesn’t compile. And the loop bound is s.length() with parentheses (String method), i < length, not <=.

Drill 1 — Input and arithmetic

Read two integers and print their sum, difference, product, and the result of dividing the first by the second as a double with 2 decimals.

import java.util.Scanner;
public class Main {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);
    int a = sc.nextInt();
    int b = sc.nextInt();
    System.out.println(a + b);
    System.out.println(a - b);
    System.out.println(a * b);
    System.out.printf("%.2f%n", (double) a / b);   // cast BEFORE dividing
  }
}

Drill 2 — Even/odd with edge case

Read an integer; print "EVEN", "ODD", or "ZERO".

int n = sc.nextInt();
if (n == 0)            System.out.println("ZERO");
else if (n % 2 == 0)   System.out.println("EVEN");
else                   System.out.println("ODD");
// Watch: negative odd numbers → n % 2 is -1, not 1. (n % 2 != 0) catches both.

Drill 3 — String reversal (no built-in reverse)

String s = sc.nextLine();
String rev = "";
for (int i = s.length() - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
    rev += s.charAt(i);
}
System.out.println(rev);
// Alternative they also accept: new StringBuilder(s).reverse().toString()

Drill 4 — Vowel counter

Count vowels in a line, case-insensitive.

String line = sc.nextLine().toLowerCase();
int count = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < line.length(); i++) {
    char c = line.charAt(i);
    if (c=='a' || c=='e' || c=='i' || c=='o' || c=='u') count++;

System.out.println(count);

Drill 5 — Grade calculator (if/else chain)

int score = sc.nextInt();
String grade;
if      (score >= 90) grade = "A";
else if (score >= 80) grade = "B";
else if (score >= 70) grade = "C";
else if (score >= 60) grade = "D";
else                  grade = "F";
System.out.println(grade);
// Order matters: check from highest down, no need for "score < 90 &&"

Drill 6 — Sum until sentinel

Read integers until -1 is entered; print their sum (excluding the -1).

int sum = 0;
int n = sc.nextInt();
while (n != -1) {
    sum += n;
    n = sc.nextInt();   // read the NEXT value at the END of the loop
}
System.out.println(sum);
// Classic bug: reading inside the loop FIRST adds the sentinel. Pattern: read → test → process → read.

Drill 7 — Multiplication table (nested-ish loop)

int n = sc.nextInt();
for (int i = 1; i <= 10; i++) {
    System.out.println(n + " x " + i + " = " + (n * i));
}
// Note the parentheses around (n * i): without them, + concatenates strings.

Drill 8 — FizzBuzz (the eternal classic)

for (int i = 1; i <= 100; i++) {
    if (i % 15 == 0)      System.out.println("FizzBuzz");  // test 15 FIRST
    else if (i % 3 == 0)  System.out.println("Fizz");
    else if (i % 5 == 0)  System.out.println("Buzz");
    else                  System.out.println(i);

// The order trap: testing %3 before %15 means "FizzBuzz" never prints.

Valid if: length ≥ 8, contains a digit, contains an uppercase letter. Print VALID or INVALID.

String pw = sc.nextLine();
boolean hasDigit = false, hasUpper = false;

int choice;

Exam focus: safe odd test and printf newline

Odd test: in Java, x % 2 == 1 FAILS for negative numbers (−3 % 2 is −1). The safe odd test that also handles negatives is x % 2 != 0. printf newline: in format strings, %n writes the platform-appropriate line separator (\n is a literal linefeed and is not platform-aware).

What to practise, and why

These drills exist to make the mechanical parts automatic so that exam time goes to reasoning. Concretely, you should be able to do each of these without hesitation:

  • Trace a loop and state the value of every variable after each pass.
  • Predict integer-division and modulo results, including with negatives.
  • Walk a String character by character with charAt and length().
  • Say whether a given if/switch falls through, and which branch fires.
  • Spot the off-by-one in a loop bound at a glance.

The patterns that recur

Accumulator: declare a total before the loop, add inside. Counter with a condition: count items matching a test. Max/min so far: initialize from the first element (not 0, which breaks with negative data). Search with a flag: set found = true and break. Building a string: use StringBuilder inside loops. Swap: always via a temporary variable.

Recognizing which pattern a question wants is faster than reasoning from scratch, and these five cover most exam code.

How to practise properly

Predict the output before you check. If you were wrong, do not just read the answer — find the exact line where your mental model diverged. That gap is the thing being tested, and it is what will otherwise repeat on the exam.

public static int max(int[] arr) {
    int best = arr[0];                    // start with the FIRST element
    for (int i = 1; i < arr.length; i++) {
        if (arr[i] > best) {
            best = arr[i];
        }
    }
    return best;
}

int[] data = {4, 9, 2, 9, 5};
System.out.println(max(data));   // 9
Trace: best=4 → 9>4, best=9 → 2 no → 9 no (not >) → 5 no → returns 9. Seeds: max starts at arr[0] (NOT 0 — fails on all-negative arrays); min starts at arr[0] too. This find-the-extreme skeleton, plus sum/average and count-matching, covers most array drills on the OA.
⚠️ START best AT arr[0], NOT 0
Initializing max to 0 breaks on {−5, −2} (returns 0, which isn’t even in the array). Start from the first element and loop from index 1 — the version graders expect.
📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Round two covers the heavier half of the OA: arrays, ArrayLists, methods, classes, and exceptions. These tasks earn more points and separate passing from failing. Same protocol: write first, compare after.

Drill 11 — Array statistics

Read n, then n integers into an array; print max, min, and average (2 decimals).

int n = sc.nextInt();
int[] arr = new int[n];
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) arr[i] = sc.nextInt();

int max = arr[0], min = arr[0], sum = 0;
for (int x : arr) {
    if (x > max) max = x;
    if (x < min) min = x;
    sum += x;
}
System.out.println(max);
System.out.println(min);
System.out.printf("%.2f%n", (double) sum / n);
// Initialize max/min from arr[0], NOT from 0 — all-negative arrays break the 0 version.

Drill 12 — Linear search with position

int target = sc.nextInt();
int foundAt = -1;
for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) {
    if (arr[i] == target) { foundAt = i; break; }
}
System.out.println(foundAt >= 0 ? "Found at index " + foundAt : "Not found");

Drill 13 — Reverse an array in place

for (int i = 0; i < arr.length / 2; i++) {
    int temp = arr[i];
    arr[i] = arr[arr.length - 1 - i];
    arr[arr.length - 1 - i] = temp;
}
// Loop only to the MIDDLE — going further swaps everything back.

Drill 14 — ArrayList filtering

Read words until "stop"; print only words longer than 4 characters.

import java.util.ArrayList;
ArrayList<String> words = new ArrayList<>();
String w = sc.next();
while (!w.equals("stop")) {     // .equals, never ==
    words.add(w);
    w = sc.next();
}
for (String word : words) {
    if (word.length() > 4) System.out.println(word);
}

Drill 15 — Remove from ArrayList safely

// Remove all even numbers from an ArrayList<Integer>
for (int i = list.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) {   // iterate BACKWARD when removing
    if (list.get(i) % 2 == 0) list.remove(i);
}
// Forward iteration skips elements after each removal — the classic ArrayList trap.

Drill 16 — Method with return value

Write a method countOccurrences(int[] arr, int target) returning how many times target appears, and a main that uses it.

public class Main {
  public static int countOccurrences(int[] arr, int target) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int x : arr) {
        if (x == target) count++;
    }
    return count;
  }
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    int[] data = {3, 7, 3, 1, 3};
    System.out.println(countOccurrences(data, 3));   // 3
  }
}
// Methods called from main without an object must be STATIC.

Drill 17 — Method overloading

public static double area(double radius) {            // circle
    return Math.PI * radius * radius;
}
public static double area(double w, double h) {       // rectangle
    return w * h;
}
// Same name, different parameter lists = overloading. Return type alone is NOT enough.

Drill 18 — A complete class

Create a Student class: name, score fields; constructor; getters; a passed() method (score ≥ 60); toString. Main creates two students and prints them.

class Student {
    private String name;
    private int score;

    public Student(String name, int score) {
        this.name = name;          // this. resolves field vs parameter shadowing
        this.score = score;
    }
    public String getName() { return name; }
    public int getScore()   { return score; }
    public boolean passed() { return score >= 60; }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return name + ": " + score + (passed() ? " (PASS)" : " (FAIL)");
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student s1 = new Student("Ana", 84);
        Student s2 = new Student("Raj", 51);
        System.out.println(s1);    // println calls toString automatically
        System.out.println(s2);
    }
}

Drill 19 — try/catch for robust input

import java.util.InputMismatchException;
try {
    int n = sc.nextInt();
    System.out.println(100 / n);
} catch (InputMismatchException e) {
    System.out.println("Not a number");
} catch (ArithmeticException e) {          // division by zero
    System.out.println("Cannot divide by zero");
} finally {
    System.out.println("Done");            // runs ALWAYS — exception or not
}
// Catch order: specific exceptions before general (Exception last if at all).

Drill 20 — Putting it together

Read n scores into an ArrayList; use a method to compute the average; handle the n=0 case with an exception or guard; print "No scores" or the average.

public static double average(ArrayList<Integer> scores) {
    if (scores.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("No scores");
    int sum = 0;
    for (int s : scores) sum += s;
    return (double) sum / scores.size();
}
public static void main(String[] args) {
    Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);
    ArrayList<Integer> scores = new ArrayList<>();
    int n = sc.nextInt();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) scores.add(sc.nextInt());
    try {
        System.out.printf("%.2f%n", average(scores));
    } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
        System.out.println(e.getMessage());
    }
}
⚠ THE FIVE HEAVYWEIGHT TRAPS

(1) max/min initialized to 0 instead of arr[0]; (2) forward iteration while removing from ArrayList; (3) non-static method called from main; (4) == on Strings/Integers (autoboxing makes small ints "work" then big ints fail!); (5) array.length vs list.size() vs string.length() — three different spellings.

✓ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Reverse in place: swap to the middle only; remove from lists: iterate backward
  • this. in constructors; static for main-called methods; toString for printing objects
  • Catch specific exceptions first; finally always runs
  • length (array) / length() (String) / size() (ArrayList) — memorize the trio
🔬 GOING DEEPER — drilling arrays, methods, classes and exceptions

What the harder half of the exam looks like

Later questions combine topics: an array traversal inside a method that throws, or a subclass overriding a method that uses a field the parent initialized. Handle these by identifying each mechanism in play rather than reading the code as one lump.

Reference semantics — the recurring theme

Most "why did this change / not change?" questions reduce to one rule: Java passes a copy of the reference. Therefore mutating the object (arr[0] = 9, list.add(x), sb.append()) is visible to the caller, while reassigning the parameter (arr = new int[5]) is not. Apply that test and the answer follows every time.

Object questions

Check the constructor chain (does an implicit super() exist to call?), whether a method is overridden or merely overloaded, and whether the reference type permits the call while the object type supplies the behavior. For static members, ask whether the code is reaching instance state from a static context — the standard planted compile error.

Exception questions

Trace the flow explicitly: which line throws, which catch matches first, and remember that finally runs regardless — including when the try block returns. Then check the ordering rule: a broader catch above a narrower one is a compile error, not a runtime surprise.

Before the exam

Rehearse the failure modes rather than the successes. Most exam code is deliberately near a boundary — an empty array, a null reference, the last index, a zero divisor. If you can name what breaks, you can pick the answer.

📊 FIGURE — the three spellings, and what a method can change
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Removing while iterating forward really does skip elements
System.out.println("start:    " + make());
System.out.println("forward:  " + forward(make()));
System.out.println("backward: " + backward(make()));
start: [1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8] forward: [1, 4, 7] backward: [1, 7]
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Removing element i shifts everything after it one place left, and the loop's i++ then steps over the element that moved into that slot.
  2. Trace it: removing the 2 at index 1 slides the 4 down into index 1, but i has already become 2 — so the 4 is never examined and survives. The 6 and 8 happen to line up and are removed.
  3. Counting downward means each removal only shifts positions the loop has already passed, so nothing is skipped and every even number goes.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Two claims about arrays and == worth seeing fail
int[] negatives = { -5, -2, -9 };
System.out.println("seeded with 0:    " + maxFromZero(negatives));
System.out.println("seeded with a[0]: " + maxFromFirst(negatives));

Integer a = 127, b = 127;
Integer c = 128, d = 128;
System.out.println("127 == 127 : " + (a == b));
System.out.println("128 == 128 : " + (c == d));
System.out.println("equals     : " + c.equals(d));
seeded with 0: 0 seeded with a[0]: -2 127 == 127 : true 128 == 128 : false equals : true
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Seeding the maximum with 0 returns 0 for an all-negative array — a value that is not even in the data, from code that never errors.
  2. The Integer comparison is worse: == gives true at 127 and false at 128, because Java caches small Integer objects and hands back the same one.
  3. That is why a test with small numbers passes and the graded one with larger numbers fails. equals is right at every value.
🎯 EXAM TIP
For any "why did this change / not change?" question, apply one rule: Java passes a copy of the reference. Mutating the object through it — arr[0] = 9, list.add(x), sb.append(…) — is visible to the caller. Reassigning the parameter itself — arr = new int[5] — is not. That single test answers the whole family.

📖 Learn it step by step — Generics (types as parameters)

WORKED EXAMPLE — why <String> saves you
ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
names.add("Ana");
// names.add(42);          ← COMPILE error — caught before running
String first = names.get(0);   // no cast needed

// without generics (old style):
ArrayList raw = new ArrayList();
raw.add("Ana"); raw.add(42);            // both allowed!
String s = (String) raw.get(1);         // compiles… CRASHES at runtime
Generics move type errors from RUNTIME to COMPILE TIME and remove casting. The <> “diamond” on the right lets the compiler infer the type parameter.
GENERIC METHODS & BOUNDS
static <T> T first(List<T> list) works for ANY element type. Bounds constrain it: <T extends Comparable<T>> = “any T that can compare itself” — required to write a generic max/sort. Primitives can’t be type arguments: use Integer, not int (autoboxing bridges the gap).
⚠️ ArrayList<int> DOES NOT COMPILE
Type parameters must be reference types: ArrayList<Integer>. Java auto-boxes int ↔ Integer on the way in and out, so usage still looks natural.
🎯 QUICK CHECK
The main benefit of ArrayList<String> over a raw ArrayList is:
  1. Type errors are caught at compile time
  2. It runs faster
  3. It can hold more items
Show answer
A. The compiler enforces the element type — no bad adds, no casts, no runtime ClassCastException.

Generics — type-safe collections & methods

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A generic is a type placeholder. Instead of writing a separate Box class for a String, an Integer, and a Dog, you write Box<T> once and let the caller fill in T. ArrayList<String> is just ArrayList<T> with T set to String — so the list can only hold Strings, and the compiler enforces it.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

The angle brackets after a type — <String>, <Integer> — are the type argument. They give you two things: (1) the compiler rejects the wrong type at compile time instead of throwing a ClassCastException at runtime, and (2) you get elements back already typed, so no casting is needed.

Generics work only with reference types, never primitives: you write ArrayList<Integer>, not ArrayList<int>. Autoboxing converts int ↔ Integer automatically.

WORKED EXAMPLE — with vs. without generics
Raw (old, unsafe)Generic (safe)
ArrayList list = new ArrayList();ArrayList<String> list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add("hi"); list.add(42); — both allowedlist.add("hi"); ✓   list.add(42); ✗ compile error
String s = (String) list.get(0); — cast neededString s = list.get(0); — no cast
⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

You can write your own generic type. The <T> after the class name declares the placeholder:

class Box<T> { private T item; void set(T x){ item = x; } T get(){ return item; } }

A generic method declares its own placeholder before the return type: public static <T> T first(T[] a){ return a[0]; }. A bounded type restricts it: <T extends Number> means "T must be Number or a subclass," so you can safely call .doubleValue().

📝 EXAM WORDING

<T> is a type parameter; <String> is a type argument. <> on the right is the diamond operator (Java infers the type). Generics give compile-time type safety and remove casts. Common letters: T type, E element, K/V key/value.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

You cannot use a primitive as a type argument (ArrayList<int> won't compile — use Integer). And generics are checked by the compiler only; at runtime the type is "erased" (type erasure), which is why you can't write new T() or new T[10].

🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
Why does ArrayList<String> not need a cast on get()?
  1. The compiler already knows every element is a String
  2. ArrayList stores the class name with each element
  3. Casting is done automatically at runtime
  4. Strings never need casting
Show answer
A. The type argument tells the compiler the element type, so get() returns String directly — no cast, and a wrong-type add() is caught at compile time.
🔬 GOING DEEPER — generics — why the compiler, not the runtime, catches the bug

The problem generics solve

Before generics, a collection held Object, so anything could go in and every retrieval needed a cast. A wrong cast compiled fine and blew up at run time with ClassCastException. Generics move that failure to compile time: List<String> refuses a non-String at the point you write it, and retrieval needs no cast.

Type erasure

Generics are enforced by the compiler and then erased — the bytecode has no type parameter. That explains several rules: you cannot create new T[], you cannot test x instanceof List<String>, and List<String> and List<Integer> are the same class at run time.

Generic methods and bounds

You can parameterize a single method: <T> void printAll(List<T> items). A bounded parameter constrains it — <T extends Comparable<T>> guarantees the type supports compareTo, so a generic max() can compare safely.

The inheritance trap

List<Dog> is not a subtype of List<Animal>, even though Dog is an Animal — generics are invariant. If it were allowed you could insert a Cat into a list of Dogs through the Animal reference. Wildcards restore flexibility safely: <? extends Animal> to read, <? super Dog> to write.

📖 Learn it step by step — equals(), hashCode() & toString()

WORKED EXAMPLE — what breaks when you skip them
public class Point {
    int x, y;
    Point(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }
}
Point a = new Point(1, 2), b = new Point(1, 2);
System.out.println(a.equals(b));   // false! (inherited == identity)
System.out.println(a);             // Point@6d06d69c (default toString)
Without overrides, equals() means “same object in memory” and printing shows class@hash. Override them:
@Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
    if (this == o) return true;
    if (!(o instanceof Point)) return false;
    Point p = (Point) o;
    return x == p.x && y == p.y;
}
@Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(x, y); }
@Override public String toString() { return "(" + x + "," + y + ")"; }
Now a.equals(b) is true and printing shows (1,2).
⚠️ equals AND hashCode TRAVEL TOGETHER
Equal objects MUST have equal hash codes — override one without the other and HashSet/HashMap “lose” your objects (contains() returns false for an equal object). This pairing rule is the section’s most-tested fact.
🎯 QUICK CHECK
If you override equals(), you must also override:
  1. hashCode()
  2. toString()
  3. main()
Show answer
A — hashCode(), so equal objects hash identically and hash-based collections behave.

equals(), hashCode() & toString() — the Object contract

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Every class in Java secretly extends Object, inheriting three methods worth overriding: toString() (how the object prints), equals() (when two objects count as "the same"), and hashCode() (a number used by hash-based collections). The defaults compare memory addresses, which is rarely what you want.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

toString() — the default prints something like Dog@1b6d3586 (class name + hash). Override it to return something readable; System.out.println(dog) and string concatenation call it automatically.

equals(Object o) — default == checks if two references point to the same object. Override it to compare field values so two different Point(3,4) objects are considered equal.

hashCode() — returns an int bucket used by HashMap and HashSet. It must be consistent with equals().

THE equals/hashCode CONTRACT
If a.equals(b) is true, then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode() MUST also be true. Override both together — never just one. (The reverse isn't required: equal hashes don't force equal objects — that's a hash collision.)
WORKED EXAMPLE — why override both

You put two Point(1,2) objects in a HashSet. If you override equals() but NOT hashCode(), the two points land in different buckets (different default hashes), so the set stores both — the duplicate is never detected. Overriding hashCode() to match equals() sends equal points to the same bucket, and the set correctly keeps one.

📝 EXAM WORDING

== compares references (identity); .equals() compares values when overridden. String, Integer, and the wrapper classes already override equals()/hashCode() — that's why "ab".equals("ab") is true. Always use .equals() for object content comparison.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

The signature MUST be public boolean equals(Object o) — with parameter type Object. Writing equals(Point p) instead overloads rather than overrides, so collections (which call equals(Object)) won't use it. Add @Override and the compiler will catch the mistake.

🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
You override equals() but not hashCode(). What breaks?
  1. Nothing
  2. HashSet/HashMap may store logical duplicates
  3. The program won't compile
  4. toString stops working
Show answer
B. Equal objects can produce different hash codes, so they land in different buckets and hash-based collections fail to detect them as duplicates. Override both together.
🔬 GOING DEEPER — the Object contract — equals, hashCode and toString

Why you must override equals

The inherited Object.equals() compares references, so two objects with identical field values are "unequal" by default. If your class represents a value — a Point, a Money, a Student — you override equals() to compare contents. Until you do, list.contains(myObject) and list.remove(myObject) will fail even when a matching object is present.

The rule that catches everyone

If you override equals(), you must override hashCode(). The contract: equal objects must return equal hash codes. Hash-based collections (HashMap, HashSet) find the bucket by hash code and only then compare with equals. Override equals alone and two equal objects land in different buckets — so a HashSet accepts an apparent duplicate and a HashMap lookup silently misses. Note the converse is allowed: equal hash codes do not require equality (that is just a collision).

Writing equals correctly

The contract requires it to be reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent, and false for null. In practice: check this == obj first, reject null and mismatched types, cast, then compare fields — using .equals() for object fields and == for primitives.

toString

The default prints ClassName@1b6d3586 — the class and a hash in hex, useless in a log. Overriding toString() to return meaningful text pays off everywhere, because System.out.println(obj) and string concatenation call it automatically.

📖 Learn it step by step — Comparable & Comparator

TWO WAYS TO DEFINE ORDER
• Comparable — the class defines its OWN natural order: implement compareTo(other); then Collections.sort(list) just works. ONE order per class.
• Comparator — a SEPARATE object defines an order: as many different orders as you like, passed to sort.
WORKED EXAMPLE — both, on a Student
class Student implements Comparable<Student> {
    String name; double gpa;
    public int compareTo(Student o) {
        return this.name.compareTo(o.name);      // natural: by name
    }
}

Collections.sort(students);                       // by name (Comparable)

students.sort(Comparator.comparingDouble(s -> s.gpa));         // by GPA
students.sort(Comparator.comparingDouble((Student s) -> s.gpa)
                        .reversed());                          // GPA high→low
compareTo returns negative (this first), zero (tie), positive (other first). Comparators bolt on alternative orders without touching the class.
⚠️ RETURN SIGN, NOT VALUE
Only the SIGN of compareTo matters: −, 0, +. Returning a−b works for ints (overflow aside); for doubles use Double.compare(a, b). “One natural order = Comparable; many external orders = Comparator” answers most questions here.
🎯 QUICK CHECK
To sort the same list three different ways, you’d use:
  1. Three Comparators
  2. Three compareTo methods in the class
  3. Three copies of the class
Show answer
A. A class gets ONE compareTo (natural order); every extra ordering is a Comparator.

Comparable & Comparator — sorting your own objects

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Collections.sort() and Arrays.sort() know how to order numbers and Strings, but they have no idea whether one Employee comes before another. You teach them by supplying an ordering — either built into the class (Comparable) or as a separate rule (Comparator).

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Comparable<T> — the class implements it and defines public int compareTo(T other). This is the object's natural ordering (String's is alphabetical, Integer's is numeric). Collections.sort(list) uses it with no extra argument.

Comparator<T> — a separate object defining public int compare(T a, T b). Pass it as a second argument: Collections.sort(list, bySalary). Use it when you want multiple orderings or can't modify the class.

THE RETURN-VALUE RULE (both methods)
Return a negative int if this/first should come BEFORE, zero if they are equal in order, positive if it should come AFTER. A common trick for numbers is Integer.compare(a, b) (never a - b, which can overflow).
WORKED EXAMPLE — natural vs custom order
GoalCode
Sort employees by natural order (name)class Employee implements Comparable<Employee> { public int compareTo(Employee e){ return name.compareTo(e.name);} } then Collections.sort(list);
Sort by salary insteadCollections.sort(list, (a,b) -> Integer.compare(a.salary, b.salary));
Reverse salarylist.sort(Comparator.comparingInt((Employee e) -> e.salary).reversed());
📝 EXAM WORDING

Comparable = compareTo(other), one natural ordering, implemented BY the class. Comparator = compare(a, b), an external/alternate ordering, passed TO sort. Mnemonic: Comparable = the object is able to compare itself; Comparator = a separate -ator object that compares two others.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Sorting objects that don't implement Comparable with a plain Collections.sort(list) throws a ClassCastException at runtime. Either implement Comparable or pass a Comparator.

🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
compareTo returns a positive number. What does that mean?
  1. this object comes before the other
  2. this object comes after the other
  3. they are equal
  4. an error occurred
Show answer
B. Positive means "this" is greater / comes after; negative means before; zero means equal in order.
🔬 GOING DEEPER — Comparable vs Comparator — one natural order, many alternatives

The difference in one line

Comparable is implemented by the class itself and defines its single natural ordering via compareTo(other). Comparator is a separate object defining one of many alternative orderings via compare(a, b). A Student can be Comparable by ID, while separate Comparators sort by name, GPA or enrollment date.

The return-value convention

Both return an int, and the sign is what matters: negative means this comes first, zero means equal ordering, positive means this comes after. For numeric fields Integer.compare(a, b) is safer than a - b, which can overflow for extreme values.

Where they get used

Collections.sort(list) and Arrays.sort(arr) require Comparable elements, and throw ClassCastException at run time if the type does not implement it. Pass a Comparator as the second argument to override the natural order. TreeMap and TreeSet keep keys sorted the same way.

Consistency with equals

Best practice is that compareTo returns 0 exactly when equals returns true. When they disagree, sorted collections behave surprisingly — TreeSet treats "compareTo == 0" as duplicate and silently drops an element that equals considers distinct.

try (Scanner fin = new Scanner(new File("scores.txt"))) {
    while (fin.hasNextInt()) {

• The resource must implement AutoCloseable (Scanner, readers/writers, streams all do).
• FileNotFoundException / IOException are checked: catch or declare throws.
• Writing: try (PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter("out.txt")) { out.println("hi"); }.

If an exception fires before your close() line, the file stays open (a resource leak). try-with-resources closes on success AND on failure — which is why it’s the exam’s “best practice” answer.

A resource declared in try (...) is closed:
  1. Automatically, even when an exception occurs
  2. Only if you call close()
  3. Never

try-with-resources & File I/O

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

When you open a file, a Scanner, or any resource, you must close it or you leak file handles. The old way — closing in a finally block — is verbose and easy to get wrong. try-with-resources closes the resource for you, automatically, even if an exception is thrown.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Declare the resource in parentheses right after try:

try (Scanner fileIn = new Scanner(new File("data.txt"))) {
  while (fileIn.hasNextLine()) System.out.println(fileIn.nextLine());
}

When the block ends — normally OR via exception — Java calls close() automatically. Any resource whose class implements AutoCloseable (Scanner, BufferedReader, PrintWriter, FileWriter…) works this way. You can declare several, separated by semicolons; they close in reverse order.

WORKED EXAMPLE — read then write, safely
TaskCode
Read a file line by linetry (Scanner s = new Scanner(new File("in.txt"))) { while (s.hasNextLine()) process(s.nextLine()); }
Write to a filetry (PrintWriter pw = new PrintWriter("out.txt")) { pw.println("Hello"); }

No explicit close() — the resource is released as soon as the block exits.

CHECKED EXCEPTIONS FOR FILES
File operations throw checked exceptions: FileNotFoundException (reading a missing file) and IOException. You must either catch them or declare throws IOException on the method — the compiler forces it.
📝 EXAM WORDING

try-with-resources = resource declared in try(...), auto-closed via AutoCloseable.close(). It replaces the finally { resource.close(); } pattern. Scanner(new File(f)) reads a file; Scanner(System.in) reads the keyboard. PrintWriter/FileWriter write. Reading a missing file → FileNotFoundException (a checked exception).

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

new Scanner("data.txt") does NOT open a file — it scans the literal string "data.txt"! You must wrap a File: new Scanner(new File("data.txt")). That's a classic OA trap.

🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
What is the main advantage of try-with-resources?
  1. It runs faster
  2. It closes the resource automatically, even on exception
  3. It ignores exceptions
  4. It avoids importing Scanner
Show answer
B. The resource declared in try(...) is closed automatically when the block exits — normally or via an exception — preventing leaks without a finally block.
🔬 GOING DEEPER — try-with-resources and file I/O

The leak that finally was invented to stop

Open files, streams and sockets hold operating-system resources that must be released. Closing them in finally works but is verbose and easy to get wrong — especially when the close itself can throw. try-with-resources replaces all of it: try (Scanner sc = new Scanner(file)) { ... } closes the resource automatically when the block exits, normally or by exception.

The mechanism is an interface: any class implementing AutoCloseable can be declared in the parentheses. Multiple resources are closed in reverse order of declaration.

Reading and writing

Reading a file throws the checked IOException (or FileNotFoundException), so the compiler forces you to catch it or declare throws — a direct application of the checked/unchecked rule from Unit 4. Typical patterns are Scanner or BufferedReader for input and PrintWriter or FileWriter for output.

Two practical points that show up in questions: opening a writer in the default mode overwrites the file, so appending requires the append flag; and buffered writers hold data in memory until flushed, so failing to close (or flush) can lose the last chunk of output entirely.

📖 Learn it step by step — Nested, Inner & Anonymous Classes

Java lets you define a class inside another class. Three kinds matter, and the difference is what they can see and when you use them.

THE THREE KINDS
• Static nested class — declared static inside the outer class. It does NOT see the outer instance’s fields; it’s just a namespaced helper: Outer.Nested n = new Outer.Nested();
• Inner class (non-static) — tied to an INSTANCE of the outer class and can read its fields directly. Created via an outer object.
• Anonymous class — a one-off, unnamed class defined at the point of use, usually to implement an interface inline.
WORKED EXAMPLE — an anonymous class implementing an interface
Runnable task = new Runnable() {
    @Override
    public void run() {
        System.out.println("running!");
    }
};
task.run();   // prints: running!
Reading it: new Runnable() { ... } creates an object of a brand-new unnamed class that implements Runnable, overriding run() on the spot. Since Java 8 the same thing is usually written as a lambda: Runnable task = () -> System.out.println("running!");
⚠️ STATIC NESTED ≠ INNER
The exam tell: a static nested class cannot touch the outer object’s instance fields (there is no outer object); an inner class can. If the code accesses outer instance state, it must be a (non-static) inner class.

Nested, inner & anonymous classes

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Sometimes a helper class only makes sense inside another class. Java lets you declare a class within a class. There are four flavors, and the OA mostly wants you to tell them apart: static nested, inner (non-static), local (inside a method), and anonymous (a class with no name, created on the spot).

Static nested class
Declared static inside another class. Does NOT need an outer instance; behaves like a top-level class scoped inside its outer class: Outer.Nested n = new Outer.Nested();
Inner (non-static) class
Non-static; each inner object is tied to an outer instance and can access its private fields. Created via an outer object: Outer.Inner i = outer.new Inner();
Local class
Declared inside a method body; visible only within that method.
Anonymous class
A one-off class with no name, declared and instantiated at once — usually to implement an interface or extend a class inline: Runnable r = new Runnable(){ public void run(){ ... } };
⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

The big distinction is static nested vs inner. A static nested class is independent — no outer object required. A (non-static) inner class always belongs to an instance of the outer class and can read that instance's private members directly. That's why inner classes are handy for tightly-coupled helpers (like an iterator over the outer list).

📝 EXAM WORDING

static nested = no outer instance needed (new Outer.Nested()). inner = needs an outer instance (outer.new Inner()), can access outer's privates. anonymous = no name, defined and instantiated in one expression, often for a listener/callback. Modern code frequently replaces small anonymous classes with lambdas.

🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
Which class type does NOT require an instance of the outer class to create?
  1. Non-static inner class
  2. Static nested class
  3. Neither can be created
  4. Both always need one
Show answer
B. A static nested class is created like a normal class (new Outer.Nested()) — no outer instance. A non-static inner class requires an outer instance.
🔬 GOING DEEPER — nested, inner and anonymous classes

The four kinds, and what distinguishes them

  • Static nested class — declared static inside another class. It is just a top-level class in a namespace: it has no reference to an outer instance and cannot touch outer instance fields.
  • Inner (non-static nested) class — holds an implicit reference to the outer object, so it can use the outer instance fields. It requires an outer instance to exist: outer.new Inner().
  • Local class — declared inside a method, visible only there.
  • Anonymous class — declared and instantiated in one expression, with no name, typically to implement an interface on the spot (a Comparator, an event listener).

The distinction that gets tested

An inner class can access the enclosing object's private members — including via Outer.this.field when names collide. A static nested class cannot, because there is no enclosing instance. If a nested class does not need outer state, make it static: the hidden reference in an inner class keeps the outer object alive and is a known source of memory leaks.

Why anonymous classes exist

They avoid a named file for a one-use implementation. A local or anonymous class may only use local variables that are final or effectively final — because the value is captured (copied), so allowing reassignment would make the two copies disagree.

📖 Exam terms — compilation, parsing & loop patterns (with examples)

COMPILATION — what actually runs
javac Hello.java compiles source into bytecode (Hello.class); java Hello starts the JVM, which executes that bytecode. Java is compiled ONCE to bytecode, then run anywhere a JVM exists — that’s “write once, run anywhere.”
PARSING — text to number
int n = Integer.parseInt("42"); turns the STRING "42" into the int 42. Feed it "4x" and it throws NumberFormatException. (Double.parseDouble for decimals; Scanner’s nextInt parses as it reads.)
THE for LOOP’S THREE COMPONENTS
for (init; condition; update) — run init once, test the condition before each pass, run the update after each pass. for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++): i starts 0, loops while i<5, bumps i each time.
WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — countdown loop
for (int i = 5; i >= 1; i--) {
    System.out.print(i + " ");
}
Start high, test i ≥ 1, step DOWN with i--. Output: 5 4 3 2 1. (Forgetting to flip the condition when counting down gives a loop that never runs.)
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — the accumulate pattern
int total = 0;
int[] prices = {3, 5, 2};
for (int p : prices) {
    total += p;      // running sum: 3, then 8, then 10
}
System.out.println(total);   // 10
Initialize OUTSIDE the loop, add INSIDE. The same shape computes counts, sums, max — it’s the most reused pattern in the course.
WORKED EXAMPLE 3 — recursion, traced properly
int fact(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return 1;      // base case — STOPS the calls
    return n * fact(n - 1);    // smaller problem
}
Trace fact(3): fact(3) = 3 · fact(2) = 3 · 2 · fact(1) = 3 · 2 · 1 = 6. Every recursive method needs a base case and a call that moves toward it — remove either and you get a StackOverflowError.

📖 Worked example — trace a program exactly like the exam

WORKED EXAMPLE — what is printed?
int total = 0;
for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
    total += i * 2;
    System.out.print(total + " ");
}
Trace with a table — one row per loop pass:
• i = 1: total = 0 + 2 = 2 → prints “2 ”
• i = 2: total = 2 + 4 = 6 → prints “6 ”
• i = 3: total = 6 + 6 = 12 → prints “12 ”
Output: 2 6 12. The discipline: write the variable values down EVERY pass; never run the loop in your head all at once.

Why tracing beats memorizing

The D286 OA rewards people who can run the code in their head. Java's arithmetic is driven by the compile-time types of the operands, not the values. 7/2 is int division and yields 3; only if one side is a double literal (7.0/2) do you get 3.5. An int silently wraps on overflow: Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 becomes the most negative int.

Promotion and precedence

In any numeric expression, operands narrower than int (byte, short, char) are promoted to int first. So 'A' + 1 is 66, an int, not the char 'B'. Precedence binds * and / tighter than + and -, so 2 + 3 * 4 - 8 / 2 is 2 + 12 - 4 = 10.

Identity vs equality

== on reference types compares object identity; .equals() compares content. A string literal is interned, but new String("hi") is a fresh object, so == is false while .equals() is true.

Control flow traps

A switch without break falls through into later cases. A labeled break exits the named outer loop, not just the inner one. Overload resolution prefers the most specific applicable method using widening (char to int before long before Object) before boxing. Finally, Java is strictly pass-by-value: a method can mutate the object an array reference points to, but reassigning a primitive parameter never changes the caller's variable. Short-circuit && skips its right side when the left is false, which can prevent an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

📖 Exam terms — objects, failures & containers (with examples)

ACCESSORS & MUTATORS (getters/setters)
Fields stay private; the class exposes accessors (getName — read) and mutators (setName — change). That’s encapsulation: outside code goes through methods, so the class can validate changes.
WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — this disambiguation
public class Part {
    private String name;
    public Part(String name) {
        this.name = name;   // this.name = the FIELD; name = the parameter
    }
}
When a parameter has the same name as a field, the parameter wins inside the method — this. reaches past it to the object’s field. Without this, the line name = name assigns the parameter to itself and the field stays null.
AIOOBE — ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
Valid indices run 0 to length−1. int[] a = new int[3]; then a[3] throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException at RUNTIME (it compiles fine). Classic causes: using <= in a loop condition, or indexing with length.
ARRAYLIST RESIZING
An ArrayList grows automatically: when its internal array fills, it allocates a bigger one and copies the elements over. You never set a size — that’s the difference from a plain array, whose length is fixed forever at creation.
CONTAINMENT (has-a) vs INHERITANCE (is-a)
Containment/composition: a class holds another as a field — a Car HAS-An Engine. Inheritance: a class IS-A specialized parent — a Truck IS-A Vehicle (extends). Exam tell: “has a” → field; “is a” → extends.
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — the equals contract
A correct equals() must be:
• Reflexive: x.equals(x) is true.
• Symmetric: x.equals(y) ⇔ y.equals(x).
• Transitive: x.equals(y) and y.equals(z) ⇒ x.equals(z).
And whenever you override equals, override hashCode too — equal objects must share a hash code, or HashSet/HashMap misplace them. (Same three words as relation properties in discrete math — same meaning.)
WORKED EXAMPLE 3 — string performance
String s = "";
for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) s += i;        // SLOW: copies every pass

StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) sb.append(i);  // FAST: edits in place
String done = sb.toString();
String is immutable — each += builds a whole new string, so a loop of appends is O(n²) copying. StringBuilder mutates one buffer and turns the loop O(n). Rule: concatenating in a loop → StringBuilder.

📖 Worked example — objects and references, the classic trap

WORKED EXAMPLE — two references, one object
int[] a = {1, 2, 3};
int[] b = a;        // b points to the SAME array
b[0] = 99;
System.out.println(a[0]);   // ?
b = a copies the reference, not the array. Both names point at one array in memory, so changing b[0] changes what a sees: it prints 99.

Contrast with primitives: int x = 5; int y = x; y = 9; leaves x = 5, because primitives copy the VALUE. Reference-vs-value is the single most-tested Java idea.

Objects, failures, and containers

Construction runs bottom-up the class hierarchy but top-down in execution: this(...) and super(...) must be the first statement, so the superclass constructor body finishes before the subclass body runs. Only instance methods are polymorphic. Fields and static methods are resolved by the reference's compile-time type (hiding), while overridden instance methods dispatch on the runtime object.

Interfaces and exceptions

When two interfaces supply the same default method, the implementing class must override it and may call A.super.m() explicitly. Exceptions split into checked (subclasses of Exception that are not RuntimeException, e.g. IOException — must be declared or caught) and unchecked (RuntimeException and its subclasses like NullPointerException). A finally block always runs; a return inside finally replaces any value the try was returning.

Collections gotchas

Autoboxing caches Integer objects for -128..127, so == is true for 127 but false for 128 — always use .equals() for value comparison. List<Integer>.remove(int) removes by index, while remove(Object) removes by value; list.remove(1) deletes index 1. If you override equals but not hashCode, hash-based lookups fail because equal objects land in different buckets. Generics use type erasure: List<String> and List<Integer> are the same class at runtime, generic types are invariant (a List<String> is not a List<Object>), and you cannot write new T(). Prefer an ArrayList over a raw array when you need dynamic sizing, and remember it stores boxed Integer objects, not primitives — which is exactly why the remove overload and == traps above bite so often.

A program is a list of instructions a computer carries out in order, one after another, without judgement. That last part is the whole difficulty of programming: the machine does exactly what you wrote, not what you meant, so almost every bug you will ever write is a gap between those two things.

Java specifically is compiled then interpreted. You write .java source, the compiler (javac) turns it into bytecode in a .class file, and the JVM runs that bytecode on whatever machine it is installed on. That two-step is why the same compiled Java file runs on Windows, macOS and Linux unchanged — the phrase the exam uses is "write once, run anywhere".

Hello.java   --javac-->   Hello.class   --java (JVM)-->   output
 (source)                    (bytecode)                     (running program)

Inside the JVM: interpretation and JIT

The JVM does not simply interpret bytecode line by line for ever. It starts by interpreting, and watches which methods run often — the hot ones. Those get handed to the JIT (just-in-time) compiler, which translates them into native machine code for the actual processor, once, and reuses that from then on.

That is why a Java program is often slow for its first second and fast afterwards, and why the old claim that "Java is slow because it is interpreted" is out of date. Bytecode gives portability; the JIT gives back most of the speed.

ToolIsContains
JDKJava Development Kit — to write Javacompiler (javac), tools, and a JRE
JREJava Runtime Environment — to run Javathe JVM and the standard libraries
JVMJava Virtual Machine — executes bytecodethe interpreter and the JIT compiler

The nesting is the exam point: JDK contains the JRE, which contains the JVM. To compile you need the JDK; to run only, the JRE is enough.

Why the two-step matters

The compile-then-run split is the reason two different kinds of failure exist, and questions rely on it. If javac refuses, no class file is produced and nothing runs — so a "compile error" never produces partial output. If compilation succeeds, any failure afterwards happens while the JVM is executing, and by then output may already have appeared. When a question shows some output followed by a crash, it is describing a runtime error; when it shows none at all, suspect a compile error.

📘 DEFINITION

Program: an ordered list of instructions a computer executes

Compiler: a tool that translates source code into another form before the program runs; in Java, into bytecode

Bytecode: the platform-independent instructions in a .class file

JVM: the Java Virtual Machine — the program that executes bytecode on a particular operating system

Interpreter: a program that executes instructions directly rather than translating them ahead of time

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

Everything in this course sits on top of this loop: edit, compile, run, read the message, edit again. When a section later says something is a "compile error" it means javac refused and no .class file was produced, so the program never ran at all — a distinction that decides several exam questions in 1.4 and 2.2.

📊 FIGURE — where a Java program can die — and what you see when it does
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a compile error produces no class file and no output

The file below has one fault: line 4 is missing its semicolon. Watch what the machine actually does with it.

public class Payroll {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int hours = 38;
        int rate = 17
        int gross = hours * rate;
        System.out.println("Gross: " + gross);
    }
}

Step 1 — run the compiler. This is the real message from javac 21:

TERMINAL
$ javac Payroll.java
Payroll.java:4: error: ';' expected
        int rate = 17
                     ^
1 error

Step 2 — look for the class file. There is none:

TERMINAL
$ ls Payroll.class
ls: cannot access 'Payroll.class': No such file or directory

Step 3 — there is nothing to run. The program never executed, so it printed nothing at all — not even the lines above the fault. That is the whole point of the two-step pipeline: javac either produces a complete .class or it produces none.

Notice also where the caret points: at the end of line 4, not at line 5. The compiler read int rate = 17, expected a semicolon next, and found int instead — so it complains at the position where the semicolon should have been.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a runtime error prints everything up to the moment it fails

This one compiles cleanly. Every type is legal and every statement is well formed — the fault is a value, and values are not the compiler's business.

System.out.println("Loading roster...");
int students = 5;
int groups = 0;
System.out.println(students / groups);
System.out.println("done");

Step 1 — javac accepts it and writes the class file. Step 2 — the JVM starts and executes line by line. Line 1 prints. Lines 2 and 3 store values. Line 4 divides 5 by 0, and integer division by zero throws.

ACTUAL OUTPUT
Loading roster...
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ArithmeticException: / by zero

Two things to read off that. First, Loading roster... did appear — the failure happened halfway through, so the earlier output is real. Second, done never printed: an uncaught exception ends the program on the spot, it does not skip the bad line and carry on.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

When a question says "this code has a compile error", the answer can never be "it prints X then crashes". No class file means no execution at all. Conversely, an answer showing some output followed by an exception name is describing a runtime error, and that means the code compiled fine — so do not go hunting for a missing semicolon.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Diagnose from the shape of the output. No output at all plus a message naming a line and a rule = compile error. Some output, then a line starting Exception in thread "main" = runtime error. Full output, wrong numbers = logic error. You can answer most Unit 1 error questions from that alone, without reading the code closely.

Every Java program is built from the same three nested wrappers, and knowing which one an error is complaining about saves you most of the guessing. The outer wrapper is a class, inside it is the main method where execution begins, and inside that are statements, each ending in a semicolon.

public class Main {                         // 1. the class, name must match Main.java
    public static void main(String[] args) {   // 2. where the JVM starts
        System.out.println("Hello");           // 3. one statement, ends with ;
    }
}

System.out.println reads left to right as: in the System class, take the standard out stream, call println on it. The ln is the only difference from print — it adds a newline after the text. That one character is the entire content of a surprising number of "what is the exact output" questions.

Input is the mirror image, and needs a Scanner:

import java.util.Scanner;                 // must be above the class

Scanner scnr = new Scanner(System.in);
int age = scnr.nextInt();                 // reads one int
String name = scnr.next();                // reads one word
String line = scnr.nextLine();            // reads the rest of the line

Reading the structure back

Almost every "what is wrong with this code" question in Unit 1 is answered by checking the three wrappers in order: is the class name identical to the file name, is the main signature exactly public static void main(String[] args), and does every statement end in a semicolon. Those three account for most early compile errors, and the signature is the one people mistype — dropping static compiles fine and then fails at launch with "main method not found", which is a runtime failure rather than a compile one.

📘 DEFINITION

Class: the outer container for Java code; the file name must match the public class name exactly, including case

main method: the method the JVM calls first; its signature is always public static void main(String[] args)

Statement: a single instruction, terminated by a semicolon

Scanner: the standard class for reading typed input, constructed with System.in

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Mixing nextInt() and nextLine() is the classic input bug. nextInt() consumes the number but leaves the newline sitting in the buffer, so the next nextLine() returns an empty string instead of waiting. The fix is an extra throwaway nextLine() after the number.

📊 FIGURE — the anatomy of a Java program, and the three rules attached to it
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — print versus println — the one character that changes the output

Both of these print the same two words. Only the line breaks differ, and "what is the exact output" questions live entirely in that difference.

System.out.print("Ada");
System.out.print("Lovelace");
System.out.println();
System.out.println("Ada");
System.out.println("Lovelace");

Trace it. print writes the characters and leaves the cursor where it is, so the first two calls land on the same line with nothing between them — no space is inserted for you. The bare println() then ends that line. The last two calls each write their text and then end the line, so they occupy two lines.

ACTUAL OUTPUT
AdaLovelace
Ada
Lovelace

Three lines of output from five statements. If you expected Ada Lovelace on the first line, the missing space is the lesson: concatenation and printing add exactly what you wrote and nothing else.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — why nextInt() followed by nextLine() reads an empty string

The user types 37, presses Enter, types Grace Hopper, presses Enter. Here is the version that looks right and is not:

Scanner scnr = new Scanner(System.in);
int age = scnr.nextInt();
String name = scnr.nextLine();
System.out.println("age=" + age);
System.out.println("name=[" + name + "]");
ACTUAL OUTPUT
age=37
name=[]

The reason is the position of the cursor in the input stream. nextInt() consumes the characters 3 and 7 and stops — it does not consume the Enter that followed them. So the newline is still waiting, and nextLine() does exactly what it is asked: it reads to the end of the current line, which is now empty, and returns "" immediately without waiting for the user.

The fix is one throwaway call that swallows the leftover newline:

Scanner scnr = new Scanner(System.in);
int age = scnr.nextInt();
String rest = scnr.nextLine();   // consumes the newline left by nextInt
String name = scnr.nextLine();   // now reads the real line
System.out.println("age=" + age);
System.out.println("rest=[" + rest + "]");
System.out.println("name=[" + name + "]");
ACTUAL OUTPUT
age=37
rest=[]
name=[Grace Hopper]

rest is the empty string — that is the leftover newline, now safely consumed — and name finally holds the full line, spaces included.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Memorise the signature as one unbroken string: public static void main(String[] args). Every word earns a question. Drop static and the file still compiles; it fails at launch with Error: Main method is not static in class ..., which makes it a runtime failure, not a compile error. Change String[] args to anything else and the JVM reports that it cannot find a main method at all.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A local variable has no default value — a field does
System.out.println(fieldInt);
System.out.println(fieldBool);
System.out.println(fieldRef);
System.out.println(fieldDouble);

int local;
local = 5;
System.out.println(local);
0 false null 0.0 5
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Fields are initialised for you: 0, false, null, 0.0.
  2. A local variable gets none of that. Writing int local; System.out.println(local); is a compile error — "variable local might not have been initialized" — not a run-time surprise and not a printed 0.
  3. That is why the assignment above comes before the use. The compiler tracks whether every path assigns the variable before it is read.
🎯 EXAM TIP
This is a favourite exam question because the two rules look alike but are not. Fields default (0 / false / null). Locals do not, and using one before assignment fails to compile. If a question shows int x; System.out.println(x); inside a method, the answer is "does not compile" — never 0.

Comments and whitespace are invisible to the compiler and essential to the reader, which makes them easy to dismiss and easy to test. Java strips them out entirely before the program runs, so they can never change behaviour — only readability.

// single-line: everything after // on this line is ignored

/* multi-line:
   ignored until the closing marker */

/** Javadoc: same as multi-line, but tools read it
 *  to generate documentation. See 6.22 and 7.17. */

Whitespace — spaces, tabs, blank lines — is free-form in Java. You could write an entire program on one line and it would compile. The convention is one statement per line and four spaces of indentation per nesting level, because the indentation is how a human sees the block structure that the braces define.

What comments cost and do not cost

Because comments are stripped before compilation, they cannot slow a program down or change its behaviour — a fact questions occasionally test directly. What they can do is mislead: a comment that no longer matches the code is worse than none, because a reader trusts it. The convention that survives is to comment the why rather than the what. // add 1 to i repeats the code; // skip the header row explains a decision the code cannot state.

📘 DEFINITION

Comment: text ignored by the compiler, written for people reading the code

Whitespace: spaces, tabs and newlines; free-form in Java, so it affects readability but never behaviour

Javadoc comment: a /** */ comment that documentation tools extract into API docs

🎯 EXAM TIP

Watch for questions where indentation misleads. Java decides what belongs to an if by braces, not by how the code is lined up, so a line that looks like it is inside the branch may not be — the specific trap is spelled out in 3.8.

📊 FIGURE — comments and whitespace never reach the generated bytecode
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the same program written unreadably still compiles and prints the same thing

Whitespace in Java is free-form, which means the layout carries no meaning to the compiler. This entire program body is one line:

int hours=38;int rate=17;System.out.println("Pay: "+hours*rate);/* all on one line */

Trace it as three statements, because that is what the semicolons say it is: store 38, store 17, then evaluate "Pay: " + hours * rate. Multiplication binds tighter than the +, so 38 × 17 = 646 happens first, and only then is 646 joined onto the text.

ACTUAL OUTPUT
Pay: 646

Reformatted across four indented lines, the output is byte-for-byte identical. The indentation was for you, not for javac — which is exactly why an exam question can indent a line misleadingly and still be a fair question.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — where a comment is not a comment

The comment markers only count when the compiler is reading code. Inside a string literal they are ordinary characters:

System.out.println("See https://www.wgu.edu/catalog");
System.out.println("a" /* mid-expression comment */ + "b");

Line 1 contains // in the middle of https://. If the compiler treated that as a comment, the closing quote and the semicolon would vanish and the file would not compile. It does not — the // is inside a string literal, so it is just text.

Line 2 shows the reverse: a /* ... */ comment sitting in the middle of an expression is stripped, and the two string literals close up around the gap as though it was never there.

ACTUAL OUTPUT
See https://www.wgu.edu/catalog
ab

So the rule is positional: // and /* start a comment everywhere except inside a string or character literal, and a quote inside a comment is likewise just a character. This is why a stray unclosed quote can produce a cascade of nonsense errors — the compiler's idea of where code ends and text begins has been shifted.

Errors are worth sorting into three kinds, because the kind tells you where to look. Two of them stop you before the program runs; the third one lets the program run and produce the wrong answer, which is why it is the dangerous one.

int x = "hello";       // COMPILE  error — types do not match, no .class produced
int y = 5 / 0;         // RUNTIME  error — compiles, then throws ArithmeticException
int avg = a + b / 2;   // LOGIC    error — runs happily, answer is simply wrong

A warning sits below all three: the compiler is uneasy but produces the class file anyway. Unchecked casts and deprecated methods are the usual causes. Warnings do not stop you, so they accumulate quietly.

Which error you are looking at

The practical value of the three-way split is that it tells you where to look before you start looking. A compile error names a line and a rule, so you read that line and the one above it. A runtime error names an exception type, and the type is the diagnosis — ArithmeticException means a division, NullPointerException means something was never assigned, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException means a bound was wrong. A logic error names nothing at all, which is why it needs a trace table rather than a message.

📘 DEFINITION

Syntax / compile-time error: code that breaks the rules of the language; the compiler refuses and nothing runs

Runtime error: the program compiles but fails while running, usually by throwing an exception

Logic error: the program compiles and runs but computes the wrong result

Warning: a compiler complaint that does not prevent compilation

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

This split reappears constantly. Unit 2 hinges on it (an uninitialised local is a compile error while integer overflow is a silent logic error), and Unit 12 exists entirely to handle the second category deliberately rather than by accident.

✅ Also covered in depth: Intro to CS → from source code to running program

📊 FIGURE — reading the symptom backwards to the kind of error
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a runtime error, read from its own message

Every type here is correct, so javac has no objection. The fault is an index that does not exist, and only the running program can discover that.

int[] scores = {88, 92, 79};
System.out.println("first: " + scores[0]);
System.out.println("fourth: " + scores[3]);
ACTUAL OUTPUT
first: 88
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 3 out of bounds for length 3

Read the message as three separate facts. The type — ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException — says the fault is an index. The detail — "Index 3 out of bounds for length 3" — says which index and what the limit was, and reading it carefully answers the question on its own: three elements are numbered 0, 1, 2. The partial output — first: 88 — says the program got that far, which locates the failure at the line after it.

That triple is the whole technique for runtime errors: type tells you the category, detail tells you the value, and the last line of output tells you the place.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a logic error: the code that runs perfectly and is wrong

Two students score 88 and 92. Their average is obviously 90. This code is entirely legal Java:

int a = 88, b = 92;
int wrong = a + b / 2;
int right = (a + b) / 2;
System.out.println(wrong);
System.out.println(right);
ACTUAL OUTPUT
134
90

Step by step: / binds tighter than +, so a + b / 2 means 88 + (92 / 2) = 88 + 46 = 134. The average of two scores between 0 and 100 came out as 134, and nothing anywhere reported a problem — no red underline, no exception, no warning.

That is the defining property of a logic error: the only detector is a value you worked out beforehand. Had you not known the answer was 90, 134 would simply have been the answer.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

A missing semicolon is a compile error even when the offending line looks perfect, because the compiler reports it where the semicolon should have been. Given int rate = 17 on line 4 followed by another statement on line 5, javac says Payroll.java:4: error: ';' expected with the caret past the end of line 4. Students read line 4, see nothing wrong with the assignment, and start editing line 5. The caret position, not the line number alone, is the thing to read.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Learn the four common exception types as a lookup table, because the type is the diagnosis: ArithmeticException ⇒ integer division or modulo by zero; NullPointerException ⇒ a method called on something never assigned; ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException ⇒ an index outside 0..length−1; NumberFormatException ⇒ Integer.parseInt handed something that is not a number. Questions usually give the message and ask for the cause.

A computer only ever manipulates numbers, and only ever in binary. Text, images and instructions are all encodings on top of that, which is the single fact that makes 2.13 (binary), 2.14 (characters) and 2.16 (overflow) make sense rather than feel arbitrary.

The layers are worth naming from the bottom up: transistors form logic gates, gates form circuits, circuits execute machine instructions, machine instructions are what your bytecode is eventually turned into. Each layer hides the one below it, which is exactly why you can write x + y without knowing any of this — until a value overflows and the hidden layer shows through.

Why everything reduces to numbers

Saying a computer stores only numbers sounds like trivia until it explains behaviour. Text is numbers under an encoding, so comparing strings compares character codes and 'Z' sorts before 'a'. Colours are numbers, so image files are arrays. And because every type is a fixed number of bits, every numeric type has a hard ceiling — which is not a Java quirk but the hardware showing through, and it is what makes integer overflow in 2.16 possible at all.

📘 DEFINITION

Bit: a single binary digit, 0 or 1

Byte: eight bits; the smallest normally addressable unit of memory

Machine instruction: a single operation the processor executes directly

Memory: numbered storage locations, each holding a byte

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

Because every type is a fixed number of bits, every numeric type has a hard maximum. That is not a Java quirk — it is the hardware showing through, and it is why int stops at about 2.1 billion (2.13, 2.16).

📊 FIGURE — the abstraction stack, and the one place it leaks
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a character is a number wearing a costume

The claim "a computer only stores numbers" is testable in four lines. A char holds a Unicode code value; printing it shows a letter, and doing arithmetic on it shows the number.

char grade = 'B';
System.out.println(grade);
System.out.println((int) grade);
System.out.println(grade + 1);
System.out.println((char)(grade + 1));
ACTUAL OUTPUT
B
66
67
C

Line by line: printing the char itself shows B, because println has a version that formats a char as a character. Casting to int exposes the stored number, 66. Adding 1 promotes the char to an int first, so the expression has type int and prints 67 — not C. Casting the result back to char finally gives C.

So the same 66 bits are a letter or a number depending only on how they are interpreted. Nothing about the storage changed between line 2 and line 3.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — counting the values a fixed number of bits can hold

If a type is n bits wide it has exactly 2n distinct bit patterns, so it has exactly 2n possible values — no more. For signed whole numbers Java splits them evenly around zero: 2n−1 negatives, zero, and 2n−1−1 positives.

System.out.println(Integer.MAX_VALUE);
System.out.println(Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1);
System.out.println(Byte.MAX_VALUE);
System.out.println(Integer.toBinaryString(11));
ACTUAL OUTPUT
2147483647
-2147483648
127
1011

Work the arithmetic yourself. An int is 32 bits, so 232 = 4,294,967,296 patterns; half of them are negative, giving a top value of 231−1 = 2,147,483,647 — exactly line 1. A byte is 8 bits, so 27−1 = 127 — exactly line 3.

Line 2 is the leak. Adding one to the largest pattern carries out of the top bit; the carry has nowhere to go and is discarded, and the sign bit flips. The answer is the most negative int, printed with no warning whatsoever. Line 4 confirms the underlying representation: 11 in binary is 1011, which is 8 + 2 + 1.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

"The computer stores the letter B" is the wrong mental model and it makes several later sections look arbitrary. It stores 66. That is why 'A' < 'a' is true (65 < 97), why '7' - '0' gives 7, and why System.out.println('A' + 1) prints 66 rather than B. Whenever character behaviour surprises you, replace each character with its code and re-read the line.

🎯 EXAM TIP

The exam turns bit width into range questions. Memorise one worked chain rather than four numbers: n bits ⇒ 2n patterns ⇒ signed range −2n−1 to 2n−1−1. From that, 8 bits gives −128..127, 16 bits gives −32,768..32,767, and 32 bits gives roughly ±2.1 billion — all three derived, none memorised.
