An IDE bundles the editor, the compiler and the debugger into one window so that the edit-compile-run loop takes a keystroke instead of three commands. Nothing it does is magic: everything an IDE performs, javac and java can do from a terminal, which is worth remembering when a question asks what is actually required to run Java.

What an IDE genuinely adds is speed of feedback — it underlines a type error as you type rather than at compile time — plus refactoring, autocompletion and a visual debugger. What it cannot do is find logic errors for you, because to the IDE a wrong answer looks exactly like a right one.

The IDEs you will meet by name

Exam questions ask you to recognise a Java IDE rather than to use one, so the names are worth knowing. Eclipse, IntelliJ IDEA, NetBeans and Visual Studio Code are the common ones; BlueJ and DrJava are teaching-oriented. Note what is not an IDE: a plain text editor such as Notepad, and the JDK itself, which is a toolchain rather than an environment.

What the IDE is not doing for you

An IDE removes typing, not thinking. It will underline a type error as you type, autocomplete a method name and jump to a definition — all of which catch syntax problems early. It cannot tell you that your average is computed with integer division, because to the tool a wrong number looks exactly like a right one. That boundary is worth holding: the IDE handles the errors the compiler would have caught anyway, and the ones that actually cost marks are the ones it cannot see.

📘 DEFINITION

IDE: Integrated Development Environment — editor, compiler and debugger in one application

JDK: Java Development Kit — the compiler and tools; required to write Java

JRE: Java Runtime Environment — the JVM and libraries; enough to run Java, not to compile it

Debugger: a tool that pauses a running program so you can inspect variables

🎯 EXAM TIP

JDK versus JRE is a favourite question. To compile you need the JDK; to only run a compiled program the JRE is enough. The JDK contains a JRE, so a machine with the JDK can do both.

✅ Also covered in depth: Java Basics → JVM, JRE, and JDK

What actually happens when you press Run

Two separate programs are involved, and the exam expects you to name which does what.

📊 FIGURE — source to bytecode to execution
StepToolProduces
Compilejavac Hello.javaHello.class — bytecode
Runjava Hellothe JVM executes the bytecode

Write once, run anywhere is exactly this split: javac targets the JVM rather than any real processor, so the bytecode is portable and only the JVM has to be rewritten per platform.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

The file name must match the public class exactly, capitals included — Hello.java for public class Hello. And you run java Hello, not java Hello.class.

📊 FIGURE — what is inside the JDK, and which layer each task needs
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the whole edit-compile-run loop with no IDE at all

An IDE is a convenience over two commands. Here is the entire loop in a terminal — this is the real transcript, and the IDE's Run button does exactly this behind the scenes.

public class Hello {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello, WGU!");
    }
}
TERMINAL
$ javac Hello.java          # the compiler; silence means success
$ ls
Hello.class  Hello.java
$ java Hello                # note: no .class on the end
Hello, WGU!

Three details are examined. The compiler is given the file name Hello.java; the launcher is given the class name Hello, with no extension — java Hello.class fails. And javac printing nothing is success: compilers report problems, not progress.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the error an IDE cannot underline

Twenty questions, seventeen correct. The percentage is obviously 85. This compiles with no error, no warning, and no red underline anywhere:

int correct = 17;
int items = 20;
int percent = correct / items * 100;
System.out.println("Score: " + percent + "%");
ACTUAL OUTPUT
Score: 0%

Trace it in the order Java actually uses. / and * have equal precedence, so evaluation runs strictly left to right: 17 / 20 is computed first, both operands are int, so the result is the truncated 0. Then 0 * 100 is 0.

The tool cannot help here, because every type is legal and every value is a valid int. To the IDE a wrong number looks exactly like a right one — which is precisely the boundary the section is drawing. Writing correct * 100 / items gives 85, because the multiplication happens while the value is still large enough to survive truncation.

Following one statement through the hardware explains why some operations are thousands of times slower than others. The processor fetches an instruction from memory, decodes it, executes it, and stores the result — the fetch-decode-execute cycle — billions of times per second.

The speed differences come from distance. Registers live inside the processor and are effectively instant. Cache is close and fast. Main memory (RAM) is further and noticeably slower. Disk is slower again by orders of magnitude, which is why file operations in Unit 9 are treated so differently from ordinary variable access.

Input, output and storage devices

The hardware categories are asked directly. Input devices send data in — keyboard, mouse, scanner, microphone, camera. Output devices send results out — monitor, printer, speakers. A few are both, and touchscreens are the standard example. Storage devices — hard disk, SSD, USB drive — are a separate category again, because they retain data rather than moving it in or out.

Why the speed ladder matters to your code

The distances in the hardware explain performance differences you will meet later. A variable lives in registers or cache and is effectively free to read. An object on the heap is slightly further away. A file is thousands of times slower again, which is why Unit 9 treats file access so differently from ordinary assignment, and why reading a file line by line inside a loop is a very different proposition from reading a variable inside one.

📘 DEFINITION

CPU: the processor; fetches, decodes and executes instructions

Register: a tiny storage location inside the CPU; the fastest memory there is

RAM: main memory; fast, addressable, and erased when power is lost

Storage: disk or SSD; slow compared with RAM but survives power loss

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

RAM being volatile is the reason files exist at all. Everything your program holds in variables disappears when it ends, so anything that must outlive the run has to be written to a file — the problem Unit 9 solves.

📊 FIGURE — distance from the processor is the whole explanation for speed
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — one Java statement, expanded into the steps the processor runs

The fetch–decode–execute cycle is not a metaphor. Compile this class and disassemble it with javap -c — a JDK tool — and the individual steps are printed out.

public class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int total = 0;
        int price = 42;
        total = total + price;
        System.out.println(total);
    }
}
TERMINAL
$ javac Demo.java
$ javap -c Demo
  public static void main(java.lang.String[]);
    Code:
       0: iconst_0
       1: istore_1
       2: bipush        42
       4: istore_2
       5: iload_1
       6: iload_2
       7: iadd
       8: istore_1
       9: getstatic     #7   // System.out
      12: iload_1
      13: invokevirtual #13  // println
      16: return

Read the middle four instructions against the source line total = total + price;. iload_1 fetches total into the working area. iload_2 fetches price. iadd executes the addition. istore_1 stores the result back into total. Fetch, fetch, execute, store — one readable line of Java became four separate machine-level steps, each one moving a value between storage and the processor.

That is also why the memory ladder matters: every iload and istore is a trip to storage, and the price of that trip depends entirely on which rung the value is sitting on.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — RAM is erased, disk is not — demonstrated in one program

The reason Unit 9 exists is visible in nine lines. A value is held in a variable, written to a file, then destroyed in memory and read back from disk.

int reading = 72;
System.out.println("in RAM: " + reading);

PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter("sensor.txt");
out.println(reading);
out.close();

reading = 0;                       // the variable is gone
System.out.println("variable cleared: " + reading);

BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("sensor.txt"));
System.out.println("read back from disk: " + in.readLine());
in.close();
ACTUAL OUTPUT
in RAM: 72
variable cleared: 0
read back from disk: 72

The variable genuinely lost its value — line 2 of the output proves it. The 72 survived anyway, because a copy had been pushed down the ladder to storage, which does not depend on power or on the program still running.

Note what it cost. The two file operations are the slowest lines in the program by several orders of magnitude, and they are the only ones that needed close() and a throws declaration. Persistence is bought with time and ceremony; that trade is the whole content of the file chapter.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

"Variables are stored on the hard disk" is a common wrong answer. Variables live in registers, cache and RAM — all volatile. Nothing your program holds in a variable survives the program ending, let alone the power going off. The related confusion is memory versus storage: RAM is measured in gigabytes and cleared on shutdown, storage is measured in hundreds of gigabytes and is not.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Two orderings are worth being able to write from memory. Speed, fastest first: register, cache, RAM, SSD, hard disk. The cycle, in order: fetch, decode, execute, store. Questions are usually "which is faster" or "what comes after decode", and both are answered straight from those lists.

📊 FIGURE — the hardware a program actually runs on
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Where a running program's data actually sits
int[] inMemory = new int[3];
inMemory[0] = 42;
System.out.println("in RAM while running: " + inMemory[0]);

out.println(42);
out.close();

java.util.Scanner in = new java.util.Scanner(new java.io.File("kept.txt"));
System.out.println("read back from storage: " + in.nextInt());
in.close();
in RAM while running: 42 read back from storage: 42
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The array lives in RAM. RAM is volatile — cut the power and it is gone, which is why the value has to be written somewhere else to survive.
  2. Writing to a file puts the value on storage, which persists; reading it back proves it outlived the variable.
  3. The motherboard is the main circuit board holding the CPU, RAM and the sockets and buses connecting them. A peripheral is a device attached to the machine that is not part of that core — a keyboard, printer, or external drive.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Keep the split straight: RAM is fast and volatile and holds your variables while the program runs; storage is slower and persistent and holds files between runs. The motherboard connects the components, and peripherals are what plug into it.

Java was released by Sun Microsystems in 1995, designed around a goal earlier languages had not met: compile once, run on any machine. C and C++ compiled straight to machine code, which meant recompiling for every platform; Java compiled to bytecode and let the JVM absorb the differences.

Its other design decisions were reactions to C++ pain points. Automatic garbage collection removed manual memory freeing (Unit 8). Removing pointer arithmetic removed a whole family of crashes. Enforced exception handling made failure explicit (Unit 12). Generics arrived later, in Java 5 (Unit 13), and var later still, in Java 10 (2.22).

What the design decisions bought

Each Java feature the exam mentions was a response to a specific pain. Automatic garbage collection removed the crashes caused by freeing memory twice or never. Dropping pointer arithmetic removed a family of security holes. Checked exceptions made failure visible in the method signature rather than in a comment. Bytecode removed the need to ship a different binary per platform. If a question asks what a feature is for, the answer is nearly always "it removed a whole class of bug that the previous language allowed".

📘 DEFINITION

Platform independence: the property that compiled bytecode runs unchanged on any machine with a JVM

Garbage collection: automatic reclaiming of memory no longer reachable by the program

Java SE: Java Standard Edition — the core language and libraries this course covers

🎯 EXAM TIP

The exam does not ask for release dates. It asks what problem a feature solved — platform independence, automatic memory management, explicit error handling. Learn the "why", not the timeline.

✅ Also covered in depth: Java Basics → JVM, JRE, and JDK

📊 FIGURE — what "write once, run anywhere" actually moves
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a class file is aimed at a JVM version — and you can read which one

"Platform independent" does not mean "version independent". Compile the smallest possible class and inspect the header that javac wrote into it:

TERMINAL
$ javac Hello.java
$ javap -v Hello.class
  Compiled from "Hello.java"
public class Hello
  minor version: 0
  major version: 65
  flags: (0x0021) ACC_PUBLIC, ACC_SUPER

Major version 65 is Java 21 (the scheme is simple: 52 = Java 8, 55 = Java 11, 61 = Java 17, 65 = Java 21). That number is a floor, not a preference. Hand this exact file to a Java 17 JVM and it refuses to load it with UnsupportedClassVersionError — a runtime failure, not a compile one, because the compiler is long finished by then.

So the promise is precise: the same bytecode runs on any operating system that has a JVM of at least that version. The portability Java bought is across platforms, and the price is a version contract that shows up in the class file itself.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a feature that did not exist yet — the same file, two compilers

var arrived in Java 10, and the compiler can be told to pretend it is older. That makes the history concrete rather than a date to memorise:

public class Modern {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var total = 1250;
        System.out.println("Total: " + total);
    }
}
TERMINAL
$ javac --release 8 Modern.java
Modern.java:3: error: cannot find symbol
        var total = 1250;
        ^
  symbol:   class var
  location: class Modern
1 error

Read that message closely, because it says exactly what "the feature did not exist" means. The Java 8 compiler does not know var is a keyword at all — it assumes you meant a class called var and reports that no such class exists.

TERMINAL
$ javac Modern.java        # the modern compiler, no --release flag
$ java Modern
Total: 1250

Same file, same text, two different answers. Every feature the exam mentions — generics in Java 5, var in Java 10 — works this way: it is a rule the compiler learned on a specific date, not a change in the hardware.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Three confusions in this section are worth separating. Bytecode is not machine code — the CPU cannot run a .class file; the JVM has to. Portable means portable across operating systems, not across JVM versions — newer bytecode on an older JVM throws UnsupportedClassVersionError. Problem solving is the part that does not look like programming and decides whether the programming works. The order that survives contact with real problems is: understand the problem, work one example by hand, write the steps in plain language, then translate those steps into code — and only then worry about syntax.

Working an example by hand is the step people skip and the step that catches the most bugs. If you cannot compute the answer for one specific input on paper, no amount of Java will get you there, because you do not yet know what you are asking the machine to do.

Problem: average of three test scores
By hand: (88 + 92 + 79) / 3  ->  259 / 3  ->  86.33
Steps:   1. read three scores   2. add them   3. divide by 3   4. print
Trap:    if all four are int, step 3 gives 86 — see 2.5 and 2.11

Why the hand-trace is not optional

Working one example by hand feels like a delay and is the fastest route to a correct program, because it converts a vague understanding into a specific expectation. Once you know that three scores of 88, 92 and 79 must give 86.33, you have a test: if the program prints 86, you know immediately that the division truncated, and you know where to look. Without that number you only know the output "looks wrong", which is a far harder position to debug from — and on an exam it is the same technique, since a trace table answers the question directly.

📘 DEFINITION

Algorithm: a finite sequence of unambiguous steps that solves a problem

Pseudocode: steps written in structured plain language rather than a programming language

Decomposition: breaking a problem into smaller sub-problems that can be solved separately

Trace: stepping through code by hand, tracking each variable value

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

Tracing by hand is also the exam skill. Most "what does this print" questions are answered by writing the variables in a column and updating them line by line — not by recognising the pattern.

📊 FIGURE — why working one case by hand comes before writing any code
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the average of three test scores, done both ways

Follow the four steps. Understand: add three scores, divide by three. By hand: 88 + 92 + 79 = 259, and 259 ÷ 3 = 86.33. Steps: read three, total them, divide, print. Translate:

int s1 = 88, s2 = 92, s3 = 79;
int total = s1 + s2 + s3;
System.out.println("total = " + total);

int avgInt = total / 3;
System.out.println("int average    = " + avgInt);

double avgD = (double) total / 3;
System.out.println("double average = " + avgD);
System.out.printf("rounded        = %.2f%n", avgD);
ACTUAL OUTPUT
total = 259
int average    = 86
double average = 86.33333333333333
rounded        = 86.33

The hand-worked 259 confirms the totalling. Then the two averages diverge, and the hand-worked 86.33 tells you instantly which one is wrong: total / 3 has two integer operands, so the .33 is discarded before it is ever stored. Casting one operand to double first keeps it.

Had you not computed 86.33 in advance, 86 would have looked entirely plausible — which is exactly the failure step 2 prevents.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — decomposing a problem into two operations you already have

"A project takes 45 days. Express that as whole weeks plus leftover days." There is no weeks() method; the problem has to be broken into pieces the language already provides.

By hand first: 45 ÷ 7 is 6 remainder 3, so 6 weeks and 3 days. Two separate quantities, so two separate operations: the whole part of the division, and the remainder.

int days = 45;
int weeks = days / 7;       // whole groups: integer division keeps only the whole part
int leftover = days % 7;    // what did not fill a group
System.out.println(days + " days = " + weeks + " weeks and " + leftover + " days");
ACTUAL OUTPUT
45 days = 6 weeks and 3 days

This is the shape decomposition usually takes: not one clever operation, but two ordinary ones applied to the same value. Note also that integer division — the villain of the previous example — is exactly the right tool here, because "whole weeks" genuinely means "throw the remainder away". The operation is not wrong or right on its own; it is right when the hand-worked answer says the fraction should be discarded.

🎯 EXAM TIP

For any "what does this print" question, build a two-column trace table: variable names across the top, one row per statement, and update only the variables that change. It is slower for the first two lines and much faster after that, and it is immune to the pattern-matching mistakes that the distractors are built to catch. Write the table even when you are confident — the questions are designed so that confidence is the trap.

The practical case for programming in this degree is narrower than the general one: D286 is the gate to every later software course, and the concepts here are the vocabulary those courses assume. Loops and arrays in Units 4 and 5 become the data structures course. Classes in Unit 7 become the object-oriented design course. Big-O in 17.3 becomes algorithms.

Within Java itself, the payoff is automation of anything repetitive and exact — which is precisely what a loop is. The rest of the course is a series of tools for describing that repetition more precisely.

Where the effort pays

Weighting revision by exam weight rather than by unit count is worth doing deliberately. Units 2 to 7 — variables, branches, loops, arrays, methods and classes — carry most of the questions, and they are also the units everything later is built from: exceptions are branches on failure, collections are arrays that grow, and inheritance is classes reusing classes. Time spent on Unit 2 pays twice, once directly and once through everything that assumes it.

📘 DEFINITION

Automation: having a program perform a repetitive task reliably and identically each time

Abstraction: hiding detail behind a name so it can be used without being re-derived

🎯 EXAM TIP

Weight your revision by exam weight, not by section count. Units 2 to 7 — variables, branches, loops, arrays, methods, classes — carry the majority of the questions. Units 15, 16 and 18 carry far fewer.

📊 FIGURE — the dependency graph the rest of the course hangs off
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — automation: the same calculation, exactly, every time

The case for a program is not that it is clever but that it is repeatable. Sales tax on a $12.99 item at 7.25%:

double price = 12.99;
double taxRate = 0.0725;
double tax = price * taxRate;
System.out.printf("tax  = %.4f%n", tax);
System.out.printf("total = %.2f%n", price + tax);
ACTUAL OUTPUT
tax  = 0.9418
total = 13.93

Two things worth noticing beyond the arithmetic. The exact tax is 0.941775, and %.4f shows 0.9418 — the format string rounds for display without changing the stored value, which is why the total uses the full precision and comes out at 13.93 rather than 13.9318 rounded twice.

And the point of the variables: change taxRate to 0.08 and every figure updates consistently. Done by hand across a hundred items, a rate change is a hundred chances to make an arithmetic slip; done here it is one character.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — abstraction: a name that hides a calculation you no longer have to do

Square roots are computed by repeated refinement. Here are two rounds of that refinement done by hand, next to the library call that does the whole thing:

double n = 2;
double guess = 1;

guess = (guess + n / guess) / 2;
System.out.println("one step by hand:  " + guess);

guess = (guess + n / guess) / 2;
System.out.println("two steps by hand: " + guess);

System.out.println("Math.sqrt(2):      " + Math.sqrt(2));
ACTUAL OUTPUT
one step by hand:  1.5
two steps by hand: 1.4166666666666665
Math.sqrt(2):      1.4142135623730951

Two rounds of hand work gets three digits right. Math.sqrt gets sixteen, in one call, and you never had to know the method it used.

That is what abstraction buys: a name standing in for a procedure, so the procedure stops being your problem. The same move happens at every scale in this course — a method name hides a block of statements (Unit 6), a class name hides a set of fields and methods (Unit 7), and System.out.println has been hiding the entire output system since your first line of code.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

The commonest revision mistake here is treating all eighteen units as equally weighted because they are equally numbered. They are not. Units 2 to 7 carry the bulk of the questions and everything later is built from them, so a gap in Unit 2 costs marks twice — once in its own questions and again in every loop, array and method question that assumes it. If your time is limited, the correct order is not "start at 1 and go forwards", it is "make Units 2–7 solid first".

Two of the specific ways Java is unforgiving are worth isolating early, because they cause errors that read as mysterious. The first is that Java is case-sensitive everywhere: Count, count and COUNT are three different names, and system.out.println simply does not exist.

The second is that whitespace is free-form but punctuation is not. A missing semicolon, an unmatched brace, or a missing closing quote produces an error message that often points at the following line, because that is where the compiler finally noticed something was wrong.

System.out.println("hi")     // missing ;   error reported on the NEXT line
if (x > 5) {                 // missing }   error reported at end of file
String s = "unterminated ;   // missing "   error mentions an illegal character

Where the compiler points, and where the error is

The two rules combine into a practical habit. Because Java is case-sensitive, an identifier that "looks right" may still be wrong, and the compiler will report it as an unknown symbol rather than a typo. Because punctuation errors are noticed late, the reported line is often one below the real fault. So the routine when a message makes no sense is: check the line above for a missing semicolon or brace, then check the spelling and capitalisation of every name on the reported line. Between them those two checks resolve most early compile errors.

📘 DEFINITION

Case sensitivity: the rule that upper and lower case letters are distinct in identifiers and keywords

Syntax: the grammar rules of the language; violations stop compilation

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

When the compiler points at a line that looks fine, check the line above it. Missing semicolons and unclosed braces are almost always reported one line late.

📊 FIGURE — a missing brace is reported at the end of the file, not at the brace
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — one wrong capital letter, and the message that follows

Java is case-sensitive everywhere — in keywords, in class names and in method names. This file has exactly one capital letter out of place:

public class Greeter {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String name = "Ada";
        System.out.Println("Hello, " + name);
    }
}
TERMINAL
$ javac Greeter.java
Greeter.java:4: error: cannot find symbol
        System.out.Println("Hello, " + name);
                  ^
  symbol:   method Println(String)
  location: variable out of type PrintStream
1 error

The message is worth decoding, because "cannot find symbol" is the message you will see most often in this course. symbol: names what it looked for — a method called Println taking a String. location: names where it looked — on out, which is a PrintStream. The caret sits under the dot before the name.

So the compiler is not saying "you made a typo"; it has no concept of a typo. It is saying "there is no such thing here". Whenever you see cannot find symbol, check spelling and capitalisation of the name under the caret before anything else.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — an unclosed brace, and why the line number is useless

Here the mistake is a missing closing brace for the if block on line 4:

public class Roster {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int students = 24;
        if (students > 20) {
            System.out.println("Split into two sections");
        System.out.println("Roster complete");
    }
}
TERMINAL
$ javac Roster.java
Roster.java:8: error: reached end of file while parsing
}
 ^
1 error

Trace what the compiler did. It opened a brace at line 1 for the class, another at line 2 for main, another at line 4 for the if. It then read three closing braces — lines 7 and 8 close the if and main — and reached the end of the file still owing one. Only at that moment could it know something was wrong, so line 8 is where it complains.

The reported line is therefore the last place the error could have been detected, not the first place it existed. Nothing on line 8 needs fixing. The habit that follows: for "reached end of file while parsing", count braces from the top; for ';' expected, look at the end of the line named and at the line above it.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Two messages, two fixed responses, and between them they cover most Unit 1 compile errors. cannot find symbol ⇒ a name is misspelled, miscapitalised, or not declared yet — look at the token under the caret. ';' expected or reached end of file while parsing ⇒ punctuation — look at the end of the named line and upwards, never below it. Answering "which line has the error" by trusting the reported number is the mistake these questions are built to catch.

This section puts 1.2 and 1.3 together in one worked program: read two names, join them, print a sentence. Nothing new appears — it exists so you see the whole loop of import, class, main, input, output at real size.

import java.util.Scanner;

public class MarriedNames {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Scanner scnr = new Scanner(System.in);

        System.out.println("Enter first name:");
        String first = scnr.next();
        System.out.println("Enter last name:");
        String last  = scnr.next();

        System.out.println("Mr. and Mrs. " + first + " " + last);
    }
}

The + here is doing something different from arithmetic: when either operand is a String, + concatenates instead of adding. That double meaning is set up properly in 2.15, and it is the reason "total: " + 3 + 4 prints total: 34 rather than total: 7.

Why this example is placed here

The program is deliberately small so that the whole loop is visible at once: import at the top, class, main, read, compute, print. It is also the first place the double meaning of + appears — joining text rather than adding numbers — which is worth noticing now because it becomes a trap in 2.15. And the choice of next() over nextLine() is doing real work: the program depends on reading exactly one word at a time, and swapping the two would break it in a way that produces no error message at all.

📘 DEFINITION

Concatenation: joining strings with +, producing a new String

next(): Scanner method that reads a single whitespace-delimited word

Prompt: output printed to tell the user what input is expected

🎯 EXAM TIP

Use next() for one word and nextLine() for a whole line including spaces. A full name typed as "Ada Lovelace" needs nextLine(); two separate next() calls would split it — which is exactly what this program relies on.

📊 FIGURE — the data path through the married-names program
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — running the program, prompts and all

The complete program, run with Ada and Lovelace typed on separate lines:

import java.util.Scanner;

public class MarriedNames {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Scanner scnr = new Scanner(System.in);
        System.out.println("Enter first name:");
        String first = scnr.next();
        System.out.println("Enter last name:");
        String last  = scnr.next();
        System.out.println("Mr. and Mrs. " + first + " " + last);
    }
}
ACTUAL OUTPUT
Enter first name:
Enter last name:
Mr. and Mrs. Ada Lovelace

Three lines of output, and the prompts are two of them — a prompt is just output, so it counts in "what does this print" questions. The typed input itself is not in the program's output; it appears on your screen because the terminal echoes what you type, not because the program printed it. That distinction catches people out on trace questions that supply the input separately.

Count the spaces in the last line. There is one after Mrs. because the literal "Mr. and Mrs. " ends with a space, and one between the names because + " " + put it there. Remove that middle piece and the output becomes Mr. and Mrs. AdaLovelace.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the + that adds and the + that joins

The same symbol does two different jobs, and which one it does depends on the operand types — evaluated strictly left to right.

System.out.println("total: " + 3 + 4);
System.out.println("total: " + (3 + 4));
System.out.println(3 + 4 + " total");
ACTUAL OUTPUT
total: 34
total: 7
7 total

Line 1: the leftmost + has a String on its left, so it concatenates, producing "total: 3". The next + now also has a String on its left, so it concatenates too, giving "total: 34". No addition ever happened.

Line 2: parentheses force 3 + 4 to be evaluated first. Both operands are int, so that + adds, giving 7, and only then is the 7 joined onto the text.

Line 3: the leftmost + has two ints, so it adds — giving 7 — and the String appears only in the second +. Same three values, three arrangements, three answers. The rule to carry: once a String has appeared on the left, every + after it in that expression joins rather than adds.

A variable is a named box in memory that holds one value at a time. Three things happen to it, and keeping them apart explains most early confusion: you declare it (give it a name and a type), you initialize it (put the first value in), and you assign to it (replace whatever is there).

int x;          // declaration — the box exists, nothing in it yet
x = 5;          // assignment — 5 goes in
int y = 7;      // declaration + initialization together
y = 9;          // assignment — 7 is gone, replaced by 9

The equals sign is the source of the confusion. It is not a statement of fact, it is an instruction: work out the right-hand side, then put the result in the left. That is why x = x + 1 is perfectly sensible in code and nonsense in algebra.

Why the three operations are worth separating

Declaration, initialization and assignment get conflated because a single line often does two of them. Keeping them apart explains error messages precisely: "already defined" means you declared twice, "might not have been initialized" means you declared but never gave a value, and a wrong result with no message at all means you assigned something you did not intend. The equals sign is not a claim of equality but an instruction — evaluate the right, store into the left — which is why x = x + 1 is ordinary code and nonsense as algebra.

📘 DEFINITION

Variable: a named location in memory holding one value of a declared type

Declaration: names a variable and its type

Initialization: giving a variable its first value at the moment of declaration

Assignment: storing a value into an existing variable, replacing what was there

🎯 EXAM TIP

Assignment copies the value for primitives. int b = a; gives b its own copy, so changing a afterwards leaves b alone. For objects, what gets copied is the reference — the same distinction returns in 2.15 with Strings and again in Unit 7.

📊 FIGURE — declare, initialize, assign — and what the equals sign really means
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — following one variable through every operation

Three lines, three different things happening to the same slot. Track the value after each statement.

int quantity = 3;
int unitCents = 1299;
System.out.println("quantity=" + quantity + " unitCents=" + unitCents);

quantity = quantity + 2;
System.out.println("after +2: quantity=" + quantity);

int totalCents = quantity * unitCents;
System.out.println("totalCents=" + totalCents);
ACTUAL OUTPUT
quantity=3 unitCents=1299
after +2: quantity=5
totalCents=6495

Line 1 is a declaration with initialization: the name quantity and the type int are fixed, and 3 is put in. Line 4 is a pure assignment: the right-hand side quantity + 2 is evaluated using the current contents (3), giving 5, and only then is 5 stored back. The old 3 is not recoverable — nothing kept a copy.

Line 7 declares a new slot and initialises it from an expression: 5 × 1299 = 6495. Note that quantity was read here, not changed; reading a variable never alters it.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — why swapping two variables needs a third

The order "evaluate right, then store into left" has a consequence that is examined regularly. Swapping two values by the obvious route does not work:

int front = 42, back = 17;
System.out.println("before: front=" + front + " back=" + back);

front = back;    // front is now 17 — the 42 is gone
back  = front;   // back = 17, because that is what front now holds
System.out.println("naive : front=" + front + " back=" + back);

int a = 42, b = 17;
int temp = a;    // park the value that is about to be overwritten
a = b;
b = temp;
System.out.println("temp  : a=" + a + " b=" + b);
ACTUAL OUTPUT
before: front=42 back=17
naive : front=17 back=17
temp  : a=17 b=42

Trace the naive version one statement at a time. After front = back, front holds 17 and the 42 no longer exists anywhere — a slot holds exactly one value, and the previous one is not stored elsewhere. So the next line copies 17 onto 17.

The three-line version works because temp preserves the value that is about to be destroyed. This is the standard swap idiom, and the reason it needs a third variable is precisely the assignment rule from the figure.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Two different confusions live on this one symbol. First, = is assignment and == is comparison — if (x = 5) does not even compile for an int, because an assignment produces an int where if demands a boolean. Second, assignment does not create a link. int copy = original; takes a snapshot; changing original afterwards leaves copy alone. Running int original = 100; int copy = original; original = 250; prints original=250 copy=100.

int is the default choice for whole numbers, and the one you will use most. It holds a value from about -2.1 billion to +2.1 billion, which is enough for counts, indexes and years, but not for populations of the world or amounts in cents.

The detail that catches people is what happens before you assign anything, and it depends on where the variable lives:

public class Demo {
    static int field;                 // FIELD  — automatically 0

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int local;                    // LOCAL  — no default at all
        System.out.println(field);    // prints 0
        System.out.println(local);    // COMPILE ERROR:
                                      // variable local might not have been initialized
    }
}

The compiler is deliberately strict here. It rejects any path where a local might be unread, even one you can prove never happens — which is why an if without an else can trigger it.

Where the compiler is strict on purpose

The rule that locals must be assigned before use is stricter than it first appears: the compiler rejects any path where the variable might be unread, even one you can prove never happens. An if without an else triggers it, because as far as the compiler is concerned the condition might be false. The fix is to give the variable a value at declaration, or to make every branch assign one. Fields escape this because they are given type defaults automatically — which is the whole distinction the exam tests.

📘 DEFINITION

int: a 32-bit whole-number type, roughly -2.1 to +2.1 billion

Field: a variable belonging to a class or object; gets a default value automatically

Local variable: a variable declared inside a method; has no default and must be assigned before use

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Reading a local variable before assigning it is a compile error, not a runtime one — the message is "variable might not have been initialized". Remember it as: fields get defaults, locals do not.

What a variable actually holds

📊 FIGURE — a primitive stores the value; a reference stores the way to it

This one distinction explains a whole family of exam questions. Assigning a primitive copies the value, so the two are independent afterwards. Assigning a reference copies the arrow, so both names reach the same object and a change through one is visible through the other.

Primitive (int, double, char, boolean…)Reference (String, arrays, objects)
A variable holdsthe value itselfthe address of an object
b = a copiesthe valuethe arrow, not the object
Changing b affects a?NoYes, if you change the object
Default value of a field0 / 0.0 / '\u0000' / falsenull
Compared with ==valuesaddresses — use .equals for content
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

A local variable has no default at all — Java refuses to compile a read before assignment. Only fields are auto-initialised, and that difference is examined directly.

📊 FIGURE — why a local variable "might not have been initialized"
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — fields get defaults, locals get a compile error

Same four types, two different places to declare them. First as fields of the class:

public class Demo {
    static int totalOrders;
    static double averageValue;
    static String lastCustomer;
    static boolean isOpen;

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(totalOrders);
        System.out.println(averageValue);
        System.out.println(lastCustomer);
        System.out.println(isOpen);
    }
}
ACTUAL OUTPUT
0
0.0
null
false

Those four values are the type defaults: 0 for whole-number types, 0.0 for decimals, null for any reference type, false for boolean. Nothing in the program assigned them; the JVM did it while creating the class.

Now move one of them inside main, making it a local:

int shipping;
System.out.println(shipping);
TERMINAL
Demo.java:5: error: variable shipping might not have been initialized
System.out.println(shipping);
                   ^
1 error

No .class file, no output, no default. The distinction is not stylistic: fields are auto-initialised, locals are not, and reading an unassigned local is caught at compile time rather than producing garbage at run time.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the branch that "obviously" always runs, and the compiler that disagrees

Here weightKg is 12, so any reader can see the branch is taken and shipping ends up as 15. javac still refuses.

int weightKg = 12;
int shipping;
if (weightKg > 10) {
    shipping = 15;
}
System.out.println(shipping);
TERMINAL
Demo.java:9: error: variable shipping might not have been initialized
System.out.println(shipping);
                   ^
1 error

The rule the compiler applies is definite assignment: a local must be assigned on every path that reaches the read. It deliberately does not evaluate weightKg > 10 to see whether the false path is possible — it only checks that a false path exists in the code.

Adding the missing path fixes it:

int weightKg = 12;
int shipping;
if (weightKg > 10) {
    shipping = 15;
} else {
    shipping = 5;
}
System.out.println(shipping);
ACTUAL OUTPUT
15

The other fix is to initialise at the declaration — int shipping = 0; — which removes the error by making every path start with a value. Both are legitimate; the second is safer when more branches are added later.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Remember the two halves as one sentence: fields get type defaults, locals get a compile error. The exact message, variable x might not have been initialized, is quoted verbatim in questions, and the word "might" is the giveaway — it means the compiler found a path, not necessarily the path your data takes. If a question shows an if without an else assigning a local, the answer is a compile error, not the value the branch would have produced.

An identifier is any name you invent — variables, methods, classes. Two separate sets of rules apply to them, and exam questions deliberately mix the two up: what the compiler enforces, and what programmers merely agree on.

// LEGAL — the compiler accepts all of these
int count;      int _total;     int $rate;
int myValue2;   int Total;      int CLASS;

// ILLEGAL — the compiler rejects all of these
int 2ndPlace;   // may not start with a digit
int my-score;   // hyphens are not allowed
int class;      // reserved word
int my score;   // no spaces

Conventions sit on top of that. Nothing breaks if you ignore them, but every reader and grader expects camelCase for variables and methods, PascalCase for classes, and ALL_CAPS for the constants you will meet in 2.9.

Rules versus conventions

Identifier questions are nearly always testing which of the two you are looking at. The rules are enforced by the compiler: start with a letter, underscore or dollar sign, no spaces, not a reserved word. Break one and the code will not compile. The conventions are agreements the compiler ignores entirely — camelCase for variables, PascalCase for classes, ALL_CAPS for constants. Break one and the code runs perfectly and reads badly. A question asking which name "will not compile" is about rules; one asking which is "best" or "conventional" is about style.

📘 DEFINITION

Identifier: a programmer-chosen name for a variable, method or class

Reserved word: a name Java has claimed for itself, such as class, int, for or new — never usable as an identifier

camelCase: the convention for variables and methods: first word lowercase, later words capitalized

🎯 EXAM TIP

Watch the wording. int Total; is legal but breaks convention; int 1st; is illegal. If a question asks which are "valid", it is asking about the rules, not the style. And identifiers are case sensitive, so count and Count are two different variables.

📊 FIGURE — the two filters every identifier passes through
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — sorting a list of names into legal, illegal and merely ugly

Take six names the compiler accepts. Nothing here is good style, but every one of them compiles:

int count = 1;
int _total = 2;
int $rate = 3;
int myValue2 = 4;
int Total = 5;
int CLASS = 6;
System.out.println(count + _total + $rate + myValue2 + Total + CLASS);
ACTUAL OUTPUT
21

The sum 1+2+3+4+5+6 = 21 proves all six exist as separate variables. Now the illegal ones, each with the real message javac produces:

TERMINAL
int 2ndPlace = 5;
  error: not a statement          — a name may not start with a digit

int class = 5;
  error: not a statement          — class is a reserved word
  error: <identifier> expected

int _ = 5;
  error: as of release 9, '_' is a keyword, and may not be used as an identifier

Notice how unhelpful these messages are compared with the missing-semicolon one. The compiler cannot say "bad identifier" because, having failed to read a name, it no longer knows what kind of statement it is looking at — which is why one bad name can produce four or five errors at once. Fix the first and the rest usually vanish.

And CLASS is worth a second look: it is legal, because only the exact lowercase class is reserved. Total and CLASS are filter-1 legal and filter-2 wrong.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — case sensitivity makes two names, not one

Because identifiers are case-sensitive, a capitalisation slip does not produce an error — it produces a second, unrelated variable.

int totalPrice = 120;
int totalprice = 7;
System.out.println("totalPrice=" + totalPrice);
System.out.println("totalprice=" + totalprice);
ACTUAL OUTPUT
totalPrice=120
totalprice=7

Two declarations, two slots, two values — the compiler sees no relationship between them at all. That is the good case, where both are declared. The dangerous case is a program that declares totalPrice and then reads totalprice, which produces cannot find symbol and sends you hunting for a missing declaration when the real fault is one capital letter.

The same rule applies to everything: String and string are not the same type, System and system are not the same class, and println and Println are not the same method.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Three specific traps here. Reserved words — class, int, for, new, static, void — are illegal as names, but capitalised versions like Class or CLASS are perfectly legal, which questions exploit. A single underscore _ was legal in old Java and has been a keyword since Java 9, so it is now rejected. And true, false and null are not technically keywords but are still reserved literals, so they cannot be used as identifiers either.

Arithmetic in Java follows the precedence you already know from maths, with one addition and one trap. Multiplication, division and modulo bind tighter than addition and subtraction, and parentheses beat everything.

2 + 3 * 4        = 14      // * before +
10 - 4 / 2       = 8       // / before -
10 + 7 % 3       = 11      // % ranks with * and /
-3 + 5           = 2       // unary minus applies to 3 first
(2 + 3) * 4      = 20      // parentheses win

The trap is equal precedence. When two operators rank the same, Java works strictly left to right — it does not group them the way your eye wants to:

20 / 5 * 2       = 8       // (20/5)*2, NOT 20/(5*2)
100 / 10 / 2     = 5       // (100/10)/2
10 - 4 - 3       = 3       // (10-4)-3

Precedence before arithmetic

Expression questions are decided before any arithmetic happens, by the order the operators bind in. Parentheses first, then multiplication, division and modulo left to right, then addition and subtraction. The consequence that costs marks is the invisible division bar: a formula written as a fraction has implied parentheses round the whole numerator, so (a + b + c) / 3 is right and a + b + c / 3 divides only the last term. When a computed average is wildly too small, that is almost always the cause.

📘 DEFINITION

Operator precedence: the order in which operators are applied when an expression has several

Associativity: the direction operators of equal precedence are applied — in Java, left to right

Modulo (%): the remainder after integer division; ranks with multiplication and division

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

20 / 5 * 2 is 8, not 2 — the most commonly missed line in this unit, because people read the whole 5 * 2 as the divisor. Note too that ^ is bitwise XOR, not a power operator: use Math.pow or plain multiplication.

📊 FIGURE — why 20 / 5 * 2 is 8 and not 2
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — eight expressions, evaluated by the rules rather than by eye

Work each one out before reading the output. The only two rules needed are: higher precedence binds first, and equal precedence goes left to right.

System.out.println(2 + 3 * 4);
System.out.println(10 - 4 / 2);
System.out.println(10 + 7 % 3);
System.out.println(-3 + 5);
System.out.println((2 + 3) * 4);
System.out.println(20 / 5 * 2);
System.out.println(100 / 10 / 2);
System.out.println(10 - 4 - 3);
ACTUAL OUTPUT
14
8
11
2
20
8
5
3

The first four are precedence: 3 * 4 before the + gives 12 + 2 = 14; 4 / 2 before the - gives 10 − 2 = 8; 7 % 3 is 1, ranking with * and /, so 10 + 1 = 11; unary minus applies to the 3 alone, so −3 + 5 = 2.

The last three are associativity, and they are the ones that catch people. 20 / 5 * 2 is (20 / 5) * 2 = 8, not 20 / (5 * 2) = 2. 100 / 10 / 2 is (100 / 10) / 2 = 5, not 100 / (10 / 2) = 20. 10 - 4 - 3 is (10 - 4) - 3 = 3, not 10 - (4 - 3) = 9. In each case the wrong reading is the one that groups the two rightmost operands.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the division bar that exists on paper and not in code

A formula written as a fraction has invisible brackets round the whole numerator. Typing it out left to right loses them, and the answer stays plausible enough not to notice.

double a = 88, b = 92, c = 79;
System.out.println(a + b + c / 3);
System.out.println((a + b + c) / 3);

double celsius = 37.0;
System.out.println(celsius * 9 / 5 + 32);
System.out.println(celsius * (9 / 5) + 32);
ACTUAL OUTPUT
206.33333333333334
86.33333333333333
98.6
69.0

Line 1: / binds tighter, so only c / 3 is divided — the expression means 88 + 92 + (79/3) = 206.33. Line 2 restores the numerator brackets and gives the real average, 86.33.

Lines 3 and 4 show the mirror-image mistake. celsius * 9 / 5 is (37.0 * 9) / 5 = 333 / 5 = 66.6, plus 32 = 98.6 — correct. Adding "helpful" brackets around 9 / 5 changes it into integer division: 9 / 5 with two int literals is 1, so the result collapses to 37 + 32 = 69.0.

The lesson is not "always add brackets" but "add brackets where the paper formula has them, and check what types are inside the ones you add".

🎯 EXAM TIP

When a computed value is wildly too small, check for a missing numerator bracket; when it is wildly too large, check for a missing denominator bracket. On the exam, rewrite the expression with every implied bracket made explicit before evaluating anything — 20 / 5 * 2 becomes (20 / 5) * 2 on your paper, and the arithmetic then has only one possible reading. Note also that ^ is bitwise XOR, never a power operator: use Math.pow or repeated multiplication.

This is the single most expensive rule in the unit, because it produces a wrong answer silently. When both operands of / are integer types, Java performs integer division: it computes the whole-number part and throws the remainder away. No warning, no exception.

int a = 7, b = 2;

int    r1 = a / b;              // 3     truncated
double r2 = a / b;              // 3.0   the division happened FIRST, in int
double r3 = (double) a / b;     // 3.5   CORRECT — cast BEFORE dividing
double r4 = (double)(a / b);    // 3.0   WRONG — cast AFTER the damage
double r5 = a / 2.0;            // 3.5   one double operand is enough

Look carefully at r2. Storing the result in a double does not help, because the division has already finished by the time the assignment happens. Widening cannot recover a digit that was discarded — which is why the fix is always to change one operand, never the result type.

Truncation also moves toward zero rather than downward, so it behaves differently from rounding on negatives:

  7 / 2  =  3        // not 3.5, and not 4
 -7 / 2  = -3        // toward zero, so not -4

The one rule that decides the most questions

Integer division discarding the remainder is the single most examined behaviour in this unit, and it is silent — no warning, no error, just a smaller number. The rule is that int / int is always an int, so 7 / 2 is 3 and 1 / 2 is 0. Declaring the result as a double does not save you, because the truncation happens first and the whole number is then widened. To get a fractional answer at least one operand must be a decimal — either a literal like 2.0 or a cast like (double) a.

📘 DEFINITION

Integer division: division where both operands are integer types; the fractional part is discarded

Truncation: discarding the fractional part, always toward zero

Cast: explicitly converting a value to another type, written (double) x

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

double avg = sum / count; with two ints looks right and even produces a double — but a truncated one. This one line is behind almost every wrong-average answer. The fix is (double) sum / count: cast one operand before the division.

Precedence, drawn

📊 FIGURE — 2 + 3 * 4 as an expression tree
LevelOperatorsAssociativity
1 (tightest)()—
2++ -- (cast) ! unary -right to left
3* / %left to right
4+ -left to right
5< <= > >=left to right
6== !=left to right
7&&left to right
8||left to right
9 (loosest)= += -= *= /= %=right to left
🎯 EXAM TIP

When unsure, add brackets. They cost nothing at run time and they remove the entire category of precedence bugs — and the exam cannot mark you down for being explicit.

📊 FIGURE — int / int truncates before anything else can help
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the five ways to divide 7 by 2, and the three that lose the half

One pair of values, five expressions. The only thing that varies is where the decimal type appears.

int a = 7, b = 2;
int    r1 = a / b;
double r2 = a / b;
double r3 = (double) a / b;
double r4 = (double)(a / b);
double r5 = a / 2.0;

System.out.println(r1);
System.out.println(r2);
System.out.println(r3);
System.out.println(r4);
System.out.println(r5);
System.out.println(7 / 2);
System.out.println(-7 / 2);
ACTUAL OUTPUT
3
3.0
3.5
3.0
3.5
3
-3

r1 is the plain case: two ints, so integer division, so 3. r2 is the one that surprises people — the answer is a double and it is still 3.0, because the division finished in int arithmetic before the assignment ever happened. Widening cannot restore a digit that was already discarded.

r3 casts an operand, so the expression becomes 7.0 / 2; the int 2 is promoted and the division runs in double, giving 3.5. r4 casts the result, which is 3 by then, so it prints 3.0 — the cast is in the wrong place. r5 shows the simpler fix: make one literal a decimal.

The last line is the negative case. Truncation moves toward zero, not downward, so -7 / 2 is −3 rather than −4.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — splitting a price in cents into dollars and cents

Integer division is not always the villain. When the question genuinely is "how many whole units", it is the right tool — and % supplies what is left over.

int totalCents = 1299;
int dollars = totalCents / 100;   // whole dollars
int cents   = totalCents % 100;   // the leftover
System.out.println("$" + dollars + "." + cents);

double wrong = totalCents / 100;    // both int — truncates first
double right = totalCents / 100.0;  // one decimal operand
System.out.println("wrong=" + wrong);
System.out.println("right=" + right);
ACTUAL OUTPUT
$12.99
wrong=12.0
right=12.99

Line 2 wants the whole part, so int division is exactly correct: 1299 / 100 = 12. Line 3 wants the remainder: 1299 % 100 = 99. Together they reconstruct the value with no floating point anywhere, which is why money is normally stored in whole cents.

Lines 6 and 7 are the same expression twice, differing by a single character. 100 is an int so the division truncates to 12 and then widens to 12.0; 100.0 is a double so the int 1299 is promoted and the answer keeps its fraction. Declaring the variable double did nothing for the first one.

One caution on the first output: "$" + dollars + "." + cents would print $12.9 for 1209 cents, because 9 has no leading zero. Formatting is a separate job from arithmetic — printf("$%d.%02d%n", dollars, cents) handles it.

This example puts 2.4 and 2.5 together on a real calculation. BMI is weight divided by height squared, and every decision in these nine lines is one the exam tests.

Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);

double weightKg = in.nextDouble();
double heightM  = in.nextDouble();

if (heightM <= 0) {
    System.out.println("Height must be positive.");
    return;
}

double bmi = weightKg / (heightM * heightM);
System.out.printf("BMI: %.1f%n", bmi);

Why double and not int: 70.5 kg would truncate to 70 (2.5). Why the parentheses: without them w / h * h runs left to right and cancels back to w (2.4). Why the guard: a zero height gives Infinity for doubles rather than an exception, so the bad value spreads silently instead of stopping. Why printf: a raw println would print 22.857142857142858.

Reading a worked example for the trap

Worked examples in this course are constructed so that one specific mistake produces a plausible wrong answer. Here it is the division: a BMI or average computed with two integers loses the fraction and produces a number that looks reasonable enough not to notice. The habit worth taking from this is to check every division in a formula and ask what types are on each side before trusting the result — which is faster than tracing the whole calculation.

📘 DEFINITION

Formatted output: printf with a format string such as "%.1f" to control decimal places

Guard clause: an early check that rejects invalid input before the real work begins

Infinity: the double result of dividing by 0.0 — no exception is thrown

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

w / h * h is not a typo you can catch by reading — it computes exactly w, and for realistic inputs that looks like a plausible BMI. It is a logic error: it compiles, it runs, and it lies. Only checking against a hand-computed answer finds it.

📊 FIGURE — every decision in the BMI line, and the wrong answer it prevents
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the calculation, and the version that quietly returns the weight

A person weighing 70.5 kg and standing 1.75 m tall. Work it by hand first: 1.75 × 1.75 = 3.0625, and 70.5 ÷ 3.0625 = 23.02.

double weightKg = 70.5;
double heightM  = 1.75;

double bmi = weightKg / (heightM * heightM);
System.out.println(bmi);
System.out.printf("BMI: %.1f%n", bmi);

double wrong = weightKg / heightM * heightM;   // brackets removed
System.out.println("w / h * h = " + wrong);
ACTUAL OUTPUT
23.020408163265305
BMI: 23.0
w / h * h = 70.5

The first line shows why printf is in the program at all: the raw double carries seventeen digits, none of which a person wants. %.1f rounds for display only — bmi itself is unchanged.

The last line is the trap in its purest form. / and * have equal precedence, so weightKg / heightM * heightM means (weightKg / heightM) * heightM — the two heights cancel and the expression returns the weight. It compiles, it runs, and for an adult it produces a number in a believable BMI range. Only checking against the hand-computed 23.02 catches it.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — what a height of zero actually does

The guard clause exists because floating-point division by zero does not behave like integer division by zero. Remove the guard and watch what happens:

double weightKg = 70.5;
double heightM  = 0.0;
double bmi = weightKg / (heightM * heightM);
System.out.println("bmi = " + bmi);
System.out.println("bmi > 25? " + (bmi > 25));
System.out.printf("BMI: %.1f%n", bmi);

int bad = 70 / 0;    // the integer version, for contrast
ACTUAL OUTPUT
bmi = Infinity
bmi > 25? true
BMI: Infinity
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ArithmeticException: / by zero

Three lines of output appeared before anything went wrong. Dividing a double by zero produces the special value Infinity — no exception, no warning. Worse, Infinity compares as larger than everything, so a later if (bmi > 25) classifies this nonsense as overweight and the program reports it confidently.

Only the last line throws, and only because both operands there are int. So the two types fail in opposite ways: integer division by zero stops the program loudly, floating-point division by zero corrupts the answer silently. The guard clause converts the silent failure into a message you control.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Questions on worked examples like this one almost never ask you to recompute the formula. They ask which single change breaks it: removing the brackets, using int for a measurement, or dropping the guard. Scan for those three before doing any arithmetic. And remember the pair of behaviours for division by zero — int throws ArithmeticException, double gives Infinity or NaN — because that contrast is a question on its own.

double is the default for anything with a fractional part. It stores values in binary, and that single fact causes the behaviour that surprises everyone: just as one third cannot be written exactly in decimal, one tenth cannot be written exactly in binary. It repeats forever and gets cut off.

System.out.println(0.1 + 0.2);            // 0.30000000000000004
System.out.println(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3);     // false

So doubles are approximations, and the practical consequence is that you must never test them for exact equality. Compare the difference against a small tolerance instead:

if (Math.abs(a - b) < 0.0001) { ... }     // "close enough to equal"

Two smaller rules follow from the type system. A decimal literal is a double by default, so assigning one to a float needs an f suffix. And doubles do not crash on overflow — they produce special values instead:

float f = 3.14;      // ERROR — 3.14 is a double
float f = 3.14f;     // fine

1.0 / 0              // Infinity, no exception
0.0 / 0              // NaN — "not a number"

Why floating point is approximate

A double stores a number as a sign, an exponent and a mantissa — scientific notation in binary. That buys enormous range and costs exactness, because any fraction whose denominator is not a power of two cannot be represented, exactly as one third cannot be written in decimal. So 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3, adding a tiny number to a huge one can lose it entirely, and money is never stored as a double. Those are not bugs to work round; they are the format, and 3.18 is where the consequence becomes a rule.

📘 DEFINITION

double: a 64-bit floating-point type, about 15 significant digits — the default for decimals

Epsilon comparison: testing Math.abs(a - b) < tolerance instead of a == b

NaN: the "not a number" result of an undefined operation such as 0.0/0 or Math.sqrt(-1)

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

NaN is not equal to anything, including itself. So a NaN produced upstream does not throw — it quietly makes every later comparison false, sending an if-else chain down the wrong branch. Test for it with Double.isNaN(x).

📊 FIGURE — why a double is an approximation, and where the error comes from
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the arithmetic that does not add up, and the comparison that fixes it

Every one of these is exact arithmetic in decimal and inexact in binary.

System.out.println(0.1 + 0.2);
System.out.println(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3);
System.out.println(Math.abs((0.1 + 0.2) - 0.3) < 0.0001);
System.out.println(1.0 / 3.0);
System.out.println(0.1 + 0.7);
ACTUAL OUTPUT
0.30000000000000004
false
true
0.3333333333333333
0.7999999999999999

Line 1 shows the error itself — the stored values for 0.1 and 0.2 are each a hair off, and adding them accumulates the discrepancy into the sixteenth decimal place. Line 2 is the practical damage: an exact equality test on values that should match returns false.

Line 3 is the fix and the pattern to memorise: subtract, take the absolute value, and compare against a small tolerance. Math.abs is needed because you do not know which of the two is larger.

Line 5 is included because it errs in the other direction — 0.799999… rather than 0.800000…4. There is no rule about which way the error goes, which is exactly why < and > comparisons on computed doubles are also unreliable at the boundary.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the values a double produces instead of crashing

Integer arithmetic throws when it cannot answer. Floating-point arithmetic answers anyway, with three special values:

System.out.println(1.0 / 0);
System.out.println(-1.0 / 0);
System.out.println(0.0 / 0);

double nan = 0.0 / 0;
System.out.println(nan == nan);
System.out.println(Double.isNaN(nan));
System.out.println(Math.sqrt(-4));
ACTUAL OUTPUT
Infinity
-Infinity
NaN
false
true
NaN

Note line 4 carefully: NaN == NaN is false. NaN is not equal to anything, including itself, which is the only reason Double.isNaN exists — you cannot test for it with ==.

The danger is what this does to branching. A NaN produced early makes every later comparison false: nan > 0, nan < 0 and nan == 0 are all false at once, so an if-else chain falls through to whichever branch handles "none of the above". The bad value never announces itself; it just steers the program.

One more rule from the same section, this time caught at compile time:

float f = 3.14;   // ERROR: incompatible types: possible lossy conversion from double to float

A decimal literal is a double by default, and a double does not fit in a 32-bit float, so it needs the suffix: float f = 3.14f;.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Three facts carry nearly every double question. Never compare computed doubles with == — use Math.abs(a - b) < EPSILON. Division by zero differs by type — int throws, double gives Infinity or NaN. A decimal literal is a double, so a float needs an f suffix. If a question shows 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3, the answer is false every single time.
