Scientific notation is a compact way of writing very large or very small numbers, and Java reads the e as "times ten to the power of". It is a convenience for the literal only — the value is an ordinary number once stored.

2.5e3    // 2500.0
1e-3     // 0.001      — a negative exponent divides
6.02e23  // readable without counting 23 zeros

The rule that costs marks is the type: any literal written this way is a double, even when the value is a whole number. That connects straight back to 2.12 — assigning it to an int needs an explicit cast.

int n = 1e3;          // ERROR — 1e3 is the double 1000.0
int n = (int) 1e3;    // fine

int million = 1_000_000;   // underscores are allowed for readability
int bad     = 1,000,000;   // commas are NOT

Where scientific notation appears

Scientific notation matters less as a way of writing numbers and more as an explanation of how a double works internally. 6.02e23 is a mantissa of 6.02 and an exponent of 23, and that is precisely the structure the bits are divided into. Recognising that makes the range and precision trade obvious: the exponent buys reach, the mantissa buys accuracy, and the total number of bits is fixed, so one is always paid for with the other.

📘 DEFINITION

Scientific notation: a literal of the form mEn meaning m x 10 to the power n

Digit separator: an underscore inside a numeric literal, ignored by the compiler, used for readability

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

6.02 * 10e23 is wrong for 6.02 x 10²³ — it means 6.02 x 10 x 10²³, one power too many. The e already contains the "times ten to the", so the correct literal is simply 6.02e23.

📊 FIGURE — scientific notation: what each part of the literal means
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — six literals and the values they really stand for

The e is not a variable and not multiplication — it is part of the literal, and it means "times ten to the power of".

System.out.println(2.5e3);
System.out.println(1e-3);
System.out.println(6.02e23);
System.out.println(6.02 * 10e23);
System.out.println(1_000_000);
System.out.println(2.5e3 == 2500.0);
ACTUAL OUTPUT
2500.0
0.001
6.02E23
6.019999999999999E24
1000000
true

Line 1: 2.5 × 10³ = 2500, printed as 2500.0 because it is a double. Line 2: a negative exponent divides, giving 0.001. Line 3 prints in scientific form itself, because Java switches to that notation for very large and very small magnitudes.

Line 4 is the classic error, and the output makes it unmistakable. 10e23 already means 10 × 10²³ = 10²⁴, so multiplying by 6.02 gives 6.02 × 10²⁴ — ten times too big. Writing Avogadro's number as 6.02 * 10e23 instead of 6.02e23 is off by a factor of ten, and the stray ...99999 is the ordinary floating-point error from section 2.7.

Line 5 shows underscores as digit separators — the compiler ignores them entirely, so 1_000_000 is the int 1000000. Commas are not allowed. Line 6 confirms the value is exactly 2500.0, since 2500 is representable exactly in binary.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the type rule that trips the assignment up

The value 1e3 is a whole number, which makes the next line look reasonable:

int n = 1e3;
TERMINAL
error: incompatible types: possible lossy conversion from double to int
int n = 1e3;
        ^

The compiler is not objecting to the value — 1000 fits in an int comfortably. It is objecting to the type: any literal with an e or a decimal point is a double, and narrowing from double to int is never automatic, because in general it would lose data. The compiler applies the rule to the type, not to the particular value.

int n = (int) 1e3;
System.out.println(n);

long bytes = 2_000_000_000L;
System.out.println(bytes);

double tiny = 4.5e-8;
System.out.println(tiny);
ACTUAL OUTPUT
1000
2000000000
4.5E-8

The cast is you accepting responsibility for any loss; here there is none. The other two lines show the neighbouring literal rules: L marks a long, and very small doubles print back in scientific notation.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Two things get asked. What is the value — count the exponent as places to shift the decimal point, right for positive and left for negative. What is the type — anything with e or a decimal point is a double, so assigning it to an int or float needs a cast or a suffix. And watch for 10e23: if the mantissa already ends in a power of ten, the answer is off by that factor.

"}, "D286/u2/z2_9": {"body": "

Some values should never change once set — a tax rate, a maximum size, the number of days in a week. Marking them final lets the compiler enforce that, turning a rule you were relying on into one the language guarantees.

final double TAX_RATE = 0.07;
TAX_RATE = 0.08;          // COMPILE ERROR — cannot assign to a final variable

The reason to bother is not performance. It is that a rate change becomes a one-line edit instead of a hunt through the file, and that the name explains the number to whoever reads it next. if (x > 86400) means nothing; if (x > SECONDS_PER_DAY) explains itself.

What final guarantees is narrower than people assume. It locks the variable, not the object the variable points at:

final int[] a = {1, 2, 3};
a[0] = 99;        // ALLOWED — the contents are not final
a = new int[5];   // ERROR   — repointing the variable is what is blocked

What a constant is really for

A named constant is worth three things and only one of them is convenience. It documents — LEGAL_AGE says what 18 means. It centralises — one edit changes every use, so a rate change cannot be half-applied. And it protects — final turns an accidental reassignment into a compile error rather than a silent bug. The alternative, a bare number scattered through the code, is the magic-number anti-pattern, and the reason it is worth naming is that nobody can safely find all the copies later.

📘 DEFINITION

final: a modifier preventing a variable from being reassigned after its first value

Named constant: a final variable given a meaningful name, conventionally in ALL_CAPS

Magic number: an unexplained numeric literal sitting directly in the code

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

For a primitive, "the variable" and "the value" are the same thing, so final feels absolute. For an array or object they are not, and the contents stay editable. That distinction is the whole reason final fields holding mutable objects are not as safe as they look — a point that returns in Unit 7.

📊 FIGURE — what final actually protects
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Declaring and using a constant
final int MAX_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS = 3;
int attempts = 4;
System.out.println(attempts > MAX_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS);
System.out.println("limit is " + MAX_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS);
true limit is 3
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. final says this name may be assigned exactly once.
  2. The comparison reads clearly because the number has a name.
  3. Change the policy in one place and every use follows.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — final protects the reference, not the object
final int[] scores = {90, 80};
scores[0] = 55;
System.out.println(scores[0] + "," + scores[1]);
55,80
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. scores may never point at a different array.
  2. But the array it points at is still mutable, so element 0 can change.
  3. This distinction is worth a mark on its own.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Thinking final freezes the contents. It freezes the binding. final int[] a means you cannot say a = somethingElse, but a[0] = 99 is perfectly legal.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Constants are written UPPER_SNAKE_CASE by convention, and a final field with no initial value must be assigned in the constructor or the code will not compile.
"}, "D286/u2/z2_10": {"body": "

The Math class collects the arithmetic that operators cannot express. Every method is static, so you call it on the class itself, and Math lives in java.lang, so it needs no import.

Math.abs(-7)        // 7        int in, int out
Math.pow(2, 3)      // 8.0      ALWAYS returns double
Math.sqrt(16)       // 4.0      always double
Math.max(3, 9)      // 9
Math.round(5.6)     // 6        rounds — unlike a cast, which truncates
Math.random()       // [0.0, 1.0)  — 0 possible, 1.0 not

Two of those return types cause most of the errors here. pow and sqrt hand back a double whatever you feed them, so storing the result in an int needs a cast (2.12):

int n = Math.pow(2, 3);          // ERROR — double will not narrow on its own
int n = (int) Math.pow(2, 3);    // 8

Reading library methods rather than memorising them

The Math methods are all static, so they are called on the class and never on an object. Beyond that, the useful skill is reading the signature: Math.pow returns a double even for whole numbers, which is why Math.pow(2, 3) gives 8.0 rather than 8. Math.round returns a long, so assigning it to an int needs a cast. Those return types are what questions test, more often than what the methods compute.

📘 DEFINITION

static method: a method called on the class rather than on an object, as in Math.sqrt(x)

Math.round: rounds to the nearest whole number, in contrast to a cast, which truncates

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Math.sqrt of a negative returns NaN rather than throwing. Nothing stops, nothing warns — the NaN simply flows into the rest of the calculation and poisons every comparison downstream, exactly as described in 2.7.

📊 FIGURE — the Math methods that actually appear
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Math.pow always returns a double
int base = 5;
double squared = Math.pow(base, 2);
System.out.println(squared);
int asInt = (int) Math.pow(base, 2);
System.out.println(asInt);
25.0 25
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Math.pow returns double whatever you feed it.
  2. So it prints with a decimal point.
  3. Assigning it to an int needs an explicit cast.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Rounding is not truncation
System.out.println(Math.round(2.5));
System.out.println(Math.round(-2.5));
System.out.println((int) 2.9);
3 -2 2
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Math.round rounds half up — towards positive infinity.
  2. So −2.5 rounds to −2, not −3.
  3. A cast truncates instead, discarding the fraction entirely.
🎯 EXAM TIP
The exam's favourite is that Math.pow returns a double. int x = Math.pow(2,3); does not compile without a cast.
"}, "D286/u2/z2_11": {"body": "

Modulo gives the remainder after integer division, and it is far more useful than that description suggests. It is the standard way to test divisibility, to pull digits apart, and to wrap a value around a range.

17 % 5    =  2        // 17 = 3*5 + 2
10 % 2    =  0        // no remainder, so 10 is even
 7 % 10   =  7        // when a < b, the answer is a

The three patterns worth memorising:

n % 2 == 0                 // is n even?
n % 10                     // the last digit of n
n / 10                     // n with the last digit removed

// together they walk every digit
while (n > 0) {
    int digit = n % 10;
    n = n / 10;
}

Negatives behave in a way that trips a very common test. The sign of the result follows the left operand, not the right:

-7 % 3    = -1        // not 2
 7 % -3   =  1

What modulo is actually for

Modulo looks like a niche operator and does three jobs you will use constantly. n % 2 == 0 tests whether a number is even. n % 10 extracts the last digit, and n / 10 removes it, which together let a loop walk the digits of a number. And i % k cycles through 0…k−1 as i increases, which is how anything wraps round — clock arithmetic, array indices, alternating rows. In Java the result takes the sign of the left operand, so −7 % 2 is −1, and that is why n % 2 == 1 fails to detect negative odd numbers.

📘 DEFINITION

Modulo (%): the remainder left after integer division

Divisibility test: n % d == 0 means d divides n exactly

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Because -7 % 2 is -1 and not 1, the test n % 2 == 1 is false for negative odd numbers. Use n % 2 != 0 to test for odd. And 5 % 0 throws ArithmeticException, exactly like dividing by zero.

Division and remainder are one calculation

Integer division answers how many whole groups; % answers what is left. They always satisfy (a / b) * b + (a % b) == a.

📊 FIGURE — 17 items in groups of 5
ExpressionValueNote
17 / 53truncated, not rounded — 3.4 becomes 3
17 % 52the leftover
-7 / 2-3truncation is toward zero, so not -4
-7 % 2-1the remainder takes the sign of the LEFT operand
n % 2 == 0even testnothing left over after halving
🎯 EXAM TIP

The two negative rows are the ones that catch people, because several other languages answer -4 and 1 there. Java truncates toward zero and keeps the dividend's sign.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — One operand decides the whole division
System.out.println(7 / 2);
System.out.println(7 / 2.0);
System.out.println(7 % 2);
System.out.println((double) 7 / 2);
3 3.5 1 3.5
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. 7 / 2 — both int, so integer division truncates to 3.
  2. 7 / 2.0 — one double, so real division gives 3.5.
  3. % gives the remainder, 1.
  4. Casting one operand first is the usual fix.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Splitting a total into units
int totalMinutes = 145;
int hours = totalMinutes / 60;
int minutes = totalMinutes % 60;
System.out.println(hours + "h " + minutes + "m");
2h 25m
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Integer division gives how many whole hours fit.
  2. Modulo gives what is left over.
  3. Division and remainder together are how any total is broken into units.
"}, "D286/u2/z2_12": {"body": "

Java converts between numeric types in two directions, and it treats them very differently depending on whether information can be lost.

Widening moves to a larger type and happens automatically, because nothing can be lost. Narrowing moves to a smaller type and requires an explicit cast — the cast is you telling the compiler you accept the loss.

byte -> short -> int -> long -> float -> double      // widening: automatic

int n = 5;
double d = n;        // fine, implicit

double x = 5.9;
int m = x;           // ERROR: possible lossy conversion
int m = (int) x;     // 5 — and note it TRUNCATES, it does not round

A cast silences the compiler; it does not prevent the loss. That distinction decides where you put it, and it is the same lesson as 2.5: convert before the operation, not after.

long r = (long) a * b;     // CORRECT — widened first, so the multiply is in long
long r = (long)(a * b);    // WRONG   — overflows in int, then widens the wrong answer

Which conversions are free and which are not

Widening — int to double, char to int — is automatic because the target can hold everything the source could, so nothing is lost. Narrowing is the reverse and always needs an explicit cast, because information will be discarded and the language wants you to say you meant it. The specific behaviour to remember is that a cast from a decimal type truncates toward zero rather than rounding: (int) 3.9 is 3, and (int) −3.9 is −3, not −4.

📘 DEFINITION

Widening: converting to a larger type; automatic and lossless

Narrowing: converting to a smaller type; requires an explicit cast and may lose data

Promotion: when operands of different types meet, the smaller is widened before the operation

🎯 EXAM TIP

Promotion is why 5 / 2.0 gives 2.5 and why 'a' + 1 gives the int 98 rather than a char. When two types meet in an expression, the smaller one is widened first — then the operation runs in the larger type.

Which conversions Java will do for you

📊 FIGURE — widening is free, narrowing is not
ConversionAllowed?Why
double d = 3;Yes, automaticint fits inside double without loss
int x = 3.5;No — compile errorthe .5 would be silently destroyed
int x = (int) 3.5;Yesthe cast says you accept the loss — x becomes 3
long L = 5;Yes, automaticwidening
int n = 5L;No — needs (int)narrowing
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Casting a double to int truncates toward zero; it does not round. (int) 3.99 is 3 and (int) -3.99 is -3. Use Math.round when you want rounding.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Widening happens by itself; narrowing must be demanded
int i = 42;
double d = i;
System.out.println(d);
double price = 9.87;
int truncated = (int) price;
System.out.println(truncated);
42.0 9
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. int to double is widening — no information can be lost, so Java does it silently.
  2. double to int is narrowing — the fraction is lost, so you must write the cast.
  3. The cast truncates towards zero. It does not round.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Mixed arithmetic promotes before it computes
int count = 3;
double total = 10.0;
System.out.println(total / count);
System.out.println(1 / 2 * 2.0);
System.out.println(2.0 * 1 / 2);
3.3333333333333335 0.0 1.0
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. count is promoted to double, so the division is real.
  2. In 1 / 2 * 2.0 the integer division happens FIRST and gives 0.
  3. Reordering so a double leads keeps the precision.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Declared is not the same as initialized
int declaredAndSet = 7;
System.out.println(declaredAndSet);

int later;
boolean condition = true;
if (condition) {
    later = 1;
} else {
    later = 2;
}
System.out.println(later);
7 1
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Declaring int later; reserves the name but stores nothing in it.
  2. Both branches of the if assign it, so by the time it is printed the compiler can prove it has a value — this compiles.
  3. Delete the else and it stops compiling, because one path would reach the print with nothing assigned. The compiler requires every path to assign, not just the likely one.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Assuming an int local starts at 0 the way a field does. It does not start at anything — reading it before assignment is a compile error, so the program never runs at all.
"}, "D286/u2/z2_13": {"body": "

Computers store everything in binary, because two states are far easier to build reliably than ten. Each position is a power of two, and reading a binary number is just adding up the positions that are switched on.

Position:   128  64  32  16   8   4   2   1
Binary 1011:                  1   0   1   1   = 8 + 2 + 1 = 11
Binary 11111111:                              = 255

Going the other way, repeatedly subtract the largest power of two that fits: 10 needs an 8 (leaving 2) and a 2 (leaving 0), so 10 is 1010.

This is also where the type sizes in 2.17 come from. A type with n bits can hold 2ⁿ distinct values, which is exactly why an int stops near 2.1 billion — and why it overflows the way 2.16 describes.

4 bits  = 2^4  = 16 values
8 bits  = 2^8  = 256 values
32 bits = 2^32 = about 4.3 billion  ->  int spans -2.1bn to +2.1bn

Why bit width shows up later

Binary is worth understanding here rather than memorising, because two later topics depend on it. Every numeric type is a fixed number of bits, so each has a hard maximum — which is exactly what overflow in 2.16 is. And the widths in 2.17 are not arbitrary trivia: they are the reason an int stops near 2.1 billion and a long does not. The single fact worth carrying is that binary place values double leftward — 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 — which is enough to read any byte.

📘 DEFINITION

Bit: a single binary digit, 0 or 1

Byte: eight bits, able to represent 256 distinct values

Hexadecimal: base 16, written with the prefix 0x — each hex digit is exactly four bits

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

A leading zero on an integer literal makes it octal, not decimal: int x = 010; is 8, not 10. It compiles silently, which makes it a genuinely nasty bug. 0x means hexadecimal and 0b means binary.

📊 FIGURE — place values in a byte
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Converting by subtracting place values
System.out.println(Integer.toBinaryString(45));
System.out.println(Integer.parseInt("101101", 2));
System.out.println(0b101101);
101101 45 45
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. 45 = 32 + 8 + 4 + 1, so the bits at those places are 1.
  2. parseInt with radix 2 reads a binary string back.
  3. A 0b literal writes binary directly in source.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Why 8 bits stop at 255
System.out.println(Math.pow(2, 8));
System.out.println((int) Math.pow(2, 8) - 1);
System.out.println(Integer.toBinaryString(255));
256.0 255 11111111
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. n bits give 2^n distinct patterns.
  2. Counting from 0, the largest is 2^n − 1.
  3. 255 is eight 1s — every place value filled.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Two facts cover most questions: n bits give 2^n values, and the largest unsigned value is 2^n − 1. Do not confuse the count with the maximum.
"}, "D286/u2/z2_14": {"body": "

A char holds one character, but underneath it is a 16-bit number — the Unicode code value. That dual nature explains every behaviour in this section: chars compare, sort and do arithmetic like numbers, and only print like letters.

char c = 'A';
System.out.println(c);          // A
System.out.println((int) c);    // 65   the code value
System.out.println(c + 1);      // 66   char PROMOTES to int in arithmetic
System.out.println((char)(c + 1)); // B   cast back to see the letter

You rarely need the code values themselves. What you need are the differences, because those turn a character into the number it represents:

char digit = '7';
int value = digit - '0';        // 7  — NOT (int) digit, which is 55

char letter = 'd';
int position = letter - 'a';    // 3  — d is the 4th letter, zero-indexed

For classification, the Character class saves you from remembering ranges: isDigit, isLetter, isLetterOrDigit, isWhitespace, toUpperCase.

Why char arithmetic works at all

A char holds a number, so arithmetic on it is ordinary arithmetic on that number. That explains the whole family of behaviours: 'A' + 1 is 66 because the addition promotes the char to an int, and getting back to a character requires a cast. It also explains the digit idiom — '7' − '0' is 7, because subtracting the code for zero from the code for seven leaves the numeric value. The trap is that System.out.println('A' + 1) prints 66, not B, because the expression is an int by the time it reaches the print.

📘 DEFINITION

char: a 16-bit type holding one Unicode character, written in single quotes

Code value: the number a character is stored as — 48 for '0', 65 for 'A', 97 for 'a'

Promotion: a char automatically becomes an int when used in arithmetic

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

(int) '7' is 55, not 7 — it gives the code value, not the digit. Subtract '0' to get the numeric value. And 'a' and "a" are different types entirely: single quotes make a char, double quotes make a String.

📊 FIGURE — a char is a number with a costume
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Arithmetic on a char produces an int
char c = 'A';
System.out.println((int) c);
System.out.println(c + 1);
System.out.println((char) (c + 1));
65 66 B
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. A char holds a numeric code — 'A' is 65.
  2. Adding 1 promotes to int, so it prints 66.
  3. Cast back to char to see the letter.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Converting a digit character to its value
char digit = '7';
System.out.println(digit - '0');
System.out.println(Character.isDigit(digit));
System.out.println(Character.toUpperCase('m'));
7 true M
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. '7' is code 55 and '0' is 48, so the difference is the digit's value.
  2. This works for any digit because the codes are consecutive.
  3. The Character class carries the tests and conversions.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Remember '0' is 48 and 'A' is 65, and that lower-case letters come after upper-case ('a' is 97). Any question about ordering follows from those.
"}, "D286/u2/z2_15": {"body": "

A String is a sequence of characters, and it is immutable — once created, its contents can never change. Every method that looks like it edits a String actually returns a brand-new one and leaves the original untouched.

String s = "WGU";
s.concat(" rocks");
System.out.println(s);          // WGU  — unchanged!

s = s.concat(" rocks");         // you must ASSIGN the result
System.out.println(s);          // WGU rocks

That applies to all of them — toUpperCase, trim, replace, substring. Calling one without using the result does nothing at all, silently.

"Hello".length()           // 5    a METHOD for Strings (arrays use .length)
"Hello".charAt(0)          // 'H'  zero-indexed
"Hello".substring(1, 3)    // "el" start INCLUSIVE, end EXCLUSIVE
"Hello".indexOf("l")       // 2    or -1 if absent
"  hi  ".trim()            // "hi"

Immutability also decides how you compare Strings. Because two Strings with the same text can be two different objects, == asks the wrong question — it asks whether they are the same object, not whether they read the same.

Why immutability is the whole story

Every surprising String behaviour comes from one fact: no method ever changes the string it is called on. toUpperCase, trim, replace and substring all return a new String and leave the original untouched, which is why forgetting to assign the result is the most common String bug there is. It is also why += in a loop is expensive — each pass allocates another String — and why StringBuilder exists. And it is why == is unreliable: two Strings with the same characters may or may not be the same object.

📘 DEFINITION

String: an immutable sequence of characters, written in double quotes

Immutable: cannot be changed after creation; operations return a new value instead

equals: the method that compares String contents, as opposed to == which compares identity

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Two consequences bite constantly. Comparison: use .equals(), because == can be false for identical text. Performance: s += x inside a loop builds a whole new String every pass, making the loop O(n²) — which is what StringBuilder exists to fix.

📊 FIGURE — a String is indexed from 0
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Length, index, and the last position
String s = "Java";
System.out.println(s.length());
System.out.println(s.charAt(0));
System.out.println(s.charAt(s.length() - 1));
System.out.println(s.substring(1, 3));
4 J a av
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. length() counts characters — 4.
  2. Indexes run 0 to length()−1, so the last is 3.
  3. substring(1, 3) takes index 1 up to but NOT including 3.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Strings are immutable
String a = "cat";
a.toUpperCase();
System.out.println(a);
a = a.toUpperCase();
System.out.println(a);
cat CAT
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. toUpperCase() RETURNS a new String; it cannot change the old one.
  2. Ignoring the return value therefore does nothing at all.
  3. Assigning the result back is what makes the change visible.
🎯 EXAM TIP
substring(a, b) is inclusive of a and exclusive of b, so its length is b − a. That off-by-one is the most tested detail in this section.
"}, "D286/u2/z2_16": {"body": "

An int has a fixed 32 bits (2.13), so there is a largest value it can hold. Go past it and Java does not throw, warn, or stop — it wraps around to the most negative value, like an odometer rolling over.

int max = Integer.MAX_VALUE;      // 2,147,483,647
System.out.println(max + 1);      // -2147483648

int a = 2_000_000_000;
System.out.println(a + a);        // -294967296   silently negative

Because nothing is thrown, an overflowed value simply flows onward as a plausible-looking wrong number. The defence is to choose a big enough type before the arithmetic, which brings back the cast-placement rule from 2.12:

long r = (long) a * b;     // CORRECT — widened before multiplying
long r = (long)(a * b);    // WRONG   — already overflowed in int

Why overflow is silent

Overflow produces no exception and no warning. The arithmetic simply wraps: add 1 to Integer.MAX_VALUE and you get Integer.MIN_VALUE, because the carry out of the top bit is discarded and the sign bit flips. That silence is what makes it dangerous — the program continues confidently with a negative total. The practical defences are to use long when a value might exceed about two billion, and to be suspicious of any total that comes out negative when every input was positive.

📘 DEFINITION

Overflow: exceeding a type's range, causing the value to wrap to the opposite end

Integer.MAX_VALUE: 2,147,483,647 — the largest int

long: a 64-bit whole-number type, up to about 9.2 quintillion

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

You cannot catch overflow — no exception is thrown, so try/catch is useless. Either use long from the start, or use Math.addExact / Math.multiplyExact, which do throw when the result will not fit.

📊 FIGURE — int wraps around at its limits
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Adding one to the maximum
int max = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
System.out.println(max);
System.out.println(max + 1);
System.out.println(max + 1 == Integer.MIN_VALUE);
2147483647 -2147483648 true
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. An int holds 32 bits, so its range is fixed.
  2. Exceeding it wraps around to the most negative value.
  3. No error, no warning — the program simply continues with a wrong number.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The fix is a wider type, chosen early
int a = 2_000_000_000;
System.out.println(a + a);
long b = 2_000_000_000L;
System.out.println(b + b);
System.out.println((long) a + a);
-294967296 4000000000 4000000000
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Two ints are added AS ints, so the overflow happens before any assignment.
  2. Making the variables long avoids it.
  3. Casting one operand first also works — casting the result afterwards would be too late.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Overflow is silent. If a question shows a large int calculation and offers a negative answer, that is almost certainly the intended one.
"}, "D286/u2/z2_17": {"body": "

Java has exactly eight primitive types, and everything else in the language — String, arrays, your own classes — is an object. Choosing between the primitives comes down to two questions: does the value have a fractional part, and how large can it get?

TypeBitsHolds
byte8-128 to 127
short16-32,768 to 32,767
int32±2.1 billion — the default
long64±9.2 quintillion — needs the L suffix
float32~7 digits — needs the f suffix
double64~15 digits — the default for decimals
char16one Unicode character
boolean—true or false only

The bit counts are not trivia — they are where the ranges come from (2.13) and why overflow happens where it does (2.16). Note also that Java fixes these sizes on every platform, unlike C.

Choosing a numeric type

The choice is nearly always int for whole numbers and double for decimals, and the exceptions are worth knowing because questions are built on them. Use long when the value can exceed about 2.1 billion — populations, milliseconds since 1970, file sizes in bytes. Use byte and short only when memory genuinely matters, which in this course means almost never. And use neither float nor double for money: store whole cents in an int or long, because a rounding error in a balance is a real error.

📘 DEFINITION

Primitive type: one of the eight built-in value types; not an object and never null

Reference type: everything else — String, arrays, and any class; holds a reference to an object

Literal suffix: L marks a long literal, f marks a float literal

🎯 EXAM TIP

String is a reference type, not a primitive — a very frequent exam question. It behaves a little like one because it is immutable and has literal syntax, but it is an object, which is why it uses .equals() and can be null.

📊 FIGURE — the ranges worth memorising
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Choosing between int, long and double
int people = 250;
long nationalDebt = 34_000_000_000L;
double weight = 72.5;
System.out.println(people + " " + nationalDebt + " " + weight);
250 34000000000 72.5
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. A count that fits comfortably: int.
  2. A value beyond ~2.1 billion: long, and the literal needs the L suffix.
  3. A measurement with a fraction: double.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — float and double are approximate
System.out.println(0.1 + 0.2);
System.out.println(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3);
System.out.println(Math.abs((0.1 + 0.2) - 0.3) < 1e-9);
0.30000000000000004 false true
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. 0.1 has no exact binary representation, so the sum is a hair off.
  2. Comparing with == therefore fails.
  3. Compare within a tolerance instead.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Writing long big = 34000000000; without the L. The literal is treated as an int first, and the compiler rejects it before the assignment ever happens.
"}, "D286/u2/z2_18": {"body": "

Java randomness is pseudorandom: an algorithm produces a sequence that passes statistical tests but is completely determined by a starting seed. That is a feature, not a limitation — a fixed seed makes a buggy run reproducible while you debug it.

Random r = new Random();

r.nextInt(6)          // 0 to 5    the bound is EXCLUSIVE
r.nextInt(6) + 1      // 1 to 6    a die roll
r.nextDouble()        // [0.0, 1.0)

Random r = new Random(42);   // fixed seed -> identical sequence every run

The general shape for any inclusive range, which is worth memorising because the off-by-one is so easy:

// random int from min to max INCLUSIVE
int v = r.nextInt(max - min + 1) + min;

// example: 10 to 20 -> 11 possible values
int v = r.nextInt(11) + 10;

Getting a random number in the right range

The method that matters is nextInt(n), and its range is the part questions test: it returns a value from 0 to n−1 inclusive, never n itself. So a die roll is rand.nextInt(6) + 1, and a value between lo and hi inclusive is rand.nextInt(hi − lo + 1) + lo. The + 1 inside the parentheses is the part people drop, and it is what makes the top of the range reachable. Seeding with new Random(42) gives the same sequence every run, which is what makes randomised code testable.

📘 DEFINITION

Pseudorandom: generated by a deterministic algorithm from a seed, not physically random

Seed: the starting value that determines the whole sequence

Exclusive bound: nextInt(n) returns 0 up to n-1; n itself never appears

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Forgetting the + 1 is the classic die bug: nextInt(6) returns 0 through 5 and never returns 6. Whenever you write a range, check both ends by hand — what is the smallest value it can give, and the largest?

📊 FIGURE — nextInt's argument is a COUNT, not a maximum
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A fixed seed makes randomness repeatable
import java.util.Random;
Random r = new Random(42);
System.out.println(r.nextInt(100));
System.out.println(r.nextInt(100));
Random again = new Random(42);
System.out.println(again.nextInt(100));
30 63 30
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The same seed always produces the same sequence.
  2. That is what makes a test involving randomness repeatable.
  3. A new Random with the same seed restarts the sequence.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Building a range
import java.util.Random;
Random r = new Random(7);

The API documentation is the reference for every class in the standard library, and reading a method signature is a skill worth ten minutes of practice. Everything you need is in one line.

public int indexOf(String str, int fromIndex)
   |     |      |         |
   |     |      |         +-- parameters, in order, with their types
   |     |      +-- the method name
   |     +-- RETURN TYPE — what you get back
   +-- access — callable from anywhere

Four things to extract before using an unfamiliar method: what it returns (void means it acts rather than produces), whether it is static (class name versus object), what the boundaries mean, and what special values signal failure — -1 for indexOf, null for a missing map key.

What to read in a method signature

Two lines of any API entry decide whether you can use it correctly. The return type tells you whether the result must be assigned — the mistake that makes s.trim(); on its own do nothing. The throws clause tells you what can fail and whether the compiler will force you to handle it. Everything else is detail you can look up. Getting into the habit of reading those two before calling something unfamiliar removes a whole category of bug.

📘 DEFINITION

Signature: the method name together with its parameter types

Return type: the type of value the method hands back; void means none

API: the published set of classes and methods available to you, with their contracts

🎯 EXAM TIP

A guessed method name that does not exist is harmless — the compiler rejects it. The dangerous case is a method that does exist but behaves slightly differently than you assumed: substring(1,3) returning "el" rather than "ell" is the classic, and only the docs tell you the end index is exclusive.

📊 FIGURE — how to read a method signature
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Reading the return type before you assign
System.out.println(Math.pow(2, 10));
System.out.println(Math.max(3, 7));
System.out.println(Math.max(3.0, 7));
1024.0 7 7.0
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The docs say pow returns double, so it prints 1024.0 and not 1024.
  2. Math.max has overloads; with two ints it returns an int.
  3. With one double it uses the double overload, so the result prints as a double.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — static or not decides how you call it
String s = "hello";
System.out.println(s.toUpperCase());
System.out.println(String.valueOf(42).length());
HELLO 2
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. toUpperCase is an instance method — call it ON a String.
  2. valueOf is static — call it on the class itself.
  3. The word static in the signature is what tells you which.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Assuming a method changes the object it is called on. The documentation's return type is the giveaway: if a String method returns a String, it is handing you a new one and leaving the original alone.

Debugging is finding the cause of wrong behaviour, not changing code until the symptom disappears. A repeatable procedure beats intuition, especially under exam pressure.

1. Reproduce it with one specific input — if you cannot reproduce it, you cannot confirm a fix. 2. Read the top line of the stack trace: the exception type and line number say what and where. 3. Print state at the midpoint of the suspect region, then halve again — each check eliminates half the code. 4. Compare actual against expected. 5. Change one thing at a time. 6. Re-run earlier tests, because fixes routinely break something else.

// print the state, not just the answer
for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
    total += a[i];
    System.out.println("i=" + i + " a[i]=" + a[i] + " total=" + total);
}

Debugging as a procedure

Debugging becomes reliable when it stops being inspection and becomes a procedure: reproduce the failure, narrow it to the smallest input that still fails, print or inspect the values around that point, form one hypothesis, change one thing, and re-test. Changing several things at once is what makes a bug appear to move rather than disappear. The single most useful tool is still a print statement showing a variable together with the loop index that produced it — a value on its own rarely tells you which pass went wrong.

📘 DEFINITION

Stack trace: the list of method calls active when an exception was thrown, innermost first

Regression: a bug introduced by a change that previously worked

Reproduce: to trigger the fault reliably with a known input

🎯 EXAM TIP

Diagnose by symptom. A result one too small is a loop-bound error. A result of 0 means the accumulator was declared inside the loop and reset every pass. A total equal to the last value only means = was used where += was meant.

📊 FIGURE — three kinds of error, found at three different times
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A logic error runs perfectly and is still wrong
int[] scores = {80, 90, 100};
int sum = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < scores.length; i++) sum += scores[i];
System.out.println(sum / scores.length);
System.out.println((double) sum / scores.length);
90 90.0
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Both lines compile and both run.
  2. The first prints an integer average because both operands are int.
  3. Nothing reports it — only checking the value against an expectation finds it.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Tracing by printing the state
int total = 0;
for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
    total += i;
    System.out.println("i=" + i + " total=" + total);
}
i=1 total=1 i=2 total=3 i=3 total=6
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Print the variables that change, inside the loop.
  2. The table it produces shows exactly where a value first goes wrong.
  3. This is the cheapest debugging technique there is.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Treating "it compiled" as "it works". The compiler checks grammar, not intent — a logic error passes every compile and produces a confidently wrong answer.

None of this is enforced by the compiler. It is enforced by every person who reads the code afterwards — and since most programming time is spent reading rather than writing, that is the majority of a program's life.

class BankAccount        // PascalCase for classes
int studentCount         // camelCase for variables
void calculateTotal()    // camelCase verb for methods
final int MAX_SIZE       // ALL_CAPS for constants

if (x > 5) {             // brace at the end of the line
    doSomething();       // 4-space indent per level
}                        // one statement per line

The naming test that matters: can a reader tell what it holds without tracing the code? int d fails, int daysRemaining passes. Short names like i are fine for a tight, obvious loop counter and nowhere else.

Why style is examined at all

Style questions look like opinion and are actually about a shared convention the exam expects you to know. camelCase for variables and methods, PascalCase for classes, ALL_CAPS_WITH_UNDERSCORES for constants. The reason it is worth marks is that these conventions carry information: seeing MAX_SIZE tells a reader it cannot change, and seeing BankAccount tells them it is a type rather than a value. A name that follows the convention is doing part of the documenting.

📘 DEFINITION

camelCase: variables and methods: studentCount, calculateTotal

PascalCase: class names: BankAccount, StudentRecord

ALL_CAPS: constants: MAX_SIZE, TAX_RATE

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

A boolean reads best with an is or has prefix, because it makes the call site read as a sentence: if (isValid(domain)) rather than if (validate(domain)). Methods that return a value should be named for what they return; methods that act should be named for the action.

📊 FIGURE — the naming conventions Java expects
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Naming that carries meaning
int d = 30;
int daysRemaining = 30;
System.out.println(d + " " + daysRemaining);
30 30
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Both compile and both behave identically.
  2. Only the second tells the next reader what the number means.
  3. Style is about the reader, not the compiler.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Whitespace and braces do not change behaviour
int x = 5;
if (x > 3) { System.out.println("big"); }
if (x > 3)
    System.out.println("big again");
big big again
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Java ignores the layout entirely.
  2. Both forms run the same.
  3. Braces are still recommended, because adding a second line to the second form silently breaks it.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Omitting the braces on a single-statement if, then adding a second line later. Only the first line stays inside the branch — the second runs unconditionally, and the indentation hides it.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Conventions are not enforced by the compiler but ARE assessed: class names capitalised, variables and methods lowerCamelCase, constants UPPER_SNAKE_CASE.

var asks the compiler to work out a local variable's type from its initializer. Java stays statically typed — the type is fixed permanently at that moment, and the compiled result is identical to writing the type out. This is not the dynamic var of JavaScript.

var name = "Ana";        // inferred as String — permanently
var count = 5;           // inferred as int

name = 42;               // COMPILE ERROR — name is a String, always

The restrictions all follow from that one idea: if there is nothing to infer from, var cannot be used.

var x;                   // ERROR — no initializer to infer from
var y = null;            // ERROR — null could be any reference type

// locals only
var field = 1;           // ERROR at class level
void f(var p) { }        // ERROR — parameters need explicit types

What var does and does not do

var is not a dynamic type and does not make Java loosely typed. The compiler infers the type from the initialiser at compile time and fixes it permanently, so var n = 5 is an int and cannot later hold a String. Two restrictions follow and are examined: it works only for local variables, not fields or parameters, and it requires an initialiser on the same line, because otherwise there is nothing to infer from.

📘 DEFINITION

Type inference: the compiler deducing a type instead of you writing it

Statically typed: every variable has one type, fixed at compile time

var: a reserved type name usable only for local variables with an initializer

🎯 EXAM TIP

Use var when the type is obvious from the right-hand side — var list = new ArrayList<String>() — and avoid it when it is not. var total = compute(); hides exactly the information the reader needs.

📊 FIGURE — var is inferred, not dynamic
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The type is fixed at the declaration
var count = 5;
count = 10;
System.out.println(count);
var name = "Priya";
System.out.println(name.length());
10 5
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. count is inferred as int from the literal 5.
  2. It stays an int — assigning a String would not compile.
  3. name is a String, so String methods are available.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — var needs something to infer from
var total = 0;
for (var i = 1; i <= 4; i++) total += i;
System.out.println(total);
10
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Each var has an initialiser, so each type is knowable.
  2. var i in a for-loop is inferred as int.
  3. A declaration with no initial value cannot use var at all.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Reading var as "any type", as in a dynamically typed language. Java infers the type once, at compile time, and then enforces it exactly as if you had written it out.

This example brings the whole unit together on one calculation. Every line uses a rule from an earlier section, and the mistakes available here are the mistakes those sections warned about.

final double OVERTIME_THRESHOLD = 40.0;     // 2.9  named constants
final double OVERTIME_MULTIPLIER = 1.5;
final double TAX_RATE = 0.20;

double rate  = 20.0;                        // 2.7  double, not int
double hours = 45.0;

double gross;
if (hours > OVERTIME_THRESHOLD) {
    double regular  = rate * OVERTIME_THRESHOLD;
    double overtime = rate * OVERTIME_MULTIPLIER * (hours - OVERTIME_THRESHOLD);
    gross = regular + overtime;             // 2.4  parenthesised correctly
} else {
    gross = rate * hours;
}

double net = gross * (1 - TAX_RATE);
System.out.printf("Gross: %.2f  Net: %.2f%n", gross, net);   // 950.00  760.00

Check the overtime arithmetic by hand: 40 hours at 20.00 is 800, plus 5 hours at 30.00 is 150, giving 950. The common wrong version applies the 1.5 multiplier to all 45 hours and produces 1350.

What the example is checking

The salary calculation exists to test whether the arithmetic rules of this unit survive contact with a realistic formula. The rate is a decimal, the salary may be entered as a whole number, and the result must keep its fraction — so the types on each side of every operation decide the answer. Working it with all-integer arithmetic produces a number that is plausible and wrong, which is exactly the failure the question is built around.

📘 DEFINITION

Gross pay: total earnings before deductions

Net pay: what remains after tax — gross x (1 - rate)

Time and a half: the overtime multiplier applied only to hours beyond the threshold

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Keeping 80% is gross * (1 - TAX_RATE), or equivalently gross - gross * TAX_RATE. Writing gross - TAX_RATE subtracts twenty cents rather than twenty percent — it compiles, runs, and is wrong by an amount small enough to look believable.

📊 FIGURE — the shape of every calculation program
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Annual to monthly, with the division trap
int annualSalary = 55000;
System.out.println(annualSalary / 12);
System.out.println(annualSalary / 12.0);
System.out.printf("%.2f%n", annualSalary / 12.0);
4583 4583.333333333333 4583.33
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Both int, so the first division truncates — the cents vanish.
  2. Dividing by 12.0 keeps them.
  3. printf("%.2f") formats to two decimal places for money.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Applying a percentage raise
double salary = 55000;
double raised = salary * 1.04;
System.out.println(raised);
System.out.printf("%.2f%n", raised);
57200.0 57200.00
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. A 4% rise multiplies by 1.04.
  2. The raw double carries more digits than you want to show.
  3. Formatting at the point of OUTPUT keeps the stored value exact.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Money questions almost always hinge on integer division. If both operands are int, the cents are gone before formatting can help.

The same program written twice shows what variables actually buy you. The first version hard-codes the numbers into every expression; the second names them once.

// version 1 — literals everywhere
System.out.println(20.0 * 45.0);
System.out.println(20.0 * 45.0 * 0.8);

// version 2 — named variables
double rate = 20.0, hours = 45.0;
double gross = rate * hours;
double net   = gross * 0.8;
System.out.println(gross);
System.out.println(net);

Three concrete gains, and the exam asks about all of them conceptually. One place to change: a new rate is a single edit rather than a search. No recomputation: gross is calculated once and reused, so the two outputs cannot disagree. The names document the arithmetic: rate * hours needs no comment.

Why the same program is repeated with variables

Rewriting a hard-coded calculation with variables is not busywork; it is the step that makes a program reusable rather than a one-off answer. It also introduces the arc this course follows for the rest of its length: literals become variables here, variables become parameters in Unit 6, and parameters become fields in Unit 7. Each step widens where the value can come from, and recognising that progression makes the later units feel like continuations rather than new topics.

📘 DEFINITION

Hard-coded value: a literal written directly into an expression rather than stored in a variable

Single point of change: the property that one edit updates every use

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

This is the first step of an arc that runs through the whole course. Literals become variables here in Unit 2; variables become parameters in Unit 6; parameters become fields of an object in Unit 7. Each step moves the data closer to the logic that owns it.

📊 FIGURE — why a named variable beats a repeated literal
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Naming the rate
final double TAX_RATE = 0.07;
double gross = 4583.33;
double tax = gross * TAX_RATE;
double net = gross - tax;
System.out.printf("%.2f %.2f%n", tax, net);
320.83 4262.50
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The rate appears once and is named.
  2. Every use reads as intent rather than as a magic number.
  3. Changing the rate is a one-line edit that cannot be applied inconsistently.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Order of operations still applies
double gross = 1000;
System.out.println(gross - gross * 0.07);
System.out.println((gross - gross) * 0.07);
930.0 0.0
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Multiplication binds tighter than subtraction, so the tax is computed first.
  2. Adding brackets changes the meaning completely.
  3. When in doubt, bracket what you mean.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Repeating a literal like 0.07 in several places. When the rate changes, one occurrence gets missed and the program produces two different answers for the same quantity.
🎯 EXAM TIP
If a value appears twice, name it. Marks in the performance assessment are lost for magic numbers more often than for wrong arithmetic.

Reading input turns a fixed program into one that works for anybody, and Scanner is how Java does it. The only real decision is how much you want to read at a time.

Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);

String first = in.next();       // ONE word — stops at whitespace
String last  = in.next();
System.out.println(first + " " + last);

String full = in.nextLine();    // the WHOLE line, spaces included

Joining the pieces uses +, which concatenates exactly what it is given and never adds a space of its own — so every space in the output has to exist as a literal in the code:

first + last            // "AnnLee"
first + " " + last      // "Ann Lee"
last + ", " + first     // "Lee, Ann"

What changed from the Unit 1 version

Compared with the version in 1.12, only the storage has changed — the logic is identical. That is deliberate: it shows that variables do not add capability, they add flexibility. The program can now be adapted by changing one assignment rather than by editing the middle of a print statement, and the values can come from input rather than from the source code. It is the smallest possible demonstration of why the previous twenty-four sections were worth reading.

📘 DEFINITION

Scanner: the class that reads input, constructed with new Scanner(System.in)

next(): reads one whitespace-delimited token

nextLine(): reads everything up to the end of the current line

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Mixing the two is the classic input bug. nextInt() and next() stop before the newline and leave it behind, so a following nextLine() reads that leftover and returns an empty String with no error — the program looks like it skipped a prompt. Call in.nextLine() once to discard the newline before reading the real line.

📊 FIGURE — + means two different things
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Building a full name
String first = "Ana";
String last = "Marsh";
String full = first + " " + last;
System.out.println(full);
System.out.println(full.length());
Ana Marsh 9
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. + between Strings joins them.
  2. The space is a String literal of its own.
  3. The length counts that space too.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — When + stops adding and starts joining
int a = 1, b = 2;
System.out.println("sum: " + a + b);
System.out.println("sum: " + (a + b));
System.out.println(a + b + " total");
sum: 12 sum: 3 3 total
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Evaluation runs left to right: once a String appears, everything after it is joined.
  2. Brackets force the addition to happen first.
  3. Before any String appears, + is still addition.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Whenever a question mixes a String with numbers and +, work left to right and switch to concatenation at the first String.

Everything in Unit 2 ran straight down the page — every statement, every time. A branch is the first thing that changes that: it lets the program choose a path based on a condition, so the same code produces different behaviour for different data.

if (temp > 100) {
    System.out.println("boiling");     // runs only when the condition is true
} else if (temp > 0) {
    System.out.println("liquid");      // checked only if the first was false
} else {
    System.out.println("frozen");      // runs when every condition above failed
}

The chain rule is what makes else if different from separate if statements: at most one block in a chain runs, and evaluation stops at the first true condition. Separate if statements each get tested independently, so several can run. This distinction is the entire content of 3.6 and half of 3.8.

Why the chain rule is the whole unit

The difference between an if-else chain and a run of separate if statements decides more questions in this unit than any other single fact. In a chain, evaluation stops at the first true condition and at most one block runs — every later condition is skipped even if it would also be true. With separate statements each is tested independently, so several can fire. Neither is more correct; the choice depends on whether the cases are alternatives or independent adjustments, and reading which one the code uses is the first thing to establish in any trace.

📘 DEFINITION

Branch: a block of statements that runs only when a condition is true

Condition: an expression that evaluates to true or false

if-else chain: a sequence of conditions where the first true one runs and the rest are skipped

Relational operator: one of <, >, <=, >=, ==, != — produces a boolean

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

Branching plus the looping in Unit 4 is the whole of control flow. Every program you write for the rest of the course is variables (Unit 2) moved around by branches and loops.

✅ Also covered in depth: Control Flow → if/else and switch Statements

📊 FIGURE — IF-ELSE IS A FORK IN THE ROAD
🎯 EXAM TIP
On the OA, trace with the given value before reading the answer choices: write down which branch runs, then evaluate only that branch. Half the distractors are the output of the branch that did not run.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Only one branch of a chain ever runs
int score = 95;
if (score >= 90) System.out.println("A");
else if (score >= 80) System.out.println("B");
else if (score >= 70) System.out.println("C");
else System.out.println("F");
A
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The first true test wins and the rest are skipped.
  2. 95 is also >= 80, but that line is never reached.
  3. That is the whole point of else-if: the tests are mutually exclusive.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Separate ifs are not a chain
int score = 95;
if (score >= 90) System.out.println("A");
if (score >= 80) System.out.println("B");
if (score >= 70) System.out.println("C");
A B C
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Without else, each if is tested independently.
  2. 95 satisfies all three, so all three print.
  3. Dropping the elses changes the meaning entirely.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Writing a grade chain as separate if statements. Every condition is then evaluated, so a high score matches several branches and the program prints more than one answer.

Testing "are these equal" is where Java splits into two rules that look identical and behave differently, and it is worth learning now rather than in 3.13 when the bug appears.

For primitives, == compares values and is correct. For objects — including Strings — == compares references: it asks "are these the same object in memory", not "do these hold the same characters".

int a = 5, b = 5;
a == b                     // true — primitives compare by value

String s1 = "cat";
String s2 = "cat";
String s3 = new String("cat");
s1 == s2                   // true  — but only because the pool reused one object
s1 == s3                   // FALSE — different objects, same characters
s1.equals(s3)              // true  — .equals compares contents

The s1 == s2 case is a trap dressed as a rule. Java keeps identical string literals in a shared pool, so two literals often are the same object — which makes == appear to work right up until a String comes from input or new, and then it silently stops working.

Why == on Strings appears to work

The reason this trap survives is that == on Strings often gives the right answer by accident. Java keeps identical string literals in a shared pool, so two literals with the same characters usually are the same object and == reports true. The moment a String comes from input, from concatenation at run time, or from new, it is a different object and the comparison silently starts returning false. Code that worked in testing then fails on real data — which is exactly why the rule is to use .equals() always, not just when it seems necessary.

📘 DEFINITION

==: compares values for primitives, and reference identity for objects

.equals(): compares contents; the correct choice for Strings and other objects

String pool: a shared store of string literals, which is why two identical literals can be the same object

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

== on Strings is the single most common Java error on this exam. Always use .equals(). And do not confuse = with == — if (x = 5) does not compile in Java for ints, because the assignment produces an int and if requires a boolean.

✅ Also covered in depth: Control Flow → if/else and switch Statements

📊 FIGURE — == compares what the variable holds
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — = assigns, == compares
int a = 5;
int b = 5;
System.out.println(a == b);
System.out.println(a != b);
boolean same = (a == b);
System.out.println(same);
true false true
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. == asks a question and produces a boolean.
  2. = would instead store a value.
  3. A comparison can be stored in a boolean variable.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Equality for numbers and for text
int x = 3;
String s = "abc";
String t = "ab" + "c";
System.out.println(x == 3);
System.out.println(s.equals(t));
System.out.println(s.equalsIgnoreCase("ABC"));
true true true
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. For primitives, == compares the values themselves.
  2. For Strings, always use .equals to compare contents.
  3. equalsIgnoreCase ignores letter case.
🎯 EXAM TIP
In a condition, if (x = 5) does not compile in Java for ints — it is an assignment, not a boolean. With boolean variables it DOES compile and is a real bug, so read carefully.
