Ranges are the natural next step from equality, and the mistake is importing mathematical notation. Java has no 0 <= x <= 100. That expression parses as (0 <= x) <= 100, which compares a boolean with an int and fails to compile.

if (0 <= x && x <= 100) { ... }    // correct: two comparisons joined by &&

The four relational operators to keep straight are <, <=, > and >=, and the boundary is where the exam lives. "At least 18" is >= 18; "over 18" is > 18. Read the wording, not the number.

Reading the boundary in the wording

Range questions almost always turn on a single word. "At least 18" and "18 or over" are >= 18; "over 18" and "more than 18" are > 18. "Between 10 and 20" is ambiguous in English and the question will disambiguate it with "inclusive" or by the answer options. The reliable technique is to test the boundary value itself: work out what the code does at exactly 18, and compare that with what the sentence says should happen at 18. If they differ, the operator is wrong.

📘 DEFINITION

Range check: testing that a value falls between two bounds, written as two comparisons joined by &&

Inclusive bound: a boundary value that counts as inside the range — uses <= or >=

Exclusive bound: a boundary value that counts as outside the range — uses < or >

🎯 EXAM TIP

When you check a range question, test the boundary itself. If the answer differs at exactly 18, the question is about > versus >= and nothing else.

✅ Also covered in depth: Control Flow → if/else and switch Statements

📊 FIGURE — a range needs two bounds
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Both ends must be stated
int t = 15;
System.out.println(t > 10 && t < 20);
System.out.println(t >= 15 && t <= 15);
System.out.println(t > 20 && t < 10);
true true false
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Two comparisons joined by && express a range.
  2. The bounds may coincide, which selects a single value.
  3. An impossible range is legal code that is simply always false.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Ordering the tests removes the second bound
int t = 15;
if (t < 10) System.out.println("low");
else if (t < 20) System.out.println("middle");
else System.out.println("high");
middle
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Reaching the second test already means t >= 10.
  2. So only the upper bound needs stating.
  3. An ordered chain is why range code is usually shorter than it looks.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Writing 10 < x < 20. Java evaluates 10 < x to a boolean and then tries to compare a boolean with 20, which does not compile. Each bound needs its own full comparison.
"}, "D286/u3/z3_4": {"body": "

With a range you can also order the checks so each one does less work. In an else if chain every later condition already knows that all the earlier ones were false, so you never need to restate the lower bound.

if (score >= 90) {
    grade = 'A';
} else if (score >= 80) {          // we already know score < 90
    grade = 'B';
} else if (score >= 70) {
    grade = 'C';
} else {
    grade = 'F';
}

Order is not optional here. Reverse it — put score >= 70 first — and everything above 70 becomes a C, because the first true condition wins and the rest are never tested. The chain reads correctly only from the most restrictive condition to the least.

Why ordering a chain is a correctness issue

In a chain, each condition is only reached when every earlier one failed, so the conditions carry hidden context. Written from most restrictive to least — 90, then 80, then 70 — each test needs only its lower bound, because the upper bound is implied by the ones above. Reverse the order and the chain still compiles, still runs, and gives everyone above 70 a C, because score >= 70 is now the first true condition for a score of 95. It is a logic error of the purest kind: no message, no crash, just wrong grades.

📘 DEFINITION

Cascading conditions: an else-if chain ordered so each condition assumes all previous ones were false

Mutually exclusive: conditions where at most one can be true for any input

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Writing the grade chain from lowest to highest is the classic version of this bug. It compiles, it runs, and every score above 70 gets a C — a logic error (1.4) that no compiler will catch.

✅ Also covered in depth: Control Flow → if/else and switch Statements

📊 FIGURE — where the boundary belongs
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Testing the boundary itself
int[] marks = {89, 90, 91};
for (int m : marks) {
    String g = (m >= 90) ? "A" : "B";
    System.out.println(m + " -> " + g);
}
89 -> B 90 -> A 91 -> A
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Always test the exact boundary value.
  2. 89 falls below, 90 and 91 are at or above.
  3. Most range bugs live on one value, not across the whole range.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A chain must cover everything
int age = 65;
if (age < 13) System.out.println("child");
else if (age < 20) System.out.println("teen");
else if (age < 65) System.out.println("adult");
else System.out.println("senior");
senior
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Each test assumes the previous ones failed.
  2. 65 is not < 65, so it falls through to the final else.
  3. The bare else is what guarantees every value is handled.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Test three values for any range question: just below the boundary, exactly on it, and just above. That finds nearly every off-by-one.
"}, "D286/u3/z3_5": {"body": "

Once ranges get more complicated than a single band, the logical operators do the joining. There are three, and the truth of each is worth holding in one sentence rather than a table.

&&   AND   true only when BOTH sides are true
||   OR    true when EITHER side is true
!    NOT   flips true to false and false to true

if (age >= 13 && age <= 19)        // teenager: both must hold
if (day == 6  || day == 7)         // weekend: either will do
if (!isValid)                       // shorthand for isValid == false

Precedence matters when they mix: ! binds tightest, then &&, then ||. So a || b && c means a || (b && c). Parenthesise when you mix them — not because Java is unclear, but because a reader will read it in English order and get it wrong.

Precedence between the logical operators

When && and || appear in the same expression, && binds tighter — so a || b && c means a || (b && c), not (a || b) && c. English reads it the other way round, which is why this is worth parenthesising even when the default happens to be what you meant. The related skill is negation: !(a && b) becomes !a || !b and !(a || b) becomes !a && !b. The operator flips along with each side, and forgetting to flip it is the standard wrong answer.

📘 DEFINITION

&& (AND): true only when both operands are true

|| (OR): true when at least one operand is true

! (NOT): inverts a boolean

Operator precedence: the order operators bind in: ! before && before ||

🎯 EXAM TIP

Negating a compound condition follows De Morgan: !(a && b) is !a || !b, and !(a || b) is !a && !b. The operator flips along with each side — forgetting to flip it is the standard wrong answer.

✅ Also covered in depth: Control Flow → if/else and switch Statements

📊 FIGURE — A RANGE IS A BAND ON THE NUMBER LINE
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
20 <= x <= 40 is not legal Java — the compiler reads it left to right, gets a boolean, and cannot compare a boolean to 40. A range always needs two comparisons joined by &&.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — && narrows, || widens
int n = 25;
System.out.println(n > 10 && n < 30);
System.out.println(n < 10 || n > 30);
System.out.println(!(n > 10 && n < 30));
true false false
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. && requires both sides — it selects the overlap.
  2. || requires either — it selects everything outside.
  3. Negating a range gives exactly the outside of it.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — De Morgan in Java
int n = 5;
System.out.println(!(n > 10 && n < 30));
System.out.println(n <= 10 || n >= 30);
System.out.println(!(n > 10 || n < 3));
System.out.println(n <= 10 && n >= 3);
true true true true
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Negating an AND gives an OR of the negations.
  2. Negating an OR gives an AND of the negations.
  3. Each pair prints the same, which is what equivalence means.
"}, "D286/u3/z3_6": {"body": "

A range with a gap is where separate if statements and an if-else chain stop being interchangeable. If the valid values are 1–10 and 20–30, the gap between them has to be expressed, not assumed.

// two accepted bands, everything else rejected
if ((n >= 1 && n <= 10) || (n >= 20 && n <= 30)) {
    System.out.println("accepted");
} else {
    System.out.println("rejected");     // covers the 11-19 gap AND everything outside
}

Note that the else is doing real work: it catches the gap and both outer regions at once. Trying to enumerate the rejected values instead is how ranges end up with holes.

Why the else does the work

With a gap in the accepted range, the temptation is to enumerate the rejected values, and that is where holes appear — it is easy to cover 11 to 19 and forget everything above 30. Expressing the accepted bands and letting a single else catch everything else is both shorter and complete by construction, because "not accepted" needs no enumeration. That is a general habit worth carrying: describe the smaller, well-defined set and let the else handle the remainder.

📘 DEFINITION

Gap: a span of values between two accepted ranges that must be excluded

Compound condition: a condition built from several comparisons joined by logical operators

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Dropping the inner parentheses changes the meaning. Because && binds tighter than ||, n >= 1 && n <= 10 || n >= 20 && n <= 30 happens to be correct here — but the moment the shape changes it will not be, so parenthesise deliberately.

📊 FIGURE — a gap is an OR of two ranges
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Two separate bands, joined with ||
int[] ages = {10, 30, 70};
for (int a : ages) {
    boolean discount = (a < 18) || (a >= 65);
    System.out.println(a + " discount? " + discount);
}
10 discount? true 30 discount? false 70 discount? true
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The qualifying ages are not one continuous range.
  2. || joins the two bands into a single condition.
  3. The middle band is what is left over.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The same thing as a chain
int a = 70;
if (a < 18) System.out.println("child");
else if (a < 65) System.out.println("standard");
else System.out.println("senior");
senior
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Ordering the bands lets each test state only one bound.
  2. 70 fails both earlier tests and lands in the else.
  3. A chain is usually clearer than one long boolean expression.
🎯 EXAM TIP
When a question describes a discount for the young AND the old, the condition is an OR of two ranges, not an AND. An AND there is always false.
"}, "D286/u3/z3_7": {"body": "

Sometimes the checks are genuinely independent — a product can be both on sale and in stock — and then separate if statements are right, precisely because you want more than one to run.

// independent features: each is tested, several can fire
if (hasDiscount) { price -= 5; }
if (isMember)    { price -= 3; }
if (isBulk)      { price -= 2; }

// versus a chain: at most ONE of these ever runs
if (hasDiscount)      { price -= 5; }
else if (isMember)    { price -= 3; }

So the choice between else if and separate ifs is not stylistic. Ask: can two of these be true at once, and if so should both take effect? Yes means separate statements; no means a chain.

Choosing between a chain and separate ifs

The decision has a test that always works: can two of these conditions be true at the same time, and if so should both take effect? Discounts stack, so they are separate if statements. Grade bands do not, so they are a chain. Getting this wrong produces bugs in opposite directions — a chain where you wanted stacking applies only the first discount, and separate statements where you wanted a chain apply every band at once. Both compile, and neither reports anything.

📘 DEFINITION

Independent conditions: conditions that can be true simultaneously and should each take effect

Nested if: an if placed inside another, used when the inner test only makes sense if the outer one passed

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

This one decision quietly determines the output of many trace questions. When you read code in an exam, mark the chains first — everything in a chain after a true condition is dead.

📊 FIGURE — independent features need independent ifs
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Several features can be true at once
boolean sunroof = true, heatedSeats = true, towbar = false;
int extra = 0;
if (sunroof) extra += 900;
if (heatedSeats) extra += 400;
if (towbar) extra += 550;
System.out.println("extras cost " + extra);
extras cost 1300
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Each feature is independent, so each gets its own if.
  2. The costs accumulate.
  3. An else-if chain would have counted only the first.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The same code written wrongly
boolean sunroof = true, heatedSeats = true;
int extra = 0;
if (sunroof) extra += 900;
else if (heatedSeats) extra += 400;
System.out.println(extra);
900
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. else if makes the options exclusive.
  2. The heated seats are never charged for.
  3. Ask whether the cases exclude one another; if not, do not use else.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Using an else-if chain for features that can coexist. Only one branch runs, so every option after the first is silently ignored.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Mutually exclusive (a grade band, a category) → else-if chain. Independently true (features, permissions, flags) → separate ifs.
"}, "D286/u3/z3_8": {"body": "

The branching errors that cost marks are not exotic; they are four specific things, and all four compile cleanly.

if (x > 5);                    // 1. stray semicolon — the branch body is empty,
    System.out.println("hi");  //    so this line ALWAYS prints

if (x > 5)
    a = 1;
    b = 2;                     // 2. no braces — b = 2 is NOT in the branch,
                               //    despite the indentation

if (name == "Ada")             // 3. == on a String — compares references (3.2)

if (x = 5)                     // 4. = instead of == — will not compile for int

Three of the four are silent. The compiler is happy with an empty branch body, happy with a one-statement branch followed by an unrelated statement, and happy comparing references. Only the last one is caught for you.

Why three of the four are silent

The branching errors that matter are the ones the compiler accepts. A stray semicolon after if (x > 5); makes the branch body empty, so the indented line below runs unconditionally. Omitting braces means only the first statement belongs to the branch, however the code is indented — Java reads braces, not layout. And == on a String compares references. Only if (x = 5) is caught, and only because an assignment produces an int where a boolean is required. Using braces always removes the first two permanently.

📘 DEFINITION

Empty statement: a lone semicolon; legal Java, and the cause of the if(x>5); bug

Dangling else: an else binds to the nearest unmatched if, not to the one the indentation suggests

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Always use braces, even for one statement. It costs two characters and removes bug 1 and bug 2 permanently.

✅ Also covered in depth: Control Flow → if/else and switch Statements

📊 FIGURE — three that compile and still misbehave
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The stray semicolon
int x = 3;
if (x > 5);
    System.out.println("runs anyway");
System.out.println("and so does this");
runs anyway and so does this
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The semicolon right after the condition IS the body — an empty statement.
  2. The indented line is therefore outside the if entirely.
  3. It compiles without complaint and prints even though 3 is not > 5.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Missing braces around two statements
int t = 2;
if (t > 5)
    System.out.println("hot");
    System.out.println("fan on");
fan on
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Only the FIRST statement belongs to the if.
  2. The second runs unconditionally, whatever the indentation suggests.
  3. Braces would have made the intent enforceable.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Whenever a question shows an if whose output looks impossible, check for a semicolon straight after the condition or a missing pair of braces. Those two account for most of them.
"}, "D286/u3/z3_9": {"body": "

A toll calculation is the standard worked example because it forces every idea in the unit into one small program: a chain, a range with boundaries, and a compound condition.

// weekday rush hour (6-9 or 16-19) costs more; weekends are flat
double toll;
boolean weekday   = (day >= 1 && day <= 5);
boolean rushHour  = (hour >= 6 && hour <= 9) || (hour >= 16 && hour <= 19);

if (weekday && rushHour) {
    toll = 5.00;
} else if (weekday) {
    toll = 2.50;
} else {
    toll = 1.00;
}

Naming the two conditions as booleans first is the technique worth copying. It turns an unreadable four-way compound test into two named ideas, and the chain then reads as ordinary English — which is also how you avoid ordering it wrongly.

Naming conditions before using them

The technique this example demonstrates is worth more than the toll rules. Assigning a compound condition to a well-named boolean first — weekday, rushHour — turns an unreadable four-clause test into two named ideas, after which the chain reads as English and its ordering can be checked by eye. It also makes tracing far faster: work out the two booleans for the given input once, then walk the chain, instead of re-evaluating a long condition at every step.

📘 DEFINITION

Boolean variable: a variable holding true or false, often used to name a condition

Decision table: a listing of every input combination and its expected result, used to check a chain is complete

🎯 EXAM TIP

When a trace question has a chain this long, write out the boolean sub-conditions for the given input first. The chain then resolves in one pass instead of re-reading each condition.

📊 FIGURE — ordered bands, one charge each
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Charging by weight band
int[] weights = {1200, 5000, 12000};
for (int w : weights) {
    double toll;
    if (w <= 3500) toll = 2.40;
    else if (w <= 7500) toll = 5.80;
    else toll = 11.50;
    System.out.printf("%d kg -> %.2f%n", w, toll);
}
1200 kg -> 2.40 5000 kg -> 5.80 12000 kg -> 11.50
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Bands are ordered lightest first, so each test needs one bound.
  2. The first matching band sets the toll and the rest are skipped.
  3. The final else catches everything heavier.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — An off-peak discount on top
double toll = 5.80;
boolean offPeak = true;
if (offPeak) toll = toll * 0.80;
System.out.printf("%.2f%n", toll);
4.64
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The discount is independent of the band, so it is a separate if.
  2. Multiplying by 0.80 takes 20% off.
  3. Combining it into the band chain would have been wrong.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Ordering the bands from heaviest to lightest while still using <=. The first test then catches everything and every vehicle pays the same toll.
"}, "D286/u3/z3_10": {"body": "

Order of evaluation decides what an expression means before any branching happens. Java evaluates in a fixed precedence order, and it is short enough to memorise for the exam.

1.  ()                       parentheses
2.  ++  --  !  (unary)       including unary minus
3.  *  /  %                  multiplicative
4.  +  -                     additive
5.  <  <=  >  >=             relational
6.  ==  !=                   equality
7.  &&                       logical AND
8.  ||                       logical OR
9.  =  +=  -=  *=  /=        assignment (right to left)

Two consequences catch people. Arithmetic always resolves before comparison, so a + b > c is (a + b) > c. And comparison always resolves before &&, so x > 0 && y > 0 needs no inner parentheses.

What the precedence table is really for

You will not be asked to recite the table; you will be asked what an expression evaluates to, and that is the same thing. The two consequences that appear most are that arithmetic always finishes before comparison — so a + b > c is (a + b) > c — and that comparison always finishes before the logical operators, so x > 0 && y > 0 needs no inner parentheses. Assignment being right-associative is the third: a = b = c = 5 works because the rightmost assignment happens first and produces a value.

📘 DEFINITION

Precedence: which operator binds first when several appear in one expression

Associativity: the direction operators of equal precedence group in; left to right for arithmetic, right to left for assignment

🎯 EXAM TIP

a = b = 0 works because assignment is right-associative: b = 0 happens first and produces 0, which is then assigned to a.

✅ Also covered in depth: Control Flow → if/else and switch Statements

📊 FIGURE — what binds tightest
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Arithmetic before comparison, comparison before &&
int a = 2, b = 3, c = 10;
System.out.println(a + b * 2);
System.out.println(a + b < c);
System.out.println(a < b && b < c);
8 true true
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. b * 2 is computed before the addition.
  2. a + b is computed before the comparison with c.
  3. Both comparisons finish before && combines them.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — && binds tighter than ||
boolean p = true, q = false, r = false;
System.out.println(p || q && r);
System.out.println((p || q) && r);
true false
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The first reads as p || (q && r), which is true.
  2. Forcing the OR first makes it false.
  3. Brackets are the only reliable way to say which you meant.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Assuming || and && have equal precedence and run left to right. && binds tighter, so p || q && r is p || (q && r).
"}, "D286/u3/z3_11": {"body": "

A switch is a chain restricted to one thing: comparing a single variable against a list of constant values. That restriction buys readability, and costs you the ability to test ranges — a switch cannot express "greater than 90".

switch (day) {
    case 1:
    case 2:
    case 3:
    case 4:
    case 5:
        System.out.println("weekday");
        break;                       // without break, execution FALLS THROUGH
    case 6:
    case 7:
        System.out.println("weekend");
        break;
    default:
        System.out.println("invalid");
}

Fall-through is the defining behaviour and the source of nearly every switch question. Without break, control continues into the next case regardless of whether that case matched. Stacked empty cases (1 through 5 above) use this on purpose; a missing break anywhere else is a bug.

When a switch is the wrong tool

A switch compares one value against a list of compile-time constants, and everything it cannot do follows from that. It cannot test a range, so grade bands must stay an if chain. It cannot use a variable as a case label. It does not work with double or boolean. What it does buy is readability when there genuinely are many discrete values, and the stacked-case idiom — several case labels sharing one body — which is the one legitimate use of fall-through. Everywhere else, a missing break is a bug that produces extra output rather than an error.

📘 DEFINITION

switch: a multi-way branch comparing one expression against constant case labels

case: one labelled entry point in a switch

break: exits the switch; without it, execution falls through to the next case

default: the case that runs when nothing else matched; optional, and may appear anywhere

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

A switch works with int, char, String and enum, but not with double or boolean. And every case label must be a compile-time constant — a variable is not allowed.

✅ Also covered in depth: Control Flow → if/else and switch Statements

📊 FIGURE — SWITCH: BREAK EXITS, NO BREAK FALLS THROUGH
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Fall-through when break is missing
int day = 2;
switch (day) {
    case 1: System.out.println("Mon");
    case 2: System.out.println("Tue");
    case 3: System.out.println("Wed");
        break;
    default: System.out.println("other");
}
Tue Wed
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Execution ENTERS at the matching case.
  2. With no break it keeps running into the cases below.
  3. So case 2 prints Tue and then Wed, stopping at the break.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Deliberate grouping, and the arrow form
char grade = 'B';
switch (grade) {
    case 'A': case 'B': System.out.println("pass"); break;
    case 'C': System.out.println("borderline"); break;
    default: System.out.println("fail");
}
int m = 4;
String season = switch (m) {
    case 12, 1, 2 -> "winter";
    case 3, 4, 5 -> "spring";
    default -> "other";
};
System.out.println(season);
pass spring
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Stacked labels with no code between them share one body deliberately.
  2. The arrow form does not fall through at all.
  3. It can also produce a value, assigned straight into a variable.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Any switch question showing more output than expected is testing fall-through. Trace from the matching label downwards until you meet a break.
"}, "D286/u3/z3_12": {"body": "

boolean is the type every condition in this unit has actually been producing. It holds exactly two values, true and false, and — unlike C — Java will not accept a number in its place.

boolean isValid = (age >= 18);       // a comparison IS a boolean value
boolean canVote = isValid && isRegistered;

if (isValid) { ... }                 // idiomatic
if (isValid == true) { ... }         // legal but redundant
if (1) { ... }                       // COMPILE ERROR — int is not boolean

Because a comparison is a value, you can store it, pass it and return it. That is what makes 3.9 readable, and it is the basis of the boolean-returning methods in 6.5.

Booleans as values, not just conditions

The step that makes conditions manageable is realising a comparison is a value. age >= 18 produces a boolean that can be stored, passed to a method, returned from one, or combined with others — which is what makes the named-condition technique in 3.9 possible and what makes predicate methods in 6.5 natural. It also explains why if (isValid == true) is redundant: isValid already is the boolean the if wants.

📘 DEFINITION

boolean: a primitive type with exactly two values, true and false

Boolean expression: any expression producing a boolean, including comparisons and logical combinations

Flag: a boolean variable used to record whether something happened

🎯 EXAM TIP

A boolean field defaults to false; a boolean local, like every local, has no default at all (2.2). The wrapper class Boolean defaults to null, which is a third possibility and a source of runtime failures (7.13).

📊 FIGURE — a condition IS a boolean
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Storing and negating a condition
int stock = 0;
boolean inStock = stock > 0;
System.out.println(inStock);
System.out.println(!inStock);
if (!inStock) System.out.println("reorder");
false true reorder
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The comparison produces a boolean, which can be named.
  2. ! flips it.
  3. A well-named boolean makes the if read like a sentence.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Comparing to true is redundant
boolean ready = true;
if (ready) System.out.println("go");
if (ready == true) System.out.println("also go");
go also go
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. ready is already a boolean.
  2. ready == true produces the same boolean again.
  3. The shorter form is preferred, and avoids the = typo.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Writing if (ready = true) with one equals sign. For booleans this COMPILES — it assigns true and then tests it — so the branch always runs and the compiler never warns you.
"}, "D286/u3/z3_13": {"body": "

String comparison is where 3.2 stops being theoretical. Java gives you three methods, and choosing between them is a real decision rather than a style question.

s1.equals(s2)             // exact content match, case-sensitive -> boolean
s1.equalsIgnoreCase(s2)   // content match, ignoring case            -> boolean
s1.compareTo(s2)          // dictionary order                        -> int

"apple".compareTo("banana")   // negative — apple comes first
"banana".compareTo("apple")   // positive
"apple".compareTo("apple")    // 0 — equal

compareTo returns an int, not a boolean, and the exact number is not meaningful — only its sign is. It is the method that makes sorting possible, which is why it returns in 13.5 with the Comparable interface.

Choosing between the three comparisons

The three String comparisons answer different questions and questions test whether you picked the right one. equals asks "are these identical", equalsIgnoreCase asks "identical apart from case", and compareTo asks "which comes first in dictionary order". Only the last returns an int, and only its sign is meaningful — the magnitude is an implementation detail. Putting the literal on the left, as "yes".equals(input), is worth doing habitually because it cannot throw when the variable is null.

📘 DEFINITION

equals(): content comparison, case-sensitive, returns boolean

equalsIgnoreCase(): content comparison ignoring letter case

compareTo(): returns negative, zero or positive to indicate dictionary order

Lexicographic order: dictionary ordering based on character codes, so all uppercase letters sort before all lowercase

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Calling a method on a null String throws NullPointerException. Writing the literal first — "yes".equals(input) instead of input.equals("yes") — is safe even when input is null.

✅ Also covered in depth: Java Basics → Operators, Strings, and Scanner

📊 FIGURE — == against .equals
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Why == sometimes appears to work
String a = "hello";
String b = "hello";
String c = new String("hello");
System.out.println(a == b);
System.out.println(a == c);
System.out.println(a.equals(c));
true false true
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Identical literals are pooled, so a and b are the same object and == is true.
  2. new String forces a separate object, so == is false.
  3. .equals compares the characters and is true either way.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Ordering text with compareTo
System.out.println("apple".compareTo("banana"));
System.out.println("banana".compareTo("apple"));
System.out.println("apple".compareTo("apple"));
System.out.println("Apple".equalsIgnoreCase("APPLE"));
-1 1 0 true

  2. Positive means after, zero means equal.

Strings are indexed like arrays and, crucially, are immutable: no method changes the string it is called on. Every one of them returns a new String and leaves the original untouched.

String s = "Hello";

s.length()          // 5
s.charAt(0)         // 'H'      — indexes start at 0, so the last is length()-1
s.substring(1, 3)   // "el"     — from index 1 UP TO but NOT including 3
s.substring(2)      // "llo"    — from index 2 to the end
s.toUpperCase()     // "HELLO"  — s is still "Hello"

s = s.toUpperCase();   // to keep the result you must assign it

The half-open range in substring is not an inconsistency — it is the same convention as loop bounds in Unit 4, and it means substring(a, b) always has length b - a.

Why the half-open range is consistent

substring(a, b) including the start and excluding the end looks like an inconsistency and is the same convention as loop bounds and array indices. Its practical advantage is that the length of the result is always b − a, with no adjustment, and that consecutive substrings tile without overlap: substring(0,3) and substring(3,6) fit together exactly. Once you expect it, the off-by-one disappears. The other half of this section is immutability — every method returns a new String, so an unassigned call does nothing at all.

📘 DEFINITION

Immutable: cannot be changed after creation; every String method returns a new String

Index: the position of a character, counting from 0

substring(start, end): the characters from start up to but not including end

charAt(i): the single char at position i

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Forgetting to assign the result is the number one String bug: s.toUpperCase(); on its own does nothing. And an index equal to length() throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException — the last valid index is length() - 1.

✅ Also covered in depth: Java Basics → Operators, Strings, and Scanner

📊 FIGURE — index positions in "Java"
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Reading characters and slices
String s = "Programming";
System.out.println(s.length());
System.out.println(s.charAt(0));
System.out.println(s.substring(0, 7));
System.out.println(s.substring(7));
11 P Program ming
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. substring(a, b) stops just BEFORE b.
  2. So (0, 7) gives seven characters.
  3. One argument means from there to the end.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The index that does not exist
String s = "Java";
System.out.println(s.charAt(s.length() - 1));
try {
    System.out.println(s.charAt(s.length()));
} catch (StringIndexOutOfBoundsException e) {
    System.out.println("out of bounds");
}
a out of bounds
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The last character sits at length() − 1.
  2. Asking for index length() is one past the end.
  3. Java throws rather than returning anything.
🎯 EXAM TIP
The length of substring(a, b) is exactly b − a. Use that to check any substring answer in one step.

char is a numeric type wearing a costume. It stores a 16-bit Unicode code, which is why arithmetic on characters works and why 'A' and 65 are interchangeable in the right context.

char c = 'A';
int  n = c;              // 65 — automatic widening
char next = (char)(c + 1);   // 'B' — the cast is required to get back to char

'0' is 48    'A' is 65    'a' is 97      // the three anchors worth knowing

int digit = '7' - '0';   // 7 — converts a digit character to its value

The Character class supplies the tests you would otherwise write with ranges:

Character.isDigit(c)       Character.isLetter(c)
Character.isUpperCase(c)   Character.isWhitespace(c)
Character.toUpperCase(c)   Character.toLowerCase(c)

Why characters and integers are interchangeable

A char is a 16-bit number, so every behaviour in this section follows from ordinary arithmetic. Comparisons work because codes are ordered — which is why 'Z' < 'a' is true, since uppercase codes come first. Ranges work for the same reason, so c >= 'a' && c <= 'z' tests for a lowercase letter. And the Character methods exist to say the same thing more readably: Character.isDigit(c) is clearer than comparing against '0' and '9', and it is correct for characters beyond ASCII where the range test is not.

📘 DEFINITION

char: a 16-bit primitive holding a single Unicode character; single quotes

ASCII: the character encoding covering the first 128 codes; the basis for the numeric values above

Character class: the utility class of static methods for classifying and converting characters

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Single quotes make a char, double quotes make a String. 'A' and "A" are different types, and char c = "A"; does not compile.

📊 FIGURE — the Character tests worth knowing
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Classifying each character of a string
String s = "a1 B";
for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
    char c = s.charAt(i);
    System.out.println(c + " digit=" + Character.isDigit(c) + " letter=" + Character.isLetter(c));
}
a digit=false letter=true 1 digit=true letter=false digit=false letter=false B digit=false letter=true
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. charAt pulls one character out at a time.
  2. The Character class answers the questions about it.
  3. A space is neither a digit nor a letter.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Changing case returns a new value
char c = 'q';
System.out.println(Character.toUpperCase(c));
System.out.println(c);
System.out.println(Character.isUpperCase('Q'));
Q q true
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. toUpperCase RETURNS the converted character.
  2. The original variable is unchanged.
  3. Assign the result if you want to keep it.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Character.isDigit(c) tests a char. Character.getNumericValue(c) — or c - '0' — converts it to the number it represents. Questions often offer both and mean the second.

Searching within a String is the other half of 3.14, and the whole family shares one convention: -1 means not found. Nothing throws; you get a sentinel value you have to check.

String s = "hello world";

s.indexOf("o")        // 4   — first occurrence
s.indexOf("o", 5)     // 7   — first occurrence at or after index 5
s.lastIndexOf("o")    // 7
s.indexOf("z")        // -1  — NOT FOUND
s.contains("wor")     // true
s.replace("l", "L")   // "heLLo worLd" — a NEW string, s is unchanged

Because indexOf returns -1 rather than throwing, forgetting to check it turns into a StringIndexOutOfBoundsException later, when the -1 is handed to substring. Test the result before you use it.

Why −1 rather than an exception

The whole indexOf family returns −1 for "not found" rather than throwing, which makes it cheap to call and dangerous to ignore. The failure mode is delayed: indexOf quietly returns −1, the value is passed to substring or used as an index, and that throws — so the exception appears on a line that is not where the mistake was. Testing the result before using it is what keeps the error where it happened. The other detail questions test is that replace replaces every occurrence, not just the first.

📘 DEFINITION

indexOf(): the position of the first match, or -1 if absent

lastIndexOf(): the position of the last match, or -1

contains(): true if the substring appears anywhere

replace(): returns a new String with every occurrence replaced

🎯 EXAM TIP

replace replaces all occurrences, not just the first. If a question shows only the first one changing, the answer is wrong.

✅ Also covered in depth: Java Basics → Operators, Strings, and Scanner

📊 FIGURE — what each search returns
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — indexOf returns a position, or -1
String s = "order-4821-ship";
System.out.println(s.indexOf("4821"));
System.out.println(s.indexOf("9999"));
System.out.println(s.contains("ship"));
System.out.println(s.substring(s.indexOf("-") + 1, s.lastIndexOf("-")));
6 -1 true 4821
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. A found substring reports where it starts.
  2. Absent gives −1, which is why you must test before using it as an index.
  3. indexOf and lastIndexOf together pull out the middle field.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — replace does not modify the original
String s = "grey shoes, grey hat";
s.replace("grey", "blue");
System.out.println(s);
String t = s.replace("grey", "blue");
System.out.println(t);
grey shoes, grey hat blue shoes, blue hat
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The first call computes a new String and throws it away.
  2. The original is untouched, because Strings are immutable.
  3. Capturing the return value is what makes the change stick.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Using the result of indexOf without checking for −1. Passing −1 to substring throws, and the message points at the substring rather than at the failed search.

The conditional operator compresses a two-way if-else that assigns to one variable into a single expression. It is the only ternary operator in Java, which is why it is often just called "the ternary".

int max = (a > b) ? a : b;

// identical to
int max;
if (a > b) { max = a; } else { max = b; }

It is an expression, so it produces a value and can be used anywhere a value fits — inside a println, as an argument, inside another ternary. That last option is where readability collapses; nesting more than one is where an if is simply better.

When the ternary earns its place

The conditional operator is an expression, so it produces a value and fits where a value fits — inside a println, as an argument, on the right of an assignment. That is exactly when it is worth using: assigning one of two values to one variable. It stops being worth it the moment it nests, because a ternary inside a ternary is harder to read than the if it replaced. Both branches must also produce compatible types, which is why it cannot contain a statement that returns nothing.

📘 DEFINITION

Conditional operator: condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse — an expression, not a statement

Ternary: an operator taking three operands; Java has exactly one

🎯 EXAM TIP

Both branches must produce compatible types, and the whole thing must produce a value — so a ternary cannot contain a statement like System.out.println used as a branch result of type void.

✅ Also covered in depth: Control Flow → if/else and switch Statements

📊 FIGURE — the ternary is an expression
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Choosing a value inline
int stock = 0;
String label = (stock > 0) ? "In stock" : "Sold out";
System.out.println(label);
int a = 7, b = 4;
System.out.println(a > b ? a : b);
Sold out 7
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The condition comes first, then the value if true, then if false.
  2. The whole thing evaluates to one value.
  3. That is why it can sit on the right of an assignment.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The same logic written both ways
int n = -5;
String sign = (n >= 0) ? "non-negative" : "negative";
System.out.println(sign);
String sign2;
if (n >= 0) sign2 = "non-negative";
else sign2 = "negative";
System.out.println(sign2);
negative negative
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Both produce exactly the same result.
  2. The ternary is shorter when the ONLY job is picking a value.
  3. An if/else is clearer as soon as either branch does more than one thing.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Reaching for a ternary when each branch has to perform several statements. It cannot hold statements, only values — the attempt does not compile, and forcing it produces unreadable code.

Comparing floating-point values with == is the one comparison that is wrong for a reason unrelated to references. Values like 0.1 have no exact binary representation, so arithmetic accumulates a tiny error, and two numbers that should match do not.

0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3        // FALSE
0.1 + 0.2               // actually 0.30000000000000004

// the correct test: is the difference small enough
final double EPSILON = 0.0001;
if (Math.abs(a - b) < EPSILON) {
    // treat as equal
}

This is the same underlying fact as 2.7: double stores an approximation. It is not a rounding bug you can avoid by being careful — it is how binary fractions work, and it is why money is normally stored in whole cents as an int.

Why == on doubles is a rule, not a caution

Comparing computed doubles with == fails for a structural reason, not an occasional one: values like 0.1 have no exact binary representation, so arithmetic accumulates a tiny error and two numbers that should match do not. It is not fixable by being careful, which is why the remedy is a tolerance — Math.abs(a − b) < EPSILON — rather than more precision. The same fact is why money is stored as whole cents in an integer, and it connects directly back to 2.7.

📘 DEFINITION

Epsilon: a small tolerance value; two doubles are treated as equal when their difference is below it

Math.abs(): absolute value; used so the comparison works regardless of which is larger

Representation error: the gap between a decimal value and its nearest binary approximation

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Never write if (total == 0.3) for a computed double. Compare against a tolerance, or use int cents, or BigDecimal.

✅ Also covered in depth: Java Basics → Primitive Types and Type Casting

📊 FIGURE — compare within a tolerance
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Why == fails on doubles
double a = 0.1 + 0.2;
double b = 0.3;
System.out.println(a);
System.out.println(a == b);
System.out.println(Math.abs(a - b) < 0.000000001);
0.30000000000000004 false true
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary form, so the sum is slightly off.
  2. == demands the bits match exactly, and they do not.
  3. Comparing the difference against a small tolerance is the fix.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Money is safest in whole units
double total = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) total += 0.1;
System.out.println(total);
System.out.println(total == 1.0);
int cents = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) cents += 10;
System.out.println(cents);
0.9999999999999999 false 100
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Ten additions accumulate ten small errors.
  2. The total is not exactly 1.0, so the test fails.
  3. Counting in whole cents avoids the problem entirely.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Never compare doubles with == in an exam answer. The expected answer is always a tolerance test, or storing the value as an integer number of the smallest unit.

Short-circuit evaluation is a promise Java makes about how much of a condition it bothers to run: with &&, if the left side is false the right side is never evaluated, because the answer is already settled. With ||, a true left side settles it the same way.

if (count != 0 && total / count > 5) { ... }
//   ^ if count is 0, the division never happens — no ArithmeticException

if (s != null && s.length() > 0) { ... }
//   ^ the null check GUARDS the method call — order is not optional here

This is why the guard has to come first. Swap the two halves and the protection disappears entirely, because the side that would crash gets evaluated before the side that would have prevented it.

Short-circuiting as a tool

Short-circuit evaluation is usually introduced as an efficiency detail and is more useful as a correctness tool. Because a false left operand of && means the right is never evaluated, a guard placed first makes the following test safe: count != 0 && total / count > 5 cannot divide by zero, and s != null && s.length() > 0 cannot throw. Reverse the order and the protection vanishes entirely. Exam questions that count how many times a method is called inside a condition are testing exactly this.

📘 DEFINITION

Short-circuit evaluation: skipping the right operand when the left already determines the result

Guard condition: a test placed first specifically to make the following test safe

& and |: the non-short-circuiting versions; both sides are always evaluated

🎯 EXAM TIP

If an exam question counts how many times a method is called inside a condition, short-circuiting is the point. Work left to right and stop the moment the result is determined.

✅ Also covered in depth: Control Flow → if/else and switch Statements

📊 FIGURE — SHORT CIRCUIT: THE RIGHT SIDE MAY NEVER RUN
🎯 EXAM TIP
This is why (x != 0) && (total / x > 2) is safe but the reversed order crashes when x is 0. If a question swaps the operand order, the answer usually changes.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The right side may never run
int count = 0, total = 50;
if (count != 0 && total / count > 5) System.out.println("high");
else System.out.println("skipped safely");
skipped safely
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. count != 0 is false.
  2. && already knows the answer, so the division is never evaluated.
  3. Swapping the two conditions would divide by zero and crash.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Watching the short circuit happen
System.out.println(check(false) && check(true));
System.out.println("---");
System.out.println(check(true) || check(false));
evaluated false false --- evaluated true true
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The first prints only one 'evaluated' line — the right side of && is skipped.
  2. The second also prints only one — || stops as soon as it sees true.
  3. Only the side that can still change the answer is evaluated.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Putting a side effect on the right of && or || — an increment, or a method that writes something. It may never run, and the bug appears only for certain inputs.

This worked example runs the whole unit through a salary problem: a rate chosen by a chain, then a discount applied only under a compound condition.

double rate;
if (salary >= 100000)      { rate = 0.28; }
else if (salary >= 50000)  { rate = 0.22; }
else if (salary >= 25000)  { rate = 0.15; }
else                       { rate = 0.10; }

double tax = salary * rate;

// the sale discount is independent, so it is a separate if
if (isMember && purchase > 100) {
    purchase *= 0.90;
}

Notice the two structures side by side and doing different jobs: the chain picks exactly one rate (3.4), while the separate if applies an independent adjustment (3.7). Getting this pairing right is what the section is testing.

Two structures doing different jobs

This example puts a chain and an independent if side by side deliberately. The tax rate is one of several mutually exclusive bands, so it is a chain ordered highest-first. The member discount is an independent adjustment that should apply on top, so it is a separate statement. Swapping either produces a program that runs and is wrong: a chain for the discount would suppress it whenever a band matched, and separate statements for the bands would apply every rate in turn.

📘 DEFINITION

Tiered rate: a value selected from bands by an ordered else-if chain

Compound discount condition: two requirements joined by &&, both of which must hold

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Ordering the chain lowest-first breaks it silently, and using || where the wording says "and" gives the discount to everyone. Read the requirement sentence once per operator.

📊 FIGURE — band first, then adjustments
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A tiered commission
double sales = 12000;
double rate;
if (sales < 5000) rate = 0.02;
else if (sales < 20000) rate = 0.05;
else rate = 0.08;
System.out.printf("%.2f%n", sales * rate);
600.00
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The bands are mutually exclusive, so an else-if chain is right.
  2. 12000 fails the first test and passes the second.
  3. Formatting happens once, at output.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Stacking an independent discount
double price = 250.00;
boolean member = true;
boolean clearance = true;
if (member) price *= 0.90;
if (clearance) price *= 0.80;
System.out.printf("%.2f%n", price);
180.00
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Both discounts can apply, so each gets its own if.
  2. They compound: 10% off, then 20% off what remains.
  3. That is not the same as a single 30% off.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Read carefully whether discounts stack or replace each other. Two 10% discounts applied in turn give 19% off, not 20% — a favourite exam distinction.

The final example combines the String methods of 3.13 to 3.16 with branching: given a name and a list, decide whether it matches, ignoring case and surrounding spaces.

String input = scnr.nextLine().trim();          // strip stray spaces first

if (input.equalsIgnoreCase("Ada")) {
    System.out.println("exact match");
} else if (input.toLowerCase().contains("ad")) {
    System.out.println("partial match at index " + input.toLowerCase().indexOf("ad"));
} else {
    System.out.println("no match");
}

The order of operations in the second branch matters: lowercase first, then search, so that "AD", "Ad" and "ad" all match. Doing it the other way — searching then lowercasing — would search the original case and miss.

The rest of the String search family

Beyond indexOf and contains, three more methods appear constantly in matching problems and all return a boolean.

s.startsWith("A")     true if the string begins with "A"
s.endsWith(".com")    true if it ends with ".com"
s.isEmpty()           true if the length is 0
s.isBlank()           true if it is empty or only whitespace (Java 11+)

startsWith and endsWith are case-sensitive, like equals, so a case-insensitive prefix test means normalising first: s.toLowerCase().startsWith("a").

Normalise, then compare

The order of operations in the matching logic is what makes it work. Trimming first removes stray spaces that would defeat any comparison; lowercasing before searching means every capitalisation of the target matches. Searching first and lowercasing afterwards would search the original case and miss. That sequence — normalise the input, then test it — is the general habit worth taking from this section, and it is the reason equalsIgnoreCase exists at all.

📘 DEFINITION

trim(): returns a new String with leading and trailing whitespace removed

Normalisation: converting input to a consistent form (case, spacing) before comparing it

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

Normalise, then compare. That single habit removes most String-matching bugs, and it is the same reasoning that makes equalsIgnoreCase exist in the first place.

📊 FIGURE — searching with a flag
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Searching a list of names
String[] names = {"Ada", "Grace", "Alan"};
String target = "Grace";
boolean found = false;
for (int i = 0; i < names.length; i++) {
    if (names[i].equals(target)) { found = true; break; }
}
System.out.println(found ? "found" : "not found");
found
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The flag starts false — the assumption before any evidence.
  2. .equals compares the characters, which is what matters.
  3. break stops as soon as the answer is known.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Reporting where it was found
String[] names = {"Ada", "Grace", "Alan"};
int index = -1;
for (int i = 0; i < names.length; i++) {
    if (names[i].equalsIgnoreCase("alan")) { index = i; break; }
}
System.out.println(index);
System.out.println(index >= 0 ? "at " + index : "absent");
2 at 2
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. −1 is the conventional 'not found' marker, matching indexOf.
  2. equalsIgnoreCase makes the search case-insensitive.
  3. Testing index >= 0 is how you distinguish found from absent.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Comparing the names with ==. It compares object identity, so a name read from input will not match a literal even when the text is identical.

Set the flag or index BEFORE the loop, never inside it. Declaring it inside means it is destroyed on each pass and the result is unreadable afterwards.

A branch chooses whether a block runs. A loop chooses how many times. That is the only difference, and it is the reason loops are where beginners stall: an if you can read once, but a loop you have to trace.

Every loop, whatever its syntax, has the same three moving parts. Miss any one of them and you get an infinite loop or a loop that never starts.

int i = 0;              // 1. INITIALISE  — set up the loop variable
while (i < 5) {         // 2. CONDITION   — checked BEFORE each pass
    System.out.println(i);
    i++;                // 3. UPDATE      — move toward making the condition false
}

Java has three loop forms and they are interchangeable in power: while when you do not know the count in advance, for when you do, and do-while when the body must run at least once (19.1). Choosing between them is about clarity, never about capability.

The three moving parts, named

Every loop — whatever the syntax — is made of the same three things, and naming them is what lets you debug one you did not write.

PartDoesIf you get it wrong
Initialisationsets the starting value before the first testthe loop starts in the wrong place, or does not compile
Conditionis tested before each pass; the loop runs while it is truethe loop never starts, or never stops
Updatechanges something the condition depends oninfinite loop — the classic cause
int i = 0;              // initialisation
while (i < 5) {         // condition
    System.out.println(i);
    i++;                // update  <- forget this and it never ends
}

An infinite loop is almost always a missing or ineffective update: the condition tests something the body never changes. The other half of the pair is a loop that never runs at all, which happens when the condition is already false at the first test — often correct behaviour, not a bug, when the data is empty.

📘 DEFINITION

Loop: a construct that repeats a block of statements while a condition holds

Iteration: one pass through the loop body

Loop variable: the variable the condition tests and the update changes

Infinite loop: a loop whose condition never becomes false, usually because the update is missing or moves the wrong way

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

Nearly every trace question in the exam is a loop question. The reliable method is a table: one column per variable, one row per iteration. It is slower than reading and it is right far more often.

📊 FIGURE — a loop is a branch with one extra arrow — the one going back
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — folding a repeated block into a loop

A warehouse program scans four crates. Written out by hand it is the same two lines copied four times, with only the crate number changing — which is the signal that a loop is wanted.

int crate = 1;                          // 1. INITIALISE
while (crate <= 4) {                    // 2. CONDITION
    System.out.println("Crate " + crate + " scanned");
    crate++;                            // 3. UPDATE
}
System.out.println("Total crates: " + (crate - 1));
Test #cratecrate <= 4What happens
11trueprints "Crate 1 scanned", crate becomes 2
22trueprints "Crate 2 scanned", crate becomes 3
33trueprints "Crate 3 scanned", crate becomes 4
44trueprints "Crate 4 scanned", crate becomes 5
55falseloop exits — the body does not run
OUTPUTCrate 1 scanned Crate 2 scanned Crate 3 scanned Crate 4 scanned Total crates: 4

Two counts come out of that table and the exam asks for both. The body ran four times; the condition was evaluated five times, because the failing test is what ends the loop. And crate is left holding 5, not 4 — which is why the last line subtracts one.

Answer: four passes, five tests, and crate ends at 5
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — naming the three parts in code you did not write

An electric van charges from 12 percent, gaining 17 points every 10 minutes. How long until it reaches 80?

int minutes = 0;
int charge  = 12;
while (charge < 80) {
    charge  += 17;
    minutes += 10;
}
System.out.println(charge + " " + minutes);
  1. Initialisation is the two declarations above the loop: charge = 12 is the value the condition will test, minutes = 0 is the accumulator.
  2. Condition is charge < 80. It is tested before every pass, including the first.
  3. Update is charge += 17. Note that minutes += 10 is not the update — the condition does not test it, so it could never stop the loop.
Passcharge at the testcharge < 80charge afterminutes after
112true2910
229true4620
346true6330
463true8040
580false——

A for loop is a while loop with the three parts collected onto one line. Nothing about it is more powerful — it is more readable, and it keeps the loop variable from leaking, which matters in 4.10.

    System.out.println(i);         // prints 0 1 2 3 4
}

The order of events per pass is: condition, body, update. So the update runs after the last statement of the body, and the condition is checked once more after that — which is why i ends up as 5, not 4, when the loop finishes.

The two idiomatic bounds are worth memorising as shapes rather than derived each time:

for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)   // n iterations, i from 1 to n     <- counting

The order of events in a for loop is fixed, and tracing it once removes most off-by-one confusion.

for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) { ... }

  2  is i < 5?  yes  -> body, then i++     (i = 1)
  3  is i < 5?  yes  -> body, then i++     (i = 2)

  6  is i < 5?  yes  -> body, then i++     (i = 5)
  7  is i < 5?  NO   -> loop ends

The body ran five times, with i taking 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — but i finishes holding 5, because the update runs before the final test. That final increment is the whole reason the loop stops.

    }

// 2 4 6 8
// 3 6 9 12

The inner loop runs to completion for every single pass of the outer one, then starts over from its own initialisation. Writing out the first few pairs is faster than reasoning about it.

    for (int c = 1; c <= 2; c++) {
        System.out.print(r + "" + c + " ");
    }
    System.out.println();          // OUTER loop — once per row
}

31 32                              3 x 2 = 6 inner passes

Move that println() inside the inner loop and every pair lands on its own line; delete the braces around the inner body and only the first statement belongs to it. A triangle pattern is the same shape with the inner bound depending on the outer variable: for (int c = 1; c <= r; c++) gives 1, then 2, then 3 stars.

Developing incrementally means writing the smallest thing that runs, checking it, then adding one piece. It sounds like advice; it is actually a debugging strategy, because a bug in code you just added is far cheaper to find than a bug somewhere in 60 lines.

// step 1: get the loop running at all
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { System.out.println(i); }

// step 2: add the real work, keep the print
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { sum += arr[i]; System.out.println(i + " " + sum); }

// step 3: remove the trace print once it is correct

The temporary print inside the loop is the cheapest debugger there is, and 11.4 makes the same point for recursion. Print the loop variable together with whatever it changed — a value alone rarely tells you which pass produced it.

Stubs, and what "smallest thing that runs" means

A stub is a method that exists with the right name and signature but does something trivial — returns 0, prints a fixed line — so the rest of the program can be compiled and run before that part is written.

public static double taxFor(double pay) {
    return 0.0;                   // stub: correct shape, wrong answer, compiles
}

That is what makes incremental development a debugging strategy rather than advice. You always have a running program, so when it breaks you know the cause is in the few lines you just added. The alternative — writing sixty lines and then compiling — gives you a list of errors with no ordering and no way to tell which are consequences of which.

Hard-coding the input first is the same idea applied to data: get the calculation right with a fixed value you can check by hand, and only then read the value from the user.

📘 DEFINITION

Incremental development: building a program in small verified steps rather than all at once

Trace output: temporary print statements used to observe variable values while running

Stub: a placeholder implementation that lets the surrounding code run before the real logic exists

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

On a timed exam the same habit works in reverse: when a loop question looks tangled, trace two iterations by hand rather than trying to see the whole answer at once.

📊 FIGURE — why small steps are a debugging strategy, not just tidiness
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — building a payroll loop in two verified steps

Step one is not the program. It is the smallest thing that runs: the loop shape, a stub value, and a trace print that shows the loop is going round the right number of times.

// STEP 1 — shape only. pay is a stub that returns nothing useful yet.
double total = 0;
for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
    double pay = 0.0;                       // stub
    total += pay;
    System.out.println("pass " + i + " total " + total);
}
OUTPUTpass 1 total 0.0 pass 2 total 0.0 pass 3 total 0.0

Three passes, the accumulator surviving between them, no crash. Everything structural is now known to be right, so step two can only break the arithmetic.

// STEP 2 — the real calculation, trace print kept for one more run.
double total = 0;
double[] hours = {38, 46, 40};
for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
    double h = hours[i - 1];
    double pay = (h <= 40) ? h * 18.50
                           : 40 * 18.50 + (h - 40) * 18.50 * 1.5;
    total += pay;
    System.out.printf("pass %d pay %.2f total %.2f%n", i, pay, total);
}

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — hard-coding the input to check the formula by hand

Before any of that, the overtime formula itself is worth pinning down with one fixed value you can verify on paper — 46 hours at £18.50.

double hours = 46, rate = 18.50;

System.out.printf("%.2f%n", pay);
System.out.printf("%.2f%n", hours * rate * 1.5);   // the tempting wrong version

break and continue interrupt the normal flow of a loop, and the difference between them is exactly one word: break leaves the loop, continue skips to the next iteration.

for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    if (i == 5) { break; }       // stops the loop entirely — prints 0 1 2 3 4
    System.out.println(i);
}

for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    if (i % 2 == 0) { continue; }  // skips the rest of THIS pass
    System.out.println(i);         // prints 1 3 5 7 9
}

In a nested loop, both affect only the loop they sit directly inside — break in an inner loop returns to the outer loop, it does not leave both. And in a while loop continue is dangerous: it jumps past the update if the update is at the bottom of the body, which turns the loop infinite.

Where continue jumps to

for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    if (i == 2) continue;         // skip the REST of this pass
    System.out.print(i);          // i++ still runs
}                                 // prints 0134

int i = 0;
while (i < 5) {
    if (i == 2) continue;         // DANGER: i++ below is skipped too
    System.out.print(i);
    i++;                          // never reached when i == 2 -> infinite
}

In a for loop continue jumps to the update, so the loop still advances. In a while loop it jumps to the condition, skipping any update at the bottom of the body — which hangs the program. That asymmetry is the point of the topic.

In nested loops, an unlabelled break leaves only the loop it sits directly inside. To leave both, Java allows a label: outer: for (...) { for (...) { break outer; } }.

📘 DEFINITION

break: exits the innermost enclosing loop or switch immediately

continue: skips the remainder of the current iteration and proceeds to the next

Early exit: leaving a loop as soon as the answer is known, e.g. a found flag in a search

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

continue in a for loop still runs the update, because the update is part of the header. continue in a while loop does not. That asymmetry is a favourite exam question.

✅ Also covered in depth: Control Flow → for Loops, break, and continue

📊 FIGURE — break leaves the loop; continue leaves only the pass — and in a while it skips the update
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — break inside a nested loop leaves only the inner one

This is the single most-tested fact about break: it is not a "leave everything" instruction.

for (int r = 1; r <= 3; r++) {
    for (int c = 1; c <= 3; c++) {

        System.out.print(r + "" + c + " ");

}

OUTPUT11 21 31

The outer loop ran all three of its passes. If the intention really is to leave both, Java needs a label: outer: for (...) { for (...) { break outer; } }. A plain break answering "it stops the program" or "it stops both loops" is the classic wrong option.

Scope is the region of code where a name exists. The rule is simple and its consequences are not: a variable exists from its declaration to the closing brace of the block containing it, and nowhere else.

for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    int temp = i * 2;         // temp is created and destroyed each pass
}
System.out.println(i);        // ERROR — i does not exist out here
System.out.println(temp);     // ERROR — neither does temp

int j;
for (j = 0; j < 5; j++) { }   // declared OUTSIDE, so it survives
System.out.println(j);        // 5 — usable

So if you need the loop variable after the loop — the index where a search succeeded, for instance — declare it before the loop. That is the whole reason the "found index" pattern in 5.4 declares its variable outside.

Scope, lifetime, and shadowing

Scope answers where can this name be seen; lifetime answers when does the value exist. For a local variable they coincide — it is created when execution reaches the declaration and destroyed at the closing brace — which is why a variable declared inside a loop is genuinely a new variable each pass.

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    int temp = i * 2;             // new variable every pass
}
// i and temp are both gone here — using either is a compile error

int found = -1;                   // declared OUTSIDE so it survives the loop
for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
    if (a[i] == target) { found = i; break; }
}
if (found >= 0) { ... }

Declaring a name inside a block when the same name already exists outside is shadowing: the inner one hides the outer for the rest of that block. It compiles, so the symptom is an outer variable that mysteriously never changes.

The working rule is to declare a variable in the smallest block that needs it. Narrow scope means fewer places a value can be corrupted, and the compiler catches misuse instead of the value silently surviving into code that should not see it.

📘 DEFINITION

Scope: the region of code in which a name is visible

Block scope: the rule that a variable declared in a block exists only until that block closes

Shadowing: an inner declaration hiding an outer variable of the same name

🎯 EXAM TIP

Declaring a variable inside a loop resets it every pass. If your accumulator keeps coming out as one iteration’s worth of value, its declaration is in the wrong place.

✅ Also covered in depth: Control Flow → for Loops, break, and continue

📊 FIGURE — nested blocks: an inner block sees out, an outer block cannot see in
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the accumulator that keeps coming out too small

The same addition written with the total declared in two different places. Both compile; only one is a total.

int totalOutside = 0;                       // OUTSIDE the loop
for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) { totalOutside += i; }
System.out.println(totalOutside);

for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) {
    int totalInside = 0;                    // INSIDE — a NEW variable each pass
    totalInside += i;
    System.out.print(totalInside + " ");
}

The inner version is not "resetting" a variable; it is creating a different one on every pass, because the declaration is inside the block. That is why the printed values are just the loop variable back again — the symptom to recognise is a total that always equals the last item.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a search result has to outlive the loop that found it

Room codes are stored as a String; find where the letter C appears.

String rooms = "B4C7";
int found = -1;                     // OUTSIDE — must survive the loop
for (int i = 0; i < rooms.length(); i++) {
    if (rooms.charAt(i) == 'C') { found = i; break; }
}
System.out.println(found);

  2. found is declared before the loop, so the assignment inside the if reaches outward and the value survives.

An enum is a type whose values are a fixed named list. It exists so that a set of constants — days, states, suits — becomes a real type the compiler can check, instead of loose ints that anything can be assigned to.

enum Day { MON, TUE, WED, THU, FRI, SAT, SUN }

Day today = Day.WED;

switch (today) {
    case MON: case TUE: case WED: case THU: case FRI:
        System.out.println("weekday"); break;
    default:
        System.out.println("weekend");
}

for (Day d : Day.values()) { System.out.println(d); }   // every value in order

The advantage over int constants is compile-time safety: Day d = 9; will not compile, whereas int day = 9; happily accepts a nonsense day. Inside a switch the case labels drop the type name — case MON, not case Day.MON.

What an enum gives you beyond a list of names

enum Day { MON, TUE, WED, THU, FRI }

Day d = Day.WED;
switch (d) {
    case MON: ... break;          // no "Day." prefix inside a switch
    case WED: ... break;
}

for (Day each : Day.values()) { ... }   // values() — every constant, in order
Day.valueOf("TUE")                       // String -> enum (exact match, or throws)
d.ordinal()                              // position: MON=0, TUE=1, WED=2
d.name()                                 // "WED"

Compare enum constants with ==, not equals — there is exactly one object per constant, so reference comparison is both correct and the convention.

ordinal() is worth treating with suspicion: it returns the declaration position, so reordering the constants silently changes every stored ordinal. If a number matters, give the enum a field for it rather than relying on position.

enum Planet {
    MERCURY(3.30e23), VENUS(4.87e24);
    private final double mass;
    Planet(double m) { mass = m; }
    public double mass() { return mass; }
}
📘 DEFINITION

enum: a type whose instances are a fixed, named set of constants

values(): the automatically provided method returning an array of all constants, in declaration order

ordinal(): the zero-based position of a constant in its declaration

name(): the constant’s identifier as a String

🎯 EXAM TIP

Enum constants are conventionally ALL_CAPS, matching the constant naming from 2.9 — and for the same reason, since they are constants.

📊 FIGURE — an enum is a closed set of constant objects the compiler can police
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — values(), ordinal() and an enum in a switch

A rota program models the three shifts. Because the set is fixed and named, the compiler can check every use of it.

enum Shift { MORNING, AFTERNOON, NIGHT }

for (Shift s : Shift.values()) {
    System.out.println(s + " " + s.ordinal());
}
Shift s = Shift.valueOf("NIGHT");
switch (s) {
    case NIGHT: System.out.println("premium"); break;   // no "Shift." prefix
    default:    System.out.println("standard");
}
OUTPUTMORNING 0 AFTERNOON 1 NIGHT 2 premium
  1. values() returns an array of every constant in declaration order, so the enhanced for loop visits them once each.
  2. Printing an enum prints its name() — "MORNING", not a number. That is the free toString every enum gets.
  3. ordinal() is the declaration position, counting from 0.
  4. Inside a switch the case labels are bare: case NIGHT:. Writing case Shift.NIGHT: is a compile error, which surprises people who expect the opposite.
Answer: MORNING 0 / AFTERNOON 1 / NIGHT 2 / premium
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — comparing enum constants, and why ordinal is fragile

There is exactly one object per constant, which changes how you compare them.

Shift a = Shift.AFTERNOON;
Shift b = Shift.valueOf("AFTERNOON");
System.out.println(a == b);
System.out.println(a.name() + " " + a.ordinal() + " " + Shift.values().length);
OUTPUTtrue AFTERNOON 1 3

a == b is true — unlike Strings, where the same comparison is a trap. valueOf does not build anything; it looks up the one existing constant, so both variables hold the same reference. That is why == is the idiomatic comparison for enums and equals is merely equivalent.

The fragile part is ordinal(). AFTERNOON is 1 only because it is declared second. Insert an EVENING constant before it and every stored 1 now means something else, with nothing to warn you. If a number matters — a shift multiplier, a planet's mass — give the enum a field for it and a constructor, rather than leaning on declaration order.

Answer: true, then AFTERNOON 1 3
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

valueOf requires an exact match, capitals included. Shift.valueOf("night") compiles perfectly and throws IllegalArgumentException: No enum constant Shift.night at run time. Normalise with toUpperCase() before converting user input, or check against values() first.

This example replaces the fixed calculation from 3.20 with a loop over many employees, which is what makes the tiered-rate chain worth writing once.

double totalPayroll = 0;
int n = scnr.nextInt();

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    double salary = scnr.nextDouble();

    double rate;
    if      (salary >= 100000) { rate = 0.28; }
    else if (salary >=  50000) { rate = 0.22; }
    else                       { rate = 0.15; }

    totalPayroll += salary * (1 - rate);
}
System.out.printf("Total: %.2f%n", totalPayroll);

Two things are placed deliberately. totalPayroll is declared before the loop, so it accumulates (4.10); rate is declared inside, because each employee needs a fresh one. Swapping those placements is the bug this example is designed to teach.

Reading the placement decisions

double totalPayroll = 0.0;            // OUTSIDE — accumulates across employees
for (int e = 0; e < count; e++) {
    double rate = baseRate;           // INSIDE — fresh for each employee
    double hours = scnr.nextDouble();
    double pay = (hours <= 40)
               ? hours * rate
               : 40 * rate + (hours - 40) * rate * 1.5;
    totalPayroll += pay;
}
System.out.printf("Total: $%.2f%n", totalPayroll);

Move totalPayroll inside and it resets every pass, so the printed total is the last employee's pay. Move rate outside and any change one employee makes to it carries into the next. Those two mistakes look identical in the source and produce completely different wrong answers, which is why the example exists.

The overtime line is the tiered-rate idea from 3.20 applied per pass: the first 40 hours at the base rate, everything beyond at 1.5×. Computing hours * rate * 1.5 for an overtime week overpays the first 40 hours as well.

📘 DEFINITION

printf: formatted output; %.2f prints two decimal places, %n a newline (see 9.2)

Loop-invariant declaration: a variable declared outside the loop because its value must persist across iterations

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Declaring the accumulator inside the loop resets it to zero every pass, so the final total equals only the last employee. It compiles, it runs, and the answer is silently wrong.

Four salaries, three tax bands, one running total. The Scanner is built over a fixed String so the run is reproducible.

double totalPayroll = 0;                        // OUTSIDE — accumulates
for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
    double salary = scnr.nextDouble();
    double rate;                                // INSIDE — fresh per employee
    if      (salary >= 100000) { rate = 0.28; }
    else if (salary >=  50000) { rate = 0.22; }
    else                       { rate = 0.15; }
    double net = salary * (1 - rate);

  3. 62000 fails the first and matches the second, 22 percent: 62000 × 0.78 = 48360.00.
  4. 24000 takes the else again: 24000 × 0.85 = 20400.00, and the four nets sum to 185160.00.

The band order is not decorative. Test 50000 before 100000 and every high earner matches the 22 percent band first and stops there, so the top rate is never applied — a silent under-taxing bug with no error anywhere.
