Domain validation puts loops and Strings together: walk the characters, and reject the whole string the moment any character breaks a rule.

String domain = scnr.next();
boolean valid = domain.length() >= 3 && domain.contains(".");

for (int i = 0; i < domain.length() && valid; i++) {
    char c = domain.charAt(i);
    if (!Character.isLetterOrDigit(c) && c != '.' && c != '-') {
        valid = false;                 // the condition ends the loop next check
    }
}
System.out.println(valid ? "valid" : "invalid");

The flag appears in the loop condition, so the loop stops as soon as it is falsified — the same early-exit idea as break in 4.9, expressed without one. Either is fine; what is not fine is continuing to scan after the answer is known and then overwriting it.

Validating with a flag versus breaking out

boolean valid = domain.length() > 0;
boolean hasDot = false;
int i = 0;
while (valid && i < domain.length()) {      // stops the moment valid turns false
    char c = domain.charAt(i);
    if (c == '.') hasDot = true;
    else if (!Character.isLetterOrDigit(c) && c != '-') valid = false;
    i++;
}
valid = valid && hasDot;

Two rules are being checked at once and they behave differently. "Every character must be legal" fails on the first counter-example, so it can stop early. "At least one dot" cannot be decided until the whole string has been read, so it must be a flag that survives the loop.

Putting valid in the loop condition is early exit without break — equivalent here, and it keeps the exit rule visible at the top. What is genuinely wrong is scanning to the end and then overwriting valid in a later pass, which is what happens if the final line is written valid = hasDot; instead of combining the two.

📘 DEFINITION

Validation flag: a boolean set to false the first time a rule is broken and never reset

Early termination: stopping a loop once the result is determined

🎯 EXAM TIP

Never set the flag back to true inside the loop. A flag that can flip both ways ends up reporting only the last character, which is the standard broken version of this pattern.

📊 FIGURE — a validation flag falls once and stays down
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — validating a domain with the flag in the loop condition

Two rules are being checked at once, and they behave differently: "every character is legal" can fail early, while "there is at least one dot" cannot be decided until the end.

String domain = "shop-01.example.com";
boolean valid = domain.length() >= 3;
boolean hasDot = false;
int i = 0;
while (valid && i < domain.length()) {          // early exit without break
    char c = domain.charAt(i);
    if (c == '.') hasDot = true;
    else if (!Character.isLetterOrDigit(c) && c != '-') valid = false;
    i++;
}
valid = valid && hasDot;
System.out.println("chars examined: " + i + ", valid: " + valid);
OUTPUTchars examined: 19, valid: true
  1. Every character of "shop-01.example.com" is a letter, a digit, a hyphen or a dot, so valid is never falsified and all 19 characters are examined.
  2. The two dots set hasDot, and the else if means a dot is never also tested as an illegal character.
  3. valid && i < length() puts the early exit in the condition: had character 3 been a space, valid would drop to false and the very next test would end the loop with i at 4 — the same effect as break, with the exit rule visible at the top.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the assignment that turns a flag into a last-character report

One character of difference — valid = ... instead of if (...) valid = false; — and the same input gives the opposite answer.

String domain = "my site.net";              // illegal space at index 2

boolean valid = true;                       // RESET every pass — wrong
for (int i = 0; i < domain.length(); i++) {
    char c = domain.charAt(i);
    valid = Character.isLetterOrDigit(c) || c == '.' || c == '-';
}
System.out.println("reset-each-pass version says: " + valid);

boolean valid2 = true;                      // STICKY — right
for (int i = 0; i < domain.length(); i++) {
    char c = domain.charAt(i);
    if (!(Character.isLetterOrDigit(c) || c == '.' || c == '-')) valid2 = false;
}
System.out.println("sticky-flag version says: " + valid2);
OUTPUTreset-each-pass version says: true sticky-flag version says: false

The reset version does detect the space at index 2 — and then overwrites that discovery on every later character. By the end it is reporting only whether the final "t" is legal, which it is. The sticky version can only ever move from true to false, so one bad character survives to the answer. Both compile, both run, and only one of them is a validator.

Answer: true from the broken version, false from the correct one
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

The same fault appears in a "found" flag written the other way round: found = (a[i] == target); inside a loop reports only whether the last element matched. A search flag starts false and may only rise; a validation flag starts true and may only fall. If an assignment inside a loop can move a flag in both directions, it is wrong.

Up to now every value needed its own variable. That works for three test scores and collapses at thirty. An array is one name holding many values of the same type, reached by position — which is what finally makes the loops of Unit 4 useful for real data.

Two properties define an array and cause almost every array bug. Its length is fixed at creation and can never change, and its indexes run from 0 to length - 1.

scores[0]  scores[1]  scores[2]  scores[3]  scores[4]
   88        92        79        95        61        <- length 5
                                                     <- last index is 4, not 5

Because the index is just an int, it can be a loop variable — and that single fact is the whole reason arrays and for loops are taught together.

Why index 0, and what the exception tells you

An index is not a position in a list, it is an offset from the start of the block of memory. The first element is zero elements from the start, so it is a[0]. Every consequence follows from that one fact.

Array of length 5Value
first index0
last index4, written a.length - 1
a.length5 — a count, never a valid index
a[5]ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException at run time

That exception is a runtime error, not a compile error: the compiler cannot know what the index will be, so nothing warns you. The message names the offending index — "Index 5 out of bounds for length 5" — which tells you immediately that a bound used <= where it needed <.

The length being fixed at creation is the other half. An array cannot grow; to "add" an element you allocate a bigger array and copy across, which is exactly what ArrayList does for you behind the scenes.

📘 DEFINITION

Array: a fixed-size, ordered collection of values of one type, accessed by index

Index: the position of an element, starting at 0

Element: one value stored in the array

Length: the number of elements; fixed when the array is created

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

Everything from here to Unit 14 is a variation on this idea. ArrayList (7.14) is an array that can grow; a HashMap (14.3) is the same lookup idea keyed by something other than a number.

📊 FIGURE — why the first index is 0, and why the last one is length − 1
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — reading an array by its bounds

A week of rainfall in millimetres. Three questions about it are answered without a loop at all — just by indexing.

int[] rainfall = {12, 0, 31, 8, 26, 4, 19};
System.out.println("days: " + rainfall.length);
System.out.println("first: " + rainfall[0] + ", last: " + rainfall[rainfall.length - 1]);
System.out.println("third: " + rainfall[2]);
OUTPUTdays: 7 first: 12, last: 19 third: 31
  1. length is 7 — the number of elements, and it is a field, so there are no parentheses.
  2. rainfall[0] is the first element, 12. Zero elements along from the start.
  3. rainfall[rainfall.length - 1] is rainfall[6], the last one, 19. Learn that whole expression as one symbol meaning "the last".
  4. "Third" in ordinary speech is index 2, not 3. That off-by-one between how people count and how arrays are indexed is the source of most of the confusion in this unit.

Note that rainfall[1] is 0 — a real recorded value of zero millimetres. A stored 0 and an absent element are different things, which matters once the array is longer than the data.

Answer: 7 days; first 12, last 19; the third day is 31
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — what going out of bounds actually reports

The exception is worth meeting deliberately once, because its message names the mistake precisely.

int[] rainfall = {12, 0, 31, 8, 26, 4, 19};
try { System.out.println(rainfall[7]); }
catch (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException e) { System.out.println("threw: " + e.getMessage()); }
try { System.out.println(rainfall[-1]); }
catch (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException e) { System.out.println("threw: " + e.getMessage()); }
OUTPUTthrew: Index 7 out of bounds for length 7 threw: Index -1 out of bounds for length 7

Two things to take from this. First, index 7 on a length-7 array is one past the end, and the message says so in exactly those words — so when you see it in a real run, the fix is almost always a loop bound written <= that should be <. Second, this is a runtime exception, not a compile error: rainfall[7] compiles happily, because the compiler cannot in general know what an index will be.

Answer: both throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, naming the index and the length
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

length is a count and indexes are offsets, so they never match. An array of length 7 has no element 7. The moment you write a[a.length] — or a loop bound of i <= a.length — you have asked for one element past the end, and the program will get all the way to the final pass before telling you.

🎯 EXAM TIP

When a question gives you an array and asks for "the last element" or "the middle element", write the index as an expression in length rather than a number: a[a.length - 1] and a[a.length / 2]. Answers that hard-code a number are the distractors, because they break the moment the length changes.

There are three ways to bring an array into existence, and choosing between them comes down to whether you already know the values.

int[] a = new int[5];              // 5 elements, all 0 by default
int[] b = {10, 20, 30};            // literal — length 3, inferred
int[] c;  c = new int[]{1, 2, 3};  // the long form of the literal

a[0] = 88;                         // store
int x = a[0];                      // read
int n = a.length;                  // LENGTH — a field, no parentheses

New arrays are filled with the default for their type, and the defaults come from the same table as fields in 2.2: 0 for numeric types, false for boolean, null for objects and Strings. That last one matters — a new String[] is an array of nulls, not of empty strings.

Three ways to create one, and what is in it

int[] a = new int[5];                 // 5 elements, all 0
int[] b = {10, 20, 30};               // literal — size taken from the list
int[] c;                              // declared, refers to nothing yet
c = new int[3];                       // now it exists

int[] d = {1,2,3};                    // only legal AT the declaration
d = {4,5,6};                          // compile error
d = new int[]{4,5,6};                 // this is the way to reassign
Element typeDefault value
int, long, short, byte0
double, float0.0
char'\u0000' — prints as blank
booleanfalse
String and any objectnull

The last row is the one that bites. new String[3] gives three nulls, not three empty strings, so calling .length() on any of them throws a NullPointerException until you assign real values.

📘 DEFINITION

new int[5]: creates an array of 5 elements, each set to the type default

Array literal: the {…} form that creates and fills an array in one step

length: a public final field on every array; note that String uses length() instead

Default value: 0, 0.0, false or null depending on the element type

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

arr.length() does not compile — arrays use the field length, Strings use the method length(). Reversing them is one of the most reliably tested details in the course (see 4.6).

✅ Also covered in depth: Arrays → 1D Arrays

📊 FIGURE — AN ARRAY IS NUMBERED BOXES, STARTING AT 0
🎯 EXAM TIP
The last valid index is always length - 1. Loops written i <= scores.length crash on the final pass — spot that <= instantly.
📊 FIGURE — what is actually in an array the instant it is created
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — three ways to create an array, and what is in each

Creation with new fills every slot with the type default; creation from a literal fills it with your values and infers the length.

int[] counts     = new int[4];
double[] avgs    = new double[2];
boolean[] flags  = new boolean[2];
String[] names   = new String[3];
System.out.println(counts[0] + " " + avgs[0] + " " + flags[0] + " " + names[0]);
System.out.println(Arrays.toString(counts) + " " + Arrays.toString(names));
int[] b = {10, 20, 30};
System.out.println("literal length " + b.length);
OUTPUT0 0.0 false null [0, 0, 0, 0] [null, null, null] literal length 3
  1. The defaults are the same table as uninitialised fields: 0 for the integer types, 0.0 for the floating types, false for boolean, null for anything that is an object.
  2. Arrays.toString is the readable way to print a whole array; printing the array variable itself gives something like [I@1b6d3586, which is the type and a hash, not the contents.
  3. The literal form {10, 20, 30} takes its length from the list — three elements, so length is 3, and no size is written anywhere.

The literal form is only legal at the declaration. b = {40, 50, 60}; on a later line does not compile; the reassignment form is b = new int[]{40, 50, 60};.

Answer: 0, 0.0, false, null — and a literal length of 3
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the null that an array of objects hands you

An array of Strings is an array of references, and a new one holds no Strings at all.

String[] codes = new String[3];
codes[0] = "AB1";
System.out.println(codes[0].length());
try { System.out.println(codes[1].length()); }
catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("NullPointerException on codes[1]"); }
OUTPUT3 NullPointerException on codes[1]

codes[0] was assigned, so it refers to a real String and length() works. codes[1] is still null — it refers to nothing — so calling any method on it fails at run time. Note what did not happen: codes[1] is a perfectly valid index, so this is not an out-of-bounds problem. The array exists and has three slots; two of them are simply empty.

This is why a loop over an array of objects often needs if (codes[i] != null) where a loop over an array of ints needs nothing — an int cannot be null, so it always has a usable value.

Answer: 3, then a NullPointerException on the unassigned element

Before writing array code, it is worth being fluent at reading it, because most exam array questions are traces rather than constructions. The drill is always the same: draw the array, draw the index, update both line by line.

int[] a = {4, 8, 15, 16, 23};

a[2]            // 15
a[a.length - 1] // 23  — the idiom for "last element"
a[0] + a[4]     // 27
a[a[0]]         // a[4] -> 23   — an element used as an index

for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) { a[i] = a[i] * 2; }
// {8, 16, 30, 32, 46}

a[a.length - 1] is worth learning as a single symbol for "the last one". Writing a[a.length] instead is the most common runtime crash in Java, and the exception names the index it tried.

How to trace an array question

int[] a = {4, 8, 15, 16};
int sum = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) sum += a[i];

  i    a[i]    sum
  0      4       4
  1      8      12
  2     15      27
  3     16      43
  4    stop — 4 < 4 is false

Write the table. Every trace question in this unit is answerable in under a minute this way, and reasoning about it in your head is where the mistakes come from. Track exactly the variables the question asks about, one row per pass.

The two boundary rows are the ones worth checking twice: the first pass, where an accumulator's starting value shows up, and the row where the condition fails, which decides whether the last element was included.

📘 DEFINITION

Bounds: the valid index range, 0 through length - 1

🎯 EXAM TIP

The exception is a runtime error, not a compile error (1.4). a[10] on a 5-element array compiles fine — Java only checks the index while running.

Four loop patterns cover the overwhelming majority of array work, and recognising which one a question wants is most of the answer.

// 1. SUM / AVERAGE
int sum = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) { sum += a[i]; }
double avg = (double) sum / a.length;      // cast, or integer division (2.5)

// 2. MAXIMUM  — start from the first element, never from 0
int max = a[0];
for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++) { if (a[i] > max) { max = a[i]; } }

// 3. SEARCH   — index declared OUTSIDE so it survives the loop (4.10)
int found = -1;
for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) { if (a[i] == target) { found = i; break; } }

// 4. COUNT matching a condition
int evens = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) { if (a[i] % 2 == 0) { evens++; } }

The maximum pattern is where people lose marks. Initialising max = 0 works only if the data is guaranteed non-negative; with all-negative data it returns 0, a value not even in the array. Starting from a[0] is always right.

The four patterns, and the maximum trap

int sum = 0;                          // TOTAL
for (int x : a) sum += x;

int count = 0;                        // COUNT MATCHING
for (int x : a) if (x > 10) count++;

int max = a[0];                       // MAXIMUM — start from a real element
for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++) if (a[i] > max) max = a[i];

int found = -1;                       // SEARCH — index, or -1 for absent
for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) if (a[i] == target) { found = i; break; }

Starting max = 0 is the classic error: on all-negative data it returns 0, which is not even in the array. Starting from a[0] is always correct — and start the loop at i = 1, since element 0 is already accounted for.

The search pattern returns −1 rather than 0 for "not found", because 0 is a legitimate index. Callers must test found >= 0, not found being truthy — Java will not let you do the latter anyway.

📘 DEFINITION

Linear search: checking each element in turn until a match is found; O(n) — see 17.1

Sentinel -1: the conventional "not found" result, matching indexOf in 3.16

Running maximum: a variable holding the largest value seen so far

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

sum / a.length with two ints performs integer division and truncates. Cast one side to double first — the same trap as 2.5, now with arrays.

✅ Also covered in depth: Arrays → 1D Arrays

📊 FIGURE — the running maximum: where the starting value comes from
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the maximum that is not in the array

Five overnight temperatures, every one below freezing. Two versions of the same loop differ only in the starting value of max.

int[] temps = {-3, -11, -7, -19, -5};

int wrong = 0;                                  // starts outside the data
for (int i = 0; i < temps.length; i++) if (temps[i] > wrong) wrong = temps[i];

int right = temps[0];                           // starts from a real element
for (int i = 1; i < temps.length; i++) if (temps[i] > right) right = temps[i];

System.out.println("max=0 start: " + wrong + "   max=a[0] start: " + right);
OUTPUTmax=0 start: 0 max=a[0] start: -3
  1. In the first loop nothing is ever greater than 0, so no assignment happens and the reported maximum is 0 — a value that appears nowhere in the data.
  2. In the second, max starts at temps[0] = −3, which is in the data, and no later element beats it.
  3. The second loop starts at i = 1, because element 0 has already been accounted for. Starting at 0 is harmless — it just compares −3 with itself once.

The same reasoning applies to a minimum, with Integer.MAX_VALUE as the only other defensible starting point. Starting from a[0] needs no such constant and works for any data — its one requirement is that the array is not empty, which is worth a guard.

Answer: 0 from the broken version, −3 from the correct one
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — an average that loses its fraction

Summing is easy; the division is where the marks are lost.

int[] scores = {88, 92, 79, 95, 60};
int sum = 0;
for (int x : scores) sum += x;
System.out.println("sum " + sum);
System.out.println("int division: " + (sum / scores.length));
System.out.println("cast first:   " + ((double) sum / scores.length));
OUTPUTsum 414 int division: 82 cast first: 82.8
  1. 414 and 5 are both int, so sum / scores.length is integer division: 82.8 is truncated to 82, and the 0.8 is gone before anything else happens.
  2. Assigning that to a double afterwards does not rescue it — double avg = sum / scores.length; stores 82.0.
  3. (double) sum makes the left operand a double, so the whole division is done in floating point and gives 82.8. Casting either side works; casting the result does not.

A second detail hides here: scores.length is the divisor only when the array is a perfect fit for the data. Over an oversize array it must be the element count instead, or the unused zeros drag the average down.

Answer: 82 from integer division, 82.8 done correctly
🎯 EXAM TIP

Recognise the four patterns by their starting value, which is the fastest way to spot a broken one on sight: a total starts at 0, a product starts at 1, a count starts at 0, a maximum starts at a[0], and a search result starts at −1. If a snippet's initialiser is not on that list, look hard at it before you trace anything.

Parallel arrays hold related data in separate arrays where the same index refers to the same thing: names[3] and scores[3] describe one student. It works, and it is how you handle records before Unit 7 gives you classes.

String[] names  = {"Ada", "Alan", "Grace"};
int[]    scores = {95, 88, 99};

for (int i = 0; i < names.length; i++) {
    System.out.println(names[i] + ": " + scores[i]);
}

// finding the name of the top scorer means tracking the INDEX, not the value
int best = 0;
for (int i = 1; i < scores.length; i++) { if (scores[i] > scores[best]) { best = i; } }
System.out.println("top: " + names[best]);

The fragility is that nothing links the arrays. Sort one and the correspondence is destroyed silently. That weakness is the argument for classes in 7.6 — one Student object keeps its own name and score together, so they cannot drift apart.

Keeping parallel arrays in step

String[] names  = {"Ana", "Ben", "Cy"};
int[]    scores = {88, 71, 95};
// names[i] and scores[i] describe the SAME student

for (int i = 0; i < names.length; i++)
    System.out.println(names[i] + ": " + scores[i]);

Three rules keep them usable. They must be the same length; every insert or delete must touch all of them; and any sort must move all of them together, which means sorting by hand rather than calling Arrays.sort on one of them.

Arrays.sort(scores) is precisely the operation that destroys the data: the scores end up in order and the names do not move, so every student now has somebody else's mark. Nothing throws, nothing warns — the program keeps running with silently wrong data. That is the argument for a Student class in 7.6.

📘 DEFINITION

Parallel arrays: two or more arrays where matching indexes describe one entity

Index of maximum: tracking the position of the largest value rather than the value itself

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

When you meet "choosing classes to create" in 7.6, this is the problem it is answering. Parallel arrays are the before picture.

📊 FIGURE — parallel arrays are held together by the index and by nothing else
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — finding the name of the top scorer

The value alone is not the answer here — the question asks who, so the loop must track the index rather than the maximum score.

String[] names = {"Ada", "Grace", "Alan"};
int[] scores   = {88, 95, 71};

int best = 0;                                     // an INDEX, not a score
for (int i = 1; i < scores.length; i++)
    if (scores[i] > scores[best]) best = i;
System.out.println("top: " + names[best] + " with " + scores[best]);

int worst = 0;
for (int i = 1; i < scores.length; i++)
    if (scores[i] < scores[worst]) worst = i;
System.out.println("bottom: " + names[worst] + " with " + scores[worst]);
iscores[i]scores[best]best after
——88 (index 0)0
195881 — 95 beats 88
271951 — unchanged
OUTPUTtop: Grace with 95 bottom: Alan with 71

Because best holds a position, it unlocks both arrays: names[best] and scores[best] describe one student. Had the loop tracked int bestScore = scores[0]; instead, it would know the mark was 95 and have no way back to the name.

Answer: Grace with 95; Alan with 71
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the one line that destroys the data

Sorting looks like an obvious improvement, and on parallel arrays it is a data-loss bug.

String[] names = {"Ada", "Grace", "Alan"};
int[] scores   = {88, 95, 71};
Arrays.sort(scores);                    // moves scores only
for (int i = 0; i < names.length; i++)
    System.out.println(names[i] + ": " + scores[i]);
OUTPUTAda: 71 Grace: 88 Alan: 95

Every line is wrong, and nothing threw. Arrays.sort rearranged scores into 71, 88, 95 and never touched names, so index 0 now pairs Ada with Alan's mark. The program is still running, the output still looks like a report, and the data is ruined.

Sorting parallel arrays correctly means writing the sort yourself and swapping both arrays on every exchange — which is precisely the bookkeeping a Student class removes, because then one swap moves the name and the mark together.

Answer: Ada: 71, Grace: 88, Alan: 95 — every pairing broken
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Parallel arrays must be the same length and must be edited together. Inserting into one and forgetting the other shifts everything after that point by one, so the data looks correct at the start of the array and is wrong from the insertion point onward — which is the hardest kind of bug to see in a spot check.

🎯 EXAM TIP

When an exam question tracks "the position of the largest" rather than the largest itself, that is the parallel-array pattern and the answer needs names[best]. Watch for the distractor that compares scores[i] > best — comparing a score against an index — which compiles and produces nonsense.

Swapping two values needs a third variable, and the reason is worth stating precisely: assignment overwrites, so the first assignment destroys the value you still need.

int temp = a;
a = b;
b = temp;

// the broken version
a = b;      // a's original value is now GONE
b = a;      // b gets b's own value — both end up as b

In an array the swap is the same, just with indexes, and it is the primitive operation underneath reversing (5.8), selection sort (17.6) and quicksort (17.8).

int temp = arr[i];
arr[i] = arr[j];
arr[j] = temp;

Why the third variable is unavoidable

int x = 3, y = 7;

x = y;          // x is now 7 — the original 3 is GONE
y = x;          // y = 7. Both are 7. The swap failed.

int temp = x;   // save what is about to be overwritten
x = y;
y = temp;       // x = 7, y = 3

Assignment overwrites, and nothing keeps a copy. The temporary exists to hold the value that the first assignment is about to destroy — which is why the order save, overwrite, restore is fixed.

int t = a[i]; a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = t;   // the same thing with indexes

The arithmetic trick x = x + y; y = x - y; x = x - y; does swap two numbers without a temp, and it is a bad answer on an exam and worse in code: it overflows for large values, breaks for floating-point precision, and does not work at all for objects or Strings.

📘 DEFINITION

Swap: exchanging the values of two variables, requiring one temporary

Temporary variable: a variable that briefly holds a value so it is not overwritten

🎯 EXAM TIP

A method cannot swap two int parameters, because primitives are passed by value (6.8). It can swap two array elements, because the array reference gives it access to the original array (6.10).

📊 FIGURE — SWAP NEEDS A THIRD BOX
📊 FIGURE — the same swap done to two slots of one array
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — watching the value disappear

Both versions are run side by side on the same starting values, so the loss is visible rather than argued.

int x = 3, y = 7;

int a = x, b = y;
a = b;                       // a is now 7 — the 3 is GONE
b = a;                       // b gets 7 back from a
System.out.println("broken: a=" + a + " b=" + b);

int c = x, d = y;
int temp = c;                // save the value about to be overwritten
c = d;
d = temp;
System.out.println("correct: c=" + c + " d=" + d);

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — swapping array elements, and the no-temp trick

Inside an array the swap is identical, just with subscripts — and this three-line block is the primitive underneath reversing and every exchange sort.

int[] a = {4, 8, 15, 16, 23};
int i = 1, j = 3;
int t = a[i];
a[i] = a[j];
a[j] = t;
System.out.println(Arrays.toString(a));

double p = 0.1, q = 0.3;                    // the "clever" arithmetic swap
p = p + q;  q = p - q;  p = p - q;
System.out.println("doubles after the no-temp trick: " + p + " " + q);

The array swap exchanged positions 1 and 3 and left everything else alone. The arithmetic trick — p = p + q; q = p - q; p = p - q; — did move the values, but look at what came back: 0.1 became 0.10000000000000003, because two floating-point roundings do not cancel. It also cannot be used at all on Strings or objects, and it is unreadable. Use the temporary.

Answer: [4, 16, 15, 8, 23], and a corrupted 0.1 from the trick
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

A method cannot swap two int parameters. swap(a, b) exchanges the method's own copies and the caller sees nothing, because primitives are passed by value. It can swap two elements of an array it is given, because the array reference reaches the one real array — which is the same distinction that governs every parameter question in Unit 6.

Three operations on whole arrays behave differently from what the syntax suggests, and each has a specific correct form.

// COPYING — this does NOT copy
int[] b = a;             // b and a now refer to the SAME array
b[0] = 99;               // a[0] is also 99

// copy properly
int[] b = new int[a.length];
for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) { b[i] = a[i]; }
// or
int[] b = Arrays.copyOf(a, a.length);

// COMPARING — this compares references, not contents
a == b                   // almost always false
Arrays.equals(a, b)      // compares element by element   <- correct

Both traps are the same trap as == on Strings in 3.2, for the same reason: an array variable holds a reference, so plain assignment and == operate on the reference and not on the contents. The idea is set out fully in 7.10 and 7.12.

Assignment, comparison and copying

int[] a = {1, 2, 3};
int[] b = a;                 // NOT a copy — two names, one array
b[0] = 99;                   // a[0] is now 99 as well

int[] c = Arrays.copyOf(a, a.length);       // a real copy
int[] d = a.clone();                        // also a real copy (1D)

a == c                       // false — different objects, even if equal
Arrays.equals(a, c)          // true  — compares element by element

An array variable holds a reference. Plain assignment copies the reference, so both names reach the same array; == compares references, so it asks "the same array?" and never "the same contents?". This is the identical distinction as == versus .equals on Strings.

For a 2D array, clone() and copyOf are shallow: the new outer array holds references to the same rows, so changing an element still shows through both. A deep copy needs a loop that copies each row.

Removing an element means shifting everything after it left by one and treating the array as one shorter — the length itself cannot change.

📘 DEFINITION

Reference copy (shallow): copying the reference, leaving one array with two names

Element copy (deep): copying each element into a separate array

Arrays.copyOf: library method returning a new array with the copied contents

Arrays.equals: compares two arrays element by element

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Modifying an array through a second variable and being surprised the first one changed is the classic aliasing bug. If two names point at one array, there is only one array.

✅ Also covered in depth: Arrays → 1D Arrays

📊 FIGURE — assignment copies the arrow; copyOf copies the array
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — two names, one array

The aliasing demonstration, with a real copy alongside it for contrast.

int[] a = {5, 9, 2};
int[] b = a;                              // NOT a copy
int[] c = Arrays.copyOf(a, a.length);     // a real copy
b[0] = 99;
System.out.println(Arrays.toString(a) + " " + Arrays.toString(b) + " " + Arrays.toString(c));
System.out.println((a == b) + " " + (a == c) + " " + Arrays.equals(a, c));
OUTPUT[99, 9, 2] [99, 9, 2] [5, 9, 2] true false false
  1. Writing through b changed what a reports, because there is only one array and both variables hold its address.
  2. c was taken before the write, so it still holds 5 — a genuinely separate array.
  3. a == b is true: the same address. a == c is false: different addresses, even though the contents were identical at the moment of copying.
  4. Arrays.equals(a, c) is false now only because a[0] has since become 99. Immediately after the copy it would have been true.

The final line of the run makes the point completely: comparing a with a freshly written literal {99, 9, 2} gives false for == and true for Arrays.equals — identical contents, different objects.

Answer: [99, 9, 2] [99, 9, 2] [5, 9, 2] — then true, false, false
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — why clone() is not enough for a 2D array

A 2D array is an array of references to rows, so copying the outer array copies the references and not the rows.

int[][] g = {{1, 2}, {3, 4}};

int[][] shallow = g.clone();              // copies the ROW REFERENCES only
shallow[0][0] = 99;
System.out.println("after shallow write, g[0][0] = " + g[0][0]);

int[][] deep = new int[g.length][];       // copy each row separately
for (int r = 0; r < g.length; r++) deep[r] = Arrays.copyOf(g[r], g[r].length);
deep[1][1] = 77;
System.out.println("after deep write,    g[1][1] = " + g[1][1]);
OUTPUTafter shallow write, g[0][0] = 99 after deep write, g[1][1] = 4

The shallow copy produced a new outer array whose two slots point at the original rows, so writing into it wrote into g. The deep copy allocated a fresh row for each one, so g is untouched. Arrays.copyOf and clone() behave identically here — both are one level deep, which is enough for a 1D array of primitives and never enough for a 2D one.

Answer: 99 after the shallow write; 4 after the deep write
🎯 EXAM TIP

Any exam question showing b = a followed by a write through b is asking about aliasing, and the answer is that both variables report the change. Any question comparing two arrays with == is answered false unless one was assigned from the other. Both are the same rule as == on Strings, for the same reason.

Reversing an array in place is the standard debugging example because the obvious version is wrong in an instructive way.

// WRONG — this reverses, then reverses back to the original
for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
    int temp = a[i];
    a[i] = a[a.length - 1 - i];
    a[a.length - 1 - i] = temp;
}

// RIGHT — stop at the middle
for (int i = 0; i < a.length / 2; i++) {
    int temp = a[i];
    a[i] = a[a.length - 1 - i];
    a[a.length - 1 - i] = temp;
}

Going the whole way swaps every pair twice, and the second swap undoes the first. Halving the bound is the fix, and integer division handles an odd length correctly for free: the middle element has nothing to swap with and is left alone.

Why the bound is half

// WRONG — swaps every pair twice, ending where it started
for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
    int t = a[i]; a[i] = a[a.length-1-i]; a[a.length-1-i] = t;
}

// RIGHT
for (int i = 0; i < a.length / 2; i++) {
    int t = a[i]; a[i] = a[a.length-1-i]; a[a.length-1-i] = t;
}

Each swap handles two elements — i and its mirror — so running the full length processes every pair a second time from the other end and undoes it. Half the length is exactly one pass per pair.

Integer division handles an odd length for free: length 5 gives 5 / 2 = 2, so i takes 0 and 1, and the middle element at index 2 is left where it is — which is correct, since its mirror is itself.

The mirror index is a.length - 1 - i. Writing a.length - i is off by one and throws on the very first pass, which at least fails loudly.

📘 DEFINITION

In-place algorithm: one that rearranges the existing array without allocating another

Mirror index: the position length - 1 - i, which pairs with i from the other end

🎯 EXAM TIP

For a length-5 array, a.length / 2 is 2, so i takes 0 and 1 and index 2 stays put — exactly right. Trust the integer division here rather than special-casing odd lengths.

📊 FIGURE — running the whole length swaps every pair twice and undoes the reversal
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the two bounds, run side by side

The only difference between the working reverse and the broken one is a.length against a.length / 2.

int[] a = {4, 8, 15, 16};
for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {                 // WRONG
    int t = a[i]; a[i] = a[a.length-1-i]; a[a.length-1-i] = t;
}
System.out.println("full length: " + Arrays.toString(a));

int[] b = {4, 8, 15, 16};
for (int i = 0; i < b.length / 2; i++) {             // RIGHT
    int t = b[i]; b[i] = b[b.length-1-i]; b[b.length-1-i] = t;
}
System.out.println("half length: " + Arrays.toString(b));
OUTPUTfull length: [4, 8, 15, 16] half length: [16, 15, 8, 4]
imirror indexarray after the swap
03[16, 8, 15, 4]
12[16, 15, 8, 4] — reversed here
21[16, 8, 15, 4] — undoes pass 1
30[4, 8, 15, 16] — undoes pass 0, back to the start

The broken version is not "not reversing" — it reverses correctly halfway through and then reverses again. That is why the symptom is an array that looks completely untouched, which sends people hunting for a swap that is not happening at all.

Answer: the full-length loop gives back the original; the half-length loop reverses it
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — an odd length, and the element with no partner

Five elements, so one of them is its own mirror. Integer division handles it with no special case.

int[] a = {4, 8, 15, 16, 23};
System.out.println("bound is " + (a.length / 2));
for (int i = 0; i < a.length / 2; i++) {
    int t = a[i]; a[i] = a[a.length-1-i]; a[a.length-1-i] = t;
    System.out.println("i=" + i + " -> " + Arrays.toString(a));
}
OUTPUTbound is 2 i=0 -> [23, 8, 15, 16, 4] i=1 -> [23, 16, 15, 8, 4]
  1. 5 / 2 is integer division, so the bound is 2 and i takes 0 and 1.
  2. Pass 0 exchanges indexes 0 and 4; pass 1 exchanges 1 and 3.
  3. Index 2 is never touched — and it should not be, because its mirror (5 - 1 - 2) is 2, itself. Swapping an element with itself is a waste at best and, written carelessly, a way to zero it out.

The mirror expression is a.length - 1 - i. Writing a.length - i is off by one and throws on the very first pass, which is the friendly failure — you find it immediately instead of shipping a subtly wrong array.

Answer: [23, 16, 15, 8, 4] after two passes, with index 2 left in place
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Reversing into a second array is a different algorithm and needs no halving: for (i = 0; i < a.length; i++) out[i] = a[a.length - 1 - i]; runs the full length and is correct, because it never writes back into what it is reading. Halving that loop fills only half the output. The bound depends on whether the reversal is in place, so read that first.

A two-dimensional array is an array of arrays: the outer array holds references to rows, and each row is itself an array. Once you picture it that way, the syntax follows.

int[][] grid = new int[3][4];        // 3 rows, 4 columns

grid[1][2] = 7;                       // row 1, column 2

grid.length        // 3  — number of ROWS
grid[0].length     // 4  — number of COLUMNS in row 0

int[][] g = { {1, 2, 3},
              {4, 5, 6} };            // literal form

for (int r = 0; r < g.length; r++) {
    for (int c = 0; c < g[r].length; c++) {
        System.out.print(g[r][c] + " ");
    }
    System.out.println();             // ends the row — outer loop (4.7)
}

Because rows are separate arrays, they need not all be the same length — a jagged array. That is why the inner bound is g[r].length and not g[0].length: writing the latter is correct for rectangular data and breaks the moment it is not.

Rows, columns, and the two bounds

int[][] g = new int[3][4];        // 3 rows, each of 4 columns
g[1][2] = 7;                      // row 1, column 2

g.length        // 3  — number of ROWS
g[0].length     // 4  — number of columns in row 0

for (int r = 0; r < g.length; r++)
    for (int c = 0; c < g[r].length; c++)     // g[r], not g[0]
        System.out.print(g[r][c] + " ");

The first index is always the row, and g.length counts rows rather than total cells — a 3×4 grid has g.length == 3 and 12 elements. Total cells is rows × columns.

int[][] jag = new int[3][];       // rows not yet created
jag[0] = new int[2];
jag[1] = new int[5];              // rows may differ in length

Because each row is its own array, rows can have different lengths — a jagged array. That is why the inner bound must be g[r].length: g[0].length is right only for rectangular data and throws the moment it is not.

📘 DEFINITION

2D array: an array whose elements are themselves arrays

Row-major order: the convention that the first index selects the row

Jagged array: a 2D array whose rows have different lengths

grid[r].length: the length of one specific row

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

grid.length is the row count, never the total number of elements. For a 3×4 grid the total is grid.length * grid[0].length = 12.

✅ Also covered in depth: Arrays → 2D Arrays and ArrayList

📊 FIGURE — A 2D ARRAY IS ROWS OF ARRAYS
📊 FIGURE — a jagged array: why the inner bound must be jag[r].length
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — row totals and a column total on a rectangular grid

Four stores, three quarters of sales. The first subscript is always the row.

int[][] sales = { {120, 95, 140},
                  { 88, 210,  76},
                  {150, 130, 190},
                  { 60,  45,  80} };
System.out.println("rows " + sales.length + ", cols " + sales[0].length);
for (int r = 0; r < sales.length; r++) {
    int rowTotal = 0;
    for (int c = 0; c < sales[r].length; c++) rowTotal += sales[r][c];
    System.out.println("store " + r + " total " + rowTotal);
}
int colTotal = 0;
for (int r = 0; r < sales.length; r++) colTotal += sales[r][1];   // fix the COLUMN
System.out.println("column 1 total " + colTotal);
System.out.println("sales[2][0] = " + sales[2][0]);
OUTPUTrows 4, cols 3 store 0 total 355 store 1 total 374 store 2 total 470 store 3 total 185 column 1 total 480 sales[2][0] = 150
  1. sales.length is 4 — the number of rows, not the 12 elements. Total cells is rows × columns.
  2. The row total fixes r and walks c; the column total does the opposite, fixing the second subscript at 1 and walking r. Swapping those is the standard error.
  3. rowTotal is declared inside the outer loop, so each store starts from zero — the accumulator-placement rule from Unit 4, now one level deeper.
  4. sales[2][0] is 150: row 2 (the third store), column 0 (the first quarter).
Answer: row totals 355, 374, 470, 185; column 1 totals 480
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a jagged array, and the bound that breaks it

Rows are separate arrays, so they need not be the same length — and code that assumes they are fails in two different ways.

int[][] jag = new int[3][];        // three row slots, no rows yet
jag[0] = new int[] {5, 8};
jag[1] = new int[] {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
jag[2] = new int[] {9};
for (int r = 0; r < jag.length; r++)
    System.out.println("row " + r + " length " + jag[r].length + " " + Arrays.toString(jag[r]));
int total = 0;
for (int r = 0; r < jag.length; r++)
    for (int c = 0; c < jag[r].length; c++) total += jag[r][c];
System.out.println("total " + total);
OUTPUTrow 0 length 2 [5, 8] row 1 length 5 [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] row 2 length 1 [9] total 37

Now replace the inner bound with jag[0].length, which is 2. Row 0 is fine, row 1 is silently truncated to its first two elements, and row 2 — which has only one element — throws Index 1 out of bounds for length 1. One bound produces both a silent wrong answer and a crash, depending on the row.

new int[3][] with the second bracket empty creates the outer array only: its three slots are null until a row is assigned. new int[3][4] creates all four rows at once, every element 0.

Answer: lengths 2, 5 and 1; total 37
🎯 EXAM TIP

For a 2D trace question, write the grid out with its row and column indexes labelled before doing anything else. Then check which subscript the loop is holding still: an inner loop over the second subscript walks a row, an inner loop over the first walks a column. Half the marks on these questions turn on that one distinction.

The enhanced for loop — the "for-each" — removes the index when you do not need it. It reads each element in turn, from first to last, and there is no counter to get wrong.

for (int value : a) {
    System.out.println(value);
}

// same thing with an index
for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) { System.out.println(a[i]); }

The restriction is the whole point of the trade: value is a copy of the element, so assigning to it changes nothing in the array. Modifying elements needs the indexed form.

for (int value : a) { value = 0; }      // array is UNCHANGED
for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) { a[i] = 0; }   // this works

What the for-each can and cannot do

for (int x : a) sum += x;             // reading — ideal

for (int x : a) x = x * 2;            // does NOTHING to the array
for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) a[i] = a[i] * 2;   // this works

The loop variable is a fresh copy of each element, so assigning to it changes the copy and nothing else. For objects the copy is a copy of the reference, which means you cannot replace an element but you can still call a method that mutates the object it points at.

UseWhich loop
reading every element, order irrelevantfor-each — no index to get wrong
assigning to elementsindexed for
needing the positionindexed for
going backwards, or skippingindexed for
comparing neighbours a[i] and a[i+1]indexed for

A for-each over an empty array runs zero times and is safe. A for-each over a null array throws a NullPointerException — empty and null are not the same thing.

📘 DEFINITION

Enhanced for loop: for (Type v : collection) — iterates every element without an index

Read-only iteration: the enhanced loop gives a copy for primitives, so writes to the variable do not persist

🎯 EXAM TIP

Use the enhanced loop when you only read, and every element, in order. Use the indexed loop when you need to write, need the index, need to skip, or need to go backwards. The same loop works on collections in 14.1.

✅ Also covered in depth: Control Flow → for Loops, break, and continue

📊 FIGURE — the for-each variable is a copy, which is exactly why it cannot write back
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the assignment that does nothing

Both loops look like they zero the array. Only one of them does.

int[] readings = {14, 22, 9, 31};

for (int v : readings) v = 0;                 // assigns the COPY
System.out.println("after for-each writes: " + Arrays.toString(readings));

for (int i = 0; i < readings.length; i++) readings[i] = 0;
System.out.println("after indexed writes:  " + Arrays.toString(readings));
OUTPUTafter for-each writes: [14, 22, 9, 31] after indexed writes: [0, 0, 0, 0]

On each pass of the first loop, v is created, filled with a copy of the element, assigned 0, and destroyed. The array is never addressed at all — there is no readings[...] anywhere on that line, which is the give-away. It compiles without so much as a warning.

The second loop names the storage: readings[i] on the left of the assignment is the array slot itself. Any exam option claiming a for-each can modify an array of primitives is wrong for this reason.

Answer: unchanged by the for-each; all zeros after the indexed loop
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — empty, null, and an array of objects

Three edge cases the enhanced loop is asked about, and they do not behave the same way.

int[] empty = new int[0];
int n = 0;
for (int v : empty) n++;
System.out.println("empty array passes: " + n);

int[] missing = null;
try { for (int v : missing) n++; }
catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("null array threw NullPointerException"); }

String[] words = {"alpha", "beta"};
for (String w : words) w = w.toUpperCase();
System.out.println(Arrays.toString(words));
OUTPUTempty array passes: 0 null array threw NullPointerException [alpha, beta]
  1. A length-0 array is a perfectly real array with nothing in it. The loop runs zero times, which is correct and needs no guard.
  2. A null array is not an array at all. The enhanced loop has to ask it for its length before it can start, so it throws immediately — before the first pass.
  3. Over an array of objects the loop variable is a copy of the reference. Assigning a new String to w repoints the copy, so the array still holds the originals. What would work is calling a method that changes the object itself — impossible for a String, which is immutable, but the reason a for-each over your own objects can mutate them.
Answer: 0 passes; a NullPointerException; and the words unchanged
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

"Empty" and "null" are different states and the exam separates them deliberately. new int[0] is safe to loop over, has a length of 0, and is the right thing to return when there are no results. null throws on the loop, on .length, and on every element access. A guard has to test a == null first, or it throws while checking.

Tax brackets are the natural array example because the long else if chain from 3.20 becomes two arrays plus one loop — and adding a new bracket then means editing data, not code.

double[] limits = {25000, 50000, 100000, Double.MAX_VALUE};
double[] rates  = {0.10,  0.15,  0.22,   0.28};

double rate = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < limits.length; i++) {
    if (salary < limits[i]) { rate = rates[i]; break; }
}
double tax = salary * rate;

This is parallel arrays (5.5) doing real work: limits[i] and rates[i] describe one bracket. The break matters — without it, the loop keeps testing and every salary ends up in the top bracket.

Why break decides the answer

double[] limits = {10000, 40000, 85000, Double.MAX_VALUE};
double[] rates  = {0.10,  0.22,  0.30,  0.37};

double rate = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < limits.length; i++) {
    if (salary <= limits[i]) { rate = rates[i]; break; }   // FIRST match wins
}

The brackets are in ascending order, so the first limit the salary fits under is the right one. Without break the loop keeps testing, every later limit also passes, and rate ends up as the last one assigned — so every salary is taxed at the top rate. The bug is silent and uniform, which makes it hard to spot from one test value.

The final Double.MAX_VALUE entry is a sentinel that guarantees a match, so rate can never be left at 0. Adding a bracket is now editing two array literals rather than rewriting an else if chain — the whole point of the rewrite.

📘 DEFINITION

Table-driven logic: replacing a branch chain with data in arrays plus one loop

Bracket lookup: finding the first limit a value falls under and taking the matching rate

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

Table-driven code is easier to get right because the ordering rule from 3.4 becomes visible as data. The list is sorted low to high on the page, so you can see the bug rather than trace it.

📊 FIGURE — bracket lookup: the break is what makes "first match wins" true
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — four salaries through one table-driven loop

An else if chain becomes two arrays and one loop, and adding a band becomes an edit to data rather than to code.

double[] limits = {25000, 50000, 100000, Double.MAX_VALUE};
double[] rates  = {0.10, 0.15, 0.22, 0.28};
double[] tests  = {18000, 42000, 61000, 250000};
for (double salary : tests) {
    double rate = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < limits.length; i++) {
        if (salary < limits[i]) { rate = rates[i]; break; }   // FIRST match wins
    }
    System.out.printf("%.0f -> rate %.2f, tax %.2f%n", salary, rate, salary * rate);
}
OUTPUT18000 -> rate 0.10, tax 1800.00 42000 -> rate 0.15, tax 6300.00 61000 -> rate 0.22, tax 13420.00 250000 -> rate 0.28, tax 70000.00
  1. 18000 fits under the first limit, so the loop takes rates[0] and breaks after one test.
  2. 42000 fails < 25000 and passes < 50000, so it takes rates[1] after two tests.
  3. 61000 needs three tests; 250000 falls through to the sentinel Double.MAX_VALUE, which is there precisely so that something always matches and rate is never left at 0.
  4. limits[i] and rates[i] describe one band — parallel arrays doing real work.
Answer: rates 0.10, 0.15, 0.22 and 0.28
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — deleting the break, one pass at a time

The same loop with the break removed, printing rate after every test so the damage is visible.

double[] limits = {25000, 50000, 100000, Double.MAX_VALUE};
double[] rates  = {0.10, 0.15, 0.22, 0.28};
double salary = 18000, rate = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < limits.length; i++) {
    if (salary < limits[i]) { rate = rates[i]; }        // no break
    System.out.printf("  after i=%d rate is %.2f%n", i, rate);
}
System.out.printf("no break: %.0f taxed at %.2f%n", salary, rate);
OUTPUT after i=0 rate is 0.10 after i=1 rate is 0.15 after i=2 rate is 0.22 after i=3 rate is 0.28 no break: 18000 taxed at 0.28

18000 is under every limit, so every test passes and each one overwrites the rate. The final value is the last band — the top rate, for the lowest earner. Worse, the bug is uniform: every salary comes out at 0.28, so a single test value gives no hint that anything is wrong.

Two fixes exist and only one is the topic here. Adding break stops at the first match. Alternatively, reversing the array order and testing salary >= limits[i] also works without a break — but then the data must be sorted descending, and mixing the two conventions is how this loop usually goes wrong.

Answer: 0.28 for an 18000 salary — the highest band, applied to everyone
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Whether the comparison is < or <= decides who sits exactly on a boundary. With salary < 25000, a salary of exactly 25000 falls to the next band. Boundary values are precisely where exam questions are set, so read the operator before you read the numbers.

🎯 EXAM TIP

The final example stores a list of registered domains in an array and checks a candidate against it — the search pattern of 5.4 applied to Strings, with the comparison rules of 3.13.

String[] taken = {"example.com", "wgu.edu", "java.org"};
String candidate = scnr.next().toLowerCase().trim();

boolean available = true;
for (int i = 0; i < taken.length; i++) {
    if (taken[i].equalsIgnoreCase(candidate)) {
        available = false;
        break;
    }
}
System.out.println(candidate + (available ? " is available" : " is taken"));

Three earlier ideas are load-bearing here and each one is a place the exam plants an error: .equalsIgnoreCase rather than == (3.2), normalising the input before comparing (3.21), and break so the flag is not overwritten by later non-matches (4.13).

Rules as data

char[] allowed = {'-', '.'};

boolean legal(char c) {
    if (Character.isLetterOrDigit(c)) return true;
    for (char ok : allowed) if (c == ok) return true;
    return false;
}

Putting the permitted characters in an array turns the rule into data: extending it is a one-element edit rather than another clause in a growing boolean expression. It is the same move as the tax brackets in 5.11, applied to validation.

The loop returns as soon as it finds a match, and returns false only after every possibility has been checked — the shape of every "is this in the set?" search. Returning false inside the loop instead would reject on the first non-match, which rejects everything.

📘 DEFINITION

Membership test: searching an array for an element equal to a target

Case-insensitive search: normalising both sides, or using equalsIgnoreCase, so case does not affect the match

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Using == here would compile and would report every domain as available, because the input String is never the same object as the literals in the array.

📊 FIGURE — a membership search, and the comparison that decides whether it finds anything
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — is this domain taken?

The search pattern of 5.4 with Strings in place of numbers, plus the normalisation that makes the comparison fair.

String[] taken = {"example.com", "wgu.edu", "java.org"};
String[] tries = {"WGU.edu", "newsite.com"};
for (String raw : tries) {
    String candidate = raw.trim().toLowerCase();
    boolean available = true;
    for (int i = 0; i < taken.length; i++) {
        if (taken[i].equalsIgnoreCase(candidate)) { available = false; break; }
    }
    System.out.println(candidate + (available ? " is available" : " is taken"));
}
OUTPUTwgu.edu is taken newsite.com is available
  1. trim().toLowerCase() normalises the input first, so trailing spaces and capitals cannot produce a false "available".
  2. The flag starts true and can only be falsified — the sticky-flag rule from 4.13.
  3. break stops the scan at the match. Without it the loop keeps testing, and since the remaining entries do not match, nothing resets the flag — so here it is an efficiency point rather than a correctness one. It becomes a correctness point the moment the loop assigns available = ... instead of only assigning false.
  4. "newsite.com" survives all three comparisons, so the flag stays true.
Answer: wgu.edu is taken; newsite.com is available
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — why == compiles and finds nothing

The candidate arrives as input rather than as a literal, which is what makes this the realistic case.

String[] taken = {"example.com", "wgu.edu"};
Scanner scnr = new Scanner("wgu.edu");
String candidate = scnr.next();          // built at run time — a NEW object
boolean byEquals = false, byIdentity = false;
for (String t : taken) {
    if (t.equals(candidate)) byEquals = true;
    if (t == candidate)      byIdentity = true;
}
System.out.println("equals found it: " + byEquals);
System.out.println("==     found it: " + byIdentity);
OUTPUTequals found it: true == found it: false

The characters are identical and == still says no, because it asks "the same object?" and the Scanner built a fresh String. The array entries are compile-time literals living in the string pool; the input is not. So a registry written with == reports every domain as available, forever, and never throws.

There is a trap inside the trap: written as String candidate = "wgu" + ".edu"; the compiler folds two literals into one pooled literal and == would be true. That is why demonstrations of this rule must use a value built at run time — and why == on Strings can appear to work in testing and fail in production.

Answer: equals finds it; == does not
🎯 EXAM TIP

Two things make a "rules as data" answer right on this topic: the permitted values live in an array so extending them is a one-element edit, and the search returns as soon as it finds a match but only reports failure after the whole array has been checked. A loop that returns false from inside the body rejects on the first non-match, which rejects everything.

public static int square(int n) {
//     ^      ^   ^      ^
//     |      |   |      parameter list: what it needs
//     |      |   name
//     |      return type: what it gives back  (void = nothing)
//     modifiers

    return n * n;               // hands the value back and exits immediately
}

int result = square(6);         // 36 — the CALL

The vocabulary is worth separating now because the exam uses it precisely. The method definition is written once; the call can happen many times; the parameter is the name in the definition; the argument is the value supplied at the call.

Reading a method header

public static double average(int a, int b) { ... }
  |      |      |        |        |
  |      |      |        |        +-- parameter list (types AND names)
  |      |      |        +----------- method name (camelCase, a verb)
  |      |      +-------------------- return type — what comes back
  |      +--------------------------- static: called on the class, not an object
  +---------------------------------- visibility

Parameterthe variable in the definition — int a
Argumentthe value at the call — average(3, 5)

Method: a named, reusable block of code that may take inputs and return a value

Parameter: a variable in the method definition that receives an argument

Argument: the actual value passed at the call site

Return type: the type of value the method hands back; void means none

Signature: the method name plus its parameter types — what distinguishes overloads (6.12)

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

Every remaining unit is built from methods. Classes in Unit 7 are data plus methods; recursion in Unit 11 is a method calling itself; the library you have been using since Unit 1 is nothing but methods.

📊 FIGURE — A METHOD CALL IS A ROUND TRIP
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The four parts of a method
System.out.println(applyDiscount(200, 10));
System.out.println(applyDiscount(89, 25));

Read the signature before the body. The return type tells you whether the call can be assigned, and the parameter list tells you exactly what the call must supply.

The simplest useful methods return nothing and exist purely to avoid repeating output code. Their return type is void, and a void method ends either at its closing brace or at a bare return;.

public static void printBanner(String title) {
    System.out.println("=================");
    System.out.println("  " + title);
    System.out.println("=================");
}

printBanner("Results");        // a STATEMENT — it produces no value

int x = printBanner("Hi");     // COMPILE ERROR — void gives nothing to assign

The distinction between a method that prints and one that returns is a real design decision, not a formality. A method that prints can only ever print; a method that returns can be printed, stored, compared or passed on. Prefer returning — it is also what makes the unit testing in 6.7 possible.

A void method ends at its closing brace, or early at a bare return; used as a guard. Writing return value; in a void method is a compile error, and so is using its result: int x = printReport(); will not compile because there is nothing to assign.

public static void banner(String title) {
    if (title == null) return;          // early exit, no value
    System.out.println("=== " + title + " ===");
}

The choice between printing and returning is a design decision that shows up again in 6.7: a method that prints can only be checked by eye, while a method that returns can be unit tested. Prefer returning the value and letting the caller decide whether to display it.

📘 DEFINITION

void: a return type meaning the method produces no value

return;: in a void method, exits early without a value

Side effect: anything a method does other than return a value, such as printing

🎯 EXAM TIP

If a question asks why a method returns a String instead of printing it, the answer is testability and reuse — you cannot assert on something that has already gone to the screen.

📊 FIGURE — print, println and printf

System.out.print("a");
System.out.print("b");
System.out.println("c");
System.out.println("d");
System.out.printf("%.2f%n", 3.14159);
abc d 3.14

  1. print leaves the cursor on the same line, so a and b run together.

Three reasons justify pulling code into a method, and they are the reasons an exam question will list.

Reuse removes duplication, so a fix happens in one place rather than five. Abstraction lets you use calculateTax(salary) without holding the brackets in your head. Decomposition breaks a large problem into pieces small enough to test separately (1.9).

// before: the same six lines in three places
// after:
double tax = calculateTax(salary);

The practical rule of thumb: if you have copied a block of code, or if you find yourself writing a comment to explain what the next ten lines do, that block wants to be a method with the comment as its name.

ReasonWhat it buysSymptom when ignored
Reuseone copy of the logicthe same fix applied in five places, four correctly
Abstractiona name instead of the detailcode you must re-read to understand
Testabilitycallable in isolationthe only way to test is to run the whole program
Maintainabilitychange in one placeedits ripple unpredictably

The practical rule is one job per method. If describing what it does needs the word "and", it is probably two methods — and each half is then independently reusable and independently testable.

Method names should be verbs for actions (calculateTax) and questions for booleans (isValid, hasNext). A name that reads like a sentence at the call site is the point of the exercise.

📘 DEFINITION

Reuse: calling one definition from many places instead of duplicating code

Abstraction: using a method by its name and contract without knowing its implementation

Decomposition: splitting a problem into smaller solvable parts

Cohesion: a method doing one clearly-named job rather than several

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

This is the same argument the whole course keeps making at larger scale: methods group statements, classes group methods and data (7.6), packages group classes (7.20).

📊 FIGURE — what a method buys you
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The same logic, repeated versus named
double a = 100, b = 250;
System.out.println(a * 0.20 + b * 0.20);
System.out.println(vat(a) + vat(b));
70.0 70.0
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Both lines compute the same total.
  2. The second says what the number MEANS.
  3. If the rate changes, the second needs one edit and the first needs every occurrence found.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Decomposition makes the main flow readable
double[] prices = {19.99, 5.50, 3.75};
System.out.printf("%.2f%n", subtotal(prices));
System.out.printf("%.2f%n", withVat(subtotal(prices)));
29.24 35.09
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Each method does one job with a name that says so.
  2. The last line reads as a sentence rather than as arithmetic.
  3. Each piece can also be tested on its own.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Believing methods make a program faster. A call carries a small overhead, so raw speed usually goes very slightly DOWN. The gain is correctness and maintenance — that is the answer the exam wants.
🎯 EXAM TIP
If a question asks for the PRIMARY benefit of methods, the answer is reuse and maintainability — not performance and not memory.

A mathematical method is the cleanest kind: values in, value out, nothing else touched. Every path through it must return, and the compiler enforces that.

public static double average(int a, int b, int c) {
    return (a + b + c) / 3.0;      // 3.0 not 3 — else integer division (2.5)
}

public static int max(int a, int b) {
    if (a > b) { return a; }
    return b;                       // reached only when a <= b
}

The 3.0 in the first method is the same trap as ever, now hidden inside a method where it is harder to see. Declaring the return type as double does not rescue an integer division — the truncation happens first, and the whole number is then widened.

A pure method depends only on its parameters and changes nothing outside itself. Same inputs, same output, every time — which is what makes it trivially testable and safe to call from anywhere.

public static double circleArea(double r) {
    return Math.PI * r * r;              // pure
}

public static double triangleArea(double b, double h) {
    return (b * h) / 2.0;                // 2.0, not 2
}

The 2.0 is deliberate. With 2, if b and h were ints the whole expression would be integer division and lose the half. Writing the literal as a double forces real division regardless of what the operands are.

Math.PI rather than 3.14, and Math.pow(r, 2) is legal but r * r is faster and clearer for a square.

📘 DEFINITION

Pure method: one whose result depends only on its arguments and which changes nothing else

Return path: every route through the method must reach a return statement

Math class: the standard library of static maths methods: abs, pow, sqrt, min, max, round

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

"Missing return statement" means one branch has no return — usually an if with no else. The compiler will not reason about whether that branch can actually happen; it demands a return on every path.

📊 FIGURE — a maths method is just input to output
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Return the value; let the caller print it
System.out.println(circleArea(2));
System.out.printf("%.2f%n", circleArea(2));
System.out.printf("%.2f%n", circleArea(2) * 3);
12.566370614359172 12.57 37.70
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The method computes and returns; it never prints.
  2. That lets the caller format it, or use it in further arithmetic.
  3. A method that printed instead could not be reused in the third line.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Integer division inside a maths method
System.out.println(averageBad(7, 8));
System.out.println(averageGood(7, 8));
7.0 7.5
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Both parameters are int, so (a + b) / 2 is integer division.
  2. The declared double return type does NOT rescue it — the value is already truncated.
  3. Dividing by 2.0 forces real division before the return.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Declaring the return type as double does not make the arithmetic inside it double. Check the operands, not the signature.

Methods that return boolean turn a condition into a name, and that is worth more than it sounds: if (isLeapYear(y)) reads correctly, while the same condition written out does not.

public static boolean isLeapYear(int year) {
    if (year % 400 == 0) { return true; }
    if (year % 100 == 0) { return false; }
    return year % 4 == 0;              // return the expression directly
}

public static char grade(int score) {
    if (score >= 90) { return 'A'; }
    if (score >= 80) { return 'B'; }
    return 'F';
}

Note the last line of the first method. return year % 4 == 0; is preferred over an if that returns true or false — the comparison already is a boolean (3.12), so wrapping it adds nothing.

Using return instead of else if also flattens the chain: once a return executes, the method is over, so no else is required to prevent the later checks.

// verbose
public static boolean isEven(int n) {
    if (n % 2 == 0) return true;
    else return false;
}

// the condition IS the answer
public static boolean isEven(int n) {
    return n % 2 == 0;
}

Any if (c) return true; else return false; collapses to return c;. The exam asks you to spot it, and the reverse — return !c; for the negated version.

A guard clause handles the exceptional case first and returns, leaving the main path unindented:

public static double divide(int a, int b) {
    if (b == 0) return 0;                // guard
    return (double) a / b;               // the real work, not nested
}

Every path must return. A method whose last statement is inside an if with no else fails to compile even when you can see the condition is always true — the compiler does not reason about values.

📘 DEFINITION

Predicate method: a method returning boolean, named as a question: isValid, hasNext

Guard clause: an early return that handles a special case and leaves the rest unindented

Early return: returning as soon as the answer is known

🎯 EXAM TIP

if (x) return true; else return false; is always reducible to return x;. Exam questions include the long form as a "which is equivalent" distractor.

📊 FIGURE — every path must return
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Returning from a branch
System.out.println(band(95));
System.out.println(band(80));
System.out.println(band(12));
A B F

  2. So the first matching band wins and nothing below runs.
  3. The final unconditional return guarantees every path returns something.

System.out.println(isEvenLong(4) + " " + isEven(4));
System.out.println(isEvenLong(7) + " " + isEven(7));

actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The condition is ALREADY a boolean.
  2. So the if/else pair is redundant.
  3. Both versions agree; the second is what a marker expects.

"Missing return statement" when a method returns inside every if but has nothing after them. The compiler must see a return on every possible path, even one you can argue is unreachable.

A method containing a loop is where the accumulate patterns of 4.3 get a name and become reusable. The accumulator is a local variable, so each call starts fresh — which is the fix for the bug in 4.12 by construction.

public static int sumTo(int n) {
    int sum = 0;                    // local: reset on every call
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) { sum += i; }
    return sum;
}

public static int countVowels(String s) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
        if ("aeiouAEIOU".indexOf(s.charAt(i)) >= 0) { count++; }
    }
    return count;
}

"aeiouAEIOU".indexOf(c) >= 0 is a compact membership test using 3.16: indexOf returns -1 when the character is absent, so a non-negative result means it was found.

public static int sum(int[] a) {
    int total = 0;                       // LOCAL — fresh every call
    for (int x : a) total += x;
    return total;                        // after the loop
}

public static int indexOf(int[] a, int target) {
    for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++)
        if (a[i] == target) return i;    // early return — no break needed
    return -1;                           // reached only if nothing matched
}

Putting the accumulator inside the method rather than outside is what fixes the reset bug from 4.12 permanently: each call gets its own, so calls cannot interfere.

In a search, return replaces break — it leaves the loop and the method at once. The final return -1 is not optional; without it the method has a path with no return value and will not compile.

An empty array is not an error for sum (the loop runs zero times and 0 is right) but it is for an average, which must guard against dividing by a.length == 0.

📘 DEFINITION

Local accumulator: a variable declared inside the method, so each call gets its own

Loop-and-return: the pattern of accumulating in a loop and returning the result after it

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Putting a return inside the loop body without a condition ends the method on the first iteration. Return after the loop unless you genuinely want an early exit.

System.out.println(sumTo(100));

  2. Each pass adds one more term.

  2. So the method exits during the first pass.

Unit testing means calling a method with known inputs and checking the outputs — and it is the direct payoff of returning values rather than printing them (6.2).

public static void main(String[] args) {
    // normal cases
    System.out.println(max(3, 7) == 7);      // expect true
    System.out.println(max(9, 2) == 9);

    // EDGE cases — where the bugs live
    System.out.println(max(5, 5) == 5);      // equal
    System.out.println(max(-3, -8) == -3);   // negatives
}

The valuable tests are the edge cases: empty input, a single element, zero, negatives, the exact boundary of a range, the first and last index of an array. A method that passes three ordinary cases and fails on an empty array is the normal state of untested code.

A unit test calls one method with known inputs and checks the result against what you worked out by hand. It is only possible because the method returns something — which is the concrete reason 6.2 prefers returning to printing.

Test kindFor max(int[])
typical{3, 9, 4} → 9
boundaryone element {5} → 5; max at the first position; max at the last
edgeempty array; all values equal; all negative
invalidnull — does it throw, or return a default?

Boundaries earn their keep because that is where off-by-one errors live: a bound that is wrong by one behaves correctly for every value except at the very edge of the range.

Tests must be independent — each sets up its own data — so that one failure does not cascade. Re-running the whole set after a change is regression testing, and its purpose is to catch the fix that broke something else.

📘 DEFINITION

Unit test: a check that one method produces the expected output for a specific input

Test case: one input plus its expected result

Edge case: an input at the boundary of what is valid: empty, zero, first, last, maximum

Regression: a previously working behaviour broken by a later change

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

Edge cases are also where exam questions are set. When you see a trace question with an empty array or a single-element array, that is deliberate — the interesting answer is at the boundary.

📊 FIGURE — what to test
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Testing a method by asserting values
System.out.println(clamp(5, 1, 10) == 5);
System.out.println(clamp(0, 1, 10) == 1);
System.out.println(clamp(99, 1, 10) == 10);
System.out.println(clamp(1, 1, 10) == 1);
true true true true
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Each line states an expectation and prints whether it held.
  2. The boundary values 1 and 10 matter more than the middle ones.
  3. All true means the method behaves as specified.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A test that catches a real bug
int[] xs = {4, 8, 15};
System.out.println(lastIndexBug(xs) == 2);
System.out.println(lastIndex(xs) == 2);
false true
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The buggy version returns 3, one past the end.
  2. The test prints false, which is the bug being caught.
  3. The corrected version passes.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Testing only the happy path. The bugs live at the boundaries — an empty array, a zero, the first and last index — which is exactly where a casual test never looks.
🎯 EXAM TIP
A good test names the expected value explicitly. "It ran without crashing" is not a test; "clamp(99, 1, 10) equals 10" is.
