Understanding how a call works mechanically explains several behaviours that otherwise look arbitrary. When a method is called, Java pushes a stack frame holding that call’s parameters and locals; when it returns, the frame is discarded.

main            calls  average(a, b)
  |                        |
  | frame: a, b, result    | frame: its OWN a, b  (copies)
  |                        |
  |  <---- returns 86.3 ---+   frame destroyed, locals gone

The consequence that matters most is pass by value: the parameter is a copy of the argument, so assigning to a parameter cannot change the caller’s variable.

public static void tryToChange(int x) { x = 99; }

int n = 5;
tryToChange(n);
System.out.println(n);       // still 5

The call stack, and pass-by-value

Each call pushes a stack frame holding that call's parameters, its local variables and the address to return to. The frame is destroyed when the method returns, which is why locals do not survive and why infinite recursion ends in StackOverflowError.

Java is always pass-by-value. The subtlety is what the value is.

static void f(int n)   { n = 99; }          // copies the number
static void g(int[] a) { a[0] = 99; }       // copies the REFERENCE
static void h(int[] a) { a = new int[3]; }  // reassigns the copy — caller unaffected

int x = 1;      f(x);   // x is still 1
int[] arr={1};  g(arr); // arr[0] IS now 99  — same array, reached through the copy
                h(arr); // arr still points at the original array

For a primitive, the copied value is the number. For an object or array, the copied value is the reference — so the method can reach and modify the same object, but assigning a whole new object to the parameter only rebinds its private copy.

📘 DEFINITION

Call stack: the stack of frames, one per active method call

Stack frame: the memory holding one call’s parameters and local variables

Pass by value: the argument’s value is copied into the parameter

Return address: where execution resumes in the caller after the method returns

🎯 EXAM TIP

outer();

The common method errors are a short list, and all but one are compile errors — which is the good news.

int x = printTotal();          // 1. using the result of a void method
double avg(int a, int b) { }   // 2. missing return statement
max(3);                         // 3. wrong number of arguments
max("a", "b");                  // 4. wrong argument types
int max(int a, int b) { ... }   // 5. defined inside main — methods go beside it

The one silent failure is argument order. divide(b, a) compiles perfectly when both parameters are the same type and gives the wrong answer forever — a logic error (1.4) that no compiler can catch, which is what makes named parameters in the call site comment worthwhile.

ErrorWhen it bites
missing return on some pathcompile
wrong number of argumentscompile
argument of the wrong typecompile

defining a method inside another methodcompile
arguments in the wrong ordernever — silently wrong answers

Only the last one is dangerous. divide(b, a) compiles perfectly when both parameters are int, and the result is simply wrong. Naming parameters meaningfully and keeping the list short is the only real defence; a method taking four ints in a row is an accident waiting to happen.

Type mismatch: an argument whose type does not convert to the parameter type

System.out.println(msg);

  1. The first call computes the upper-case text and discards it.
  2. Nothing changes, and the compiler does not complain.

Passing an array to a method is the first place where pass-by-value stops feeling like pass-by-value — and it is worth being exact, because the exam tests the exact boundary.

public static void doubleAll(int[] a) {
    for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) { a[i] *= 2; }   // caller SEES this
}

public static void replace(int[] a) {
    a = new int[]{9, 9, 9};        // caller does NOT see this
}

The reference is copied, so the method has a second name for the same array — modifying elements through it modifies the one array everyone shares. But reassigning the parameter only repoints the copy; the caller’s variable still points at the original.

Because the length travels with the array, an array parameter needs no separate size parameter — a.length is always available inside the method.

static void doubleAll(int[] a) {
    for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) a[i] *= 2;   // caller SEES this
}

static void replace(int[] a) {
    a = new int[]{9, 9, 9};                        // caller sees NOTHING
}

The exact boundary: you may change what the array contains, because the copy of the reference reaches the same array; you may not change which array the caller's variable points at, because that variable was never handed over.

The array's length travels with it — a.length works inside the method with no extra parameter. That is only true for a perfect size array; an oversize one must pass its count separately, which is the whole of 6.17.

static int sum(int... nums) { ... }   // varargs: call as sum(1,2,3) or sum(arr)

A null array parameter is legal to pass and throws only when dereferenced, so a method that might receive one should guard with if (a == null || a.length == 0).

📘 DEFINITION

Array parameter: declared as Type[] name; receives a copy of the reference

Aliasing: two variables referring to the same array

Reassignment vs mutation: changing what a variable points to, versus changing what it points at

🎯 EXAM TIP

The rule in one line: a method can change an array’s contents but not which array the caller holds. The same rule governs objects in 7.18.

✅ Also covered in depth: Arrays → 1D Arrays

📊 FIGURE — arrays are handed over by reference
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Changing elements is visible to the caller
int[] data = {7, 8, 9};
zeroFirst(data);
System.out.println(data[0] + "," + data[1]);
0,8
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The method receives a copy of the reference, pointing at the SAME array.
  2. Writing to an element changes that one array.
  3. So the caller sees 0.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Reassigning the parameter is not
int[] data = {7, 8, 9};
replace(data);
System.out.println(data[0] + "," + data[1] + "," + data[2]);
7,8,9
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Assigning to a repoints only the method's own copy of the reference.
  2. The caller's variable still points at the original array.
  3. So nothing changed outside — this is the distinction the exam tests.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Concluding that Java is "pass by reference" because array contents change. Java is always pass by value — for an array, the VALUE being copied happens to be a reference.

Scope for methods extends the block scope of 4.10 upward. A local variable lives inside its method and is invisible everywhere else, including inside other methods — even ones called from it.

public class Demo {
    static int shared = 10;                 // FIELD: visible to every method

    public static void a() {
        int local = 5;                      // visible only inside a()
        System.out.println(shared);         // fine
    }

    public static void b() {
        System.out.println(local);          // ERROR — local does not exist here
    }
}

Two methods can each declare a variable called count with no conflict, because the names never meet. And a local with the same name as a field shadows it: inside that method the local wins, and the field is reachable only through this (7.11).

A local variable is visible only inside its own method — not in methods that method calls, and not in the caller. Methods do not see each other's locals at all; the only channels between them are parameters in and the return value out.

static void a() {
    int x = 5;
    b();                      // b cannot see x
}
static void b() {
    System.out.println(x);    // compile error: x does not exist here
}

A field declared in the class is visible to every method of that class, which is how objects hold state across calls (Unit 7). A parameter with the same name as a field shadows it, which is exactly why constructors and setters are written this.name = name; — the bare name refers to the parameter.

📘 DEFINITION

Local scope: a variable visible only within the method that declares it

Class scope (field): a variable declared in the class, visible to its methods

Shadowing: a local variable hiding a field of the same name

Method scope: methods in a class can call each other regardless of declaration order

🎯 EXAM TIP

Methods, unlike variables, do not need to be declared before use. A method defined at the bottom of the class can be called from main at the top.

✅ Also covered in depth: OOP → Encapsulation and Access Modifiers

📊 FIGURE — where a name is visible

for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
    int doubled = i * 2;
    total += doubled;
}
System.out.println(total);

actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. doubled exists only inside the loop body.
  2. Using it after the closing brace would not compile.
  3. total is declared outside, so it survives and holds the sum.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A local shadows a field of the same name
show();
System.out.println(count);
5 100
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Inside show the local count hides the field.
  2. Printing inside shows 5.
  3. The field is untouched and still prints 100.

Declaring a variable inside a loop when you need its value afterwards. It is created fresh each pass and destroyed at the closing brace, so the total you wanted never survives.

Overloading lets several methods share one name as long as their parameter lists differ. The compiler picks the match at compile time from the argument types.

static int    add(int a, int b)            { return a + b; }
static double add(double a, double b)      { return a + b; }
static int    add(int a, int b, int c)     { return a + b + c; }

add(2, 3);        // the int version
add(2.0, 3.0);    // the double version
add(1, 2, 3);     // the three-parameter version

The rule that catches people: the return type alone is not enough. Two methods differing only in what they return will not compile, because at the call site there is nothing for the compiler to choose on.

static int    f(int x) { ... }
static double f(int x) { ... }        // COMPILE ERROR — same signature
static int    max(int a, int b)          { ... }   // OK
static double max(double a, double b)    { ... }   // OK — different types
static int    max(int a, int b, int c)   { ... }   // OK — different count

static double max(int a, int b)          { ... }   // ERROR — return type
                                                   // alone is not enough

Overloads must differ in the parameter list — the number of parameters, their types, or their order. The return type is not part of the signature, so two methods differing only there cannot coexist: the compiler chooses from the arguments at the call, and the arguments would be identical.

Parameter names do not matter either. Selection happens at compile time from the static types of the arguments, so max(1, 2) picks the int version and max(1.0, 2) widens the 2 and picks the double one.

📘 DEFINITION

Overloading: multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists

Signature: the method name plus the number, types and order of its parameters

Resolution: the compile-time choice of which overload a call matches

🎯 EXAM TIP

Overloading is decided at compile time from the declared types; overriding (10.3) is decided at run time from the actual object. Confusing the two is the most common inheritance mistake in Unit 10.

✅ Also covered in depth: OOP → Static Members and Method Overloading

📊 FIGURE — what makes an overload legal
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Java picks the overload from the arguments
System.out.println(describe(5));
System.out.println(describe(5.0));
System.out.println(describe(2, 3));
int 5 double 5.0 two ints 5
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The argument types decide which version runs.
  2. The name is shared; the parameter list is the real identity.
  3. This is resolved at compile time.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — An int argument will widen if it must
System.out.println(only(7));
double version got 7.0
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. There is no int overload.
  2. Java widens the int to a double, which is safe and automatic.
  3. So the double version runs, printing 7.0.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Trying to overload on the return type alone. int f(int) and double f(int) is a compile error — the call site could not say which one it meant.

A method that trusts its arguments will eventually be handed a negative length or a null String. Checking parameters at the top is the cheap version of the exception handling in Unit 12.

public static double divide(int a, int b) {
    if (b == 0) {
        System.out.println("Error: divide by zero");
        return 0;                    // a sentinel — the caller must check it
    }
    return (double) a / b;
}

// stricter, and usually better: refuse rather than invent a value
public static double divideStrict(int a, int b) {
    if (b == 0) { throw new IllegalArgumentException("b must not be 0"); }
    return (double) a / b;
}

The difference between the two is who handles the problem. Returning a sentinel puts the burden on every caller and is silently ignored if they forget; throwing forces the issue at the point of the mistake. Unit 12 formalises the second approach.

public static double average(int[] a) {
    if (a == null)      return 0;           // guard: null
    if (a.length == 0)  return 0;           // guard: empty
    int sum = 0;
    for (int x : a) sum += x;
    return (double) sum / a.length;         // safe by here
}

Guards go at the top and return immediately, so the body below can assume its inputs are sane. The alternative — wrapping the real work in a deep if — indents the important code and hides the normal path.

Answer to a bad argumentUse when
return a safe defaultthere is an obviously right answer, like 0 for an empty average
return a sentinel (-1, null)the caller can reasonably check it
throw IllegalArgumentExceptioncontinuing would be meaningless — this is Unit 12

Validating in the method rather than at every call site means the rule is written once and cannot be forgotten by one caller out of six.

📘 DEFINITION

Precondition: something that must be true of the arguments for the method to work

Defensive programming: validating inputs at the boundary rather than assuming them

IllegalArgumentException: the standard exception for an argument that violates a precondition

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

This is why 12.2 exists. Once you have written a few sentinel returns and watched a caller ignore one, throwing becomes obviously preferable.

📊 FIGURE — validate at the boundary
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Guarding against a bad argument
System.out.println(safeDivide(10, 2));
System.out.println(safeDivide(10, 0));
5.0 cannot divide by zero 0.0
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The guard runs before any arithmetic.
  2. The bad case is reported and a safe value returned.
  3. The good case is unaffected.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Throwing is often better than returning a fake value
System.out.println(factorial(5));
try { factorial(-1); }
catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println("rejected: " + e.getMessage()); }
120 rejected: n must be >= 0
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Returning 0 for an invalid input would be indistinguishable from a real 0.
  2. Throwing makes the failure impossible to ignore.
  3. The caller decides how to handle it.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Checking the argument AFTER using it. A guard placed below the first calculation has already let the division by zero or the negative index happen.
🎯 EXAM TIP
For the performance assessment, validate at the top of the method and say in a comment what is rejected. Evaluators look for the check, not just for correct output.

Passing a Scanner to a method works, and there is one rule: create one Scanner in main and pass it around. Creating a second one on System.in inside a method causes input to be lost.

public static int readValidAge(Scanner scnr) {
    int age = scnr.nextInt();
    while (age < 0 || age > 120) {
        System.out.println("Invalid, try again:");
        age = scnr.nextInt();
    }
    return age;
}

// in main
Scanner scnr = new Scanner(System.in);
int age = readValidAge(scnr);

The reason is buffering: each Scanner keeps its own buffer over the same stream, so a second one can consume data the first has already pulled in. The same argument reappears in 9.4 for file input.

Create one Scanner on System.in in main and pass it as a parameter to anything that needs input.

public static void main(String[] args) {
    Scanner scnr = new Scanner(System.in);
    int age = readAge(scnr);              // pass the SAME scanner
}
static int readAge(Scanner scnr) { return scnr.nextInt(); }

A second new Scanner(System.in) inside a method opens a second reader over the same stream. Scanner buffers ahead, so the first one may already hold input the second will never see — and closing either one closes System.in for both, after which every later read throws NoSuchElementException.

The other Scanner trap is the newline: nextInt() consumes the number but leaves the line-ending behind, so an immediately following nextLine() returns an empty String. The fix is an extra scnr.nextLine(); to discard it.

📘 DEFINITION

Scanner parameter: passing the existing Scanner so all input shares one buffer

Buffer: the internal store of characters read ahead from the stream

Input method: a method that encapsulates prompting, reading and validating one value

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Never call new Scanner(System.in) in more than one place in a program. It is the standard cause of input that mysteriously disappears.

✅ Also covered in depth: Java Basics → Operators, Strings, and Scanner

📊 FIGURE — pass the Scanner in
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The newline nextInt leaves behind
import java.util.Scanner;
Scanner sc = new Scanner("42\nAda Lovelace\n");
int id = sc.nextInt();
String leftover = sc.nextLine();
String name = sc.nextLine();
System.out.println(id);
System.out.println("leftover=[" + leftover + "]");
System.out.println("name=[" + name + "]");
42 leftover=[] name=[Ada Lovelace]
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. nextInt takes the 42 but stops before the newline.
  2. The first nextLine therefore returns the EMPTY remainder of that line, not the name.
  3. Only the second nextLine reaches the name.
  4. Skip that extra nextLine and the name comes back empty — the commonest Scanner bug there is.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Sharing one Scanner between methods
import java.util.Scanner;
Scanner sc = new Scanner("31 27");
System.out.println(askAge(sc));
System.out.println(askAge(sc));
31 27
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The Scanner is created once and passed in as a parameter.
  2. Each call continues from where the last one stopped.
  3. Creating a new Scanner inside the method would restart or fight over the same input.
🎯 EXAM TIP
After nextInt(), an extra nextLine() is needed to consume the rest of the line before reading text. That single line is the most common Scanner exam question.

A perfect size array is exactly as long as the data it holds: a.length is the count, so nothing extra needs tracking.

int[] scores = new int[n];        // n known before the array is created
for (int i = 0; i < scores.length; i++) { scores[i] = scnr.nextInt(); }

// every loop bound is simply .length
for (int s : scores) { total += s; }

It is the simpler design and the one to prefer whenever the count is known up front. The limitation is the fixed length from 5.1: if the count is not known until the data has been read, you cannot size the array in advance — which is the problem 6.16 exists to solve.

In a perfect size array, a.length is the element count, so there is nothing else to keep in step and every loop bound is simply a.length.

int n = scnr.nextInt();          // count first
int[] a = new int[n];            // then the exact array
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) a[i] = scnr.nextInt();

It requires knowing the count before creating the array, which is why the count is read first. When the input ends with a sentinel instead of a count, you cannot size it up front — and that is exactly the case oversize arrays exist for.

Prefer it whenever the count is knowable: it uses no wasted memory and removes an entire class of bug, because there is no separate size variable to fall out of step with the data.

📘 DEFINITION

Perfect size array: an array whose length equals the number of elements stored

Element count: in a perfect size array, identical to length

🎯 EXAM TIP

In a perfect size array every loop is i < arr.length and the enhanced for loop (5.10) is always safe. Both become wrong for an oversize array.

📊 FIGURE — a perfect size array
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — length is the count, so loops are simple
int[] temps = {18, 21, 19, 24};
int total = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < temps.length; i++) total += temps[i];
System.out.println(temps.length);
System.out.printf("%.2f%n", (double) total / temps.length);
4 20.50
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Every slot is real data, so length is the item count.
  2. The loop runs to length with no separate counter.
  3. The average divides by length directly.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Growing one means copying
int[] a = {1, 2, 3};
int[] bigger = new int[a.length + 1];
for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) bigger[i] = a[i];
bigger[a.length] = 4;
System.out.println(bigger.length + " " + bigger[3]);
4 4
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. An array's length is fixed once created.
  2. Adding an item means allocating a new array and copying.
  3. That cost is the reason oversize arrays exist.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Assuming a perfect size array can grow. a.length is final — there is no add. Either allocate a new array, or use an oversize array with a separate count.

An oversize array is deliberately longer than the data it holds, with a separate int tracking how many slots are actually in use. It is the standard way to handle a growing collection before ArrayList (7.14).

final int CAPACITY = 100;
int[] values = new int[CAPACITY];
int numValues = 0;                    // how many are REAL

// adding
if (numValues < values.length) {      // capacity check — required
    values[numValues] = newItem;
    numValues++;
}

// every loop uses numValues, NOT values.length
for (int i = 0; i < numValues; i++) { System.out.println(values[i]); }

The count and the array must travel together everywhere. Passing the array to a method without the count leaves the method unable to tell data from the zeros beyond it — which is the argument for a class that holds both (7.6).

A note on the size variable's name

Different sources name the count differently — numValues, numElements, size, count. They all mean the same thing: how many slots hold real data. What matters is that the loop bound is that variable and never arr.length.

for (int i = 0; i < numElements; i++) { ... }   // correct
for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++)   { ... }   // reads the unused slots

arr[numElements] = value;   // append at the first free slot
numElements++;              // then advance the count
final int CAPACITY = 100;
int[] a = new int[CAPACITY];     // room for 100
int size = 0;                    // how many are ACTUALLY used

// add
if (size < CAPACITY) { a[size] = value; size++; }   // check capacity FIRST

// traverse — size, never a.length
for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) System.out.println(a[i]);

Two numbers now describe the array and they mean different things: a.length is capacity (how many it could hold) and size is count (how many it does). Looping to a.length walks over the unused slots and prints their defaults — zeros for numbers, null for objects.

Removing element i means shifting everything after it one place left and decrementing size; the vacated slot at the end still holds its old value, which is harmless precisely because nothing reads past size.

This is exactly how ArrayList works internally — an oversize array plus a size, reallocated to a bigger one when it fills.

📘 DEFINITION

Oversize array: an array with spare capacity plus a separate count of used elements

Capacity: the array’s physical length

Size / count: how many elements are actually in use

Unused slots: the elements beyond the count, still holding default values

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Looping to values.length instead of numValues processes the unused zeros. It is the defining bug of oversize arrays, and it makes averages wrong rather than crashing.

📊 FIGURE — capacity is not size
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Two numbers, and only one of them is the count
int[] scores = new int[10];
int numScores = 0;
scores[numScores++] = 88;
scores[numScores++] = 92;
scores[numScores++] = 75;
System.out.println(scores.length);
System.out.println(numScores);
int total = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < numScores; i++) total += scores[i];
System.out.println(total);
10 3 255
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. length is 10 — the capacity allocated.
  2. numScores is 3 — how many are real.
  3. The loop must run to numScores, never to length.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Looping to length instead
int[] scores = new int[10];
int numScores = 3;
scores[0] = 88; scores[1] = 92; scores[2] = 75;
int total = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < scores.length; i++) total += scores[i];
System.out.println(total);
System.out.printf("%.2f%n", (double) total / scores.length);
255 25.50
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The seven unused slots hold 0, the default for int.
  2. The total happens to be right, because adding 0 changes nothing.
  3. But the AVERAGE is wrong — divided by 10 instead of 3.
🎯 EXAM TIP
In any oversize-array question, find which variable holds the count and loop to that. length is the capacity and is almost never the right bound.

A method taking an oversize array needs both pieces, and the count must be a parameter because there is no way to recover it from the array.

public static int sum(int[] a, int size) {
    int total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) { total += a[i]; }   // size, not a.length
    return total;
}

// adding an element returns the NEW count, because an int parameter
// cannot be changed for the caller (6.8)
public static int add(int[] a, int size, int value) {
    if (size < a.length) { a[size] = value; size++; }
    return size;
}

numValues = add(values, numValues, 42);       // caller must reassign

That return-the-new-count idiom exists precisely because of pass by value. The array contents change through the shared reference (6.10), but the count is an int and cannot be updated in place — so it comes back as the return value and the caller stores it.

static void print(int[] a, int size) {          // BOTH pieces
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) System.out.println(a[i]);
}

static int add(int[] a, int size, int value) {  // returns the NEW size
    if (size < a.length) { a[size] = value; size++; }
    return size;
}

size = add(a, size, 42);                        // caller must reassign

The count must be a parameter because it cannot be recovered from the array — the unused slots hold defaults that are indistinguishable from real data.

And the new count must be returned, because size is an int and Java passes it by value: incrementing it inside the method changes only the copy. The array's contents do change, since the reference is shared — so forgetting size = at the call gives you an array that quietly grows while the count says otherwise.

Needing two things kept in step, in every signature, is the argument for wrapping them in one object — which is Unit 7, and what ArrayList already does.

📘 DEFINITION

int[] a = new int[8];
a[0] = 5; a[1] = 6; a[2] = 7;
int n = 3;
System.out.println(sum(a, n));
System.out.println(sum(a, a.length));

  2. Passing it gives the right answer.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A method that appends returns the new size
int[] a = new int[5];
int n = 0;
n = add(a, n, 10);
n = add(a, n, 20);
System.out.println(n + " " + a[0] + " " + a[1]);

Choosing between the two array designs comes down to one question: is the number of elements known before the array is created?

                  PERFECT SIZE              OVERSIZE
length            equals the data           larger than the data
extra tracking    none                      a separate count
loop bound        arr.length                numValues
enhanced for      safe                      UNSAFE — reads unused slots
add elements      impossible                yes, up to capacity
wasted memory     none                      capacity minus count

Perfect size is simpler and should be the default. Oversize buys the ability to grow, and pays for it with a second variable that has to be kept correct in every method it passes through. ArrayList (7.14) is the resolution: it hides the capacity and keeps the count itself.

Perfect sizeOversize
Element counta.lengtha separate size variable
Loop bounda.lengthsize
Addingnot possible — length is fixedwrite at size, then size++
Memoryexactwastes the unused capacity
Passing to a methodthe array alonethe array and the count
Main risknone of this kindthe two falling out of step

The deciding question is whether the count is known before the array is created. Known → perfect size, and prefer it. Not known, or the collection must grow → oversize.

ArrayList is the oversize design with the bookkeeping hidden: it stores an array plus a size, exposes size(), and allocates a larger array and copies when the old one fills.

📘 DEFINITION

Trade-off: simplicity and safety versus the ability to grow

Wasted capacity: allocated slots that hold no data

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

This comparison is why ArrayList feels like a relief when you meet it. It is an oversize array that manages its own count, which removes the entire class of bugs described in 6.16.

📊 FIGURE — choosing between them
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The same total, two shapes
int[] perfect = {4, 9, 2};
int t1 = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < perfect.length; i++) t1 += perfect[i];

int[] over = new int[10];
over[0] = 4; over[1] = 9; over[2] = 2;
int n = 3, t2 = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) t2 += over[i];

System.out.println(t1 + " " + t2);
15 15
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The perfect size array bounds its loop with length.
  2. The oversize array bounds its loop with the count.
  3. Both give 15 — the difference is which bound is correct.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Where they diverge
int[] over = new int[10];
over[0] = 4; over[1] = 9; over[2] = 2;
int n = 3;
System.out.printf("%.2f%n", (double)(4+9+2) / n);
System.out.printf("%.2f%n", (double)(4+9+2) / over.length);
5.00 1.50
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Dividing by the count gives the true average.
  2. Dividing by the capacity silently dilutes it with empty slots.
  3. Sums hide the mistake; averages expose it.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Using a.length on an oversize array. It is the capacity, so every average, percentage and "how many" comes out wrong while the sums still look fine.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Ask one question of any array in an exam: is every slot real data? If yes, use length. If not, there is a count variable and you must use that.

Once objects arrive in Unit 7, the rules of 6.10 apply to them unchanged, because an object variable is a reference just as an array variable is.

public static void giveRaise(Employee e) {
    e.setSalary(e.getSalary() * 1.1);    // caller SEES this — same object
}

public static void replace(Employee e) {
    e = new Employee("New");             // caller does NOT see this
}

So a method can change the state of an object it is given, but cannot make the caller’s variable refer to a different object. The one exception in the whole language is immutable types — a method cannot change a String at all (3.14), because nothing can.

An object variable holds a reference, exactly as an array variable does, so every rule from 6.10 carries over unchanged.

static void rename(Student s) { s.setName("Ana"); }   // caller SEES it
static void swap(Student s)   { s = new Student("Bo"); } // caller sees nothing

A method can change the state of an object it is handed, but cannot change which object the caller's variable refers to. That is the single sentence that answers most pass-by-value exam questions.

A reference may also be null, meaning it points at no object. Calling any method on it throws NullPointerException — the most common runtime failure in Java, and the reason a method that may receive null should say so or guard for it.

📘 DEFINITION

Reference parameter: a parameter holding a copy of a reference to an object

Mutation: changing an object’s internal state through its methods

Immutable object: one whose state cannot change after construction, e.g. String

🎯 EXAM TIP

If a method is supposed to hand back a different object, it must return it. Reassigning the parameter is the standard non-working attempt.

✅ Also covered in depth: Concepts Made Clear → Pass-by-value

📊 FIGURE — WHAT A METHOD CAN AND CANNOT CHANGE
🎯 EXAM TIP
Reassigning the parameter itself (nums = new int[5]) never affects the caller — you bent your copy of the arrow, not theirs. Changing what the arrow points AT (nums[0] = 99) does.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — One array, two names
int[] xs = {1, 2, 3};
int[] alias = xs;
bump(xs);
System.out.println(alias[0] + "," + alias[1] + "," + alias[2]);
2,3,4
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. alias and xs refer to the same array.
  2. The method changes the elements through its own copy of the reference.
  3. Every name pointing at that array sees the change.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Copying the reference is not copying the array
int[] a = {1, 2, 3};
int[] shallow = a;
int[] real = a.clone();
a[0] = 99;
System.out.println(shallow[0]);
System.out.println(real[0]);
99 1
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. shallow = a copies only the reference — one array, two names.
  2. a.clone() allocates a second array and copies the contents.
  3. Changing the original moves the alias and leaves the clone alone.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Writing int[] copy = original; and expecting an independent copy. It is the same array under a second name; use clone() or Arrays.copyOf for a real copy.

A method can return an array, which is the way around the "cannot reassign a parameter" limit: build a new array inside and hand back the reference.

public static int[] doubled(int[] a) {
    int[] result = new int[a.length];      // a NEW array
    for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) { result[i] = a[i] * 2; }
    return result;                          // the reference is returned
}

int[] b = doubled(a);      // a is untouched; b is the new array

Returning a new array leaves the input untouched, which is usually what a caller expects. The alternative — modifying in place and returning void — is also valid, but the two must not be mixed: a method that both modifies its argument and returns an array is the kind that gets used wrongly.

static int[] doubled(int[] a) {
    int[] out = new int[a.length];      // new array, input untouched
    for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) out[i] = a[i] * 2;
    return out;                          // the reference survives the call
}

Returning an array is the way around "you cannot reassign a parameter": build a new one inside and hand back the reference. The local variable out disappears when the frame is destroyed, but the array it pointed at does not — objects live on the heap, and the returned reference keeps it alive.

For a filter, the length is not known until you have counted, so the usual shape is two passes — count the matches, allocate exactly that many, then fill. The alternative is an oversize array plus Arrays.copyOf(out, n) at the end.

Return an empty array rather than null for "no results". An empty array loops zero times and needs no special case; null forces every caller to remember a check.

📘 DEFINITION

Array return type: declared as Type[]; returns a reference to an array

New array vs in-place: building a fresh result versus modifying the argument

Local array lifetime: an array created in a method survives the return, because the reference is returned; only the local variable disappears

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

The returned array survives the method’s stack frame because arrays live on the heap (8.3). Only the local variable naming it disappears when the frame is popped.

📊 FIGURE — returning an array
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Building and returning a new array
int[] in = {1, 2, 3};
int[] result = doubled(in);
System.out.println(result[0] + "," + result[1] + "," + result[2]);
System.out.println(in[0] + "," + in[1] + "," + in[2]);
2,4,6 1,2,3
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. A fresh array is allocated inside the method.
  2. Returning it hands back the reference — the object is not destroyed with the frame.
  3. The input is untouched, because a new array was built rather than edited.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Returning the argument instead of a copy
int[] in = {1, 2, 3};
int[] out = doubleInPlace(in);
out[0] = 100;
System.out.println(in[0] + "," + in[1] + "," + in[2]);
100,4,6
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. This version edits the caller's array and returns the same reference.
  2. So in and out are one array.
  3. Changing out changes in — rarely what the caller expects.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Thinking an array created inside a method is destroyed when it returns. The local VARIABLE goes away; the array object survives as long as something still references it.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Decide deliberately whether a method should return a NEW array or modify the one it was given, and make the name say which — doubled against doubleInPlace.

Null is the one worth guarding: an array parameter can legitimately be null, which is a different state from an array of length 0. if (a == null || a.length == 0) covers both, and the order matters because of short-circuiting (3.19).

b = a expecting a copyboth names share one array — silent
a == b to compare contentscompares references — silent, usually false

Javadoc turns a structured comment into browsable documentation, and it is how every method in the standard library you have used since Unit 1 is described.

/**
 * Returns the average of three test scores.
 *
 * @param a the first score
 * @param b the second score
 * @param c the third score
 * @return  the arithmetic mean as a double
 */
public static double average(int a, int b, int c) {
    return (a + b + c) / 3.0;
}

The tags are the point: @param once per parameter, @return for the result, @throws for each exception it can raise. The habit worth taking from this is the same one 2.19 asked for — read the contract before calling something, and write the contract before someone calls yours.

/**
 * Returns the average of the values.
 * @param a the values; must not be null
 * @return the mean, or 0 if the array is empty
 */
public static double average(int[] a) { ... }

A Javadoc comment starts /** and sits immediately above what it documents. @param describes each argument and @return the result; together they state the method's contract — what it expects and what it guarantees — which is where the guards of 6.13 come from.

Read the official API the same way: the signature tells you the types, the description tells you the contract, and the "Throws" section tells you what it does with bad input. String.substring(int, int) is the standard example — the second index is exclusive, and only the documentation says so.

📘 DEFINITION

Javadoc: a /** */ comment processed into API documentation

@param: documents one parameter

@return: documents the returned value

@throws: documents an exception the method may throw

🎯 EXAM TIP

A Javadoc comment must sit immediately above the method with no blank line between. Placed anywhere else it is just an ordinary comment.

📊 FIGURE — reading a Javadoc entry
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Writing a Javadoc comment

System.out.println(larger(-2, -7));

actual output, captured from the JVM

  2. @param describes each input and @return the output.
  3. Tools and IDEs read these to show help at the call site.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Using the signature to predict the type
System.out.println(Math.max(3, 7));
System.out.println(Math.max(3.0, 7));
System.out.println(String.valueOf(42).length());

The salary program returns for the third time, and the difference now is structural: the calculation that was inline in 3.20 and looped in 4.12 becomes two named methods that can be tested on their own.

public static double taxRate(double salary) {
    if (salary >= 100000) { return 0.28; }
    if (salary >=  50000) { return 0.22; }
    if (salary >=  25000) { return 0.15; }
    return 0.10;
}

public static double netPay(double salary) {
    return salary * (1 - taxRate(salary));
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    System.out.println(taxRate(60000) == 0.22);      // testable (6.7)
    System.out.printf("%.2f%n", netPay(60000));
}

Note the guard-clause style from 6.5: each return ends the method, so no else is needed and the ordering rule of 3.4 still applies unchanged — highest bracket first.

📘 DEFINITION

Extracted method: logic pulled out of a larger routine into its own named method

Composition: one method calling another to build a larger result

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

This is the shape of every well-organised program you will write: main reads input and prints, and the real work happens in small methods that take values and return values.

📊 FIGURE — one method per idea
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Splitting the salary program into methods
double annual = 55000;
System.out.printf("%.2f%n", monthly(annual));
System.out.printf("%.2f%n", withRaise(annual, 4));
System.out.printf("%.2f%n", monthly(withRaise(annual, 4)));
4583.33 57200.00 4766.67
actual output, captured from the JVM

  2. Because they return rather than print, they compose.
  3. The last line reads as "the monthly value of the raised salary".

System.out.println(monthlyBad(55000));
System.out.println(monthlyGood(55000));
4583.0 4583.333333333333

Domain validation, done for the third time, becomes a set of small predicates — and the improvement is that each rule can now be tested in isolation.

public static boolean hasValidChars(String d) {
    for (int i = 0; i < d.length(); i++) {
        char c = d.charAt(i);
        if (!Character.isLetterOrDigit(c) && c != '.' && c != '-') { return false; }
    }
    return true;                        // only if the loop finished
}

public static boolean isValidDomain(String d) {
    return d != null
        && d.length() >= 3
        && d.contains(".")
        && hasValidChars(d);            // short-circuits (3.19) in order
}

The return false inside the loop replaces the flag of 4.13 entirely — it is an early exit that cannot be accidentally overwritten. And the null check leads the chain deliberately, so the later calls are safe.

📘 DEFINITION

Predicate composition: building a complex test from small boolean methods joined by &&

Return-false-early: exiting the moment a rule is broken, instead of tracking a flag

🎯 EXAM TIP

Ordering the conditions in isValidDomain is not cosmetic. d != null must come first or every other test can throw, and the cheap checks before the loop avoid scanning strings that were already disqualified.

📊 FIGURE — validation returns a boolean
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A validator built from small checks
System.out.println(isValidDomain("wgu.edu"));
System.out.println(isValidDomain("nodot"));
System.out.println(isValidDomain(".leading.com"));
System.out.println(isValidDomain(""));
true false false false
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Each rule is one early return, so the method reads as a checklist.
  2. The null and empty test comes FIRST, before any method is called on d.
  3. The caller receives a boolean and decides what to say about it.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Why the order of the checks matters
System.out.println(safeCheck("wgu.edu"));
System.out.println(safeCheck(null));
true false
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. d != null is tested first.
  2. Because && short-circuits, d.length() never runs when d is null.
  3. Reversing the two would throw a NullPointerException.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Calling a method on the string before checking it for null. d.isEmpty() || d == null throws on null — the null test has to come first, and && short-circuiting is what makes that work.

Unit 5 left an unsolved problem: parallel arrays keep a student’s name and score in two places, and nothing stops them drifting apart. An object is the fix — one thing that holds its own data and the methods that operate on it.

// before: two arrays that must be kept in step
String[] names;  int[] scores;

// after: one object per student, name and score inseparable
Student s = new Student("Ada", 95);
s.getName();  s.getScore();

A class is the blueprint; an object is one thing built from it. The class is written once and describes what every instance will have; each object gets its own copy of the fields, so a thousand Students have a thousand names and one class definition.

The four pillars, named

Object-oriented programming is conventionally summarised as four principles, and questions ask you to name the one a scenario describes.

PillarMeansIn this course
Encapsulationdata kept private, reached only through methods7.3, 7.4
Abstractionexpose what it does, hide how7.4, and abstract classes in 10.7
Inheritancea class takes on another's fields and methods10.1
Polymorphismone reference type, many actual behaviours10.5

Encapsulation and abstraction are the pair most often confused, because both involve hiding. Encapsulation hides data so the rules can be enforced in one place; abstraction hides complexity so a caller need not understand the internals. A locked bonnet is encapsulation; the steering wheel is abstraction.

A class is the description; an object is a thing built from it. One class, any number of objects, each with its own copy of the fields — which is the entire reason parallel arrays (5.5) stop being necessary.

Student a = new Student("Ana", 88);
Student b = new Student("Ben", 71);
// one Student class, two objects, two separate name/score pairs
Instance memberStatic member
belongs toeach objectthe class itself
one copyper objectshared by all objects
called ona.getName()Math.max(...)
can use thisyesno — there is no object

this is a reference to the object the method was called on. A static method is not called on an object, so this has nothing to refer to and using it is a compile error — which is also why a static method cannot read an instance field directly.

📘 DEFINITION

Class: a blueprint describing the fields and methods its objects will have

Object / instance: one concrete thing created from a class

Field / instance variable: a variable belonging to each object

Encapsulation: keeping data private and exposing it only through methods

Instantiation: creating an object with new

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

Everything after this unit assumes objects. Inheritance (Unit 10), exceptions (Unit 12) and every collection in Unit 14 are classes; even a String has been an object since Unit 1.

✅ Also covered in depth: OOP → Classes, Objects, and Constructors

Counter a = new Counter();
Counter b = new Counter();
a.bump(); a.bump(); b.bump();
System.out.println(a.count + " " + b.count);
2 1
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. new builds a separate object each time.
  2. Each object carries its own copy of the fields.
  3. Changing one leaves the other alone — that separation is the point of objects.

Rect r = new Rect(3, 4);
System.out.println(r.area());
r.w = 10;
System.out.println(r.area());
12.0 40.0

Treating a class as if it were an object. Counter.count does not exist — count belongs to each instance, so it is reached through a variable such as a.count.

You have been using classes since Unit 1 without naming it. Scanner, String, Math and Random are all classes, and using one always follows the same three-step shape.

import java.util.Scanner;                 // 1. make the name available

Scanner scnr = new Scanner(System.in);    // 2. create an instance
int n = scnr.nextInt();                   // 3. call methods on it

Math breaks the pattern deliberately, and the reason is worth noticing: its methods are static, so they belong to the class rather than to any instance. Math.sqrt(9) needs no object, and in fact you cannot create a Math.

Math.sqrt(16)      // static — called on the CLASS
scnr.nextInt()     // instance — called on an OBJECT
Scanner scnr = new Scanner(System.in);
//  |         |       |
//  |         |       +-- constructor call: builds the object
//  |         +---------- the variable name
//  +-------------------- the reference type

scnr.nextInt();          // instance method — needs an object
Math.max(3, 7);          // static method — called on the CLASS

new does two things: it allocates the object and runs the constructor. The variable does not hold the object, it holds a reference to it — so Scanner s2 = scnr; gives a second name for one Scanner, not a second Scanner.

Classes outside java.lang need an import — java.util.Scanner, java.util.ArrayList. String, Math and System are in java.lang, which is imported automatically, which is why they never need one.

📘 DEFINITION

import: makes a class from another package usable by its short name

new: allocates an object and runs its constructor

Defining a class means listing what each object holds and what it can do. Fields go at the top, methods below, and the fields are private by default choice rather than by language rule.

public class Student {
    private String name;          // FIELDS — one copy per object
    private int score;

    public Student(String n, int s) {      // CONSTRUCTOR — same name, no return type
        name = n;
        score = s;
    }

    public String getName()  { return name; }        // ACCESSOR
    public void setScore(int s) { score = s; }       // MUTATOR
}

Fields are private so that outside code cannot reach in and set a score to -400. Everything that changes the object goes through a method, and that method is where the rule lives. That is encapsulation, and it is the whole argument of 7.4.

public class Student {          // file MUST be Student.java
    private String name;        // field — one per object
    private int score;          // private: reachable only inside this class

    public Student(String name, int score) {   // constructor
        this.name = name;
        this.score = score;
    }
    public String getName() { return name; }   // instance method
}

Fields declared but not assigned get the same defaults as array elements — 0, false, null — unlike local variables, which must be assigned before use. That difference catches people: a field silently holds null, a local refuses to compile.

A public class must live in a file of exactly its own name, and only one class per file may be public. A class needs no main — Student is a type to be used by other code, not a program to run.

Convention: class names are PascalCase nouns; fields and methods are camelCase.

📘 DEFINITION

public: accessible from anywhere

private: accessible only from inside this class

Constructor: a special method with the class name and no return type, run by new

Instance variable: a field; each object has its own, and it gets a type default (2.2)

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

A constructor has no return type, not even void. Writing public void Student(...) makes it an ordinary method that happens to share the class name, so new Student(...) stops finding it — and the error is confusing.

✅ Also covered in depth: OOP → Classes, Objects, and Constructors

📊 FIGURE — what goes inside a class
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A complete small class
Student s = new Student("Priya", 15);
System.out.println(s.getName());
System.out.println(s.isFullTime());
Student p = new Student("Sam", 6);
System.out.println(p.isFullTime());
Priya true false
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Fields are private, so nothing outside can set them directly.
  2. The constructor fills them once, at creation.
  3. The public methods are the only way in — that is encapsulation.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Fields get default values if the constructor does not set them
Box b = new Box();
System.out.println(b.n);
System.out.println(b.label);
System.out.println(b.ready);
0 null false
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Unlike local variables, FIELDS are initialised automatically.
  2. Numbers default to 0, booleans to false, references to null.
  3. That null default is where many NullPointerExceptions begin.
🎯 EXAM TIP
The standard shape is private fields plus public methods. If a question offers a class with public fields, that is usually the wrong answer — it breaks encapsulation.

Three kinds of method make up the public face of a class, and naming them the way the exam does saves confusion later.

// ACCESSOR (getter) — reports state, changes nothing
public int getScore() { return score; }

// MUTATOR (setter) — changes state, usually returns void
public void setScore(int s) {
    if (s >= 0 && s <= 100) { score = s; }     // the RULE lives here
}

// PRIVATE HELPER — internal, not part of the public interface
private boolean isValid(int s) { return s >= 0 && s <= 100; }

The validation inside the setter is the point of the whole design. Make the field public and there is no place to put that check; make it private and every change in the program’s lifetime passes through this one line.

Encapsulation is fields private, access through methods. The reason is not secrecy — it is that a rule enforced in one setter cannot be bypassed.

private int score;

public int getScore() { return score; }            // accessor / getter
public void setScore(int s) {                      // mutator / setter
    if (s >= 0 && s <= 100) score = s;             // the rule lives HERE
}

With score public, any line anywhere can write s.score = -5; and the object is invalid with nothing to blame. With it private, there is exactly one door and the check is on it.

ModifierVisible to
publiceverywhere
protectedthe same package, and subclasses anywhere
(none) — package-privatethe same package only
privatethe same class only — not even subclasses

A private helper is a method the class uses internally and no caller should see — it can be changed or deleted freely, because nothing outside can depend on it.

📘 DEFINITION

Accessor / getter: returns a field value without modifying state

Mutator / setter: modifies a field, usually after validating

Private helper: a method used internally and not exposed to callers

Interface (of a class): the set of public methods — what callers may rely on

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

Making every field public and dropping the getters looks simpler and removes the only place a rule can be enforced. This is the difference between a class and a bag of variables.

✅ Also covered in depth: OOP → Encapsulation and Access Modifiers

📊 FIGURE — three kinds of method
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A getter, a setter, and validation between them
Thermostat t = new Thermostat();
t.setTarget(21);
System.out.println(t.getTarget());
t.setTarget(99);
System.out.println(t.getTarget());
21 rejected 99 21
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The getter simply reports the state.
  2. The setter is where the rule lives, so no caller can bypass it.
  3. The rejected value leaves the object unchanged.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A private helper the outside never sees
Invoice i = new Invoice(100);
System.out.printf("%.2f%n", i.total());
120.00
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. vat() is an implementation detail, so it is private.
  2. total() is the public interface.
  3. Calling i.vat() from outside would not compile.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Making fields public "to save writing getters". Anything can then assign an invalid value directly, and the validation in the setter is bypassed entirely.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Accessor returns and does not change; mutator changes and returns void. If a question asks which method is the mutator, look for the one with a void return type and a parameter.

A constructor runs once, at new, and its job is to leave the object in a valid state. If you write none, Java supplies a no-argument default that leaves every field at its type default (2.2) — and the moment you write any constructor, that free one disappears.

public class Student {
    private String name;
    private int score;

    public Student() {                    // no-arg
        name = "unknown";
        score = 0;
    }

    public Student(String n, int s) {     // parameterised
        name = n;
        setScore(s);                      // reuse the validation from the setter
    }
}

Student a = new Student();                // needs the no-arg constructor
Student b = new Student("Ada", 95);

Calling setScore from the constructor rather than assigning the field directly means the validation rule exists in exactly one place. That habit is worth adopting as a default.

A constructor runs once, when new builds the object, and its job is to leave the object in a valid state. It has the class's exact name and no return type — not even void. Writing void Student(...) makes it an ordinary method that never runs at construction, which is a favourite exam trap.

public class Student {
    private String name;
    public Student() { this("unknown"); }        // must be the FIRST statement
    public Student(String name) { this.name = name; }
}

If you write no constructor, Java supplies a no-argument default that leaves fields at their defaults. The moment you write any constructor, that free one disappears — so adding Student(String) makes new Student() stop compiling until you write it yourself.

this(...) calls another constructor of the same class and must be the first statement, so the object is fully set up once rather than in overlapping halves.

📘 DEFINITION

Default constructor: the no-argument constructor Java provides only when you define none

Parameterised constructor: one taking arguments to initialise fields

Initialisation: putting the object into a usable state before anyone can call its methods

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Defining only Student(String, int) and then calling new Student() is a compile error — the free default is gone. If you need both, write both (7.9).

✅ Also covered in depth: OOP → Classes, Objects, and Constructors

📊 FIGURE — what a constructor is
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The constructor runs once, at creation
Account a = new Account("Ada", 250.0);
System.out.println(a.getBalance());
created for Ada 250.0
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The constructor is called by new, not by you.
  2. It has no return type — writing void would make it an ordinary method.
  3. By the time new finishes, the object is fully set up.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Writing a constructor removes the free one
Widget w = new Widget(5);
System.out.println(w.size);
5
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Java supplies a no-argument constructor only when you write none.
  2. This class defines one that takes an int, so the free one is gone.
  3. new Widget() would now be a compile error.
🎯 EXAM TIP
A "constructor" with a return type is not a constructor — it is a method that merely shares the class's name, and new will not call it. That trick appears in exam code.

Deciding what should be a class is design rather than syntax, and the reliable test is a grammatical one: nouns in the problem description tend to be classes, verbs tend to be methods, and adjectives tend to be fields.

"A library lends books to members. Each book has a title and an ISBN.
 A member can borrow up to five books."

nouns      -> Library, Book, Member          (classes)
adjectives -> title, isbn, borrowedCount     (fields)
verbs      -> lend(), borrow(), returnBook() (methods)

The signal to watch for is the one from 5.5: whenever two arrays must be kept in step, or a value must always travel with a count (6.16), that pairing is a class waiting to be written. A class is exactly a set of things that belong together.

Two questions identify a class worth creating: which values always travel together, and what does the program do to them. The first gives the fields, the second gives the methods.

SignWhat it suggests
parallel arrays kept in step by handthose items are one class
the same three arguments passed to many methodsthey belong in one object
a class with data and no behaviourfine as a record, but look for the logic acting on it
a class that would need "and" to describesplit it — one job each

A noun in the problem statement is a candidate class; a verb is a candidate method. Student, Domain, Employee are classes; calculatePay, isAvailable, register are their methods.

Not everything deserves a class. A single value with no rules attached is a variable, and a method used once by one caller is a method — creating a class for either adds ceremony without buying anything.

📘 DEFINITION

Class identification: finding the entities in a problem that own their own data

Responsibility: what one class is accountable for; a class should have one

Has-a relationship: a class holding another class as a field — see 10.9

🎯 EXAM TIP

If a class has one field and one method, it is probably not a class. If it has fifteen fields covering three unrelated ideas, it is probably three classes.

📊 FIGURE — what deserves a class
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Splitting one blob into two classes
Product bike = new Product("Bike");
bike.parts.add(new Part("Wheel", 40));
bike.parts.add(new Part("Frame", 120));
System.out.println(bike.parts.size());
System.out.printf("%.2f%n", bike.cost());
2 160.00
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Each noun in the problem became a class.
  2. Each class holds the data that belongs to it.
  3. The cost calculation lives with Product, because that is whose question it answers.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — One responsibility per class
Temperature t = new Temperature(-4);
System.out.println(t.toFahrenheit());
System.out.println(t.isFreezing());
24.8 true
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Everything here is about one temperature.
  2. Printing, saving to a file or reading input would be someone else's job.
  3. A class that does one thing is the one you can test.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Creating a class for a verb — a Calculator that only holds methods and no state is usually a sign the behaviour belongs on the data it operates on.

main is an ordinary static method that the JVM happens to call first, and it can live in any class — including the class it is testing. That is convenient during development and is why the pattern appears throughout this unit.

public class Student {
    private String name;
    public Student(String n) { name = n; }
    public String getName() { return name; }

    public static void main(String[] args) {       // test driver
        Student s = new Student("Ada");
        System.out.println(s.getName().equals("Ada"));
    }
}

Because main is static, it has no object, so it cannot touch name directly — it must create a Student first. That restriction is not arbitrary: a static method exists before any object does, so there is no this for it to read from (7.19).

public class Calc {
    public static int square(int n) { return n * n; }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(square(4));       // static -> static: fine
        Calc c = new Calc();
        System.out.println(c.hashCode());    // instance member needs an object
    }
}

main is static because it must run before any object exists — the JVM has nothing to call it on. Everything main touches directly must therefore also be static, or reached through an object it creates first.

"Non-static method cannot be referenced from a static context" is that rule being enforced: the method needs an object, and main has not made one. From another class, a static method is called on the class — Calc.square(4).

📘 DEFINITION

Test driver: a main method written to exercise a class

static context: code with no associated object, so instance fields are unreachable

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

"Non-static variable cannot be referenced from a static context" always means the same thing: you used an instance field inside main without creating an object. Create the object, or make the field static.

📊 FIGURE — the signature that starts a program
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Why main must be static
Greeter g = new Greeter();
g.hello();
hello
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. main runs before any object exists.
  2. A non-static method needs an object to be called on, so main could never start.
  3. That is why main creates the first objects itself, as here.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Reading the command-line arguments
String[] args = {"alpha", "beta"};
System.out.println(args.length);
for (String a : args) System.out.println(a);
2 alpha beta
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. args is an ordinary array of Strings.
  2. Its length is the number of arguments supplied.
  3. Running with none gives an array of length 0, not null.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Any change to the signature — dropping static, renaming it Main, returning int — compiles fine and then fails at launch with "main method not found".

Testing a class means testing it through its public methods — create an object, drive it into a state, check the state came out right. The edge cases from 6.7 apply unchanged, plus one new category: invalid input that the setter is supposed to reject.

Student s = new Student("Ada", 95);

System.out.println(s.getScore() == 95);      // constructor worked

s.setScore(80);
System.out.println(s.getScore() == 80);      // setter worked

s.setScore(-5);
System.out.println(s.getScore() == 80);      // rejected, state UNCHANGED

That last assertion is the one people forget to write, and it is the only one that actually tests the validation. Checking that a bad value was refused matters more than checking that a good value was accepted.

Testing a class means building an object, calling methods in a realistic order, and checking the resulting state through its accessors — not just single return values.

Account a = new Account(100);
a.withdraw(30);
// expect getBalance() == 70

Account b = new Account(100);
b.withdraw(500);                 // more than the balance
// expect getBalance() == 100 and the withdrawal refused

Each test builds a fresh object. Reusing one across tests means test three depends on what tests one and two did, so a failure tells you nothing about which is broken.

The valuable tests are the ones that attack the rules the setters enforce: the overdraft, the negative score, the empty name. The constructor deserves its own test — build an object and immediately check every field came out as intended.

📘 DEFINITION

State-based testing: setting state through methods and asserting on what the accessors report

Invalid input test: confirming a bad value is rejected and the object is left unchanged

Object state: the current values of all an object’s fields

🎯 EXAM TIP

Test the constructor as carefully as the setters. If a constructor assigns fields directly and skips validation, an invalid object can be created that no setter would ever allow.

📊 FIGURE — testing an object
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Arrange, act, assert
Cart c = new Cart();
System.out.println(c.size() == 0);
c.add(3);
System.out.println(c.size() == 3);
c.add(-5);
System.out.println(c.size() == 3);
true true true
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Construct the object into a known state.
  2. Call exactly one method.
  3. Compare the result against what was specified — including that a bad input changes nothing.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A test that catches a real defect
BadCart c = new BadCart();
c.add(3);
c.add(4);
System.out.println(c.size() == 7);
System.out.println(c.size());
false 4
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. add assigns instead of accumulating.
  2. One call would have passed; two reveal it.
  3. The test prints false, which is the bug being caught.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Testing with a single call. Many state bugs — assigning instead of adding, resetting a counter — only appear on the second call.

Constructor overloading is method overloading (6.12) applied to constructors: several ways to build an object, distinguished by their parameter lists.

public class Student {
    private String name;
    private int score;

    public Student()                    { this("unknown", 0); }
    public Student(String n)            { this(n, 0); }
    public Student(String n, int s)     { name = n; setScore(s); }
    //                                     ^ the ONE that does the real work
}

this(...) calls another constructor of the same class, and it lets every version funnel into one. It must be the first statement in the constructor — that is a hard rule, because the object cannot be half-initialised by two constructors at once.

public class Rect {
    private int w, h;
    public Rect()               { this(1, 1); }        // delegates
    public Rect(int side)       { this(side, side); }  // delegates
    public Rect(int w, int h) {                        // the real one
        this.w = w; this.h = h;
    }
}

Overloaded constructors differ in their parameter lists, exactly like overloaded methods. Chaining them with this(...) puts the validation and assignment in one place — add a check to the two-argument version and all three benefit.

this(...) must be the very first statement, so you cannot validate before delegating. And a constructor has no return type at all, so public void Rect() is not a constructor — it is a method that happens to share the class's name and will never run at construction.

📘 DEFINITION

Constructor overloading: multiple constructors distinguished by parameter list

this(...): calls another constructor of the same class; must be the first statement

Telescoping constructors: a chain of constructors each supplying more defaults to the next

🎯 EXAM TIP

this(...) chains to a constructor in the same class; super(...) chains to the parent’s (10.1). Both must be first, so a constructor can use one or the other, never both.

✅ Also covered in depth: OOP → Classes, Objects, and Constructors

📊 FIGURE — several ways to build one object
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Three constructors, one class
System.out.println(new Pizza());
System.out.println(new Pizza("large"));
System.out.println(new Pizza("small", "olive"));
medium/cheese large/cheese small/olive
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The argument list decides which constructor runs.
  2. this(...) chains to another constructor so the real work is written once.
  3. A chained this(...) call must be the FIRST statement.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The default disappears once you write one
Ticket t = new Ticket(12);
System.out.println(t.row);
12
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Java gives a free no-argument constructor only when a class defines none.
  2. This class defines one, so the free one is gone.
  3. Add Ticket() { } explicitly if you still want it.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Expecting new Thing() to work after adding a constructor that takes parameters. The compiler-supplied no-argument constructor vanishes the moment you write any constructor of your own.

An object variable does not hold the object. It holds a reference — the address of an object living on the heap — and every confusing behaviour in this area follows from that one fact.

Student a = new Student("Ada", 95);
Student b = a;                    // b points at the SAME object

b.setScore(50);
a.getScore();                     // 50 — there was only ever one object

Student c = new Student("Ada", 95);
a == c                            // false — different objects
a.equals(c)                       // false too, unless Student overrides equals (10.4)

This is the same rule as arrays in 5.7 and Strings in 3.2, and now the reason is visible: the variable is a reference in all three cases. null is the reference that points at nothing, and calling a method on it is the NullPointerException of 6.21.

Student a = new Student("Ana");
Student b = a;               // same object, two names
b.setName("Bo");
a.getName();                 // "Bo"

Student c = new Student("Bo");
a == c                       // false — different objects
a.equals(c)                  // false too, unless Student overrides equals

== on objects asks "the same object?", never "the same contents?". equals asks about contents — but only if the class defines it. The inherited default compares references, so it behaves identically to == until you override it.

null means the variable refers to no object. Calling anything on it throws NullPointerException, and the message names the method you tried to call, which is usually enough to find it.

toString() is what System.out.println(obj) calls. Without an override you get Student@1b6d — the class name and a hash — which is the giveaway that the class has not defined one.

📘 DEFINITION

Reference: a value identifying an object’s location; what an object variable actually stores

null: a reference pointing at no object; the default for uninitialised object fields

Aliasing: two references to one object

Shallow copy: copying the reference rather than the object

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

== on objects asks "same object", not "same contents". Two Students with identical fields are not equal by ==, and will not be equal by .equals() either until you write an equals method (10.4).

✅ Also covered in depth: OOP → Classes, Objects, and Constructors

📊 FIGURE — TWO REFERENCES, ONE OBJECT
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
== on objects compares arrows (same object?), .equals() compares contents. Two different String objects with the same letters: equals true, == false.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Two names, one object
Dog a = new Dog("Rex");
Dog b = a;
b.name = "Bella";
System.out.println(a.name);
System.out.println(a == b);
Bella true
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. b = a copies the REFERENCE, not the object.
  2. Both names point at one Dog, so changing through b is visible through a.
  3. == is true because they are literally the same object.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — == compares identity, equals compares content
String a = new String("hi");
String b = new String("hi");
System.out.println(a == b);
System.out.println(a.equals(b));
String c = a;
System.out.println(a == c);
false true true
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Two separately constructed objects are different objects, so == is false.
  2. equals compares the characters, so it is true.
  3. Only an assignment of the reference itself makes == true.
🎯 EXAM TIP
For objects, == asks "the same object?" and .equals() asks "the same value?". Unless a class overrides equals, the two mean the same thing — which is why comparing your own objects usually needs an override.

Inside an instance method, this is a reference to the object the method was called on. It is normally invisible — score and this.score mean the same thing — and it becomes necessary in exactly one common situation.

public class Student {
    private String name;

    public Student(String name) {       // parameter SHADOWS the field (6.11)
        this.name = name;               // this.name = the field, name = the parameter
    }

    public void copyFrom(Student other) {
        this.name = other.name;         // private is per CLASS, not per object
    }
}

Note the second method: a class can read the private fields of another object of the same class, because private restricts access by class, not by instance. That surprises people and it is a legitimate exam question.

public void setName(String name) {
    name = name;              // assigns the parameter to itself — field unchanged
    this.name = name;         // field  =  parameter
}

When a parameter shares a field's name it shadows it: the bare name means the parameter for the rest of the method. this.name reaches past the shadow to the field. The self-assignment version compiles and silently does nothing, which is why it is the standard exam question.

this is an implicit parameter every instance method receives — a reference to the object it was called on. a.setName("Bo") passes a as this. That is precisely why a static method cannot use it.

Its other uses: this(...) to chain constructors, and passing this as an argument when an object needs to hand itself to something else.

📘 DEFINITION

this: a reference to the object the current instance method was invoked on

Implicit parameter: the object before the dot in a call; passed invisibly as this

Shadowing resolution: using this.field to reach a field hidden by a parameter of the same name

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Writing name = name; in a constructor whose parameter is also called name assigns the parameter to itself. It compiles, it does nothing, and the field stays null.

✅ Also covered in depth: OOP → Classes, Objects, and Constructors

📊 FIGURE — this = the object the method was called on
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — this separates the field from the parameter
System.out.println(new Point(3, 7));
3,7
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The parameter x hides the field x inside the constructor.
  2. this.x is unambiguous — the field of this object.
  3. Writing x = x would assign the parameter to itself and leave the field at 0.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Forgetting this
Broken b = new Broken(42);
System.out.println(b.get());
0
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. size = size assigns the parameter to itself.
  2. The field is never touched, so it keeps its default of 0.
  3. It compiles and runs — the output is simply wrong.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Any constructor whose parameters share their names with the fields needs this. on the left of every assignment. Its absence is a silent zero, not an error.
