Java’s types split cleanly in two, and almost every "why did that happen" in this unit is answered by which side a type is on.

PRIMITIVE                      REFERENCE
int, double, char, boolean     String, arrays, Scanner, your classes
byte, short, long, float

holds the value itself         holds an address
stored in the stack frame      object lives on the heap (8.3)
== compares values             == compares identity
no methods                     has methods
cannot be null                 can be null
default 0/false                default null

There are exactly eight primitives and everything else is a reference type. That is worth memorising as a list, because a question asking "which of these is a primitive" is testing whether String is on the list. It is not.

PrimitiveReference
Examplesint, double, char, boolean, longString, arrays, Scanner, your classes
Holdsthe value itselfthe address of an object
Default0, 0.0, falsenull
== comparesthe valuesthe references
Can be nullnoyes
Has methodsnoyes

Java has exactly eight primitives — byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, boolean — and everything else is a reference type. String looks primitive because of literals and +, but it is a class: it has methods, it can be null, and == on two Strings compares references.

This one distinction explains pass-by-value (6.8), == versus equals, why arrays copy by reference, and why generics such as ArrayList<int> are illegal.

📘 DEFINITION

Primitive type: one of the eight built-in value types

Reference type: any class, interface or array type

Heap: where objects live; survives the method that created them

Stack: where locals and parameters live; discarded when the method returns

🎯 EXAM TIP

Every rule about ==, null, defaults and parameter passing in this course follows from this table. When a question puzzles you, work out which column the type is in first.

✅ Also covered in depth: Concepts Made Clear → Pass-by-value

📊 FIGURE — what the variable holds
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Assignment copies different things
int a = 5;
int b = a;
b = 9;
System.out.println(a);

Bag x = new Bag();
x.n = 5;
Bag y = x;
y.n = 9;
System.out.println(x.n);
5 9
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. For a primitive, the VALUE is copied — the two are independent.
  2. For an object, the REFERENCE is copied — both names reach one object.
  3. That single difference explains most surprises in this unit.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Only reference types can be null
String s = null;
System.out.println(s);
int i = 0;
System.out.println(i);
null 0
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. null means "references nothing".
  2. A primitive always holds a value, so it can never be null.
  3. int i = null; would not compile.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Calling .equals() or any method on a reference that is null. The variable exists, but there is no object to run the method on, so it throws at run time.

Each primitive has a matching wrapper class that turns it into an object — needed because collections such as ArrayList hold objects only, and a primitive is not one.

int    -> Integer      double -> Double      char    -> Character
boolean-> Boolean      long   -> Long        float   -> Float

Integer boxed = 5;              // AUTOBOXING     — int to Integer
int back = boxed;               // UNBOXING       — Integer to int

ArrayList list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add(5);                    // autoboxed automatically

// parsing text into numbers — the most-used wrapper methods in the course
int n = Integer.parseInt("42");
double d = Double.parseDouble("3.14");

Two traps come with wrappers. An Integer can be null, so unboxing one throws NullPointerException. And == on two Integer objects compares references — it appears to work for small values, because Java caches -128 to 127, and stops working above that.

valueOf, and how it differs from parse

Every wrapper class offers valueOf alongside parseInt, and the difference is what comes back.

int      a = Integer.parseInt("42");   // returns a PRIMITIVE int
Integer  b = Integer.valueOf("42");   // returns an Integer OBJECT
Integer  c = Integer.valueOf(42);     // also works from an int

String   s = String.valueOf(42);      // "42" — the reverse direction

valueOf also uses the wrapper cache for values from −128 to 127, which is exactly why Integer.valueOf(127) == Integer.valueOf(127) is true and the same comparison at 128 is false. new Integer(42) always allocates and so is never cached — which is one reason it is deprecated.

Every primitive has a wrapper class that holds the same value as an object — because collections and generics only accept objects.

PrimitiveWrapper
intInteger
charCharacter
doubleDouble
booleanBoolean
ArrayList<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add(5);                 // autoboxing:  int  -> Integer
int x = list.get(0);         // unboxing:    Integer -> int

int n = Integer.parseInt("42");        // String -> primitive int
Integer o = Integer.valueOf("42");     // String -> Integer OBJECT

The two irregular names are Integer and Character — not Int or Char. Autoboxing hides the conversion until something is null: unboxing a null Integer into an int throws NullPointerException, and the line looks like plain arithmetic.

📘 DEFINITION

Wrapper class: an object type wrapping a primitive value

Autoboxing: automatic conversion from primitive to wrapper

Unboxing: automatic conversion from wrapper back to primitive

parseInt / parseDouble: static methods converting a String to a number; throw NumberFormatException on bad text

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Integer a = 200, b = 200; a == b is false, while the same code with 100 is true. Always use .equals() — or better, unbox to int and compare that.

✅ Also covered in depth: Java Basics → Primitive Types and Type Casting

📊 FIGURE — every primitive has a wrapper
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Boxing, unboxing and parsing
Integer boxed = 42;
int plain = boxed;
System.out.println(boxed + 1);
System.out.println(Integer.parseInt("123") + 1);
System.out.println(Integer.valueOf("7") + 1);
System.out.println(Integer.MAX_VALUE);
43 124 8 2147483647
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Autoboxing wraps the int without you asking.
  2. Unboxing takes it back out again.
  3. parseInt returns a primitive int; valueOf returns an Integer.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Why == on Integers is dangerous
Integer a = 127, b = 127;
System.out.println(a == b);
Integer c = 128, d = 128;
System.out.println(c == d);
System.out.println(c.equals(d));
true false true
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Java caches Integer objects from −128 to 127, so a and b are the same object.
  2. Above that range new objects are created, so == compares two different objects and is false.
  3. equals compares the values and is true either way.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Compare wrapper objects with .equals(), never ==. The cache makes == appear to work for small numbers, which is exactly what makes the bug so hard to find.

ArrayList is the answer to the oversize array of 6.16: a list that grows on demand and keeps its own count. It removes the entire category of bugs that came from tracking a size by hand.

import java.util.ArrayList;

ArrayList names = new ArrayList<>();

names.add("Ada");            // append
names.add(0, "Grace");       // insert at index 0
names.get(1);                // "Ada"          — NOT names[1]
names.set(1, "Alan");        // replace
names.remove(0);             // remove by index; everything after shifts down
names.size();                // count          — NOT .length or .length()
names.contains("Alan");      // true
names.isEmpty();

Three names for the same idea now exist and the exam checks you know which is which: arrays use length, Strings use length(), and lists use size(). Indexing also differs — square brackets for arrays, get and set for lists.

ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
names.add("Ana");            // append
names.add(0, "Zed");         // insert at index 0
names.get(1);                // read      — NOT names[1]
names.set(1, "Bo");          // replace
names.remove(0);             // delete and shift left
names.size();                // count     — NOT length or length()

Three different words for "how many" now exist and the exam tests all three: a.length for an array, s.length() for a String, list.size() for an ArrayList.

An ArrayList grows on demand — it is the oversize array of 6.16 with the bookkeeping hidden. It stores objects only, so ArrayList<int> is illegal and ArrayList<Integer> is the way, with autoboxing making it look seamless.

remove(int) removes by index while remove(Object) removes by value — so on an ArrayList<Integer>, remove(1) deletes position 1 and remove(Integer.valueOf(1)) deletes the value 1.

📘 DEFINITION

ArrayList: a resizable list backed by an array, from java.util

Type parameter: the <String> that says what the list holds; see Unit 13

Diamond operator: the empty <> on the right-hand side, which infers the type

size(): the number of elements currently in the list

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Removing while looping forward skips elements, because everything shifts down into the index you just processed. Loop backwards, or use an iterator, when removing.

✅ Also covered in depth: Arrays → 2D Arrays and ArrayList

📊 FIGURE — ArrayList against a plain array
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The operations you actually need
import java.util.ArrayList;
ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
names.add("Ada");
names.add("Grace");
names.add(1, "Alan");
System.out.println(names);
System.out.println(names.size());
System.out.println(names.get(0));
names.remove("Alan");
System.out.println(names.contains("Alan"));
System.out.println(names);
[Ada, Alan, Grace] 3 Ada false [Ada, Grace]
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. add appends, or inserts at an index.
  2. size() is the count — there is no .length.
  3. remove shifts everything after it down.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — It must hold objects, so ints are boxed
import java.util.ArrayList;
ArrayList<Integer> nums = new ArrayList<>();
nums.add(10);
nums.add(20);
int total = 0;
for (int n : nums) total += n;
System.out.println(total);
System.out.println(nums.get(0) + 5);
30 15
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. ArrayList<int> is illegal — generics need a reference type.
  2. ArrayList<Integer> works, and autoboxing hides the conversion.
  3. The loop unboxes each Integer back to an int.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Arrays use length and [i]; ArrayLists use size() and get(i). Mixing them up is the most common compile error in this section.

A list of your own objects is where classes and collections finally combine, and it replaces parallel arrays completely.

ArrayList roster = new ArrayList<>();
roster.add(new Student("Ada", 95));
roster.add(new Student("Alan", 88));

for (Student s : roster) {                    // enhanced for (5.10)
    System.out.println(s.getName() + ": " + s.getScore());
}

// finding the top scorer: track the OBJECT, not an index
Student best = roster.get(0);
for (Student s : roster) {
    if (s.getScore() > best.getScore()) { best = s; }
}

Compare this with 5.5, where the same job required an index to keep two arrays aligned. Here the name and score cannot separate, because they are one object — which is the payoff the whole unit has been building toward.

ArrayList<Student> roll = new ArrayList<>();
roll.add(new Student("Ana", 88));

for (Student s : roll)                       // read every one
    System.out.println(s.getName());

for (Student s : roll)                       // MUTATING is fine —
    s.setScore(s.getScore() + 5);            // the reference reaches the object

Unlike an array of primitives, a for-each over objects can change them: the loop variable is a copy of the reference, which still points at the same object. What it cannot do is replace an element — that needs set(i, ...).

for (int i = roll.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--)   // remove BACKWARDS
    if (roll.get(i).getScore() < 40) roll.remove(i);

Removing while looping forwards skips elements, because everything after the removed item shifts left while the index still advances. Going backwards avoids it entirely; removing inside a for-each throws ConcurrentModificationException.

📘 DEFINITION

Collection of objects: a list whose elements are references to your own class’s instances

Object accumulator: tracking a whole object as the current best rather than an index

🎯 EXAM TIP

roster.get(0) on an empty list throws IndexOutOfBoundsException. Guard with isEmpty() before assuming a first element exists.

✅ Also covered in depth: Arrays → 2D Arrays and ArrayList

📊 FIGURE — a list of your own objects
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Building and searching a list of objects
import java.util.ArrayList;
ArrayList<Part> parts = new ArrayList<>();
parts.add(new Part("Wheel", 40));
parts.add(new Part("Frame", 120));
double total = 0;
for (Part p : parts) total += p.getPrice();
System.out.printf("%.2f%n", total);
for (Part p : parts) if (p.getName().equals("Frame")) System.out.println("found " + p.getPrice());
160.00 found 120.0
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Each entry is a reference to a Part object.
  2. The enhanced for loop hands you each one in turn.
  3. Searching compares with .equals, because the names are Strings.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The list holds references, not copies
import java.util.ArrayList;
Item i = new Item(1);
ArrayList<Item> list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add(i);
i.qty = 99;
System.out.println(list.get(0).qty);
99
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Adding an object to a list stores a reference to it.
  2. The original variable still points at the same object.
  3. Changing it through either name is visible through both.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Expecting list.add(obj) to store a snapshot. It stores a reference, so later changes to that object show up inside the list.

Treating ArrayList as an abstract data type means separating what it does from how it does it. The operations — add, get, remove, size — are the contract; the array-with-spare-capacity underneath is an implementation detail you are free to ignore.

ADT operation      what it costs
add(e)             O(1) usually; O(n) when it has to grow
get(i)             O(1)   — direct index into the backing array
remove(i)          O(n)   — everything after i shifts down
contains(e)        O(n)   — a linear search

Knowing the costs is what lets you choose. The shifting on remove is exactly what makes LinkedList (14.2) attractive for heavy insertion and deletion, and the linear contains is why HashSet (14.4) exists.

An abstract data type is a type defined by the operations it offers, not by how it stores anything. ArrayList is the ADT; "an oversize array that reallocates when full" is the implementation, and it is deliberately invisible.

OperationDoes
add(x) / add(i, x)append / insert at a position
get(i)read by position
set(i, x)replace at a position — does not grow the list
remove(i)delete and shift left
indexOf(x)the position of a value, or -1
contains(x)true/false — indexOf(x) >= 0
size()how many elements

get takes a position and returns a value; indexOf takes a value and returns a position — they are inverses, and mixing them up is the usual slip. set overwrites and add(i, x) inserts, so only one of them changes the size.

Capacity is invisible from outside. size() is the number of elements; the underlying array may be larger, and that is exactly what the ADT is hiding.

📘 DEFINITION

Abstract data type (ADT): a set of operations defined independently of any implementation

Implementation: the concrete data structure providing those operations

Amortised cost: the average cost per operation over many, allowing for occasional expensive resizes

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

This split is what Unit 14 is organised around, and the O-notation attached to it is Unit 17. The same operation name can cost wildly different amounts depending on the structure underneath.

✅ Also covered in depth: Arrays → 2D Arrays and ArrayList

📊 FIGURE — the ADT and its implementation
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The interface is what you program against
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
List<String> items = new ArrayList<>();
items.add("a");
items.add("b");
items.add("c");
System.out.println(items.indexOf("b"));
items.remove(0);
System.out.println(items);
System.out.println(items.isEmpty());
1 [b, c] false
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Declaring the variable as List commits you only to the ADT.
  2. The implementation could be swapped without changing this code.
  3. That separation is exactly what an abstract data type means.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Why removing from the front costs more
import java.util.ArrayList;
ArrayList<Integer> a = new ArrayList<>();
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) a.add(i);
System.out.println(a);
a.remove(0);
System.out.println(a);
System.out.println(a.get(0));
[0, 1, 2, 3, 4] [1, 2, 3, 4] 1
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. An ArrayList is a resizing array underneath.
  2. Removing index 0 shifts every later element down one place.
  3. get(i) stays fast because the position is computed, not searched.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
list.remove(1) on an ArrayList<Integer> removes the element at INDEX 1, not the value 1. Use remove(Integer.valueOf(1)) to remove by value.
🎯 EXAM TIP
An ADT specifies the operations and their behaviour, not the storage. If a question asks what an ADT defines, the answer is the interface — never the implementation.

Reading the Java API documentation for a class is a skill the exam assumes, and the layout is always the same: constructors first, then methods, each with parameters, return type and exceptions.

public boolean add(E e)
       ^       ^   ^
       |       |   parameter: the element to append
       |       method name
       return type — true if the collection changed

Throws: NullPointerException - if the specified element is null
        and this list does not permit null elements

The two lines to read before calling anything unfamiliar are the return type and the throws clause. The return type tells you whether you need to assign the result — the mistake from 3.14 with Strings — and the throws clause tells you what can go wrong.

/**
 * A student's name and exam score.
 * An instance always has a non-null name and a score in 0..100.
 */
public class Student {
    /** @return the score, always between 0 and 100 */
    public int getScore() { return score; }
}

Class documentation states the invariant — what is always true of every instance — and that is more useful than describing the fields. "Score is always 0 to 100" tells a reader they need not check it, and tells you the setter must enforce it.

Document the contract, not the implementation. "Returns the average" survives a rewrite; "loops through the array adding to a total" becomes a lie the moment the storage changes, and stale documentation is worse than none because it is trusted.

Private helpers need only enough comment for the next maintainer; public members need the full contract, because callers cannot see inside.

📘 DEFINITION

API: the published set of classes and methods available to you

Method summary: the documentation table listing every method with its signature

Throws clause: the exceptions a method may raise

🎯 EXAM TIP

When the docs show E, T or K, V, those are type parameters (Unit 13), not real classes. E is whatever type you supplied in the angle brackets.

📊 FIGURE — reading a class's docs
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The docs tell you the return type before you assign
import java.util.ArrayList;
ArrayList<String> l = new ArrayList<>();
l.add("x");
boolean added = l.add("y");
System.out.println(added);
String removed = l.remove(0);
System.out.println(removed);
System.out.println(l);
true x [y]
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. add is documented as returning boolean — always true for a list.
  2. remove(int) is documented as returning the element removed.
  3. Knowing the return type is what lets you use it rather than discard it.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Constructors are documented separately
import java.util.ArrayList;
ArrayList<String> a = new ArrayList<>();
ArrayList<String> b = new ArrayList<>(50);
b.add("one");
System.out.println(a.size() + " " + b.size());
0 1
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. One constructor takes nothing; another takes an initial capacity.
  2. Capacity is not size — the list still contains nothing.
  3. The docs are where you find which constructors exist.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Assuming a documented method changes the object it is called on. Check the return type: a method that returns a value is usually handing you a result and leaving the receiver alone.
"}, "D286/u7/z7_18": {"body": "

Passing an object to a method follows the rule already established for arrays in 6.10, because both are references.

public static void promote(Student s) {
    s.setScore(100);          // caller SEES this — same object
}

public static void swapOut(Student s) {
    s = new Student("Other"); // caller does NOT see this — copy repointed
}

Student ada = new Student("Ada", 50);
promote(ada);     ada.getScore();   // 100
swapOut(ada);     ada.getName();    // still "Ada"

The precise statement — the one to give if the exam asks — is: Java is always pass by value, and for an object the value being copied is the reference. That single sentence explains both lines of behaviour above.

static void promote(Student s) { s.setScore(100); }   // caller SEES it
static void swap(Student s)    { s = new Student("X"); } // caller sees nothing

Identical to arrays in 6.10, for an identical reason: the reference is copied, so the method reaches the same object but cannot rebind the caller's variable.

A defensive copy is the answer when a class must not let outsiders mutate its internals: return new ArrayList<>(items) rather than items, or the caller can modify your private list through the reference you handed out — encapsulation defeated without a single public field.

Passing null is legal and only fails when the method dereferences it, so a method taking an object should either guard or document that null is not allowed. String is immutable, so passing one is always safe.

📘 DEFINITION

Pass by value (references): the reference is copied, so both names reach one object

Mutation through a parameter: changing the object’s state, which the caller observes

Reassigning a parameter: repointing the local copy, which the caller never sees

🎯 EXAM TIP

If a method must give back a different object, return it. And beware of returning a reference to a private field — the caller can then modify the object’s internals, defeating the encapsulation of 7.4.

✅ Also covered in depth: Concepts Made Clear → Pass-by-value

📊 FIGURE — passing an object to a method
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Changing a field is visible; reassigning is not
Box box = new Box(1);
changeField(box);
System.out.println(box.n);
reassign(box);
System.out.println(box.n);
99 99
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. changeField follows the reference and edits the one object.
  2. reassign only repoints the method's own copy of the reference.
  3. The caller's variable still points at the original object.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The same rule for a String — but Strings are immutable
String msg = "hello";
shout(msg);
System.out.println(msg);
hello
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The method reassigns its own copy of the reference.
  2. A String cannot be changed in place anyway.
  3. So the caller's text is unaffected — return the new value instead.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Concluding Java is pass-by-reference because an object's fields can be changed. Java is always pass-by-value; for objects the value copied is the reference, which is why reassigning the parameter changes nothing outside.
"}, "D286/u7/z7_19": {"body": "

A static member belongs to the class rather than to any object: there is exactly one copy no matter how many objects exist. That makes it the right home for counters and constants, and the wrong home for anything describing one particular object.

public class Student {
    private static int count = 0;         // ONE copy, shared by all
    private String name;                  // one per object

    public Student(String n) {
        name = n;
        count++;                          // every construction increments the same counter
    }

    public static int getCount() { return count; }   // no object needed
}

Student.getCount();       // called on the CLASS

The restriction follows from the definition: a static method has no object, so it cannot read an instance field. The reverse is fine — an instance method can read static members, because the class exists whenever an object does.

Static initializer blocks

A static field sometimes needs more than one expression to set up. A static initializer block runs once, when the class is first loaded, before any object exists and before main runs.

class Config {
    static Map defaults;

    static {                            // runs ONCE, at class load
        defaults = new HashMap<>();
        defaults.put("theme", "dark");
    }
}

An instance initializer block — the same thing without static — runs before each constructor instead. The full order at object creation is: static blocks once at class load, then instance initializers, then the constructor body.

public class Counter {
    private static int made = 0;      // ONE copy, shared by every object
    private int id;                   // one per object

    public Counter() { made++; id = made; }
    public static int total() { return made; }   // no object needed
}
Counter.total();                      // called on the CLASS

A static field belongs to the class, so every object sees the same one — which is what makes "how many have been created" possible at all. An instance field could not do it, because each object would have its own count of one.

A static method may not touch instance fields or this, because it runs without an object. The reverse is fine: an instance method can freely use static members, since the class always exists.

static final is the constant idiom — public static final double PI = 3.14159; — one shared copy that cannot change, named in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE.

📘 DEFINITION

static field: one shared copy belonging to the class

static method: called on the class; cannot access instance fields or this

static final constant: a shared, unchangeable value — the pattern of 2.9

Instance counter: a static field incremented in the constructor to count objects created

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

A static method cannot use this or any instance field — which is exactly why main has to create an object before it can use one (7.7).

✅ Also covered in depth: OOP → Static Members and Method Overloading

📊 FIGURE — INSTANCE FIELDS VS ONE SHARED STATIC FIELD
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — One static field shared by every object
Visitor a = new Visitor();
Visitor b = new Visitor();
Visitor c = new Visitor();
System.out.println(a.id + " " + b.id + " " + c.id);
System.out.println(Visitor.total);
1 2 3 3
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. id is an instance field, so each object has its own.
  2. total is static, so there is exactly ONE for the whole class.
  3. A static field is reached through the class name, not an object.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A static method cannot touch instance state
System.out.println(MathHelper.twice(21));
MathHelper m = new MathHelper();
System.out.println(m.countedTwice(21) + " calls=" + m.calls);
42 42 calls=1
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. twice is static, so it runs with no object and cannot see calls.
  2. countedTwice is an instance method and can.
  3. That is why Math.max is static — it needs no state.
🎯 EXAM TIP
"Non-static variable cannot be referenced from a static context" always means the same thing: a static method tried to use an instance field. Either make the field static, or create an object first.
"}, "D286/u7/z7_20": {"body": "

A package is a namespace for classes: it prevents name collisions and groups related code. You have been consuming packages since import java.util.Scanner.

package com.wgu.school;              // FIRST line of the file, if present

import java.util.ArrayList;          // one class
import java.util.*;                  // every class in the package (not sub-packages)

java.lang     — String, Math, System, Integer   (imported automatically)
java.util     — Scanner, ArrayList, HashMap, Random
java.io       — File, FileReader, PrintWriter   (Unit 9)

Package membership also affects visibility: a member with no access modifier at all is package-private, visible inside its package and nowhere else. That is a fourth level alongside public, private and protected (10.2).

package com.example.school;        // FIRST line, matches the folder path
import java.util.ArrayList;        // one class
import java.util.*;                // everything in that package (not subpackages)

A package is a namespace and a folder path at once: com.example.school means the file lives in com/example/school/. Two classes may share a name if they are in different packages, which is the problem packages exist to solve.

java.lang is imported automatically — that is why String, Math, System and the wrappers never need one, while java.util.Scanner and java.util.ArrayList do.

A member with no access modifier is package-private: visible to other classes in the same package and nowhere else. It is the default, and it is not the same as public.

📘 DEFINITION

Package: a named grouping of related classes

The salary program becomes a class, and the difference from 6.23 is that the data now travels with the behaviour instead of being handed in on every call.

public class Employee {
    private String name;
    private double salary;

    public Employee(String n, double s) { name = n; salary = s; }

    public double taxRate() {
        if (salary >= 100000) { return 0.28; }
        if (salary >=  50000) { return 0.22; }
        return 0.15;
    }

    public double netPay() { return salary * (1 - taxRate()); }
    public String getName() { return name; }
}

ArrayList staff = new ArrayList<>();
staff.add(new Employee("Ada", 95000));
for (Employee e : staff) {
    System.out.printf("%s: %.2f%n", e.getName(), e.netPay());
}

taxRate() takes no parameter now because it reads its own salary field. That is the shift from Unit 6 to Unit 7 in a single line: methods stop being given the data and start owning it.

public class Employee {
    private String name;
    private double rate;                       // private: the rule is protected
    public Employee(String name, double rate) {
        this.name = name; this.rate = rate;
    }
    public double payFor(double hours) {       // the logic lives WITH the data
        return hours <= 40 ? hours * rate
                           : 40 * rate + (hours - 40) * rate * 1.5;
    }
    public String getName() { return name; }
}

double payroll = 0;
for (Employee e : staff) payroll += e.payFor(hoursFor(e));

Compare this with the Unit 6 version. There, the rate lived in a loop variable and the overtime rule was written inline, so every place that needed pay had to repeat it. Here each Employee carries its own rate and knows how to compute its own pay — the rule exists once, and a rate cannot drift away from the person it belongs to.

The accumulator is still declared before the loop for the same reason as 4.12. What has changed is that the per-employee state moved from a variable that must be reset into a field that cannot be shared by accident.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

Adding a new field — a bonus, a department — now means editing one class. In the parallel-array version of 5.11 it meant adding an array and updating every loop that touched it.

📊 FIGURE — the data and its rules together
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — An Employee class that owns its own rules
Employee e = new Employee("Ada", 55000);
System.out.printf("%.2f%n", e.monthly());
e.raise(4);

The domain example becomes a class too, and the win is that the rules and the registry finally live in one place.

public class DomainRegistry {
    private ArrayList taken = new ArrayList<>();

    public boolean isAvailable(String d) {
        String candidate = normalise(d);
        for (String t : taken) {
            if (t.equalsIgnoreCase(candidate)) { return false; }
        }
        return true;
    }

    public boolean register(String d) {
        if (!isAvailable(d)) { return false; }
        taken.add(normalise(d));
        return true;
    }

    private String normalise(String d) { return d.trim().toLowerCase(); }
}

normalise is private because it is an implementation detail — callers should not have to know that names are stored lowercased. And register reuses isAvailable instead of repeating the search, so a change to the matching rule happens once.

public class Domain {
    private String name;
    private boolean registered;

    public Domain(String name) { this.name = name; this.registered = false; }

    public boolean isValid()     { /* the 4.13 character rules */ }
    public boolean isAvailable() { return isValid() && !registered; }
    public boolean register() {
        if (!isAvailable()) return false;       // guard: cannot register twice
        registered = true;
        return true;
    }
}

registered is private and there is no setter, so the only way to change it is register() — which refuses unless the domain is valid and still free. The rule cannot be bypassed because there is no other door, which is encapsulation doing something concrete rather than being a definition.

isAvailable() composes isValid() instead of repeating the character checks, so the validation rules live in exactly one method. register() returning a boolean lets the caller react to a refusal rather than silently assume success.

📘 DEFINITION

Encapsulated state: the list is private, so the only way to change it is through register()

Private helper reuse: sharing internal logic between public methods

Class invariant: a property kept true by every method — here, that stored names are always normalised

🎯 EXAM TIP

Returning boolean from register rather than printing keeps the class usable from a GUI, a test, or a file-driven program — the argument from 6.2, now at class scale.

📊 FIGURE — a small class with one clear job
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A Domain class that validates itself
System.out.println(new Domain("wgu.edu").isValid());
System.out.println(new Domain("nodot").isValid());
System.out.println(new Domain("").isValid());
true false false
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The object answers a question about its own state.
  2. The null and empty check comes first, before any String method is called.
  3. The method returns a boolean and prints nothing — the caller decides the wording.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Checking against a list of taken names
import java.util.List;
List<String> taken = List.of("wgu.edu", "example.com");
System.out.println(new Dom("wgu.edu").isAvailable(taken));
System.out.println(new Dom("newsite.org").isAvailable(taken));
false true
actual output, captured from the JVM

  2. contains uses equals, which is the correct comparison for Strings.

Calling name.isEmpty() before the null check. Ordering the guards the other way round throws a NullPointerException on exactly the input the guard was meant to catch.

Unit 7 said objects live "on the heap" without explaining what that costs. Memory management is that explanation, and in Java the headline is that you never free anything by hand — the garbage collector does it — but you can still keep memory alive by accident.

Two questions decide everything in this unit: where does this value live, and what is still pointing at it? A local int lives in the stack frame and vanishes when the method returns. An object lives on the heap and survives exactly as long as something can still reach it.

void demo() {
    int n = 5;                    // stack — gone when demo() returns
    Student s = new Student();    // s is on the stack, the OBJECT is on the heap
}                                 // s vanishes; the object becomes unreachable
                                  // and is collected at some later point

Memory management is deciding when storage is claimed and when it is given back. In C you do both by hand; in Java new claims and the garbage collector gives back, automatically, once nothing can reach the object any more.

Manual (C/C++)Automatic (Java)
claimmalloc / newnew
releasefree / delete — yoursthe garbage collector
forget to releasememory leakcannot happen this way
release too earlydangling pointer, crashcannot happen at all

Java can still leak, but only in one way: an object you no longer use is still reachable — left in a list, held by a static field — so the collector must keep it. Filling memory that way ends in OutOfMemoryError.

So the programmer's job is not freeing, it is not holding on. Removing something from a collection when you are done with it is the whole of the discipline.

📘 DEFINITION

Memory management: deciding when memory is allocated and when it is reclaimed

Allocation: reserving memory for a new object, done by new

Reachable: an object is reachable if some live reference chain leads to it

Garbage: an allocated object that is no longer reachable

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

In C you would call free and risk freeing twice or never. Java removes that entire class of bug and replaces it with a subtler one — holding a reference longer than you meant to, which is the leak described in 8.5.

📊 FIGURE — WHO GIVES THE MEMORY BACK
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — WHERE EACH NAME LIVES, AND WHAT SURVIVES

Four printed lines answer the two questions this unit is built on: where does this value live, and what is still pointing at it.

static class Student { String name; Student(String n){ name = n; } }
static void rename(Student s, String n) { s.name = n; }

public static void main(String[] args) {
    int count = 2;
    Student s1 = new Student("Ada");
    Student s2 = s1;
    rename(s1, "Grace");
    System.out.println(s1.name);
    System.out.println(s2.name);
    s1 = null;
    System.out.println(s2.name);
    System.out.println(count);
}
  1. int count = 2; — the value 2 itself sits in main's stack frame. There is no heap object anywhere in this line.
  2. new Student("Ada") — one Student object is created on the heap. The variable s1 is a stack slot holding the address of it.
  3. Student s2 = s1; — a second stack slot holding the same address. Still one object, now two references to it.
  4. rename(s1, "Grace") — the parameter s is a third reference to that same object, so s.name = n edits the one object everybody points at. Both later reads see "Grace".
  5. s1 = null; — this overwrites one stack slot. It does not touch the heap object, and s2 still reaches it, so the next line prints normally.
  6. count was never involved: primitives are copied, so nothing a method does to a copy can be seen here.
OUTPUT
Grace
Grace
Grace
2

The whole unit in one trace: three references, one object, and assigning null to a reference removes a path rather than deleting anything.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — AN ACCIDENTAL LEAK, MEASURED

Java cannot leak the C way. It leaks exactly one way — an object you have finished with is still reachable. Here a logging list is the culprit.

static class Reading { double value; Reading(double v){ value = v; } }
static ArrayList<Reading> log = new ArrayList<>();

static void sample(double v) {
    Reading r = new Reading(v);      // local — dies at the closing brace
    log.add(r);                      // but the LIST keeps a reference
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) { sample(i * 1.5); }
    System.out.println("locals gone, list still holds " + log.size());
    log.clear();
    System.out.println("after clear: " + log.size());
}
  1. Each call to sample creates one Reading and stores a reference in log. When the method returns, r disappears — but it was never the only reference.
  2. log is a static field, so it lives for the whole run. Anything inside it is reachable, and therefore cannot be collected, no matter how long ago the program stopped caring about it.
  3. After five calls the size is 5 — five objects the collector must keep. Run this loop ten million times instead of five and the program dies with OutOfMemoryError, having never called anything resembling malloc.
  4. log.clear() releases the list's references. Now nothing reaches the readings and they become collectable.
OUTPUT
locals gone, list still holds 5
after clear: 0

The fix is never "free the memory" — it is clear(), remove(), or not storing it in the first place. Not holding on is memory management in Java.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

"The object is destroyed when the method returns." It is not. The variable is destroyed when the frame is popped; the object is destroyed only when nothing anywhere can reach it. In the second worked example the local r vanished five times over and not one object was freed, because the list still pointed at all of them.

How to notice it: whenever a method hands an object to a collection, a static field, or a caller, ask who else now holds this? That second holder, not the local variable, decides the lifetime.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Two facts answer most memory questions on this exam:

① Java cannot have a dangling pointer or a double free — the collector makes both impossible, so any option offering them is wrong by construction.
② Java can still run out of memory, by keeping references to objects it no longer uses. If an option says "memory leaks are impossible in Java", it is wrong; the accurate statement is "leaks caused by forgetting to free are impossible".

When asked "what reclaims this?", the answer is the garbage collector, and the trigger is unreachability — never free, never delete, never the end of a method.

A linked list is the clearest demonstration of references doing structural work: each node holds a value and a reference to the next node, and the list is nothing but that chain.

class Node {
    int value;
    Node next;              // a reference to another Node — null marks the end
    Node(int v) { value = v; }
}

Node a = new Node(1);
Node b = new Node(2);
a.next = b;                 // a -> b -> null

// walking the chain
Node cur = a;
while (cur != null) {
    System.out.println(cur.value);
    cur = cur.next;          // move along
}

Compare this with an array (5.1). The array is one contiguous block with instant indexing and a fixed length; the list is scattered nodes with no indexing at all, but it grows by allocating one node. That trade — get(i) versus insert — is exactly the comparison drawn again in 14.2.

class Node {
    int data;
    Node next;            // a Node holding a reference to another Node
}

head -> [4|*] -> [8|*] -> [15|null]

Each node stores a value and a reference to the next; the last node's next is null, and that null is what ends every traversal. The head reference is the only way in — lose it and the whole list becomes unreachable and is collected.

for (Node cur = head; cur != null; cur = cur.next)
    System.out.println(cur.data);

Node n = new Node();  n.data = 1;
n.next = head;  head = n;          // insert at the FRONT — O(1), no shifting
Array / ArrayListLinked list
get element iinstant — computed addresswalk from the head — O(n)
insert at the frontshift everything rightO(1)
memoryone contiguous blockscattered, plus a reference per node

The trade is direct access against cheap insertion. Assigning head = n.next before saving n is how nodes get lost — nothing refers to them afterwards and the data is gone.

📘 DEFINITION

Node: an object holding a value and a reference to the next node

Head: the reference to the first node; losing it loses the whole list

Traversal: walking the chain by following next until null

null terminator: the null next reference marking the end of the list

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Reassigning the head before saving it — head = head.next without keeping the old head — makes the earlier nodes unreachable. In C that leaks; in Java the collector takes them, and either way the data is gone.

📊 FIGURE — A LINKED LIST AS IT ACTUALLY SITS IN MEMORY
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — BUILDING AND WALKING A THREE-NODE LIST

Nothing here is a list type — just a class holding a value and a reference, plus a loop that follows references until one is null.

static class Node {
    int data;
    Node next;
    Node(int d) { data = d; }
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    Node head = new Node(4);
    head.next = new Node(8);
    head.next.next = new Node(15);

    int count = 0, sum = 0;
    for (Node cur = head; cur != null; cur = cur.next) {
        System.out.print(cur.data + " ");
        count++; sum += cur.data;
    }
    System.out.println();
    System.out.println("nodes=" + count + " sum=" + sum);
}
  1. new Node(4) runs the constructor, which sets data = 4. next is never assigned, so it holds its default — null. Every fresh node ends the list until you say otherwise.
  2. head.next = new Node(8) — the second node is created and its address is stored inside the first node. The chain is now 4 → 8 → null.
  3. head.next.next = new Node(15) reads two references to get to node 8, then writes into its next field. Chain: 4 → 8 → 15 → null.
  4. The loop starts with cur = head. Test cur != null — true, print 4, then cur = cur.next moves to node 8. Print 8, move to node 15. Print 15, move to null.
  5. The fourth test fails and the loop ends. Three iterations, one per node — count is 3 and sum is 4 + 8 + 15 = 27.
OUTPUT
4 8 15 
nodes=3 sum=27

Notice there is no index anywhere. The only way to reach node 15 was to walk through nodes 4 and 8, which is the whole cost model of a linked list.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — INSERT AT THE FRONT, THEN UNLINK THE MIDDLE

Both operations are pure reference rewiring. No element moves and no memory is copied.

static String show(Node head) {
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("head");
    for (Node c = head; c != null; c = c.next) sb.append(" -> ").append(c.data);
    return sb.append(" -> null").toString();
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    Node head = new Node(8);
    head.next = new Node(15);
    System.out.println(show(head));

    Node n = new Node(4);      // INSERT AT FRONT
    n.next = head;             // ① new node points at the old first
    head = n;                  // ② head now names the new node
    System.out.println(show(head));

    head.next = head.next.next;   // UNLINK the second node
    System.out.println(show(head));
}
  1. Start: head → 8 → 15 → null.
  2. Insert. n.next = head makes the new node point at 8. The order matters: had we written head = n first, head would no longer name node 8 and the rest of the list would be unreachable.
  3. head = n completes it. Two assignments, list length 3, nothing shifted.
  4. Unlink. head.next.next is node 15. Assigning it to head.next makes node 4 point straight at 15, so node 8 is skipped in every future traversal.
  5. Node 8 still exists in memory for a moment, but nothing refers to it any more — it is unreachable, and the collector takes it (8.4). You do not free it and you must not try.
OUTPUT
head -> 8 -> 15 -> null
head -> 4 -> 8 -> 15 -> null
head -> 4 -> 15 -> null

Compare with an array: inserting 4 at the front would shift every element right, and deleting the middle would shift every later element left. Here both are two-line reference edits.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Linked-list questions on this exam are almost always one of three shapes, and all three are answered by drawing boxes and arrows rather than by reading the code twice.

① "How many nodes does the loop visit?" — count nodes, not statements. A while (cur != null) loop runs exactly once per node.
② "Which line loses data?" — look for a reference being overwritten before it has been saved. head = head.next with nothing else holding the old head is the classic.
③ "Where does the traversal stop?" — at the first null. If a question sets the last node's next back to head, the loop never ends.

And know the cost pair cold: insert at front O(1), access by index O(n) — exactly the reverse of an array.

Java splits memory in two, and knowing which region a value is in answers most questions about lifetime.

STACK                                HEAP
one frame per active call            all objects, created by new
holds parameters and locals          holds fields
popped automatically on return       reclaimed by garbage collection
fast, small, fixed size              larger, managed
StackOverflowError when too deep     OutOfMemoryError when exhausted

A local variable of object type sits on the stack and holds a reference into the heap. So the variable and the object have different lifetimes: when the method returns, the variable disappears immediately, while the object waits until nothing else points at it.

That gap is exactly why returning an array from a method works (6.20) — the array itself was never on the stack.

StackHeap
holdsstack frames: parameters, local variablesevery object created with new
a local intthe value itself—
a local Student sthe referencethe Student object
fields of an object—inside the object, on the heap
freed whenthe method returns — automaticnothing can reach it — garbage collector
runs outStackOverflowErrorOutOfMemoryError
void f() {
    int n = 5;                     // n: on the stack
    int[] a = new int[3];          // a: on the stack, the ARRAY: on the heap
}                                  // n and a vanish; the array survives only
                                   // if something else still refers to it

This is why a method can return a locally created object safely: the variable died with the frame, but the object was never on the stack, and the returned reference keeps it alive.

It is also why deep recursion fails before memory does — each call adds a frame, and the stack is small compared with the heap.

📘 DEFINITION

Stack: per-call memory for parameters and locals; freed automatically on return

Heap: the region where all objects live

StackOverflowError: too many nested calls — the failure mode of runaway recursion (11.8)

OutOfMemoryError: the heap is full and nothing can be collected

🎯 EXAM TIP

Every primitive local is on the stack. Every object, including arrays and Strings, is on the heap — even when the variable naming it is a local.

✅ Also covered in depth: Advanced → Nested, Inner and Anonymous Classes

📊 FIGURE — STACK HOLDS FRAMES, HEAP HOLDS OBJECTS
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — RETURNING AN ARRAY FROM A METHOD — WHY IT IS SAFE

A local array looks like it should die with the method. It does not, because the array was never on the stack — only the reference to it was.

static int[] makeScores() {
    int[] local = new int[3];      // local: STACK.  the array: HEAP
    local[0] = 91; local[1] = 78; local[2] = 84;
    return local;                   // returns the ADDRESS, not the array
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    int[] scores = makeScores();
    System.out.println(scores.length + " " + scores[0] + " " + scores[2]);

    int[] alias = scores;
    alias[0] = 100;
    System.out.println(scores[0]);

    int n = scores[0];
    n = 5;
    System.out.println(scores[0] + " " + n);
}
  1. Inside makeScores, the frame holds one stack slot named local. The three-element array itself is heap memory allocated by new.
  2. return local; copies the address out. When the frame is popped, the slot local is gone — the array is untouched, because it was never in that frame.
  3. scores in main now holds that address, so the array is still reachable and prints 3 91 84.
  4. int[] alias = scores; copies the address again. alias[0] = 100 writes into the one heap array, so reading scores[0] shows 100. One object, two names.
  5. int n = scores[0]; copies a value out of the heap into a stack slot. Changing n to 5 cannot possibly affect the array, so the last line prints 100 5.
OUTPUT
3 91 84
100
100 5

Steps 4 and 5 are the same syntax doing two different things. alias = scores copies a reference; n = scores[0] copies an int. Which one you get depends entirely on the type.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — WHAT A METHOD CAN AND CANNOT CHANGE

Java passes everything by value. For a primitive the value is the number; for an object the value is the reference — and that single sentence predicts all four lines of this output.

static void bump(int prim, int[] arr, StringBuilder sb, String s) {
    prim = prim + 1;          // changes a COPY of the number
    arr[0] = arr[0] + 1;      // follows the reference into the heap
    sb.append("!");           // follows the reference into the heap
    s = s + "!";              // rebinds a COPY of the reference
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    int prim = 10;
    int[] arr = { 10 };
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("hi");
    String s = "hi";
    bump(prim, arr, sb, s);
    System.out.println(prim);
    System.out.println(arr[0]);
    System.out.println(sb);
    System.out.println(s);
}
  1. prim — the parameter is a fresh stack slot in bump's frame holding a copy of 10. Incrementing it edits that frame, which is then discarded. main still prints 10.
  2. arr — the parameter is a copy of the reference, but it points at main's array. arr[0] = arr[0] + 1 writes into the heap object both frames can see, so main prints 11.
  3. sb — same story. append mutates the StringBuilder on the heap, so main prints hi!.
  4. s — s + "!" creates a new String on the heap and stores its address in the parameter slot. main's s still points at the original, and Strings are immutable, so main prints hi.
OUTPUT
10
11
hi!
hi

The rule that separates lines 3 and 4: mutating the object the reference points at is visible to the caller; reassigning the parameter is not, because you only overwrote a stack slot in the callee's own frame.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

"Strings and arrays are small, so they live on the stack." Size has nothing to do with it. Every object created with new — arrays, Strings, ArrayLists, your own classes — is on the heap. The only things on the stack are stack frames: the parameters and locals of calls that are currently running, which for an object variable means the reference and nothing more.

How to notice it: ask "did a new make this?" If yes, the object is heap. The name you gave it may be a stack slot, but the name and the object are two different things with two different lifetimes — and confusing them is what makes questions about returning locals, aliasing and pass-by-value look hard.

The mirror-image error: "a field is on the stack because the method that uses it is." Fields live inside their object, on the heap, for as long as the object does.

The garbage collector reclaims objects that can no longer be reached from any live variable. Reachability, not counting, is the criterion — which is why two objects pointing at each other are still collected once nothing outside points to either.

Student s = new Student("Ada");
s = null;                     // the Ada object is now unreachable -> collectable

Student a = new Student("A");
Student b = new Student("B");
a = b;                        // the "A" object is unreachable -> collectable

You cannot force collection and you cannot predict when it happens. System.gc() is a suggestion the JVM may ignore, and finalize() is deprecated and must not be relied on. The right way to release a scarce resource such as a file handle is close(), not the collector (9.4).

The collector reclaims an object when it becomes unreachable — no chain of references from a running method, a local variable or a static field leads to it. Not "when it goes out of scope" and not "when nobody is using it".

Student s = new Student("Ana");
s = new Student("Ben");        // the Ana object is now unreachable -> collectable

Student a = new Student("Cy");
Student b = a;
a = null;                      // still reachable through b — NOT collected

Setting a reference to null does not free anything; it removes one path. If any other path remains the object stays. That is why a forgotten entry in a long-lived ArrayList is the classic Java leak.

System.gc() is a request the JVM may ignore, and calling it is almost always a mistake. Collection timing is not something a program should depend on, which is also why finalizers are deprecated — there is no guarantee they run at all.

📘 DEFINITION

Garbage collector: the JVM component that reclaims unreachable objects

Reachability: whether a chain of references from a live variable leads to the object

System.gc(): a request to run collection; not a guarantee

Memory leak (in Java): keeping references to objects you no longer need, so they can never be collected

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Setting a variable to null does not delete the object; it removes one reference. If any other reference remains, the object stays alive — which is the aliasing point from 7.10 seen from the other side.

📊 FIGURE — COLLECTED WHEN THE LAST REFERENCE DROPS — NOT BEFORE
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — WHICH LINE MAKES WHICH OBJECT COLLECTABLE

Exam questions phrase this as "after which statement is object X eligible for garbage collection?". Answer it by tracking arrows, one line at a time.

static class Sensor {
    String id;
    Sensor(String id) { this.id = id; }
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    Sensor a = new Sensor("S-1");   // line 1
    Sensor b = new Sensor("S-2");   // line 2
    Sensor c = a;                    // line 3
    a = b;                           // line 4
    System.out.println(a.id + " " + b.id + " " + c.id);
    c = null;                        // line 5
    System.out.println(a.id + " " + b.id);
    b = null;                        // line 6
    System.out.println(a.id);
}
After linePoints at S-1Points at S-2Eligible for collection
1a—nothing
2abnothing
3a, cbnothing
4ca, bnothing — c still holds S-1
5nobodya, bS-1 — line 5 dropped the last reference
6nobodyastill only S-1
  1. Line 4 is the tempting answer and it is wrong. a = b does remove a path to S-1, but line 3 made a second one through c.
  2. Line 5 removes that last path, so S-1 becomes unreachable exactly there.
  3. Line 6 sets b to null, but a also points at S-2, so S-2 survives. It is only collectable when main ends.
  4. Every print still works, because reassigning references never harms the objects they used to name.
OUTPUT
S-2 S-2 S-1
S-2 S-2
S-2

The last printed line proves the point: after b = null, S-2 is perfectly usable through a.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — TWO OBJECTS POINTING AT EACH OTHER — BOTH COLLECTED

Some languages reclaim memory by counting references, and a cycle defeats them: each object has a count of 1 for ever. Java asks a different question, so the cycle is not special.

static class Cart {
    String owner; Cart peer;
    Cart(String o) { owner = o; }
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    Cart x = new Cart("Ana");
    Cart y = new Cart("Ben");
    x.peer = y;
    y.peer = x;                       // a cycle: x -> y -> x
    System.out.println(x.peer.owner + " " + y.peer.owner);
    System.out.println(x.peer.peer.owner);
    x = null;
    y = null;
    System.out.println("both roots dropped");
    System.gc();
    System.out.println("gc requested, program continues");
}
  1. x.peer = y and y.peer = x build the cycle. Following it twice — x.peer.peer — arrives back at the Ana cart, which is why the second line prints Ana.
  2. After x = null; y = null; every reference to either object is inside the other object. A reference count would still say 1 apiece.
  3. Java's test is different: can a chain of references starting from a root reach it? Roots are the locals of running methods and static fields. No root leads into the pair, so the whole cycle is garbage and both are collected together.
  4. System.gc() is a request, not a command. The JVM may run a collection, may run a partial one, or may do nothing — which is why nothing about the output can depend on it, and why the program simply carries on to the final line.
OUTPUT
Ben Ana
Ana
both roots dropped
gc requested, program continues

Nothing observable tells you when — or whether — the two carts were reclaimed. That is by design: collection timing is not part of the language's contract with your program.

🎯 EXAM TIP

The eligibility question, answered in ten seconds. Number the lines, then for the object named in the question write down every variable that currently points at it. The answer is the first line after which that list becomes empty.

Three traps built into these questions:

① a second reference created earlier (Sensor c = a;) that the question hopes you forgot;
② an object still inside an ArrayList or a static field, which counts as reachable;
③ a cycle, which does not save anything — if no root reaches the cycle, all of it goes.

Also memorise the exact wording: an object becomes eligible for collection. Java never guarantees it is collected, so any option saying "the memory is freed immediately" or "System.gc() forces collection" is wrong.

Scope (4.10, 6.11) and garbage collection meet here: when a variable goes out of scope, the reference it held disappears, and if it was the last one the object becomes collectable at that moment.

void process() {
    {
        Student temp = new Student("X");
        // temp is usable here
    }                        // temp out of scope -> the object is collectable

    ArrayList cache = new ArrayList<>();
    cache.add(new Student("Y"));
    // as long as cache is reachable, EVERY Student in it stays alive
}

The second half is where real leaks come from. A long-lived collection holds references, so anything added to it is immune to collection until it is removed. A cache nobody ever clears is the standard Java memory leak, and no amount of setting other variables to null helps.

for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
    Student s = new Student("x");   // 1000 objects created
}                                   // each becomes unreachable at the brace

ArrayList<Student> kept = new ArrayList<>();
for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
    kept.add(new Student("x"));     // the list still refers to all 1000
}                                   // none can be collected

Scope ending makes an object eligible only if that variable was the last route to it. The two loops differ in exactly that: the second stores a second reference somewhere that outlives the loop.

Circular references are not a problem for Java. A refers to B and B refers to A, but if nothing outside reaches either, both are unreachable and both are collected — reachability from a root, not reference counting, is the test.

Practical guidance is short: let variables fall out of scope naturally, remove things from collections when you are done, and do not sprinkle = null around.

📘 DEFINITION

Out of scope: past the closing brace, where the name no longer exists

Eligible for collection: unreachable, and therefore collectable at some unspecified later time

Retained reference: a reference held by a long-lived object that keeps another object alive

🎯 EXAM TIP

For an exam question asking when an object becomes eligible for collection, look for the line where the last reference to it is overwritten, reassigned or falls out of scope.

📊 FIGURE — SCOPE ENDING IS NOT THE SAME AS BEING COLLECTED
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — THE SAME LOOP, TWICE, WITH ONE LINE OF DIFFERENCE

Both loops create a thousand objects. One loop leaves nothing behind; the other retains every single one — and the only difference is a single add.

static class Ticket { int id; Ticket(int id){ this.id = id; } }

public static void main(String[] args) {
    for (int i = 1; i <= 1000; i++) {
        Ticket t = new Ticket(i);          // unreachable at the closing brace
    }
    System.out.println("loop A finished");

    ArrayList<Ticket> audit = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 1; i <= 1000; i++) {
        Ticket t = new Ticket(i);
        audit.add(t);                      // a SECOND reference outlives the loop
    }
    System.out.println("loop B kept " + audit.size() + " objects alive");
    System.out.println("first id still readable: " + audit.get(0).id);
    audit.clear();
    System.out.println("after clear: " + audit.size());
}
  1. Loop A. On each iteration t is created, assigned, and goes out of scope at the closing brace. At that moment nothing else refers to that Ticket, so it becomes eligible immediately — one object born and abandoned a thousand times over.
  2. Loop B. audit.add(t) stores a copy of the reference inside the list. When t goes out of scope the object still has one arrow pointing at it.
  3. audit itself is a local of main, which runs for the whole program, so every element stays reachable. audit.size() printing 1000 is direct evidence: you cannot have a size of 1000 without holding 1000 references.
  4. audit.get(0).id reads the very first Ticket, created a thousand iterations earlier — it was never collected because it was never unreachable.
  5. audit.clear() drops all 1000 references at once, and only then does loop B's worth of objects become collectable.
OUTPUT
loop A finished
loop B kept 1000 objects alive
first id still readable: 1
after clear: 0

Scope ended identically in both loops. Lifetime did not. Scope governs names; reachability governs objects.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A STATIC FIELD OUTLIVES EVERY BLOCK

Static fields are garbage-collection roots: they are reachable for the entire run, so anything they point at is too, regardless of where it was created.

static class Session { String user; Session(String u){ user = u; } }
static Session current;                    // a static field = a GC ROOT

public static void main(String[] args) {
    {
        Session temp = new Session("guest");
        System.out.println("inside block: " + temp.user);
    }                                      // temp out of scope
    System.out.println("block ended");

    {
        Session temp = new Session("ada");
        current = temp;                    // stored in the static field
    }                                      // temp out of scope AGAIN
    System.out.println("still alive via static: " + current.user);
    current = null;
    System.out.println("now unreachable");
}
  1. The first block creates the "guest" session and lets it go. temp was the only reference, so at the closing brace the object is eligible — and the name temp can be reused afterwards, because it no longer exists.
  2. The second block creates "ada" and copies the reference into current. Now two references exist; one is about to die and one is not.
  3. At that closing brace temp is gone, yet current.user reads "ada" perfectly. A static field kept an object alive past the end of the scope it was created in.
  4. current = null is the line that finally makes the ada session collectable — and it is also the only cleanup this program can do, since there is no other way to reach it.
OUTPUT
inside block: guest
block ended
still alive via static: ada
now unreachable

This is the whole anatomy of a real Java memory leak: a long-lived root (a static field, a cache, a listener list) holding references to short-lived objects. Nothing is broken, nothing is illegal, and memory grows until the program dies.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

"Setting variables to null helps the garbage collector, so do it everywhere." It does not. A local that is about to go out of scope is already about to lose its reference — the assignment is noise, and scattering = null through a method makes it harder to read while achieving nothing.

= null is worth writing in exactly one situation: a long-lived field that is holding an object you have finished with, like current = null above, where nothing else will drop that reference for you.

The related misconception is the opposite one: "two objects pointing at each other leak in Java." They do not. Java tests reachability from roots, not reference counts, so an unreferenced cycle is collected whole. If you remember one sentence from this section, make it: the question is never how many references exist, only whether a root can reach it.

The employee list ties Unit 7 and Unit 8 together: an ArrayList holds references, so removing from the list is what makes an object collectable.

ArrayList staff = new ArrayList<>();
staff.add(new Employee("Ada", 95000));      // the only reference is in the list
staff.add(new Employee("Alan", 88000));

staff.remove(0);        // the Ada object is now unreachable -> collectable
staff.clear();          // every element unreachable

// but this does NOT make it collectable:
Employee held = staff.get(0);
staff.clear();          // held still points at it — object stays alive

The last three lines are the whole lesson. Removing from a collection releases the collection’s reference and nothing else; any other variable you handed the object to keeps it alive.

ArrayList<Employee> staff = new ArrayList<>();
staff.add(new Employee("Ana", 22.50));

for (int i = staff.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--)          // remove BACKWARDS
    if (staff.get(i).getRate() < 15) staff.remove(i);

double total = 0;
for (Employee e : staff) total += e.payFor(40);

Compared with the oversize array of 6.16, the list carries its own count — staff.size() is always right, with no second variable to fall out of step, and adding never needs a capacity check.

Two things still catch people. remove(i) shifts everything after i left, so a forward loop skips the element that moved into the gap; going backwards avoids it. And the list stores references, so modifying an object through the list changes the same object the rest of the program sees.

📘 DEFINITION

Collection as an owner: the list holds references, so membership determines lifetime

clear(): removes every element, releasing the list’s references

Escaped reference: a reference handed out to a caller, which then outlives the collection

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

This is the same escape problem as returning a private field from a getter (7.18). Once a reference leaves the class that owns it, that class no longer controls the object’s lifetime or its state.

📊 FIGURE — THE LIST HOLDS REFERENCES — UNTIL YOU HAND ONE OUT
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — REMOVING WHILE LOOPING — BACKWARDS, AND WHY

Filtering a list in place is the single most common ArrayList bug in this course. Here is the correct version, traced.

ArrayList<Employee> staff = new ArrayList<>();
staff.add(new Employee("Ana", 22.50));
staff.add(new Employee("Ben", 14.00));
staff.add(new Employee("Cy",  13.25));
staff.add(new Employee("Dee", 31.00));

for (int i = staff.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) {      // BACKWARDS
    if (staff.get(i).rate < 15) { staff.remove(i); }
}
for (Employee e : staff) { System.out.print(e.name + " "); }
System.out.println();
System.out.println("size=" + staff.size());
iElement at irate < 15?List after this step
3Deeno (31.00)Ana, Ben, Cy, Dee
2Cyyes (13.25)Ana, Ben, Dee
1Benyes (14.00)Ana, Dee
0Anano (22.50)Ana, Dee
  1. remove(i) shifts every element after index i one place left. Going backwards, everything after i has already been examined, so the shift can never move an unchecked element past the cursor.
  2. Starting at staff.size() - 1 — index 3, not 4 — is what puts the cursor on the last element rather than one past it.
  3. The removals leave Ana and Dee, in their original relative order.
  4. Once removed, the Ben and Cy objects have no reference anywhere and become collectable. That is 8.4 applied: the list was their only owner.
OUTPUT
Ana Dee 
size=2

Two clean alternatives exist for the same job: staff.removeIf(e -> e.rate < 15);, or an explicit Iterator with it.remove(). Both avoid index arithmetic entirely.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — THE FORWARD LOOP SKIPS — AND A REFERENCE ESCAPES

The same filter written forwards produces a wrong answer silently, and the second half of this example shows why clear() does not always mean gone.

for (int i = 0; i < staff.size(); i++) {          // FORWARD — buggy
    if (staff.get(i).rate < 15) { staff.remove(i); }
}
for (Employee e : staff) { System.out.print(e.name + " "); }
System.out.println();

Employee held = staff.get(0);
staff.clear();
System.out.println("list size " + staff.size() + ", held still reads " + held.name);
held.rate = 25.00;
System.out.printf("%.2f%n", held.rate);
  1. i = 0: Ana, 22.50, kept. List is Ana, Ben, Cy, Dee.
  2. i = 1: Ben, 14.00, removed. Cy shifts down into index 1 and the list is Ana, Cy, Dee.
  3. i = 2: the loop increments past the element it just pulled into position 1, so it reads Dee, not Cy. Cy is never tested and survives the filter.
  4. The loop ends with Ana, Cy, Dee printed — one element that should have gone is still there, with no exception and no warning.
  5. Employee held = staff.get(0); copies a reference out of the list. staff.clear() then empties the list, so size() is 0.
  6. The Ana object is still perfectly alive, because held points at it: reading its name works and writing held.rate = 25.00 works. The list gave up its reference; the escaped one is still holding on.
OUTPUT
Ana Cy Dee 
list size 0, held still reads Ana
25.00

The second half is the lifetime lesson: membership in a collection is one reference among possibly many. Removing is only the last word if nobody else took a copy.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Removing inside a forward-counting loop. Because remove(i) shifts everything left, the element that slides into index i is skipped when i++ runs. The result is not a crash — it is a list that quietly kept an element it should have dropped, which is far harder to spot.

How to notice it: the bug only shows when two removable elements are adjacent. In the trace above, Ben and Cy sit next to each other and Cy survives; had Cy been elsewhere in the list, the forward loop would have looked correct. Test with consecutive matches.

The other half of the same trap: modifying the list inside a for-each loop. for (Employee e : staff) staff.remove(e); compiles and then throws ConcurrentModificationException at run time. Use a backwards index loop, removeIf, or an explicit iterator — never a for-each.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Three things this section is tested on, in order of frequency:

① What is in the list after a removal loop? Write the list out and cross elements off as you trace; do not reason about it in your head. A forward loop with remove skips the element after each removal — if the options include a list that is one element too long, that is the distractor for the backwards-loop answer, and vice versa.
② When is an element collectable? When the list no longer holds it and no variable took a copy. clear() alone is not enough if a get happened first.
③ Does changing an object through the list change it everywhere? Yes — the list stores references, so staff.get(0).rate = 30 and held.rate = 30 edit the same object.

And remember size() is a method call on an ArrayList — staff.size() — while an array uses the field arr.length and a String uses s.length(). Exams mix all three deliberately.
