Everything you have printed or read so far went through a stream: an ordered sequence of data flowing in one direction. Naming the abstraction matters, because file input in 9.4 is the same code as keyboard input with a different source.

System.out    standard output — the screen
System.err    standard error  — also the screen, but a separate stream
System.in     standard input  — the keyboard

Scanner scnr = new Scanner(System.in);         // read from the keyboard
Scanner file = new Scanner(new File("in.txt")); // read from a file — same methods

Because Scanner takes the source as a constructor argument, a method that accepts a Scanner (6.14) works with either without changing a line. That is the practical payoff of the abstraction.

When the input is not what you asked for

nextInt() assumes the next token really is an integer. Hand it "abc" and it throws InputMismatchException — and, importantly, it does not consume the bad token, so a naive retry loop reads the same rubbish for ever.

Scanner scnr = new Scanner(System.in);
int age;
while (true) {
    if (scnr.hasNextInt()) { age = scnr.nextInt(); break; }
    scnr.next();                       // DISCARD the bad token — essential
    System.out.println("Numbers only, please:");
}

Two safe patterns exist: test first with hasNextInt() as above, or catch InputMismatchException and call scnr.next() inside the catch to clear it. Either way the discard is what stops the infinite loop.

StreamIsUsed for
System.instandard inputusually wrapped in a Scanner
System.outstandard outputprintln, print, printf
System.errstandard errorerror messages, kept separate from output

A stream is a one-way sequence of data with a source or a destination. The point of the abstraction is that the same code shape reads from the keyboard, a file or a String — only the object you construct changes.

Scanner kb   = new Scanner(System.in);          // keyboard
Scanner file = new Scanner(new File("in.txt"));  // file
Scanner str  = new Scanner("10 20 30");          // a String

println adds a line ending and print does not — which is why building output with print in a loop and one println after it is the standard way to put values on one line.

📘 DEFINITION

Stream: a sequence of data flowing to or from a source

Standard output / input / error: the three streams every program starts with

System.out.print vs println: print leaves the cursor on the line; println ends it

Buffering: holding output briefly before writing it, for efficiency

🎯 EXAM TIP

System.err exists so error messages can be separated from normal output when a program is redirected to a file. They interleave unpredictably on screen because they are buffered differently.

📊 FIGURE — STREAMS: DATA FLOWING OUT AND IN
printf specifiermeansprintf("...", 3.14159) gives
%dwhole number (int/long)3 (with an int argument)
%.2ffloating point, 2 decimals3.14
%5.1fwidth 5, 1 decimal, right-aligned  3.1
%sstringtext as-is
%nnewline(line break)
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — ONE METHOD, TWO SOURCES — THE POINT OF THE ABSTRACTION

Because Scanner takes its source as a constructor argument, a method that accepts a Scanner neither knows nor cares where the data came from.

static int total(Scanner in) {          // works with ANY source
    int sum = 0;
    while (in.hasNextInt()) { sum += in.nextInt(); }
    return sum;
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    Scanner fromString = new Scanner("12 7 31");
    System.out.println(total(fromString));

    Scanner mixed = new Scanner("12 7 oops 31");
    System.out.println(total(mixed));
    System.out.println("stopped at: " + mixed.next());
    System.out.println(total(mixed));
}
  1. The first Scanner reads a String; new Scanner(System.in) or new Scanner(new File("in.txt")) would work with the same total method, unchanged. That substitutability is what "stream" buys you.
  2. hasNextInt() is the loop control. It reports whether the next token can be read as an int — it does not consume anything, so the following nextInt() gets that token.
  3. First call: 12 + 7 + 31 = 50. The loop ends because the stream is exhausted and hasNextInt() is false.
  4. Second call: 12 + 7 = 19, then hasNextInt() sees oops and returns false. The loop stops at the bad token, having consumed nothing of it.
  5. mixed.next() reads oops as a plain String, which advances the cursor past it.
  6. Calling total again on the same Scanner now resumes from 31 and returns 31. A stream is a position as well as a source.
OUTPUT
50
19
stopped at: oops
31

The last two lines are the practical shape of every "keep reading until the data runs out" loop: test, read, and when the test fails, deal with whatever stopped it.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — THE BAD-TOKEN LOOP — AND WHY IT HANGS WITHOUT THE DISCARD

nextInt() on non-numeric input throws and leaves the token in the stream. That single fact is what turns a naive retry loop into an infinite one.

Scanner scnr = new Scanner("abc 4.5 19 rest");
int age = -1;
while (age < 0) {
    if (scnr.hasNextInt()) {
        age = scnr.nextInt();
    } else {
        String bad = scnr.next();          // DISCARD — essential
        System.out.println("rejected: " + bad);
    }
}
System.out.println("age = " + age);
System.out.println("next token still waiting: " + scnr.next());

Scanner s2 = new Scanner("abc");
try {
    int n = s2.nextInt();
} catch (InputMismatchException e) {
    System.out.println("caught: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName());
    System.out.println("token NOT consumed: " + s2.next());
}
  1. Token 1 is abc. hasNextInt() is false, so the else branch runs scnr.next(), which consumes and returns it — printing rejected: abc and, crucially, moving the cursor forward.
  2. Token 2 is 4.5. hasNextInt() is also false — a decimal is not an int. It is rejected the same way. (hasNextDouble() would have accepted it.)
  3. Token 3 is 19, so nextInt() reads it, age becomes 19 and the loop condition fails.
  4. scnr.next() afterwards returns rest, proving the Scanner is sitting exactly where the loop left it.
  5. The second half shows the same fact from the exception side. nextInt() on abc throws InputMismatchException, and the very next next() still returns abc — the failed read consumed nothing.
  6. So a try/catch retry loop must call scnr.next() inside the catch. Without it, the loop retries the same unreadable token for ever and the program appears to freeze.
OUTPUT
rejected: abc
rejected: 4.5
age = 19
next token still waiting: rest
caught: InputMismatchException
token NOT consumed: abc

Two safe patterns, then: look before you leap with hasNextInt(), or try it and see with catch (InputMismatchException e) { scnr.next(); }. Both work; only the versions that advance the cursor terminate.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Mixing nextInt() and nextLine(). nextInt() reads the number and stops before the newline that follows it. The next nextLine() therefore returns the empty remainder of that line rather than the line you wanted, and the program appears to skip an input.

Scanner in = new Scanner("7\nAda Lovelace\n");
int n    = in.nextInt();     // reads 7, leaves the newline
String a = in.nextLine();    // returns "" — the rest of line 1
String b = in.nextLine();    // "Ada Lovelace" — what you wanted first time

How to notice it: a prompt that seems to be ignored, or a String variable that is empty when you know the user typed something. The fix is one extra in.nextLine(); immediately after the nextInt(), to swallow the leftover newline — or read everything with nextLine() and parse with Integer.parseInt.

The same trap applies to nextDouble(), next() and any other token-based read followed by a line-based one. Token reads stop at whitespace; line reads stop at newlines, and the two disagree about who owns it.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The compiler's definite-assignment rule, seen from both sides
System.out.println("field default: " + counter);
System.out.println("sum: " + safeSum(new int[] { 1, 2, 3 }));

int x;
for (int i = 0; i < 1; i++) { x = 9; }
x = 10;
System.out.println(x);
field default: 0 sum: 6 10
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. total = 0 is not decoration — without it the total += x would not compile.
  2. The loop assigning x is not enough on its own: the compiler cannot prove a loop body runs at all, so it does not count as a definite assignment.
  3. The explicit x = 10 is what makes the print legal here.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Any accumulator you declare must be seeded on the same line — int total = 0;, double sum = 0;, String out = "";. Forgetting it is a compile error rather than a wrong answer, which on a graded coding task costs the whole item.

printf gives you control over exactly how a value is rendered, which println cannot do. It takes a format string containing placeholders, followed by one value per placeholder.

System.out.printf("%s is %d years old%n", name, age);
System.out.printf("%.2f%n", 3.14159);          // 3.14   — rounded, not truncated
System.out.printf("%8.2f%n", 3.14159);         // "    3.14" — width 8, right aligned
System.out.printf("%-8s|%n", "hi");            // "hi      |" — left aligned

%d   integer        %f   floating point     %s   String
%c   char           %b   boolean            %%   a literal percent
%n   newline (portable)      \n  newline (Unix-style)

Two details are reliably examined. %.2f rounds rather than truncating, so 3.567 prints as 3.57. And the number of arguments must match the number of placeholders exactly, or you get a runtime exception rather than a compile error.

System.out.printf("%s scored %d (%.2f%%)%n", name, score, pct);
//                  |       |      |        |
//                  string  int    2 dp     literal % (doubled)
SpecifierForExample
%dinteger42
%ffloating point — 6 dp by default3.140000
%.2ffixed to 2 decimals3.14
%sString, or anything via toString()Ana
%ccharA
%8.2fwidth 8, right-aligned, 2 dp 3.14
%-8swidth 8, left-alignedAna
%nnewline

Handing a double to %d throws IllegalFormatConversionException at run time — the compiler does not check the pairing, so a mismatch survives to the moment the line executes. The count must match too: too few arguments throws, extra ones are ignored.

String.format takes the identical arguments and returns the String instead of printing it, which is what you want when the text is going somewhere other than the console.

📘 DEFINITION

Format specifier: a %-prefixed placeholder describing how to render one value

Precision: the .2 in %.2f — digits after the decimal point

Field width: the 8 in %8.2f — minimum total characters, padded with spaces

String.format: the same formatting, returning a String instead of printing it

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

%d with a double throws IllegalFormatConversionException at run time. The specifier must match the argument type — and the compiler will not check it for you.

📊 FIGURE — A FORMAT SPECIFIER, TAKEN APART AND APPLIED
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — EVERY SPECIFIER, WITH THE BRACKETS SHOWN

Printing each result inside [ ] makes the padding visible, which is the only way to check a format string without counting spaces by hand.

double v = 3.14159;
System.out.printf("[%f]%n", v);
System.out.printf("[%.2f]%n", v);
System.out.printf("[%8.2f]%n", v);
System.out.printf("[%-8.2f]%n", v);
System.out.printf("[%d]%n", 42);
System.out.printf("[%5d]%n", 42);
System.out.printf("[%-5d]|%n", 42);
System.out.printf("[%s]%n", "Ana");
System.out.printf("[%10s]%n", "Ana");
System.out.printf("[%-10s]|%n", "Ana");
System.out.printf("[%c] [%b] [%%]%n", 'A', true);
System.out.printf("%.2f %.2f %.2f%n", 3.567, 2.5, 3.5);
System.out.printf("%.0f %.0f%n", 2.5, 3.5);
OUTPUT
[3.141590]
[3.14]
[    3.14]
[3.14    ]
[42]
[   42]
[42   ]|
[Ana]
[       Ana]
[Ana       ]|
[A] [true] [%]
3.57 2.50 3.50
3 4
  1. %f with no precision gives six decimals — 3.141590, not 3.14159. That default catches people out constantly; if you want a specific number of places you must say so.
  2. %8.2f produces 3.14 preceded by four spaces: the value is 4 characters and the field is 8, so 4 spaces are added in front because numbers are right-aligned by default.
  3. %-8.2f puts the same four spaces after. The minus sign is a left-align flag, never a negative number.
  4. %5d and %-5d behave identically for integers — width is width, regardless of conversion.
  5. Strings pad the same way: %10s right-aligns, %-10s left-aligns. In practice you left-align text columns and right-align number columns, which is why a report almost always mixes them.
  6. Rounding, not truncation. 3.567 at two places becomes 3.57, and 2.5 and 3.5 at zero places become 3 and 4 — Java rounds half away from zero here, so 2.5 goes up rather than to the even number.
  7. %% prints one literal percent sign. A single % followed by an ordinary letter is an unknown conversion and throws.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — AN ALIGNED REPORT, AND THE THREE WAYS IT CAN THROW

Column alignment is the reason printf exists. It is also the place mismatched arguments show up, and the failures are all at run time.

record Row(String item, int qty, double price) {}

Row[] rows = {
    new Row("Widget", 12, 4.5),
    new Row("Bracket", 3, 19.99),
    new Row("Gasket kit", 140, 0.75)
};
System.out.printf("%-12s %5s %9s %10s%n", "ITEM", "QTY", "PRICE", "TOTAL");
double grand = 0;
for (Row r : rows) {
    double line = r.qty() * r.price();
    grand += line;
    System.out.printf("%-12s %5d %9.2f %10.2f%n", r.item(), r.qty(), r.price(), line);
}
System.out.printf("%-12s %5s %9s %10.2f%n", "GRAND", "", "", grand);
OUTPUT
ITEM           QTY     PRICE      TOTAL
Widget          12      4.50      54.00
Bracket          3     19.99      59.97
Gasket kit     140      0.75     105.00
GRAND                            218.97
  1. The header uses %5s, %9s and %10s — the same widths as the data rows but with the s conversion, because "QTY" is text. Matching the widths is what makes the columns line up.
  2. %-12s left-aligns the item names; every numeric column is right-aligned so the decimal points stack.
  3. The total line reuses the layout with empty strings as placeholders, keeping 218.97 in the same column as the other totals.

Now the failures. Each of these compiles cleanly and throws when the line executes:

System.out.printf("%d%n", 4.5);                 // double into %d
System.out.printf("%s scored %d%n", "Ana");      // one argument short
System.out.printf("%s%n", "Ana", "ignored");     // one argument too many
String s = String.format("%05.1f", 3.14159);    // zero-padding flag
OUTPUT
threw IllegalFormatConversionException
Ana scored threw MissingFormatArgumentException
Ana
003.1
  1. %d with a double throws IllegalFormatConversionException. The compiler cannot check the pairing, because the arguments are a varargs array of Object.
  2. Too few arguments throws MissingFormatArgumentException — and notice Ana scored was already printed before it threw. printf writes as it goes, so a partial line reaches the screen first.
  3. Too many arguments is not an error at all: extras are silently ignored, which is why a value that "disappeared" is usually a missing specifier rather than a missing argument.
  4. %05.1f uses the 0 flag: pad the field with zeros instead of spaces. Width 5, one decimal, so 3.1 becomes 003.1.
  5. String.format takes exactly the same arguments as printf and returns the text instead of printing it — the right choice when the result is going into a file, a label or a message.
🎯 EXAM TIP

Read the specifier right to left. The last letter is the type, the number after the dot is the decimals, the number before it is the total width, and a minus sign means left-aligned. %-10.3f = float, 3 decimals, 10 wide, left.

Two answers worth memorising because they are asked directly:

① printf("%.2f", 3.567) gives 3.57 — it rounds. Any option offering 3.56 is testing whether you think it truncates.
② %f with no precision gives six decimal places.

For "what does this print" questions, count the padding by writing the value out and subtracting its length from the width. %8.2f on 3.14159 → the text is 3.14, 4 characters, so 4 leading spaces.

Finally: %n versus \n. Both end the line; %n is the portable one and is what printf examples use. \n inside a format string works too — it is just a character in the text.

A Scanner can read from a String exactly as it reads from the keyboard, which makes it the simplest way to pull a line apart into typed pieces.

Scanner s = new Scanner("Ada 95 3.7");
String name = s.next();        // "Ada"
int score   = s.nextInt();     // 95
double gpa  = s.nextDouble();  // 3.7

// splitting on something other than whitespace
String csv = "Ada,95,3.7";
String[] parts = csv.split(",");        // {"Ada", "95", "3.7"}
int n = Integer.parseInt(parts[1]);     // Strings must be parsed (7.13)

// building a String piece by piece
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
sb.append("Ada").append(": ").append(95);

split returns an array of Strings, always — even the numeric-looking pieces. Converting them is Integer.parseInt or Double.parseDouble, and a piece that is not a number throws NumberFormatException, which is one of the cases Unit 12 handles.

StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for (String w : words) sb.append(w).append(" ");
String line = sb.toString();          // ONE String at the end

String[] parts = "a,b,c".split(",");  // {"a","b","c"}
String joined  = String.join("-", parts);   // "a-b-c"

A String is immutable, so += in a loop allocates a new String every pass. StringBuilder is mutable — append writes into a buffer that grows — so n appends cost one object rather than n.

split takes a regular expression, not a plain string, so splitting on a dot needs split("\\.") — a bare "." matches every character and returns an empty array. A Scanner over a String is the alternative when the input is whitespace-separated and typed.

📘 DEFINITION

Scanner over a String: parsing a String with the same next/nextInt methods used for input

split(delimiter): breaks a String into an array on a delimiter; takes a regular expression

StringBuilder: a mutable buffer for assembling text without creating a String per step (4.6)

🎯 EXAM TIP

split takes a regular expression, so characters like . and | must be escaped: split("\\.") to split on a dot. Splitting a domain name on "." unescaped returns an empty array.

📊 FIGURE — ONE STRING, TWO WAYS TO TAKE IT APART
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — PARSING A CSV RECORD BOTH WAYS

Two tools, two shapes of input. split handles a delimiter you choose; a Scanner handles whitespace-separated tokens and does the typing for you.

String record = "Ada Lovelace,95,3.71";
String[] parts = record.split(",");
System.out.println("pieces: " + parts.length);
for (int i = 0; i < parts.length; i++)
    System.out.println(i + " -> [" + parts[i] + "]");

String name  = parts[0];
int    score = Integer.parseInt(parts[1]);
double gpa   = Double.parseDouble(parts[2]);
System.out.printf("%s | %d | %.2f%n", name, score + 5, gpa);

Scanner s = new Scanner("Ada 95 3.71");
String first = s.next();
int    sc    = s.nextInt();
double g     = s.nextDouble();
System.out.println(first + "/" + sc + "/" + g);
System.out.println("more tokens? " + s.hasNext());
  1. split(",") cuts at every comma and returns a String[] of length 3. The name keeps its internal space, because only commas were delimiters.
  2. Printing each piece inside [ ] is worth doing while debugging — it exposes stray spaces that parseInt would reject.
  3. parts[1] is the String "95", not the number 95. Integer.parseInt converts it; score + 5 then prints 100, which proves the conversion happened. Had you written parts[1] + 5 you would have got the text 955.
  4. Double.parseDouble("3.71") gives the double 3.71, printed as 3.71 by %.2f.
  5. The Scanner version never mentions parsing: next(), nextInt() and nextDouble() each consume one whitespace-separated token and return it already typed.
  6. hasNext() is false afterwards because all three tokens were consumed — the cursor is at the end of the String.
OUTPUT
pieces: 3
0 -> [Ada Lovelace]
1 -> [95]
2 -> [3.71]
Ada Lovelace | 100 | 3.71
Ada/95/3.71
more tokens? false

Choose by the separator: commas, tabs or semicolons mean split; plain spaces mean a Scanner. A Scanner cannot easily read Ada Lovelace as one field, because the space inside it is a token boundary.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — THE REGEX TRAP AND THE BUFFER

split takes a regular expression, not a literal string, and String is immutable. Both facts have visible consequences.

String[] words = { "total", "orders", "shipped" };
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for (String w : words) sb.append(w).append(" ");
System.out.println("[" + sb.toString().trim() + "]");
System.out.println("length " + sb.length());

String host = "shop.example.co.uk";
System.out.println(host.split("\\.").length);
System.out.println(host.split("\\.")[0]);
System.out.println("dot-unescaped pieces: " + host.split(".").length);

String csv = "12,,7";
System.out.println("empty middle -> " + csv.split(",").length + " [" + csv.split(",")[1] + "]");
System.out.println(String.join("-", "a", "b", "c"));

String s = "hi";
String t = s;
s += "!";
System.out.println(s + " " + t);
  1. The StringBuilder ends up holding "total orders shipped " — 21 characters including the trailing space, which is why sb.length() is 21 while the trimmed text printed is 20.
  2. split("\\.") — a backslash-escaped dot in the regex, written as \\. in Java source — splits on literal dots and gives 4 pieces, the first being shop.
  3. split(".") is the bug. In a regex . means "any character", so every character is a delimiter, every piece is empty, trailing empties are discarded, and the result is an array of length 0. No exception is thrown — you simply get nothing.
  4. "12,,7".split(",") gives 3 pieces with an empty String in the middle. Empty fields are preserved inside the data; only trailing ones are dropped. This is exactly what breaks a naive parseInt on real CSV.
  5. String.join("-", ...) is the inverse of split.
  6. The last three lines are immutability: s += "!" does not edit the original text, it builds a new String and points s at it. t still names the old one, so the output is hi! hi.
OUTPUT
[total orders shipped]
length 21
4
shop
dot-unescaped pieces: 0
empty middle -> 3 []
a-b-c
hi! hi

That final pair is why += in a loop is expensive: each pass allocates a brand-new String and abandons the previous one. A hundred appends means a hundred objects; a StringBuilder means one buffer.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Treating split's argument as plain text. It is a regular expression, so the characters . | * + ? ( ) [ ] { } ^ $ \ all mean something else. The two that bite in this course:

split(".") returns an empty array — length 0, no exception. Splitting a filename or a domain this way silently produces nothing, and the next line throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException a long way from the real cause.
split("|") on pipe-delimited data splits between every character, because | is the regex alternation operator with two empty alternatives.

How to notice it: print parts.length immediately after the split. If it is 0 or suspiciously large, the delimiter needs escaping — split("\\.") and split("\\|"). Alphanumeric delimiters and the comma need no escape, which is why split(",") lulls you into trusting the rest.

File input is 9.1 with a different source, plus two obligations the keyboard did not have: the file may not exist, and the file must be closed.

import java.io.File;
import java.io.FileNotFoundException;
import java.util.Scanner;

public static void main(String[] args) throws FileNotFoundException {
    File f = new File("data.txt");
    Scanner in = new Scanner(f);            // may throw FileNotFoundException

    while (in.hasNextLine()) {              // the standard read-until-empty loop
        String line = in.nextLine();
        System.out.println(line);
    }
    in.close();                              // release the handle
}

hasNextLine() is what replaces the sentinel value of 4.2 — the stream itself reports when it is exhausted, so no magic value is needed. The throws clause on main is the minimal way to satisfy the compiler; try-catch (12.3) is the version that can actually respond to a missing file.

try (Scanner in = new Scanner(new File("data.txt"))) {
    while (in.hasNextLine()) {
        String line = in.nextLine();
        // ...
    }
} catch (FileNotFoundException e) {
    System.out.println("Could not open the file");
}

FileNotFoundException is a checked exception: the compiler refuses to build code that neither catches it nor declares throws. That is the difference from ArrayIndexOutOfBounds, which is unchecked and only appears at run time.

hasNextLine() before nextLine() is what stops the read at the end of the file; calling nextLine() with nothing left throws NoSuchElementException. The same pairing applies to hasNextInt/nextInt.

The resource declared in the try(...) parentheses is closed automatically, in reverse order, before any catch runs — which is why this form is preferred over closing by hand in a finally block. A relative path is resolved against the directory the program was started from, not the source file's directory.

📘 DEFINITION

File: an object naming a path; creating one does not open or read anything

FileNotFoundException: a checked exception — the compiler forces you to handle or declare it

hasNextLine() / hasNextInt(): tests whether more input of that kind is available

close(): releases the operating-system file handle

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Forgetting close() leaves the handle open — and the garbage collector will not fix it (8.4), because collection is about memory, not operating-system resources. Use try-with-resources if the syntax is available to you.

✅ Also covered in depth: Advanced → try-with-resources and File I/O

📊 FIGURE — READING A FILE: THE SAME LOOP, A DIFFERENT SOURCE
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — WRITE A FILE, READ IT BACK, THEN ASK FOR ONE THAT IS NOT THERE

Everything about file input is in this one program: creating the file, the read-until-exhausted loop, and what happens when the path is wrong.

File f = new File("readings.txt");
try (PrintWriter setup = new PrintWriter(f)) {
    setup.println("Ana 22.50");
    setup.println("Ben 14.00");
    setup.println("Cy 31.25");
}
System.out.println("exists? " + f.exists() + "  (a File object alone creates nothing)");

double total = 0;
int lines = 0;
try (Scanner in = new Scanner(f)) {
    while (in.hasNextLine()) {
        String line = in.nextLine();
        lines++;
        String[] p = line.split(" ");
        total += Double.parseDouble(p[1]);
    }
}
System.out.println("lines=" + lines);
System.out.printf("total=%.2f%n", total);

File missing = new File("nope.txt");
System.out.println("missing exists? " + missing.exists());
try {
    Scanner bad = new Scanner(missing);
} catch (FileNotFoundException e) {
    System.out.println("caught " + e.getClass().getSimpleName());
}
  1. new File("readings.txt") builds an object that names a path. On its own it opens nothing, creates nothing and reads nothing — which is why the last few lines can construct a File for a non-existent path without any error at all.
  2. The PrintWriter is what actually creates the file. f.exists() is then true.
  3. new Scanner(f) opens the file for reading. This is the call that can throw FileNotFoundException, and because it is checked, the compiler will not let the line stand unguarded.
  4. The loop shape is while (hasNextLine()) { nextLine(); }. The stream itself reports when it is exhausted — no sentinel value, no line count known in advance.
  5. Each line is split on the space and p[1] parsed as a double: 22.50 + 14.00 + 31.25 = 67.75, and three lines were read.
  6. The failure case is explicit at the end: missing.exists() is false, and constructing the Scanner throws FileNotFoundException, caught and named.
OUTPUT
exists? true  (a File object alone creates nothing)
lines=3
total=67.75
missing exists? false
caught FileNotFoundException

Both Scanners are declared inside try (...), so both are closed automatically at the end of their block — before any catch runs, and whether or not anything threw.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — READING PAST THE END, AND THE nextInt / nextLine COLLISION

Two failures that look like file problems and are actually cursor problems. Both are reproduced here with a String source so the behaviour is identical and visible.

Scanner in = new Scanner("7\nAda Lovelace\n");
int    n    = in.nextInt();
String rest = in.nextLine();
String name = in.nextLine();
System.out.println("n=" + n);
System.out.println("rest=[" + rest + "]");
System.out.println("name=[" + name + "]");

Scanner two = new Scanner("42");
System.out.println(two.nextInt());
System.out.println("hasNextInt now? " + two.hasNextInt());
try {
    two.nextInt();
} catch (NoSuchElementException e) {
    System.out.println("caught " + e.getClass().getSimpleName());
}
  1. nextInt() reads 7 and stops. The newline after the 7 is still sitting in the stream — token reads never consume the line ending.
  2. The first nextLine() therefore returns everything from the cursor to that newline, which is nothing: rest is the empty String.
  3. The second nextLine() gets Ada Lovelace. In a real program, that is the input the user thought they were giving to the first prompt — the notorious "it skipped my question" bug.
  4. The second Scanner reads its only token, 42. hasNextInt() is then false because the stream is exhausted.
  5. Calling nextInt() anyway throws NoSuchElementException. This is the exception you get from reading past the end of a file, and it is exactly what the hasNextLine() / hasNextInt() test exists to prevent.
OUTPUT
n=7
rest=[]
name=[Ada Lovelace]
42
hasNextInt now? false
caught NoSuchElementException

The fix for the first is one throwaway in.nextLine(); after the nextInt(). The fix for the second is never calling a next… method without the matching hasNext… test in front of it.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Pair every read with its test. hasNextLine() guards nextLine(); hasNextInt() guards nextInt(). Mixing them — while (in.hasNextLine()) { in.nextInt(); } — is a favourite wrong answer, because a line that exists is not necessarily an int.

Know which exception goes with which mistake:

SituationExceptionChecked?
the file does not existFileNotFoundExceptionyes — catch or declare
reading past the endNoSuchElementExceptionno
the token is the wrong typeInputMismatchExceptionno
the text will not parseNumberFormatExceptionno

Only the first one the compiler forces you to deal with — which is why throws FileNotFoundException appears on so many main methods in examples. That is the minimum to compile, not the right answer to a design question: a program that can respond usefully should catch instead.

And remember that a relative path is resolved against the directory the program was launched from, not the folder holding the source file. "File not found" when the file is plainly there is almost always this.

File output mirrors input, with one extra hazard: opening a file for writing erases it unless you explicitly ask to append.

import java.io.PrintWriter;
import java.io.FileWriter;
import java.io.IOException;

PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter("out.txt");        // TRUNCATES the file
out.println("Ada,95");
out.printf("%.2f%n", 3.7);                            // same formatting as 9.2
out.close();                                          // REQUIRED — flushes the buffer

// appending instead of overwriting
PrintWriter app = new PrintWriter(new FileWriter("out.txt", true));

close() is not optional here in a way it almost is for reading: output is buffered, so without the close the last writes may never reach the disk and the file ends up short or empty. That is the single most common file-output bug.

try (PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter("report.txt")) {
    out.println("Total: " + total);
    out.printf("%-10s %6.2f%n", name, pay);
}                                  // closed here — and only now guaranteed on disk

new PrintWriter("report.txt") creates the file if it does not exist and truncates it to empty if it does. There is no warning and no undo. Appending instead needs new PrintWriter(new FileWriter("report.txt", true)) — the true is the append flag.

Output is buffered, so text may sit in memory rather than on disk until the writer is closed or flushed. A program that writes and then crashes without closing leaves an empty or truncated file, which is the usual explanation for "my file is blank".

PrintWriter offers the same print, println and printf as System.out, so formatting code moves between console and file unchanged.

📘 DEFINITION

PrintWriter: a writer offering print, println and printf to a file

FileWriter(path, true): the append mode constructor; false or omitted truncates

Flush: forcing buffered output out to the destination; close() flushes

IOException: the checked exception for output failures

🎯 EXAM TIP

A missing input file throws; a missing output file is created. The asymmetry catches people out — and an existing output file is silently destroyed, which is worth remembering before you run the program on real data.

✅ Also covered in depth: Advanced → try-with-resources and File I/O

📊 FIGURE — OUTPUT SITS IN A BUFFER UNTIL YOU FLUSH OR CLOSE
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — THE BUFFER, MEASURED IN BYTES

"Close the writer or your file may be empty" is usually asserted. Here it is measured: the file length is checked on disk after each step.

PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter("notes.txt");
out.println("line one");
out.println("line two");
System.out.println("written, not closed: " + new File("notes.txt").length() + " bytes");
out.flush();
System.out.println("after flush()        : " + new File("notes.txt").length() + " bytes");
out.println("line three");
out.close();
System.out.println("after close()        : " + new File("notes.txt").length() + " bytes");

PrintWriter w = new PrintWriter("out.txt");
w.println("this never reaches the disk");
System.out.println("no close at all      : " + new File("out.txt").length() + " bytes");
  1. Two full lines have been "written" and the file is 0 bytes. The text is in a buffer in memory; the constructor created the file, but nothing has travelled to the disk.
  2. flush() pushes the buffer out. The file jumps to 18 bytes — "line one\n" and "line two\n", nine characters each.
  3. A third line is written and close() called. close() flushes first, then releases the handle, so the file reaches 29 bytes (18 + "line three\n").
  4. The last two lines are the failure: a writer that is never closed and never flushed leaves the file at 0 bytes even though the program clearly wrote to it. The JVM exiting does not rescue you.
OUTPUT
written, not closed: 0 bytes
after flush()        : 18 bytes
after close()        : 29 bytes
no close at all      : 0 bytes

This is the whole explanation for "my output file is blank". The program ran, the writes happened, and the buffer was discarded at exit. close() — or a try (PrintWriter out = ...) that calls it for you — is what makes the writing real.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — TRUNCATE VERSUS APPEND, DEMONSTRATED ON THE SAME FILE

The same file is written three times. Watch the length: the second open destroys the first two lines, and only the third open preserves anything.

static void dump(String path) throws IOException {
    File f = new File(path);
    System.out.println("--- " + path + " (" + f.length() + " bytes)");
    try (Scanner in = new Scanner(f)) {
        while (in.hasNextLine()) System.out.println("| " + in.nextLine());
    }
}

try (PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter("payroll.txt")) {
    out.printf("%-10s %8.2f%n", "Ana", 22.5 * 40);
    out.printf("%-10s %8.2f%n", "Ben", 14.0 * 40);
}
dump("payroll.txt");

try (PrintWriter again = new PrintWriter("payroll.txt")) {      // TRUNCATES
    again.printf("%-10s %8.2f%n", "Cy", 31.25 * 40);
}
dump("payroll.txt");

try (PrintWriter app = new PrintWriter(new FileWriter("payroll.txt", true))) {
    app.printf("%-10s %8.2f%n", "Dee", 18.0 * 40);
}
dump("payroll.txt");
  1. The first block writes two payroll lines. %-10s left-aligns the name in ten columns and %8.2f right-aligns the pay in eight — the identical formatting you would use on the console, because PrintWriter offers the same print, println and printf. 40 bytes: two lines of 20.
  2. new PrintWriter("payroll.txt") a second time truncates the file to empty before writing a single character. Ana and Ben are gone with no warning and no way back; the file is down to 20 bytes holding only Cy.
  3. The third block wraps a FileWriter with the append flag set to true. Now Dee is added after Cy and the file grows to 40 bytes again.
  4. Each block is a try-with-resources, so each writer is closed at its closing brace — which is why dump can read complete, flushed data immediately afterwards.
OUTPUT
--- payroll.txt (40 bytes)
| Ana          900.00
| Ben          560.00
--- payroll.txt (20 bytes)
| Cy          1250.00
--- payroll.txt (40 bytes)
| Cy          1250.00
| Dee          720.00

The append constructor is the awkward one to remember because it is on FileWriter, not PrintWriter: new PrintWriter(new FileWriter(path, true)). There is no new PrintWriter(path, true) that means append — that overload sets the character encoding.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Opening an output file to "check" it, or to write a second batch. new PrintWriter(path) truncates on construction — before any println, before any condition is tested, before you decide you had nothing to write after all. Running the program twice therefore leaves you with only the second run's output, and running it once on a file of real data destroys that data.

How to notice it: the file is shorter than expected, or contains only the last few records. If a program opens the same path in a loop — for (Order o : orders) { PrintWriter p = new PrintWriter("out.txt"); ... } — the finished file holds exactly one record, the last, which is the classic symptom.

The rule to carry: open once outside the loop, write inside it, close at the end. And when you genuinely want to add to an existing file, it must be new FileWriter(path, true) — nothing else appends.

Two classes often share most of their content — a Manager is an Employee with a bonus. Inheritance lets the second class take everything the first has and add to it, so the shared part is written once.

public class Employee {
    protected String name;                    // protected: visible to subclasses
    private double salary;
    public Employee(String n, double s) { name = n; salary = s; }
    public double getSalary() { return salary; }
}

public class Manager extends Employee {
    private double bonus;

    public Manager(String n, double s, double b) {
        super(n, s);                          // MUST be the first statement
        bonus = b;
    }

    public double totalPay() { return getSalary() + bonus; }
}

super(...) calls the parent constructor, and it has to come first for the same reason this(...) does (7.9): the inherited part of the object must be built before the subclass can add to it. If you omit it, Java inserts a call to the parent’s no-argument constructor — and if the parent has none, that is a compile error.

public class Employee { ... }
public class Manager extends Employee {      // Manager IS-A Employee
    public Manager(String n, double r) {
        super(n, r);                         // FIRST statement, always
    }
}

A derived class inherits every field and method of its base class and adds its own. Java allows a class to extend exactly one class — single inheritance — while it may implement any number of interfaces.

Constructors are not inherited. The subclass constructor must run a superclass constructor first, and if you do not write super(...) Java inserts super() — the no-argument one. If the base class has no no-argument constructor, that inserted call does not compile, which is the usual cause of "constructor Employee in class Employee cannot be applied to given types".

Construction runs base-first: Employee's constructor completes before Manager's body starts, so the inherited half of the object is ready before the subclass touches it.

📘 DEFINITION

Inheritance: a class taking on the fields and methods of another

Superclass / base class: the class being extended

Subclass / derived class: the class doing the extending

extends: the keyword declaring inheritance; a class may extend only one class

super(...): calls the superclass constructor; must be the first statement

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

Inheritance is why Unit 12 works: every exception type extends Exception, so one catch (Exception e) can catch all of them. It is also the mechanism behind every collection interface in Unit 14.

✅ Also covered in depth: Inheritance → Inheritance with extends and super

📊 FIGURE — ONE OBJECT, TWO HALVES — AND THE BASE HALF IS BUILT FIRST
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — WATCHING THE CONSTRUCTORS RUN IN ORDER

Printing inside both constructors makes the ordering visible instead of asserted.

static class Employee {
    protected String name;
    private double salary;
    Employee(String n, double s) {
        System.out.println("  Employee ctor: " + n);
        name = n; salary = s;
    }
    double getSalary() { return salary; }
}
static class Manager extends Employee {
    private double bonus;
    Manager(String n, double s, double b) {
        super(n, s);                                   // MUST be first
        System.out.println("  Manager ctor: bonus " + b);
        bonus = b;
    }
    double totalPay() { return getSalary() + bonus; }
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    System.out.println("building a Manager:");
    Manager m = new Manager("Ada", 90000, 10000);
    System.out.println("name    = " + m.name);
    System.out.println("salary  = " + m.getSalary());
    System.out.println("total   = " + m.totalPay());
}
  1. new Manager(...) allocates one object big enough for both halves, then runs Manager's constructor.
  2. The first statement is super(n, s), so Employee's constructor runs to completion before anything else — its print appears first.
  3. Only then does Manager's own body execute. The output order proves it: Employee, then Manager, never the reverse.
  4. m.name works because name is protected and Manager inherited it. It is not a copy — it is the same field, in the same object.
  5. m.getSalary() works even though salary is private. The field is inside the object; the inherited public method is the only way to read it, which is encapsulation surviving inheritance intact.
  6. totalPay() is Manager's own addition, combining an inherited method with a new field: 90000 + 10000 = 100000.
OUTPUT
building a Manager:
  Employee ctor: Ada
  Manager ctor: bonus 10000.0
name    = Ada
salary  = 90000.0
total   = 100000.0
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — THE INVISIBLE super() — AND WHEN IT STOPS COMPILING

If you do not write super(...), Java inserts super() — the no-argument one. Here the chain is three deep, so the effect is easy to see.

static class Vehicle {
    Vehicle() { System.out.println("Vehicle()"); }
    Vehicle(String tag) { System.out.println("Vehicle(" + tag + ")"); }
}
static class Car extends Vehicle {
    Car() { System.out.println("Car()"); }                 // implicit super()
    Car(String tag) { super(tag); System.out.println("Car(" + tag + ")"); }
}
static class Taxi extends Car {
    Taxi() { super("fleet"); System.out.println("Taxi()"); }
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    new Car();
    System.out.println("---");
    new Taxi();
}
  1. new Car() runs Car(), which contains no super call — so the compiler put super(); at the top for you. Vehicle() prints first, then Car().
  2. new Taxi() runs Taxi(), whose explicit super("fleet") selects Car(String).
  3. Car(String) in turn calls super(tag), selecting Vehicle(String). The chain runs to the top before any body executes.
  4. Unwinding, the bodies print from the top down: Vehicle, then Car, then Taxi. Every constructor chain runs root-first.
OUTPUT
Vehicle()
Car()
---
Vehicle(fleet)
Car(fleet)
Taxi()

Now remove Vehicle(), leaving only Vehicle(String). The inserted super() in Car() has nothing to call, and the compiler says so:

class Employee {
    Employee(String n) { }        // no no-arg constructor
}
class Manager extends Employee {
    Manager() { }                  // compiler inserts super();
}
OUTPUT
error: constructor Employee in class Employee cannot be applied to given types;
    Manager() { }
              ^
  required: String
  found:    no arguments

That message is one of the most common in this course, and the cause is always the same: a base class with no no-argument constructor, and a subclass constructor that did not call super(...) explicitly. The fix is to write the call.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Expecting constructors to be inherited. They are not. Giving Employee a (String, double) constructor does not give Manager one — new Manager("Ada", 90000) will not compile unless Manager declares that constructor itself and passes the values up with super(...).

The related slip: putting super(...) somewhere other than the first line, usually after a validation check. That is a compile error — "call to super must be first statement in constructor" — because the inherited half of the object has to be built before any code can touch it. Validate inside the argument instead, or use a static helper method in the call.

How to notice both: any error mentioning constructor … cannot be applied or call to super must be first statement is this, not a problem with the fields.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Four facts about extends answer nearly every question in this section:

① One superclass only. class A extends B, C is a compile error. Multiple interfaces are fine — that is the distinction being tested.
② Constructors are never inherited, and super(...) must be the first statement.
③ Construction runs base-first, so if a question prints from several constructors, the topmost class prints first.
④ Private members are inherited but not accessible. The field exists in the object; the subclass simply cannot name it.

When a question shows a hierarchy and asks "what prints?", write the constructor chain top-down before you read the options. The order of print statements is usually the whole answer.

Access modifiers decide what a subclass can reach, and this is where protected finally earns its place — it is the level that exists specifically for inheritance.

                same class   same package   subclass   everywhere
public              yes           yes            yes        yes
protected           yes           yes            yes        no
(no modifier)       yes           yes            no         no
private             yes           no             no         no

So a subclass cannot touch a private field of its parent — not because inheritance is broken, but because private means private. The inherited field is there in the object; it is simply reachable only through the parent’s public or protected methods.

public class Manager extends Employee {
    void demo() {
        name = "x";           // OK if name is protected
        salary = 1;           // ERROR if salary is private
        getSalary();          // the correct route
    }
}
ModifierSubclass in another package can see it?
publicyes
protectedyes — this is what protected is for
package-private (no modifier)no
privateno — not even a subclass

A private field is inherited — the subclass object contains it — but the subclass cannot name it. It must go through an inherited public or protected accessor, which is exactly the encapsulation of 7.4 continuing to hold.

protected is the middle setting that exists for inheritance: visible to subclasses anywhere and to the whole of its own package, but not to unrelated classes. Making everything protected "so subclasses can get at it" gives away the ability to change those fields later.

📘 DEFINITION

protected: accessible within the package and to subclasses anywhere

Package-private: the default with no modifier; package only, not subclasses in other packages

Inherited but inaccessible: a private field exists in the subclass object but cannot be named there

🎯 EXAM TIP

Prefer private plus a protected getter over a protected field. It keeps the validation point of 7.4 intact even for subclasses.

✅ Also covered in depth: Inheritance → Inheritance with extends and super

📊 FIGURE — HOW FAR EACH MODIFIER REACHES
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — WHAT A SUBCLASS CAN TOUCH, LINE BY LINE

Three fields with three different modifiers, and a subclass that uses each in the only way it is allowed to.

static class Account {
    public    String id      = "AC-1";
    protected double balance = 250.00;
    private   String pin     = "1234";
    protected double read() { return balance; }
    public String toString() { return id + " " + balance + " " + pin; }
}
static class Savings extends Account {
    double withdraw(double amt) {
        // pin;                                   // would NOT compile
        if (amt <= balance) { balance -= amt; }   // protected — fine
        return balance;
    }
    String describe() { return id + " has " + read(); }   // public + protected
}

Savings s = new Savings();
System.out.println(s.describe());
System.out.println(s.withdraw(80));
System.out.println(s);
  1. id is public, so describe() names it directly.
  2. balance is protected, so withdraw can both read and assign it. This is the level that exists specifically so subclasses can work with inherited state.
  3. read() is a protected method — inherited and callable from the subclass for the same reason.
  4. pin is private. The commented line would fail with error: pin has private access in Account. Note the wording: the field is there, it simply has private access.
  5. The proof that pin exists in the Savings object is the last line. toString() was inherited from Account, it prints pin, and it prints correctly — because that method is inside Account, where pin is visible.
  6. withdraw(80) takes the balance from 250.00 to 170.00, and the final toString() shows all three fields including the one the subclass could never name.
OUTPUT
AC-1 has 250.0
170.0
AC-1 170.0 1234

That is the whole idea of "inherited but inaccessible": the data is part of the object, and the base class's own methods are the door to it.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — CHOOSING A MODIFIER FOR A REAL FIELD

The question is never "what is legal" but "who should be able to change this". Work through balance on an Account with a Savings subclass in another package.

ChoiceWho can assign balanceWhat goes wrong
public double balanceevery class in the programany code anywhere can set a negative balance; the class can no longer guarantee anything about its own state
protected double balanceAccount, its package, and every subclasssafer, but every future subclass can still bypass validation — and subclasses are written by people who did not read your rules
private double balance + protected double getBalance()Account only; subclasses read through the methodnothing — the single assignment point stays inside Account, where the checks live
  1. Start at private and widen only when something concrete cannot be written. That is the opposite of the instinct to make everything protected "so subclasses can get at it".
  2. A protected field is part of your class's permanent contract with every subclass, present and future. You cannot rename it, retype it, or start validating it later without breaking them.
  3. A protected method costs far less: you can change the field behind it whenever you like, as long as the method keeps behaving.
  4. The default — no modifier at all — is package-private, and the important thing to know is that it does not reach subclasses in other packages. It is the one people assume means "protected-ish", and it does not.

So the practical rule for this course: fields private, accessors protected or public. The worked example above is the proof it costs nothing — Savings got everything it needed through read().

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Believing "no modifier" means public, or means protected. It means package-private: visible to the whole package, invisible to a subclass in a different package. In single-file exercises everything is in one package, so the mistake is invisible — and then it appears the first time real code is split into packages.

The second half of the same trap: expecting protected to be narrower than package-private. It is not — it is wider in one direction and equal in the other. protected = package-private plus subclasses anywhere. There is no modifier meaning "subclasses only, not the package".

How to notice it: whenever an exam option involves "a subclass in a different package", the answer hinges on exactly one row of the reach chart. public and protected reach it; the default and private do not.

Overriding replaces an inherited method with a new version in the subclass. It is not overloading (6.12): overriding keeps the signature identical and changes the behaviour.

public class Employee {
    public String describe() { return "Employee " + name; }
}

public class Manager extends Employee {
    @Override
    public String describe() {
        return "Manager " + name + " (" + super.describe() + ")";
    }                          //          ^ calls the PARENT version
}

The @Override annotation is optional and worth always writing: it makes the compiler check that you really are overriding something, which turns a silent typo — describe() misspelled as discribe() — into a compile error instead of a method nobody calls.

class Employee { public double pay() { return base; } }

class Manager extends Employee {
    @Override
    public double pay() {
        return super.pay() + bonus;      // reuse the base version, then extend
    }
}

An override replaces an inherited method with one of the same signature. Same name, same parameter list — change either and it is an overload, a second unrelated method, and the base version still runs.

@Override is optional and worth writing every time: it asks the compiler to check that something really is being overridden, which turns a silent typo (Pay(), or a wrong parameter type) into a compile error.

OverridingOverloading
wheresubclass replaces a base methodsame class, several methods, one name
signaturemust be identicalmust differ
chosenat run time, by the objectat compile time, by the arguments

An override may widen visibility (protected → public) but never narrow it, and must not throw broader checked exceptions.

📘 DEFINITION

Overriding: redefining an inherited method with the same signature

@Override: an annotation asking the compiler to verify the override

super.method(): calls the superclass version from inside the override

Covariant return: an override may return a subtype of the original return type

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Overloading versus overriding is the most-tested pair in Unit 10. Same name, different parameters, same class → overloading, resolved at compile time. Same name, same parameters, subclass → overriding, resolved at run time.

✅ Also covered in depth: Inheritance → Method Overriding and Polymorphism

📊 FIGURE — OVERRIDING: THE OBJECT DECIDES, NOT THE VARIABLE
🎯 EXAM TIP
Two-step check for these questions: ① does the declared type HAVE the method (else compiler error)? ② which class’s VERSION runs — always the actual object’s. Fields, unlike methods, follow the declared type.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — OVERRIDE, OVERLOAD AND FIELD HIDING IN ONE PROGRAM

Three things that look alike in source and behave completely differently at run time. The output separates them.

static class Employee {
    protected String name = "Employee";
    String describe() { return "Employee " + name; }
    String describe(String prefix) { return prefix + " " + describe(); }   // OVERLOAD
}
static class Manager extends Employee {
    protected String name = "Manager";                  // HIDES the field
    @Override String describe() { return "Manager (" + super.describe() + ")"; }
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    Manager  m = new Manager();
    Employee e = m;                       // same object, base-typed variable
    System.out.println(m.describe());
    System.out.println(e.describe());
    System.out.println(e.describe("Staff:"));
    System.out.println(e.name);
    System.out.println(m.name);
    System.out.println(((Employee) m).name);
}
  1. m.describe() runs Manager's override, which calls super.describe() — Employee's version. Inside that method, the unqualified name means Employee's field, because fields are resolved where the code is written. So it produces Employee Employee, wrapped as Manager (Employee Employee).
  2. e.describe() prints exactly the same thing. The variable is typed Employee, but the object is a Manager, and methods are chosen by the object.
  3. e.describe("Staff:") resolves to the one-argument overload, which exists only in Employee. Overloads are picked at compile time from the argument list. That method then calls describe() with no arguments, which dispatches to Manager's override — so the Manager text still appears.
  4. e.name prints Employee. Fields do not dispatch. Two fields named name exist in this object, and which one you get is decided by the declared type of the variable.
  5. m.name prints Manager — same object, different variable type, different field.
  6. ((Employee) m).name prints Employee, proving the point: casting changes nothing about the object, only about which field name is visible.
OUTPUT
Manager (Employee Employee)
Manager (Employee Employee)
Staff: Manager (Employee Employee)
Employee
Manager
Employee

Lines 4 to 6 are why field hiding is a bug rather than a technique: the same object answers name differently depending on how you happen to be holding it. Give the subclass field a different name, or reuse the inherited one.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — WHAT COUNTS AS AN OVERRIDE — AND WHAT THE COMPILER SAYS WHEN IT IS NOT

Same name is not enough. The parameter list must match exactly; the return type may narrow; the visibility may only widen.

static class Shape {
    double area() { return 0; }
    Object copy() { return this; }
    void scale(double f) { System.out.println("Shape.scale " + f); }
}
static class Circle extends Shape {
    double r;
    Circle(double r) { this.r = r; }
    @Override double area() { return Math.PI * r * r; }      // true override
    @Override Circle copy() { return new Circle(r); }        // COVARIANT return — still an override
    void scale(int f) { System.out.println("Circle.scale(int) " + f); }   // OVERLOAD
}

Shape s = new Circle(2);
System.out.printf("%.4f%n", s.area());
s.scale(3);
s.scale(3.0);
Circle c = new Circle(2);
c.scale(3);
c.scale(3.0);
Circle copy = new Circle(5).copy();
System.out.printf("%.4f%n", copy.area());
  1. s.area() runs Circle's version: π × 2² = 12.5664. A genuine override, chosen by the object.
  2. s.scale(3) — the variable is a Shape, and Shape has only scale(double). The int 3 widens to 3.0 and Shape's method runs. Circle.scale(int) is invisible from this variable.
  3. s.scale(3.0) — same method, same output. Nothing surprising yet.
  4. c.scale(3) with a Circle variable now sees both methods, and scale(int) is an exact match, so Circle's runs. Changing only the variable's type changed which method executes — the signature of an overload, not an override.
  5. c.scale(3.0) falls back to Shape's. One object, two methods called scale, chosen entirely at compile time by the argument type.
  6. copy() returns Circle where the base returned Object. That is a covariant return and it is a legal override — which is why Circle copy = ...copy(); compiles with no cast. π × 5² = 78.5398.
OUTPUT
12.5664
Shape.scale 3.0
Shape.scale 3.0
Circle.scale(int) 3
Shape.scale 3.0
78.5398

Two overrides that are not allowed, with the compiler's exact words:

class Sub extends Base { protected String describe() { … } }   // Base had public
OUTPUT
error: describe() in Sub cannot override describe() in Base
  attempting to assign weaker access privileges; was public
class Sub extends Base { @Override public String discribe() { … } }   // typo
OUTPUT
error: method does not override or implement a method from a supertype

The second is the whole argument for writing @Override: without it, discribe() compiles perfectly as a brand-new method that nothing ever calls, and the program silently keeps using the base version.

Every class in Java extends Object, directly or through its parents. That is why every object already has toString(), equals() and hashCode() — and why the inherited versions are usually not what you want.

public class Student {
    private String name;
    private int score;

    @Override
    public String toString() {                 // called automatically by println
        return name + " (" + score + ")";
    }

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        if (!(o instanceof Student)) { return false; }
        Student other = (Student) o;
        return name.equals(other.name) && score == other.score;
    }
}

Without the override, System.out.println(student) prints something like Student@1b6d3586 — the class name and a hash. And equals inherited from Object is just ==, which is the identity comparison of 7.10 and almost never the comparison you want.

Every class extends Object, directly or through its ancestors, so every object has these whether you write them or not.

MethodDefault behaviourOverride it to
toString()Student@1b6d — class name and hashprint something meaningful
equals(Object)reference comparison, same as ==compare contents
hashCode()derived from the addressagree with equals

System.out.println(obj) and String concatenation both call toString() automatically — so the Student@1b6d output is the visible sign that a class has not defined one.

The contract that matters: if two objects are equals they must return the same hashCode. Overriding equals without hashCode breaks HashMap and HashSet, which look the object up by hash first and never find it.

📘 DEFINITION

Object: the root of the class hierarchy; every class inherits from it

toString(): the String form of an object; called implicitly by println and concatenation

equals(Object): content comparison; must take Object as its parameter to be a true override

hashCode(): must be overridden alongside equals for HashMap and HashSet to work (14.3)

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Writing equals(Student o) instead of equals(Object o) creates an overload, not an override. The inherited identity version is still what collections call — which is why @Override is worth writing.

✅ Also covered in depth: Advanced → equals(), hashCode() and toString()

📊 FIGURE — EVERY CLASS DESCENDS FROM Object — AND THE HASH CONTRACT
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — WHAT toString, equals AND hashCode DO BEFORE AND AFTER YOU OVERRIDE THEM

The default versions are inherited from Object and are almost never what you want. This program shows both states side by side.

static class Plain { int id = 7; }                       // no overrides
static class Student {
    String name; int score;
    Student(String n, int s) { name = n; score = s; }
    @Override public String toString() { return name + " (" + score + ")"; }
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        if (this == o) return true;
        if (!(o instanceof Student)) return false;
        Student other = (Student) o;
        return score == other.score && name.equals(other.name);
    }
    @Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(name, score); }
}

Plain p = new Plain();
String s = p.toString();
System.out.println(s.startsWith("M104a$Plain@"));
System.out.println(s.equals("M104a$Plain@" + Integer.toHexString(p.hashCode())));

Student a = new Student("Ada", 95);
Student b = new Student("Ada", 95);
System.out.println(a);
System.out.println("a == b      : " + (a == b));
System.out.println("a.equals(b) : " + a.equals(b));
System.out.println("same hash   : " + (a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()));

Set<Student> set = new HashSet<>();
set.add(a); set.add(b);
System.out.println("set size    : " + set.size());
System.out.println("contains    : " + set.contains(new Student("Ada", 95)));
System.out.println("list toString: " + Arrays.asList(a, b));
  1. Plain overrides nothing, so its toString() is the inherited one. The two true results prove its exact recipe: the class name, an @, and the hash code in hexadecimal. That output — Plain@1b6d3586 — is the visible sign that a class has no toString.
  2. System.out.println(a) calls toString() automatically, so the Student prints as Ada (95). The same happens inside String concatenation.
  3. a == b is false — two separate objects, two different addresses. == compares identity and always will; overriding equals does not change it.
  4. a.equals(b) is true, because the override compares contents. The instanceof test also handles null safely: null instanceof Student is false, so a null argument returns false rather than throwing.
  5. hashCode() agrees with equals: equal objects give equal hashes.
  6. That agreement is what makes the collection lines work. Adding both to a HashSet gives size 1, and contains finds a brand-new but equal Student.
  7. The last line shows toString being used by the collection itself — a list prints its elements by calling theirs.
OUTPUT
true
true
Ada (95)
a == b      : false
a.equals(b) : true
same hash   : true
set size    : 1
contains    : true
list toString: [Ada (95), Ada (95)]
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — THE TWO WAYS equals GOES WRONG, WITH THE DAMAGE MEASURED

One class overloads instead of overriding; the other overrides equals but forgets hashCode. Both compile. Both are broken, in different places.

static class Badly {
    String code;
    Badly(String c) { code = c; }
    public boolean equals(Badly o) { return code.equals(o.code); }   // OVERLOAD
}
static class Half {
    String code;
    Half(String c) { code = c; }
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return (o instanceof Half) && code.equals(((Half) o).code);
    }
    // hashCode deliberately NOT overridden
}

Badly x = new Badly("A1"), y = new Badly("A1");
System.out.println("Badly, typed:  " + x.equals(y));
Object yo = y;
System.out.println("Badly, as Object: " + x.equals(yo));
List<Badly> bl = new ArrayList<>(); bl.add(x);
System.out.println("list.contains: " + bl.contains(y));

Half h1 = new Half("A1"), h2 = new Half("A1");
System.out.println("Half equals:   " + h1.equals(h2));
List<Half> hl = new ArrayList<>(); hl.add(h1);
System.out.println("list.contains: " + hl.contains(h2));
Set<Half> hs = new HashSet<>(); hs.add(h1);
System.out.println("set.contains:  " + hs.contains(h2));
  1. x.equals(y) with both typed Badly picks the overload and returns true. Everything looks fine, which is why this bug survives testing.
  2. Assign y to an Object variable and call again: now the argument type is Object, so the inherited identity version runs and returns false. Same two objects, opposite answer.
  3. bl.contains(y) is false, because ArrayList.contains is written against equals(Object) — the version that was never overridden. The library can only call the real override, and there isn't one.
  4. Half gets this right: equals(Object), so h1.equals(h2) is true and hl.contains(h2) is true — an ArrayList searches linearly, calling equals on each element.
  5. But hs.contains(h2) is false. A HashSet computes the hash first to choose a bucket, and the inherited hashCode is address-based, so h1 and h2 land in different buckets. contains looks in one bucket and never sees the equal object sitting in another.
OUTPUT
Badly, typed:  true
Badly, as Object: false
list.contains: false
Half equals:   true
list.contains: true
set.contains:  false

The fix in both cases is mechanical. Write equals(Object), mark it @Override, and override hashCode() in the same commit — return Objects.hash(field1, field2); using exactly the fields equals compares.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Recognise Student@1b6d3586 instantly. It means "this class has no toString()", and the format is always class name @ hash in hex. If a question shows that output, the answer involves a missing override.

The equals/hashCode contract, stated the way it is tested: if a.equals(b) then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode() must hold. The reverse is not required — unequal objects may share a hash, which is just a collision.

Three near-certain question shapes:

① equals(Student o) versus equals(Object o) — the first is an overload and collections ignore it.
② == versus .equals() on two objects with identical contents: == false, equals true (assuming a proper override).
③ Overriding equals without hashCode — breaks HashSet and HashMap, leaves ArrayList.contains working. The asymmetry is the point.

Also worth knowing: toString() is called implicitly by println, by String concatenation, and by a collection printing its elements. You never have to call it by name.

Polymorphism is the payoff of the whole unit: a variable of the parent type can hold any subclass object, and calling an overridden method runs the subclass version. The decision is made at run time from the actual object, not at compile time from the declared type.

Employee e = new Manager("Ada", 90000, 10000);   // legal — a Manager IS an Employee

e.describe();      // runs Manager's version — DYNAMIC DISPATCH
e.totalPay();      // COMPILE ERROR — the declared type is Employee,
                   // which has no totalPay

((Manager) e).totalPay();       // a downcast makes it visible again

The two halves are easy to state together: the declared type decides what you may call, and the actual object decides which version runs. Nearly every polymorphism exam question is that sentence applied to specific code.

Employee e = new Manager("Ana", 30);   // base-type reference, subclass object
e.pay();                               // runs MANAGER's pay — decided at run time
e.approveLeave();                      // COMPILE ERROR — not on Employee

Employee[] staff = { new Employee(...), new Manager(...) };
for (Employee x : staff) total += x.pay();   // each runs its own version

Two different rules apply at two different times, and keeping them apart answers nearly every polymorphism question:

Decided byWhenGoverns
the reference typecompile timewhich methods you are allowed to call
the object typerun timewhich version actually runs

So a base-type reference can only call base-type methods, but the subclass's override is what executes — dynamic dispatch. That is what lets one loop over an array of mixed subclasses do the right thing for each.

Fields do not work this way. A field with the same name in a subclass hides rather than overrides, and which one you get is decided by the reference type — which is why field hiding is a bug, not a technique.

📘 DEFINITION

Polymorphism: one reference type behaving as any of its subtypes

Dynamic dispatch: choosing the method implementation at run time from the object’s real class

Upcast: treating a subclass reference as its parent type; always safe and implicit

Downcast: casting back to the subclass; requires an explicit cast and can throw ClassCastException

🎯 EXAM TIP

Guard a downcast with instanceof. if (e instanceof Manager) { ((Manager) e).totalPay(); } is the safe idiom; casting blind throws ClassCastException at run time.

✅ Also covered in depth: Inheritance → Method Overriding and Polymorphism

📊 FIGURE — TWO DECISIONS, TWO DIFFERENT TIMES
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — ONE OBJECT, THREE BEHAVIOURS, AND THE TWO RULES IN ACTION

Every line below is one of the two rules applied. Read the declared type to decide whether it compiles; read the object to decide what it prints.

static class Employee {
    String name; double base;
    Employee(String n, double b) { name = n; base = b; }
    double pay()   { return base; }
    String role()  { return "Employee"; }
    String card()  { return role() + " " + name + " earns " + pay(); }
}
static class Manager extends Employee {
    double bonus;
    Manager(String n, double b, double bo) { super(n, b); bonus = bo; }
    @Override double pay()  { return super.pay() + bonus; }
    @Override String role() { return "Manager"; }
    void approveLeave() { System.out.println(name + " approves leave"); }
}
static class Contractor extends Employee {
    double hours, rate;
    Contractor(String n, double h, double r) { super(n, 0); hours = h; rate = r; }
    @Override double pay()  { return hours * rate; }
    @Override String role() { return "Contractor"; }
}

Employee e = new Manager("Ada", 90000, 10000);
System.out.println(e.pay());
System.out.println(e.role());
System.out.println(e.card());
// e.approveLeave();                 // COMPILE ERROR
((Manager) e).approveLeave();

Employee c = new Contractor("Bo", 120, 85);
System.out.println(c.card());

Employee[] staff = { new Employee("Cy", 50000), e, c };
double total = 0;
for (Employee x : staff) { total += x.pay(); }
System.out.println("total " + total);
  1. e.pay() — the variable is an Employee, so the call is legal; the object is a Manager, so Manager's override runs: 90000 + 10000 = 100000.0.
  2. e.role() is Manager for the same reason.
  3. e.card() is the interesting one. card() exists only in Employee and was written long before Manager. Yet the role() and pay() calls inside it dispatch to Manager's versions — a parent method calling child methods without knowing they exist.
  4. e.approveLeave() does not compile, because Employee has no such method. The error is cannot find symbol … location: variable e of type Employee — the compiler names the declared type explicitly.
  5. ((Manager) e).approveLeave() works: the cast changes what the compiler is willing to let you call. It changes nothing about the object.
  6. The Contractor prints Contractor Bo earns 10200.0 — 120 × 85 — through exactly the same card() method.
  7. The loop adds 50000 + 100000 + 10200 = 160200.0. It never mentions Manager or Contractor: adding a fourth subclass tomorrow would not change a character of it.
OUTPUT
100000.0
Manager
Manager Ada earns 100000.0
Ada approves leave
Contractor Bo earns 10200.0
total 160200.0
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — CASTING SAFELY — instanceof, THE PATTERN VARIABLE, AND THE CRASH

A downcast is a claim about the object. If the claim is false the JVM stops you, at run time, with no compiler warning beforehand.

Employee e = new Manager("Ada", 90000, 10000);
Employee c = new Contractor("Bo", 120, 85);

Object o = e;
System.out.println(o instanceof Manager);
System.out.println(c instanceof Manager);
try {
    Manager bad = (Manager) c;
} catch (ClassCastException ex) {
    System.out.println("caught " + ex.getClass().getSimpleName());
}
  1. o instanceof Manager is true. The variable is typed Object, but instanceof asks about the object, not the variable.
  2. c instanceof Manager is false: a Contractor is an Employee, but it is not a Manager. Sibling subclasses are unrelated to each other.
  3. (Manager) c compiles — the compiler allows any cast between related types, because it cannot know what the variable will hold at run time.
  4. At run time the JVM checks the actual class, finds a Contractor, and throws ClassCastException. That is the whole reason to test first.
OUTPUT
true
false
caught ClassCastException

The three shapes worth knowing, in increasing order of preference:

// ① blind — throws when it is wrong
Manager m = (Manager) e;

// ② guarded — the classic idiom
if (e instanceof Manager) {
    Manager m = (Manager) e;
    m.approveLeave();
}

// ③ pattern variable — test and declare in one step
if (e instanceof Manager m) {
    m.approveLeave();
}

Also useful: an upcast is the opposite direction — Employee e = new Manager(...) — and needs no cast and can never fail, because a Manager genuinely is an Employee. Only downcasts are claims that can be wrong.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Expecting fields to be polymorphic. They are not. If both classes declare a field with the same name, the one you get depends on the declared type of the variable, not the object — so e.name and ((Manager) e).name can print different values for the very same object. Methods dispatch; fields do not.

The second half: expecting the cast to change the object. ((Manager) e).approveLeave() does not turn e into a Manager and does not create one — it was always a Manager, and the cast merely persuades the compiler to let you say so. Casting a Contractor to Manager does not convert anything; it throws.

How to notice both: if an exam option claims a cast "converts" an object, or that a subclass field "overrides" the parent's, it is wrong. Only methods are overridden, and only objects decide which one runs.
