Polymorphism plus a collection is where it becomes genuinely useful: one list holds mixed subclasses, and one loop calls the right version for each.

ArrayList staff = new ArrayList<>();
staff.add(new Employee("Bob", 50000));
staff.add(new Manager("Ada", 90000, 10000));

for (Employee e : staff) {
    System.out.println(e.describe());     // each runs ITS OWN version
}

// reaching subclass-only behaviour requires a check plus a cast
double total = 0;
for (Employee e : staff) {
    total += (e instanceof Manager) ? ((Manager) e).totalPay() : e.getSalary();
}

The loop never mentions Manager in the first case, and adding a third subclass tomorrow requires no change to it at all. That is the argument for polymorphism over a chain of instanceof checks — the second loop is the version you should be slightly unhappy about.

ArrayList<Employee> staff = new ArrayList<>();
staff.add(new Manager("Ana", 30));

for (Employee e : staff) {
    System.out.println(e.pay());          // polymorphic — no cast needed
    if (e instanceof Manager) {           // guard BEFORE casting
        Manager m = (Manager) e;
        m.approveLeave();                 // subclass-only method
    }
}

A list declared with the base type holds any subclass, and calling an overridden method needs no cast — that is the whole benefit. A cast is needed only to reach something the subclass adds.

Casting without checking throws ClassCastException at run time, so instanceof comes first. Modern Java combines them: if (e instanceof Manager m) { m.approveLeave(); } tests and declares in one step.

Frequent instanceof chains usually mean the behaviour belongs in an overridden method instead — let each subclass answer for itself rather than asking the list what type everything is.

📘 DEFINITION

Heterogeneous collection: a collection holding several subclasses through their common parent type

instanceof: tests whether an object is of a given type, including subtypes

ClassCastException: thrown at run time by a cast the actual object does not satisfy

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

If you find yourself writing a long chain of instanceof tests, the behaviour probably belongs in an overridden method instead. That is the design lesson 10.7 formalises.

📊 FIGURE — ONE LIST, ONE LOOP, THREE DIFFERENT METHOD BODIES
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A MIXED PAYROLL IN ONE LIST

Four classes, three of them subclasses, one loop that mentions none of them.

static abstract class Employee {
    String name;
    Employee(String n) { name = n; }
    abstract double pay();
    @Override public String toString() {
        return String.format("%-10s %8.2f", name, pay());
    }
}
static class Salaried extends Employee {
    double annual;
    Salaried(String n, double a) { super(n); annual = a; }
    @Override double pay() { return annual / 26; }
}
static class Hourly extends Employee {
    double hours, rate;
    Hourly(String n, double h, double r) { super(n); hours = h; rate = r; }
    @Override double pay() { return hours * rate; }
}
static class Manager extends Salaried {
    double bonus;
    Manager(String n, double a, double b) { super(n, a); bonus = b; }
    @Override double pay() { return super.pay() + bonus; }
    void approveLeave() { System.out.println("  " + name + " approved leave"); }
}

ArrayList<Employee> staff = new ArrayList<>();
staff.add(new Salaried("Ana", 78000));
staff.add(new Hourly("Ben", 72, 22.50));
staff.add(new Manager("Cy", 104000, 1500));

double total = 0;
for (Employee e : staff) {
    System.out.println(e);
    total += e.pay();
}
System.out.printf("%-10s %8.2f%n", "TOTAL", total);

for (Employee e : staff) {
    if (e instanceof Manager m) { m.approveLeave(); }
}
System.out.println(staff.get(1).getClass().getSimpleName());
System.out.println(staff.get(2) instanceof Salaried);
  1. The list is declared ArrayList<Employee>, so it accepts any subclass. That single declaration is what makes the mixture legal.
  2. System.out.println(e) calls the inherited toString(), which calls pay() — and pay() dispatches to whichever subclass the element actually is. Ana: 78000 / 26 = 3000.00. Ben: 72 × 22.50 = 1620.00. Cy: 104000 / 26 = 4000, + 1500 = 5500.00.
  3. Manager extends Salaried, not Employee directly, so super.pay() reaches Salaried's version. Dispatch walks up from the actual class, however deep the chain is.
  4. The total, 10120.00, was accumulated by a loop containing the single expression e.pay().
  5. approveLeave() exists only on Manager, so the second loop guards with instanceof Manager m — the pattern form, which tests and declares m in one step. Only Cy matches.
  6. getClass().getSimpleName() reports Hourly for element 1 — the real class, regardless of the declared element type.
  7. staff.get(2) instanceof Salaried is true: instanceof accepts any ancestor type, not just the exact class.
OUTPUT
Ana         3000.00
Ben         1620.00
Cy          5500.00
TOTAL      10120.00
  Cy approved leave
Hourly
true
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — WHY THE POLYMORPHIC LOOP BEATS THE instanceof CHAIN

Both versions produce the same total today. Only one of them survives a new requirement.

// ① the instanceof chain — every type named, in one place
double total = 0;
for (Employee e : staff) {
    if (e instanceof Manager m)        total += m.annual / 26 + m.bonus;
    else if (e instanceof Hourly h)    total += h.hours * h.rate;
    else if (e instanceof Salaried s)  total += s.annual / 26;
}

// ② the polymorphic loop — no type named at all
double total = 0;
for (Employee e : staff) total += e.pay();
  1. Ordering. Version ① only works because Manager is tested before Salaried. Manager extends Salaried, so a Manager matches both tests — put Salaried first and every manager silently loses their bonus. Version ② has no ordering to get wrong.
  2. Fields. Version ① reads m.annual and h.rate from outside, so those fields cannot be private and the payroll formula now lives in two places. Version ② asks the object and lets it answer.
  3. Adding a class. A new Intern subclass needs a new branch in ① — and if you forget one, the total is quietly wrong rather than a compile error. In ② the new class supplies pay() and every existing loop is already correct.
  4. Counting the branches. Version ① has one branch per subclass per loop. With four loops and five subclasses that is twenty places to keep in step; version ② has five method bodies and nothing to keep in step.

The abstract pay() makes this enforceable rather than merely advisable: a subclass that fails to supply one does not compile — error: Intern is not abstract and does not override abstract method pay(). The compiler becomes the checklist that version ① needs a human for.

The legitimate use of instanceof is the one in the first worked example: reaching behaviour that genuinely exists on only one subclass, like approveLeave(). Reaching for it to compute something every subclass has is the smell.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Testing subclasses in the wrong order. instanceof matches ancestors too, so in a hierarchy where Manager extends Salaried, the test e instanceof Salaried is true for a Manager. Put the general test first and the specific branch becomes unreachable — silently, at run time, with no compiler complaint at all (unlike catch blocks, where the compiler does object).

How to notice it: draw the hierarchy and check that each instanceof chain runs most specific first, exactly like catch blocks in Unit 12. If one type extends another in your chain, the deeper one must be tested earlier.

The second, quieter version: e.getClass() == Manager.class is not the same test as e instanceof Manager. The first is exact-class and excludes any future subclass of Manager; the second includes them. Mixing them up produces code that works until someone extends your class.

🎯 EXAM TIP

For "what does this loop print?" questions, resolve each element separately: what is the actual class, and does that class override the method being called? Work up the chain from the actual class until you find a body. The declared type of the list only decides which methods you are allowed to call.

Facts that get tested directly:

① ArrayList<Employee> can hold any subclass. It cannot hold an unrelated class, and it cannot hold a primitive — ArrayList<int> is a compile error.
② No cast is needed to call an overridden method; a cast is needed to call a method the subclass adds.
③ instanceof is true for the class and every ancestor, and false for null — which is why if (x instanceof Manager) never needs a null check in front of it.

Watch for the sneaky ArrayList<Object> variant: it holds anything, but you can then call only Object's methods without casting, which is precisely the pre-generics problem Unit 13 exists to solve.

Sometimes the parent class has no sensible implementation of a method. What area does a generic Shape have? An abstract class answers this: it declares the method, refuses to implement it, and forbids anyone from creating a plain Shape.

public abstract class Shape {
    protected String name;
    public Shape(String n) { name = n; }        // abstract classes CAN have constructors

    public abstract double area();               // no body — subclasses must supply one

    public String describe() {                   // concrete method — inherited as is
        return name + " with area " + area();
    }
}

Shape s = new Shape("x");     // COMPILE ERROR — cannot instantiate an abstract class

Note that describe() calls area(), a method that does not exist yet. That works because of dynamic dispatch (10.5): by the time it runs, the object is a real subclass with a real area.

public abstract class Shape {
    private String name;
    public Shape(String n) { name = n; }       // abstract classes DO have constructors
    public String getName() { return name; }   // concrete: inherited as-is
    public abstract double area();             // no body — subclasses must supply one
}

Shape s = new Shape("x");                      // COMPILE ERROR
Shape s = new Circle(2);                       // fine — Circle is concrete

An abstract class cannot be instantiated because it is deliberately incomplete: there is no sensible area() for "a shape in general". It can still have fields, constructors and fully written methods, and its constructor runs via super(...) when a subclass is built.

Any class containing an abstract method must itself be declared abstract. A subclass must implement every inherited abstract method or be declared abstract in turn, which is how the requirement passes down until some class finally satisfies it.

📘 DEFINITION

abstract class: a class that cannot be instantiated, meant to be extended

abstract method: a method with a signature and no body; subclasses must implement it

Concrete subclass: a subclass implementing every abstract method, so it can be instantiated

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

A subclass that does not implement every abstract method must itself be declared abstract, or it will not compile. There is no way to leave one unimplemented in a concrete class.

✅ Also covered in depth: Inheritance → Abstract Classes and Interfaces

📊 FIGURE — AN ABSTRACT CLASS IS A CLASS WITH A HOLE IN IT
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A CONCRETE METHOD CALLING A METHOD THAT DOES NOT EXIST YET

Shape.describe() calls area(), which has no body anywhere in Shape. It works, and the reason is dynamic dispatch.

static abstract class Shape {
    private String name;
    Shape(String n) { name = n; System.out.println("  Shape ctor for " + n); }
    String getName() { return name; }
    abstract double area();                               // no body
    String describe() { return String.format("%s area %.2f", name, area()); }
}
static class Circle extends Shape {
    private double r;
    Circle(double r) { super("Circle"); this.r = r; }
    @Override double area() { return Math.PI * r * r; }
}
static class Rect extends Shape {
    private double w, h;
    Rect(double w, double h) { super("Rect"); this.w = w; this.h = h; }
    @Override double area() { return w * h; }
}
static abstract class Quad extends Shape { Quad(String n) { super(n); } }   // still abstract
static class Square extends Quad {
    private double s;
    Square(double s) { super("Square"); this.s = s; }
    @Override double area() { return s * s; }
}

ArrayList<Shape> shapes = new ArrayList<>();
shapes.add(new Circle(2));
shapes.add(new Rect(3, 4));
shapes.add(new Square(5));
System.out.println("--");
for (Shape s : shapes) System.out.println(s.describe());
double total = 0;
for (Shape s : shapes) total += s.area();
System.out.printf("total %.2f%n", total);
System.out.println(shapes.get(2) instanceof Quad);
System.out.println(shapes.get(0).getClass().getSimpleName());
  1. Abstract classes have constructors, and they run. All three "Shape ctor" lines appear before the --, once per object created — a constructor is not the same thing as an instantiation.
  2. describe() is a fully written, inherited method. Its call to area() is a normal virtual call: by the time it executes, the object is a real Circle, Rect or Square, and the JVM finds a real body.
  3. π × 2² = 12.57, 3 × 4 = 12.00, 5² = 25.00. One method, three answers, and Shape knows about none of the formulas.
  4. Quad extends Shape without implementing area(), so it must itself be declared abstract — the requirement is passed down rather than dropped.
  5. Square extends Quad and finally supplies area(), which is what makes it concrete and instantiable.
  6. instanceof Quad is true for the Square, and getClass().getSimpleName() reports Circle — the abstract types are perfectly real types, they simply have no instances of their own.
OUTPUT
  Shape ctor for Circle
  Shape ctor for Rect
  Shape ctor for Square
--
Circle area 12.57
Rect area 12.00
Square area 25.00
total 49.57
true
Circle

This is the template method shape: the parent writes the algorithm (describe) and leaves the varying step (area) abstract. Every subclass gets the formatting for free and supplies only what is genuinely different.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — THE TWO COMPILE ERRORS ABSTRACTION IS BUILT FROM

An abstract class enforces its contract through the compiler. These are the exact messages, and each one is a rule stated as an error.

abstract class Shape { abstract double area(); }
class Use { void f() { Shape s = new Shape(); } }
OUTPUT
error: Shape is abstract; cannot be instantiated
class Use { void f() { Shape s = new Shape(); } }
                                 ^
  1. The caret points at new, not at the variable. Shape s is perfectly legal — declaring a variable of an abstract type is the entire reason abstract types exist. Only the new is refused.
  2. The fix is never "remove abstract". It is to instantiate a concrete subclass and keep the variable typed as Shape: Shape s = new Circle(2);
abstract class Shape { abstract double area(); }
class Circle extends Shape { }        // forgot area()
OUTPUT
error: Circle is not abstract and does not override abstract method area() in Shape
class Circle extends Shape { }
^
  1. A concrete subclass must implement every inherited abstract method. There is no way to leave one out.
  2. Two fixes exist, and the choice is a design decision: implement area(), or declare Circle itself abstract and push the obligation to its subclasses — which is exactly what Quad did in the previous example.
  3. This is what makes the abstract method a genuine guarantee. Every object of type Shape that can exist has an area(), checked at compile time, in every subclass, for ever.

Three further rules follow from the same idea, each worth checking against the code above:

RuleWhy
a class with any abstract method must be declared abstractotherwise it could be instantiated with a hole in it
an abstract class may have zero abstract methodsthe keyword alone prevents instantiation — useful for a base that is never meaningful alone
an abstract class may have fields, constructors and full method bodiesit is a normal class in every respect except that new is refused
🎯 EXAM TIP

The two-line test for any abstract-class question. Ask: (1) does this class still contain an unimplemented abstract method? If yes it must be declared abstract. (2) Is there a new on an abstract type? If yes, that line is the error.

Statements that are true and get offered as if they were false:

• an abstract class can have a constructor — and it runs, via super(...)
• an abstract class can have concrete methods, fields and static members
• an abstract class can have no abstract methods at all
• Shape[] arr = new Shape[3]; is legal — it creates references, not Shapes

Statements that are false and get offered as if they were true:

• "abstract methods can be private" — no: a private method cannot be overridden, so the combination is a compile error. The same goes for abstract static and abstract final.
• "an abstract class cannot be used as a variable type" — it is used that way constantly.

Working with abstract classes settles into one shape: the parent holds what is common, declares what varies, and every subclass fills in the gaps.

public class Circle extends Shape {
    private double radius;
    public Circle(double r) { super("Circle"); radius = r; }

    @Override
    public double area() { return Math.PI * radius * radius; }
}

public class Rectangle extends Shape {
    private double w, h;
    public Rectangle(double w, double h) { super("Rectangle"); this.w = w; this.h = h; }

    @Override
    public double area() { return w * h; }
}

ArrayList shapes = new ArrayList<>();
shapes.add(new Circle(2));
shapes.add(new Rectangle(3, 4));
for (Shape s : shapes) { System.out.println(s.describe()); }

The list is declared as Shape even though no Shape can exist. That is not a contradiction: the type is a promise about what every element can do, and abstract classes are useful precisely as that promise.

Abstract classInterface
a class may haveonemany
fieldsyes, any kindonly public static final constants
constructorsyesno
method bodiesyesdefault and static methods only
members areany visibilityimplicitly public
expressesis-a, with shared codecan-do, a capability

Choose an abstract class when subclasses share state and implementation as well as a contract; choose an interface when unrelated classes need to promise the same capability. Shape is an abstract class; Comparable is an interface, and a Student and an Invoice can both be comparable while sharing nothing else.

Neither can be instantiated. Both can be used as a reference type, which is what makes polymorphism through them possible.

📘 DEFINITION

Template method: a concrete parent method that calls abstract methods the subclasses supply

Common state: fields the parent holds on behalf of every subclass

Polymorphic collection of an abstract type: valid because every element is a concrete subclass

🎯 EXAM TIP

An abstract class may have zero abstract methods and still be abstract — the abstract keyword alone is enough to prevent instantiation.

✅ Also covered in depth: Inheritance → Abstract Classes and Interfaces

📊 FIGURE — ABSTRACT CLASS versus INTERFACE — WHAT EACH ONE CAN CARRY
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — THE SAME HIERARCHY USING BOTH AT ONCE

This is the normal arrangement in real code: an abstract class for the shared state, an interface for the capability, and a class that uses both.

interface Payable {
    double RATE = 15.0;                       // implicitly public static final
    double pay();                             // implicitly public abstract
    default String label() { return "Payable earning " + pay(); }
    static String unit() { return "USD"; }
}
interface Printable { void print(); }

static abstract class Person implements Payable {
    protected String name;                    // STATE — only a class can hold this
    Person(String n) { name = n; }            // a constructor — only a class can have one
    public String toString() { return name; }
}
static class Contractor extends Person implements Printable {
    double hours;
    Contractor(String n, double h) { super(n); hours = h; }
    public double pay() { return hours * RATE; }        // must be PUBLIC
    public void print() { System.out.println("Contractor " + name); }
}
static class Volunteer extends Person {
    Volunteer(String n) { super(n); }
    public double pay() { return 0; }
    @Override public String label() { return "Volunteer, unpaid"; }   // overrides the default
}

Contractor c = new Contractor("Bo", 20);
Volunteer  v = new Volunteer("Vi");
System.out.println(c.pay());
System.out.println(c.label());
System.out.println(v.label());
System.out.println(Payable.RATE + " " + Payable.unit());
Payable[] all = { c, v };
double t = 0;

p.print();

The choice is decided by two questions: is there shared state? and are the classes otherwise related?

RequirementChoiceWhy

• A field in an interface is silently public static final. RATE = 15.0; is a constant, cannot be reassigned, and belongs to the interface rather than to any object. There is no such thing as an interface instance field.

Two relationships between classes are constantly confused, and choosing the wrong one produces designs that fight you later.

IS-A  (inheritance)          A Manager IS-A Employee     -> extends
HAS-A (composition)          A Car HAS-A Engine          -> a field

class Car {
    private Engine engine;       // composition: Car HAS-A Engine
}

class SportsCar extends Car { }  // inheritance: SportsCar IS-A Car

The test is the sentence. "A Car is an Engine" is nonsense, so Car extends Engine is wrong even though a Car needs an Engine. Composition is also the more flexible choice — an object can have many parts, but a class can extend only one class.

RelationshipMeansImplemented as
is-aa Manager is an Employeeextends — inheritance
has-aa Car has an Enginea field — composition

The test is the sentence. "A Car is an Engine" is false, so class Car extends Engine is wrong however convenient the inherited methods look. "A Car has an Engine" is true, so Engine becomes a field.

Inheriting for convenience is the classic error: Stack extends ArrayList gives a stack every list method, including add(int, E) in the middle, which breaks the one rule a stack has. Composition — a private list inside the stack — exposes only what should be exposed.

The Square/Rectangle case is the standard warning: a square is a rectangle mathematically, but a Square that inherits setWidth and setHeight can be made non-square, so the inheritance breaks the type's own guarantee.

📘 DEFINITION

Is-a relationship: a subtype relationship, expressed by extends or implements

Has-a relationship: containment, expressed by a field holding another object

Composition: building a class from other objects rather than by inheriting

Single inheritance: Java allows only one superclass; interfaces are the way around it (10.11)

🎯 EXAM TIP

When a question asks whether one class should extend another, read it out loud as "an X is a Y". If that sentence is false, the answer is a field.

✅ Also covered in depth: Inheritance → Inheritance with extends and super

📊 FIGURE — IS-A POINTS UP, HAS-A POINTS ACROSS
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — THE SAME PROGRAM WRITTEN BOTH WAYS

SportsCar extends Car and Car has-a Engine sit side by side here, so the difference in what each buys you is visible in one run.

static class Engine {
    int hp; boolean running;
    Engine(int hp) { this.hp = hp; }
    void start() { running = true; }
    String status() { return hp + "hp " + (running ? "running" : "stopped"); }
}
static class Car {
    private Engine engine;                    // HAS-A
    private String model;
    Car(String m, int hp) { model = m; engine = new Engine(hp); }
    void start() { engine.start(); }          // delegation
    String report() { return model + ": " + engine.status(); }
}
static class SportsCar extends Car {          // IS-A
    SportsCar(String m) { super(m, 460); }
}

Car c = new SportsCar("GT");
c.start();
System.out.println(c.report());
System.out.println(c instanceof Car);

ArrayList<Car> fleet = new ArrayList<>();
fleet.add(new Car("Sedan", 180));
fleet.add(new SportsCar("GT"));
for (Car x : fleet) System.out.println(x.report());
  1. SportsCar adds nothing but a constructor. It still gets start(), report(), and — the part that matters — it is a Car, so it fits in a Car variable and a List<Car>.
  2. That substitutability is what extends is for. Composition would not give it: a class holding a Car field is not a Car and cannot go in the list.
  3. Car holds an Engine as a private field. Car.start() does not inherit engine behaviour, it forwards to it — one line of delegation.
  4. The payoff is control. Car exposes start() and report() and nothing else; the Engine's own methods are not part of Car's interface unless Car chooses to forward them.
  5. Only the GT is started, so the loop prints Sedan: 180hp stopped and GT: 460hp stopped — the second SportsCar is a different object from c, with its own engine.
OUTPUT
GT: 460hp running
true
Sedan: 180hp stopped
GT: 460hp stopped

Had Car extends Engine been used instead, Car would have inherited hp and status() and the code would compile — but every Car would then be an Engine, fit in a List<Engine>, and expose engine internals to the whole program. Convenience is not a reason to inherit.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — WHEN "IS-A" IS TRUE IN ENGLISH AND WRONG IN CODE

A square is a rectangle — every geometry textbook says so. Inherit on that basis and you get a compiling program that breaks its own guarantee.

static class Rectangle {
    protected double w, h;
    void setWidth(double w)  { this.w = w; }
    void setHeight(double h) { this.h = h; }
    double area() { return w * h; }
}
static class Square extends Rectangle {
    Square(double s) { w = s; h = s; }
}

Rectangle r = new Square(4);
System.out.println("square area " + r.area());
r.setWidth(10);
System.out.println("after setWidth(10): " + r.area()
                 + "  still a Square? " + (r instanceof Square));
  1. new Square(4) sets both sides to 4, so the area is 16.0. Everything is fine so far.
  2. r is declared Rectangle, so setWidth is available — it was inherited, and there is no way to un-inherit it.
  3. After setWidth(10) the object has width 10 and height 4. Its area is 40.0, and instanceof Square is still true.
  4. The object now claims to be a Square while being 10 × 4. The class's one invariant — all sides equal — has been broken by a method the class never wrote and cannot remove.
  5. Overriding setWidth to set both sides does not rescue it either: code written against Rectangle reasonably expects setWidth(10); setHeight(4); to give area 40, and would now silently get 16.
OUTPUT
square area 16.0
after setWidth(10): 40.0  still a Square? true

The test that catches this is stronger than the English sentence: can the subclass honour every promise the parent makes? A Rectangle promises independently settable sides; a Square cannot honour it. The fix is composition — a Square with a side field, offering only the operations it can actually support.

The everyday version of the same error is class Stack extends ArrayList: convenient, compiles, and hands every user add(int, E) so they can insert into the middle of a stack.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Inheriting to reuse code. The reasoning goes: "Invoice needs the date-formatting methods in Report, so I will extend Report." It compiles, the methods work, and you have now declared that every Invoice is a Report — so it can be passed to any method expecting one, stored in a List<Report>, and given every other Report method whether it makes sense or not.

How to notice it: say the sentence out loud. If "an Invoice is a Report" makes you hesitate, the answer is a field — private Report formatter; — or a static utility method.

The second signal is overriding a method to make it do nothing, or to throw. If a subclass has to disable something it inherited, the is-a relationship was false; the parent promised behaviour the child cannot deliver. Composition exposes only what you choose to forward, and that is the whole difference.

+-------------------+

+-------------------+

Three arrows carry most of the meaning: a hollow triangle for inheritance pointing at the parent, a plain line or arrow for association (has-a), and a dashed line with a hollow triangle for implementing an interface.

+-------------------+

+-------------------+

+-------------------+

+-------------------+

+-------------------+

hollow triangle, solid lineinheritance — is-a
hollow triangle, dashed lineimplements an interface
filled diamondcomposition — the part dies with the whole
hollow diamondaggregation — the part can outlive it
+ / - / #public / private / protected

<<interface>>the stereotype above an interface name

The arrow always points from the subclass up to the base class, which is the direction people most often draw backwards.

📘 DEFINITION

UML class diagram: a diagram of classes, their members and their relationships

Visibility markers: - private, + public, # protected

Generalisation arrow: the hollow triangle pointing from subclass to superclass

Multiplicity: the 1, 0..1 or * on an association showing how many objects are involved

🎯 EXAM TIP

The arrow always points from the more specific class to the more general one — subclass to superclass, implementer to interface. Reversing it is the usual diagram-reading error.

Exam questions give you the picture and ask for the code, or give you the code and ask which picture matches. Both directions are the same table read in opposite orders.

Employee in italicspublic abstract class Employee
- name : Stringprivate String name;
# salary : doubleprotected double salary;
+ getSalary() : doublepublic double getSalary()

  2. Read the symbol before every member — it is the access modifier, and it is the single most-tested detail in these questions. - is private, + public, # protected.
  3. Type comes after the colon, which is the reverse of Java. - name : String becomes String name, never name String.

  5. Follow the arrow to decide extends vs implements: solid line for a class, dashed for an interface, hollow triangle either way.

A student draws a payroll model. Each of these is a real error with a specific consequence.

  1. The triangle points at Manager. A hollow triangle always sits at the more general end, so this diagram says "Employee extends Manager" — every Employee would be a Manager. The arrow direction is the most common diagram-reading error, in both directions: reading one and drawing one.
  2. Payable is joined with a solid line. A solid line plus a triangle means extends, so this claims Payable is a class. If Payable is an interface the line must be dashed, and the class would then be able to implement several of them.
  3. Car and Engine are joined with a triangle instead of a diamond. That turns a has-a into an is-a — the 10.9 error, drawn. It should be a filled diamond at the Car end, meaning Car holds an Engine field.

triangle at Payable, dashedPayable is an interfaceclass Manager implements Payable
filled diamond at CarCar owns an Engineprivate Engine engine;

A fourth detail worth checking on any diagram you are handed: multiplicity. A 1 at the far end of an association means one object; * means many, and in code that is a collection field rather than a single reference. 0..1 means the field may legitimately be null.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Drawing the generalisation arrow from the parent down to the child. It goes the other way. The line starts at the subclass and the hollow triangle touches the superclass — the arrow points at the more general type, always. The same rule covers implements: the triangle sits at the interface.

How to notice it: read the picture as a sentence in the direction of the arrow. "Manager → Employee" reads "a Manager is an Employee", which is true. If the sentence comes out false, the arrow is backwards.

The other frequent mix-up is solid versus dashed. Solid + hollow triangle = extends a class; dashed + hollow triangle = implements an interface. Since a class can implement many interfaces but extend only one class, getting the line style wrong changes what the diagram claims is even legal.

An interface is a pure contract: a list of method signatures with no state and (traditionally) no bodies. A class can extend only one class but implement any number of interfaces, which is how Java gets the useful part of multiple inheritance without the ambiguity.

public interface Payable {
    double calculatePay();                 // implicitly public abstract
}

public interface Printable {
    void print();
}

public class Contractor implements Payable, Printable {
    public double calculatePay() { return hours * rate; }
    public void print() { System.out.println(name); }
}

Payable p = new Contractor();      // polymorphism through an interface
p.calculatePay();

The choice between an abstract class and an interface comes down to whether there is shared state. Shared fields and partial implementation mean an abstract class; a capability that unrelated classes might have — comparable, printable, payable — means an interface.

public interface Payable {
    double pay();                          // implicitly public abstract
    double RATE = 15.0;                    // implicitly public static final

    default String label() { return "Payable"; }   // a body — optional to override
}

public class Contractor implements Payable, Comparable<Contractor> {
    public double pay() { ... }            // must be PUBLIC
}

An interface is a contract: implement it and you promise to supply every abstract method. Missing one leaves the class abstract, and a concrete class then fails to compile.

Interface methods are implicitly public, so an implementation that writes them without public is narrowing visibility and will not compile — a very common slip.

Multiple interfaces are allowed because an interface carries no state, so there is nothing to inherit twice. A default method supplies a body so that adding a method to an interface does not break every existing implementer.

📘 DEFINITION

Interface: a contract of method signatures a class promises to implement

implements: the keyword declaring that a class satisfies an interface

Multiple interfaces: a class may implement any number, unlike extends

default method: since Java 8, an interface method may have a body marked default

🎯 EXAM TIP

Comparable (13.5) is the interface you will actually use. Implementing it means writing one compareTo, after which Collections.sort can sort your objects.

✅ Also covered in depth: Inheritance → Abstract Classes and Interfaces

📊 FIGURE — AN INTERFACE IS A CONTRACT
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — IMPLEMENTING TWO INTERFACES AND EXTENDING A CLASS AT ONCE

The rule "one extends, many implements" is easiest to believe when you watch it work.

interface Payable {
    double RATE = 15.0;                                // public static final
    double pay();                                      // public abstract
    default String label() { return "Payable earning " + pay(); }
    static String unit() { return "USD"; }
}
interface Printable { void print(); }

static abstract class Person implements Payable {
    protected String name;
    Person(String n) { name = n; }
    public String toString() { return name; }
}
static class Contractor extends Person implements Printable {
    double hours;
    Contractor(String n, double h) { super(n); hours = h; }
    public double pay() { return hours * RATE; }
    public void print() { System.out.println("Contractor " + name); }
}
static class Volunteer extends Person {
    Volunteer(String n) { super(n); }
    public double pay() { return 0; }
    @Override public String label() { return "Volunteer, unpaid"; }
}

Contractor c = new Contractor("Bo", 20);
Volunteer  v = new Volunteer("Vi");
System.out.println(c.pay());
System.out.println(c.label());
System.out.println(v.label());
System.out.println(Payable.RATE + " " + Payable.unit());
System.out.println(c instanceof Payable);
System.out.println(c instanceof Printable);
System.out.println(v instanceof Printable);
Printable p = c;
p.print();
  1. Person implements Payable but never writes pay(). Legal — because Person is abstract, so the obligation simply passes to its subclasses. A concrete class could not get away with it.
  2. Contractor extends one class and implements one interface in the same declaration, and both obligations are checked: it must supply pay() (from Payable, via Person) and print() (from Printable).
  3. RATE is used unqualified: interface constants are inherited by implementers. 20 × 15.0 = 300.0.
  4. label() is a default method. Contractor never declares it and gets the interface's body; Volunteer overrides it. Adding label() to Payable later therefore broke nothing — which is precisely what default methods are for.
  5. Payable.unit() is a static interface method, called on the interface itself. It is not inherited by implementers — c.unit() would not compile.
  6. c instanceof Printable is true, v instanceof Printable is false. The two share a superclass, but only one advertises this capability — which is exactly the distinction that makes interfaces worth having.
  7. Printable p = c; — an interface is a reference type like any other, and calling p.print() dispatches to the Contractor's body.
OUTPUT
300.0
Payable earning 300.0
Volunteer, unpaid
15.0 USD
true
true
false
Contractor Bo
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — WHAT AN INTERFACE ACTUALLY ENFORCES

An interface is a promise the compiler checks. Here is each promise, broken, with the message it produces.

interface Payable { double pay(); }

class Contractor implements Payable {
    // pay() not written
}
OUTPUT
error: Contractor is not abstract and does not override abstract method pay() in Payable

The identical wording to the abstract-class error in 10.7 — because it is the identical rule. Implement it, or declare the class abstract.

class Contractor implements Payable {
    double pay() { return 0; }        // no "public"
}
OUTPUT
error: pay() in Contractor cannot implement pay() in Payable
  attempting to assign weaker access privileges; was public

Interface methods are implicitly public; leaving the keyword off is narrowing, and narrowing is never allowed on an override.

interface Payable { double RATE = 15.0; }

class Contractor implements Payable {
    void bump() { RATE = 20.0; }
}
OUTPUT
error: cannot assign a value to final variable RATE
  1. An interface field is implicitly public static final — a constant, shared, and unassignable. There is no way to declare an interface instance field.
  2. These three messages cover almost every interface compile error you will meet: does not override, weaker access privileges, and cannot assign a value to final variable.
  3. Notice what an interface does not enforce: nothing about how pay() is calculated, nothing about fields, nothing about constructors. It is a signature list, so implementers are free to be as unrelated as they like — which is the entire source of its usefulness.

And the one rule that makes multiple interfaces safe: an interface carries no instance state, so there is nothing to inherit twice. That is why class A implements B, C, D is fine while class A extends B, C is not.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Writing implements where a bound needs extends, and vice versa. Two different contexts use opposite keywords for the same idea:

• In a class declaration: class Contractor extends Person implements Payable. Class with extends, interface with implements.
• In a generic bound (13.2): <T extends Comparable<T>> — extends, even though Comparable is an interface. <T implements Comparable> does not compile.
• Between interfaces: interface Manager extends Payable, Printable — an interface extends other interfaces, and may extend several.

How to notice it: the compiler error for the class-declaration case is blunt — interface expected here or no interface expected here — and points straight at the keyword. The generic-bound case is the one worth memorising in advance, because there extends simply means "is or is below", covering classes and interfaces alike.

The employee example demonstrates overriding across a hierarchy, with each subclass computing pay its own way.

public class Employee {
    protected String name;
    protected double baseSalary;
    public Employee(String n, double s) { name = n; baseSalary = s; }

    public double pay() { return baseSalary; }

    @Override
    public String toString() { return name + ": " + pay(); }
}

public class Manager extends Employee {
    private double bonus;
    public Manager(String n, double s, double b) { super(n, s); bonus = b; }

    @Override
    public double pay() { return super.pay() + bonus; }
}

for (Employee e : staff) { System.out.println(e); }   // toString called implicitly

Two mechanisms are quietly cooperating in the last line. println calls toString(), which is defined only in Employee — and inside it, pay() dispatches to the subclass version. The parent’s code calls the child’s method, which is the whole point of 10.5.

class Employee {
    public double pay() { return 40 * rate; }
    public String toString() { return name + ": " + pay(); }
}
class Manager extends Employee {
    @Override public double pay() { return super.pay() + bonus; }
}

for (Employee e : staff) System.out.println(e);   // each prints ITS OWN pay

super.pay() reaches the version this method is replacing — the way to extend behaviour rather than restate it. Without super., calling pay() inside the override calls itself and recurses until the stack overflows.

Notice that the inherited toString() calls pay() and gets the Manager version for a Manager, even though toString was written in Employee and knows nothing about managers. That is dynamic dispatch doing the work, and it is the point the example exists to make.

📘 DEFINITION

super.pay(): reusing the parent implementation inside the override rather than duplicating it

Inherited toString: defined once in the parent, correct for every subclass through dispatch

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

Adding a Contractor subclass tomorrow requires no change to toString, to the loop, or to anything else. That is what a hierarchy buys you.

📊 FIGURE — THE PARENT'S toString CALLS THE CHILD'S pay
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — THE WHOLE HIERARCHY, PRINTED BY ONE LOOP

Three pay formulas, one toString, one loop. Watch which class each printed number came from.

static class Employee {
    protected String name;
    protected double rate;
    Employee(String n, double r) { name = n; rate = r; }
    double pay() { return 40 * rate; }
    @Override public String toString() {
        return String.format("%-9s %8.2f", name, pay());
    }
}
static class Manager extends Employee {
    private double bonus;
    Manager(String n, double r, double b) { super(n, r); bonus = b; }
    @Override double pay() { return super.pay() + bonus; }
}
static class Contractor extends Employee {
    private double hours;
    Contractor(String n, double r, double h) { super(n, r); hours = h; }
    @Override double pay() { return hours * rate; }
}

ArrayList<Employee> staff = new ArrayList<>();
staff.add(new Employee("Ana", 22.50));
staff.add(new Manager("Ben", 30.00, 500));
staff.add(new Contractor("Cy", 45.00, 12));
double total = 0;
for (Employee e : staff) { System.out.println(e); total += e.pay(); }
System.out.printf("%-9s %8.2f%n", "TOTAL", total);
  1. Ana is a plain Employee: 40 × 22.50 = 900.00.
  2. Ben is a Manager. super.pay() runs Employee's body — 40 × 30.00 = 1200 — and the override adds the 500 bonus: 1700.00.
  3. Cy is a Contractor and ignores the 40-hour assumption entirely: 12 × 45.00 = 540.00.
  4. System.out.println(e) never calls toString() by name — println does it for you, and String concatenation would too.
  5. The toString() being run is Employee's, in every case. It was written before Manager and Contractor existed and mentions neither. Its call to pay() dispatches to whichever subclass the object actually is.
  6. The loop body accumulates the same dispatched values: 900 + 1700 + 540 = 3140.00.
  7. %-9s %8.2f is what lines the columns up — names left-aligned in nine characters, money right-aligned in eight with two decimals (9.2).
OUTPUT
Ana         900.00
Ben        1700.00
Cy          540.00
TOTAL      3140.00

A parent method calling a child method it has never heard of is the single most useful consequence of inheritance, and this output is the proof it happens.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — WHAT super. IS FOR, AND WHAT HAPPENS WITHOUT IT

Manager.pay() needs the base salary and the bonus. There are three ways to write it and only one is right.

VersionResultVerdict
return super.pay() + bonus;1700.00correct — reuses the base formula
return 40 * rate + bonus;1700.00 todayduplicates the formula. Change the base to a 37-hour week and this silently keeps paying 40.
return pay() + bonus;StackOverflowErrorcalls itself — the unqualified name resolves to the override it is inside
  1. super.pay() is the only syntax that reaches a method you are replacing. It is not "the parent object" — there is one object — it is an instruction to start the method lookup one level up.
  2. The second version compiles and produces the right number, so tests pass. It is still wrong: the base formula now exists in two places, and the day it changes only one of them will be updated.
  3. The third version is the classic accident. Inside Manager.pay(), a bare pay() means this.pay(), which dispatches straight back to Manager.pay(). Each call pushes a stack frame, nothing ever returns, and the stack is exhausted in milliseconds (11.8).
  4. super. only reaches one level up, and only from inside the subclass. super.super.pay() is not valid Java, and super cannot be used from a static method — there is no this for it to work from.

The same reasoning applies to toString. If Manager wanted extra detail, the right override is:

@Override public String toString() {
    return super.toString() + "  (bonus " + bonus + ")";
}

which reuses the parent's formatting rather than restating the %-9s %8.2f layout in a second place.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Calling the overriding method from inside itself. Writing pay() instead of super.pay() inside Manager.pay() compiles perfectly — a method calling another method of the same object is ordinary Java — and then recurses infinitely, ending in StackOverflowError the first time the line runs.

How to notice it: the stack trace is hundreds of identical lines naming the same method and the same line number. If you see one method repeating, look for a missing super. before deciding you have a recursion bug.

The mirror-image mistake is using super. when you meant this. Writing super.pay() in a method that is not an override skips the polymorphic call deliberately, which is almost never what you want — it hard-wires the base version and defeats the dispatch that makes the hierarchy useful.

🎯 EXAM TIP

For "what does this hierarchy print?" questions, work object by object, not line by line. For each element: what is its actual class, does that class override the method, and does the override call super? Compute the base value first, then apply the override.

The reliable traps in this exact style of question:

① a toString() defined only in the parent that calls an overridden method — the parent's text layout with the child's numbers;
② super.pay() + bonus versus a restated formula — both give the same number, so the question has to be about design rather than output;
③ println(obj) with no toString() anywhere — the answer is ClassName@hexhash, not a compile error.

And when a question asks why the design is good, the answer is almost always the same sentence: adding another subclass requires no change to the loop, to toString, or to any existing code.

The final example is the one people get wrong under exam conditions: you cannot instantiate an abstract class, but you constantly declare variables of its type.

Shape s = new Shape("x");         // ERROR — abstract
Shape s = new Circle(2);          // FINE  — the variable type is Shape,
                                  //        the OBJECT is a Circle

Shape[] shapes = new Shape[3];    // FINE  — an array of Shape REFERENCES,
                                  //        all null, no Shape created
shapes[0] = new Circle(2);
shapes[1] = new Rectangle(3, 4);

for (Shape sh : shapes) {
    if (sh != null) { System.out.println(sh.area()); }   // null check matters
}

new Shape[3] creates no Shape objects at all — it creates three null references (5.2). That is why it is legal for an abstract type, and why the null check in the loop is not optional.

Shape[] shapes = { new Circle(2), new Rect(3, 4) };   // a Shape[] of subclasses
for (Shape s : shapes)
    System.out.printf("%s: %.2f%n", s.getName(), s.area());

You cannot instantiate Shape, but you can declare an array of it — the reference type is abstract while every object in it is concrete. That combination is what makes an abstract class useful: it guarantees every element answers area() without needing to know which shape it is.

The subclass supplies the missing method and passes shared data up with super(name). Adding a new shape needs no change to this loop at all, which is the practical payoff and the usual exam framing.

📘 DEFINITION

Declared type vs actual type: the variable’s type limits what you may call; the object decides what runs

Array of abstract type: an array of references, initially null; no instances are created

Abstract instantiation error: the compile error from calling new on an abstract class

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

"Shape is abstract; cannot be instantiated" always points at a new on the abstract type. The fix is to instantiate a concrete subclass — the variable can stay declared as the abstract type.

📊 FIGURE — AN ARRAY OF AN ABSTRACT TYPE IS AN ARRAY OF REFERENCES
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — THREE NULL SLOTS, THEN TWO REAL SHAPES

new Shape[3] is legal for an abstract type, and the reason is visible in the very first printed value.

static abstract class Shape {
    private String name;
    Shape(String n) { name = n; }
    String getName() { return name; }
    abstract double area();
}
static class Circle extends Shape {
    double r;
    Circle(double r) { super("Circle"); this.r = r; }
    @Override double area() { return Math.PI * r * r; }
}
static class Rect extends Shape {
    double w, h;
    Rect(double w, double h) { super("Rect"); this.w = w; this.h = h; }
    @Override double area() { return w * h; }
}

Shape[] shapes = new Shape[3];
System.out.println("length " + shapes.length + ", slot 0 = " + shapes[0]);
shapes[0] = new Circle(2);
shapes[1] = new Rect(3, 4);
for (Shape s : shapes) {
    if (s != null) System.out.printf("%s: %.2f%n", s.getName(), s.area());
    else System.out.println("(empty slot)");
}
try {
    System.out.println(shapes[2].area());
} catch (NullPointerException e) {
    System.out.println("caught " + e.getClass().getSimpleName());
}
Shape[] filled = { new Circle(1), new Rect(2, 5) };
double t = 0;
for (Shape s : filled) t += s.area();
System.out.printf("total %.4f%n", t);
  1. slot 0 = null is the whole explanation. new Shape[3] allocates three reference slots, all null. Not one Shape was constructed, so the "cannot instantiate an abstract class" rule was never even approached.
  2. Assigning new Circle(2) and new Rect(3, 4) fills two of them. The array is declared to hold Shape references; a Circle reference is a Shape reference, so it fits.
  3. The loop calls getName() — a concrete inherited method — and area() — an abstract one, dispatched to the subclass. π × 2² = 12.57, 3 × 4 = 12.00.
  4. The third slot is still null, so the guard prints (empty slot). That check is not optional housekeeping: it is the direct consequence of the array being references.
  5. Removing the guard proves it — shapes[2].area() throws NullPointerException. This is the single most common bug when arrays of objects are filled partially.
  6. The array initialiser form { new Circle(1), new Rect(2, 5) } avoids the problem entirely by creating and filling in one step: π + 10 = 13.1416.
OUTPUT
length 3, slot 0 = null
Circle: 12.57
Rect: 12.00
(empty slot)
caught NullPointerException
total 13.1416

Every use of Shape below is legal except one. The dividing line is simple: anything that names a type is fine; only new Shape(...) is refused.

CodeLegal?Why
Shape s;yesdeclaring a variable creates no object
Shape s = new Circle(2);yesthe variable type is abstract, the object is concrete
Shape[] a = new Shape[3];yesthree null references, no Shapes
ArrayList<Shape> listyesthe element type is abstract; the elements are not
void draw(Shape s)yesa parameter is a variable
Shape make() { … }yesthe return type is a promise about what comes back
new Shape("x")NOerror: Shape is abstract; cannot be instantiated
  1. Read down the table and notice that six of the seven rows are the abstract class being useful. Its whole purpose is to be a type — the guarantee that whatever arrives can answer area().
  2. void draw(Shape s) is the payoff. One method accepts every present and future shape, and calls area() on all of them without knowing a single subclass name.
  3. Shape make() is the other half — a method that decides which shape to build and returns it as a Shape, so the caller does not have to know either.
  4. The single illegal row is illegal for a concrete reason: Shape has no area() body, so a plain Shape object would be an object with a hole in it. The compiler refuses to create one rather than letting it fail later.

The mirror-image case is worth stating too. Once the object is a Circle, calling something Circle adds needs a cast, because the variable is still a Shape:

Shape s = new Circle(2);
s.area();                          // fine — declared on Shape
// s.getRadius();                  // COMPILE ERROR — Circle-only
if (s instanceof Circle c) { c.getRadius(); }    // the safe way

Which is 10.5's two rules again, arriving through abstraction instead of plain inheritance.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Find the new. In any question about abstract classes, scan for new followed by the abstract type's name. That line is the error; every other mention of the type is legal.

The four options these questions usually offer, and why three are wrong:

• "Shape[] a = new Shape[3]; does not compile" — false. It creates three nulls. This is the most common wrong answer in the whole unit.
• "Shape s; does not compile" — false. Declaring a variable creates nothing.
• "the array creates three Shape objects" — false. It creates three references, all null.
• "new Shape("x") does not compile" — true, and that is the answer.

One more that appears regularly: after Shape[] a = new Shape[3];, what does a[0].area() do? Not a compile error — a NullPointerException at run time. The slot is empty, and the compiler has no way to know.

Recursion is a method calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem. It is not a trick — it is the natural shape for anything defined in terms of itself, and it needs exactly two things to work.

public static int factorial(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) { return 1; }              // BASE CASE — stops the recursion
    return n * factorial(n - 1);           // RECURSIVE CASE — smaller input
}

factorial(4)
  -> 4 * factorial(3)
       -> 3 * factorial(2)
            -> 2 * factorial(1)
                 -> 1              base case
            <- 2
       <- 6
  <- 24

Miss the base case and the calls never stop; fail to shrink the input and they never reach it. Both produce StackOverflowError (11.8), because each call pushes a stack frame (6.8) and nothing pops.

A recursive method calls itself on a smaller version of the same problem. Two parts are compulsory, and every recursion question turns on one of them.

PartJobMissing it gives
base caseanswers the smallest input directly, with no further callinfinite recursion → StackOverflowError
recursive casecalls itself on a smaller input and builds the answerno progress → also a stack overflow

"Smaller" is the part people skip. f(n) calling f(n) has a base case and still never reaches it; the argument must move towards the base case on every call.

Anything recursive can be written with a loop and the reverse is also true. Recursion costs a stack frame per call, so a loop is cheaper — recursion earns its place when the data is itself nested, as with trees and divide-and-conquer.

📘 DEFINITION

Recursion: a method that calls itself on a smaller instance of the problem

Base case: the input small enough to answer without recursing

Recursive case: the branch that calls itself with a reduced input

Recursive depth: how many calls are on the stack at the deepest point

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

Recursion is not just an alternative to loops. Trees, permutations (11.7) and merge sort (17.9) have no natural iterative form, because the problem itself branches.

📊 FIGURE — every recursive method needs both halves
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Counting down, then counting up
countdown(3);
before 3 before 2 before 1 liftoff after 1 after 2 after 3
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Each call prints, then calls itself with a smaller n.
  2. The base case stops the descent.
  3. The 'after' lines print in REVERSE order — that is the calls unwinding as they return.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Recursion and iteration solve the same problem
System.out.println(sumRec(5));
System.out.println(sumIter(5));
System.out.println(sumRec(100) == sumIter(100));
15 15 true
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Both compute the same total.
  2. The recursive version mirrors the definition: the sum to n is n plus the sum to n−1.
  3. The iterative version uses less memory, because there is no stack of calls.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Writing a recursive case that does not get smaller. f(n) calling f(n), or calling f(n - 0), recurses for ever — the base case is never reached however correct it looks.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Check two things in any recursive method: is there a base case, and does every recursive call move towards it? Those two questions answer most exam items in this unit.

Writing one is a two-question routine, and doing it in this order is what stops recursion feeling like guesswork.

First: what input is small enough that I can answer immediately? That is the base case. Second: assuming the method already works for a smaller input, how do I build my answer from it? That is the recursive case — and the key move is trusting the smaller call rather than tracing it.

// sum of 1..n
public static int sumTo(int n) {
    if (n == 0) { return 0; }              // base: sum of nothing is 0
    return n + sumTo(n - 1);               // trust it for n-1, add n
}

// reverse a String
public static String reverse(String s) {
    if (s.length() <= 1) { return s; }
    return reverse(s.substring(1)) + s.charAt(0);
}

Compare sumTo with the loop version in 6.6. They produce the same answer; the recursive one describes the definition, the loop describes the procedure.

static int factorial(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return 1;              // base case
    return n * factorial(n - 1);       // recursive case, n gets smaller
}

factorial(4)
  4 * factorial(3)
      3 * factorial(2)
          2 * factorial(1)  -> 1      <- base case reached, unwinding starts
          2 * 1 = 2
      3 * 2 = 6
  4 * 6 = 24

The multiplications happen on the way back up: every call waits for the one below it before it can finish. factorial(4) makes 4 calls in total, and 4 frames exist at once at the deepest point.

n <= 1 rather than n == 1 is deliberate — it catches 0 (whose factorial is 1) and stops a negative input from recursing forever downwards.

📘 DEFINITION

Recursive leap of faith: assuming the smaller call is correct rather than tracing it

Reduction step: the change that makes the argument closer to the base case

Direct recursion: a method calling itself, as opposed to two methods calling each other

🎯 EXAM TIP

If tracing your own recursion confuses you, that is expected and not a sign of a bug. Verify the base case and verify one level of the recursive step; the rest follows by induction.

📊 FIGURE — RECURSION GOES DOWN TO THE BASE CASE, THEN RESULTS CLIMB BACK UP
🎯 EXAM TIP
To trace recursion fast, find the base case FIRST and compute upward from it — much faster than expanding downward and less error-prone under exam time pressure.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Factorial, traced by its own definition
System.out.println(fact(1));
System.out.println(fact(4));
System.out.println(4 * 3 * 2 * 1);
1 24 24
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. fact(4) waits for fact(3), which waits for fact(2), and so on.
  2. fact(1) returns 1 without recursing — the base case.
  3. The multiplications then happen on the way back up.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The base case must come first
System.out.println(goodFact(5));
System.out.println(badFact(5));
120 120
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. goodFact tests for the base case before recursing.
  2. badFact multiplies first and only then delegates.
  3. Both give 120 here, but the second has no stopping rule of its own — the helper is doing all the real work.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Putting the recursive call before the base-case test. The test then never gets a chance to run on the way down, and the method descends until the stack is exhausted.

Binary search is the standard recursive search, and it is recursive for a real reason: each step reduces the problem to a genuinely smaller version of the same problem.

// the array MUST be sorted
public static int bsearch(int[] a, int target, int lo, int hi) {
    if (lo > hi) { return -1; }                       // base: empty range
    int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;

    if (a[mid] == target) { return mid; }             // base: found
    if (a[mid] < target)  { return bsearch(a, target, mid + 1, hi); }
    return bsearch(a, target, lo, mid - 1);
}

There are two base cases here, and both are needed: found, and searched-everything. The halving is what makes it O(log n) — 1,000,000 elements take about 20 comparisons — and that analysis is 17.2.

static int bsearch(int[] a, int target, int lo, int hi) {
    if (lo > hi) return -1;                       // base case: not found
    int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
    if (a[mid] == target) return mid;             // base case: found
    if (a[mid] < target) return bsearch(a, target, mid + 1, hi);
    else                 return bsearch(a, target, lo, mid - 1);
}

Two base cases, and both are needed: one succeeds, one gives up. The range shrinks by half each call, so 1,000 elements take about 10 calls — O(log n), and the recursion depth is that same small number.

The precondition is that the array is sorted. On unsorted data binary search does not fail loudly; it simply misses values that are there, which is worse.

mid + 1 and mid - 1 rather than mid is what guarantees progress. Passing mid unchanged leaves the range the same size and the recursion never reaches lo > hi.

📘 DEFINITION

Binary search: repeatedly halving a sorted range to locate a value

Search space: the lo..hi range still under consideration

Divide and conquer: splitting a problem into smaller instances, solving each, combining

Precondition: binary search requires sorted data; on unsorted data it silently returns wrong answers

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

lo > hi is the empty-range test; writing lo == hi misses the single-element case and the recursion never terminates properly.

📊 FIGURE — binary search halves the range
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Binary search, recursively
int[] a = {2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38};
System.out.println(bsearch(a, 23, 0, a.length - 1));
System.out.println(bsearch(a, 2, 0, a.length - 1));
System.out.println(bsearch(a, 7, 0, a.length - 1));
5 0 -1
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Each call throws away half the remaining range.
  2. There are TWO base cases: found it, or the range is empty.
  3. −1 is the conventional 'not found' marker.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — How few comparisons it really takes
int[] a = new int[1000];
for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) a[i] = i * 2;
System.out.println(steps(a, 1998, 0, a.length - 1, 0));
System.out.println(a.length);
10 1000
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. A thousand elements are searched in a handful of comparisons.
  2. Each step halves the range, so the cost grows as log₂ n.
  3. A linear search would have taken up to 1,000.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Binary search REQUIRES a sorted array. If a question shows an unsorted array, binary search is the wrong answer however tempting the numbers look.

Debugging recursion with print statements is the technique from 4.8, with one addition that makes all the difference: print the depth, so you can see the shape rather than a flat list.

public static int fact(int n, int depth) {
    String pad = "  ".repeat(depth);
    System.out.println(pad + "enter n=" + n);

    if (n <= 1) {
        System.out.println(pad + "base -> 1");
        return 1;
    }
    int result = n * fact(n - 1, depth + 1);
    System.out.println(pad + "exit  n=" + n + " -> " + result);
    return result;
}

Printing on the way in and on the way out is what shows you the two phases: descending to the base case, then combining on the way back up. Most recursion bugs are visible in the exit lines, because that is where the combining happens.

static int fact(int n, int depth) {
    System.out.println("  ".repeat(depth) + "enter n=" + n);
    if (n <= 1) { System.out.println("  ".repeat(depth) + "base -> 1"); return 1; }
    int r = n * fact(n - 1, depth + 1);
    System.out.println("  ".repeat(depth) + "return " + r);
    return r;
}

Print on the way in and on the way out, and indent by the depth. The indentation is what makes the shape visible: each level steps right, and the returns line up with their matching entries.

Infinite recursion is instantly recognisable in that output — the same argument repeating, or the indentation marching right without a base case ever printing. Passing a depth parameter costs nothing and is the cheapest recursion debugger there is.

Trace with a small input. fact(4) produces readable output; fact(40) produces a wall of text that hides the very thing you are looking for.

📘 DEFINITION

Trace output: temporary prints showing entry, exit and arguments

Depth parameter: an extra argument used only to indent the trace

Winding / unwinding: the descent to the base case and the return back up through the calls

🎯 EXAM TIP

In an exam, draw the call stack instead: one indented line per call, then fill in return values from the deepest line upward. It is the same diagram the prints would have produced.

Leaving the debugging output in. It is fine while you are working and wrong in a submission — the marker sees pages of trace instead of the program's real output.

Creating a recursive method from scratch follows a fixed procedure, and following it beats intuition every time.

1. State the problem for input n.
2. Find the smallest input you can answer with no work    -> base case
3. Express the answer for n in terms of the answer for a smaller input
4. Check that every recursive call is CLOSER to the base case
5. Check the base case is actually REACHABLE from every path

// count digits
public static int digits(int n) {
    if (n < 10) { return 1; }          // 2: one digit
    return 1 + digits(n / 10);         // 3: one more than the rest (4.3)
}

Step 4 is the one people skip and the one that causes infinite recursion. digits(n / 10) shrinks because integer division truncates; digits(n - 1) would also shrink but would take far longer to reach the base case, and digits(n) never would.

Designing a recursive method is a fixed four-step order, and doing it out of order is what makes recursion feel like guesswork.

1  What is the smallest input, and what is its answer?      -> base case
2  How does one step make the problem smaller?              -> recursive call
3  How do I build my answer from the smaller answer?        -> combine
4  Does every path reach the base case?                     -> check

Step 3 requires trusting the recursion: assume the smaller call returns the right answer and use it. Trying to trace all the way down while writing the method is where people lose the thread — the trace is for debugging, not for designing.

static String reverse(String s) {
    if (s.length() <= 1) return s;                     // 1
    return reverse(s.substring(1)) + s.charAt(0);      // 2 and 3
}

A public wrapper is common when the recursion needs extra bookkeeping: search(a, target) calls the private search(a, target, lo, hi), so callers do not have to supply indices they should not have to know about.

📘 DEFINITION

Termination argument: the reason every chain of calls reaches a base case

Progress: each call must strictly reduce the problem size

Infinite recursion: calls that never reach a base case; ends in StackOverflowError

🎯 EXAM TIP

Negative or zero inputs are where base cases fail. digits(0) returns 1 correctly here; digits(-5) returns 1 too, which may or may not be what you wanted — decide deliberately.

📊 FIGURE — the recipe
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Reversing a string by the recipe
System.out.println(reverse("a"));
System.out.println(reverse("abc"));
System.out.println(reverse("recursion"));
a cba noisrucer
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Smallest case: a string of 0 or 1 characters is already reversed.
  2. Otherwise: reverse everything after the first character, then put that character on the end.
  3. Each call passes a shorter string, so it must reach the base case.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Counting a character
System.out.println(countChar("banana", 'a'));
System.out.println(countChar("banana", 'z'));
System.out.println(countChar("", 'a'));

  2. Each call handles ONE character and delegates the rest.
  3. The empty case is what makes the whole thing terminate.

The classic recursive maths methods are worth knowing by shape, because they appear in exam questions almost verbatim.

// factorial: n! = n * (n-1)!
static int fact(int n) { return (n <= 1) ? 1 : n * fact(n - 1); }

// Fibonacci: F(n) = F(n-1) + F(n-2) — TWO recursive calls
static int fib(int n) { return (n <= 1) ? n : fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2); }

// power: x^n = x * x^(n-1)
static double pow(double x, int n) { return (n == 0) ? 1 : x * pow(x, n - 1); }

// greatest common divisor — Euclid
static int gcd(int a, int b) { return (b == 0) ? a : gcd(b, a % b); }

fib is the odd one out and the interesting one: because it calls itself twice, the work grows exponentially and fib(40) recomputes the same values millions of times. It is the standard example of recursion being elegant and slow at once, and the fix — remembering results — is called memoisation.

static int fib(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return n;                    // TWO base cases: fib(0)=0, fib(1)=1
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);
}

This is correct and catastrophically slow. Each call spawns two more, so the work doubles with every increment — O(2ⁿ). fib(40) makes over a billion calls, and fib(5) already computes fib(2) three separate times.

The fix is memoization: keep an array of answers already computed and return the stored one instead of recomputing. That turns O(2ⁿ) into O(n) without changing the shape of the method.

static int gcd(int a, int b) { return b == 0 ? a : gcd(b, a % b); }
static int sumDigits(int n) { return n < 10 ? n : n % 10 + sumDigits(n / 10); }

Both of these shrink fast and reach their base case in a handful of calls, which is what makes recursion genuinely the clearer choice for them.

📘 DEFINITION

Factorial: n! = n × (n-1)!, with 0! = 1

Fibonacci: F(n) = F(n-1) + F(n-2), with F(0)=0 and F(1)=1

Exponential blow-up: two recursive calls per level giving roughly 2^n total calls

Memoisation: caching computed results so each input is solved once

🎯 EXAM TIP

Exam questions ask for the number of calls as often as the result. fib(5) makes 15 calls; counting them by drawing the tree is faster than reasoning about it.

📊 FIGURE — definitions that are already recursive
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Three classics, each a direct translation

System.out.println(gcd(48, 36));

Some problems need to try every possibility, and recursion is the natural way to express "choose one, solve the rest, then undo the choice". That undo step is what makes it backtracking.

public static void permute(String prefix, String rest) {
    if (rest.isEmpty()) {
        System.out.println(prefix);           // base: nothing left to place
        return;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < rest.length(); i++) {
        permute(prefix + rest.charAt(i),
                rest.substring(0, i) + rest.substring(i + 1));
    }
}

permute("", "abc");     // abc acb bac bca cab cba

The loop chooses each remaining character in turn as the next one; the recursion handles everything after it. There are n! permutations of n characters, so this is only usable for small inputs — a real limit, not a caution.

Exhaustive search is recursion's natural home: at each step, try every choice, recurse, then undo the choice before trying the next. The undo is backtracking, and leaving it out is the standard bug — the shared state carries into branches it should not.

static void subsets(int[] a, int i, List<Integer> cur) {
    if (i == a.length) { System.out.println(cur); return; }   // base case
    subsets(a, i + 1, cur);                    // choice 1: leave a[i] out
    cur.add(a[i]);
    subsets(a, i + 1, cur);                    // choice 2: put a[i] in
    cur.remove(cur.size() - 1);                // UNDO — backtrack
}

Every element is either in or out, so a set of n elements has 2ⁿ subsets; arrangements of all n give n! permutations. Both grow fast enough that exhaustive search is only practical for small n — 20 elements is a million subsets, 20 items is 2.4 × 10¹⁸ permutations.

Pruning is abandoning a branch as soon as it cannot lead to a solution. It does not change the worst case but usually makes the difference between usable and not.

📘 DEFINITION

Backtracking: trying an option, recursing, then undoing it and trying the next

Permutation: one ordering of a set of items; n items have n! orderings

Search tree: the tree of partial solutions the recursion explores

Combinatorial explosion: the factorial or exponential growth in the number of possibilities

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

This is the shape behind maze solving, N-queens and sudoku solvers. The pattern never changes: choose, recurse, undo.

📊 FIGURE — exploring a branching choice
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Every subset of a set
subsets(new int[]{1, 2, 3}, 0, "");
{1,2,3} {1,2} {1,3} {1} {2,3} {2} {3} {}
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. At each element there are exactly two choices: include it, or do not.
  2. Each choice leads to a recursive call on the rest.
  3. Three elements give 2³ = 8 subsets, and all eight are printed.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Counting the leaves of the tree
System.out.println(count(3));
System.out.println(count(10));
System.out.println((int) Math.pow(2, 10));
8 1024 1024
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Two recursive calls per level double the work each time.
  2. The total is 2ⁿ.
  3. That is why exhaustive search becomes impossible quite quickly.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Forgetting to undo a choice before trying the next one. If the state is shared rather than passed along, the second branch starts from the first branch's leftovers.
🎯 EXAM TIP
If a question asks how many possibilities are explored, count the choices per step and raise it to the number of steps — two choices over n items gives 2ⁿ.

StackOverflowError is what happens when recursion goes too deep. Each call pushes a frame (8.3) and the stack has a fixed size, so a few thousand levels is typically all you get.

public static int bad(int n) {
    return bad(n - 1);          // no base case — overflows in milliseconds
}

public static int alsoBad(int n) {
    if (n == 0) { return 0; }
    return alsoBad(n);          // base case exists but is UNREACHABLE
}

The two causes are a missing base case and a call that does not shrink the input. A third, legitimate case exists: correct recursion on genuinely deep data — a 100,000-element linked list — where the fix is to rewrite it as a loop rather than to hunt for a bug.

Each call takes a stack frame, and the stack is a fixed, fairly small region — typically a few thousand frames deep. Exceed it and the JVM throws StackOverflowError.

StackOverflowErrorOutOfMemoryError
regionthe stackthe heap
causerecursion too deep, usually missing a base casetoo many reachable objects
is anError, not an ExceptionError

Both are Errors rather than Exceptions, which is why you do not catch them: they signal that the program's assumptions have failed, not a condition to be handled.

The stack trace itself names the cause — the same method repeating for hundreds of lines. If the argument never changes between those lines the recursive case is not shrinking; if it does change but the base case never matches, the base case is testing the wrong thing.

For a genuinely deep problem the fix is to rewrite it as a loop, since a loop uses one frame no matter how many times it runs.

📘 DEFINITION

StackOverflowError: an Error thrown when the call stack is exhausted

Error vs Exception: an Error signals a condition a program should not try to recover from (12.1)

Tail recursion: recursion whose recursive call is the last operation; some languages optimise it into a loop, but Java does not

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

StackOverflowError is an Error, not an Exception, so catch (Exception e) will not catch it. That is deliberate — it is not meant to be recovered from.

📊 FIGURE — why the stack runs out
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Watching it actually happen
depth = 0;
try {
    forever();
} catch (StackOverflowError e) {
    System.out.println("StackOverflowError caught");
    System.out.println("frames before it broke: more than 1000? " + (depth > 1000));
}
StackOverflowError caught frames before it broke: more than 1000? true
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Each call adds a frame and never returns, so nothing is ever popped.
  2. The stack has a fixed size, so it fills.
  3. Java throws a StackOverflowError — an Error, not an Exception.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The same method, with a base case
System.out.println(countdown(1000));
System.out.println(countdown(9000));
0 0
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Now each call gets closer to 0.
  2. The base case returns, and the frames unwind normally.
  3. Deep but finite recursion is fine; unbounded recursion is not.
🎯 EXAM TIP
A StackOverflowError almost always means a missing or unreachable base case — check the stopping condition first, not the recursive step. An infinite LOOP by contrast just hangs; it does not throw.
