The permutation example from 11.7 written as a complete program, with the pieces named so the structure is visible.

public class Permutations {

    public static void permute(String prefix, String rest) {
        if (rest.length() == 0) {
            System.out.println(prefix);
            return;
        }
        for (int i = 0; i < rest.length(); i++) {
            char chosen  = rest.charAt(i);
            String left  = rest.substring(0, i) + rest.substring(i + 1);
            permute(prefix + chosen, left);
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        permute("", "abc");        // 3! = 6 lines of output
    }
}

Naming chosen and left instead of nesting the expressions is the difference between code you can trace and code you can only run. The recursion is unchanged; the readability is not.

static void permute(char[] a, int k) {
    if (k == a.length) { System.out.println(new String(a)); return; }
    for (int i = k; i < a.length; i++) {
        swap(a, k, i);            // choose: put a[i] in position k
        permute(a, k + 1);        // permute the rest
        swap(a, k, i);            // UNDO — restore before the next choice
    }
}

Position k is filled in turn by every remaining character, and the rest is permuted recursively. The base case is reaching the end of the array, which is where a completed arrangement is printed — output happens at the leaves, never on the way down.

The second swap is the whole reason the loop works. Without it the array stays scrambled and the next iteration chooses from data the previous branch left behind, producing duplicates and missing arrangements.

n characters give n! permutations — 5 gives 120, 10 gives 3.6 million, 13 exceeds two billion. Repeated characters produce visually duplicate lines, since the algorithm permutes positions rather than distinct values.

📘 DEFINITION

Prefix accumulator: the choices made so far, carried down the recursion

Remaining set: the items still available at this level

Output at the base case: printing when nothing remains, which is one complete solution

🎯 EXAM TIP

Count the output lines before running it: n characters give n! lines. Four characters give 24, five give 120 — which is how you know at a glance whether an input is reasonable.

📊 FIGURE — permutations by choosing a first character
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — All permutations of a short string
permute("", "abc");
abc acb bac bca cab cba
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Each loop pass chooses a different character to come next.
  2. The chosen character moves to the prefix and leaves the remainder.
  3. When nothing remains, the prefix is one complete permutation.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — How many there are
System.out.println(countPerms("abc"));
System.out.println(countPerms("abcd"));
System.out.println(countPerms("abcde"));
6 24 120
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Three characters give 3! = 6.
  2. Four give 24, five give 120.
  3. The count is n!, which is why permutation problems become impossible faster than almost anything else.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Removing the chosen character with replace instead of by index. replace removes EVERY copy, so a string with a repeated letter loses too much and the permutations come out wrong.

6.13 left a question open: when a method is handed a zero divisor, what should it do? Returning a made-up value pushes the problem onto a caller who may ignore it. An exception is the alternative — the method refuses, and the failure travels up until someone deals with it.

try {
    int result = 10 / divisor;          // may throw ArithmeticException
    System.out.println(result);
} catch (ArithmeticException e) {
    System.out.println("cannot divide by zero: " + e.getMessage());
} finally {
    System.out.println("always runs, thrown or not");
}

The flow is worth stating exactly, because trace questions depend on it: if nothing throws, the whole try runs and every catch is skipped. If something throws, the rest of the try is abandoned and the first matching catch runs. finally runs either way — even after a return.

try {
    int x = a[i] / d;
} catch (ArithmeticException e) {      // most SPECIFIC first
    ...
} catch (Exception e) {                // most GENERAL last
    ...
} finally {
    // runs whether or not an exception was thrown, and even after a return
}

Catch blocks are tested top to bottom and the first matching one wins, so they must run specific to general. Putting catch (Exception e) first makes every later block unreachable, and that is a compile error rather than a subtle bug.

CheckedUnchecked
extendsExceptionRuntimeException
compiler forces you to handle ityesno
examplesIOException, FileNotFoundExceptionNullPointerException, ArithmeticException, ArrayIndexOutOfBounds

The distinction is about who can be expected to recover. A missing file is a normal possibility the caller should plan for; a null reference is a programming error, and wrapping every dereference in a try block would be absurd.

finally is for releasing what must be released. It runs after the try block, after any catch, and even if the method returns from inside the try — which is why cleanup goes there rather than at the end of the try.

📘 DEFINITION

Exception: an object describing a runtime failure, thrown up the call stack

try: the block whose failures you want to handle

catch: the handler for one exception type, including its subtypes

finally: a block that always runs, used for cleanup such as close()

Stack unwinding: the search up the call stack for a matching catch

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

This is the mechanism behind every failure in Units 9 and 13. A missing file, an unparseable number and a bad cast all arrive as exceptions, and one structure handles all of them.

✅ Also covered in depth: Arrays → Exception Handling

📊 FIGURE — TRY / CATCH / FINALLY: THE TWO PATHS
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
If NO catch matches, finally still runs and THEN the exception keeps propagating up the call stack. And catch blocks are checked top-down — a parent type like Exception listed first swallows everything below it (the compiler rejects unreachable catches).
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — try, catch and finally, in the order they actually run
int[] a = { 10, 20, 30 };

try {
    System.out.println("before");
    System.out.println(a[5]);
    System.out.println("never reached");
} catch (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException e) {
    System.out.println("caught: " + e.getMessage());
} finally {
    System.out.println("finally always runs");
}

System.out.println("execution continues");
before caught: Index 5 out of bounds for length 3 finally always runs execution continues
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The moment a[5] throws, the rest of the try block is abandoned — "never reached" never prints.
  2. Control jumps straight to the matching catch.
  3. finally runs whether or not anything was thrown, which is what makes it the right place for cleanup.
  4. After the whole statement, the program carries on normally — a caught exception is not a crash.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Several catch blocks, and why the order matters
String[] inputs = { "4", "0", "seven" };
for (String s : inputs) {
    System.out.println("input \"" + s + "\"");
    attempt(s);
}
input "4" 100 / 4 = 25 input "0" arithmetic problem: / by zero input "seven" not a number: seven
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Java picks the first catch whose type matches, then stops looking — exactly like an else if chain.
  2. The specific types come first and the general Exception last.
  3. Reversing that order is a compile error, because a catch after Exception could never be reached.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Know what each of the three blocks is for: try holds the risky code, catch handles one kind of failure, finally cleans up either way. A question asking which lines print after a throw is really asking whether you know the rest of the try block is skipped but finally is not.

Throwing is how a method reports that it cannot do what was asked. The throw statement ends the method immediately and hands an exception object to the caller.

public static double divide(int a, int b) {
    if (b == 0) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("divisor must not be zero");
    }
    return (double) a / b;
}

// the two families
UNCHECKED (extends RuntimeException)   CHECKED (extends Exception)
  ArithmeticException                    IOException
  NullPointerException                   FileNotFoundException
  ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException         ClassNotFoundException
  IllegalArgumentException
  NumberFormatException
  -> compiler does not force handling    -> compiler REQUIRES catch or throws

The checked/unchecked split is the most-tested idea in the unit. Checked exceptions describe things outside your control — a file that might be missing — and the compiler insists you plan for them. Unchecked exceptions describe programming errors, and forcing a try around every array access would be absurd.

throw  new IllegalArgumentException("age must not be negative");  // an ACTION
                                                                     // one exception, now

void load(String f) throws IOException { ... }                       // a DECLARATION
                                                                     // this may throw

throw is a statement that raises an exception immediately; throws is part of a method header announcing what may escape. One letter apart, and the exam relies on that.

Throwing beats returning an error code because it cannot be ignored: a caller who does nothing about a -1 carries on with bad data, while an unhandled exception stops the program at the point of failure with a stack trace.

Integer division by zero throws ArithmeticException. Floating-point division by zero does not — it produces Infinity or NaN, which then propagates silently through every later calculation. That asymmetry is a favourite question.

📘 DEFINITION

throw: raises an exception, ending the method immediately

throws: a method declaration saying "I do not handle this; my caller must"

Checked exception: must be caught or declared; the compiler enforces it

Unchecked exception: a RuntimeException or Error; no compiler requirement

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

throw and throws are different keywords. throw is a statement that raises one exception; throws is part of a method signature listing what may escape. Swapping them is a compile error and an exam distractor.

✅ Also covered in depth: Arrays → Exception Handling

📊 FIGURE — throw, throws, and the two families
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Throwing on bad input instead of returning nonsense
System.out.println(sqrtOf(9));
System.out.println(Math.sqrt(-9));
try {
    System.out.println(sqrtOf(-9));
} catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
    System.out.println("rejected -> " + e.getMessage());
}
3.0 NaN rejected -> negative input: -9.0
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Math.sqrt(-9) quietly returns NaN, and NaN then poisons every calculation it touches without ever complaining.
  2. Throwing stops the program at the point the bad value arrived, which is the only place that knows what went wrong.
  3. IllegalArgumentException is unchecked, so the caller is free to catch it or not — no throws clause is needed.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Checked versus unchecked, in one program
try {
    checkedOne();
} catch (Exception e) {
    System.out.println("1: " + e.getMessage());
}
try {
    uncheckedOne();
} catch (RuntimeException e) {
    System.out.println("2: " + e.getMessage());
}
System.out.println(RuntimeException.class.isAssignableFrom(IllegalStateException.class));
System.out.println(RuntimeException.class.isAssignableFrom(java.io.IOException.class));
1: I am checked - the signature must say so 2: I am unchecked - no throws needed true false

  2. uncheckedOne compiles with no declaration at all, because it extends RuntimeException.
  3. The last two lines ask the runtime directly which family each belongs to: IllegalStateException sits under RuntimeException, IOException does not. (Writing this as new IOException("x") instanceof RuntimeException will not even compile — Java rejects an instanceof between types that can never be related.)
🎯 EXAM TIP
Test yourself on the split, because questions lean on it: IOException and FileNotFoundException are checked and force a throws or a catch. NullPointerException, ArithmeticException, NumberFormatException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException and IllegalArgumentException are unchecked and the compiler never mentions them.

File work is where checked exceptions become unavoidable, because 9.4 quietly used throws FileNotFoundException on main to make the compiler stop complaining. Catching it is the version that can actually respond.

Scanner in = null;
try {
    in = new Scanner(new File("data.txt"));
    while (in.hasNextLine()) { System.out.println(in.nextLine()); }
} catch (FileNotFoundException e) {
    System.out.println("No such file — using defaults instead.");
} finally {
    if (in != null) { in.close(); }        // cleanup happens either way
}

// try-with-resources: closes automatically, no finally needed
try (Scanner in2 = new Scanner(new File("data.txt"))) {
    while (in2.hasNextLine()) { System.out.println(in2.nextLine()); }
} catch (FileNotFoundException e) {
    System.out.println("missing");
}

The finally block has to test for null, because if the constructor threw, in was never assigned. Try-with-resources exists precisely to remove that awkwardness — it closes anything declared in its parentheses, in reverse order, whatever happens.

What try-with-resources actually requires

Try-with-resources closes anything declared in its parentheses, and it can only do that for a type that implements AutoCloseable — the interface whose single method is close(). Scanner, PrintWriter, FileReader and every stream implement it, which is why they all work in that position.

class Resource implements AutoCloseable {
    public void close() { System.out.println("closed"); }
}

try (Resource r = new Resource()) { ... }   // close() runs automatically

Resources are closed in reverse order of declaration, and closing happens before any catch or finally block runs — which is the ordering questions ask about.

try (Scanner in = new Scanner(new File("data.txt"))) {
    ...
} catch (FileNotFoundException e) {        // subclass of IOException
    ...
} catch (IOException e) {                  // more general — must come after
    ...
}

File work is where checked exceptions become unavoidable: the compiler will not build code that opens a file without either catching or declaring the failure. That is the language insisting you decide what happens when the file is not there.

try-with-resources closes anything declared in its parentheses whose type implements AutoCloseable — every stream, reader, writer and Scanner. Resources close in reverse order of declaration, and before any catch or finally block runs.

Without it, the close call has to go in finally, needs its own try block because closing can itself throw, and is skipped entirely if an exception fires before it — which is why the older pattern is no longer taught as the default.

📘 DEFINITION

try-with-resources: a try whose declared resources are closed automatically

Resource leak: an unclosed file handle or connection; not fixed by the garbage collector (8.4)

Recovery: responding to a failure with a usable alternative rather than crashing

🎯 EXAM TIP

Catching an exception and doing nothing — an empty catch block — is worse than not catching it. The failure still happened; now nobody will ever know.

✅ Also covered in depth: Advanced → try-with-resources and File I/O

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A missing file, handled rather than crashing

w.println("alpha");
w.println("beta");
w.close();

System.out.println("notes.txt:");
readIt("notes.txt");
System.out.println("gone.txt:");
readIt("gone.txt");
System.out.println("still running");
notes.txt: alpha beta gone.txt: could not open gone.txt still running

  2. The try-with-resources form closes the Scanner automatically, even if an exception escapes the block.
  3. The missing file produces one sentence and the program keeps going — nothing about it is fatal.

java.io.PrintWriter w = new java.io.PrintWriter("mixed.txt");
w.println("7 hello");
w.close();

java.util.Scanner in = new java.util.Scanner(new java.io.File("mixed.txt"));
System.out.println("first int: " + in.nextInt());
try {
    System.out.println(in.nextInt());
} catch (java.util.InputMismatchException e) {
    System.out.println("InputMismatchException - 'hello' is not an int");
}

try {
    in.nextInt();
} catch (java.util.NoSuchElementException e) {
    System.out.println("NoSuchElementException - nothing left to read");
}
in.close();

  2. next() then consumes it as a String, which is how you recover.
  3. Asking for another token at end of file throws NoSuchElementException; guarding with hasNextInt() avoids both.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Catching FileNotFoundException but never checking that the file was actually read. The catch block prints a warning, execution continues, and the rest of the program then works on empty data as though everything succeeded. Either recover properly or stop — do not carry on with nothing.

A method has two options for an exception it cannot resolve: handle it, or declare it and let the caller decide. Choosing correctly is a design decision about who has enough context to respond.

// PROPAGATE — this method cannot sensibly recover
public static int readAge(String file) throws FileNotFoundException {
    Scanner in = new Scanner(new File(file));
    return in.nextInt();
}

// HANDLE — the caller knows what to do about it
public static void main(String[] args) {
    try {
        System.out.println(readAge("ages.txt"));
    } catch (FileNotFoundException e) {
        System.out.println("Using default age 0");
    }
}

Multiple catches are searched in order and the first match wins, which makes ordering a hard rule: specific types before general ones. catch (Exception e) placed first makes every later catch unreachable, and that is a compile error.

try { ... }
catch (FileNotFoundException e) { ... }    // specific
catch (IOException e)           { ... }    // its parent
catch (Exception e)             { ... }    // most general — LAST

An uncaught exception propagates: it leaves the method, then that method's caller, and so on up the call stack until something catches it or the program stops and prints the trace. The trace is that path, innermost call first.

void a() { b(); }                         // no try — the exception passes through
void b() throws IOException { c(); }      // declared, not handled
void c() throws IOException { throw new IOException(); }

Catch where you can actually do something. A method that has no sensible response should declare throws and let a caller with more context decide — catching and logging at every level buries the real failure in noise.

An empty catch block is the one thing never to write. It converts a failure into silently wrong behaviour, and the reason a program "does nothing" with no error is very often a catch (Exception e) { } several layers down.

Unchecked exceptions may be declared in a throws clause as documentation, but nothing requires it and nothing enforces it.

📘 DEFINITION

Propagation: declaring an exception with throws so it travels to the caller

Catch ordering: subclasses must be caught before their superclasses

Multi-catch: catch (IOException | SQLException e) handles several types in one block

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

A general catch above a specific one gives "exception has already been caught". The compiler is telling you the second block can never run.

✅ Also covered in depth: Arrays → Exception Handling

📊 FIGURE — how an exception travels up the call stack
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — One catch, three levels up
try {
    level1();
} catch (IllegalStateException e) {
    System.out.println("caught in main: " + e.getMessage());
}
level1 entered level2 entered level3 entered caught in main: broke at level 3
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The exception is thrown three calls deep and no method in between catches it.
  2. Each unfinished method is abandoned on the way up — neither "level2 finished" nor "level1 finished" prints.
  3. The first enclosing catch of a matching type handles it, however far up the stack that is.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — finally runs on the way out, even when the exception escapes
System.out.println("ok case: " + risky(false));
try {
    System.out.println(risky(true));
} catch (RuntimeException e) {
    System.out.println("caught: " + e.getMessage());
}
cleanup ran ok case: 1 cleanup ran caught: boom
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. In the success case finally runs after the return value is computed but before the method actually returns.
  2. In the failure case there is no catch in risky at all, yet finally still runs as the exception passes through.
  3. That guarantee is why files and connections are closed in finally — or, better, with try-with-resources.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Trace these questions by walking the call stack downward to the throw, then back up looking for the first matching catch. Any statement after the call that threw, in any method on that path, does not run — but every finally on the path does.

When no built-in type describes your failure, define one. A user-defined exception is just a class extending Exception or RuntimeException, and which one you extend decides whether it is checked.

public class InsufficientFundsException extends Exception {   // CHECKED
    private double shortfall;

    public InsufficientFundsException(String msg, double shortfall) {
        super(msg);                       // the message goes to the parent
        this.shortfall = shortfall;
    }

    public double getShortfall() { return shortfall; }
}

// throwing it
if (amount > balance) {
    throw new InsufficientFundsException("Balance too low", amount - balance);
}

The advantage over a generic exception is the extra data: the catcher can ask how much was missing and act on it. That is the argument for a custom type — not the name, but the information it can carry.

Catching a user-defined exception

Once you have defined an exception, it can be caught either by its own type or by any supertype it inherits from — because a catch block matches the named type and all of its subclasses.

catch (InsufficientFundsException e)  // its own type — most specific
catch (Exception e)                    // a supertype — also matches
catch (RuntimeException e)             // matches ONLY if it extends RuntimeException

That is the same ordering rule as 12.4: specific before general, or the general block makes the specific one unreachable.

public class InsufficientFundsException extends Exception {   // CHECKED
    private final double shortfall;
    public InsufficientFundsException(String msg, double shortfall) {
        super(msg);                      // pass the message up to Exception
        this.shortfall = shortfall;      // carry extra data with the failure
    }
    public double getShortfall() { return shortfall; }
}

if (amount > balance)
    throw new InsufficientFundsException("Balance too low", amount - balance);

Extend Exception for a checked one the caller must handle, or RuntimeException for an unchecked one signalling a programming error. That single choice is what the exam asks about.

A custom exception is worth defining when callers need to distinguish this failure from others — you can catch InsufficientFundsException specifically instead of inspecting the text of a generic message. The convention is a name ending in Exception, and a constructor that passes the message to super.

Carrying a field, as with shortfall here, lets the handler respond with detail rather than just reporting that something went wrong.

📘 DEFINITION

User-defined exception: a class extending Exception or RuntimeException

super(msg): passes the message to the parent, where getMessage() reads it

Extends Exception: makes it checked — callers must handle or declare it

Extends RuntimeException: makes it unchecked — no compiler requirement

🎯 EXAM TIP

Name exceptions ending in "Exception" and extend Exception for conditions a caller could reasonably recover from. Extend RuntimeException for programming errors that should be fixed rather than caught.

📊 FIGURE — writing your own exception type
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A named exception that carries the details with it
try {
    withdraw(20);
    System.out.println("balance now " + balance);
    withdraw(80);
    System.out.println("never reached");
} catch (InsufficientFundsException e) {
    System.out.println("declined: " + e.getMessage());
    System.out.printf("needs %.2f more%n", e.getShortfall());
}

actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. super(message) is what makes getMessage() return that text — without it the message is null.
  2. The class carries an extra field, so the handler gets the number as data instead of having to parse the sentence.
  3. Because it extends Exception, withdraw must declare throws and callers must handle it.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The one decision that changes everything: which class you extend
try { mustDeclare(); } catch (CheckedProblem e) { System.out.println(e.getMessage()); }
try { neednt(); } catch (UncheckedProblem e) { System.out.println(e.getMessage()); }

try { neednt(); } catch (Exception e) {
    System.out.println("a catch of Exception still catches it: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName());

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Writing printArray once for int[], again for String[] and again for double[] is the problem generics solve. A generic method is written once with a type placeholder and works for every type.

public static  void printAll(T[] items) {
//            ^ declares the type parameter, before the return type
    for (T item : items) { System.out.println(item); }
}

printAll(new String[]{"a", "b"});      // T is String
printAll(new Integer[]{1, 2});         // T is Integer — NOT int

The gain over using Object is compile-time checking. With Object[] the compiler cannot stop you mixing types and every element needs a cast on the way out; with <T> the type is known and the compiler enforces it.

public static <T> void printAll(List<T> items) {    // <T> declared before the return type
    for (T x : items) System.out.println(x);
}

ArrayList<String> l = new ArrayList<>();          // diamond — type inferred
ArrayList raw = new ArrayList();                   // RAW type — no checking

A generic method takes the type as a parameter, so one method serves every element type without casting. The <T> before the return type is what declares it — leaving it out makes T an unknown class name and the method will not compile.

The point is compile-time type safety. Before generics, a collection held Object, every read needed a cast, and a wrong type failed at run time with ClassCastException. With generics the mistake is caught while you are typing it.

A raw type compiles with a warning and gives all that up. And a type argument must be a reference type — List<int> is illegal, List<Integer> is the way, which is why wrappers exist.

📘 DEFINITION

Generic method: a method with its own type parameter, usable with many types

Type parameter: the placeholder, conventionally T, E, K or V

Type inference: the compiler working out T from the arguments so you need not state it

Type safety: errors caught at compile time rather than as a ClassCastException at run time

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Generics do not work with primitives. <int> is a compile error — use Integer and let autoboxing (7.13) handle the conversion.

✅ Also covered in depth: Advanced → Generics

📊 FIGURE — the shape of a generic method
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — One method, any element type
String[] words = { "red", "green", "blue" };
Integer[] nums = { 3, 1, 4 };
Double[] reals = { 1.5, 2.5 };

printAll(words);
printAll(nums);
printAll(reals);

System.out.println(firstOf(words).toUpperCase());
System.out.println(firstOf(nums) + 10);
red green blue 3 1 4 1.5 2.5 RED 13
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The <T> sits before the return type — that is what declares T, and leaving it out is the usual compile error.
  2. T is inferred from the argument at each call, so nothing has to be spelled out.
  3. Because firstOf returns T, the result is already a String or an Integer — no cast is needed, and that is the whole point over using Object.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Why the array is Integer[] and not int[]
Integer[] boxed = { 1, 2, 3 };
System.out.println(count(boxed));

int primitive = 7;
Integer wrapped = primitive;
int back = wrapped;
System.out.println(wrapped + " " + back);

A plain <T> accepts anything, which means the method can only use the handful of operations every object supports. A bound narrows it and unlocks more.

public static > T max(T[] items) {
    T best = items[0];
    for (T item : items) {
        if (item.compareTo(best) > 0) { best = item; }   // legal BECAUSE of the bound
    }
    return best;
}

max(new Integer[]{3, 9, 2});        // 9
max(new String[]{"b", "a"});        // "b" — String is Comparable too

Without extends Comparable<T>, the call to compareTo would not compile, because T might be any class at all. The bound is a promise about what T can do, and the compiler holds you to it at every call site.

Wildcards

A type parameter names a type you are choosing. A wildcard — written ? — stands for a type you are not naming, and it exists because List<Integer> is not a subtype of List<Number>, however much it looks like one.

void printAll(List list)                  // any element type at all
void sum(List list)        // Number or any subtype — READ from it
void addInts(List list)     // Integer or any supertype — WRITE to it

The memory aid is PECS — Producer Extends, Consumer Super. If the collection produces values for you to read, use ? extends; if it consumes values you put in, use ? super. A plain <?> lets you read only as Object and add nothing but null.

public static <T extends Comparable<T>> T max(List<T> items) {
    T best = items.get(0);
    for (T x : items) if (x.compareTo(best) > 0) best = x;   // compareTo is now legal
    return best;
}

An unbounded T could be anything, so the only methods available are Object's — no compareTo, no length(). A bound narrows what may be substituted and in exchange lets you call that type's methods.

The keyword is always extends, even when the bound is an interface: <T extends Comparable<T>>, not implements. Multiple bounds are joined with & — <T extends Number & Comparable<T>> — with the class first if there is one.

Passing a type that does not satisfy the bound is a compile error at the call site, which is the whole benefit: the restriction is checked once, where the mistake is, rather than failing later inside the method.

📘 DEFINITION

Bounded type parameter: <T extends Something> — T must be that type or a subtype

extends (in generics): used for both classes and interfaces here, unlike in a class declaration

Comparable<T>: the interface providing compareTo, which defines a natural ordering

Upper bound: the ceiling type a type argument must satisfy

🎯 EXAM TIP

In generics, extends means "is or is below", covering both extends and implements. <T extends Comparable> accepts any class that implements Comparable.

✅ Also covered in depth: Advanced → Generics

📊 FIGURE — bounding a type parameter
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Without a bound there is nothing you can do with T
System.out.println(maxOf(new Integer[] { 3, 9, 4 }));
System.out.println(maxOf(new String[] { "pear", "apple", "fig" }));
System.out.println(maxOf(new Double[] { 2.5, 0.5 }));

System.out.println("apple".compareTo("banana"));
System.out.println("banana".compareTo("apple"));
System.out.println("fig".compareTo("fig"));
9 pear 2.5 -1 1 0
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. An unbounded <T> would not compile here: the compiler only knows T is an Object, and Object has no compareTo.
  2. <T extends Comparable<T>> promises every T can be compared to another T, which unlocks the call.
  3. For Strings compareTo is alphabetical, so the maximum is the last one alphabetically — pear, not the longest.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A numeric bound, and what it does not give you
System.out.println(sum(new Integer[] { 1, 2, 3 }));
System.out.println(sum(new Double[] { 1.5, 2.25 }));
System.out.println(sum(new Long[] { 10L, 20L }));

Integer a = 5, b = 3;
System.out.println(a.doubleValue() + " " + a.intValue() + " " + a.compareTo(b));
6.0 3.75 30.0 5.0 5 1
actual output, captured from the JVM

  2. It does not let you write x + y on two T values; the operator is not part of the Number type, which is why the total is accumulated through doubleValue().
  3. The same bound accepts Integer, Double and Long without a single change to the method.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Writing <T implements Comparable<T>>. In a type bound the keyword is always extends, even when the bound is an interface — implements there is a syntax error.

A generic class takes its type parameter at the class level, so every method can use it. This is exactly what ArrayList<String> is — 7.14 was using generics before naming them.

public class Box {
    private T contents;

    public void put(T item)  { contents = item; }
    public T    get()        { return contents; }
    public boolean isEmpty() { return contents == null; }
}

Box b = new Box<>();      // <> infers String — the diamond operator
b.put("hello");
String s = b.get();               // no cast needed

b.put(42);                        // COMPILE ERROR — caught before it can run

That last line is the whole benefit. The non-generic version would take an Object, accept the 42 silently, and fail with a ClassCastException at run time — the difference between an error you fix now and one your user finds.

public class Box<T> {                 // T is a placeholder for the whole class
    private T item;                   // field of the parameter type
    public void set(T item) { this.item = item; }
    public T get() { return item; }
}

Box<String> b = new Box<>();
b.set("hello");
String s = b.get();                   // no cast needed

The type parameter follows the class name and is then usable throughout — as field types, parameter types and return types. Each instantiation fixes it: a Box<String> and a Box<Integer> are different types and cannot be assigned to each other.

A static member cannot use the class's type parameter, because T only exists once an object has been created with a specific type. A static method needing a type parameter must declare its own.

Several parameters are written class Pair<K, V>, which is exactly how Map<K, V> is declared.

📘 DEFINITION

Generic class: a class parameterised by one or more types

Diamond operator: the empty <> that infers the type argument from the declaration

Parameterised type: Box<String> — the class with its type argument supplied

Type erasure: generics exist at compile time only; the runtime class is just Box

🎯 EXAM TIP

Multiple parameters are ordinary: class Pair<K, V> is how HashMap<K, V> (14.3) is declared.

✅ Also covered in depth: Advanced → Generics

📊 FIGURE — A GENERIC CLASS IS A TEMPLATE WITH A TYPE HOLE
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A class parameterised by the type it holds
Box<String> s = new Box<>("note");
Box<Integer> n = new Box<>(42);

System.out.println(s + " " + n);
System.out.println(s.get().length());
System.out.println(n.get() + 8);

s.set("replaced");
System.out.println(s.get());
Box(note) Box(42) 4 50 replaced
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The <T> goes on the class name, and every T inside the body then means the same one type per object.
  2. The diamond <> on the right of new repeats the type the declaration already stated.
  3. s.get() is a String, so .length() works with no cast — the compiler knows the type, which is what a raw Object field could never give you.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A generic pair, and two type parameters
Pair<String, Integer> score = new Pair<>("Ada", 96);
System.out.println(score);
System.out.println(score.getFirst().toUpperCase());
System.out.println(score.getSecond() / 2);
System.out.println(score.swapped());

java.util.ArrayList<Pair<String, Integer>> all = new java.util.ArrayList<>();
all.add(score);
all.add(new Pair<>("Grace", 91));
for (Pair<String, Integer> p : all) System.out.println(p.getFirst() + " scored " + p.getSecond());
(Ada, 96) ADA 48 (96, Ada) Ada scored 96 Grace scored 91
actual output, captured from the JVM

  2. swapped() returns Pair<B, A> — the parameters can be reordered and reused in the body.
  3. The types survive into collections: each element of the list is known to be a Pair<String, Integer>.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Using the raw type — Box b = new Box("x"); with no <String>. It still compiles, with a warning, but b.get() now returns Object, so b.get().length() fails to compile and any cast you add is unchecked. Always name the type argument.

Bounds work at class level for the same reason as at method level: they let the class use the bounded type’s methods.

public class SortedBox> {
    private ArrayList items = new ArrayList<>();

    public void add(T item) {
        items.add(item);
        Collections.sort(items);       // legal because T is Comparable
    }

    public T max() { return items.get(items.size() - 1); }
}

SortedBox nums = new SortedBox<>();     // fine
SortedBox bad  = new SortedBox<>();     // ERROR — Scanner is not Comparable

The error appears at the declaration, not on some later call. That is the difference a bound makes: the constraint is checked once, where the type is chosen, rather than being discovered when a method fails.

public class SortedBox<T extends Comparable<T>> {
    private ArrayList<T> items = new ArrayList<>();
    public void add(T x) {
        items.add(x);
        Collections.sort(items);       // legal ONLY because of the bound
    }
}

SortedBox<String> ok  = new SortedBox<>();   // String is Comparable
SortedBox<Scanner> no = new SortedBox<>();   // compile error

A bound on a generic class works exactly as on a generic method, and for the same reason: without it the class knows nothing about T beyond it being an Object, so nothing can be sorted or compared.

The check happens where the type is supplied, so an unsuitable type is rejected at the declaration rather than blowing up later inside add. That is the difference between a compile-time and a run-time guarantee, and it is the standard exam framing of "why bound a type parameter".

📘 DEFINITION

Bounded generic class: a class whose type parameter must satisfy a constraint

Multiple bounds: <T extends A & B> requires both; a class bound must come first

Collections.sort: sorts a List whose elements are Comparable

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

This is how the standard library expresses requirements. TreeSet (14.7) demands Comparable elements for the same reason — it cannot keep things in order without a way to compare them.

✅ Also covered in depth: Advanced → Generics

📊 FIGURE — a bound on a class's type parameter
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The bound decides which type arguments the compiler will accept
Stat<Integer> ints = new Stat<>();

reals.add(1.5); reals.add(2.25);

15.0 over 3 values mean 5.00 3.75
actual output, captured from the JVM

  2. Stat<String> would be rejected at compile time — the bound is checked where the object is created, not where a method is called.
  3. This is the payoff of a bound: v.doubleValue() is only legal because T is known to be a Number.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A bounded class that sorts what it stores
Sorted<String> names = new Sorted<>();
names.add("Zoe"); names.add("Ada"); names.add("Kim");
System.out.println(names.min());
System.out.println(names.inOrder());

Sorted<Integer> nums = new Sorted<>();

Ada [Ada, Kim, Zoe] 2 [2, 5, 9]
actual output, captured from the JVM

  2. inOrder() sorts a copy, so the object's own order is left alone — returning a sorted view without mutating the source.

Expecting Stat<Number> to accept a Stat<Integer>. Generics are invariant: even though Integer is a Number, Stat<Integer> is not a subtype of Stat<Number> and assigning one to the other will not compile.

Implementing Comparable is how your own class becomes sortable, and it is one method: compareTo, returning negative, zero or positive exactly as String.compareTo did in 3.13.

public class Student implements Comparable {
    private String name;
    private int score;

    @Override
    public int compareTo(Student other) {
        return Integer.compare(this.score, other.score);   // ascending by score
        // descending: Integer.compare(other.score, this.score)
    }
}

ArrayList roster = new ArrayList<>();
Collections.sort(roster);              // now works — uses compareTo

// a different order without touching the class
roster.sort(Comparator.comparing(Student::getName));

Integer.compare(a, b) is preferred over a - b: the subtraction overflows for large values (2.16) and silently returns the wrong sign. It is a real bug and a common exam distractor.

public class Student implements Comparable<Student> {
    public int compareTo(Student o) {
        return Integer.compare(this.score, o.score);   // NOT this.score - o.score
    }
}
Collections.sort(list);                                 // uses compareTo

Collections.sort(list, (a, b) -> a.getName().compareTo(b.getName()));  // Comparator
list.sort(Comparator.comparing(Student::getName).reversed());
ComparableComparator
methodcompareTo(other) — one argumentcompare(a, b) — two
livesinside the class being sortedoutside, as a separate object
givesthe natural ordering — one per classany number of alternative orderings

The return value is a sign, not a magnitude: negative if this comes first, zero if equivalent, positive if it comes after. Any negative number will do, which is why a - b looks tempting — and it is wrong, because the subtraction overflows for large or opposite-signed values and flips the sign. Integer.compare is the safe form.

Strings compare lexicographically by Unicode value, so all uppercase letters sort before all lowercase ones — "Zoe" before "ana".

📘 DEFINITION

Comparable: the interface defining a class’s natural ordering through compareTo

compareTo: returns negative if this comes first, 0 if equal, positive if this comes after

Comparator: a separate object defining an alternative ordering

Natural ordering: the single default order a Comparable class defines

🎯 EXAM TIP

Comparable is the class’s one built-in order; Comparator supplies any number of alternatives from outside. Sort by name and by score at different times, and you need one of each.

✅ Also covered in depth: Advanced → Comparable and Comparator

📊 FIGURE — making your own class sortable
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — One class, sorted by its natural order
java.util.ArrayList<Student> roll = new java.util.ArrayList<>();
roll.add(new Student("Ada", 3.6));
roll.add(new Student("Kim", 3.9));
roll.add(new Student("Zoe", 2.8));

System.out.println("before: " + roll);
java.util.Collections.sort(roll);
System.out.println("after:  " + roll);

java.util.Collections.reverse(roll);
System.out.println("desc:   " + roll);
System.out.println(java.util.Collections.max(roll));
before: [Ada(3.6), Kim(3.9), Zoe(2.8)] after: [Zoe(2.8), Ada(3.6), Kim(3.9)] desc: [Kim(3.9), Ada(3.6), Zoe(2.8)] Kim(3.9)
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Collections.sort sorts the list in place and returns nothing — assigning its result is a compile error.
  2. Double.compare(a, b) returns the sign the interface asks for and avoids the rounding problems of subtracting two doubles.
  3. Once a class is Comparable, max, min and binarySearch all work on it for free.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The sign is the whole contract
Student a = new Student("Ada", 3.6);
Student k = new Student("Kim", 3.9);

System.out.println(a.compareTo(k));
System.out.println(k.compareTo(a));
System.out.println(a.compareTo(a));

System.out.println("apple".compareTo("banana"));
System.out.println(Integer.valueOf(7).compareTo(3));

java.util.ArrayList<Student> l = new java.util.ArrayList<>(java.util.List.of(k, a));
l.sort(java.util.Comparator.comparing(s -> s.name));
System.out.println("by name: " + l);
-1 1 0 -1 1 by name: [Ada, Kim]
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Only the sign matters, not the size: any negative value means "comes first".
  2. The three calls show the contract in both directions plus the equal case.
  3. A Comparator sorts by a different key without touching the class — compareTo defines the one natural order, comparators supply the alternatives.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Writing return (int)(this.gpa - other.gpa);. The cast truncates, so 3.9 and 3.6 both give 0 and the two students are reported as equal — the list comes back looking unsorted. Use Double.compare, and for ints Integer.compare rather than subtraction, which can also overflow.

A generic method that maps values shows the mechanics with two type parameters, and it is the shape behind every transform you will meet later.

public static  V lookup(K[] keys, V[] values, K target, V fallback) {
    for (int i = 0; i < keys.length; i++) {
        if (keys[i].equals(target)) { return values[i]; }   // equals, not == (3.2)
    }
    return fallback;
}

String[] codes = {"US", "GB", "JP"};
String[] names = {"United States", "United Kingdom", "Japan"};

lookup(codes, names, "GB", "Unknown");     // "United Kingdom"
lookup(codes, names, "ZZ", "Unknown");     // "Unknown"

Two parallel arrays again (5.5), and the same fragility again — which is exactly what HashMap (14.3) fixes by storing the pairs together and finding them without a loop.

public static <T, R> List<R> map(List<T> in, Function<T, R> f) {
    List<R> out = new ArrayList<>();
    for (T x : in) out.add(f.apply(x));      // input untouched, new list returned
    return out;
}

List<Integer> lengths = map(names, s -> s.length());   // T=String, R=Integer

Two type parameters are needed because the input and output element types differ — T in, R out. Writing it with one would force the result to have the same element type as the source, which defeats the purpose.

Neither is written at the call: the compiler infers both from the arguments. That inference is what makes generic code readable rather than ceremonial.

Returning a new list rather than modifying the input is the same choice as 6.20 — the caller keeps the original, and the method has no side effect to reason about.

📘 DEFINITION

Multiple type parameters: declared as <K, V>, conventionally key and value

Default / fallback value: what to return when the search finds nothing

Generic lookup: a search whose key and result types are both parameterised

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Using == instead of .equals() here breaks the method for every reference type — including the Strings above. Inside a generic method you almost always want .equals().

📊 FIGURE — a generic method that transforms a list
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — One mapping method, several different transformations
java.util.List<Integer> nums = java.util.List.of(1, 2, 3, 4);
java.util.List<String> words = java.util.List.of("red", "green", "blue");

System.out.println(mapAll(nums, x -> x * x));
System.out.println(mapAll(nums, x -> "#" + x));
System.out.println(mapAll(words, String::toUpperCase));
System.out.println(mapAll(words, String::length));
[1, 4, 9, 16] [#1, #2, #3, #4] [RED, GREEN, BLUE] [3, 5, 4]
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. T and R are independent: the second call takes Integers in and gives Strings out.
  2. The transformation arrives as a parameter, so the loop is written once and never changes.
  3. String::toUpperCase is a method reference — shorthand for the lambda s -> s.toUpperCase().
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Filter and reduce, built the same way
java.util.List<Integer> nums = java.util.List.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6);

System.out.println(keepIf(nums, x -> x % 2 == 0));
System.out.println(reduce(nums, 0, (a, b) -> a + b));
System.out.println(reduce(nums, 1, (a, b) -> a * b));

java.util.List<String> words = java.util.List.of("red", "green", "blue");
System.out.println(keepIf(words, s -> s.length() > 3));
System.out.println(reduce(words, "", (a, b) -> a + b));
[2, 4, 6] 21 720 [green, blue] redgreenblue
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Predicate<T> is the standard name for a test returning boolean; BinaryOperator<T> combines two T values into one.
  2. The starting value matters: 0 for a sum, 1 for a product, "" for joining text.
  3. Every one of these methods is written once and works on any element type — that is what generics buy.
🎯 EXAM TIP
When a generic method takes two type parameters, write down what each stands for before tracing it. In <T, R> List<R> mapAll(List<T>, Function<T, R>) the answer to "what type is the result?" is always R, whatever T happened to be.

The enhanced for loop from 5.10 works on every collection in this unit, and that is not a coincidence — it works on anything implementing Iterable, which every collection does.

for (String s : arrayOfStrings)   { }
for (String s : arrayListOfStrings) { }
for (String s : hashSetOfStrings)   { }

// a Map needs one of its views, because it holds pairs
for (String key : map.keySet())            { }
for (Integer v : map.values())             { }
for (Map.Entry e : map.entrySet()) {
    e.getKey();  e.getValue();
}

The one hard rule: you may not add to or remove from a collection while a for-each is walking it. Doing so throws ConcurrentModificationException. Removing requires an explicit Iterator and its remove(), or a plain indexed loop going backwards.

for (String s : names) { ... }        // works on arrays AND anything Iterable

for (Map.Entry<String,Integer> e : counts.entrySet())
    System.out.println(e.getKey() + " " + e.getValue());

The enhanced for works over any array and any type implementing Iterable, which every collection does. It is read-only in the sense that matters: you cannot replace an element, though you can call mutating methods on the object an element refers to.

Structurally modifying a collection while a for-each is running throws ConcurrentModificationException — adding or removing during the loop. Removing safely needs an explicit Iterator with it.remove(), or a backwards indexed loop.

📘 DEFINITION

Iterable: the interface that makes a type usable in an enhanced for loop

Iterator: the object walking a collection; has hasNext(), next() and remove()

ConcurrentModificationException: thrown when a collection is structurally modified during iteration

entrySet(): a Map view giving key-value pairs together in one pass

🎯 EXAM TIP

Iterating a HashSet or HashMap gives no guaranteed order — it can differ between runs. If a question shows hash-based output in a specific order, the order is not something you can rely on.

✅ Also covered in depth: Control Flow → for Loops, break, and continue

📊 FIGURE — THE COLLECTIONS FAMILY AT A GLANCE
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — walking a Map with entrySet and keeping a running total

A LinkedHashMap keeps insertion order, so the output below is fixed rather than "whatever the hash decides". Each pass hands you one Map.Entry, and getKey / getValue read the two halves of it.

LinkedHashMap<String,Integer> credits = new LinkedHashMap<>();
credits.put("Java Fundamentals", 4);
credits.put("Discrete Math I", 3);
credits.put("Data Management", 4);

int total = 0;
for (Map.Entry<String,Integer> e : credits.entrySet()) {
    total += e.getValue();
    System.out.println(e.getKey() + " -> " + e.getValue()
                       + "  (running total " + total + ")");
}
System.out.println("Total credits: " + total);
what it prints
Java Fundamentals -> 4  (running total 4)
Discrete Math I -> 3  (running total 7)
Data Management -> 4  (running total 11)
Total credits: 11
  1. The loop variable is one Map.Entry<String,Integer> per pass — not a key, not a value, the pair.
  2. total += e.getValue() unboxes the Integer to an int automatically, so the arithmetic is ordinary.
  3. Doing it with keySet() instead would need credits.get(k) inside the loop: a second lookup per element for information the iterator already had.
  4. total is declared before the loop. Declared inside, it would be reborn as 0 on every pass — the accumulator rule from Unit 4.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the exception, and the two legal ways to remove during a walk

Removing from a collection while a for-each is walking it is the error this section exists to prevent. The instructive part is that the removal succeeds — the failure arrives on the next pass, when the iterator notices the collection changed underneath it.

List<String> roster = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Ada","Raj","Mia","Sam"));
try {
    for (String s : roster) { if (s.equals("Raj")) roster.remove(s); }
} catch (ConcurrentModificationException e) {
    System.out.println("caught " + e.getClass().getSimpleName());
}
System.out.println("after the failed attempt: " + roster);

List<String> b = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Ada","Raj","Mia","Sam"));
Iterator<String> it = b.iterator();
while (it.hasNext()) { if (it.next().equals("Raj")) it.remove(); }
System.out.println("iterator.remove: " + b);

List<String> c = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Ada","Raj","Mia","Sam"));
c.removeIf(s -> s.equals("Raj"));
System.out.println("removeIf: " + c);
what it prints
caught ConcurrentModificationException
after the failed attempt: [Ada, Mia, Sam]
iterator.remove: [Ada, Mia, Sam]
removeIf: [Ada, Mia, Sam]
  1. Line 2 of the output is the point: Raj really was removed. The list is already modified when the exception is thrown.
  2. The iterator holds a modification count it took at creation. On the next next() it compares that count against the list’s and throws when they disagree.
  3. it.remove() works because the iterator performs the removal itself and updates its own count to match.
  4. removeIf is the one-line version of the same thing and is what you should write in new code.

One quirk worth knowing: removing the second-to-last element happens to leave hasNext() returning false, so that one case exits quietly instead of throwing. Code that "works" for one test input and throws for another is usually this.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Assigning to the loop variable changes nothing. for (String s : names) s = s.toUpperCase(); leaves names as [ada, raj] — s is a fresh copy of the reference, and reassigning it drops the copy on the floor. Calling a mutating method on the element does show up: a loop doing sb.append("-01") over a list of StringBuilder objects prints [lab-01]. If you need to replace elements, use an indexed loop with names.set(i, ...), which turns the same list into [ADA, RAJ]. All three lines were run to confirm it.

LinkedList is the linked list of 8.2 as a standard collection. It offers the same methods as ArrayList and makes the opposite performance trade, which is the only reason to choose it.

LinkedList list = new LinkedList<>();
list.add("b");
list.addFirst("a");            // O(1) — ArrayList would shift everything
list.addLast("c");
list.removeFirst();
list.getFirst();

                ArrayList        LinkedList
get(i)          O(1)             O(n)  — must walk from one end
add at end      O(1) amortised   O(1)
add at front    O(n)             O(1)
remove middle   O(n) shift       O(1) once you are there

In practice ArrayList wins most of the time, because get(i) is common and its memory layout is faster in ways the table does not show. LinkedList earns its place when you work at the ends — which is exactly what makes it the natural backing for a queue or a deque (14.5, 14.6).

ArrayListLinkedList
get(i)O(1)O(n) — walks from an end
add / remove at the frontO(n) — shifts everythingO(1)
add at the endO(1) amortisedO(1)
memoryone arraytwo references per element
in practicethe default choiceonly for heavy end-insertion

Both implement List, so declaring the variable as List<String> l = new LinkedList<>(); keeps the choice swappable — programming to the interface, and the reason exam code so often declares the interface type.

The trap is an indexed loop over a LinkedList: each get(i) walks from the head, so the loop is O(n²) while looking identical to the array version. Use a for-each, which uses one iterator and stays O(n).

In practice ArrayList wins most real comparisons even where the theory favours LinkedList, because contiguous memory is far friendlier to the CPU cache.

📘 DEFINITION

LinkedList: a doubly-linked list implementing both List and Deque

Random access: reaching element i directly; ArrayList has it, LinkedList does not

addFirst / removeFirst: constant-time operations at the head

List interface: the common contract both classes implement, so either can be swapped in

🎯 EXAM TIP

Declare the variable as List<String> rather than the concrete class. Then swapping the implementation is a one-line change — the practical use of interfaces from 10.11.

📊 FIGURE — WHERE THE TWO LISTS KEEP THEIR ELEMENTS
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a boarding line built at both ends

LinkedList is the only standard List that also implements Deque, so the end operations have their own names and cost nothing.

LinkedList<String> boarding = new LinkedList<>();
boarding.add("Raj");         // to the back
boarding.add("Mia");
boarding.addFirst("Ada");    // priority boarding — jumps the line
boarding.addLast("Sam");
System.out.println(boarding);
System.out.println("front: " + boarding.getFirst() + "   back: " + boarding.getLast());
System.out.println("boarded: " + boarding.removeFirst());
System.out.println(boarding);
what it prints
[Ada, Raj, Mia, Sam]
front: Ada   back: Sam
boarded: Ada
[Raj, Mia, Sam]
  1. add and addLast are the same operation; both append.
  2. addFirst("Ada") puts Ada ahead of Raj by rewriting two references. In an ArrayList the same call is add(0, "Ada") and copies every element right.
  3. removeFirst() returns the element it removed, which is why the boarded passenger can be printed in the same line.
  4. Read the last line as the queue discipline of 14.5 in list clothing — front out, back in.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — same result, different work — and why the variable is declared as List
List<Integer> al = new ArrayList<>(List.of(20, 30, 40));
al.add(0, 10);
System.out.println("ArrayList after add(0,10): " + al);

LinkedList<Integer> ll = new LinkedList<>(List.of(20, 30, 40));
ll.addFirst(10);
System.out.println("LinkedList after addFirst(10): " + ll);
System.out.println("same contents? " + al.equals(ll));

List<String> l = new LinkedList<>(List.of("a","b","c"));
System.out.println(l.getClass().getSimpleName()
                   + " used through the List interface: " + l);
what it prints
ArrayList after add(0,10): [10, 20, 30, 40]
LinkedList after addFirst(10): [10, 20, 30, 40]
same contents? true
LinkedList used through the List interface: [a, b, c]
  1. The contents are identical — equals on two Lists compares elements in order, not classes, so an ArrayList can equal a LinkedList.
  2. The work differs: three element copies against two reference rewrites. At three elements that is invisible; at a million it is the whole difference.
  3. The last block is the practical point of the interface. The variable is a List, the object is a LinkedList, and swapping in new ArrayList<>() changes one word and nothing else.
  4. Declaring it as LinkedList instead would let calling code use addFirst, and then you could no longer swap the implementation.

A HashMap stores key-value pairs and finds a value by its key in roughly constant time. It is the fix for the parallel-array lookup of 13.6, and it is the collection you will reach for most often after ArrayList.

HashMap scores = new HashMap<>();

scores.put("Ada", 95);            // add or REPLACE
scores.put("Ada", 97);            // replaces — keys are unique
scores.get("Ada");                // 97
scores.get("Nobody");             // null — NOT an exception
scores.getOrDefault("Nobody", 0); // 0 — usually what you want
scores.containsKey("Ada");        // true
scores.remove("Ada");
scores.size();

for (String k : scores.keySet()) { System.out.println(k + " " + scores.get(k)); }

Two behaviours cause most bugs. put with an existing key replaces rather than adding, and get on a missing key returns null rather than throwing — so assigning it straight to an int throws NullPointerException during unboxing (7.13).

Map<String,Integer> ages = new HashMap<>();
ages.put("Ana", 30);
ages.put("Ana", 31);            // same key — REPLACES, does not add
ages.get("Zed");                // null — the key is absent
ages.getOrDefault("Zed", 0);    // 0 — no null to handle

// the counting idiom
counts.put(w, counts.getOrDefault(w, 0) + 1);
counts.merge(w, 1, Integer::sum);        // the same thing, shorter

A map stores key → value pairs with unique keys. Re-putting an existing key overwrites and returns the old value; it never creates a second entry. Values may repeat freely.

get on a missing key returns null, which unboxes into a NullPointerException if you assign it to an int. getOrDefault exists to remove that whole class of bug, and containsKey is the right test when null is itself a legitimate stored value.

HashMap gives O(1) average lookup and no ordering at all — iteration order is unspecified and may change. Use LinkedHashMap for insertion order or TreeMap for sorted keys. Iterate with entrySet(), which visits keys and values together instead of looking each value up again.

A custom class used as a key must override both equals and hashCode, or lookups fail even with an identical-looking key.

📘 DEFINITION

HashMap: an unordered map from unique keys to values, with O(1) average lookup

Key / value: the lookup token and the data stored under it

getOrDefault: returns a supplied default instead of null when the key is absent

hashCode / equals contract: a key class must override both, or lookups silently fail (10.4)

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Using your own class as a key without overriding hashCode() and equals() means an equal-looking key never finds its value. It compiles, it runs, and it returns null forever.

📊 FIGURE — HASHMAP: THE KEY’S HASH PICKS THE BUCKET
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — counting words — the single most common Map idiom

A TreeMap is used here rather than a HashMap only so the printed order is fixed and can be shown; every method below behaves identically on a HashMap.

String text = "the rain in spain falls mainly in the plain";
Map<String,Integer> counts = new TreeMap<>();

for (String w : text.split(" ")) {
    counts.put(w, counts.getOrDefault(w, 0) + 1);
}
System.out.println(counts);

Map<String,Integer> m2 = new TreeMap<>();
for (String w : text.split(" ")) m2.merge(w, 1, Integer::sum);
System.out.println("merge gives the same: " + m2.equals(counts));

System.out.println("in -> " + counts.get("in")
    + ", missing -> " + counts.get("fog")
    + ", getOrDefault -> " + counts.getOrDefault("fog", 0));
what it prints
{falls=1, in=2, mainly=1, plain=1, rain=1, spain=1, the=2}
merge gives the same: true
in -> 2, missing -> null, getOrDefault -> 0
  1. First time a word is seen, getOrDefault(w, 0) returns 0, so put stores 1.
  2. Every later time it returns the stored count, and put replaces the entry — this is exactly the replace-not-add behaviour, used deliberately.
  3. merge(w, 1, Integer::sum) says: store 1 if absent, otherwise combine the old and new values with +. Same result, one call.
  4. The third line shows the three outcomes for a lookup: a real value, null for a missing key, and a supplied default that avoids the null entirely.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — what put returns, and where the NullPointerException comes from
Map<String,Integer> scores = new HashMap<>();
System.out.println("first put returns: " + scores.put("Ada", 95));
System.out.println("second put returns: " + scores.put("Ada", 97));
System.out.println("size after two puts: " + scores.size());
System.out.println("get(\"Ada\") = " + scores.get("Ada"));

try {
    int missing = scores.get("Nobody");   // Integer null -> int
    System.out.println(missing);
} catch (NullPointerException e) {
    System.out.println("caught NullPointerException while unboxing null");
}
System.out.println("getOrDefault: " + scores.getOrDefault("Nobody", 0));
System.out.println("containsKey(\"Nobody\") = " + scores.containsKey("Nobody"));
what it prints
first put returns: null
second put returns: 95
size after two puts: 1
get("Ada") = 97
caught NullPointerException while unboxing null
getOrDefault: 0
containsKey("Nobody") = false
  1. put returns the previous value for that key, or null if there was none. That return value is how you find out whether you overwrote something.
  2. Two puts, one entry: size() is 1. Keys are unique, so the second put replaced rather than added.
  3. The crash is not in get — get returned null perfectly happily. It is the assignment to int that calls .intValue() on null.
  4. Read the stack trace of that failure carefully on the exam: it points at the assignment line, not at the map.
🎯 EXAM TIP

Three things get asked. (1) Does a repeated key add a second entry? No — it replaces, and size() proves it. (2) What does get return for a missing key? null, never an exception — the exception comes later, on unboxing. (3) What order does iteration produce? For HashMap, unspecified; if an answer option depends on hash order it is wrong on principle. Reach for entrySet() when you need both halves, keySet() when you only need keys, and LinkedHashMap or TreeMap when the question says "in the order added" or "in sorted order".

"}, "D286/u14/z14_4": {"body": "

A HashSet is a collection with no duplicates and no order. It answers one question extremely fast — is this already in here — which is the linear contains of 7.16 made constant.

HashSet seen = new HashSet<>();

seen.add("a");           // true  — it was added
seen.add("a");           // false — already present, set unchanged
seen.contains("a");      // true  — O(1) average
seen.remove("a");
seen.size();

// the standard use: removing duplicates
ArrayList unique = new ArrayList<>(new HashSet<>(withDuplicates));

add returning a boolean is genuinely useful: it tells you whether the item was new, which turns "have I seen this before" into a single call. And a set that holds your own objects depends on the same equals/hashCode contract as a map key.

Set<String> seen = new HashSet<>();
seen.add("a");                  // true  — it was added
seen.add("a");                  // false — already present, set unchanged
seen.contains("a");             // O(1) average

List<String> unique = new ArrayList<>(new HashSet<>(withDuplicates));

A set holds no duplicates and has no positions — there is no get(i), because there is no i. add returning a boolean is genuinely useful: it tells you whether the value was new, which answers "have I seen this before?" in one call.

Its purpose is membership. Asking "is this in the collection?" is O(1) on a HashSet against O(n) on a list, which is the difference between a fast and a slow duplicate check on large data.

HashSet is unordered, LinkedHashSet keeps insertion order, TreeSet keeps sorted order. Duplicates are decided by equals and hashCode, so custom objects need both — without them, two identical-looking objects are two different elements.

📘 DEFINITION

HashSet: an unordered collection of unique elements

Set interface: the contract for a duplicate-free collection

add() return value: true if the element was not already present

LinkedHashSet: a Set that preserves insertion order

🎯 EXAM TIP

If a question needs "unique" or "have I seen this", the answer is a Set. If it needs "how many of each", the answer is a HashMap<T, Integer>.

📊 FIGURE — HOW A SET DECIDES SOMETHING IS ALREADY IN IT
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the boolean from add() answers "have I seen this before?"
String[] scans = {"BR-104","BR-221","BR-104","BR-880","BR-221","BR-104"};
Set<String> seen = new HashSet<>();
List<String> firstTime = new ArrayList<>();

for (String s : scans) {
    boolean isNew = seen.add(s);
    System.out.println(s + "  add() -> " + isNew);
    if (isNew) firstTime.add(s);
}
System.out.println("distinct scans: " + seen.size());
System.out.println("in arrival order: " + firstTime);
what it prints
BR-104  add() -> true
BR-221  add() -> true
BR-104  add() -> false
BR-880  add() -> true
BR-221  add() -> false
BR-104  add() -> false
distinct scans: 3
in arrival order: [BR-104, BR-221, BR-880]
  1. add returns true only when the element was not already present, so the boolean is the duplicate test — no separate contains call needed.
  2. Six scans, three distinct values: the set silently absorbed the repeats.
  3. The firstTime list exists because a HashSet has no order. Recording arrival order takes a second structure — or a LinkedHashSet, which does it for you.
  4. This is the deduplication pattern in full: one set for membership, one list for order.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — your own class in a set: what happens without equals and hashCode
static class BadgeA {                 // no equals, no hashCode
    final String id;
    BadgeA(String id){ this.id = id; }
}
static class BadgeB {                 // both overridden
    final String id;
    BadgeB(String id){ this.id = id; }
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o){
        if (this == o) return true;
        if (!(o instanceof BadgeB)) return false;
        return id.equals(((BadgeB) o).id);
    }
    @Override public int hashCode(){ return id.hashCode(); }
}

Set<BadgeA> s1 = new HashSet<>();
s1.add(new BadgeA("E-77")); s1.add(new BadgeA("E-77"));
Set<BadgeB> s2 = new HashSet<>();
s2.add(new BadgeB("E-77")); s2.add(new BadgeB("E-77"));
what it prints
without equals/hashCode: size=2, contains(new BadgeA("E-77")) = false
with equals/hashCode:    size=1, contains(new BadgeB("E-77")) = true
  1. BadgeA inherits Object.hashCode(), which is derived from identity, so two separately-created badges land in different buckets and never meet.
  2. Because they never meet, equals is never even consulted — the set is convinced they are different elements.
  3. BadgeB derives its hash from the id field, so both badges reach the same bucket, equals runs, and the second add is rejected.
  4. contains fails for the same reason add did: a freshly built lookup key hashes somewhere else entirely.

The rule the two classes demonstrate: equal objects must have equal hash codes. Override the two together or neither.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

It is not enough for two objects to look equal — a set finds an element by its hash first. Override equals alone and the object still hashes by identity, so contains returns false for something that is demonstrably in the set (verified above: size 2 where you expected 1). The symptom is a duplicate check that quietly never fires, and it is silent — nothing warns you, nothing throws.

📊 FIGURE — the three set operations, and the method that does each
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — All three, on the same pair of sets
java.util.TreeSet<Integer> u = a(); u.addAll(b());
java.util.TreeSet<Integer> i = a(); i.retainAll(b());
java.util.TreeSet<Integer> d = a(); d.removeAll(b());

System.out.println("a = " + a() + "   b = " + b());
System.out.println("union        addAll    : " + u);
System.out.println("intersection retainAll : " + i);
System.out.println("difference   removeAll : " + d);
System.out.println("containsAll            : " + a().containsAll(java.util.List.of(2, 3)));
a = [1, 2, 3, 4] b = [3, 4, 5] union addAll : [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] intersection retainAll : [3, 4] difference removeAll : [1, 2] containsAll : true
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Each call modifies the set it is invoked on — that is why a fresh copy of a is built for each line.
  2. retainAll keeps the shared elements; removeAll keeps the ones not shared. Mixing the two up is the usual error.
  3. A TreeSet prints in sorted order, which is why the results read cleanly; a HashSet gives no ordering guarantee.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Expecting these to return a new set. They return boolean (whether the set changed) and mutate the receiver, so Set<Integer> c = a.retainAll(b); does not compile — and a has already been altered.

A queue is first-in-first-out — the printer queue, the waiting line. Queue is an interface, so you instantiate something that implements it, usually a LinkedList.

Queue q = new LinkedList<>();

q.add("first");        q.offer("second");    // add to the BACK
q.peek();              // "first" — look at the front, do not remove
q.poll();              // "first" — remove and return the front
q.isEmpty();

// add/remove throw when they fail; offer/poll/peek return false or null
q.remove();            // NoSuchElementException on an empty queue
q.poll();              // null on an empty queue

That pairing is the detail the exam tests: every queue operation comes in a throwing version and a returning version. Which you want depends on whether an empty queue is an error or an ordinary state.

Runnable, and where a queue is really used

Queues appear most often where work is being handed between parts of a program, and the unit of work is usually a Runnable — the interface with one method, run(), representing a task with no arguments and no result.

Runnable task = () -> System.out.println("working");
Queue work = new LinkedList<>();
work.add(task);
work.poll().run();          // take the next task and execute it

That is the shape of every job queue and thread pool: producers offer tasks at the back, a worker polls from the front and calls run(). Because Runnable has a single abstract method, a lambda can supply it directly, which is why it appears wherever "a piece of work to do later" is needed.

Queue<String> q = new LinkedList<>();      // Queue is an INTERFACE
q.offer("a");                  // add at the back  (add() throws when full)
q.peek();                      // look at the front, do not remove
q.poll();                      // remove the front — null if empty

while (!q.isEmpty()) process(q.poll());     // the standard drain loop

A queue is FIFO — first in, first out, like a checkout line. Work arrives at the back and is taken from the front.

WantSafe form (returns null/false)Throwing form
addofferadd
removepollremove
inspectpeekelement

Prefer the left column: poll on an empty queue returns null while remove throws NoSuchElementException. The distinction is the most-tested detail in this section.

Queues model anything processed in arrival order — print jobs, task pipelines, breadth-first search. A stack is the opposite discipline, LIFO, and choosing between them is choosing the order the work comes back out.

📘 DEFINITION

Queue: a FIFO collection — first in, first out

offer / poll / peek: add, remove-front and inspect-front; return special values on failure

add / remove / element: the same three operations, throwing on failure instead

FIFO: first-in-first-out ordering

🎯 EXAM TIP

Queue<String> q = new LinkedList<>() is the standard declaration. Declaring it as LinkedList would expose list methods that break the queue discipline.

📊 FIGURE — FIFO: THE ORDER WORK COMES BACK OUT
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — draining a print queue, watching the size
Queue<String> jobs = new LinkedList<>();
jobs.offer("report.pdf");
jobs.offer("labels.png");
jobs.offer("invoice.pdf");
System.out.println("queue: " + jobs + "   size " + jobs.size());
System.out.println("peek: " + jobs.peek() + "   size still " + jobs.size());

while (!jobs.isEmpty()) {
    System.out.println("printing " + jobs.poll() + "   remaining " + jobs);
}
what it prints
queue: [report.pdf, labels.png, invoice.pdf]   size 3
peek: report.pdf   size still 3
printing report.pdf   remaining [labels.png, invoice.pdf]
printing labels.png   remaining [invoice.pdf]
printing invoice.pdf   remaining []
  1. Printing a queue shows it front-first, so the leftmost element is the next one out.
  2. peek reads the front and leaves it there — the size is unchanged, which is the whole difference from poll.
  3. poll removes and returns, so it can be used directly inside the print statement.
  4. while (!isEmpty()) with poll inside is the standard drain. Written as for (String s : jobs) instead, the queue would still be full at the end.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — empty queue: which methods return, and which throw
Queue<String> q = new LinkedList<>();
System.out.println("poll on empty:  " + q.poll());
System.out.println("peek on empty:  " + q.peek());
try { q.remove(); } catch (NoSuchElementException e) {
    System.out.println("remove on empty throws " + e.getClass().getSimpleName());
}
try { q.element(); } catch (NoSuchElementException e) {
    System.out.println("element on empty throws " + e.getClass().getSimpleName());
}
what it prints
poll on empty:  null
peek on empty:  null
remove on empty throws NoSuchElementException
element on empty throws NoSuchElementException
  1. poll and peek report emptiness as a value you can test: if (job == null) return;
  2. remove and element report it as an exception, which is right only when an empty queue means something has gone wrong.
  3. Pick by intention. A worker thread finding no work is normal — use poll. A protocol that guarantees a message is waiting is broken if there is none — use remove.
  4. The exception class is NoSuchElementException, not EmptyStackException; that one belongs to the legacy Stack in 14.9.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

remove() and remove(Object) are different methods, and on a LinkedList<Integer> there is a third: remove(int index). Declared as LinkedList<Integer>, list.remove(1) removes the element at index 1, turning [10, 20, 30] into [10, 30]. Declared as Queue<Integer>, the index version is not visible, so q.remove(Integer.valueOf(10)) removes the value 10 and gives [20, 30]. Both were run to confirm. Declaring the variable as Queue is what keeps the list methods out of reach.
