A deque — "double-ended queue" — allows adding and removing at both ends, which makes it a queue and a stack at once.

Deque d = new ArrayDeque<>();

d.addFirst("a");   d.addLast("b");
d.peekFirst();     d.peekLast();
d.pollFirst();     d.pollLast();

// as a STACK (LIFO)          // as a QUEUE (FIFO)
d.push("x");                  d.addLast("x");
d.pop();                      d.pollFirst();

ArrayDeque is the recommended implementation for both roles, and it is the reason the legacy Stack class of 14.9 is no longer advised. push and pop on a Deque work at the front, which is what makes it last-in-first-out.

Deque<Integer> d = new ArrayDeque<>();

d.push(1);      d.pop();       // used as a STACK — both at the front
d.offerLast(1); d.pollFirst(); // used as a QUEUE — in at the back, out at the front

A deque — "double-ended queue" — allows adding and removing at both ends in O(1), so one type covers both stack and queue behaviour. The method names say which end: First or Last.

ArrayDeque is the recommended implementation, and it is the modern replacement for the legacy Stack class, which extends Vector and is synchronised and slower. It rejects null elements outright, precisely so that a null from poll unambiguously means "empty".

Pick one idiom and keep it. Mixing push with pollLast in the same code is legal and unreadable, because the reader can no longer tell which discipline is intended.

📘 DEFINITION

Deque: a double-ended queue supporting insertion and removal at both ends

ArrayDeque: the standard resizable-array implementation; faster than LinkedList for this

push / pop: Deque methods operating on the front, giving stack behaviour

LIFO: last-in-first-out ordering

🎯 EXAM TIP

One class covers both disciplines, so the exam asks which end a method touches. push and pop are the front; addLast and pollFirst are the queue pair.

📊 FIGURE — A DEQUE IS A STACK AND A QUEUE, DEPENDING ON WHICH END YOU USE
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — browser history as a stack
Deque<String> history = new ArrayDeque<>();
history.push("home");
history.push("catalog");
history.push("cart");
System.out.println("deque printed front-first: " + history);
System.out.println("back button -> " + history.pop());
System.out.println("back button -> " + history.pop());
System.out.println("now showing: " + history.peek());
what it prints
deque printed front-first: [cart, catalog, home]
back button -> cart
back button -> catalog
now showing: home
  1. push inserts at the front, so the most recent page is printed first. That is why the printed order looks reversed compared with the order the pages were visited.
  2. Each pop takes from the front — the most recent page — which is exactly what a back button does.
  3. peek reads the front without removing, so "now showing" does not consume a history entry.
  4. Nothing here needed the Stack class. ArrayDeque is the recommended stack in modern Java.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — palindrome check — the operation only a deque can do

Comparing a word with its reverse needs to consume from both ends at once. A queue cannot; a stack cannot; a deque is exactly the right shape.

static boolean palindrome(String s){
    Deque<Character> d = new ArrayDeque<>();
    for (char ch : s.toCharArray()) d.addLast(ch);
    while (d.size() > 1) {
        if (d.removeFirst() != d.removeLast()) return false;
    }
    return true;
}
what it prints
racecar -> true
level   -> true
java    -> false
  1. Every character goes in at the back, so the deque holds the word left to right.
  2. Each pass removes one character from each end and compares them. Different characters mean it is not a palindrome, and the method returns immediately.
  3. The loop condition is size() > 1, not > 0: an odd-length word ends with one middle character, which has nothing to be compared against.
  4. Written with > 0, the middle character would be removed twice — removeFirst and removeLast would both take it, and the second call would throw on an empty deque.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Mixing the two idioms silently changes the discipline. push(1); push(2); push(3); then pop(), pop() gives 3, 2 — a stack. The same pushes with pollLast(), pollLast() give 1, 2 — a queue, because push loads the front while pollLast drains the back. Both were run. Choose push/pop or offerLast/pollFirst and never mix them in one structure; also note ArrayDeque rejects null, precisely so a null from pollFirst can only mean "empty".

A TreeSet is a set that keeps its elements sorted, which is the trade against HashSet: ordered iteration and range queries, in exchange for O(log n) instead of O(1).

TreeSet t = new TreeSet<>();
t.add(5); t.add(1); t.add(3);

for (int n : t) { System.out.print(n + " "); }    // 1 3 5 — always sorted

t.first();          // 1
t.last();           // 5
t.higher(3);        // 5  — smallest element strictly greater
t.lower(3);         // 1
t.headSet(3);       // [1]     — everything below
t.tailSet(3);       // [3, 5]  — 3 and above

Elements must be Comparable (13.5), or you must supply a Comparator to the constructor — otherwise the set has no way to order them and throws ClassCastException on the first add. The same requirement applies to TreeMap.

TreeSet<Integer> t = new TreeSet<>(List.of(5, 1, 9, 3));
t.first();          // 1        t.last();        // 9
t.higher(5);        // 9  — strictly greater
t.ceiling(6);       // 9  — greater than or equal
t.headSet(5);       // [1, 3]  — a live view, not a copy
t.subSet(3, 9);     // [3, 5]

A TreeSet keeps its elements sorted at all times, which costs O(log n) per operation against HashSet's O(1). You pay that only when the ordering is worth having — for the range and neighbour queries above, which a hash set cannot answer at all.

Ordering comes from compareTo, or from a Comparator passed to the constructor — and that same comparison decides duplicates. So a TreeSet uses compareTo == 0 rather than equals, and two objects the comparator calls equivalent cannot both be in the set even if equals says they differ.

It rejects null, because there is no way to compare null with anything.

📘 DEFINITION

TreeSet: a sorted set backed by a balanced tree; O(log n) operations

Comparable requirement: elements must define an ordering, or a Comparator must be supplied

first / last / higher / lower: navigation methods a HashSet cannot offer

TreeMap: the equivalent sorted map, iterating in key order

🎯 EXAM TIP

HashSet for speed, TreeSet for order, LinkedHashSet for insertion order. A question mentioning "sorted output" or "next largest" is pointing at TreeSet.

📊 FIGURE — A TREESET KEEPS ITS ORDER IN THE SHAPE OF THE TREE
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — every navigation method on one small set
TreeSet<Integer> prices = new TreeSet<>(List.of(89, 45, 120, 45, 67));
System.out.println("set: " + prices);
System.out.println("first=" + prices.first() + "  last=" + prices.last());
System.out.println("higher(67)=" + prices.higher(67) + "  ceiling(67)=" + prices.ceiling(67));
System.out.println("lower(67)=" + prices.lower(67) + "  floor(67)=" + prices.floor(67));
System.out.println("headSet(89)=" + prices.headSet(89) + "  tailSet(89)=" + prices.tailSet(89));
System.out.println("subSet(45,120)=" + prices.subSet(45,120));
System.out.println("descendingSet=" + prices.descendingSet());
what it prints
set: [45, 67, 89, 120]
first=45  last=120
higher(67)=89  ceiling(67)=67
lower(67)=45  floor(67)=67
headSet(89)=[45, 67]  tailSet(89)=[89, 120]
subSet(45,120)=[45, 67, 89]
descendingSet=[120, 89, 67, 45]
  1. The duplicate 45 vanished on the way in, and the elements came out sorted although 89 was added first.
  2. higher is strictly greater, ceiling is greater-or-equal — that is the whole difference, and it shows on 67: 89 against 67.
  3. lower/floor are the mirror pair going down.
  4. headSet(89) excludes 89, tailSet(89) includes it. The half-open convention is the same one as substring: low end in, high end out.
  5. subSet(45, 120) therefore contains 45 but not 120.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the comparator decides what counts as a duplicate

A HashSet asks equals. A TreeSet never calls equals at all — it asks the ordering whether the comparison is 0. Those can disagree, and here they do.

Set<String> plain = new TreeSet<>();
plain.add("Ada"); plain.add("ADA"); plain.add("ada");
System.out.println("natural order: " + plain + "   size " + plain.size());

Set<String> ci = new TreeSet<>(String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER);
ci.add("Ada"); ci.add("ADA"); ci.add("ada");
System.out.println("case-insensitive comparator: " + ci + "   size " + ci.size());
System.out.println("HashSet for comparison: "
    + new HashSet<>(List.of("Ada","ADA","ada")).size());
what it prints
natural order: [ADA, Ada, ada]   size 3
case-insensitive comparator: [Ada]   size 1
HashSet for comparison: 3
  1. With natural ordering, "ADA".compareTo("Ada") is not 0, so all three survive — and they sort by character code, which puts every capital before every lowercase letter.
  2. With CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER, the first comparison of "ADA" against "Ada" returns 0, so the set treats it as already present and discards it.
  3. Only the first spelling added survives: the set keeps "Ada", the one that got there first.
  4. The HashSet line is the control: equals says all three differ, so a hash set keeps all three regardless of any comparator.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

A TreeSet defines "duplicate" as compare(a, b) == 0, not a.equals(b). A comparator that ignores case, or one that compares only a price field, will silently discard elements you consider different — one product per price, and no warning. Two related traps come from the same requirement: elements must be orderable, so a class that does not implement Comparable throws ClassCastException on the second add (not the first — one element is never compared with anything), and null is rejected outright because it cannot be compared.

A PriorityQueue serves the smallest element first rather than the oldest. It is a queue by interface and a heap by behaviour, which is why the ordering rule surprises people.

PriorityQueue pq = new PriorityQueue<>();
pq.add(5); pq.add(1); pq.add(3);

pq.poll();      // 1  — smallest first, NOT insertion order
pq.poll();      // 3
pq.poll();      // 5

// largest first
PriorityQueue maxHeap = new PriorityQueue<>(Collections.reverseOrder());

Only peek and poll respect the priority. Iterating a PriorityQueue with a for-each gives the internal heap order, which is not sorted — a genuine trap, because the first element is right and the rest look wrong.

PriorityQueue<Integer> pq = new PriorityQueue<>();      // min-heap by default
pq.offer(5); pq.offer(1); pq.offer(9);
pq.poll();     // 1 — always the SMALLEST, regardless of insertion order

new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.reverseOrder());          // max-heap
new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.comparing(Task::priority));

A priority queue serves by priority rather than arrival: poll always returns the smallest element under the natural ordering. It is a heap, so offer and poll are O(log n) and peek is O(1).

The catch that catches everyone: printing it, or iterating it, does not give sorted order. The internal array is heap-ordered, not sorted — only the sequence of poll calls is ordered. To get every element in order you must drain it.

Elements must be Comparable or the queue must be given a Comparator; otherwise the first offer of a second element throws ClassCastException. peek and poll on an empty queue return null.

📘 DEFINITION

PriorityQueue: a queue ordering by priority rather than arrival, backed by a heap

Min-heap: the default: the smallest element is served first

Collections.reverseOrder(): a Comparator that turns it into a max-heap

Heap order: the partial internal ordering; only the head is guaranteed correct

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Printing a PriorityQueue directly, or iterating it, does not print sorted output. Only repeated poll() gives the true order.

📊 FIGURE — A PRIORITY QUEUE IS A HEAP: ONLY THE HEAD IS SORTED
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — printing it and draining it give different answers
PriorityQueue<Integer> triage = new PriorityQueue<>();
triage.offer(5); triage.offer(1); triage.offer(9); triage.offer(3);
System.out.println("printed straight out: " + triage);
System.out.println("peek: " + triage.peek());

StringBuilder order = new StringBuilder();
while (!triage.isEmpty()) order.append(triage.poll()).append(' ');
System.out.println("poll order: " + order.toString().trim());
what it prints
printed straight out: [1, 3, 9, 5]
peek: 1
poll order: 1 3 5 9
  1. The printed form is the backing array in heap order. 1 is correctly at the front; 9 sitting before 5 is not a bug.
  2. peek agrees with the first printed element, because both read index 0.
  3. Each poll removes the root, moves the last element into its place and sinks it back down — so the next smallest surfaces.
  4. Only that sequence of polls is sorted. If a question asks "what does printing the queue show", the answer is the heap array, not the sorted list.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — max-heap, and ordering objects by a field
PriorityQueue<Integer> max = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.reverseOrder());
max.addAll(List.of(5, 1, 9, 3));
while (!max.isEmpty()) System.out.print(max.poll() + " ");

record Job(String name, int priority) {}
PriorityQueue<Job> jobs = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.comparingInt(Job::priority));
jobs.add(new Job("backup", 5));
jobs.add(new Job("alert", 1));
jobs.add(new Job("report", 3));
while (!jobs.isEmpty()) {
    Job j = jobs.poll();
    System.out.println(j.name() + " (priority " + j.priority() + ")");
}
what it prints
max-heap drain: 9 5 3 1 
alert (priority 1)
report (priority 3)
backup (priority 5)
  1. The comparator is supplied to the constructor. Passing it later is impossible — the ordering has to be known before the first element arrives.
  2. Comparator.reverseOrder() inverts every comparison, so the largest element sinks to the root and comes out first.
  3. Comparator.comparingInt(Job::priority) orders jobs by the number in the priority field; the alert, added second, is served first.
  4. Priority 1 being "most urgent" is the usual convention and it catches people: with a min-heap, lower is served sooner.
🎯 EXAM TIP

Two question shapes recur. Trace one: ignore insertion order entirely, sort the values mentally and read them off smallest-first — that is what repeated poll gives. Choose a structure: anything phrased "always process the most urgent/cheapest/nearest next" is a PriorityQueue; "process in arrival order" is an ordinary Queue; "keep everything sorted and searchable" is a TreeSet. The classic application is the k-largest problem: keep a min-heap of size k, offer each element, and poll whenever the size exceeds k.

A stack is last-in-first-out, and you have been using one since 6.8 — the call stack is a stack of frames, which is why deep recursion overflows it (11.8).

// legacy class — works, but no longer recommended
Stack s = new Stack<>();
s.push("a"); s.push("b");
s.peek();        // "b" — top, not removed
s.pop();         // "b" — removed
s.isEmpty();

// the preferred modern form
Deque s2 = new ArrayDeque<>();
s2.push("a"); s2.pop();

Stacks are the natural structure for anything with nesting: matching brackets, undo history, expression evaluation, and the iterative rewrite of a recursive algorithm. Anywhere you would recurse, a stack is the manual version.

What the legacy Stack throws

Calling pop() or peek() on an empty Stack throws EmptyStackException, which is unchecked. The Deque alternative behaves differently and more usefully: pop() throws NoSuchElementException, while pollFirst() returns null instead of throwing. Guarding with isEmpty() before popping avoids all three.

Deque<Character> st = new ArrayDeque<>();     // preferred over Stack
for (char c : s.toCharArray()) {
    if (c == '(') st.push(c);
    else if (c == ')') {
        if (st.isEmpty()) return false;        // a closer with nothing open
        st.pop();
    }
}
return st.isEmpty();                            // leftover openers = unbalanced

A stack is LIFO — last in, first out. push adds to the top, pop removes and returns it, peek looks without removing. pop on an empty stack throws.

Bracket matching is the standard example because it needs both checks, and leaving either out passes strings it should reject. An early ) must fail on the empty test; a trailing ( must fail on the final isEmpty(). Code that only pops and never checks at the end accepts "((".

Stacks are everywhere underneath: the call stack of 8.3, undo history, expression evaluation, and depth-first search. Queue is the FIFO counterpart, and swapping one for the other changes a breadth-first traversal into a depth-first one.

📘 DEFINITION

Stack: a LIFO collection with push, pop and peek

push / pop / peek: add to the top, remove from the top, inspect the top

EmptyStackException: thrown by pop or peek on an empty Stack

Call stack: the JVM’s own stack of method frames (8.3)

🎯 EXAM TIP

Bracket matching is the standard exam use: push every opening bracket, pop on every closing one and check it matches. Balanced input ends with an empty stack.

📊 FIGURE — LIFO: A STACK OVER TIME
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — bracket matching on real-looking code

The rule needs three checks, and dropping any one of them accepts something it should reject.

static boolean balanced(String s){
    Deque<Character> st = new ArrayDeque<>();
    for (char ch : s.toCharArray()) {
        if (ch == '(' || ch == '[' || ch == '{') st.push(ch);
        else if (ch == ')' || ch == ']' || ch == '}') {
            if (st.isEmpty()) return false;              // a closer with nothing open
            char open = st.pop();
            if (ch == ')' && open != '(') return false;   // wrong kind of closer
            if (ch == ']' && open != '[') return false;
            if (ch == '}' && open != '{') return false;
        }
    }
    return st.isEmpty();                                 // leftover openers
}
what it prints
true   a[0] = (b+c);
false   if (x) { y[1] = 2;
true   return (a[0]);
false   ([)]
  1. a[0] = (b+c); — every closer meets its own opener and the stack empties. True.
  2. if (x) { y[1] = 2; — the { is never closed, so the final isEmpty() fails. Without that final check this string would pass.
  3. ([)] — the ) pops a [, and the kind check catches it. Counting brackets instead of stacking them would call this balanced.
  4. The isEmpty() guard before pop is what stops a leading ) from throwing instead of returning false.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — evaluating a postfix expression, one push at a time

Postfix — "3 4 + 2 *" — needs no parentheses because the order is already fixed by position. A stack evaluates it in one left-to-right pass.

String expr = "3 4 + 2 *";
Deque<Integer> st = new ArrayDeque<>();
for (String tok : expr.split(" ")) {
    if (tok.equals("+") || tok.equals("*") || tok.equals("-")) {
        int right = st.pop(), left = st.pop();       // RIGHT comes off first
        int r = tok.equals("+") ? left + right
              : tok.equals("-") ? left - right : left * right;
        st.push(r);
    } else {
        st.push(Integer.parseInt(tok));
    }
}
System.out.println("result: " + st.pop());
what it prints (with a trace line per token)
push 3        -> stack [3]
push 4        -> stack [4, 3]
apply + to 3 and 4 -> stack [7]
push 2        -> stack [2, 7]
apply * to 7 and 2 -> stack [14]
result: 14
  1. Numbers are pushed as they arrive; an operator pops the two most recent values.
  2. The second pop is the left operand. Getting that backwards computes 4 − 3 instead of 3 − 4 — invisible for + and *, wrong for − and /.
  3. The printed stack shows front-first, so [4, 3] means 4 is on top with 3 beneath.
  4. One value is left at the end. Two values left means the expression was malformed — a useful validity check.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Printing the two kinds of stack gives opposite orders. new Stack<>() extends Vector, so it prints bottom-first: pushing 1, 2, 3 shows [1, 2, 3] with 3 on top. An ArrayDeque used as a stack prints front-first: the same pushes show [3, 2, 1]. Both pop 3. They also fail differently on empty — Stack.pop() throws EmptyStackException, Deque.pop() throws NoSuchElementException, and pollFirst() returns null instead of throwing. All four were run to confirm.

Graphics in Swing all happen inside one method. You override paintComponent, draw with the Graphics object you are handed, and never call it yourself — the system calls it whenever the component needs redrawing.

public class Canvas extends JPanel {
    @Override
    protected void paintComponent(Graphics g) {
        super.paintComponent(g);            // clears the background — do this first

        g.setColor(Color.BLUE);
        g.fillRect(10, 10, 100, 50);        // x, y, width, height
        g.drawOval(10, 70, 80, 80);
        g.drawLine(0, 0, 200, 200);
        g.drawString("hello", 20, 180);
    }
}
repaint();     // ASK for a redraw — never call paintComponent directly

The coordinate system is the thing to internalise: (0,0) is the top left and y increases downward, which is upside down compared with school graphs. And fill methods draw solid shapes while draw methods draw outlines.

import javax.swing.*;

JFrame frame = new JFrame("Title");                 // 1. the window
frame.setDefaultCloseOperation(JFrame.EXIT_ON_CLOSE);
frame.add(new JLabel("Hello"));                     // 2. components
frame.pack();                                       // size to fit
frame.setVisible(true);                             // 3. show it — LAST

Three pieces make any Swing program: a container (the JFrame), components inside it, and listeners that react to events. Swing lives in javax.swing — note the x, which is not in most other package names.

Order matters. setVisible(true) goes last, after everything has been added; adding components afterwards may not appear until the frame is revalidated.

Without setDefaultCloseOperation(EXIT_ON_CLOSE) the window closes but the program keeps running, because Swing's event thread is still alive. That is the usual explanation for a program that will not stop.

A console program runs top to bottom and ends; a GUI is event-driven — it sets everything up, then waits, and all remaining work happens inside listeners.

📘 DEFINITION

paintComponent(Graphics g): the method you override to draw; called by the system

repaint(): requests a redraw; the system then calls paintComponent

Graphics object: the drawing surface, supplying setColor, fillRect, drawOval and the rest

Screen coordinates: origin at the top left, y increasing downward

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Calling paintComponent directly, or forgetting super.paintComponent(g), produces smeared or stale drawing. Call repaint() and let the system schedule it.

📊 FIGURE — WHO CALLS PAINTCOMPONENT, AND WHERE (0,0) IS
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a level gauge drawn from scratch

This panel draws a bar, a border, a percentage and two circles. It compiles as written; the only thing missing is a frame to put it in.

static class Gauge extends JPanel {
    private int level = 40;

    void setLevel(int v){ level = v; repaint(); }   // change state, THEN ask

    @Override protected void paintComponent(Graphics g){
        super.paintComponent(g);            // clears the previous frame — first
        g.setColor(Color.LIGHT_GRAY);
        g.fillRect(20, 20, 200, 30);        // the empty track
        g.setColor(new Color(14, 165, 233));
        g.fillRect(20, 20, 2 * level, 30);  // the filled part: width VARIES
        g.setColor(Color.BLACK);
        g.drawRect(20, 20, 200, 30);        // outline on top of both
        g.drawString(level + "%", 230, 42); // x, y is the text BASELINE
        g.drawOval(20, 70, 60, 60);         // outline circle
        g.fillOval(90, 70, 60, 60);         // solid circle
    }
    @Override public Dimension getPreferredSize(){ return new Dimension(300, 180); }
}
  1. The bar is two rectangles at the same position: a full-width grey one, then a partial coloured one over it. Drawing order is painting order — later calls cover earlier ones.
  2. 2 * level turns 0–100 into 0–200 pixels. Every varying number in a paint method comes from a field, because the method takes no parameters other than g.
  3. drawRect after both fills, so the outline is not buried underneath.
  4. drawString’s y is the baseline of the text, not its top — text drawn at y = 0 is invisible above the panel.
  5. getPreferredSize is what lets frame.pack() give the panel any room at all; without it a custom panel can come out zero-sized.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — why the drawing smears, and how repaint fixes it

Two mistakes produce the same symptom — old frames left on screen. Here is what each one does.

// (a) forgetting the super call
@Override protected void paintComponent(Graphics g){
    // super.paintComponent(g);   <-- omitted
    g.setColor(Color.BLUE);
    g.fillOval(x, 40, 30, 30);
}
// the panel background is never repainted, so every past position of the
// circle is still there: one moving dot becomes a blue smear.

// (b) calling the paint method yourself
void moveRight(){
    x += 5;
    paintComponent(getGraphics());   // WRONG — no clearing, no scheduling
}
void moveRightProperly(){
    x += 5;
    repaint();                       // right: state first, then request
}
  1. super.paintComponent(g) fills the panel with its background colour. It is the "clear the frame" step, and it must come first or it erases what you just drew.
  2. Calling paintComponent directly hands it a Graphics object outside the normal painting cycle: nothing is cleared, nothing is clipped, and the next real repaint discards your work anyway.
  3. repaint() returns immediately. It does not draw — it marks the component dirty and lets the event thread call paintComponent when it is ready.
  4. That also means several repaint() calls in a row can collapse into one paint. Correct behaviour must therefore never depend on how many times painting happened.
🎯 EXAM TIP

The three most-asked facts: (1) paintComponent is overridden, never called — you call repaint(); (2) fillRect(x, y, width, height) is position then size, and fillOval takes the same four numbers as the oval’s bounding box, so a circle of diameter 40 at (30,30) is fillOval(30, 30, 40, 40); (3) the origin is the top-left with y increasing downward, so "move it up 10 pixels" is y -= 10. Remember which package each class is in: JPanel is javax.swing, Graphics and Color are java.awt.

A Swing GUI is a containment hierarchy: a JFrame window holds panels, and panels hold controls. Building one is always the same five steps, in the same order.

import javax.swing.*;

JFrame frame = new JFrame("My App");                    // 1. the window
JPanel panel = new JPanel();                            // 2. a container
JButton button = new JButton("Click me");               // 3. controls
JLabel  label  = new JLabel("Result:");

panel.add(label);                                       // 4. assemble
panel.add(button);
frame.add(panel);

frame.setSize(400, 300);                                // 5. show it
frame.setDefaultCloseOperation(JFrame.EXIT_ON_CLOSE);
frame.setVisible(true);                                 // LAST — after everything

setVisible(true) goes last because components added afterwards may not appear until something forces a re-layout. And without setDefaultCloseOperation, closing the window hides it while the program keeps running.

The input components

Beyond buttons and labels, four input components appear in questions, and each has its own way of being read.

ComponentPurposeRead its value with
JTextFieldone line of textgetText() — always a String
JCheckBoxan independent on/off choiceisSelected() — a boolean
JRadioButtonone choice from a groupisSelected(), with a ButtonGroup enforcing exclusivity
JComboBoxa drop-down listgetSelectedItem() or getSelectedIndex()

The detail that decides questions: a ButtonGroup is what makes radio buttons mutually exclusive. Without one they behave as independent checkboxes, since nothing else links them. And getSelectedItem() returns an Object, so it usually needs a cast or toString().

ComponentFor
JLabeltext or an image the user cannot edit
JTextFieldone line of typed input
JTextAreaseveral lines
JButtonan action
JCheckBoxindependent on/off choices
JRadioButton + ButtonGroupmutually exclusive choices
JComboBoxa drop-down list
JPanelgrouping other components

Radio buttons are only mutually exclusive once added to a ButtonGroup — the group does the enforcing, not the class. Radio buttons on their own behave exactly like check boxes, which is the usual bug.

All of these extend JComponent, so they share setEnabled, setVisible, setToolTipText and the rest — which is polymorphism from Unit 10 doing real work. Read a check box with isSelected() and a text field with getText().

📘 DEFINITION

JFrame: the top-level window

JPanel: a container grouping components, and the usual drawing surface

Component: any control — JButton, JLabel, JTextField

Containment hierarchy: frame contains panels, panels contain components

EXIT_ON_CLOSE: ends the program when the window is closed

🎯 EXAM TIP

Swing classes live in javax.swing — note the x. AWT classes such as Color and Graphics live in java.awt, so most GUI files import both.

📊 FIGURE — A SWING GUI IS A TREE OF COMPONENTS
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a complete window, built in the required order

Every Swing program is these five steps. The comments mark why each one is where it is.

JFrame frame = new JFrame("Lab bench");                   // 1. the window
frame.setDefaultCloseOperation(JFrame.EXIT_ON_CLOSE);    //    or it never exits

JPanel form = new JPanel();                              // 2. a container
JLabel label = new JLabel("Sample id:");                 // 3. the controls
JTextField idField = new JTextField(12);                 //    12 columns wide
JButton submit = new JButton("Record");

form.add(label);                                         // 4. assemble
form.add(idField);
form.add(submit);
frame.add(form);

frame.pack();                                            // 5. size to contents
frame.setVisible(true);                                  //    LAST
  1. new JFrame("Lab bench") creates the window but shows nothing — a frame is invisible until told otherwise.
  2. Without EXIT_ON_CLOSE the default is HIDE_ON_CLOSE: the window disappears and the process keeps running, because the event thread is still alive. That is the classic "my program will not stop".
  3. new JTextField(12) asks for room for about 12 characters. It is a sizing hint, not a length limit — the user can type more.
  4. pack() sizes the window to its contents. setSize(400, 300) is the alternative and ignores what is inside.
  5. setVisible(true) comes last. Components added afterwards may not appear until something forces a re-layout, and "my button is invisible" is usually this.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — reading four kinds of input control

Each control type is read differently, and the return types are what questions turn on.

JTextField name = new JTextField(12);
JCheckBox urgent = new JCheckBox("Urgent");
JRadioButton small = new JRadioButton("Small");
JRadioButton large = new JRadioButton("Large");
ButtonGroup sizes = new ButtonGroup();
sizes.add(small); sizes.add(large);        // THIS is what makes them exclusive
JComboBox<String> lab = new JComboBox<>(new String[]{"North", "South"});

// reading them, typically inside a listener:
String typed   = name.getText();            // always a String, never null
boolean isUrgent = urgent.isSelected();     // boolean
boolean isSmall  = small.isSelected();      // boolean, one per button
String chosen  = (String) lab.getSelectedItem();   // Object -> needs a cast
int index      = lab.getSelectedIndex();    // -1 if nothing is selected
  1. getText() on an empty field returns "", not null — so isEmpty() is the right test, and parseInt("") throws.
  2. A checkbox is independent: several can be on at once.
  3. Radio buttons are not exclusive by class. The ButtonGroup enforces it, and it is not a visible component — you never add it to a panel, only the buttons.
  4. Reading a group means asking each button isSelected(), or keeping the answer in a listener as the user clicks.
  5. getSelectedItem() is declared to return Object, hence the cast; getSelectedIndex() avoids the cast and returns −1 when nothing is chosen.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Radio buttons without a ButtonGroup behave exactly like check boxes — all of them can be selected at once, and nothing warns you, because adding them to a panel looks like it should be enough. The group is a plain object that owns the buttons’ exclusivity; it is never added to the layout. The mirror-image mistake is adding the same button to two groups, or building the group but forgetting one button, which then stays selectable independently of the others.

A layout manager decides where components go and how they resize. GridBagLayout is the flexible one: a grid where each component states its own position and how it should stretch.

panel.setLayout(new GridBagLayout());
GridBagConstraints c = new GridBagConstraints();

c.gridx = 0;  c.gridy = 0;                 // column 0, row 0
c.insets = new Insets(5, 5, 5, 5);         // padding around the component
panel.add(new JLabel("Name:"), c);

c.gridx = 1;
c.fill = GridBagConstraints.HORIZONTAL;    // stretch to fill the cell
c.weightx = 1.0;                           // take the spare horizontal space
panel.add(new JTextField(20), c);

The one thing that catches everybody: the constraints object is read when you call add, so its fields persist between calls. Set gridx once and it stays until you change it, which is convenient and is also why leftover settings quietly land on later components.

LayoutArrangesNote
BorderLayoutNORTH, SOUTH, EAST, WEST, CENTERthe JFrame default; one component per region
FlowLayoutleft to right, wrappingthe JPanel default
GridLayoutequal-sized cellsevery cell the same size, always
GridBagLayouta flexible grid with spans and weightsthe most capable and the most verbose

A layout manager decides position and size as the window resizes, which is why absolute positioning is avoided: fixed coordinates break the moment the window changes size or the font differs.

Adding a second component to the same BorderLayout region does not stack them — it replaces the first, which is why the earlier one silently disappears. Put a JPanel in the region and add both to the panel.

Nesting panels, each with a simple layout, is usually clearer than one GridBagLayout doing everything.

📘 DEFINITION

Layout manager: the object positioning components inside a container

GridBagConstraints: the per-component settings: position, span, fill and weight

gridx / gridy: the column and row

weightx / weighty: how much spare space this cell claims when the window is resized

insets: external padding around a component

🎯 EXAM TIP

FlowLayout is the JPanel default and simply flows left to right. BorderLayout is the JFrame default with five regions. Reach for GridBagLayout only when you need real control.

📊 FIGURE — GRIDBAGLAYOUT: A GRID WHOSE CELLS STATE THEIR OWN RULES
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a label-and-field form, line by line
JPanel form = new JPanel(new GridBagLayout());
GridBagConstraints c = new GridBagConstraints();
c.insets = new Insets(4, 4, 4, 4);          // 4px padding on all sides

c.gridx = 0; c.gridy = 0;
c.anchor = GridBagConstraints.LINE_END;     // right-align the label in its cell
form.add(new JLabel("Sample id:"), c);

c.gridx = 1;                                 // gridy is STILL 0 — same row
c.fill = GridBagConstraints.HORIZONTAL;      // stretch to fill the cell
c.weightx = 1.0;                             // and claim the spare width
JTextField idField = new JTextField(12);
form.add(idField, c);

c.gridx = 0; c.gridy = 1;
c.gridwidth = 2;                             // this one spans both columns
form.add(new JButton("Record"), c);
  1. The constraints object is read when you call add, so its state is copied at that moment. Changing it afterwards affects only later components.
  2. Setting only gridx = 1 for the field is deliberate: gridy is still 0, so the field lands beside the label rather than under it.
  3. fill and weightx do different jobs. weightx decides who gets the leftover space in the window; fill decides whether the component stretches to occupy its cell or floats in the middle of it.
  4. gridwidth = 2 makes the button span both columns — and it stays 2 for every later add unless reset, which is the leak this section warns about.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — picking the layout manager from the requirement
// "a row of buttons that wraps when the window narrows"
JPanel toolbar = new JPanel(new FlowLayout());     // JPanel's default anyway

// "a toolbar on top, a status bar at the bottom, the content filling the rest"
frame.setLayout(new BorderLayout());               // JFrame's default anyway
frame.add(toolbar, BorderLayout.NORTH);
frame.add(new JScrollPane(table), BorderLayout.CENTER);   // CENTER grows
frame.add(status, BorderLayout.SOUTH);

// "a 4x3 keypad, every key the same size"
JPanel pad = new JPanel(new GridLayout(4, 3, 6, 6));      // rows, cols, hgap, vgap

// "a form of labels beside fields, with one spanning cell"
JPanel form = new JPanel(new GridBagLayout());
  1. FlowLayout keeps components at their natural size and wraps — good for buttons, useless for aligning a form.
  2. BorderLayout has five named regions and only CENTER absorbs extra space. A component in NORTH keeps its preferred height forever.
  3. GridLayout(4, 3) forces twelve identical cells. The property that makes it perfect for a keypad is what makes it wrong for a form: the label gets as much width as the field.
  4. Nesting beats configuring. A BorderLayout frame holding a FlowLayout toolbar and a GridBagLayout form is far easier to read than one grid bag doing everything.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Two components added to the same BorderLayout region do not stack — the second replaces the first, and the first simply vanishes with no error. The fix is a JPanel in that region holding both. The GridBagLayout version of the same surprise is stale constraints: gridwidth, fill and weightx persist on the constraints object, so a span set for one component quietly applies to every component added after it until you reset it.

A GUI does nothing until it responds to events. An ActionListener is a small object with one method, and the system calls it when the control is used.

JButton button = new JButton("Add");

button.addActionListener(new ActionListener() {
    @Override
    public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) {
        String text = field.getText();          // read input
        int n = Integer.parseInt(text);         // may throw (12.6)
        label.setText("Result: " + (n * 2));    // update output
    }
});

// the same thing as a lambda, since Java 8
button.addActionListener(e -> label.setText("clicked"));

This inverts the control flow you are used to. Nothing runs top to bottom; you register handlers and the system calls them whenever the user acts. Everything a handler needs must therefore be reachable from it — which is why fields, not locals, usually hold the components.

Finding out what was clicked

One listener can serve several components, and the ActionEvent carries the information needed to tell them apart.

public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) {
    if (e.getSource() == addButton) { ... }        // compare the object
    if ("Add".equals(e.getActionCommand())) { ... } // compare the label/command
}

getSource() returns the component object that fired the event; getActionCommand() returns its command string, which defaults to the button's text. Comparing by source is safer, because changing a button's label silently breaks a comparison written against the command string.

button.addActionListener(new ActionListener() {
    public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) { ... }    // the one method
});

button.addActionListener(e -> label.setText("clicked"));  // lambda — same thing
button.addActionListener(e -> { if (e.getSource() == button) ... });

A button does nothing until a listener is attached. ActionListener has exactly one method, actionPerformed, which is what allows the lambda form — a single-abstract-method interface.

One listener can serve many buttons: e.getSource() identifies which one fired, and e.getActionCommand() returns its label. That is how a calculator keypad is wired with one handler instead of twelve.

Listeners run on the event dispatch thread, which is also the thread that repaints. Doing anything slow inside one freezes the whole interface until it finishes — which is why Thread.sleep in a listener is always wrong, and a javax.swing.Timer is the right tool for anything periodic.

📘 DEFINITION

Event-driven programming: code runs in response to user actions rather than in sequence

ActionListener: the interface with one method, actionPerformed

ActionEvent: the object describing what happened, including the source

Anonymous inner class: the new ActionListener(){...} form, defining a class inline

Lambda: e -> ... — a shorter form usable for any single-method interface

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Everything from a text field arrives as a String. Parsing it needs Integer.parseInt, and non-numeric input throws NumberFormatException — wrap it in a try-catch or the handler dies silently.

📊 FIGURE — THE PATH FROM A CLICK TO YOUR CODE
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a handler that reads, validates and reports
JTextField idField = new JTextField(12);
JLabel status = new JLabel(" ");     // a space, so the row keeps its height
JButton submit = new JButton("Record");

submit.addActionListener(new ActionListener(){
    @Override public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e){
        String text = idField.getText().trim();
        if (text.isEmpty()) { status.setText("Enter a sample id"); return; }
        status.setText("Recorded " + text
            + " (source: " + ((JButton) e.getSource()).getText() + ")");
    }
});

// the same handler as a lambda, since ActionListener has one method
submit.addActionListener(e -> System.out.println(e.getActionCommand()));
  1. The listener is registered once, at build time. Its body runs later, every time the button is pressed — the inversion that makes GUI code different from console code.
  2. getText().trim() then isEmpty() is the standard input guard: a field holding only spaces must count as empty.
  3. The early return is a guard clause. A handler is a method, so the same structure applies.
  4. e.getSource() is the component that fired, typed as Object — hence the cast to JButton before calling getText().
  5. Both listeners are attached to the same button. addActionListener adds, so both run, in the order they were added. (JavaFX’s setOnAction replaces instead — 16.3.)
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — one handler for a whole keypad

Twelve buttons do not need twelve handlers. Give them all the same listener and ask the event which one fired.

JPanel pad = new JPanel(new GridLayout(4, 3, 4, 4));
JTextField display = new JTextField(10);

ActionListener keys = e -> {
    String k = e.getActionCommand();          // defaults to the button's text
    if (k.equals("C")) { display.setText(""); return; }
    display.setText(display.getText() + k);
};

for (String label : new String[]{"7","8","9","4","5","6","1","2","3","C","0","="}) {
    JButton b = new JButton(label);
    b.addActionListener(keys);                // the SAME listener object
    pad.add(b);
}
  1. One ActionListener object is created and handed to twelve buttons. Nothing is duplicated.
  2. getActionCommand() returns the button’s label unless setActionCommand changed it, so the text on the key is the identifier.
  3. That coupling is also its weakness: rename the button to "Clear" and the equals("C") test silently stops matching. Comparing e.getSource() against the button reference is immune to relabelling.
  4. GridLayout(4, 3) is chosen here precisely because every key should be the same size — the fill order is left to right, top to bottom, which is why the labels are listed in that order.
🎯 EXAM TIP

Expect one of three: which interface and method? — ActionListener, one method actionPerformed(ActionEvent e), which is why the lambda form is legal; how does one handler tell buttons apart? — e.getSource() (the object) or e.getActionCommand() (the text); why did the window freeze? — slow work on the event dispatch thread. Thread.sleep inside a listener is always the wrong answer; javax.swing.Timer is the right one for anything periodic. And an exception thrown inside a handler does not stop the program: Swing prints it and carries on, so the button just appears to do nothing.

📊 FIGURE — listener interface or adapter class
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The same handler, written both ways
// implementing the interface: every method must be present,
// even the four you do not care about
class ClickCounter implements java.awt.event.MouseListener {
    int clicks = 0;
    public void mouseClicked(java.awt.event.MouseEvent e) { clicks++; }
    public void mousePressed(java.awt.event.MouseEvent e)  { }
    public void mouseReleased(java.awt.event.MouseEvent e) { }
    public void mouseEntered(java.awt.event.MouseEvent e)  { }
    public void mouseExited(java.awt.event.MouseEvent e)   { }
}

// extending the adapter: the four empty ones are inherited
class ClickCounter2 extends java.awt.event.MouseAdapter {
    int clicks = 0;
    @Override
    public void mouseClicked(java.awt.event.MouseEvent e) { clicks++; }
}

button.addMouseListener(new ClickCounter2());
  1. An interface is all-or-nothing: implement MouseListener and the compiler requires all five methods, so four empty bodies are written purely to satisfy it.
  2. MouseAdapter is a class that already supplies those five as empty methods, so extending it lets you override just the one that matters.
  3. The trade-off is inheritance: a class may extend only one thing, so if it must already extend something else, implement the interface instead. The same pattern exists for KeyAdapter and WindowAdapter.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Whenever a question offers "implement the listener" against "extend the adapter", the adapter's advantage is always the same sentence: you override only the methods you need. Its only cost is using up the single extends slot.

A JFormattedTextField restricts what can be typed, which removes the parsing problem of 15.4 at the source rather than catching it afterwards.

NumberFormat fmt = NumberFormat.getIntegerInstance();
JFormattedTextField field = new JFormattedTextField(fmt);
field.setValue(0);

field.addPropertyChangeListener("value", evt -> {
    int n = ((Number) field.getValue()).intValue();     // already a number
    label.setText("doubled: " + (n * 2));
});

getValue() returns an Object holding a Number, not a String, so the cast replaces the parse. The field also refuses or reverts invalid input on its own, which is validation moved to the earliest possible point.

try {
    int n = Integer.parseInt(field.getText().trim());
    ...
} catch (NumberFormatException ex) {
    JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(frame, "Please enter a whole number");
}

getText() always returns a String — never a number, and never null; an empty field gives "", which parseInt rejects. So every numeric field needs the same trim-parse-catch shape from 12.6.

An uncaught exception inside a listener does not stop the program. Swing catches it, prints a trace to the console and carries on, so the window simply appears not to respond — a silent failure that is much harder to notice than a crash.

Report problems in the interface, not on the console the user cannot see. JOptionPane.showMessageDialog is the standard way, and field.setText("") clears the field afterwards.

📘 DEFINITION

JFormattedTextField: a text field that enforces a format on its content

NumberFormat: the formatter describing what counts as valid

getValue(): returns the parsed Object, typically a Number

PropertyChangeListener: fires when the committed value changes

🎯 EXAM TIP

Validating at input is better than validating at use. It is the GUI version of the precondition argument in 6.13.

📊 FIGURE — VALIDATE AT THE POINT OF INPUT, OR PARSE AND CATCH LATER
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the plain field, done correctly
JTextField massField = new JTextField(8);
JLabel status = new JLabel(" ");

record.addActionListener(e -> {
    String text = massField.getText().trim();     // trim FIRST
    if (text.isEmpty()) { status.setText("Enter a mass in grams"); return; }
    try {
        int grams = Integer.parseInt(text);
        if (grams <= 0) { status.setText("Mass must be positive"); return; }
        status.setText("Recorded " + grams + " g");
    } catch (NumberFormatException ex) {
        status.setText("\"" + text + "\" is not a whole number");
        massField.setText("");                    // clear it so they can retype
    }
});
  1. Three distinct failures get three distinct messages: empty, not a number, and out of range. One generic "invalid input" tells the user nothing.
  2. trim() comes before the emptiness test, so a field of spaces is caught by the first branch rather than by parseInt.
  3. The range check sits after the parse — you cannot compare a String against 0.
  4. Reporting goes to a label, not System.out: the user of a window is not watching a console.
  5. Integer.parseInt("42.5") also throws — a decimal point is not a whole number. Use Double.parseDouble when decimals are legal.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the formatted field, which never sees bad input
NumberFormat fmt = NumberFormat.getIntegerInstance();
JFormattedTextField massField = new JFormattedTextField(fmt);
massField.setValue(0);                     // seeds the value AND the display

massField.addPropertyChangeListener("value", evt -> {
    int grams = ((Number) massField.getValue()).intValue();
    status.setText("mass " + grams + " g");
});
  1. The formatter is supplied at construction; it defines what the field will accept and how it displays what it holds.
  2. setValue(0) is how you initialise it — setText("0") sets the display without setting the value, and the two then disagree.
  3. The listener is a PropertyChangeListener on the "value" property, not an ActionListener. It fires when the value is committed — typically on Enter or when focus leaves — not on every keystroke.
  4. getValue() returns Object. The cast is to Number rather than Integer, because the formatter may produce a Long; Number covers both and intValue() works on either.
  5. There is no try. Invalid text never becomes a value — the field reverts it — so there is nothing to catch.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

getText() and getValue() are not interchangeable. On a JFormattedTextField, getText() returns whatever characters are currently displayed, including formatting such as the comma in "1,250" — and Integer.parseInt("1,250") throws. getValue() returns the committed Number. The reverse mistake is casting the result of getValue() straight to Integer when the formatter produced a Long, which compiles and throws ClassCastException at run time; casting to Number and calling intValue() is safe either way.

A JSpinner constrains input to a range with up and down arrows, so out-of-range values become impossible rather than merely rejected.

SpinnerNumberModel model = new SpinnerNumberModel(
        50,      // initial
        0,       // minimum
        100,     // maximum
        1);      // step
JSpinner spinner = new JSpinner(model);

spinner.addChangeListener(e -> {
    int value = (Integer) spinner.getValue();
    label.setText("value: " + value);
});

Note it is a ChangeListener here rather than an ActionListener — different controls fire different event types, and using the wrong one means the handler is never called. That is the most common Swing debugging story.

class Canvas extends JPanel {
    @Override
    protected void paintComponent(Graphics g) {
        super.paintComponent(g);          // clears the background — do NOT omit
        g.setColor(Color.BLUE);
        g.fillRect(10, 20, 100, 50);      // x, y, WIDTH, HEIGHT
        g.fillOval(10, 20, 40, 40);       // a circle is an oval in a square box
    }
}
panel.repaint();                          // ASK for a redraw — never call paintComponent

Custom drawing means overriding paintComponent and letting Swing call it. Calling it yourself does not work reliably, because the system decides when painting happens; repaint() is the request.

Omitting super.paintComponent(g) leaves the previous frame on screen, so moving shapes smear — the single most common symptom in this topic.

The coordinate origin is the top-left and y increases downwards, which is upside-down compared with mathematics. Rectangle and oval parameters are position then size, not two corners.

📘 DEFINITION

JSpinner: a control cycling through a bounded sequence of values

SpinnerNumberModel: the model supplying initial value, bounds and step

ChangeListener: the listener for value changes, with method stateChanged

getValue(): returns the current value as an Object, requiring a cast

🎯 EXAM TIP

Buttons use ActionListener, spinners and sliders use ChangeListener, text fields can use either. If a handler never fires, check the listener type before anything else.

📊 FIGURE — A SPINNER IS A MODEL PLUS TWO ARROWS
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a bounded numeric spinner and its listener
SpinnerNumberModel model = new SpinnerNumberModel(50, 0, 100, 5);
JSpinner spinner = new JSpinner(model);

spinner.addChangeListener(new ChangeListener(){
    @Override public void stateChanged(ChangeEvent e){
        int v = (Integer) ((JSpinner) e.getSource()).getValue();
        status.setText("spinner " + v);
    }
});
  1. The four constructor arguments are value, minimum, maximum, step — in that order. Swapping the first two is the usual slip and produces a spinner that starts at its floor.
  2. Clicking up from 50 with a step of 5 gives 55, then 60. At 100 the up arrow does nothing: the model refuses to leave its range.
  3. The event carries no value. You ask the source — or the captured spinner variable — what it now holds.
  4. getValue() returns Object; a SpinnerNumberModel built from int literals yields Integer, so the cast is to Integer. Build the model with double literals and the cast must be to Double.
  5. stateChanged is the only method of ChangeListener, so this too could be written as a lambda.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a spinner over a list of values, not numbers

The number model is not the only one. A spinner can cycle through any fixed list, which is how a day-of-week or a shift-code picker is built.

JSpinner dates = new JSpinner(
    new SpinnerListModel(new String[]{"Mon","Tue","Wed","Thu","Fri"}));

dates.addChangeListener(e -> {
    String day = (String) dates.getValue();      // the cast follows the model
    status.setText("day " + day);
});
  1. SpinnerListModel replaces SpinnerNumberModel; nothing else about the spinner changes.
  2. The type returned by getValue() follows the model — String here, Integer for the numeric model. The cast is not decoration; get it wrong and it is a ClassCastException.
  3. A list model wraps at the ends by default, so pressing up on "Fri" returns to "Mon" — different from the number model, which simply stops.
  4. Compared with a JComboBox: the combo box shows all choices at once and suits long lists; a spinner shows one and suits short, naturally ordered ones.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Attaching an ActionListener to a spinner or a slider compiles — every JComponent inherits addMouseListener and friends, and there is nothing illegal about the call — but the handler never fires, because those controls publish ChangeEvents, not ActionEvents. The symptom is a control that visibly moves while your code does nothing. When a handler never runs, check the listener type before you suspect the logic: buttons and menu items use ActionListener, spinners and sliders use ChangeListener.

A JTextArea displays many lines, and it is nearly always wrapped in a JScrollPane — a text area alone does not scroll.

JTextArea area = new JTextArea(10, 40);      // rows, columns
area.setEditable(false);
area.setLineWrap(true);
area.setWrapStyleWord(true);

JScrollPane scroll = new JScrollPane(area);   // the AREA goes in the SCROLL PANE
panel.add(scroll);                            // and the SCROLL PANE goes in the panel

area.setText("first line\n");                 // replaces everything
area.append("second line\n");                 // adds to the end

The order in the middle is the part people get wrong: adding the text area to the panel and the scroll pane separately gives a text area that grows without ever scrolling. The scroll pane must be the component the panel holds.

Menus

Menus have a fixed three-level containment that questions ask you to put in order.

JMenuBar   contains   JMenu   contains   JMenuItem

JMenuBar bar = new JMenuBar();
JMenu file = new JMenu("File");
file.add(new JMenuItem("Open"));
bar.add(file);
frame.setJMenuBar(bar);        // NOT frame.add(bar)

Two details are tested. The bar is attached with setJMenuBar, not add — it is not an ordinary component in the layout. And a submenu is made by adding a JMenu to another JMenu rather than a JMenuItem, which is what nests one menu inside another.

JMenuBar bar = new JMenuBar();
JMenu file = new JMenu("File");
JMenuItem open = new JMenuItem("Open");
open.addActionListener(e -> ...);       // items fire ActionEvents, like buttons
file.add(open);
file.addSeparator();
bar.add(file);
frame.setJMenuBar(bar);                 // NOT frame.add(bar)

The hierarchy is fixed: JMenuBar holds JMenus, which hold JMenuItems. A JMenu added to another JMenu becomes a submenu.

The menu bar attaches with setJMenuBar, not add — using add drops it into the layout as an ordinary component, where it looks wrong and often disappears.

Menu items are AbstractButtons like JButton, so the same ActionListener can serve both a toolbar button and a menu item — one handler, two ways to reach it.

📘 DEFINITION

JTextArea: a multi-line text component

JScrollPane: a container adding scrollbars to whatever it wraps

setText vs append: replace all content versus add to the end

setLineWrap: wraps long lines instead of scrolling horizontally

🎯 EXAM TIP

setEditable(false) makes a text area an output log rather than an input box — the usual role in a course project.

📊 FIGURE — WRAPPING FOR SCROLL, AND THE THREE MENU LEVELS
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a scrolling, read-only log area
JTextArea log = new JTextArea(8, 40);       // rows, columns
log.setEditable(false);                     // output, not input
log.setLineWrap(true);                      // wrap instead of scrolling sideways
log.setWrapStyleWord(true);                 // wrap at spaces, not mid-word

JScrollPane logScroll = new JScrollPane(log);   // the AREA goes inside
panel.add(logScroll);                           // the PANE goes in the panel

log.setText("ready\n");        // replaces everything
log.append("job started\n");   // adds to the end — the one you want in a loop
  1. new JTextArea(8, 40) is a size hint in rows and columns, the same idea as new JTextField(12). It does not limit how much text the area can hold.
  2. setEditable(false) is what turns an input box into an output log; the user can still select and copy, which is usually wanted.
  3. setLineWrap(true) alone breaks lines mid-word. setWrapStyleWord(true) moves the break to the last space.
  4. setText replaces the entire contents; append adds. Using setText inside a loop leaves only the final line.
  5. Adding log to the panel instead of logScroll gives a text area that grows past the window edge and never scrolls — the mistake this figure exists for.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a File menu with a separator and a submenu
JMenuBar bar = new JMenuBar();
JMenu file = new JMenu("File");

JMenuItem open = new JMenuItem("Open");
open.addActionListener(e -> loadFile());     // items behave like buttons
file.add(open);
file.addSeparator();                         // the horizontal rule

JMenu export = new JMenu("Export");           // a JMenu inside a JMenu
export.add(new JMenuItem("CSV"));             // = a submenu
file.add(export);

bar.add(file);
frame.setJMenuBar(bar);                       // NOT frame.add(bar)
  1. Build inside out: items into menus, menus into the bar, the bar onto the frame.
  2. JMenuItem extends AbstractButton, so it fires an ActionEvent and takes the same ActionListener — one handler can serve a toolbar button and a menu item.
  3. addSeparator() belongs to the menu, not to the item; it groups the entries visually.
  4. Adding a JMenu where an item would go creates a submenu. Nothing else changes.
  5. setJMenuBar attaches the bar to the frame’s own menu slot. frame.add(bar) compiles and drops it into the layout as an ordinary component, where it typically lands in the middle of the window or disappears.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Adding the text component and the scroll pane as siblings is the classic failure: panel.add(area); panel.add(new JScrollPane(area)); looks thorough and produces an area that never scrolls, because the pane must be the parent. The same rule catches JList and JTable — and on a table there is a second symptom, since the column headers live in the scroll pane’s header row and simply do not appear without one.

📊 FIGURE — the two menu shortcuts, which are not the same thing
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Ctrl+S on a menu item, and Alt-navigation on the menu
JMenu fileMenu = new JMenu("File");
fileMenu.setMnemonic('F');            // Alt+F opens this menu

JMenuItem save = new JMenuItem("Save");
save.setMnemonic('S');                // once File is open, S picks Save
save.setAccelerator(
    KeyStroke.getKeyStroke(KeyEvent.VK_S, InputEvent.CTRL_DOWN_MASK));
// Ctrl+S now triggers Save without opening any menu at all

save.addActionListener(e -> saveDocument());
fileMenu.add(save);
  1. The accelerator is a global shortcut: pressing Ctrl+S fires the item's action directly, with the menu closed.
  2. The mnemonic only works while navigating — Alt+F opens File, then S selects Save.
  3. Swing displays the accelerator beside the item's label, so the shortcut advertises itself; the mnemonic shows as an underlined letter.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Treating setMnemonic as a keyboard shortcut. It is not — it only selects an item within a menu that is already open. The direct Ctrl+key shortcut is setAccelerator with a KeyStroke.
"}, "D286/u15/z15_8": {"body": "

A JTable displays rows and columns, and it separates the data from the display: the model holds the values, the table shows them.

String[] columns = {"Name", "Score"};
Object[][] data = { {"Ada", 95}, {"Alan", 88} };

DefaultTableModel model = new DefaultTableModel(data, columns);
JTable table = new JTable(model);
panel.add(new JScrollPane(table));         // headers only show inside a scroll pane

model.addRow(new Object[]{"Grace", 99});   // change the MODEL, not the table
model.getValueAt(0, 1);                    // 95
model.removeRow(0);

Every change goes through the model, which then tells the table to refresh itself. Trying to modify the table directly is the standard mistake, and the column headers vanishing without a scroll pane is the second.

javax.swing.Timer t = new javax.swing.Timer(1000, e -> {
    x += 5;
    panel.repaint();                    // move, then ask for a redraw
});
t.start();
// t.stop();  t.setDelay(500);

Use javax.swing.Timer, not java.util.Timer. The Swing one fires its ActionListener on the event dispatch thread, which is the only thread allowed to touch components; the utility one fires on its own thread and produces intermittent, hard-to-reproduce corruption.

The delay is in milliseconds, so 1000 is one frame per second. Animation is therefore not a loop — it is a timer that changes state and calls repaint(), letting the interface stay responsive between frames.

Thread.sleep in a listener does the opposite: it blocks the event thread, so nothing repaints and the window appears frozen for exactly as long as the sleep.

📘 DEFINITION

JTable: the component displaying tabular data

TableModel: the object holding the data; the table is only a view of it

DefaultTableModel: the standard editable implementation with addRow and removeRow

Model-view separation: keeping data and display apart so either can change independently

🎯 EXAM TIP

This split is the same idea as encapsulation in 7.4 — the data is owned in one place and the display asks for it, so nothing can change it behind the model’s back.

📊 FIGURE — MODEL AND VIEW: WHO OWNS THE ROWS
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — building a table and changing it through the model
String[] cols = {"Sample", "Mass (g)"};
Object[][] rows = {{"S-01", 12}, {"S-02", 19}};

DefaultTableModel tm = new DefaultTableModel(rows, cols);
JTable table = new JTable(tm);
panel.add(new JScrollPane(table));       // headers need the scroll pane

tm.addRow(new Object[]{"S-03", 7});      // change the MODEL
Object cell = tm.getValueAt(0, 1);       // -> 12   (row 0, column 1)
tm.setValueAt(14, 0, 1);                 // value FIRST, then row, then column
System.out.println(tm.getRowCount() + " rows, " + tm.getColumnCount() + " columns");
  1. The data is Object[][], so a column can hold numbers and another strings. Cells come back as Object and usually need a cast or toString().
  2. addRow takes an Object[] whose length must match the column count; a short array leaves trailing cells empty rather than throwing.
  3. getValueAt(row, column) is row first — the 2D-array convention, and the opposite of the JavaFX GridPane order in 16.2.
  4. setValueAt(value, row, column) puts the value first. Two adjacent methods with different argument orders is exactly the kind of detail an exam tests.
  5. Every one of these calls goes to the model. The table repaints itself because the model announces the change.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — animation with a Swing Timer, not a loop

A loop that redraws cannot work: it occupies the event thread, so nothing repaints until it finishes. A timer fires periodically and returns immediately.

javax.swing.Timer timer = new javax.swing.Timer(1000, e -> {
    x += 5;              // change the state
    panel.repaint();     // then ask for a redraw
});
timer.start();
timer.setDelay(500);     // twice as fast
timer.stop();
  1. The first argument is the delay in milliseconds: 1000 is one tick per second.
  2. The second argument is an ActionListener — a timer fires ActionEvents, exactly like a button.
  3. Use javax.swing.Timer, not java.util.Timer. The Swing one fires on the event dispatch thread, the only thread allowed to touch components; the utility one fires on its own thread and produces intermittent, unreproducible corruption.
  4. The fully qualified name in the declaration is deliberate: with both java.util.* and javax.swing.* imported, the plain name Timer is ambiguous and will not compile.
  5. Thread.sleep in a listener does the opposite of a timer — it blocks the thread that repaints, so the window freezes for exactly the sleep duration.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Calling setters on the JTable instead of the model is the standard dead end — the component is a view, and there is no table.addRow at all, so the code will not even compile. Keep a reference to the DefaultTableModel in a field and go through it. Two smaller ones travel with it: getValueAt returns Object (so (int) tm.getValueAt(0,1) needs the stored value really to be an Integer), and a table added without a JScrollPane shows its rows but no column headers, which looks like the headers were never set.

A JSlider chooses a value from a range by dragging, and it fires continuously while the user drags — which is a behaviour you have to design around.

JSlider slider = new JSlider(0, 100, 50);    // min, max, initial
slider.setMajorTickSpacing(25);
slider.setPaintTicks(true);
slider.setPaintLabels(true);

slider.addChangeListener(e -> {
    if (!slider.getValueIsAdjusting()) {     // only when the drag FINISHES
        label.setText("value: " + slider.getValue());
    }
});

getValueIsAdjusting() is the guard that matters. Without it a handler that does real work — recomputing, redrawing, writing a file — runs dozens of times per drag. Live preview wants it without the guard; anything expensive wants it with.

The simpler layout managers

GridBagLayout from 15.3 is the flexible one; three simpler managers cover most real forms and are asked about by name.

LayoutArrangesDefault for
FlowLayoutleft to right, wrapping as neededJPanel
BorderLayoutfive regions: NORTH, SOUTH, EAST, WEST, CENTERJFrame
GridLayoutequal-sized cells in a fixed grid—

GridLayout(rows, cols) forces every cell to the same size, which is why it suits calculators and keypads and not forms with a label beside a field. In BorderLayout only CENTER stretches to fill the leftover space, so a component placed there grows with the window and one in NORTH does not.

JPanel pad = new JPanel(new GridLayout(4, 3));      // equal cells suit a keypad
for (String label : keys) {
    JButton b = new JButton(label);
    b.addActionListener(handler);                   // ONE handler for all of them
    pad.add(b);
}

public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) {
    String k = e.getActionCommand();                // which key was pressed
    if (k.equals("/") && current == 0) { show("Cannot divide by zero"); return; }
}

GridLayout is the right choice here precisely because every cell is the same size — the property that makes it awkward elsewhere is what a keypad wants.

One listener plus getActionCommand() replaces a dozen near-identical handlers. Digits build the number by appending to the display text rather than doing arithmetic; the operator is stored and applied when the next one or equals arrives.

The division guard belongs before the calculation, not in a catch — and remember from 12.2 that with double operands dividing by zero does not throw at all, it produces Infinity, so nothing would be caught anyway.

📘 DEFINITION

JSlider: a control selecting a value from a range by dragging

ChangeListener: fires on every value change, including mid-drag

getValueIsAdjusting(): true while the user is still dragging

Tick marks: the visual scale, enabled with setPaintTicks and setPaintLabels

🎯 EXAM TIP

Sliders and spinners both use ChangeListener, and both return their value as an int from getValue() — unlike the spinner’s Object-returning version when a model is attached.

📊 FIGURE — WHAT A SLIDER DRAG ACTUALLY SENDS
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a slider with ticks, driving a live preview
JSlider slider = new JSlider(0, 100, 40);    // min, max, initial
slider.setMajorTickSpacing(25);              // labelled ticks every 25
slider.setMinorTickSpacing(5);
slider.setPaintTicks(true);                  // ticks are OFF by default
slider.setPaintLabels(true);                 // and so are the numbers

slider.addChangeListener(e -> {
    JSlider s = (JSlider) e.getSource();
    if (!s.getValueIsAdjusting()) {          // only when the drag finishes
        gauge.setLevel(s.getValue());        // this repaints the gauge
    }
});
  1. The three constructor arguments are minimum, maximum, initial value — the same shape as the spinner model, minus the step.
  2. setMajorTickSpacing alone shows nothing: the two setPaint… calls are what make ticks and labels visible.
  3. getValue() returns an int directly, with no cast — unlike JSpinner.getValue(), which returns Object.
  4. The guard means the gauge is redrawn once per drag rather than dozens of times. Drop the guard for a cheap live preview; keep it for anything that recomputes, writes a file, or hits a network.
  5. gauge.setLevel ends in repaint() — the pattern from 15.1: change state, then request a redraw.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — two controls, one value, kept in step

A slider and a spinner over the same quantity is a common requirement, and it is where the adjusting flag earns its keep — without care the two listeners call each other in a loop.

JSlider slider = new JSlider(0, 100, 40);
JSpinner spinner = new JSpinner(new SpinnerNumberModel(40, 0, 100, 1));

slider.addChangeListener(e -> {
    int v = slider.getValue();
    if (!spinner.getValue().equals(v)) spinner.setValue(v);   // guard first
});
spinner.addChangeListener(e -> {
    int v = (Integer) spinner.getValue();
    if (slider.getValue() != v) slider.setValue(v);
});
  1. Setting a control’s value fires its listener, so the naive version would loop: slider sets spinner, spinner sets slider, forever.
  2. The equality check breaks the cycle. When the second control already holds the value, nothing is set and no further event is generated.
  3. spinner.getValue() returns Object, so it is compared with equals and cast when an int is needed; slider.getValue() is already an int and uses !=.
  4. Both listeners are ChangeListeners — the shared listener type is exactly why these two controls pair up so often.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

A ChangeListener on a slider fires on every intermediate value, not once per drag. A handler that writes a file, re-runs a calculation or repaints a large image will run dozens of times for one gesture and make the interface stutter — and because each call is individually fast, it does not look like a performance bug. Guard with if (!slider.getValueIsAdjusting()) for expensive work. The reverse mistake is guarding a cheap live preview, which then updates only when the user lets go and feels broken.

"}, "D286/u15/z15_10": {"body": "

The seat reservation project puts the unit together: a table shows the seats, a field takes a seat number, a button reserves it, and a label reports what happened.

JTextField seatField = new JTextField(5);
JButton reserve = new JButton("Reserve");
DefaultTableModel model = new DefaultTableModel(new String[]{"Seat","Status"}, 0);

reserve.addActionListener(e -> {
    try {
        int seat = Integer.parseInt(seatField.getText().trim());
        if (seat < 1 || seat > model.getRowCount()) {
            status.setText("No such seat");
            return;
        }
        if ("taken".equals(model.getValueAt(seat - 1, 1))) {
            status.setText("Seat already taken");
            return;
        }
        model.setValueAt("taken", seat - 1, 1);
        status.setText("Reserved seat " + seat);
    } catch (NumberFormatException ex) {
        status.setText("Enter a number");
    }
});

The handler is a stack of guard clauses (6.5), and every one of them corresponds to a way a user can be wrong: not a number, out of range, already taken. A GUI handler that assumes good input is a GUI handler that crashes.

Lists and their models

A JList follows the same model-view split as JTable in 15.8: the ListModel holds the data and the component displays it.

DefaultListModel model = new DefaultListModel<>();
model.addElement("A1");                 // change the MODEL
JList list = new JList<>(model);
panel.add(new JScrollPane(list));       // scroll pane again

list.getSelectedIndex();   // -1 when nothing is selected
list.getSelectedValue();   // the element itself, or null

getSelectedIndex() returns -1 when nothing is selected — the same not-found convention as indexOf in 3.16 — so it must be checked before being used as an index.

DefaultListModel<String> model = new DefaultListModel<>();
JList<String> list = new JList<>(model);
frame.add(new JScrollPane(list));            // wrap it — JList does not scroll itself

model.addElement(field.getText());           // change the MODEL, not the view
int i = list.getSelectedIndex();
if (i != -1) model.remove(i);                // -1 means nothing selected

The component displays a model, and you modify the model — the view updates itself. Trying to change the JList directly is the usual dead end; this model-and-view split is the same idea behind JTable with a DefaultTableModel.

Scrolling is not built in. A JList, JTextArea or JTable must be wrapped in a JScrollPane, and the scroll pane is what gets added to the frame.

getSelectedIndex() returns −1 when nothing is selected, so removing without that check throws. Guard against empty input too, or the list fills with blank rows.

📘 DEFINITION

Guard clauses in a handler: early returns rejecting each invalid case before the real work

Seat index offset: seat 1 is row 0 — the off-by-one from 5.1 in user-facing form

Status label: a single label reporting the outcome instead of a dialog per error

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Users count seats from 1 and tables count rows from 0. Converting once, at the boundary, is right; converting in several places is how one of them ends up missing.

📊 FIGURE — EVERY WAY A USER CAN BE WRONG, IN ORDER
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the reserve button, guard by guard
reserve.addActionListener(e -> {
    String text = seatField.getText().trim();
    if (text.isEmpty()) { status.setText("Enter a seat number"); return; }
    try {
        int seat = Integer.parseInt(text);
        if (seat < 1 || seat > model.getRowCount()) {
            status.setText("No such seat"); return;
        }
        if ("taken".equals(model.getValueAt(seat - 1, 1))) {
            status.setText("Seat already taken"); return;
        }
        model.setValueAt("taken", seat - 1, 1);      // value, row, column
        status.setText("Reserved seat " + seat);
        seatField.setText("");
    } catch (NumberFormatException ex) {
        status.setText("Enter a number");
    }
});
  1. Four guards, four distinct messages, each with its own return. Nothing after a guard has to re-check what the guard already rejected.
  2. The range test uses model.getRowCount() rather than a hard-coded 40, so adding seats to the model cannot leave the check behind.
  3. "taken".equals(model.getValueAt(...)) puts the literal first on purpose: getValueAt returns Object and could be null, and this order cannot throw.
  4. seat - 1 appears twice, in the read and the write, and nowhere else — the single conversion point.
  5. Clearing the field on success is what makes the next reservation quick, and it also signals that something happened.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a JList of reservations, added and removed through its model
DefaultListModel<String> listModel = new DefaultListModel<>();
listModel.addElement("S-01");
JList<String> list = new JList<>(listModel);
panel.add(new JScrollPane(list));            // JList does not scroll itself

remove.addActionListener(e -> {
    int i = list.getSelectedIndex();
    if (i == -1) { status.setText("nothing selected"); return; }   // -1 GUARD
    listModel.remove(i);
});
  1. Same split as JTable: DefaultListModel owns the strings, JList displays them.
  2. getSelectedIndex() returns −1 when nothing is selected — the same not-found convention as indexOf. Passing −1 straight to remove throws.
  3. getSelectedValue() is the alternative and returns null in the same situation, so it needs a null check instead.
  4. The removal goes to the model; the list redraws itself. There is no list.remove(i) that does what you want.
🎯 EXAM TIP

Project-style questions here reward the boring answer: validate everything the user can type. Expect to be asked which guard is missing from a handler, and check them in this order — empty, unparseable, out of range, already in that state. The off-by-one is the other favourite: seats, rows and menu options are numbered from 1 for humans and from 0 for the model, so if an answer option differs from another only by ±1, the question is about that conversion. Convert once, at the boundary between the interface and the data.
