Reading a file from a GUI combines Unit 9 and Unit 12 with a file chooser, and adds one Swing-specific obligation.

JFileChooser chooser = new JFileChooser();
if (chooser.showOpenDialog(frame) == JFileChooser.APPROVE_OPTION) {
    File f = chooser.getSelectedFile();
    try (Scanner in = new Scanner(f)) {              // try-with-resources (12.3)
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        while (in.hasNextLine()) { sb.append(in.nextLine()).append("\n"); }
        area.setText(sb.toString());
    } catch (FileNotFoundException ex) {
        JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(frame, "Could not open the file");
    }
}

Checking APPROVE_OPTION is not optional — the user can cancel, and getSelectedFile() then returns null. The StringBuilder is there for the reason given in 4.6: appending to a String once per line reallocates once per line.

Converting a console program to a GUI is one rule: separate the logic from the input and output. A method that takes values and returns a result works unchanged behind either interface; a method that calls Scanner and println internally has to be rewritten.

ConsoleGUI
scnr.nextInt()Integer.parseInt(field.getText())
System.out.println(x)label.setText(x) or area.append(x)
the main while loopthe event loop — listeners fire as the user acts
a validation ifthe same if, unchanged

The main loop is the piece that disappears entirely. A console program drives the user; a GUI waits to be driven, so what was the body of the loop becomes the body of a listener.

Validation belongs in the logic, not in the listener, so both interfaces enforce the same rules — and so the logic can still be unit tested without a window, which is the practical payoff of the separation.

📘 DEFINITION

JFileChooser: the standard open and save dialog

APPROVE_OPTION: the return value meaning the user chose a file rather than cancelling

JOptionPane: the standard message, confirm and input dialogs

try-with-resources: closes the Scanner automatically, even on failure

🎯 EXAM TIP

Reporting a failure in a GUI means a dialog or a status label, not System.out.println — the user is not looking at a console.

📊 FIGURE — OPEN, READ, AND REPORT FAILURE WHERE IT CAN BE SEEN
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the whole load handler
load.addActionListener(e -> {
    JFileChooser chooser = new JFileChooser();
    if (chooser.showOpenDialog(frame) != JFileChooser.APPROVE_OPTION) {
        status.setText("load cancelled");
        return;                                   // the user pressed Cancel
    }
    File f = chooser.getSelectedFile();
    try (Scanner in = new Scanner(f)) {           // try-with-resources
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        int n = 0;
        while (in.hasNextLine()) { sb.append(in.nextLine()).append('\n'); n++; }
        log.setText(sb.toString());               // ONE update, at the end
        status.setText("loaded " + n + " lines from " + f.getName());
    } catch (FileNotFoundException ex) {
        JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(frame,
            "Could not open " + f.getName(), "Error", JOptionPane.ERROR_MESSAGE);
    }
});
  1. showOpenDialog blocks until the user answers and returns an int constant. Testing it is not optional: on Cancel, getSelectedFile() returns null and the next line throws.
  2. Writing the test as "not approve, then return" keeps the successful path unindented — the guard-clause shape again.
  3. try (Scanner in = new Scanner(f)) closes the scanner however the block exits, including on exception.
  4. The text is assembled in a StringBuilder and set once. Calling append on the text area per line works but repaints the component every time.
  5. new Scanner(File) throws the checked FileNotFoundException, so the compiler requires the catch — unlike new Scanner(System.in), which throws nothing.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — turning a console program into a GUI

The logic does not change. What changes is where input comes from and where output goes — which is only easy if the logic was in methods to begin with.

// console version
public static double average(int[] scores) { ... }   // reusable — no I/O inside

public static void main(String[] args){
    Scanner scnr = new Scanner(System.in);
    int n = scnr.nextInt();
    ...
    System.out.printf("Average: %.2f%n", average(scores));
}

// GUI version — SAME average method, different edges
compute.addActionListener(e -> {
    try {
        int n = Integer.parseInt(countField.getText().trim());   // input
        ...
        result.setText(String.format("Average: %.2f", average(scores)));  // output
    } catch (NumberFormatException ex) {
        result.setText("Enter a whole number");
    }
});
  1. scnr.nextInt() becomes Integer.parseInt(field.getText()) — and the parse can now fail, because a text field accepts anything.
  2. System.out.printf becomes setText with String.format, which does the same formatting and returns the string instead of printing it.
  3. The while loop that drove the console program disappears entirely. Its body becomes the listener; the event loop replaces it.
  4. average is untouched. A method that takes values and returns a result works behind either interface — and can still be unit tested with no window at all.
  5. A method that called Scanner and println internally would have to be rewritten, which is the practical argument for separating logic from I/O.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Reporting failures with System.out.println in a GUI means nobody sees them: the console is hidden behind the window, or absent when the program is launched by double-clicking. Use JOptionPane.showMessageDialog for something the user must acknowledge, or a status label for something minor. The related trap is silence — an uncaught exception inside a listener does not stop the program; Swing prints the trace to the console and carries on, so a broken button looks like a button that does nothing at all.

JavaFX is the newer GUI toolkit, and it does the same job as Swing (Unit 15) with a different vocabulary. Knowing the mapping is most of what you need: Stage is the window, Scene is the contents, and everything inside is a Node.

import javafx.application.Application;
import javafx.stage.Stage;
import javafx.scene.Scene;
import javafx.scene.control.Button;
import javafx.scene.layout.StackPane;

public class Demo extends Application {
    @Override
    public void start(Stage stage) {           // NOT main — the entry point is start
        Button b = new Button("Click me");
        StackPane root = new StackPane(b);

        stage.setScene(new Scene(root, 300, 200));
        stage.setTitle("Demo");
        stage.show();
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) { launch(args); }
}

Swing to JavaFX: JFrame becomes Stage, JPanel becomes a layout pane, JButton becomes Button, and setVisible(true) becomes stage.show(). The structure is identical; only the names changed.

public class App extends Application {          // 1. extend Application
    @Override
    public void start(Stage stage) {            // 2. build the UI HERE, not in main
        Label l = new Label("Hello");
        Scene scene = new Scene(l, 300, 200);   // 3. scene holds the node graph
        stage.setScene(scene);
        stage.show();                           // 4. show it last
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) { launch(args); }
}
JavaFXSwing equivalentIs
StageJFramethe window
Scenethe content panethe container for one node graph
NodeJComponentanything displayable — a control, a shape, a layout

The nesting is fixed and asked directly: a Stage holds a Scene, a Scene holds a root Node, and nodes hold children. Miss a level and nothing appears.

The UI is built in start, not main. main only calls launch, which starts the JavaFX runtime and then calls start on the JavaFX application thread — the same event-thread rule as Swing.

📘 DEFINITION

Application: the class a JavaFX program extends; start() replaces main as the entry point

Stage: the window

Scene: the content attached to a stage, with a root node and a size

Node: anything placed in a scene — controls, shapes, layout panes

launch(args): starts the JavaFX runtime, which then calls start()

🎯 EXAM TIP

Scene graph is the term for the tree of nodes. It is the same containment hierarchy as 15.2, named differently.

📊 FIGURE — JAVAFX: STAGE, SCENE, THEN THE SCENE GRAPH
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the smallest complete JavaFX program, line by line
import javafx.application.Application;
import javafx.scene.Scene;
import javafx.scene.control.Button;
import javafx.scene.layout.StackPane;
import javafx.stage.Stage;

public class Demo extends Application {          // 1. extend Application

    @Override
    public void start(Stage stage) {             // 2. the real entry point
        Button b = new Button("Click me");       // 3. nodes
        StackPane root = new StackPane(b);       // 4. a root node
        Scene scene = new Scene(root, 300, 200); // 5. scene wraps the root
        stage.setScene(scene);                   // 6. stage wears the scene
        stage.setTitle("Demo");
        stage.show();                            // 7. show it — last
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) { launch(args); }
}
  1. extends Application is what makes this a JavaFX program; start is abstract there, so the compiler forces you to write it.
  2. main does one thing: launch(args). That starts the JavaFX runtime, which creates the primary Stage and calls start on the JavaFX application thread.
  3. Building the interface in main instead does not work — the toolkit is not running yet, and touching nodes off the FX thread is exactly the rule Swing has for its event thread.
  4. The nesting is fixed: Stage → Scene → root node → children. Forget the scene and the window opens empty.
  5. new Scene(root, 300, 200) sets the initial size in the same call. stage.show() is the JavaFX spelling of setVisible(true), and it goes last for the same reason.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the same window in Swing and in JavaFX, side by side
// ---------- Swing ----------
JFrame frame = new JFrame("Demo");
frame.setDefaultCloseOperation(JFrame.EXIT_ON_CLOSE);
JPanel root = new JPanel();
JButton b = new JButton("Click me");
b.addActionListener(e -> System.out.println("clicked"));   // ADDS a listener
root.add(b);
frame.add(root);
frame.setSize(300, 200);
frame.setVisible(true);

// ---------- JavaFX ----------
StackPane root2 = new StackPane();
Button b2 = new Button("Click me");
b2.setOnAction(e -> System.out.println("clicked"));        // SETS the handler
root2.getChildren().add(b2);                               // not root2.add(b2)
stage.setScene(new Scene(root2, 300, 200));
stage.show();
SwingJavaFXnote
JFrameStagethe window
content paneSceneJavaFX adds this extra level
JComponentNodeanything displayable
JPanela layout paneVBox, HBox, GridPane, BorderPane, StackPane
panel.add(c)pane.getChildren().add(c)children are a live list
addActionListenersetOnActionadds versus replaces
setVisible(true)stage.show()last line either way
  1. The structure is identical; the vocabulary is not. Most exam questions in this unit are that mapping.
  2. getChildren() returns a real ObservableList, so addAll, remove and clear all work on it — and the display updates as the list changes.
  3. setOnAction takes an EventHandler<ActionEvent>, a one-method interface, which is why a lambda fits.
  4. JavaFX has no EXIT_ON_CLOSE to forget: closing the last stage ends the application by default.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Building the interface in main is the mistake this structure invites, because every other Java program starts there. In JavaFX main only calls launch, which returns after the application exits; anything written after it runs at shutdown, not at startup. The related slip is pane.add(node) — layout panes have no such method; children go through pane.getChildren().add(node), except on BorderPane, where they go through setTop, setCenter and friends.

GridPane is the JavaFX equivalent of GridBagLayout (15.3), and it is considerably simpler: position is passed straight to add.

GridPane grid = new GridPane();
grid.setHgap(10);
grid.setVgap(10);
grid.setPadding(new Insets(20));

grid.add(new Label("Name:"),   0, 0);      // node, COLUMN, ROW
grid.add(new TextField(),      1, 0);
grid.add(new Button("Submit"), 1, 1);
grid.add(new Label("Wide"),    0, 2, 2, 1); // plus colSpan, rowSpan

The argument order is the trap: column first, then row — the opposite of the row-then-column convention used for 2D arrays in 5.9. Getting it backwards produces a layout that is transposed rather than broken, which makes it harder to spot.

The other JavaFX layout panes

GridPane is one of several, and the JavaFX names map onto the Swing ones from 15.9.

JavaFX paneArrangesSwing equivalent
BorderPanetop, bottom, left, right, centerBorderLayout
FlowPaneleft to right, wrappingFlowLayout
GridPanerows and columnsGridBagLayout
VBox / HBoxa single column / a single row—
StackPanechildren stacked on top of each other, centred—

BorderPane is the usual root for an application window: a menu bar in setTop, content in setCenter, a status bar in setBottom. As with BorderLayout, only the centre region grows.

GridPane g = new GridPane();
g.setHgap(10); g.setVgap(10);
g.add(node, 1, 0);                    // COLUMN first, then ROW
g.add(wide, 0, 2, 3, 1);              // col, row, colSpan, rowSpan

add(node, col, row) takes the column before the row — the opposite of the (row, column) order used for 2D arrays in 5.9, and the single most common JavaFX slip.

PaneArranges
GridPanea grid, with spanning
VBox / HBoxa vertical / horizontal stack — spacing via the constructor
BorderPanetop, bottom, left, right, center
StackPanechildren on top of one another, centred

Adding two nodes to the same grid cell overlays them rather than replacing — the opposite of Swing's BorderLayout, where the second add replaces the first. StackPane makes that overlay deliberate.

📘 DEFINITION

GridPane: a layout arranging nodes in rows and columns

add(node, col, row): column comes first, unlike array indexing

Hgap / Vgap: spacing between columns and rows

VBox / HBox: simpler panes stacking nodes vertically or horizontally

🎯 EXAM TIP

For a simple form, VBox and HBox nested inside each other are often clearer than a grid, and they need no coordinates at all.

📊 FIGURE — COLUMN-THEN-ROW: THE ONE ARGUMENT ORDER TO MEMORISE
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a login form on a grid, with a spanning row
GridPane grid = new GridPane();
grid.setHgap(10);                       // space BETWEEN columns
grid.setVgap(10);                       // space BETWEEN rows
grid.setPadding(new Insets(20));        // space AROUND the whole grid

Label userLabel = new Label("User:");
TextField userField = new TextField();
Label passLabel = new Label("Password:");
PasswordField passField = new PasswordField();
Button submit = new Button("Sign in");
Label message = new Label();

grid.add(userLabel,  0, 0);             // column 0, row 0
grid.add(userField,  1, 0);             // column 1, row 0 — same row
grid.add(passLabel,  0, 1);
grid.add(passField,  1, 1);
grid.add(submit,     1, 2);
grid.add(message,    0, 3, 2, 1);       // col, row, colSpan, rowSpan
  1. Rows and columns are created implicitly by the coordinates you use — there is no "new GridPane(4, 2)".
  2. The label and the field share row 0 because only the first argument differs. That is the shape of every form built this way.
  3. Hgap/Vgap separate cells from one another; padding insets the whole grid from the edge of its parent. Both at 0 is why an untuned grid looks cramped.
  4. The four-argument add extends the two-argument one: column, row, then how many columns and rows to span. message occupies both columns of row 3.
  5. PasswordField is a real control and behaves like a TextField with masked display; getText() still returns what was typed.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — when a grid is the wrong tool

Half the layouts that look like grids are simpler as nested boxes, which need no coordinates at all.

// a vertical stack of controls
VBox column = new VBox(10);                 // 10px spacing between children
column.getChildren().addAll(new Label("Filter:"), field, applyButton);

// a row of buttons
HBox buttons = new HBox(8);
buttons.getChildren().addAll(okButton, cancelButton);

// the usual application shell
BorderPane shell = new BorderPane();
shell.setTop(menuBar);
shell.setCenter(table);                      // only the CENTRE grows
shell.setBottom(statusLabel);
shell.setLeft(column);

// deliberate overlay: a label on top of an image
StackPane badge = new StackPane();
badge.getChildren().addAll(imageView, captionLabel);   // later = on top
  1. The VBox/HBox spacing is a constructor argument, and nesting one inside the other covers most real forms.
  2. BorderPane is the JavaFX BorderLayout: five regions, set by name, and only the centre absorbs extra space.
  3. Each BorderPane region holds exactly one node, so a region with several controls gets a VBox or HBox in it.
  4. StackPane layers its children in list order — the last added is drawn on top — which is what makes overlays deliberate rather than accidental.

JavaFX event handling is the listener pattern of 15.4 with a lambda-friendly interface, and the handler still runs when the user acts rather than in sequence.

Button b = new Button("Add");
TextField field = new TextField();
Label result = new Label();

b.setOnAction(e -> {
    try {
        int n = Integer.parseInt(field.getText());
        result.setText("doubled: " + (n * 2));
    } catch (NumberFormatException ex) {
        result.setText("enter a number");
    }
});

// reacting to every keystroke, not just to the button
field.textProperty().addListener((obs, oldVal, newVal) -> {
    result.setText("typing: " + newVal);
});

The second form is what JavaFX adds over Swing: properties that can be observed or bound, so a label can track a field without any handler at all. result.textProperty().bind(field.textProperty()) keeps them in step permanently.

button.setOnAction(e -> label.setText("clicked"));    // SETS the handler
button.setOnAction(e -> other());                     // REPLACES the first one

String choice = combo.getValue();                     // typed, not a String cast
field.clear();

slider.valueProperty().addListener((obs, oldV, newV) -> label.setText("" + newV));
label.textProperty().bind(field.textProperty());      // binding — no listener at all

setOnAction sets rather than adds, so a second call replaces the first — unlike Swing's addActionListener, which stacks them. A handler that has silently stopped working is usually a second setOnAction further down.

Properties are JavaFX's addition. A property can be observed with a listener, or bound so one value follows another automatically. A bound property cannot then be set directly — the binding owns it, and assigning throws.

📘 DEFINITION

setOnAction: registers the handler for the control’s primary action

Lambda handler: e -> { ... }, the standard form for a single-method interface

Property: an observable value that can notify listeners or be bound to another

Binding: declaring that one property always follows another

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Text still arrives as a String, so Integer.parseInt and NumberFormatException apply exactly as in 15.4. Nothing about JavaFX makes input validation unnecessary.

📊 FIGURE — HANDLERS, LISTENERS AND BINDINGS
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a button, a field, and the failure path
TextField field = new TextField();
Label result = new Label();
Button doubleIt = new Button("Double");

doubleIt.setOnAction(e -> {
    String text = field.getText().trim();
    if (text.isEmpty()) { result.setText("Enter a number"); return; }
    try {
        int n = Integer.parseInt(text);
        result.setText("doubled: " + (n * 2));
    } catch (NumberFormatException ex) {
        result.setText("\"" + text + "\" is not a whole number");
    }
    field.clear();
});
  1. setOnAction takes the handler for the control’s primary action — a click for a button, Enter for a text field.
  2. The body is identical to the Swing version in 15.4. Nothing about JavaFX makes parsing safe: getText() still returns a String.
  3. field.clear() is JavaFX’s setText(""), and it runs on both paths because it sits after the try-catch.
  4. A second setOnAction on the same button anywhere later in the file would silently delete this handler.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — watching a property, and binding one to another
// (a) a listener: react to every change, with old and new values
field.textProperty().addListener((obs, oldText, newText) -> {
    charCount.setText(newText.length() + " characters");
});

slider.valueProperty().addListener((obs, oldV, newV) -> {
    // newV is a Number, not a double
    readout.setText(String.format("%.0f%%", newV.doubleValue()));
});

// (b) a binding: no handler at all
mirror.textProperty().bind(field.textProperty());   // mirror always follows
mirror.textProperty().unbind();                     // release it before setting
  1. A property listener receives three things: the property itself, the previous value and the new one. Most handlers use only the third.
  2. It fires on every keystroke, which is what makes live character counts and search-as-you-type possible — and what makes expensive work in one a bad idea.
  3. valueProperty() on a slider hands you a Number, so doubleValue() or intValue() is needed before arithmetic.
  4. bind replaces the listener entirely: the target property is now computed from the source and updates itself.
  5. A bound property is read-only from then on — calling mirror.setText(...) throws until unbind() is called. That exception is the exam-worthy detail.
🎯 EXAM TIP

The three facts this section is tested on: setOnAction replaces (Swing’s addActionListener adds); a lambda works because EventHandler has a single method; and a bound property cannot be set directly. When a question shows two setOnAction calls on one button, the answer is that only the second one ever runs. Also watch the types: ComboBox.getValue() is generic and needs no cast, unlike Swing’s getSelectedItem(), which returns Object.

JavaFX graphics differ from Swing in a fundamental way: instead of overriding a paint method, you either add shape objects to the scene graph or draw onto a Canvas.

// shapes are nodes — they persist and can be changed later
Circle c = new Circle(50, 50, 30);
c.setFill(Color.BLUE);
Rectangle r = new Rectangle(10, 10, 100, 40);
Pane root = new Pane(c, r);

c.setCenterX(80);          // moves it — no repaint call needed

// canvas — immediate-mode drawing, closer to Swing
Canvas canvas = new Canvas(300, 200);
GraphicsContext g = canvas.getGraphicsContext2D();
g.setFill(Color.RED);
g.fillRect(10, 10, 50, 50);
g.strokeOval(70, 10, 50, 50);

With shape nodes there is no repaint() (15.1) — changing a property redraws automatically, because the shape is a live object rather than a set of drawing instructions. The coordinate system is unchanged: origin top left, y increasing downward.

Fill versus stroke

JavaFX separates the inside of a shape from its outline, and the two are set independently.

circle.setFill(Color.BLUE);          // the interior colour
circle.setStroke(Color.BLACK);       // the OUTLINE colour
circle.setStrokeWidth(3);            // outline thickness

g.setFill(...)   / g.fillRect(...)   // Canvas: filled shape
g.setStroke(...) / g.strokeRect(...) // Canvas: outline only

So fill is the interior and stroke is the outline. The same pair of words applies to shape nodes and to GraphicsContext drawing, and setting only the fill leaves a shape with no visible border.

Circle c = new Circle(50, 50, 20);          // centreX, centreY, RADIUS
Rectangle r = new Rectangle(10, 10, 100, 40);  // x, y, width, height
c.setFill(Color.BLUE);                         // the interior
c.setStroke(Color.BLACK);                      // the outline
pane.getChildren().add(c);

c.setCenterX(120);                             // moves it — no repaint call needed

This is retained mode: shapes are objects in the scene graph, and changing a property redraws automatically. Swing is immediate mode — you redraw everything inside paintComponent and call repaint() yourself. That difference is the point of the comparison.

A Circle takes a radius while Swing's fillOval takes a bounding box, so the same circle is new Circle(50, 50, 20) here and fillOval(30, 30, 40, 40) there. The origin is still top-left with y increasing downwards.

Because shapes persist, animation is a Timeline or TranslateTransition changing a property over time rather than a redraw loop.

📘 DEFINITION

Shape node: a Circle, Rectangle or Line that lives in the scene graph and can be modified

Canvas: a surface for immediate drawing via a GraphicsContext

GraphicsContext: the JavaFX equivalent of Swing’s Graphics object

Retained vs immediate mode: objects the toolkit redraws for you, versus instructions you issue once

🎯 EXAM TIP

Use shape nodes when things move or change — the toolkit handles redrawing. Use a Canvas for many static elements, where thousands of nodes would be wasteful.

📊 FIGURE — RETAINED MODE VERSUS IMMEDIATE MODE
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — shapes as objects: fill, stroke, and moving one later
Circle c = new Circle(50, 50, 20);          // centreX, centreY, RADIUS
c.setFill(Color.CORNFLOWERBLUE);            // the interior
c.setStroke(Color.BLACK);                   // the outline
c.setStrokeWidth(3);

Rectangle r = new Rectangle(10, 90, 100, 40);   // x, y, WIDTH, HEIGHT
r.setFill(Color.TRANSPARENT);               // outline only
r.setStroke(Color.web("#e8795a"));

Line axis = new Line(0, 140, 200, 140);

Pane root = new Pane();
root.getChildren().addAll(c, r, axis);

c.setCenterX(120);                          // moves it — nothing else to call
c.setRadius(28);
  1. A Circle takes a radius; Swing’s fillOval takes a bounding box. The same circle is new Circle(50, 50, 20) here and fillOval(30, 30, 40, 40) there — a genuine translation question.
  2. Rectangle keeps the position-then-size convention, so only the circle differs.
  3. Fill is the inside, stroke is the outline. A shape with a fill and no stroke has no border; Color.TRANSPARENT plus a stroke gives an outline-only shape.
  4. Pane is the layout pane that leaves children exactly where their coordinates put them — a VBox or StackPane would reposition them and the coordinates would be ignored.
  5. The last two lines run at any time afterwards and the display updates. That is retained mode: the shape is an object, not a past drawing instruction.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the same picture on a Canvas
Canvas canvas = new Canvas(300, 200);
GraphicsContext g = canvas.getGraphicsContext2D();

g.setFill(Color.CORNFLOWERBLUE);
g.fillOval(30, 30, 40, 40);          // x, y, w, h — a bounding box again
g.setStroke(Color.BLACK);
g.setLineWidth(3);
g.strokeOval(30, 30, 40, 40);        // outline over the fill
g.strokeRect(10, 90, 100, 40);
g.strokeLine(0, 140, 200, 140);
g.fillText("sample", 10, 170);

// to move the circle: erase and redraw everything
g.clearRect(0, 0, canvas.getWidth(), canvas.getHeight());
g.fillOval(100, 30, 40, 40);
  1. getGraphicsContext2D() is the JavaFX equivalent of Swing’s Graphics object, and the method names line up: fill… for solid, stroke… for outline.
  2. On a canvas fillOval uses a bounding box, so the same circle is written differently from the Circle node above — the distinction worth carrying out of this section.
  3. setFill and setStroke are sticky state: they apply to every later call until changed, unlike a shape node where each object carries its own.
  4. There is no way to move something already drawn. clearRect over the whole canvas and redraw is the only option — the smearing problem of 15.1, in JavaFX.
  5. A canvas is one node no matter how much is painted on it, which is why thousands of marks belong here and a handful of moving shapes belong in the scene graph.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Reaching for repaint() is the reflex Swing leaves behind, and no such method exists on a JavaFX node — changing a property is the redraw. The mirror-image mistake is expecting a Canvas to work the same way: setting a variable does nothing there, because the pixels have no memory of which call produced them. And watch the circle constructors: new Circle(50, 50, 20) is centre-and-radius, while g.fillOval(50, 50, 20, 20) is a corner and a size, so copying coordinates between the two forms draws the circle in the wrong place at half the size.

This unit is the first that asks not "does it work" but "how long does it take". Two search algorithms make the contrast, and the difference between them is the whole point of the unit.

// LINEAR SEARCH — works on ANY array
for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
    if (a[i] == target) { return i; }
}
return -1;
// worst case: n comparisons  ->  O(n)

// BINARY SEARCH — requires a SORTED array
// worst case: log2(n) comparisons  ->  O(log n)

On a million elements, linear search takes up to a million comparisons and binary search takes about twenty. That gap is why sorting is worth doing even when you only want to search: sort once, then search cheaply for ever after.

static int linearSearch(int[] a, int target) {
    for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++)
        if (a[i] == target) return i;
    return -1;                                   // not found
}

Linear search checks every element until it matches. Best case 1 comparison, worst case n, average about n/2 — all O(n). Its one advantage is that it needs no precondition: unsorted data, linked lists, anything traversable.

Return −1 for "not found", never 0, because 0 is a valid index. For objects use .equals rather than ==, or you are comparing references and will miss equal-but-distinct objects.

On a linked list linear search is still O(n) and is the only option — binary search needs indexed access, which a linked list cannot give in constant time.

📘 DEFINITION

Linear search: checking each element in turn; O(n); no precondition

Binary search: halving a sorted range; O(log n); requires sorted data

Best / average / worst case: the fewest, typical and most operations for an input of size n

Precondition: what must be true for an algorithm to be correct — sortedness, here

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

Every collection choice in Unit 14 was really this question. HashSet.contains is O(1) and ArrayList.contains is O(n), which is the same trade in a different costume.

📊 FIGURE — LINEAR SEARCH: ONE ELEMENT AT A TIME UNTIL IT MATCHES
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — counting the comparisons on real data

A depot has seven trucks and the loading system searches by weight. The counter is only there so the cost is visible; the search itself is the four lines you already know.

static int comparisons;

static int linearSearch(int[] a, int target) {
    for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
        comparisons++;
        if (a[i] == target) return i;      // leaves the moment it matches
    }
    return -1;                             // fell off the end: not present
}

int[] weights = { 1840, 920, 2310, 1475, 880, 2050, 1310 };

comparisons = 0;
System.out.println("1475 found at index " + linearSearch(weights, 1475)
                   + " after " + comparisons + " comparisons");
comparisons = 0;
System.out.println("1500 found at index " + linearSearch(weights, 1500)
                   + " after " + comparisons + " comparisons");
comparisons = 0;
linearSearch(weights, 1840);
System.out.println("best case (first element): " + comparisons + " comparison");
what it prints
1475 found at index 3 after 4 comparisons
1500 found at index -1 after 7 comparisons
best case (first element): 1 comparison
  1. 1475 sits at index 3, so the loop tested indices 0, 1, 2, 3 — four comparisons, one more than the index. Off-by-one answers on this are almost always that confusion.
  2. The miss costs seven: every element had to be ruled out before -1 could be returned. A failed linear search is always the worst case.
  3. The best case is one comparison, and it is pure luck — it depends on where the value happens to sit, not on the algorithm.
  4. All three are O(n). Big-O reports the worst case unless the question says otherwise, and 7, 4 and 1 all come from the same single loop over n elements.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — searching objects — where == quietly fails

Everything above used int, where == compares values. The moment the elements are objects, == compares references, and a value typed in by a user is a different object from the identical value in the array.

List<String> codes = new ArrayList<>(List.of("D286", "C959", "D287", "D426"));
System.out.println("indexOf(\"D287\") = " + codes.indexOf("D287"));
System.out.println("indexOf(\"D999\") = " + codes.indexOf("D999"));
System.out.println("contains(\"C959\") = " + codes.contains("C959"));

String typed = new String("D287");        // what a Scanner would hand you
System.out.println("typed == codes.get(2) : " + (typed == codes.get(2)));
System.out.println("typed.equals(codes.get(2)) : " + typed.equals(codes.get(2)));

String[] arr = { "D286", "C959", "D287" };
int found = -1;
for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) if (arr[i] == typed) { found = i; break; }
System.out.println("hand-written search using == : " + found);
found = -1;
for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) if (arr[i].equals(typed)) { found = i; break; }
System.out.println("hand-written search using equals : " + found);
what it prints
indexOf("D287") = 2
indexOf("D999") = -1
contains("C959") = true
typed == codes.get(2) : false
typed.equals(codes.get(2)) : true
hand-written search using == : -1
hand-written search using equals : 2
  1. indexOf returns the index or -1 — the same contract as the loop you would write by hand, which is why it is the right call in real code.
  2. typed == codes.get(2) is false even though both hold "D287": new String(...) forces a separate object, exactly as reading from a Scanner does.
  3. The two hand-written searches differ in one operator and return -1 and 2. The == version is not slower or less elegant — it is wrong, and it is wrong only for input that did not come from a literal.
  4. indexOf and contains use equals internally, which is why they found it.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Two errors here cost marks reliably. First, returning 0 for "not found" — 0 is a perfectly good index, so the caller cannot tell a hit at the front from a miss; the convention is -1, and the caller must test if (idx >= 0) rather than if (idx > 0), which silently rejects a match at index 0. Second, writing if (arr[i] == target) for objects: it compiles, it passes the test where the target is a literal, and it fails the moment the target is typed in.

🎯 EXAM TIP

The question is almost always "how many comparisons" or "which search can you use here". For comparisons: a hit at index k costs k+1, a miss costs n. For applicability: linear search needs nothing at all, binary search needs a sorted, index-addressable structure — so on a LinkedList, or on any unsorted array, linear search is not merely an option, it is the only one.

Binary search is worth being able to write and to trace, because it is on the exam in both forms. 11.3 gave the recursive version; this is the iterative one.

public static int bsearch(int[] a, int target) {
    int lo = 0, hi = a.length - 1;

    while (lo <= hi) {                      // <= not < : a single element must be checked
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;       // avoids overflow (2.16)

        if (a[mid] == target) { return mid; }
        if (a[mid] <  target) { lo = mid + 1; }
        else                  { hi = mid - 1; }
    }
    return -1;
}

Two details carry the correctness. lo <= hi rather than <, or a one-element range is never examined; and mid + 1 / mid - 1 rather than mid, or the range stops shrinking and the loop never ends.

static int binarySearch(int[] a, int target) {
    int lo = 0, hi = a.length - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {                       // <= , not <
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;        // overflow-safe
        if (a[mid] == target) return mid;
        if (a[mid] < target) lo = mid + 1;   // +1 / -1 guarantee progress
        else                 hi = mid - 1;
    }
    return -1;
}

Three details carry the marks. lo <= hi rather than <, or a one-element range is never examined. mid + 1 and mid - 1, or the range stops shrinking and the loop hangs. And lo + (hi - lo) / 2 rather than (lo + hi) / 2, which overflows int for very large arrays.

Halving gives O(log n): 1,000 elements in about 10 comparisons, a million in about 20, a billion in about 30. Each doubling of the data adds one comparison.

The precondition is that the array is sorted, and violating it fails silently — the search simply misses values that are present.

📘 DEFINITION

Search space: the lo..hi range still under consideration; halves each iteration

Midpoint calculation: lo + (hi - lo) / 2 rather than (lo + hi) / 2, to avoid overflow

Loop invariant: if the target is present it is always within lo..hi

Termination: the range shrinks every pass, so the loop must end

🎯 EXAM TIP

To trace one, write lo, mid and hi in three columns and add a row per pass. A 16-element array takes at most 5 rows, so the whole trace fits in the margin.

📊 FIGURE — BINARY SEARCH HALVES THE FIELD EVERY PROBE
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — every probe of a real search, with lo, mid and hi written down

Twelve stock levels, already sorted, and we want 47. The trace prints the three variables before each test so you can see the window closing.

int[] stock = { 4, 9, 15, 22, 28, 33, 41, 47, 55, 62, 70, 78 };

int lo = 0, hi = stock.length - 1;
while (lo <= hi) {
    int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
    System.out.println("  lo=" + lo + " hi=" + hi + " mid=" + mid + " a[mid]=" + stock[mid]);
    if (stock[mid] == 47) { System.out.println("result index: " + mid); break; }
    if (stock[mid] < 47) lo = mid + 1;
    else                 hi = mid - 1;
}
what it prints
  lo=0 hi=11 mid=5 a[mid]=33
  lo=6 hi=11 mid=8 a[mid]=55
  lo=6 hi=7 mid=6 a[mid]=41
  lo=7 hi=7 mid=7 a[mid]=47
result index: 7
  1. Probe 1: mid = 0 + (11−0)/2 = 5. Integer division truncates, so a window of twelve picks the lower middle. 33 < 47, so everything from index 0 to 5 is gone — lo = 6.
  2. Probe 2: mid = 6 + (11−6)/2 = 6 + 2 = 8. 55 > 47, so the top is gone — hi = 7.
  3. Probe 3: mid = 6 + (7−6)/2 = 6. 41 < 47, so lo = 7.
  4. Probe 4: lo == hi == 7, a one-element window. This is the probe that lo <= hi buys you; with < the loop would have exited here and reported "not found" on a value that is present.
  5. Four probes for twelve elements. Linear search would have taken eight.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a value that is absent, and what the library returns instead of −1
int[] stock = { 4, 9, 15, 22, 28, 33, 41, 47, 55, 62, 70, 78 };

// hand-written version, searching for 50
// probes: mid=5 (33), mid=8 (55), mid=6 (41), mid=7 (47) -> lo becomes 8, hi is 7
System.out.println("hand-written result: " + binarySearch(stock, 50));

System.out.println("present  47 -> " + Arrays.binarySearch(stock, 47));
System.out.println("absent   50 -> " + Arrays.binarySearch(stock, 50));
int r = Arrays.binarySearch(stock, 50);
System.out.println("insertion point = " + (-r - 1)
                   + "  (stock[" + (-r - 1) + "] = " + stock[-r - 1] + ")");

int[] messy = { 22, 4, 55, 15, 70, 9, 41 };      // NOT sorted
System.out.println("55 really is at index 2");
System.out.println("binarySearch says: " + binarySearch(messy, 55));
System.out.println("Arrays.binarySearch says: " + Arrays.binarySearch(messy, 55));
what it prints
hand-written result: -1
present  47 -> 7
absent   50 -> -9
insertion point = 8  (stock[8] = 55)
55 really is at index 2
binarySearch says: -1
Arrays.binarySearch says: -8
  1. The absent search runs the same four probes and then lo passes hi. The window is empty, the loop condition fails, and -1 comes back.
  2. Arrays.binarySearch agrees on the hit (index 7) but reports a miss as −(insertion point) − 1. Here -9 means "not found; it would belong at index 8".
  3. The formula to recover the insertion point is -r - 1: -(-9) - 1 = 8. That is where 50 would be inserted to keep the array sorted, which is genuinely useful and is why the method does not simply return -1.
  4. The last block is the section’s whole warning made concrete. 55 is in messy, at index 2, and both searches miss it — one says -1, the other says -8. Neither throws, neither complains. Unsorted input does not break binary search; it makes it lie.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

The three ways to write this loop wrong all look reasonable. while (lo < hi) skips the final one-element window, so values that happen to land there are reported missing. lo = mid instead of lo = mid + 1 makes the window stop shrinking once it is two wide, and the program hangs rather than crashes — an infinite loop, not an exception. And forgetting to sort first is the one with no symptom at all: the search returns -1 for a value sitting right there, and nothing in the output says why. If a binary search "sometimes works", check the sorting, not the search.

Big-O describes how the work grows as the input grows, ignoring constants and lower-order terms. It answers a question about scaling, not about seconds.

O(1)         constant     — array access, HashMap.get
O(log n)     logarithmic  — binary search, TreeSet operations
O(n)         linear       — one pass over an array
O(n log n)   linearithmic — merge sort, quicksort average, Collections.sort
O(n^2)       quadratic    — selection sort, insertion sort, nested loops
O(2^n)       exponential  — naive recursive Fibonacci (11.6)

n = 1,000,000:  O(log n) ~ 20    O(n) = 1,000,000    O(n^2) = 10^12

Constants are dropped because they do not change the shape of the growth: 3n + 100 is O(n), and so is n/2. The rule for reading code is to count nested loops — one loop over n is O(n), a loop inside a loop is O(n²), and halving each pass is O(log n).

Big-O describes how the work grows with the input, not how long it takes. Constants and lower-order terms are dropped because they do not change the shape of that growth: 3n + 5 is O(n), and n² + 100n is O(n²).

NotationNameTypical source
O(1)constantarray index, hash lookup
O(log n)logarithmicbinary search — halving
O(n)linearone loop over the data
O(n log n)linearithmicmerge sort, quicksort average
O(n²)quadraticnested loops over the same data
O(2ⁿ)exponentialnaive Fibonacci, all subsets

Two loops one after the other add — O(n) + O(n) = O(n). Two loops nested multiply — O(n) × O(n) = O(n²). That addition-versus-multiplication rule answers most analysis questions on its own.

A counter that doubles (i *= 2) runs about log₂n times, which is where the logarithm comes from in code that has no recursion in it.

📘 DEFINITION

Big-O: an upper bound on how the running time grows with input size

Constant factor: the multiplier Big-O deliberately ignores

Dominant term: the fastest-growing term, which is the only one kept

Space complexity: the same analysis applied to extra memory rather than time

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Two sequential loops are O(n) + O(n) = O(n), not O(n²). Only nesting multiplies. That distinction is the most common Big-O error.

📊 FIGURE — THE FIVE CURVES, DRAWN FROM THE ACTUAL FUNCTIONS
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — from an exact operation count to the O

Analysis is done in two moves: count the operations exactly, then throw away everything that does not grow fastest. Here the counting is done by the program so there is nothing to take on trust.

for (int n : new int[]{ 10, 20, 40 }) {
    int ops = 0;
    int[] a = new int[n];
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { a[i] = i; ops++; }        // n
    int sum = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { sum += a[i]; ops++; }     // n
    ops += 3;                                              // three constant lines
    System.out.println("n=" + n + "  operations = 2n+3 = " + ops);
}
what it prints
n=10  operations = 2n+3 = 23
n=20  operations = 2n+3 = 43
n=40  operations = 2n+3 = 83
  1. The exact count is 2n + 3: 23, 43, 83 for n = 10, 20, 40 — the arithmetic checks out.
  2. Drop the constant term: +3 is the same three operations whether n is 10 or ten million, so it cannot affect growth.
  3. Drop the coefficient: 2n and n both double when n doubles. Look at the numbers — 23 → 43 → 83 is not exactly doubling only because of that fading +3.
  4. What is left is O(n). Writing "O(2n + 3)" is not wrong arithmetic, it is the wrong notation: Big-O names a growth class, and 2n + 3 is in the class called n.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — side by side, nested, or doubling — three shapes from three loop headers
for (int n : new int[]{ 4, 8, 16 }) {
    int seq = 0, nested = 0, doubling = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) seq++;                 // O(n)
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) seq++;                 // + O(n)
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
        for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) nested++;          // O(n) x O(n)
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i *= 2) doubling++;         // i *= 2
    System.out.println("n=" + n + "  two loops in a row = " + seq
            + "   nested = " + nested + "   i *= 2 loop = " + doubling);
}
what it prints
n=4  two loops in a row = 8   nested = 16   i *= 2 loop = 2
n=8  two loops in a row = 16   nested = 64   i *= 2 loop = 3
n=16  two loops in a row = 32   nested = 256   i *= 2 loop = 4
  1. Two loops one after another add: 8, 16, 32 — doubling n doubles the work. O(n) + O(n) = O(2n) = O(n).
  2. Nested loops multiply: 16, 64, 256 — doubling n quadruples the work. That is the signature of O(n²) and you can read it straight off the numbers.
  3. The doubling counter runs 2, 3, 4 times as n goes 4, 8, 16. Each doubling of n adds exactly one pass. That is log₂n, and it is where a logarithm comes from in code with no recursion in it.
  4. The test is mechanical: double the input, look at what happens to the count. Same → O(1). +1 → O(log n). ×2 → O(n). ×4 → O(n²).
🎯 EXAM TIP

Read the loop headers and nothing else. A loop from 0 to n is n; two of them nested is n²; a loop whose counter multiplies is log n; a loop over a fixed range such as i < 100 is a constant no matter how large the data is. Then keep only the biggest term: n² + 100n + 5000 is O(n²), because for large n the n² term dwarfs everything. The classic wrong answer is O(n² + n) — correct arithmetic, wrong notation, no marks.

Analysing an algorithm means counting the operation that dominates, as a function of n, in the worst case.

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { }                 // n         -> O(n)

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) { }            // n * n     -> O(n^2)

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    for (int j = i; j < n; j++) { }            // n(n+1)/2  -> O(n^2) still

for (int i = 1; i < n; i *= 2) { }             // log2(n)   -> O(log n)

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    for (int j = 1; j < n; j *= 2) { }         // n * log n -> O(n log n)

The third example is the instructive one. Halving the work still leaves n²/2 operations, and dropping the constant gives O(n²) — a triangular nested loop is not in a better class than a square one, even though it genuinely does half the work.

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++)      // triangular, not square
        ...
// n-1 + n-2 + ... + 1  =  n(n-1)/2  ->  still O(n²)

A triangular nesting does half the work of a square one and is still O(n²), because the constant ½ drops out. Recognising that stops the common answer of O(n) for the inner loop "because it starts at i".

CaseMeansLinear search
bestthe luckiest inputO(1) — first element
averagetypical inputO(n)
worstthe unluckiest input — what Big-O usually reportsO(n)

Space complexity counts extra memory beyond the input. Selection and insertion sort are O(1) extra; merge sort needs O(n); recursion costs O(depth) in stack frames, which is why recursive binary search is O(log n) space and the loop version is O(1).

Watch for hidden costs. s += x inside a loop is O(n²) in character copies because each concatenation builds a new String — the loop looks linear and is not.

📘 DEFINITION

Basic operation: the operation being counted, usually a comparison or a swap

Worst case: the input maximising the work; the default meaning of an O() claim

Amortised analysis: the average over a sequence, as with ArrayList growth (7.16)

🎯 EXAM TIP

Read the loop bounds, not the body. A loop multiplying its variable is logarithmic; a loop adding to it is linear. That single observation classifies most exam code.

📊 FIGURE — A TRIANGULAR NESTING IS HALF A SQUARE ONE — AND STILL QUADRATIC
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the half-square loop, counted rather than guessed
for (int n : new int[]{ 6, 10, 100 }) {
    int inner = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++)      // starts at i+1, not 0
            inner++;
    System.out.println("n=" + n + "  inner body ran " + inner
            + " times;  n(n-1)/2 = " + (n * (n - 1) / 2)
            + ";  full square n*n = " + (n * n));
}
what it prints
n=6  inner body ran 15 times;  n(n-1)/2 = 15;  full square n*n = 36
n=10  inner body ran 45 times;  n(n-1)/2 = 45;  full square n*n = 100
n=100  inner body ran 4950 times;  n(n-1)/2 = 4950;  full square n*n = 10000
  1. For n = 6 the inner loop runs 5, then 4, then 3, 2, 1, 0 times: 15 in total, matching n(n−1)/2 exactly.
  2. Compare 15 against 36 and it looks like a real saving. Now compare n = 100: 4,950 against 10,000 — the ratio is still about a half, and it always will be.
  3. Growth is what matters: from n = 10 to n = 100 the count goes 45 → 4,950, roughly ×110 for a ×10 in n. That is quadratic behaviour, ½ or no ½.
  4. So the answer is O(n²). "O(n) because the inner loop starts at i" is the standard wrong answer, and the numbers above are the fastest way to see why.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the loop that looks linear and is not

Every line of this loop is O(1) to look at, so the whole thing reads as O(n). It is O(n²), because s += "x" builds a whole new String each time — the old text is copied character by character.

for (int n : new int[]{ 100, 200, 400 }) {
    String s = "";
    long copied = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        copied += s.length() + 1;    // the old text is copied, then one char added
        s += "x";
    }
    System.out.println("n=" + n + "  characters copied = " + copied
            + "   (n(n+1)/2 = " + ((long) n * (n + 1) / 2) + ")"
            + "   final length = " + s.length());
}
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for (int i = 0; i < 400; i++) sb.append("x");
System.out.println("StringBuilder: 400 appends, length " + sb.length()
                   + ", each append copies 1 character");
what it prints
n=100  characters copied = 5050   (n(n+1)/2 = 5050)   final length = 100
n=200  characters copied = 20100   (n(n+1)/2 = 20100)   final length = 200
n=400  characters copied = 80200   (n(n+1)/2 = 80200)   final length = 400
StringBuilder: 400 appends, length 400, each append copies 1 character
  1. Doubling n from 100 to 200 takes the copying from 5,050 to 20,100 — four times the work for twice the input. Quadratic, from a loop with one statement in it.
  2. The final string is only 400 characters long, but producing it copied 80,200. The visible result is linear; the hidden cost is not.
  3. The cause is immutability: a String cannot be extended, so s += "x" allocates a new one and copies the old contents in.
  4. StringBuilder keeps a growable buffer and appends in place, so 400 appends copy 400 characters — O(n). Any loop that concatenates onto a String should be a StringBuilder.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Two traps sit next to each other. The first is reading nesting as multiplication without checking what the inner loop actually depends on: for (j = 0; j < 10; j++) inside a loop over n is O(10n) = O(n), not O(n²), because 10 does not grow. The second is counting only what you can see — a contains() on a list inside a loop over the same list is O(n²), and s += x in a loop is O(n²), even though each is written on one line. Ask what the call does, not how long the line is.

Sorting is the most-studied problem in this course, and the algorithms split cleanly into two groups by their cost.

O(n^2)  — simple, fine for small n
    selection sort   17.6
    insertion sort   17.7
    bubble sort

O(n log n) — what real libraries use
    merge sort       17.9   — stable, needs O(n) extra space
    quicksort        17.8   — in place, O(n^2) worst case
    Collections.sort / Arrays.sort

Two properties beyond speed decide which one is chosen in practice. Stability means equal elements keep their original relative order, which matters when you sort by one field after another. In-place means the algorithm needs no significant extra memory.

PropertyMeansMatters when
stableequal elements keep their original ordersorting by a second key after a first
in placeO(1) extra memorythe data is large
adaptivefaster on nearly-sorted inputdata arrives mostly ordered

Stability is what lets you sort by name, then by grade, and still have equal grades in name order. An unstable sort scrambles the first ordering as it applies the second.

Arrays.sort(intArray);                       // primitives: dual-pivot quicksort
Collections.sort(list);                      // objects: Timsort, STABLE
list.sort(Comparator.comparing(Student::getName).reversed());

Java sorts primitives with quicksort (unstable, but primitives are indistinguishable so it cannot matter) and objects with a stable merge-based sort — a deliberate choice, not an accident.

No comparison sort can beat O(n log n) in the worst case; that is a proven lower bound, which is why the good sorts all cluster there.

📘 DEFINITION

Sorting: arranging elements according to an ordering, usually compareTo (13.5)

Stable sort: preserves the relative order of equal elements

In-place sort: uses O(1) extra space beyond the input array

Comparison sort: any sort based on comparing pairs; O(n log n) is the theoretical floor

🎯 EXAM TIP

In real code you call Arrays.sort or Collections.sort. The algorithms here are taught because the exam asks you to trace them and to state their complexity.

📊 FIGURE — WHAT STABILITY ACTUALLY BUYS YOU
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — sorting twice to sort by two keys

Five runners. Sort by name, then by time. If the sort is stable, runners on the same time come out in name order without anyone asking for it.

record Runner(String name, String club, int minutes) {
    public String toString(){ return name + "/" + club + "/" + minutes; }
}

List<Runner> field = new ArrayList<>(List.of(
    new Runner("Okafor", "Harriers", 42),
    new Runner("Baptiste", "Striders", 39),
    new Runner("Lindqvist", "Harriers", 42),
    new Runner("Nakamura", "Striders", 39),
    new Runner("Alvarez", "Pacers", 45)));

field.sort(Comparator.comparing(Runner::name));
System.out.println("by name:   " + field);
field.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(Runner::minutes));
System.out.println("by time:   " + field);
what it prints
by name:   [Alvarez/Pacers/45, Baptiste/Striders/39, Lindqvist/Harriers/42, Nakamura/Striders/39, Okafor/Harriers/42]
by time:   [Baptiste/Striders/39, Nakamura/Striders/39, Lindqvist/Harriers/42, Okafor/Harriers/42, Alvarez/Pacers/45]
  1. After the first sort the list is alphabetical. Nothing surprising yet.
  2. The second sort compares only minutes. Baptiste and Nakamura are both 39, so as far as this comparator is concerned they are equal.
  3. They come out Baptiste then Nakamura — alphabetical — because List.sort is stable and refuses to reorder elements it considers equal. Lindqvist before Okafor, on 42, is the same effect.
  4. The rule to remember: sort by the secondary key first, then by the primary. It reads backwards and it is correct.

The same result in a single pass, which is what you would normally write:

again.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(Runner::minutes).thenComparing(Runner::name));
System.out.println("one pass:  " + again);
System.out.println("equal?     " + again.equals(field));
what it prints
one pass:  [Baptiste/Striders/39, Nakamura/Striders/39, Lindqvist/Harriers/42, Okafor/Harriers/42, Alvarez/Pacers/45]
equal?     true
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the library calls, and where reversed() attaches
int[] nums = { 34, 7, 23, 32, 5, 62 };
Arrays.sort(nums);
System.out.println("Arrays.sort(int[]):   " + Arrays.toString(nums));

Selection sort repeatedly finds the smallest remaining element and swaps it into place. It is the easiest to trace, and its cost never changes with the input.

for (int i = 0; i < a.length - 1; i++) {
    int minIdx = i;
    for (int j = i + 1; j < a.length; j++) {       // find the smallest in the rest
        if (a[j] < a[minIdx]) { minIdx = j; }
    }
    int temp = a[i]; a[i] = a[minIdx]; a[minIdx] = temp;   // swap (5.6)
}

// {5, 2, 9, 1}
// i=0: min is 1 -> {1, 2, 9, 5}
// i=1: min is 2 -> {1, 2, 9, 5}   (swaps with itself)
// i=2: min is 5 -> {1, 2, 5, 9}

It performs the same n(n+1)/2 comparisons whether the array is already sorted or completely reversed — best case equals worst case equals O(n²). What it minimises instead is swaps: exactly n-1, which mattered historically when writing was expensive.

for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
    int min = i;
    for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++)
        if (a[j] < a[min]) min = j;          // find the smallest remaining
    swap(a, i, min);                         // ONE swap per pass
}

Selection sort finds the smallest remaining element and puts it in place. After k passes the first k positions hold the k smallest values, finished and never touched again.

It is O(n²) in every case — best, average and worst — because the inner loop always scans the whole remainder regardless of the data. It is not adaptive: already-sorted input takes exactly as long.

Its one distinction is the swap count: at most n − 1 swaps, one per pass, far fewer than bubble sort. That matters only when a swap is expensive. It is not stable, because the long-distance swap can jump an equal element over another.

📘 DEFINITION

Selection sort: repeatedly select the minimum of the unsorted part and swap it into place

Sorted prefix: the front of the array, already in final position after pass i

Swap count: n-1, the fewest of any simple sort

Unstable: a long-distance swap can reorder equal elements

🎯 EXAM TIP

Trace questions usually ask for the array after k passes. After pass k, the first k+1 elements are in their final sorted positions — you do not need to trace the rest.

Selection sort, one frozen prefix at a time. Each pass scans the UNSORTED part for its minimum and swaps it to the front of that part; the bold prefix never moves again:

start29  10  14  37  13
110  29  14  37  13min of ALL five (10) swaps into index 0
210  13  14  37  29min of the last four (13) swaps into index 1
310  13  14  37  2914 already in place — swap with itself
410  13  14  29  37min of the last two (29) swaps into index 3
🎯 EXAM TIP
n elements need n−1 passes, and pass counting is the OA’s favourite: after pass k, the first k slots hold the k smallest values in final position. Selection sort does the same work even on sorted input — O(n²) always — while insertion sort on sorted input is O(n).

int[] temps = { 71, 64, 88, 59, 77, 62 };

    int min = i;
    for (int j = i + 1; j < temps.length; j++)
        if (temps[j] < temps[min]) min = j;
    int t = temps[i]; temps[i] = temps[min]; temps[min] = t;
    System.out.println("pass " + (i + 1) + ": smallest of the rest is " + temps[i]

The claim "O(n²) in every case" is easy to say and easy to doubt. Counting settles it.

int[][] inputs = {

    { 60, 50, 40, 30, 20, 10 },      // reverse sorted

  2. Five swaps every time: one per pass, whether or not anything needed moving. That is the algorithm’s one genuine virtue — at most n−1 swaps, which matters when a swap is expensive.
  3. Already-sorted input costs exactly as much as reverse-sorted. Selection sort is not adaptive, which is the sharpest contrast with insertion sort in the next section.
  4. Best = average = worst = O(n²). It is the only sort in this unit where all three are the same, and exam questions lean on that.

Three specific slips. Forgetting int min = i; at the top of each pass carries the previous pass’s index forward and corrupts the array. Insertion sort takes each element and slides it back into the sorted portion, the way you sort a hand of cards. Unlike selection sort, its cost depends heavily on the input.

for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++) {
    int key = a[i];
    int j = i - 1;
    while (j >= 0 && a[j] > key) {       // shift larger elements right
        a[j + 1] = a[j];
        j--;
    }
    a[j + 1] = key;                       // drop the key into the gap
}

On already-sorted data the inner while never runs, so the whole thing is O(n) — the best case of any comparison sort. On reversed data it shifts everything every time, giving O(n²). That adaptivity is why real library sorts fall back to insertion sort for small or nearly-sorted segments.

for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {            // starts at 1 — a[0] is sorted alone
    int key = a[i], j = i - 1;
    while (j >= 0 && a[j] > key) {       // j >= 0 FIRST — short-circuit matters
        a[j + 1] = a[j];                 // shift right
        j--;
    }
    a[j + 1] = key;                      // drop it into the gap
}

Insertion sort grows a sorted region at the front, taking each next element and shifting larger ones right to make room. It is what people actually do with a hand of cards.

Unlike selection sort it is adaptive: on already-sorted input the inner while never runs, giving O(n) best case, against O(n²) worst. That is why it is the algorithm real libraries switch to for small or nearly-sorted subarrays.

The condition order is not stylistic. j >= 0 must come first so short-circuit evaluation stops before a[j] is read with j == -1 — the exact mechanism from 1.3, with an out-of-bounds crash as the penalty for reversing it.

It is stable, because it shifts only elements strictly greater than the key.

📘 DEFINITION

Insertion sort: insert each element into its place in the already-sorted prefix

Best case O(n): sorted input; each element is already in position

Adaptive: runs faster on partially sorted input

Stable: the strict > comparison never moves an equal element past another

🎯 EXAM TIP

Selection sort versus insertion sort is a standard compare-and-contrast question. Both are O(n²) worst case; only insertion sort is O(n) at best, and only insertion sort is stable.

📊 FIGURE — INSERTION SORT: ONE PASS, IN THREE STAGES
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — jersey numbers, one insertion at a time
int[] jerseys = { 23, 8, 41, 15, 4, 16 };

for (int i = 1; i < jerseys.length; i++) {        // starts at 1
    int key = jerseys[i], j = i - 1;
    while (j >= 0 && jerseys[j] > key) { jerseys[j + 1] = jerseys[j]; j--; }
    jerseys[j + 1] = key;
    System.out.println("i=" + i + " key=" + key + " -> " + Arrays.toString(jerseys)
            + "   sorted prefix: "
            + Arrays.toString(Arrays.copyOfRange(jerseys, 0, i + 1)));
}
what it prints
i=1 key=8 -> [8, 23, 41, 15, 4, 16]   sorted prefix: [8, 23]
i=2 key=41 -> [8, 23, 41, 15, 4, 16]   sorted prefix: [8, 23, 41]
i=3 key=15 -> [8, 15, 23, 41, 4, 16]   sorted prefix: [8, 15, 23, 41]
i=4 key=4 -> [4, 8, 15, 23, 41, 16]   sorted prefix: [4, 8, 15, 23, 41]
i=5 key=16 -> [4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 41]   sorted prefix: [4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 41]
  1. The loop starts at i = 1 because a single element is already a sorted list of one — there is nothing for i = 0 to do.
  2. At i = 2 the key is 41 and the neighbour 23 is smaller, so the while body never runs and the array is unchanged. Zero shifts for an element already in order.
  3. At i = 3 the key 15 walks past 41 and 23, shifting each one right, and lands between 8 and 23. Two shifts.
  4. At i = 4 the key 4 walks all the way to the front — four shifts, the most expensive insertion here.
  5. Watch the prefix in the right-hand column: sorted at every step, and growing by one each pass. Unlike selection sort, its contents keep changing — 23 was in the prefix at i=1 and is still being pushed around at i=4.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — why libraries switch to insertion sort for small runs
int[][] inputs = {
    { 4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 41 },      // already sorted
    { 41, 23, 16, 15, 8, 4 },      // reverse sorted
    { 23, 8, 41, 15, 4, 16 }       // shuffled
};
String[] labels = { "already sorted", "reverse sorted", "shuffled" };
for (int k = 0; k < inputs.length; k++) {
    shifts = 0;
    insertionSort(inputs[k].clone());   // counting every a[j + 1] = a[j]
    System.out.println(labels[k] + ": elements shifted " + shifts);
}
what it prints
already sorted: elements shifted 0
reverse sorted: elements shifted 15
shuffled: elements shifted 9
  1. Already sorted costs zero shifts. Every key is bigger than its left neighbour, so the while condition fails immediately and the pass is a single comparison — the whole sort is O(n).
  2. Reverse sorted costs 15 = n(n−1)/2: every key has to travel to the front. That is the O(n²) worst case.
  3. Shuffled sits between them at 9. The work is proportional to how out of order the data actually is, which is the definition of adaptive.
  4. Compare with selection sort’s 15 comparisons on all three inputs. This difference — not the Big-O, which is the same — is why real library sorts fall back to insertion sort on small or nearly-ordered runs.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Swap the two halves of the while condition and the sort crashes. while (a[j] > key && j >= 0) reads a[-1] as soon as a key belongs at the front, and Java confirms it: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index -1 out of bounds for length 2. The guard must come first so && short-circuits before the array is touched. The other slip is writing a[j] = key at the end instead of a[j + 1] = key — the loop leaves j one position past the gap, and using it directly overwrites a value you just shifted.

Quicksort partitions around a pivot: smaller elements to the left, larger to the right, then sorts each side recursively. The partition step is what does the work, and the recursion just repeats it.

void quicksort(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
    if (lo >= hi) { return; }              // base case (11.1)
    int p = partition(a, lo, hi);
    quicksort(a, lo, p - 1);
    quicksort(a, p + 1, hi);
}

int partition(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
    int pivot = a[hi];
    int i = lo - 1;
    for (int j = lo; j < hi; j++) {
        if (a[j] < pivot) { i++; swap(a, i, j); }
    }
    swap(a, i + 1, hi);
    return i + 1;                          // the pivot’s final position
}

Average case is O(n log n) and in place. The worst case is O(n²), and it happens on already-sorted data with a last-element pivot — every partition puts nothing on one side. Choosing a random or median pivot is the standard defence.

static void quicksort(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
    if (lo >= hi) return;                     // base case
    int p = partition(a, lo, hi);             // the WORK happens here, before
    quicksort(a, lo, p - 1);
    quicksort(a, p + 1, hi);                  // p is already in its final place
}

Choose a pivot, partition so everything smaller is left of it and everything larger is right, then recurse on the two sides. The pivot lands in its final position immediately and is excluded from both recursive calls — which is what guarantees progress.

Average O(n log n) and in place with O(log n) stack. Worst case O(n²), and the input that triggers it is the surprising one: already sorted data with a first-or-last pivot, which splits off one element at a time. Random or median-of-three pivot selection is the standard defence.

Quicksort does its work before recursing; merge sort does it after. That one sentence separates them, and it is the usual exam question.

It is not stable.

📘 DEFINITION

Quicksort: partition around a pivot, then sort each side recursively

Pivot: the element everything is compared against

Partition: rearranging so smaller elements precede the pivot and larger follow it

Worst case O(n²): consistently unbalanced partitions, as with sorted input and a poor pivot

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Quicksort being "fastest" is only true on average. Its worst case is the same as selection sort’s, and the input that triggers it — sorted data — is common in practice.

📊 FIGURE — PARTITION: THE PIVOT FINDS ITS FINAL SLOT IN ONE PASS
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — one partition, every comparison shown

Lomuto partitioning with the last element as pivot. i marks the end of the "small" region; j is the scan.

static int partition(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
    int pivot = a[hi];
    int i = lo - 1;
    for (int j = lo; j < hi; j++) {
        if (a[j] <= pivot) { i++; swap(a, i, j); }
    }
    swap(a, i + 1, hi);          // the pivot into its final slot
    return i + 1;
}

int[] a = { 38, 12, 55, 27, 44, 19, 31 };
quicksort(a, 0, a.length - 1);   // trace printed below

quicksort on [38, 12, 55, 27, 44, 19, 31]  pivot = 31

   j=1  12 <= 31  -> swap it into slot 0   [12, 38, 55, 27, 44, 19, 31]
   j=2  55 >  31  -> leave it       [12, 38, 55, 27, 44, 19, 31]
   j=3  27 <= 31  -> swap it into slot 1   [12, 27, 55, 38, 44, 19, 31]
   j=4  44 >  31  -> leave it       [12, 27, 55, 38, 44, 19, 31]
   j=5  19 <= 31  -> swap it into slot 2   [12, 27, 19, 38, 44, 55, 31]
   pivot 31 swaps into slot 3  [12, 27, 19, 31, 44, 55, 38]
   -> 31 is now final at index 3; recurse on [12, 27, 19] and [44, 55, 38]
  1. Each "≤ pivot" element is swapped to i+1, immediately after the small region. The value that was sitting there is thrown into the scanned-and-larger area — which is fine, because it is already known to be larger.
  2. Notice the left region is [12, 27, 19]: not sorted. Partitioning only promises "all ≤ pivot", never any order within.
  3. The final swap puts 31 at index 3, and 31 is now in its permanent position. It will never be looked at again.
  4. The two recursive calls take lo..p-1 and p+1..hi. Excluding p is what shrinks the problem; including it would recurse forever on a one-element range.
  5. Sorting the whole array took 11 comparisons here, against 21 for selection sort on seven elements.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the input that turns O(n log n) into O(n²)

The bad case for quicksort is the one nobody expects: data that is already sorted, when the pivot is the first or last element.

int[][] inputs = {
    { 38, 12, 55, 27, 44, 19, 31, 60 },   // shuffled
    { 12, 19, 27, 31, 38, 44, 55, 60 },   // already sorted
    { 60, 55, 44, 38, 31, 27, 19, 12 }    // reverse sorted
};
String[] labels = { "shuffled      ", "already sorted", "reverse sorted" };
for (int k = 0; k < inputs.length; k++) {
    comps = 0; maxDepth = 0;
    quicksort(inputs[k].clone(), 0, inputs[k].length - 1);
    System.out.println(labels[k] + ": comparisons " + comps

shuffled      : comparisons 18, recursion depth 5
already sorted: comparisons 28, recursion depth 8
reverse sorted: comparisons 28, recursion depth 8

  2. The comparison count is 28 — exactly n(n−1)/2 for n = 8, the same as selection sort. The recursion depth is 8, one frame per element, which is how quicksort turns into a stack overflow on large sorted arrays.
  3. The shuffled case needs 18 comparisons and depth 5. That is the O(n log n) behaviour quicksort is famous for.
  4. The defence is pivot choice, not a different algorithm: median-of-three, or a random index swapped to the end before partitioning. Java’s Arrays.sort for primitives uses dual-pivot quicksort with exactly this kind of protection.
🎯 EXAM TIP

Two questions come up again and again. "Where does the work happen?" — quicksort partitions before recursing, merge sort merges after; that single sentence answers most compare-and-contrast items. "After one partition, which element is definitely in its final position?" — the pivot, and only the pivot. Nothing else on either side is known to be placed, and an option claiming the left side is sorted is the distractor.

Merge sort splits the array in half, sorts each half recursively and merges the two sorted halves. It is the algorithm whose complexity never varies.

void mergeSort(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
    if (lo >= hi) { return; }
    int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
    mergeSort(a, lo, mid);
    mergeSort(a, mid + 1, hi);
    merge(a, lo, mid, hi);                // combine two sorted halves
}

// merging {1,5,9} and {2,3,8}: compare the fronts, take the smaller, repeat
// -> 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 9

It is O(n log n) in every case — best, average and worst — because the splitting is always even. The price is O(n) extra space for the merge, which is the one thing quicksort does not need. It is also stable, which is why Collections.sort uses a variant of it for objects.

static void mergeSort(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
    if (lo >= hi) return;                     // base case: 0 or 1 element
    int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
    mergeSort(a, lo, mid);
    mergeSort(a, mid + 1, hi);
    merge(a, lo, mid, hi);                    // the WORK happens here, after
}

Split in half, sort each half, then merge two sorted halves in one linear pass. The merge is where everything happens, and it is why the recursion has to complete first.

O(n log n) in all cases — the split is always even, so there is no bad input. That guarantee is what you buy with its one real cost: O(n) extra memory for the temporary array, unlike quicksort's in-place partitioning.

It is stable, provided the merge takes from the left half when values are equal, which is exactly why Java uses a merge-based sort for objects where stability is observable.

Choosing between them: merge sort when you need a guarantee or stability, quicksort when memory is tight and the average case is good enough.

📘 DEFINITION

Merge sort: divide in half, sort each half, merge the sorted halves

Merge step: combining two sorted sequences by repeatedly taking the smaller front element

Guaranteed O(n log n): the split is always even, so the depth is always log n

Space O(n): a temporary array is required for merging

🎯 EXAM TIP

Merge sort versus quicksort in one line: merge sort guarantees O(n log n) but needs extra memory; quicksort sorts in place but can degrade to O(n²).

📊 FIGURE — MERGE SORT: SPLIT DOWN, MERGE UP
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the merge itself — one comparison decides one element

Splitting is trivial; everything interesting is in the merge. Two already-sorted halves, one finger on the front of each, and the smaller front element is taken.

// after both halves are sorted:  [8, 14, 26, 33]  and  [5, 19, 30, 41]
int i = lo, j = mid + 1, k = 0;
int[] tmp = new int[hi - lo + 1];
while (i <= mid && j <= hi) {
    if (a[i] <= a[j]) tmp[k++] = a[i++];      // <= keeps it STABLE
    else              tmp[k++] = a[j++];
}
while (i <= mid) tmp[k++] = a[i++];           // drain whatever is left
while (j <= hi)  tmp[k++] = a[j++];
for (int t = 0; t < tmp.length; t++) a[lo + t] = tmp[t];
the trace of that final merge
merge [8, 14, 26, 33] with [5, 19, 30, 41]
   8 >  5  take 5 from the right
   8 <= 19  take 8 from the LEFT
   14 <= 19  take 14 from the LEFT
   26 >  19  take 19 from the right
   26 <= 30  take 26 from the LEFT
   33 >  30  take 30 from the right
   33 <= 41  take 33 from the LEFT
   left half empty, take 41 from the right
   merged: [5, 8, 14, 19, 26, 30, 33, 41]
  1. Eight elements came out of seven comparisons. The last element needs none — once one half is exhausted, the rest of the other half is copied straight across.
  2. Only the two front elements are ever compared. Each half is already sorted, so whichever front is smaller is smaller than everything remaining.
  3. The drain loops at the end are not optional. Leave them out and the tail of the longer half is silently lost.
  4. The merge cannot be done in place with an array, which is where the O(n) extra memory comes from — the one real cost of merge sort.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the same work on every input, and the extra memory it costs
int[][] inputs = {
    { 5, 8, 14, 19, 26, 30, 33, 41 },     // already sorted
    { 41, 33, 30, 26, 19, 14, 8, 5 },     // reverse sorted
    { 26, 14, 33, 8, 41, 19, 5, 30 }      // shuffled
};
String[] labels = { "already sorted", "reverse sorted", "shuffled      " };
for (int k = 0; k < inputs.length; k++) {
    comps = 0; copies = 0;
    mergeSort(inputs[k].clone(), 0, inputs[k].length - 1);
    System.out.println(labels[k] + ": comparisons " + comps
            + ", elements copied into temporary arrays " + copies);
}
what it prints
already sorted: comparisons 12, elements copied into temporary arrays 24
reverse sorted: comparisons 12, elements copied into temporary arrays 24
shuffled      : comparisons 17, elements copied into temporary arrays 24

  2. 8 = 2³, so log₂8 = 3 levels. Each level does n copies. n × log n = 8 × 3 = 24 — the Big-O is not an estimate here, it is the arithmetic.
  3. Comparisons vary a little (12 against 17) because a sorted or reverse-sorted half runs out early and the drain loop finishes the job for free. Sorting is still O(n log n); the variation is a constant factor.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Two mistakes in the merge, both of which produce output that looks nearly right. Writing if (a[i] < a[j]) instead of <= takes the right-hand element on a tie and destroys stability — the array is still correctly sorted, so nothing looks broken until a second sort key reveals scrambled ties. And allocating the temporary array inside the merge is normal, but copying it back with the wrong offset — a[t] = tmp[t] rather than a[lo + t] = tmp[t] — writes every merged block to the front of the array, which corrupts the data quietly on every call except the first.
