This unit is conceptual rather than syntactic, and the exam treats it that way: it asks what a term means and what a technique is for, not for code. Artificial intelligence is the umbrella — systems performing tasks that normally require human intelligence — and the terms nest inside one another.

AI
 └── Machine Learning         — learns patterns from data instead of being programmed
      └── Deep Learning       — neural networks with many layers
           └── Generative AI  — produces new content
                └── LLMs      — generative models specialised for language

The distinction that matters most is rule-based versus learned. A rule-based system does exactly what a programmer wrote; a machine-learning system infers its behaviour from examples, which is why it can handle inputs nobody anticipated and why it can be confidently wrong.

TermIs
AIthe broad field — machines doing things that need intelligence
Machine learninga subset: behaviour learned from data rather than written as rules
Deep learninga subset of ML using many-layered neural networks

The nesting — AI ⊃ ML ⊃ deep learning — is the most-asked fact in this unit. The distinction that matters is where the behaviour comes from: a rule-based system does what a programmer wrote; a learned system infers it from examples.

Learning typeDataExample
supervisedlabelledspam / not spam from tagged mail
unsupervisedunlabelledclustering customers into groups
reinforcementreward signallearning a game by playing it

Rules remain better where the logic is known, must be exact and must be explainable — tax calculation, not image recognition. Learned systems are hard to explain, which is a real cost wherever a decision must be justified.

📘 DEFINITION

Artificial intelligence: systems performing tasks normally requiring human intelligence

Machine learning: inferring behaviour from data rather than from explicit rules

Training data: the examples a model learns from

Model: the learned function that maps an input to an output

Inference: using a trained model to produce an output for a new input

🎯 EXAM TIP

Get the nesting right and most questions in this unit answer themselves: every LLM is generative AI, all generative AI is machine learning, and all machine learning is AI — none of it works in reverse.

📊 FIGURE — AI ⊃ MACHINE LEARNING ⊃ DEEP LEARNING
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the same decision, once written and once learned

A property system has to label a listing "large" or "small". Written as rules, a person decides the thresholds. Learned from data, nobody writes a threshold at all — the program computes the centre of each labelled group and asks which centre a new listing is nearer to.

// the rule-based way: a human writes the logic
static String ruleBased(double area, int bedrooms) {
    if (area >= 2200 || bedrooms >= 4) return "large";
    return "small";
}

// the learned way: the logic comes from labelled examples
double[][] largeExamples = { {2400,4}, {2800,5}, {2250,4}, {3100,5} };
double[][] smallExamples = { {900,2}, {1150,2}, {1400,3}, {1050,1} };
double[] cLarge = centroid(largeExamples);      // the centre of each group
double[] cSmall = centroid(smallExamples);
// classify by whichever centre is nearer

double[][] tests = { {2600,4}, {1000,2}, {2300,2}, {1900,3} };
what it prints
centre of the LARGE examples: 2638 sq ft, 4.50 bedrooms
centre of the SMALL examples: 1125 sq ft, 2.00 bedrooms
2600 sq ft, 4 bed -> rules say large | learned says large
1000 sq ft, 2 bed -> rules say small | learned says small
2300 sq ft, 2 bed -> rules say large | learned says small
1900 sq ft, 3 bed -> rules say small | learned says small
  1. Nobody wrote 2638 or 1125. Those numbers came out of the eight labelled examples — that is the whole of "learned from data" in this small case.
  2. Three of the four test listings get the same label from both. A learned system is not mysterious; on typical input it agrees with the obvious rule.
  3. The fourth disagrees, and that is the interesting one. 2300 sq ft with 2 bedrooms trips the rule’s area >= 2200 threshold, but sits much closer to the small group once both features are weighed together.
  4. Which is right? The rules can be read and argued about — the threshold is right there in the source. The learned answer can only be explained by pointing at the training data, which is exactly the trade this section is about.
  5. Add ten more examples and the rule-based method needs a programmer; the learned one needs only the new rows.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — telling the three kinds of learning apart from the data alone

The exam question is almost never "define supervised learning". It is "here is a situation — which kind is it?" The answer is decided by what the training data contains, not by what the program does.

// SUPERVISED: every training row carries its answer
double[][] largeExamples = ...;   // labelled "large"
double[][] smallExamples = ...;   // labelled "small"
System.out.println("labelled training rows available: "
        + (largeExamples.length + smallExamples.length));

// UNSUPERVISED: no labels at all, group by similarity
double[][] unlabelled = { {920,2}, {2700,5}, {1080,2}, {2450,4}, {1350,3} };
// ... assign each row to the nearer of two centres ...
System.out.println("no labels given; grouped by similarity into "
        + groupA.size() + " and " + groupB.size()
        + " -- nobody said which group is which");

// REINFORCEMENT: no correct answer, only a score after the fact
int[] moves = { 1, -1, 1, 1, -1 };      // +1 good outcome, -1 bad
int reward = 0;
for (int m : moves) reward += m;
System.out.println("five attempts scored by a reward signal; total reward " + reward);
what it prints
labelled training rows available: 8
no labels given; grouped by similarity into 3 and 2 -- nobody said which group is which
five attempts scored by a reward signal; total reward 1
  1. Supervised: the eight rows arrived already sorted into "large" and "small". Somebody labelled them, and the labels are what the method learns from. Spam filtering trained on tagged mail is the textbook case.
  2. Unsupervised: the five rows have no labels. The program can still split them into two groups by similarity, but it cannot name the groups — "3 and 2" is all it knows. Customer segmentation works exactly like this.
  3. Reinforcement: nobody ever supplies the right move. Each attempt gets a score afterwards and the behaviour is adjusted towards higher scores. Learning a game by playing it is the standard example.
  4. The one-line test: are the right answers in the training data? Yes → supervised. No labels at all → unsupervised. Only a score after acting → reinforcement.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

The nesting is directional and it is asked in both directions. AI ⊃ machine learning ⊃ deep learning: every deep-learning system is machine learning and every machine-learning system is AI, but not the other way round. A rule-based expert system is AI and is not machine learning at all. The second slip is treating "AI" and "learned from data" as synonyms, so the answer "a program that follows rules a programmer wrote is not AI" gets picked — it is AI, it is just not learned AI.

A large language model predicts the next token given everything before it. That single mechanism explains both what it is good at and how it fails.

prompt -> tokens -> model -> probability over next tokens -> sample -> repeat

"The capital of France is"  ->  "Paris" (high probability)

Because it is predicting plausible continuations rather than retrieving facts, it can produce text that is fluent and wrong — a hallucination. It has no source to check against, which is exactly the gap that retrieval-augmented generation (18.8) exists to fill.

A large language model predicts the next token — a word or word fragment — over and over. Everything it does follows from that: it has no database of facts and no ability to look anything up unless a tool is attached.

TermMeans
tokenthe unit of text — roughly ¾ of a word
context windowhow much text it can consider at once; beyond it, the earliest text is dropped
parametersthe learned weights — a rough proxy for capacity
temperature0 = most predictable, higher = more varied
hallucinationfluent, confident and wrong
training cutoffthe date after which it knows nothing

It is stateless. It does not remember previous turns; the application re-sends the conversation each time, which is why history counts against the context window and why a long chat eventually forgets its own beginning.

Hallucination is not a bug to be patched — it is what next-token prediction does when the pattern is plausible but the fact is absent. That is why every factual output needs verification.

📘 DEFINITION

LLM: a model trained on large text corpora to predict the next token

Token: a chunk of text, roughly a word or word-piece, that the model works in

Context window: how much text the model can consider at once

Hallucination: fluent output that is factually wrong

Temperature: a setting controlling randomness; lower is more predictable

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

An LLM does not "look things up". It generates the most plausible continuation, which is why it must not be trusted for facts without verification.

📊 FIGURE — NEXT-TOKEN PREDICTION, AND THE WINDOW IT HAPPENS IN
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — counting tokens, because that is what you are billed and limited by

There is no exact token count without the model’s own tokeniser, but "about four characters per token" is close enough for English prose and is the estimate real code uses for budgeting.

static int estimateTokens(String s) { return (int) Math.ceil(s.length() / 4.0); }

String[] samples = {
    "The quarterly report is attached.",
    "unquestionably",
    "int total = 0;",
    "Reschedule the maintenance window to Tuesday at 02:00 UTC."
};
for (String s : samples) {
    System.out.printf("%-62s chars %3d  words %2d  ~tokens %3d%n",
        "\"" + s + "\"", s.length(), s.trim().split("\\s+").length, estimateTokens(s));
}
String doc = "The quarterly report is attached. ".repeat(200);
System.out.println("a 200-sentence document: " + doc.length()
        + " chars, about " + estimateTokens(doc) + " tokens");
what it prints
"The quarterly report is attached."                            chars  33  words  5  ~tokens   9
"unquestionably"                                               chars  14  words  1  ~tokens   4
"int total = 0;"                                               chars  14  words  4  ~tokens   4
"Reschedule the maintenance window to Tuesday at 02:00 UTC."   chars  58  words  9  ~tokens  15
a 200-sentence document: 6800 chars, about 1700 tokens
  1. Five words become about nine tokens — tokens are smaller than words, roughly ¾ of one each.
  2. unquestionably is one word and about four tokens. A long word is split into pieces, which is why the model has no reliable view of the letters in a word.
  3. int total = 0; is four words and four tokens: punctuation and symbols cost tokens too.
  4. The last sample shows the ratio holding at longer lengths, and the 6,800-character document is about 1,700 tokens. That single number is what decides whether a document fits in one request.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a conversation growing until it no longer fits

The window is a budget in tokens, not a number of turns. Here it is set to a deliberately tiny 60 so it fills up in six turns; a real one is tens of thousands, and fills up the same way.

int BUDGET = 60;
List<Turn> history = new ArrayList<>();
// ... six turns are added one at a time ...
for (String[] t : chat) {
    history.add(new Turn(t[0], t[1]));
    int used = 0;
    for (Turn h : history) used += estimateTokens(h.text());
    System.out.println("after " + history.size() + " turns: "
            + used + " tokens used of " + BUDGET);
}

// trimming to fit, always keeping the system turn at index 0
while (used > BUDGET && kept.size() > 2) {
    Turn dropped = kept.remove(1);
    used -= estimateTokens(dropped.text());
    System.out.println("dropped the oldest turn (" + dropped.role()
            + "), now " + used + " tokens");
}
what it prints
after 1 turns: 13 tokens used of 60
after 2 turns: 23 tokens used of 60
after 3 turns: 34 tokens used of 60
after 4 turns: 40 tokens used of 60
after 5 turns: 51 tokens used of 60
after 6 turns: 62 tokens used of 60
dropped the oldest turn (user), now 52 tokens
turns sent: 5 of 6
   system: You answer questions about the shipping schedule.
   assistant: It departs on Thursday at 06:00 local time.
   user: And the one after that?
   assistant: The following departure is Sunday at 22:00.
   user: Remind me which port I asked about first.
  1. The count rises on every turn because the whole history is re-sent each time. Nothing is stored on the other side.
  2. Turn 6 needs 62 tokens against a budget of 60. Without trimming the request is simply rejected.
  3. The trim removes index 1 — the oldest real turn — and keeps index 0, the system message, which carries the instructions and must survive.
  4. And now the damage: the final question is "which port did I ask about first", and the turn that named Rotterdam has just been deleted. The reply will be confidently wrong, and the cause is a data-structure decision, not the model.
  5. Real applications summarise the dropped turns into one short line rather than deleting them outright — the same trade-off as any fixed-size buffer.
🎯 EXAM TIP

Three facts carry most of the marks here. A token is smaller than a word (about ¾ of one). The model is stateless — memory is the application re-sending the history, which is why history counts against the window. And hallucination is not a bug: next-token prediction produces the most plausible continuation, and plausible is not the same as true. Any option that describes the model as "looking things up" or "remembering the last conversation" is the distractor.

Generative AI covers more than text, and the applications share one shape: a prompt describing what is wanted, and a generated artefact in response.

text   -> summarise, translate, draft, explain, answer
code   -> generate, complete, explain, convert between languages
images -> create from a description, edit, restyle
audio  -> speech from text, transcription, music

The tasks where it works well have a common property: many acceptable answers, and a human reviewing the output. The tasks where it fails have exactly one correct answer that must be right without review — which is a good rule for deciding when to use it.

TechniqueIs
specific promptingstating format, length, audience and constraints
few-shotgiving two or three worked examples of the pattern you want
chain of thoughtasking for the reasoning steps before the answer
role promptingsetting a perspective — "as a code reviewer"
iterationrefining the prompt against what came back

Few-shot works because the model is a pattern completer: examples define the shape of the answer far more reliably than describing it. Chain of thought helps on multi-step problems because each intermediate step becomes context for the next.

Poor fits are the mirror of how it works. Character counting and arithmetic are unreliable because text is processed as tokens rather than characters or numbers; anything after the training cutoff is unknown; and it cannot tell you what it does not know.

Good fits are drafting, rephrasing, explaining, summarising and generating variations — tasks where a fluent plausible answer is genuinely the goal.

📘 DEFINITION

Prompt: the input describing what the model should produce

Prompt engineering: writing prompts that reliably produce the output you want

Few-shot prompting: including examples in the prompt to demonstrate the expected form

Multimodal: a model handling more than one kind of data, such as text and images

🎯 EXAM TIP

Specific prompts beat vague ones. State the role, the task, the format and the constraints — the same clarity a well-written method signature provides (6.22).

📊 FIGURE — THE ANATOMY OF A PROMPT THAT WORKS
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — building the specific prompt in code, and counting what it costs
String role   = "You are a technical writer for an operations handbook.";
String task   = "Summarise the incident report below.";
String format = "Output exactly three bullet points, each under 15 words.";
String limits = "Use only facts stated in the report. "
              + "If a cause is not stated, write \"cause not stated\".";
String body   = "At 03:14 the load balancer stopped forwarding traffic "
              + "to two of six web nodes.";

String prompt = String.join("\n", role, task, format, limits, "", "REPORT:", body);
System.out.println(prompt);
System.out.println("--- " + prompt.length() + " characters, about "
        + (int) Math.ceil(prompt.length() / 4.0) + " tokens ---");
what it prints
You are a technical writer for an operations handbook.
Summarise the incident report below.
Output exactly three bullet points, each under 15 words.
Use only facts stated in the report. If a cause is not stated, write "cause not stated".

REPORT:
At 03:14 the load balancer stopped forwarding traffic to two of six web nodes.
--- 325 characters, about 82 tokens ---
  1. Compare with the whole of the vague version: "Summarise this." — 15 characters, and no way to tell whether the answer that comes back is what was wanted.
  2. String.join("\n", ...) with an empty string in the middle produces the blank line before REPORT:. Separating instructions from data matters: without it the report text reads as more instructions.
  3. The constraint line does real work. "If a cause is not stated, write 'cause not stated'" gives the model a legitimate way to not answer, which is the practical defence against an invented cause.
  4. Eighty-two tokens of instruction is a fixed cost paid on every request. That is the honest trade for specificity, and it is why the instructions live in a String constant rather than being rebuilt each call.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — few-shot, assembled with a loop

Few-shot prompting is not a special API. It is string building: a handful of input/output pairs, then the new input with the output line left dangling.

String[][] examples = {
    { "3 boxes of A4 paper",            "SUPPLIES|3" },
    { "one replacement laptop battery", "HARDWARE|1" },
    { "12 months of licence renewal",   "SOFTWARE|12" }
};
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
sb.append("Convert each request line into CATEGORY|QUANTITY.\n\n");
for (String[] ex : examples) {
    sb.append("Input:  ").append(ex[0]).append('\n');
    sb.append("Output: ").append(ex[1]).append("\n\n");
}
sb.append("Input:  2 ergonomic keyboards\n");
sb.append("Output:");
System.out.println(sb.toString());
what it prints
Convert each request line into CATEGORY|QUANTITY.

Input:  3 boxes of A4 paper
Output: SUPPLIES|3

Input:  one replacement laptop battery
Output: HARDWARE|1

Input:  12 months of licence renewal
Output: SOFTWARE|12

Input:  2 ergonomic keyboards
Output:
  1. The examples establish three things at once that prose would struggle with: the vocabulary of categories, the pipe separator, and that "one" and "12 months" both become digits.
  2. The prompt ends on "Output:" with nothing after it. The model is a continuation engine, so the most probable continuation is a line in exactly that shape.
  3. The loop is the point: examples live in an array and the prompt is generated. Adding a fourth category means adding a row, not editing a paragraph.
  4. This is also why the number of examples is a tuning decision — more examples pin the format down harder and cost more tokens on every single request.

And when any part of the prompt comes from a user, it has to be escaped before it goes into JSON:

String userLine = "3 reams of \"heavy\" paper\nand a stapler";
System.out.println("raw:     " + userLine.replace("\n", "\\n"));
System.out.println("escaped: " + jsonEscape(userLine));
what it prints
raw:     3 reams of "heavy" paper\nand a stapler
escaped: "3 reams of \"heavy\" paper\nand a stapler"
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

The characteristic mistake is asking for work the mechanism cannot do and then trusting the confident answer. Counting characters in a word, arithmetic on long numbers, and anything dated after the training cutoff are all unreliable — not because the model is careless but because it processes tokens rather than letters or numbers, and because the fact was never there. The second mistake is treating a wrong answer as proof the task is impossible: the same request, rewritten with a format and two examples, very often works, and "iterate on the prompt" is a listed technique for exactly that reason.

Using AI while coding is now normal practice, and the useful framing is that it is a fast draft rather than a source of truth. Everything it produces has to pass the same review any pull request would.

good uses                          bad uses
boilerplate and scaffolding        anything you cannot review
explaining unfamiliar code         security-critical logic taken on trust
suggesting test cases              coursework you must be able to defend
translating between languages      relying on it for facts without checking

For this course specifically, generated code that you cannot explain is worth nothing on the exam, because the exam asks you to trace and predict rather than to produce. Reading generated code and understanding why it works is the version of this that helps.

The reliable uses in coding are boilerplate, explaining unfamiliar code, drafting tests, and suggesting approaches. The unreliable ones are anything requiring the API to actually exist.

Invented APIs are the characteristic failure. A method that looks exactly like it should exist, with a plausible name and signature, that simply does not. That one at least fails at compile time.

The dangerous failure is code that compiles and runs and is subtly wrong — an off-by-one bound, a missing edge case, a check omitted. Nothing flags it, which is why generated code must be read and tested rather than accepted because it runs.

Two practical rules. Never paste secrets, credentials or proprietary code into a tool you do not control. And check your institution's academic policy before using it on coursework — the responsibility for what you submit is yours regardless of what produced it.

📘 DEFINITION

Code completion: suggesting the next lines as you type

Code review (of generated code): verifying correctness, security and licensing before use

Hallucinated API: a method or class the model invented that does not exist

Academic integrity: the requirement that submitted work is your own and defensible

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Invented library methods are the most common failure mode in generated Java. If a method name looks unfamiliar, check it in the API documentation (7.17) before assuming it exists.

📊 FIGURE — TWO KINDS OF WRONG — AND ONLY ONE HAS A SAFETY NET
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — code that compiles, runs, and quietly gives the wrong number

This is the suggestion. Read it before running it and decide whether you would have accepted it.

static double averageScore(int[] scores) {
    int sum = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < scores.length; i++) sum += scores[i];
    return sum / scores.length;
}

int[] scores = { 88, 91, 79, 95 };
System.out.println("averageScore      -> " + averageScore(scores));
System.out.println("averageScoreFixed -> " + averageScoreFixed(scores));
System.out.println("the true average is " + (88 + 91 + 79 + 95) / 4.0);

int[] empty = {};
try {
    System.out.println(averageScore(empty));
} catch (ArithmeticException e) {
    System.out.println("empty array -> " + e.getClass().getSimpleName()
                       + ": " + e.getMessage());
}
System.out.println("empty array, fixed version -> " + averageScoreFixed(empty));
what it prints
averageScore      -> 88.0
averageScoreFixed -> 88.25
the true average is 88.25
empty array -> ArithmeticException: / by zero
empty array, fixed version -> 0.0
  1. The return type is double, so 88.0 looks like a decimal answer and reads as correct. It is not: sum / scores.length is int / int, truncated to 88 before the widening to 88.0.
  2. The error is a quarter of a mark. No exception, no warning, nothing in the output that says "this is wrong" — you only find it by knowing the true answer, which is the whole problem.
  3. The fix is one cast, (double) sum / scores.length, and it is the integer-division rule from Unit 2. Generated code fails on the basics as readily as on the exotic parts.
  4. The empty array is the second omission. It throws ArithmeticException: / by zero — at least this one is loud, and one test with an empty array finds it.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the off-by-one that passes the obvious test
static String longest(String[] words) {
    String best = "";
    for (int i = 1; i < words.length; i++)            // starts at 1
        if (words[i].length() > best.length()) best = words[i];
    return best;
}

String[] a = { "kilo", "hectare", "gram" };
System.out.println("longest(a)      -> " + longest(a));
System.out.println("longestFixed(a) -> " + longestFixed(a));
String[] b = { "kilometre", "gram", "litre" };        // longest is FIRST
System.out.println("longest(b)      -> " + longest(b));
System.out.println("longestFixed(b) -> " + longestFixed(b));
what it prints
longest(a)      -> hectare
longestFixed(a) -> hectare
longest(b)      -> litre
longestFixed(b) -> kilometre
  1. On the first array the broken version gives the right answer. Test it once, casually, and it passes.
  2. The bug is i = 1. Element 0 is never examined, so the method is only wrong when the longest word happens to be first — and in a it was not.
  3. On b it returns litre (5 letters) while kilometre (9) sat at index 0 the whole time. Still no exception, still a plausible-looking answer.
  4. Three assertions catch both of this section’s bugs: a normal case, a case where the answer is at the boundary, and an empty input. That is the review, and it takes two minutes.
the three checks
check 1 (normal):      true
check 2 (first is longest): true
check 3 (empty input): true
🎯 EXAM TIP

Expect a question of the form "which failure is the dangerous one". The answer is always the code that compiles and runs and is subtly wrong — an invented method name fails at compile time and costs seconds. The other two reliable answers: never paste credentials, keys or proprietary code into a service you do not control; and the responsibility for submitted work is the student’s regardless of what produced it, so check the academic policy first.

Calling an AI service from Java is an ordinary HTTP request. Nothing about the mechanics is AI-specific — it is JSON over HTTPS, and every Java networking rule applies.

import java.net.http.*;
import java.net.URI;

HttpClient client = HttpClient.newHttpClient();

HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
    .uri(URI.create("https://api.example.com/v1/chat"))
    .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
    .header("Authorization", "Bearer " + System.getenv("API_KEY"))
    .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(jsonBody))
    .build();

HttpResponse response =
    client.send(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());

System.getenv rather than a literal is the detail that matters. A key written into source ends up in version control and stays in the history even after it is removed — which is a security failure, not a style preference.

String key = System.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY");   // NEVER hard-code the key
// POST JSON: {"model": ..., "messages": [ {"role":"user","content": ...} ]}
// check the status code BEFORE parsing the body
if (status != 200) { /* handle it — do not parse an error page as a reply */ }

An API key belongs in an environment variable or a config file kept out of version control. A key committed to a repository is a key that has been published, and rotating it is the only remedy.

Because the model is stateless, conversation memory is the application's job: keep the message list and re-send it every turn. That list grows without limit, so a real chatbot must trim or summarise old turns before it exceeds the context window.

Network calls fail, rate limits return 429, and responses can be malformed. Every one of those is an ordinary exception path from Unit 12, and user input placed into JSON must be escaped or it corrupts the request.

📘 DEFINITION

HttpClient: the standard Java HTTP client, since Java 11

API key: the credential authenticating your requests; never hard-code it

Environment variable: configuration supplied outside the source, read with System.getenv

JSON: the request and response format used by nearly every web API

Rate limit: the cap on requests per period; exceeding it returns an error status

🎯 EXAM TIP

Network calls fail — timeouts, rate limits, malformed responses. They belong in a try-catch (Unit 12), and IOException is checked, so the compiler will insist.

📊 FIGURE — EVERY TURN RE-SENDS THE WHOLE CONVERSATION
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — conversation memory is a List your program owns
record Message(String role, String content) {}

List<Message> history = new ArrayList<>();
history.add(new Message("system", "You help staff book meeting rooms."));

String[] userTurns = { "Book room 4B for Tuesday.",
                       "Make it Wednesday instead.",
                       "What time did I ask for?" };
String[] replies   = { "Room 4B is booked for Tuesday at 10:00.",
                       "Moved to Wednesday at 10:00." };

for (int t = 0; t < userTurns.length; t++) {
    history.add(new Message("user", userTurns[t]));
    System.out.println("turn " + (t + 1) + ": sending " + history.size() + " messages");
    if (t < replies.length) history.add(new Message("assistant", replies[t]));
}
for (Message m : history) System.out.println("   " + m.role() + ": " + m.content());
what it prints
turn 1: sending 2 messages
turn 2: sending 4 messages
turn 3: sending 6 messages
the whole list goes over the wire every single turn:
   system: You help staff book meeting rooms.
   user: Book room 4B for Tuesday.
   assistant: Room 4B is booked for Tuesday at 10:00.
   user: Make it Wednesday instead.
   assistant: Moved to Wednesday at 10:00.
   user: What time did I ask for?
  1. 2, 4, 6 — the request grows by two messages a turn, because the reply has to be appended as well as the question. Nothing is remembered on the far side.
  2. The system message goes first and stays first. It is the standing instruction, and it is re-sent every turn along with everything else.
  3. Turn 3 asks "what time did I ask for?" and can only be answered because messages 2 and 3 are still in the list. Delete them and the answer becomes a guess — which is the trimming problem of 18.2 arriving in real code.
  4. A record is exactly the right shape here: two final fields, a constructor, accessors and toString for free, from one line.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — escaping user text, and checking the status before parsing

Two failures happen at the boundary rather than in the model. A quotation mark in user text corrupts the JSON body; and an error response parsed as if it were a reply produces a nonsense answer with no exception thrown.

static String quote(String s) {
    StringBuilder out = new StringBuilder("\"");
    for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
        char c = s.charAt(i);
        switch (c) {
            case '"'  -> out.append("\\\"");
            case '\\' -> out.append("\\\\");
            case '\n' -> out.append("\\n");
            default   -> out.append(c);
        }
    }
    return out.append('"').toString();
}

hostile.add(new Message("user", "Cancel the \"9am\" booking\nand tell me why"));
System.out.println(toJson(hostile));

for (int status : new int[]{ 200, 401, 429, 503, 400 })
    System.out.println("HTTP " + status + " -> " + describe(status));
what it prints
{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Cancel the \"9am\" booking\nand tell me why"}]}
HTTP 200 -> parse the reply
HTTP 401 -> bad key -- do not retry, fix the credential
HTTP 429 -> rate limited -- wait and retry
HTTP 503 -> server side -- retry with backoff
HTTP 400 -> client error 400 -- fix the request
  1. Without escaping, the user’s quotation mark around 9am would close the JSON string early and the request would be rejected as malformed — a bug that only appears for certain user input.
  2. The newline becomes \n, two characters. A literal newline inside a JSON string is illegal, which is why multi-line input breaks naive string building.
  3. The status codes split into three different responses: 401 must not be retried (retrying a bad key just burns quota), 429 and 5xx should be retried after a wait, and 4xx means your request is wrong.
  4. Every one of these is ordinary exception handling from Unit 12. Nothing about calling a model needs a new technique — it needs the old ones actually applied.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

The mistake that costs real money is hard-coding the key: String key = "sk-live-…"; committed to a repository is public the moment the repository is, and rotating the key is the only remedy — deleting the commit does not help. Read it from the environment with System.getenv and fail loudly when it is absent. The second mistake is expecting the far side to remember anything: leave the history list out and every turn starts from nothing, which looks like the model "forgetting" and is actually your program never having told it.

An image-generation app follows the same request-response shape as 18.5, with two differences: the response is binary or a URL, and generation takes long enough that the user must be told something is happening.

// 1. send the prompt
// 2. receive a URL or base64 data
// 3. decode and save

byte[] imageBytes = Base64.getDecoder().decode(base64String);
try (FileOutputStream out = new FileOutputStream("result.png")) {
    out.write(imageBytes);                          // Unit 9, binary form
}

// in a GUI, do the request OFF the UI thread or the window freezes
new Thread(() -> {
    byte[] data = fetchImage(prompt);
    Platform.runLater(() -> imageView.setImage(new Image(...)));
}).start();

The threading note is the practically important one. A network call on the UI thread freezes the whole interface until it returns, and any update to the interface must go back onto that thread — Platform.runLater in JavaFX, SwingUtilities.invokeLater in Swing.

An image API differs from a text one in what comes back: usually a temporary URL that expires within the hour, or a base64-encoded blob. Either way the result must be downloaded and saved to keep it.

new Thread(() -> {
    Image img = callApi(prompt);                    // slow — OFF the UI thread
    SwingUtilities.invokeLater(() -> label.setIcon(new ImageIcon(img)));
}).start();                                          // back ON it to display

This is the threading rule of 15.4 with teeth. A network call takes seconds; on the event thread the whole window freezes for the duration. Do the call on a background thread, then return to the UI thread to touch any component.

Image generation also costs per request and is content-filtered, so a rejected prompt is a normal response to handle rather than an error.

📘 DEFINITION

Base64: a text encoding for binary data, common in JSON responses

Binary file output: writing bytes rather than text, using an output stream

UI thread: the single thread that must handle all interface updates

Background thread: where slow work belongs so the interface stays responsive

🎯 EXAM TIP

"The window went grey and stopped responding" almost always means slow work is running on the UI thread.

📊 FIGURE — THE SLOW CALL BELONGS IN THE OTHER LANE
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — watching the two threads interleave

The sleep stands in for a network call. The point is not the numbers, it is that lines from the two threads are interleaved — the main thread kept working while the other one waited.

final String[] result = new String[1];
Thread worker = new Thread(() -> {
    System.out.println("[" + Thread.currentThread().getName() + "] calling the image service...");
    result[0] = slowCall("a lighthouse at dusk");     // Thread.sleep(300) inside
    System.out.println("[" + Thread.currentThread().getName()
            + "] got " + result[0].length() + " bytes of data");
}, "worker-1");
worker.start();

for (int frame = 1; frame <= 3; frame++) {
    System.out.println("[" + Thread.currentThread().getName()
            + "] frame " + frame + " painted while waiting");
    Thread.sleep(100);
}
worker.join();
System.out.println("[" + Thread.currentThread().getName()
        + "] back on the UI thread, setting the icon");
what it prints
[main] user clicks Generate
[main] window is still repainting, menus still open
[worker-1] calling the image service...
[main] frame 1 painted while waiting
[main] frame 2 painted while waiting
[main] frame 3 painted while waiting
[worker-1] got 12 bytes of data
[main] back on the UI thread, setting the icon
  1. Read the thread names down the left. Three [main] lines are printed while [worker-1] is blocked in the call — that is the window staying responsive.
  2. Put the call directly in the button handler instead and every one of those frames would be missing: the same output minus the three middle lines, which on screen is a grey rectangle where the window was.
  3. worker.join() is the "wait for it to finish" step. In a real Swing program you would not block here at all; the worker would post back with SwingUtilities.invokeLater, and this is what a SwingWorker’s done() method does for you.
  4. The rule is symmetrical and both halves matter: slow work must leave the event thread, and every component update must return to it.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — what comes back, and saving it before it expires

An image service returns either a temporary URL or base64-encoded bytes. A URL usually expires within the hour, so "keeping" the picture always means writing bytes to disk.

String encoded = "SG93IHRvIHNhdmUgYW4gaW1hZ2U=";
byte[] bytes = Base64.getDecoder().decode(encoded);
System.out.println("decoded " + bytes.length + " bytes");

Path out = Path.of("generated.png");
Files.write(out, bytes);
System.out.println("written to " + out + ", size on disk " + Files.size(out));
System.out.println("re-read: " + new String(Files.readAllBytes(out)));

for (String status : new String[]{ "ok", "content_filtered", "rate_limited" }) {
    System.out.println(status + " -> " + switch (status) {
        case "ok" -> "display the image";
        case "content_filtered" -> "show the message, keep the prompt for editing";
        default -> "queue the request and tell the user to wait";
    });
}
what it prints
decoded 20 bytes
written to generated.png, size on disk 20
re-read: How to save an image
ok -> display the image
content_filtered -> show the message, keep the prompt for editing
rate_limited -> queue the request and tell the user to wait
  1. Base64.getDecoder().decode is standard java.util — no library required. Base64 exists because JSON is text and image bytes are not.
  2. Files.write(Path, byte[]) writes binary directly, with no Writer and no character encoding to get wrong. Sending image bytes through a PrintWriter corrupts them.
  3. The decoded content here is readable text only because the example encodes a sentence; a real payload would be PNG bytes and the same three lines would handle it unchanged.
  4. The status handling is the part students skip. A filtered prompt is a normal response, not an exception — the app should show the message and keep the prompt so the user can edit it, and a rate limit means wait, not fail.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Two threading errors, opposite in shape. Calling the service on the event thread freezes the window for the entire call, and a frozen window is often mistaken for a crash. The reverse — touching a Swing component from the worker thread, label.setIcon(...) straight out of the background code — usually appears to work, which is worse: Swing components are not thread-safe, so it fails intermittently and only under load. Slow work leaves the event thread; component updates come back to it through SwingUtilities.invokeLater. And do not hold onto the returned URL as if it were the picture; it expires.

Building a system around a model is mostly engineering rather than modelling, and the pipeline is the same regardless of what the model does.

input -> validate -> build prompt -> call model -> parse response
      -> validate output -> use it
                 |
                 +-- on failure: retry, fall back, or report

Every stage is ordinary Java. Validation is 6.13, failure handling is Unit 12, and the fallback path is what stops the whole feature disappearing when the service is unavailable. The model is one component, not the architecture.

A production AI feature is mostly ordinary software. The model call is a small part; the work is in what surrounds it.

PieceDoes
system promptsets role, rules and output format once
context assemblygathers the right information to include
output validationparses and checks the reply before trusting it
fallbackwhat happens when the reply is unusable
evaluationa fixed set of cases with known-good answers
logginginputs and outputs, so failures can be diagnosed
cachingavoids paying twice for the same request

Output validation is non-negotiable because the reply is text, not a typed object. Asking for JSON does not guarantee JSON, so parsing must be wrapped and a fallback ready — never assume the shape.

An evaluation set is what makes changes safe. Without one, "the new prompt seems better" is an impression; with one it is a measurement, which is regression testing from 6.7 applied to a non-deterministic component.

📘 DEFINITION

Pipeline: the ordered stages input passes through

Guardrails: checks on input and output that constrain what the system will accept or emit

Fallback: the behaviour when the model is unavailable or its answer fails validation

Evaluation: measuring output quality against known-good examples

Determinism: the same input giving the same output; models are not deterministic by default

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

Non-determinism is what makes these systems hard to test with the methods of 6.7. Assertions on exact output do not work, so evaluation moves to properties: is it valid JSON, is it in range, does it cite a real source.

📊 FIGURE — THE MODEL CALL IS THE SMALL PART
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — validating a reply that is only text

The reply is a String. Asking for JSON does not guarantee JSON, and even valid JSON can contain a category that does not exist. Validation is parse, then range-check, then enum-check — and any failure routes to the fallback.

record Ticket(String category, int urgency) {}

static Optional<Ticket> parse(String reply) {
    try {
        // ... pull out the {...} and read the two fields ...
        if (category == null || urgency == null) return Optional.empty();
        if (urgency < 1 || urgency > 5) return Optional.empty();
        if (!List.of("BILLING","TECHNICAL","ACCOUNT").contains(category))
            return Optional.empty();
        return Optional.of(new Ticket(category, urgency));
    } catch (RuntimeException e) {
        return Optional.empty();        // malformed is a NORMAL outcome
    }
}
the five replies, and what happens to each
accepted Ticket[category=BILLING, urgency=3]   <- {"category": "BILLING", "urgency": 3}
accepted Ticket[category=TECHNICAL, urgency=5]   <- Sure! Here is the JSON you asked for: | {"category": "TECHNICAL", "urgency": 5}
REJECTED  -> fall back to the human queue   <- {"category": "URGENT", "urgency": 3}
REJECTED  -> fall back to the human queue   <- {"category": "BILLING", "urgency": 9}
REJECTED  -> fall back to the human queue   <- I'm not able to categorise this ticket.
  1. Reply 1 is the happy path and is the only one most people test.
  2. Reply 2 has a chatty preamble before the JSON. Finding the first { and the last } rescues it — a small tolerance that removes a large class of failures.
  3. Reply 3 is valid JSON with an invented category. Syntax checking alone would accept it, which is why the enum check exists: the set of allowed values is yours, not the model’s.
  4. Reply 4 has urgency 9 on a 1–5 scale. Range checks are not paranoia; out-of-range values are a routine failure mode.
  5. Reply 5 is a refusal in plain English. It parses as nothing, throws nothing useful, and must be caught as a normal outcome rather than an exception that reaches the user.
  6. Every rejection lands on the same fallback: the human queue. A feature with no fallback is a feature that fails on reply 3.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — an evaluation set, and a cache that stops paying twice

"The new prompt seems better" is an impression. Five fixed cases with known answers turn it into a number, and the harness is ordinary code you can run on every change.

String[][] cases = {
    { "card declined twice",           "BILLING" },
    { "cannot reset my password",      "ACCOUNT" },
    { "app crashes on launch",         "TECHNICAL" },
    { "charged twice this month",      "BILLING" },
    { "screen freezes when printing",  "TECHNICAL" }
};
System.out.println("prompt A: " + score(cases, promptA) + " of " + cases.length + " correct");
System.out.println("prompt B: " + score(cases, promptB) + " of " + cases.length + " correct");

Map<String,String> cache = new HashMap<>();
int calls = 0;
for (String q : asked) {
    if (cache.containsKey(q)) { System.out.println("cache hit  : " + q); continue; }
    calls++;
    cache.put(q, "answer " + calls);
    System.out.println("model call : " + q);
}
System.out.println(asked.length + " questions asked, " + calls + " calls actually made");
what it prints
prompt A: 4 of 5 correct
prompt B: 5 of 5 correct
without this set, both prompts would just "seem fine"
model call : What is the refund window?
model call : How do I reset my password?
cache hit  : What is the refund window?
cache hit  : What is the refund window?
4 questions asked, 2 calls actually made
  1. Prompt A gets four of five; prompt B gets five. That is a measurement, and it is the difference between changing a prompt and improving one.
  2. The failing case is "cannot reset my password", which prompt A calls TECHNICAL and the key calls ACCOUNT. Knowing which case failed is what makes the next edit targeted rather than hopeful.
  3. Five cases is a small set and still catches the regression. The point is that it is fixed and re-run, not that it is large — this is the regression testing of Unit 6 applied to a component that is not deterministic.
  4. The cache is a plain HashMap: four questions, two calls. Half the requests never leave the building, which is half the latency and half the cost for one containsKey.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

The characteristic beginner system calls the model and uses the reply directly — String category = reply.trim(); straight into a database column. It works in the demo and fails on the first chatty preamble, the first invented category, and the first polite refusal. The other half of the same mistake is catching the parse failure and rethrowing it: a malformed reply is an expected outcome, not an exceptional one, so the code path for it must be a real fallback with a defined behaviour — a default value, a retry with a stricter prompt, or a human.

🎯 EXAM TIP

The reliable questions are "what surrounds the model call" and "why is an evaluation set needed". Answer the first with the pipeline: system prompt, context assembly, the call, validation, fallback, logging, caching. Answer the second with non-determinism — the same prompt can give different replies, so improvement has to be measured over a fixed set of cases rather than judged from one look. Anything describing the reply as a typed object is wrong: it is text until you have parsed and checked it.

Retrieval-augmented generation is the standard answer to the hallucination problem of 18.2: instead of trusting the model to know something, you find the relevant text first and hand it over with the question.

1. INDEX      break your documents into chunks, store them
2. RETRIEVE   given a question, find the most relevant chunks
3. AUGMENT    put those chunks into the prompt as context
4. GENERATE   ask the model to answer USING ONLY that context

String prompt = "Answer using only the context below.\n\n"
              + "Context:\n" + String.join("\n", relevantChunks) + "\n\n"
              + "Question: " + question;

The retrieval step is ordinary search — the algorithms of 17.1 and the collections of Unit 14, with a HashMap from term to document. Only step 4 involves a model, which is why RAG is more of a data-structures problem than an AI one.

How retrieval actually finds the relevant chunks

The retrieval step needs a way to measure "relevant". Each chunk is converted into an embedding — a vector of numbers representing its meaning — and the query is embedded the same way. The chunks whose vectors point in most nearly the same direction as the query are the ones retrieved.

The standard measure is cosine similarity: the cosine of the angle between two vectors, running from 1 (identical direction) through 0 (unrelated) to −1 (opposite). It compares direction rather than length, which is what makes it work when a long document and a short question are being matched.

RAG — retrieval-augmented generation — answers questions over documents the model was never trained on: retrieve the relevant passages, then include them in the prompt so the answer is grounded in real text.

indexing:  split documents into CHUNKS -> embed each -> store the vectors
query:     embed the question -> find the top-k most similar chunks
           -> put them in the prompt -> generate the answer

An embedding turns text into a vector positioned so that similar meanings sit close together; similarity is measured by cosine similarity, the angle between two vectors. Chunk size is the tuning knob — too large dilutes relevance, too small loses the surrounding context.

The weak link is retrieval, not generation. If the right chunk is not retrieved, the model answers from its own training or invents something, and the answer looks exactly as confident either way.

RAG suits changing or private knowledge; fine-tuning suits changing style or format. Choosing fine-tuning for facts is the standard wrong answer.

📘 DEFINITION

RAG: retrieval-augmented generation — supplying retrieved context with the question

Chunking: splitting documents into pieces small enough to retrieve and to fit the context window

Embedding: a numeric vector representing meaning, used to find similar text

Grounding: constraining an answer to supplied source material

Citation: reporting which retrieved chunk an answer came from

🎯 EXAM TIP

RAG reduces hallucination; it does not eliminate it. If retrieval returns nothing relevant, the model will still answer — which is why "say you do not know" belongs in the prompt.

📊 FIGURE — RAG: INDEX ONCE, RETRIEVE ON EVERY QUESTION
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — chunking, and what the overlap is actually for
static List<String> chunk(String doc, int size, int overlap) {
    List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
    int start = 0;
    while (start < doc.length()) {
        int end = Math.min(start + size, doc.length());
        out.add(doc.substring(start, end));
        if (end == doc.length()) break;
        start = end - overlap;                 // step BACK before the next chunk
    }
    return out;
}

String policy = "Refunds are issued within 14 days of purchase. "
              + "Shipping is free on orders over 50 dollars. "
              + "Damaged goods must be reported within 48 hours.";
what it prints
document length: 138 characters
-- 60-character chunks, no overlap --
  chunk 0: [Refunds are issued within 14 days of purchase. Shipping is f]
  chunk 1: [ree on orders over 50 dollars. Damaged goods must be reporte]
  chunk 2: [d within 48 hours.]
-- 60-character chunks, 25 of overlap --
  chunk 0: [Refunds are issued within 14 days of purchase. Shipping is f]
  chunk 1: [f purchase. Shipping is free on orders over 50 dollars. Dama]
  chunk 2: [ers over 50 dollars. Damaged goods must be reported within 4]
  chunk 3: [must be reported within 48 hours.]
chunks: 3 without overlap, 4 with -- overlap costs storage and saves sentences cut in half
  1. Look at chunk 1 in the first list: it begins "ree on orders over 50 dollars". The shipping sentence has been cut across a boundary, so neither chunk states the shipping rule in full.
  2. With 25 characters of overlap, chunk 1 begins "f purchase. Shipping is free on orders over 50 dollars." — the whole sentence is now inside one chunk and can be retrieved as a unit.
  3. The cost is exact and visible: 4 chunks instead of 3. Overlap trades storage and embedding cost for not slicing meaning in half.
  4. The step is size − overlap. Set overlap ≥ size and the loop never advances — the same "guarantee progress" requirement as binary search in 17.2.
  5. Real systems chunk on sentence or paragraph boundaries rather than fixed characters; the arithmetic is identical and the boundaries are simply chosen better.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — retrieval is a similarity ranking, and its failure is silent

An embedding is a vector positioned so that similar meanings sit close together. Three dimensions are used here so the numbers can be read; a real embedding has hundreds or thousands, and the arithmetic is the same.

static double cosine(double[] a, double[] b) {
    double dot = 0, na = 0, nb = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
        dot += a[i] * b[i]; na += a[i] * a[i]; nb += b[i] * b[i];
    }
    return dot / (Math.sqrt(na) * Math.sqrt(nb));
}

// [refund-ness, shipping-ness, damage-ness]
new Chunk("Refunds are issued within 14 days of purchase.",  {0.92, 0.10, 0.15});
new Chunk("Shipping is free on orders over 50 dollars.",     {0.08, 0.95, 0.05});
new Chunk("Damaged goods must be reported within 48 hours.", {0.20, 0.12, 0.90});
new Chunk("Gift cards are non-refundable.",                  {0.70, 0.05, 0.10});

double[] question = { 0.88, 0.12, 0.20 };   // "how long to get my money back?"
ranked.sort(Map.Entry.<Chunk,Double>comparingByValue().reversed());
what it prints
question vector: [0.88, 0.12, 0.2]
  0.9978  Refunds are issued within 14 days of purchase.
  0.9948  Gift cards are non-refundable.
  0.4376  Damaged goods must be reported within 48 hours.
  0.2237  Shipping is free on orders over 50 dollars.
-- prompt actually sent, top-2 chunks only --
Answer using ONLY the context below.

CONTEXT:
- Refunds are issued within 14 days of purchase.
- Gift cards are non-refundable.

QUESTION: How long do I have to get my money back?
  1. Cosine similarity is the angle between two vectors, so it lands between −1 and 1 and ignores length. Two chunks about refunds score 0.99; the shipping chunk scores 0.22.
  2. Only the top k go into the prompt. That is the whole retrieval step — a sort and a slice, with no model involved.
  3. The assembled prompt is the deliverable: the instruction, the retrieved text as CONTEXT, then the question. "Answer using ONLY the context below" is what makes the answer traceable to a document.
  4. Now the failure. An off-topic question — "what is your VAT number?" — still produces a ranking, and the top chunk is still handed over as context:
the off-topic question
  0.5354  Refunds are issued within 14 days of purchase.
  0.6476  Shipping is free on orders over 50 dollars.
  0.8575  Damaged goods must be reported within 48 hours.
  0.5028  Gift cards are non-refundable.
top score is still returned -- nothing in the pipeline says "not in the documents"

Nothing in that output flags a problem. A similarity threshold — reject anything below, say, 0.75 — is the missing line, and it is the difference between "I do not have that information" and a fluent invention.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

The weak link is retrieval, and it fails without a symptom. If the right chunk is not in the top k, the model answers from its training or invents something, and the answer is worded with exactly the same confidence as a correct one — so the fix is a similarity threshold and citing the chunk, not a better-worded prompt. The second mistake is the standard exam distractor: reaching for fine-tuning to teach the system new facts. Fine-tuning changes style and format; facts that change belong in the retrieval store, where updating them means replacing a document rather than retraining anything.

The risks are examined as concepts, and each one is worth being able to define and give an example of.

bias           the model reflects patterns in its training data,
               including unfair ones
privacy        data sent to a service may be stored or used for training
accuracy       fluent output can be confidently wrong (18.2)
attribution    generated work may closely reproduce training material
accountability who is responsible when an automated decision causes harm
transparency   users should know when they are dealing with a model

The through-line is that these are human and legal questions the code cannot settle. A model trained on biased hiring data will reproduce that bias no matter how well the Java around it is written — which is precisely why the decision to deploy it is not a technical one.

RiskWhere it comes from
biasthe training data — the model reproduces patterns in it
hallucinationplausible prediction with no fact behind it
privacyanything sent may be stored or used for training
accountabilitythe deployer is responsible, not the model
transparencypeople should know when they are talking to a machine
environmental costtraining and serving consume significant energy

Bias is not introduced by the algorithm; it is inherited from data reflecting the world as it was recorded. Testing for it means measuring outcomes across groups, not inspecting intentions.

Human review belongs wherever a decision materially affects someone — hiring, lending, medical, legal. The failure mode to guard against is automation bias: trusting a confident output more than it deserves, precisely because it is fluent.

📘 DEFINITION

Algorithmic bias: systematically unfair output arising from the training data

Data privacy: the obligation to protect information users supply

Explainability: being able to say why a model produced a particular output

Human in the loop: requiring a person to review consequential decisions

Responsible AI: the practices intended to keep these risks manageable

🎯 EXAM TIP

Exam questions here are scenario-based: given a situation, name the risk. Hiring and lending scenarios point at bias; anything with personal data points at privacy; anything with a confident wrong answer points at accuracy.

📊 FIGURE — WHERE EACH RISK ENTERS THE CHAIN
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — measuring a disparity instead of arguing about intent

Two hundred lending decisions, split evenly between two regions, every applicant equally qualified. Nothing in the code mentions the region — the model inherited the pattern from data in which one region was under-represented.

Map<String,int[]> tally = new LinkedHashMap<>();       // [approved, total]
for (Applicant a : decisions) {
    int[] t = tally.computeIfAbsent(a.group(), k -> new int[2]);
    if (a.approved()) t[0]++;
    t[1]++;
}
double lowest = 1.0, highest = 0.0;
for (Map.Entry<String,int[]> e : tally.entrySet()) {
    double rate = (double) e.getValue()[0] / e.getValue()[1];
    lowest = Math.min(lowest, rate);
    highest = Math.max(highest, rate);
    System.out.printf("%-9s approved %3d of %3d  = %.1f%%%n",
        e.getKey(), e.getValue()[0], e.getValue()[1], rate * 100);
}
System.out.printf("ratio of the lower rate to the higher: %.2f%n", lowest / highest);
what it prints
region A  approved  82 of 100  = 82.0%
region B  approved  61 of 100  = 61.0%
ratio of the lower rate to the higher: 0.74
a ratio below 0.80 is the threshold commonly used to flag a disparity: true
nothing in the code mentions the region -- the pattern came from the data
  1. Neither rate looks alarming on its own. 82% and 61% are both ordinary numbers; the disparity only appears when they are put next to each other.
  2. The ratio 0.74 is below the 0.80 figure commonly used as a flag. That is a measurement, which is the point: bias testing compares outcomes across groups, it does not inspect intentions or read the source.
  3. The (double) cast on the rate is load-bearing. Without it, 82 / 100 is integer division, every rate is 0, and the audit silently reports no disparity at all — the Unit 2 rule, in a place where getting it wrong is worse than a wrong number.
  4. computeIfAbsent creates the counter array the first time a group is seen, which is the tallying idiom from 14.3 doing the whole grouping in one line.
  5. The remedy is not in this code. It is more representative training data, or a decision threshold set per group, or a human reviewing the rejections — and choosing between those is a policy question, not a programming one.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — what must never reach a log or a request, and why confidence is not accuracy
static String redact(String s) {
    return s.replaceAll("\\b\\d{13,16}\\b", "[card]")
            .replaceAll("\\b\\d{3}-\\d{2}-\\d{4}\\b", "[id]")
            .replaceAll("[\\w.+-]+@[\\w-]+\\.[\\w.]+", "[email]");
}
for (String e : entries) System.out.println("  logged: " + redact(e));
what it prints
  logged: customer 4471 asked about invoice 90210
  logged: card [card] was declined
  logged: contact me at [email]
  logged: national id [id] on file
  1. The first line is untouched, and deliberately so — an internal customer number and an invoice number are not personal data, and redacting everything numeric would make the log useless.
  2. The card number, the email address and the national ID are replaced before the line is ever written. Anything sent to a third-party service may be stored or used for training, so redaction belongs before the request, not after the fact.
  3. Regular expressions are a filter, not a guarantee — they catch the common formats and will miss unusual ones, which is why the real control is not collecting the data in the first place.

The second half of the risk is the human reading the output:

confidence against correctness
  stated confidence 0.97  actually correct? true
  stated confidence 0.96  actually correct? false
  stated confidence 0.91  actually correct? false
average stated confidence 0.95, actual accuracy 0.33
a human reviewing only the low-confidence answers would have checked none of them
  1. Three outputs, all stated with high confidence, one of them right. A stated confidence is a number the system produced; it is not a measured accuracy.
  2. A review policy of "check anything below 0.90" would have checked none of these and passed two wrong answers straight through. That is automation bias with a process wrapped around it.
  3. The reliable policy is the opposite shape: review by consequence, not by confidence. Hiring, lending, medical and legal decisions get a human regardless of how sure the output sounds.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

The most common wrong answer is that bias is introduced by the algorithm and can be removed by inspecting the code. It cannot: the code above never mentions the region, and the disparity is still 0.74. Bias is inherited from data that recorded the world as it was, so it is found by measuring outcomes across groups and fixed upstream. The second is treating hallucination as a defect awaiting a patch — it is what next-token prediction does when the pattern is plausible and the fact is absent, which is why the control is verification rather than waiting for a fix. And accountability does not move: the organisation that deployed the system answers for its decisions.

do-while is the third loop form promised in 4.1, and its single distinguishing property is that the body runs before the condition is tested — so it always runs at least once.

int input;
do {
    System.out.println("Enter a positive number:");
    input = scnr.nextInt();
} while (input <= 0);            // note the semicolon — it is required

// the while version needs the prompt written twice, or a priming read (4.2)

That guarantee is what makes it the right choice for menus and input validation: you must show the prompt before you can possibly know whether the answer is acceptable. Everywhere else, a while loop is clearer.

do {
    System.out.print("Enter a positive number: ");
    n = scnr.nextInt();
} while (n <= 0);        // the semicolon is REQUIRED

do-while tests after the body, so it always runs at least once. That is exactly what input validation wants: ask, then decide whether to ask again. A plain while would need the prompt written twice — once before the loop and once inside it.

The semicolon after the closing while is required and its absence is a compile error, which at least fails loudly.

📘 DEFINITION

do-while: a post-test loop; the body executes before the condition is checked

Post-test loop: a loop guaranteed to run at least once

Menu loop: the classic do-while: display options, read a choice, repeat until quit

Required semicolon: the while(...) at the end of a do-while must be terminated with ;

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Forgetting the semicolon after while (condition) is a compile error unique to this form. Every other loop has none.

✅ Also covered in depth: Control Flow → while and do-while Loops

📊 FIGURE — WHILE VS DO-WHILE: WHO GOES FIRST
📊 FIGURE — while vs do-while: where the test sits
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The body runs once even when the condition is false
int i = 5;
int whileCount = 0;
while (i < 3) { whileCount++; i++; }

int j = 5;
int doCount = 0;
do { doCount++; j++; } while (j < 3);

System.out.println("while ran " + whileCount + " times");
System.out.println("do-while ran " + doCount + " times");
while ran 0 times do-while ran 1 times
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Both loops start with the condition already false.
  2. while tests first, sees false, and skips the body entirely.
  3. do-while runs the body, then tests — so it always runs at least once.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Input validation, the pattern do-while was made for
int age;
do {
    System.out.println("Enter an age above 0:");
    age = nextInput();
    System.out.println("  you typed " + age);
} while (age <= 0);
System.out.println("accepted: " + age);
Enter an age above 0: you typed -4 Enter an age above 0: you typed 0 Enter an age above 0: you typed 17 accepted: 17
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The prompt must appear before there is anything to check, so the body has to run first.
  2. The loop keeps re-asking while the value is still invalid.
  3. A plain while here would need the prompt written twice — once before the loop and once inside it.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Forgetting the semicolon after while (condition) in the do-while form. It is required, and leaving it off is a compile error — which is the friendly outcome, because the mistake fails loudly instead of quietly changing behaviour.
🎯 EXAM TIP
If a question shows a loop whose condition is false at the start and asks how many times the body runs, the answer is 0 for while and 1 for do-while. That single difference is what almost every do-while question is testing.

The engineering examples apply Units 2 to 5 to physical calculations, and they exist to test the same traps in unfamiliar clothing.

// projectile height over time
final double G = 9.81;
double height = v0 * t - 0.5 * G * t * t;

// unit conversion
double celsius = (fahrenheit - 32) * 5.0 / 9.0;      // 5.0 not 5 (2.5)

// resistors in parallel
double total = 1.0 / (1.0/r1 + 1.0/r2);              // 1.0 not 1

Every trap in these problems is the integer-division trap from 2.5, wearing a physics costume. 5 / 9 is 0, so the temperature conversion returns 0 for every input — and the answer looks like a physics error rather than a type error.

double current = voltage / resistance;              // guard resistance != 0
double force   = mass * acceleration;
double ke      = 0.5 * mass * Math.pow(velocity, 2);
double avg     = (a + b) / 2.0;                     // 2.0, not 2
double r       = total / (count * factor);          // parenthesise the denominator

Engineering formulas concentrate two hazards from earlier units. Use double throughout, because a single int operand makes the whole expression integer division and loses the fraction silently.

And a written fraction bar is an invisible pair of parentheses: total / count * factor divides then multiplies, which is not what total / (count × factor) means. Any denominator with more than one term needs brackets.

Division by a measured quantity needs a zero guard before the calculation, and results are formatted with printf("%.2f") rather than printed raw.

📘 DEFINITION

Named constant: final double G = 9.81 — the pattern from 2.9

Unit conversion: multiplying by a ratio; a common source of integer-division bugs

Formula translation: converting a written equation into an expression with correct precedence (3.10)

🎯 EXAM TIP

Write at least one operand of every division as a decimal. 5.0 / 9 is safe; 5 / 9 is zero.

📊 FIGURE — turning a formula into Java without losing precision
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Integer division silently ruins a physical formula
int f = 98;
System.out.println((f - 32) * 5 / 9);
System.out.println((f - 32) * 5.0 / 9.0);
System.out.println(5 / 9);
System.out.println(5 / 9 * (f - 32));
36 36.666666666666664 0 0
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Line 2 is all integers: 66 * 5 = 330, and 330 / 9 truncates to 36.
  2. Line 3 promotes the whole expression to double and gives the real answer.
  3. Line 5 shows the worst version — 5 / 9 is evaluated first and is 0, so the entire formula collapses to 0.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Constants and Math for a projectile
final double G = 9.81;
double v0 = 20.0;
double angleDeg = 45.0;

double rad = Math.toRadians(angleDeg);
double range = v0 * v0 * Math.sin(2 * rad) / G;
double maxHeight = Math.pow(v0 * Math.sin(rad), 2) / (2 * G);

System.out.printf("range %.2f m%n", range);
System.out.printf("height %.2f m%n", maxHeight);
range 40.77 m height 10.19 m
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Java's trig functions take radians, so the degrees are converted first.
  2. final says G is a constant — the compiler rejects any later assignment to it.
  3. printf with %.2f rounds for display only; the stored value keeps full precision.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Passing degrees straight into Math.sin. It expects radians, so Math.sin(45) is the sine of 45 radians (about 0.851), not of 45°. Nothing errors — the number is just wrong.
🎯 EXAM TIP
When a formula mixes literals and int variables, force one operand to double the moment you write it: 5.0 / 9, not 5 / 9. Position matters too — (a) * 5.0 / 9 is safe, 5 / 9 * (a) is not.

The same calculations become methods, which is where the argument of 6.3 pays off: a formula written once and tested once is a formula that is right everywhere it is used.

public static double celsiusFromF(double f) { return (f - 32) * 5.0 / 9.0; }

public static double parallelResistance(double r1, double r2) {
    if (r1 <= 0 || r2 <= 0) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("resistance must be positive");
    }
    return 1.0 / (1.0/r1 + 1.0/r2);
}

// testable in one line each (6.7)
System.out.println(Math.abs(celsiusFromF(212) - 100) < 0.0001);   // 3.18

Note the comparison in the test. Floating-point results must be compared with a tolerance, never with == — the rule from 3.18, which is easy to forget precisely when you are writing tests.

public static double current(double v, double r) {
    if (r == 0) return 0;                 // guard INSIDE the method
    return v / r;
}

One method per formula, each returning rather than printing. That is 6.2 and 6.7 applied: a returned value can be unit tested against a hand calculation, a printed one can only be checked by eye.

Guards belong inside the method so the rule is written once rather than at every call site. Adding a formula is then adding a method, with nothing else to change — which is the property the exercise is demonstrating.

These are pure functions of their arguments, so they are static: there is no object state involved.

📘 DEFINITION

Formula method: one calculation, named, taking its inputs as parameters

Precondition check: rejecting physically impossible inputs (6.13)

Epsilon comparison: comparing doubles against a tolerance rather than for equality

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

A formula in a method can be unit-tested against known values — 212°F is 100°C — which is not possible when it is buried inline in main.

📊 FIGURE — why a formula belongs in its own method
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The formula extracted, then checked
System.out.println(celsiusFromF(212));
System.out.println(celsiusFromF(32));
System.out.println(parallelResistance(4, 4));
try {
    parallelResistance(0, 4);
} catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
    System.out.println("rejected: " + e.getMessage());
}
100.0 0.0 2.0 rejected: resistance must be positive
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Each formula now has a name that says what it computes.
  2. The precondition check fails fast, at the point the bad value arrives, rather than returning Infinity for the caller to puzzle over.
  3. Two equal resistors in parallel give half the resistance — an answer you can sanity-check by hand.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Testing a double-returning method the right way
double got = celsiusFromF(212);
System.out.println("exact == check: " + (got == 100.0));

double tricky = 0.1 + 0.2;
System.out.println(tricky);
System.out.println("0.3 == check:   " + (tricky == 0.3));
System.out.println("epsilon check: " + (Math.abs(tricky - 0.3) < 0.0001));
exact == check: true 0.30000000000000004 0.3 == check: false epsilon check: true
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. This particular conversion lands exactly on 100.0, so == happens to work.
  2. 0.1 + 0.2 shows why you cannot rely on that — binary floating point cannot store those values exactly.
  3. The epsilon comparison is the habit to build: ask whether the answer is close enough, not whether it is bit-identical.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Comparing two doubles with == in a test. It passes on the examples you tried and fails on the one the grader picked. Use Math.abs(actual − expected) < 0.0001.
🎯 EXAM TIP
A method that computes something should return it, not print it. A method that prints cannot be tested, reused inside a bigger formula, or have its result formatted differently later.

args in main has been sitting there unexplained since 1.2. It holds the command-line arguments: whatever was typed after the class name when the program was run.

java MyProgram hello 42 3.14

args[0]        // "hello"
args[1]        // "42"     — a String, ALWAYS
args.length    // 3        — no program name, unlike C

int n = Integer.parseInt(args[1]);       // parsing is required (7.13)

if (args.length < 2) {                    // check FIRST
    System.out.println("usage: java MyProgram  ");
    return;
}

Two things trip people up. Every argument is a String, so numbers must be parsed. And args.length does not include the program name — unlike C, where argv[0] is the program itself.

public static void main(String[] args) {
    if (args.length < 1) {                       // ALWAYS check first
        System.out.println("Usage: java Prog <count>");
        return;
    }
    int n = Integer.parseInt(args[0]);           // args are Strings
}

args[0] is the first argument, not the program name — unlike C, where the name occupies slot 0. With no arguments args is an empty array, never null, so args.length is always safe to read.

Everything arrives as a String and must be parsed, with the NumberFormatException of 12.6 waiting for anything that is not a number. Reading args[0] without checking the length throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException — hence the usage message.

Arguments are split on spaces unless quoted, so a filename containing a space must be quoted on the command line.

📘 DEFINITION

Command-line argument: a value supplied after the class name when the program is launched

args array: the String[] parameter of main, holding those values in order

Usage message: the message printed when the arguments are missing or wrong

Argument parsing: converting the String arguments to the types the program needs

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Reading args[0] without checking args.length throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException when the program is run with no arguments — which is exactly how a grader will run it.

📊 FIGURE — what arrives in args[]
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Everything in args is a String until you parse it
String[] args = { "5", "8" };

System.out.println(args[0] + args[1]);
System.out.println(Integer.parseInt(args[0]) + Integer.parseInt(args[1]));
System.out.println("count: " + args.length);
58 13 count: 2
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. + between two Strings concatenates, so the first line prints 58, not 13.
  2. Parsing converts the text to numbers, and only then does + add.
  3. args.length counts the arguments only — running java Sum 5 8 gives 2, not 3.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Checking before you index, and reporting what went wrong
run(new String[] { "5", "8" });
run(new String[] { "5" });
run(new String[] { "5", "eight" });
sum = 13 usage: java Sum <a> <b> (got 1 args) not a number: For input string: "eight"
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The length check runs before any indexing, so a missing argument gives a usage message instead of an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
  2. parseInt throws NumberFormatException on text that is not a number — catching it turns a stack trace into a sentence.
  3. Notice the exception's message quotes the offending input, which is exactly what the user needs to see.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Assuming args[0] is the program name, the way it works in C. In Java it is the first argument — the class name never appears in args, so java Prog a b c gives args.length == 3.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Two failures to guard on every command-line program: too few arguments (check args.length first) and unparsable text (catch NumberFormatException). Questions on this unit nearly always target one of the two.
