Passing file names as arguments is what makes a program usable from a script, and it combines 19.4 with Unit 9 and Unit 12.

public static void main(String[] args) {
    if (args.length < 2) {
        System.out.println("usage: java Copy  ");
        return;
    }

    try (Scanner in = new Scanner(new File(args[0]));
         PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter(args[1])) {

        while (in.hasNextLine()) { out.println(in.nextLine()); }

    } catch (FileNotFoundException e) {
        System.out.println("Cannot open: " + e.getMessage());
    }
}

Both resources are declared in one try-with-resources and both are closed automatically, in reverse order. That matters here: the output file must be flushed and closed or the copy is truncated (9.5).

if (args.length < 1) { System.out.println("Usage: java Prog <file>"); return; }
try (Scanner in = new Scanner(new File(args[0]))) {
    while (in.hasNextLine()) process(in.nextLine());
} catch (FileNotFoundException e) {
    System.out.println("Cannot open " + args[0]);
}

This combines the whole of Units 9, 12 and 19: check the argument count, open with try-with-resources so the file closes automatically, and catch the checked FileNotFoundException the compiler insists on.

A relative path resolves against the directory the program was launched from, not the location of the source file — which is why a file that "is right there" is often not found. Report the actual name from args[0] in the error so the mismatch is visible.

📘 DEFINITION

File name argument: a path supplied on the command line rather than hard-coded

Multiple resources: several declarations in one try, separated by semicolons

Relative path: resolved against the working directory the program was started from

🎯 EXAM TIP

A path that works in the IDE and fails from a terminal is almost always a relative path resolved against a different working directory.

📊 FIGURE — opening a file named on the command line
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Write a file, then read it back the way a real program would
java.io.PrintWriter out = new java.io.PrintWriter("scores.txt");
out.println("88");
out.println("92");
out.println("79");
out.close();

report("scores.txt");
report("missing.txt");
scores.txt: 3 lines cannot open 'missing.txt' - no such file in the working directory
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. PrintWriter creates the file; without close() the text may still be sitting in a buffer when the program ends.
  2. exists() is checked first so a missing file produces a sentence, not a stack trace.
  3. The message names the file it could not find, and says where it looked — the working directory, not the folder holding the source. That one distinction solves most 'it works in the IDE' mysteries.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Summing the numbers a file contains
java.io.PrintWriter out = new java.io.PrintWriter("nums.txt");
out.println("10 20");
out.println("30");
out.close();

java.util.Scanner in = new java.util.Scanner(new java.io.File("nums.txt"));
int sum = 0, count = 0;
while (in.hasNextInt()) {
    sum += in.nextInt();
    count++;
}
in.close();
System.out.println(count + " numbers, sum " + sum);
3 numbers, sum 60
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. hasNextInt() is the loop guard: it stops cleanly at end of file instead of throwing NoSuchElementException.
  2. nextInt() skips whitespace, so it does not care that the numbers are split across lines.
  3. Reading with hasNext…/next… in that pairing is the safe file-reading shape for every question in this unit.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
A relative filename like data.txt is resolved against the working directory, not the folder holding the .java file. That is why a program opens the file from the IDE and fails from a terminal — same code, different starting directory.
🎯 EXAM TIP
When a file cannot be opened, print the filename you were given and the absolute path you tried. Guessing at a path problem is slow; printing it ends the question in one run.

Output art is nested-loop practice (4.7) with a visible answer — which is what makes it good practice, because a wrong loop bound is immediately obvious.

// right triangle
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
    for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) { System.out.print("*"); }
    System.out.println();                       // OUTER loop
}

// centred pyramid: spaces then stars
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
    for (int s = 0; s < n - i; s++) { System.out.print(" "); }
    for (int j = 0; j < 2*i - 1; j++) { System.out.print("*"); }
    System.out.println();
}

The technique is to write the relationship between the row number and the counts before writing any code. Row i has n - i spaces and 2i - 1 stars; once that is on paper, the loops write themselves.

for (int r = 1; r <= n; r++) {
    for (int s = 0; s < n - r; s++) System.out.print(" ");   // leading spaces
    for (int s = 0; s < r; s++)     System.out.print("*");   // then stars
    System.out.println();                                    // OUTER loop
}

Pattern printing is nested loops from 4.7 with the inner bound depending on the outer variable. The row loop is outer; each inner loop prints one part of the row; the println belongs to the outer loop, and moving it inside puts every character on its own line.

Right alignment is spaces before stars, with the two counts summing to n — which is why the space loop runs n - r times and the star loop r. Use print within a row and println to end it; automated checks compare output exactly, so a stray trailing space fails.

📘 DEFINITION

Nested output loop: the inner loop prints one row, the outer loop advances rows

print vs println: print stays on the line; println ends it

Row formula: the expression relating the row index to how many characters it holds

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Putting println() inside the inner loop puts every character on its own line. It belongs to the outer loop — the same brace question as 4.7.

✅ Also covered in depth: OA Exam Prep → Coding Drills 1

📊 FIGURE — row formulas for the four standard triangles
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The same nested loop, four ways
leftTri(4);
System.out.println("--");
rightTri(4);
System.out.println("--");
pyramid(4);
* ** *** **** -- * ** *** **** -- * *** ***** *******
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The outer loop counts rows; the inner loops count characters within a row.
  2. The only thing that changes between the three shapes is the arithmetic in the inner loop bounds.
  3. System.out.println() with no argument is what ends each row — it is the line break, nothing else.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A multiplication table, aligned with printf
for (int r = 1; r <= 4; r++) {
    for (int c = 1; c <= 4; c++) {
        System.out.printf("%4d", r * c);
    }
    System.out.println();
}
1 2 3 4 2 4 6 8 3 6 9 12 4 8 12 16
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. %4d pads each number to four characters wide, so the columns line up whatever the digit count.
  2. The inner loop writes one row with printf and never breaks the line.
  3. The println() after the inner loop — not inside it — is what moves to the next row.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Calling println inside the inner loop. Every character then lands on its own line and the shape disappears. Use print inside, println once after.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Do not guess these loop bounds — derive them. Write out rows 1 and n by hand, count spaces and stars in each, and find the formula that produces both. Pyramid rows are always an odd number of stars: 1, 3, 5, 7.

Grade calculation is the array patterns of 5.4 with a branch chain (3.4) on the end, and it is the most common exam program in the whole course.

int[] scores = {88, 92, 79, 95, 61};

int sum = 0;
for (int s : scores) { sum += s; }
double avg = (double) sum / scores.length;      // CAST — else integer division

char grade;
if      (avg >= 90) { grade = 'A'; }
else if (avg >= 80) { grade = 'B'; }
else if (avg >= 70) { grade = 'C'; }
else                { grade = 'F'; }

System.out.printf("Average: %.2f  Grade: %c%n", avg, grade);

Three earlier traps are all present in nine lines: the cast before the division (2.5), the chain ordered highest first (3.4), and %c matching a char rather than %s (9.2). Exam versions of this program plant errors in exactly those three places.

if      (avg >= 90) grade = 'A';
else if (avg >= 80) grade = 'B';        // descending — the first true wins
else if (avg >= 70) grade = 'C';
else                grade = 'F';

double avg = count == 0 ? 0 : (double) total / count;   // guard, and cast

The chain must run descending, because the first matching branch wins and no upper bound is needed — everything higher was already caught. Ascending order gives every passing score the lowest grade, which is 1.3's nested-conditional point in its most testable form.

Boundaries are where marks are lost: exactly 90 must be an A, so the test is >= and not >. And the average needs both the empty-class guard and the double cast, or an integer division quietly truncates it.

📘 DEFINITION

Average of an int array: sum as int, then cast before dividing by length

Grade chain: an ordered else-if chain, highest threshold first

Formatted report: printf with %.2f for the average and %c for the grade

🎯 EXAM TIP

Rounding matters at the boundary. An average of 89.5 printed as "89.50" is still a B unless the program rounds before grading — read whether the question grades the raw value or the rounded one.

✅ Also covered in depth: OA Exam Prep → Coding Drills 2

📊 FIGURE — the pieces of a grading program
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Letter grades, and why the chain order decides the answer
double[] marks = { 95, 83, 70, 59.9 };
for (double m : marks) {
    System.out.println(m + " -> " + letter(m) + "   (reversed chain: " + broken(m) + ")");
}
95.0 -> A (reversed chain: D) 83.0 -> B (reversed chain: D) 70.0 -> C (reversed chain: D) 59.9 -> F (reversed chain: F)
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. An else if chain stops at the first true test, so the cut-offs must be checked from the top down.
  2. The reversed chain gives everyone a D, because 95 ≥ 60 is true and nothing after it is ever reached.
  3. 59.9 falls through every test and lands on the else — which is exactly what the final else is for.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A weighted average with the lowest quiz dropped
int[] quizzes = { 80, 95, 40, 90 };
System.out.printf("quiz avg          %.2f%n", average(quizzes, false));
System.out.printf("quiz avg, dropped %.2f%n", average(quizzes, true));

double finalPct = 0.30 * average(quizzes, true) + 0.30 * 88 + 0.40 * 91;
System.out.printf("course total      %.2f%n", finalPct);
quiz avg 76.25 quiz avg, dropped 88.33 course total 89.30
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The single pass finds the total and the minimum together — there is no need to sort.
  2. Dropping the lowest means removing it from the total and reducing the divisor; forgetting the second is the usual bug.
  3. The weights add to 1.00, so the weighted sum is already a percentage and needs no further division.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Writing the average as total / scores.length with both operands int. That truncates — 3 scores totalling 250 gives 83, not 83.33. Multiply by 100.0 or cast one side to double.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Check a weighting scheme by adding the weights: if they do not sum to 1.0 (or 100), the program is wrong before it computes anything. It is the fastest sanity check on this whole topic.

An abbreviation decoder is a lookup problem, and it shows the same job done with the tools of three different units.

// parallel arrays (5.5) — works, fragile
String[] abbr = {"BTW", "IMO", "FYI"};
String[] full = {"by the way", "in my opinion", "for your information"};
for (int i = 0; i < abbr.length; i++) {
    if (abbr[i].equalsIgnoreCase(input)) { System.out.println(full[i]); }
}

// HashMap (14.3) — the right tool
HashMap map = new HashMap<>();
map.put("BTW", "by the way");
System.out.println(map.getOrDefault(input.toUpperCase(), "unknown"));

The map version is shorter, faster and cannot fall out of step, which is the whole argument of Unit 14 in six lines. Normalising the key with toUpperCase() is what replaces equalsIgnoreCase — a HashMap lookup is always case-sensitive.

Map<String,String> codes = new HashMap<>();
codes.put("ASAP", "as soon as possible");

String full = codes.getOrDefault(input.toUpperCase().trim(), "unknown code");

A map is the natural structure: lookup is O(1) and adding an entry is one line, against a parallel-array scan that is O(n) and must be kept in step. This is 14.3 replacing 5.5 for exactly the reason 5.5 warned about.

Normalise before looking up — toUpperCase() and trim() — or "asap " misses a key that is present. getOrDefault handles the unknown code without a null check, which is the whole reason it exists.

📘 DEFINITION

Lookup table: a mapping from key to value, by parallel arrays or by a Map

getOrDefault: returns a fallback instead of null for a missing key

Key normalisation: converting keys to one case so lookups match consistently

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

A HashMap has no case-insensitive lookup. Normalise both the stored keys and the query, or every lowercase input misses.

✅ Also covered in depth: OA Exam Prep → Coding Drills 2

📊 FIGURE — a lookup table, and the calls that matter
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Building the table and looking things up
java.util.HashMap<String, String> codes = new java.util.HashMap<>();
codes.put("ID", "Idaho");
codes.put("UT", "Utah");
codes.put("NV", "Nevada");

System.out.println(codes.get("UT"));
System.out.println(codes.get("XX"));
System.out.println(codes.getOrDefault("XX", "unknown code"));
System.out.println(codes.containsKey("ID"));
System.out.println(codes.size());
Utah null unknown code true 3
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. get on a missing key returns null — it does not throw, which is why the null slips downstream unnoticed.
  2. getOrDefault removes the null entirely and is the right call for a decoder.
  3. size() counts keys, so overwriting a key never grows the map.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Case-insensitive decoding, driven by a loop
java.util.HashMap<String, String> m = table();
String[] input = { "ut", " ID ", "Ut", "zz" };
for (String s : input) {
    System.out.println("'" + s + "' -> " + decode(m, s));
}
'ut' -> Utah ' ID ' -> Idaho 'Ut' -> Utah 'zz' -> unknown: zz
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Keys are compared with equals, so "ut" and "UT" are different keys.
  2. Normalising the input once, on the way in, means the map only ever needs one spelling of each key.
  3. trim() handles the stray spaces that always come with typed input.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Calling get and using the result straight away. A missing key gives null, and the failure surfaces later as a NullPointerException somewhere unrelated. Use getOrDefault, or test containsKey first.
🎯 EXAM TIP
put on an existing key replaces the value rather than adding a second entry — maps hold unique keys. If a question puts the same key twice and asks for size(), the answer counts it once.

Dice statistics combine random numbers (2.18) with array counting (5.4), and it is the standard demonstration that a histogram is just an array indexed by outcome.

Random rand = new Random();
int[] counts = new int[13];                     // indexes 0-12; 0 and 1 unused

for (int i = 0; i < 10000; i++) {
    int roll = rand.nextInt(6) + 1 + rand.nextInt(6) + 1;    // TWO dice
    counts[roll]++;                              // the value IS the index
}

for (int total = 2; total <= 12; total++) {
    System.out.printf("%2d: %d%n", total, counts[total]);
}

rand.nextInt(6) + 1 twice is not the same as rand.nextInt(11) + 2. Two dice give a triangular distribution peaking at 7; one roll of 2 to 12 is uniform. That is the whole point of the exercise, and it is a favourite exam question.

Random rnd = new Random();
int die = rnd.nextInt(6) + 1;            // 0..5 shifted to 1..6
int sum = d1 + d2;                       // 2..12

int[] counts = new int[13];              // index BY the sum — 0 and 1 unused
counts[sum]++;
System.out.printf("%d: %.2f%%%n", s, 100.0 * counts[s] / trials);

nextInt(6) returns 0 to 5, so + 1 is required. Sizing the array 13 rather than 11 lets the sum index it directly — two wasted slots in exchange for no arithmetic on every access, which is the usual trade.

Two dice are not uniform: 7 has six ways to occur and 2 has one, so the distribution peaks in the middle and approaches the expected 16.7% for 7 as trials increase. Multiplying by 100.0 rather than 100 keeps the percentage from being integer-divided to zero.

new Random(42) with a fixed seed repeats the same sequence, which is what makes a simulation testable.

📘 DEFINITION

Random.nextInt(n): a value from 0 to n-1 inclusive

Histogram array: an array where the index is the outcome and the value is its count

Seeding: new Random(42) gives a repeatable sequence, which is useful for testing

Uniform vs triangular: one die is uniform; the sum of two is not

🎯 EXAM TIP

Sizing the array to 13 and ignoring indexes 0 and 1 wastes two slots and removes all the index arithmetic. Trading a little memory for clarity is usually right.

✅ Also covered in depth: OA Exam Prep → Coding Drills 2

📊 FIGURE — simulating dice, repeatably
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Two dice, tallied into an array
java.util.Random rng = new java.util.Random(42);
int[] counts = new int[13];
int rolls = 60000;

for (int i = 0; i < rolls; i++) {
    int sum = (rng.nextInt(6) + 1) + (rng.nextInt(6) + 1);
    counts[sum]++;
}

for (int s = 2; s <= 12; s++) {
    System.out.printf("%2d: %5d  (%.1f%%)%n", s, counts[s], 100.0 * counts[s] / rolls);
}
2: 1675 (2.8%) 3: 3275 (5.5%) 4: 5014 (8.4%) 5: 6783 (11.3%) 6: 8329 (13.9%) 7: 10022 (16.7%) 8: 8288 (13.8%) 9: 6579 (11.0%) 10: 4944 (8.2%) 11: 3339 (5.6%) 12: 1752 (2.9%)
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The array is sized 13 so that index 12 exists — a size of 12 would throw on the first double six.
  2. Two separate nextInt(6) + 1 calls model two dice; nextInt(11) + 2 would give a flat distribution and be wrong.
  3. 7 comes out most often because six of the 36 combinations produce it — the simulation lands near 16.7%.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The seed is what makes a simulation testable
java.util.Random a = new java.util.Random(42);
java.util.Random b = new java.util.Random(42);
java.util.Random c = new java.util.Random(7);

System.out.println(a.nextInt(100) + " " + a.nextInt(100) + " " + a.nextInt(100));
System.out.println(b.nextInt(100) + " " + b.nextInt(100) + " " + b.nextInt(100));
System.out.println(c.nextInt(100) + " " + c.nextInt(100) + " " + c.nextInt(100));
30 63 48 30 63 48 36 64 85
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. Same seed, same sequence — the two generators agree exactly.
  2. A different seed gives a different sequence.
  3. new Random() with no seed picks one from the clock, which is what you want in production and never want in a test.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
nextInt(6) returns 0 through 5, not 1 through 6 — the bound is exclusive. Forgetting the + 1 lets a die roll a zero, and two of them can then sum to 0, which falls outside the 2..12 range your tally assumes.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Sizing a tally array: index by the outcome and make the array maxOutcome + 1 long. Index 0 and 1 simply stay unused for dice sums — wasting two slots is far cheaper than the arithmetic to shift every index by 2.
"}, "D286/u19/z19_10": {"body": "

The zyBooks programming window compiles and runs your code against automated tests, and the way it does so changes how you should write.

- input comes from a supplied file, not from typing
- output is compared to expected output EXACTLY
- a trailing space or a missing newline fails the test
- System.out.println adds the newline; print does not

Because matching is exact, most failures are formatting rather than logic. Check the expected output character by character before re-reading your algorithm — a printf with %.2f where the test wants %.1f fails just as hard as a wrong answer.

Automated checks compare your output against expected output character by character. A correct calculation with different spacing, capitalisation or an extra blank line still fails.

SymptomUsual cause
everything looks right but failsa trailing space, or a missing final newline
fails only on the hidden testan untested edge case — empty input, zero, one element
output interleaved oddlya prompt printed in a test that supplies input silently
first test passes, later ones failstate left over between runs, or an unconsumed newline

Where tests supply input from a file rather than a person, printing prompts adds text the comparison did not expect — so read without prompting when the specification says so.

Debug prints must be removed before submitting, since they are output too. Develop against the smallest failing case, and check the boundaries first: empty input, a single element, and the largest allowed value.

📘 DEFINITION

Auto-grader: a system running your program against fixed inputs and comparing output

Exact match: comparison including whitespace and line breaks

Test input file: the supplied stdin the program is run against

Whitespace error: a failure caused only by spacing or newlines

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Prompts you print for the user become part of the output being compared. If a test supplies input from a file and expects only the answer, an extra "Enter a number:" fails it.

📊 FIGURE — what an automated grader is really comparing
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Formatting differences a grader treats as wrong answers
double v = 2.5;
System.out.println(v);
System.out.printf("%.2f%n", v);
System.out.println(1.0 / 3);
System.out.printf("%.2f%n", 1.0 / 3);
System.out.println(10 / 4);
System.out.println(10 / 4.0);
2.5 2.50 0.3333333333333333 0.33 2 2.5
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. println(2.5) writes 2.5; a test expecting 2.50 fails on a value that is numerically correct.
  2. %.2f rounds for display — the underlying double is untouched.
  3. The last pair is the integer-division trap once more: 2 versus 2.5, from the same numbers.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Edge cases the hidden tests will reach for
System.out.println(average(new int[] { 1, 2, 3 }));
System.out.println(average(new int[] { 5 }));
System.out.println(average(new int[] { }));
System.out.println(average(new int[] { -4, 4 }));
2.0 5.0 0.0 0.0
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The empty array is the case that crashes an unguarded version with a divide-by-zero — the visible test almost never covers it.
  2. A single element and a result of exactly zero are the other two boundaries worth trying by hand.
  3. The cast to double is on the total, before the division, which is what keeps the fraction.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Leaving a prompt such as System.out.print("Enter a number: ") in a program an automated checker grades. The checker compares the whole of stdout, so the prompt is counted as unexpected output and the test fails even though the computed answer is right.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Before submitting, run the three inputs a grader always tries: empty, one element, and zero or negative values. Then read your output character by character against the expected output — a trailing space or a missing newline fails just as hard as a wrong number.

SDLC as an ordered process (WGU steps)

\\n
\ud83d\udca1 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Think of building software like building a house. You don't start nailing boards before you know what the owner wants, and you don't move people in before you inspect it. The Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) is just that ordered checklist \u2014 and WGU loves to ask \u201cyou just finished step X, what's next?\u201d So the order matters more than the vibe.

\\n
\u2699\ufe0f WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

A common WGU ordering runs: 1) Analyze/define the problem (gather requirements \u2014 what must it do?), 2) Plan the logic/design (flowcharts and pseudocode describe the steps), 3) Code/translate (write it, then translate the code so the machine can run it), 4) Test/debug (find and fix errors), 5) Put the program into production (deploy it for real use), 6) Maintain the program (fix, patch, and enhance over its life).

The biggest cost over a program's life is usually maintenance, not the original coding.

\\n
\ud83d\udcdd HOW WGU WORDS IT
\u2605 ON THE OA \u2014 WATCH FOR

Know the WGU SDLC steps in order and what each produces \u2014 requirements gather needs, design plans the solution, implementation codes it, testing verifies, deployment releases, maintenance sustains.

\u25b8 QUICK CHECK

Given a scenario ('the team is writing test cases'), name the phase: that's testing, which comes after implementation.

CPU scheduling algorithms by name

\\n
\ud83d\udca1 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

When many programs want the one CPU, the operating system plays traffic cop, deciding who goes next. Each strategy has a name, and WGU asks you to match the name to its one-line behavior. Learn them as a set of contrasts.

\\n
\u2699\ufe0f WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

First-Come, First-Served (FCFS): runs jobs in arrival order (simple, but a long job blocks everyone behind it). Shortest Job Next (SJN), also called shortest-job-first: picks the job with the smallest total execution time next. Shortest Remaining Time: picks the job with the smallest execution time remaining (the preemptive cousin of SJN). Priority scheduling: highest-priority job runs next. Round-Robin (RR): each job gets a fixed time slice in turn, cycling around \u2014 this is what gives fairness and responsiveness.

\\n

Programming paradigms & their subsets

\\n

A \u201cparadigm\u201d is just a style of organizing a program \u2014 a philosophy for how you tell the computer what to do. WGU asks you to identify the style from a description, and to know which styles are subsets of which.

Fixed partitions waste space INSIDE a block (internal); dynamic partitions leave gaps BETWEEN blocks (external); PAGING is the fix for external fragmentation. And the OS is SYSTEM software, not application software.
\n

Which technique eliminates external fragmentation?\n
  1. Paged memory
  2. Fixed partitioning
  3. Dynamic partitioning
  4. Single contiguous
\n
Show answer + steps
A. Equal-size pages fit into ANY free frame \u2014 no unusable gaps between allocations.
\n

Memory management, fair use & software types

\n
\ud83d\udca1 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Three quick but testable ideas your notes call out by name. First, how an operating system slices up memory to share it among programs. Second, the one big exception to copyright \u2014 fair use. Third, the difference between the software that runs the machine and the software you actually use.

\n
\u2699\ufe0f WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Memory-management techniques \u2014 how the OS divides RAM among programs: Single contiguous = one program plus the OS occupy all of memory at once (the simplest, oldest scheme). Fixed partitioning = memory is split into a set number of fixed-size blocks decided in advance; simple, but wastes space when a program is smaller than its block (internal fragmentation). Dynamic partitioning = partitions are created to fit each program's exact size; less waste inside, but leaves scattered gaps between programs over time (external fragmentation). Paged memory = memory is divided into equal-size frames and programs into equal-size pages that can be placed in any free frame, non-contiguously \u2014 which eliminates external fragmentation.

Fair use = a legal doctrine allowing limited use of copyrighted material without permission \u2014 for purposes like criticism, commentary, news reporting, teaching, or research. It's the main exception to copyright: quoting a short passage in a review is fair use; copying a whole book is not.

System software vs application software: system software runs and manages the computer itself and provides a platform for other programs \u2014 the operating system, device drivers, utilities. Application software is what you use to get tasks done \u2014 a browser, a word processor, a game. System software serves the machine; application software serves the user.

\n
\ud83d\udcdd EXAM WORDING

Single contiguous = one program + OS fill memory. Fixed partitioning = preset equal blocks (\u2192 internal fragmentation). Dynamic partitioning = sized to each program (\u2192 external fragmentation). Paged memory = equal pages in equal frames, non-contiguous (removes external fragmentation). Fair use = limited use of copyrighted work without permission (criticism, teaching, news). System software = runs the machine / platform for other software (OS, drivers); application software = user tasks (browser, word processor).

\n
\u26a0\ufe0f WATCH OUT

Fragmentation trap: fixed partitions waste space inside a block (internal); dynamic partitions leave gaps between blocks (external); paging is the fix for external fragmentation. And don't blur the software types \u2014 the operating system is system software, not application software.

\u2605 ON THE OA \u2014 WATCH FOR

System software (OS, drivers) manages the machine; application software does user tasks. The OS handles memory management (allocation, virtual memory, paging).

\u25b8 QUICK CHECK

An OS is system software; a spreadsheet is application software. Virtual memory gives each program its own large address space.

\ud83d\udcd6 Edge Computing (and where it fits next to the cloud)

Edge computing processes data close to where it\u2019s generated (on or near the device) instead of shipping everything to a distant cloud data center first.

WHY PUSH WORK TO THE EDGE?
\u2022 Lower latency: decisions in milliseconds, no round-trip to the cloud (a self-driving car can\u2019t wait).
\u2022 Less bandwidth: send summaries, not raw video/sensor floods.
\u2022 Works offline: keeps functioning when the connection drops.
Trade-off: edge devices have limited compute/storage \u2014 heavy analysis and long-term storage still live in the cloud. Edge and cloud are partners, not rivals.
WORKED EXAMPLE \u2014 sort the scenario
\u2022 A factory camera flags defective parts on the assembly line in real time \u2192 edge (latency-critical, high-volume video).
\u2022 The same factory runs monthly analytics over all plants\u2019 data \u2192 cloud (big compute, not time-critical).
\u2022 A smart doorbell detects motion locally but stores clips online \u2192 both: edge detection + cloud storage.
\u26a0\ufe0f EDGE \u2260 \u201cNO CLOUD\u201d
Edge computing doesn\u2019t replace the cloud \u2014 it filters and pre-processes near the source, then hands the important results to the cloud. If a question stresses \u201creal-time,\u201d \u201clow latency,\u201d or \u201creduce data sent,\u201d the answer is edge.
\ud83c\udfaf QUICK CHECK
Processing sensor data on the device itself to avoid network delay is called:
  1. Edge computing
  2. SaaS
  3. Batch processing
Show answer
A \u2014 edge computing. Compute happens at/near the data source for speed and bandwidth savings.

Cloud computing: SaaS, PaaS & IaaS

\n
\ud83d\udca1 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Cloud computing means renting computing over the internet instead of owning the hardware. The three service models are just about how much someone else manages for you. Think of getting dinner: cook it yourself from raw ingredients (most control, most work), use a meal kit (some done for you), or order delivery (you just eat). SaaS, PaaS, and IaaS are the same trade-off for software.

\n
\u2699\ufe0f WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service): you rent the raw building blocks \u2014 virtual machines, storage, networking \u2014 and manage the operating system and everything above it yourself. Most control, most responsibility. (Think: renting an empty kitchen.) Examples: AWS EC2, Google Compute Engine.

PaaS (Platform as a Service): you rent a ready-made platform to run your own code \u2014 the provider handles the servers, OS, and scaling; you just deploy your app. (The meal kit: ingredients prepped, you assemble.) Examples: Heroku, Google App Engine.

SaaS (Software as a Service): you use finished software in a browser and manage nothing but your own data and settings. (Delivery: you just eat.) Examples: Gmail, Google Docs, Netflix, Salesforce.

The rule of thumb: as you move IaaS \u2192 PaaS \u2192 SaaS, you manage less and the provider manages more.

Deployment models are a separate question \u2014 where the cloud lives: public cloud (shared, rented from a provider like AWS), private cloud (dedicated to one organization), and hybrid cloud (a mix of both).

\n
\ud83d\udcdd EXAM WORDING

IaaS = rent infrastructure (VMs/storage), you manage the OS & up. PaaS = rent a platform to run your own code, provider manages servers/OS. SaaS = use finished software in a browser (Gmail, Docs). Moving IaaS\u2192PaaS\u2192SaaS, you manage less. Deployment: public (shared), private (one org), hybrid (both). Cloud benefits: scalability, on-demand access, pay-for-what-you-use.

\n
\u26a0\ufe0f WATCH OUT

The tell-tale clues: \u201cfinished app in a browser\u201d = SaaS; \u201crun MY code without managing servers\u201d = PaaS; \u201crent VMs / full control of the OS\u201d = IaaS. Don't confuse the service model (SaaS/PaaS/IaaS = how much is managed) with the deployment model (public/private/hybrid = where it runs) \u2014 the exam mixes these.

\u2605 ON THE OA \u2014 WATCH FOR

Cloud service models: SaaS (ready software), PaaS (platform to build/deploy on), IaaS (raw compute/storage you manage).

\u25b8 QUICK CHECK

Gmail = SaaS; a managed app platform = PaaS; renting virtual machines = IaaS. More control = lower up the stack (IaaS).

Software licenses & the public domain

\n
\ud83d\udca1 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Copyright automatically protects whatever someone creates \u2014 but a license is the creator saying \u201chere's what YOU are allowed to do with it.\u201d Software licenses run on a spectrum from totally locked-down (proprietary) to totally free (public domain), with open-source licenses in the middle setting the rules for reuse.

\n
\u2699\ufe0f WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Proprietary: the owner keeps all rights; you buy a license to USE it but can't see or change the source (most commercial software).

Open-source licenses grant rights to use, modify, and share the source, with conditions. MIT license is very permissive \u2014 do almost anything, just keep the copyright notice. GNU GPL is \u201ccopyleft\u201d \u2014 you can reuse it, but anything you build on it must ALSO be open-source under the GPL.

Creative Commons (CC) licenses are for creative works (images, text, media), letting creators pick conditions like attribution or non-commercial use. Public domain means no copyright applies at all \u2014 anyone can use it freely for anything (either the creator waived rights, or the copyright expired).

\n
\ud83d\udcdd EXAM WORDING

Proprietary = closed, all rights reserved. MIT license = permissive open-source (keep the notice, do what you like). GNU GPL = copyleft (derivatives must stay open-source). Creative Commons = flexible licenses for creative works. Public domain = no copyright, free for all use.

\n
\u26a0\ufe0f WATCH OUT

The GPL's \u201ccopyleft\u201d is the classic trap: it's open-source, but it FORCES your derivative work to also be GPL open-source \u2014 unlike the permissive MIT license, which lets you do nearly anything, even in closed products. Public domain is not a \u201clicense\u201d so much as the absence of copyright.

\u2605 ON THE OA \u2014 WATCH FOR

Proprietary (closed), open-source \u2014 split into copyleft (GPL: derivatives must stay open) and permissive (MIT/Apache: few restrictions) \u2014 and public domain (no rights reserved).

\u25b8 QUICK CHECK

Ship a product built on GPL code and you must release your source under the GPL; MIT would not require that.

\ud83d\udcd6 Encryption Basics \u2014 Ciphers, Symmetric vs Asymmetric Keys

Encryption scrambles readable data (plaintext) into unreadable ciphertext using a key; decryption reverses it with a key. The exam wants the vocabulary and the symmetric/asymmetric distinction.

CLASSIC CIPHERS (the historical warm-up)
\u2022 Caesar cipher: shift every letter a fixed number of places (shift 3: A\u2192D, B\u2192E). Easy to break \u2014 only 25 shifts to try.
\u2022 Substitution cipher: replace each letter using a scrambled alphabet mapping. Broken by frequency analysis (E is the most common English letter, etc.).
These show WHY modern crypto uses math and long keys instead of letter tricks.
WORKED EXAMPLE 1 \u2014 Caesar shift of 3
Encrypt \u201cCAB\u201d with shift 3: C\u2192F, A\u2192D, B\u2192E \u2192 ciphertext \u201cFDE\u201d. Decrypt by shifting back 3. The \u201ckey\u201d is just the number 3.
SYMMETRIC vs ASYMMETRIC (the big distinction)
SymmetricAsymmetric (public-key)
KeysONE shared secret key \u2014 same key encrypts and decryptsTWO related keys \u2014 public key encrypts, private key decrypts
SpeedFastSlower
Hard partSharing the secret key safely with the other sideNone \u2014 the public key can be posted openly
ExamplesAESRSA
Real systems combine them: asymmetric to exchange a key, then fast symmetric for the data (this is how HTTPS works).
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 \u2014 who can read the message?
Amara publishes her public key. Ben encrypts a message with it and sends it. Only Amara\u2019s private key can decrypt \u2014 so even if the message is intercepted, only Amara reads it. Notice Ben and Amara never had to meet to share a secret \u2014 that\u2019s the point of asymmetric encryption.
\u26a0\ufe0f PUBLIC ENCRYPTS, PRIVATE DECRYPTS
In public-key crypto, the key that scrambles a message TO you is the one everybody can see (public); the one that unscrambles is the one only you hold (private). If a question says \u201cone shared key,\u201d it\u2019s symmetric; \u201ckey pair\u201d means asymmetric.
\ud83c\udfaf QUICK CHECK
Encryption that uses the SAME key to encrypt and decrypt is called:
  1. Symmetric
  2. Asymmetric
  3. Hashing
Show answer
A \u2014 symmetric. One shared secret key both ways. Asymmetric uses a public/private key pair.
\n\n
\ud83d\udcd6 Full lesson \u2014 every definition & detail (tap to collapse)

Digital forensics, surveillance & decryption

\n
\ud83d\udca1 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

When something goes wrong \u2014 a breach, a crime, misuse \u2014 someone has to reconstruct what happened from the digital traces. That's digital forensics. Surveillance is the ongoing monitoring of activity, and encryption/decryption is the lock-and-key that keeps data private in between.

\n
\u2699\ufe0f WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Digital forensics is the recovery, preservation, and analysis of digital evidence (files, logs, deleted data, metadata) \u2014 done carefully so it holds up in an investigation or court.

Surveillance is the monitoring of behavior or communications \u2014 from network logging to camera systems. It raises real privacy and ethics questions about consent and proportionality (a core ACM Code of Ethics concern).

Encryption scrambles readable data (plaintext) into unreadable ciphertext using a key; decryption is the reverse \u2014 using the key to turn ciphertext back into readable plaintext. Only someone with the correct key should be able to decrypt.

\n
\ud83d\udcdd EXAM WORDING

Digital forensics = recovering and analyzing digital evidence. Surveillance = monitoring activity/communications (a privacy & ethics issue). Encryption converts plaintext \u2192 ciphertext; Decryption converts ciphertext \u2192 plaintext with the key. Confidentiality depends on keeping the decryption key secret.

\n
\u26a0\ufe0f WATCH OUT

Encryption and decryption are opposite halves of the same system \u2014 encryption locks, decryption unlocks, and both need the right key. Surveillance is ethically sensitive: the ACM Code stresses respecting privacy, so \u201cbecause we can\u201d is never sufficient justification.

\u2605 ON THE OA \u2014 WATCH FOR

Digital forensics preserves evidence with a documented chain of custody. Encryption protects data; a warrant/authority is typically required to decrypt or surveil lawfully.

\u25b8 QUICK CHECK

Altering original evidence breaks the chain of custody \u2014 investigators work on verified copies (hashes match).

\ud83d\udcd6 Octal & Hex \u2014 the other two bases you must convert

Besides binary (base 2) and decimal (base 10), the exam uses octal (base 8) and hexadecimal (base 16). Same place-value idea, different base.

THE FOUR BASES AT A GLANCE
BaseDigitsPlace values
Binary (2)0\u20131\u20268, 4, 2, 1
Octal (8)0\u20137\u2026512, 64, 8, 1
Decimal (10)0\u20139\u20261000, 100, 10, 1
Hex (16)0\u20139, A\u2013F (A=10\u2026F=15)\u20264096, 256, 16, 1
WORKED EXAMPLE 1 \u2014 octal to decimal
Octal 127 = 1\u00b764 + 2\u00b78 + 7\u00b71 = 64 + 16 + 7 = 87. (Careful: the digit 8 never appears in octal \u2014 \u201c128\u201d is not a valid octal number.)
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 \u2014 the 3-bit / 4-bit grouping trick
Binary groups convert instantly:
\u2022 Octal = groups of 3 bits. 110101\u2082 \u2192 110|101 \u2192 6 and 5 \u2192 octal 65.
\u2022 Hex = groups of 4 bits. 11010110\u2082 \u2192 1101|0110 \u2192 D and 6 \u2192 hex D6.
That\u2019s why programmers like octal/hex: they\u2019re shorthand for binary.
\u26a0\ufe0f GROUP FROM THE RIGHT
When splitting binary into 3-bit (octal) or 4-bit (hex) groups, start from the right end and pad the leftmost group with leading zeros if needed. Grouping from the left gives wrong digits.
\ud83c\udfaf QUICK CHECK
Octal 34 in decimal is:
  1. 28
  2. 34
  3. 26
Show answer
A \u2014 28. 3\u00b78 + 4\u00b71 = 24 + 4 = 28.
\n\n
\ud83d\udcd6 Full lesson \u2014 every definition & detail (tap to collapse)

Why binary? Place value in any base

\n
\ud83d\udca1 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A computer is millions of tiny switches, and a switch has exactly two states: on or off. So the machine can only \u201ccount\u201d with two symbols, 0 and 1 \u2014 that's binary. Everything else (numbers, letters, images, sound) is ultimately a pattern of those on/off switches.

\n
\u2699\ufe0f WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Decimal (base 10) uses place values that are powers of ten: 1, 10, 100, 1000\u2026 The number 305 means 3\u00d7100 + 0\u00d710 + 5\u00d71. Binary works the same way, but the places are powers of two: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32\u2026

So binary 101101 = 1\u00d732 + 0\u00d716 + 1\u00d78 + 1\u00d74 + 0\u00d72 + 1\u00d71 = 45. To go the other way (decimal \u2192 binary), keep subtracting the largest power of two that fits, or repeatedly divide by 2 and read the remainders bottom-to-top.

Hexadecimal (base 16) is just shorthand for binary: one hex digit = exactly four binary digits, because 2\u2074 = 16. That's why programmers use it \u2014 compact and clean to convert.

\n
\ud83d\udcdd EXAM WORDING

Bit = one binary digit (0 or 1). Byte = 8 bits. A question may ask you to \u201cconvert 0x2F to decimal\u201d (hex 2F = 2\u00d716 + 15 = 47) or the \u201cnumber of distinct values n bits can represent\u201d \u2014 that's always 2\u207f. Know that 2\u00b9\u2070 = 1024.

\n
\u26a0\ufe0f WATCH OUT

Hex digits go 0\u20139 then A\u2013F, where A=10, B=11, C=12, D=13, E=14, F=15. Also: n bits give 2\u207f values, but the largest value is 2\u207f \u2212 1 (because one value is zero).

\u2605 ON THE OA \u2014 WATCH FOR

Place value works in any base: base-2 (binary) uses powers of 2, base-16 (hex) powers of 16. Convert binary\u2192decimal by adding the place values of the 1 bits.

\u25b8 QUICK CHECK

1011\u2082 = 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11\u2081\u2080. And 13\u2081\u2080 = 1101\u2082 (8+4+1).

\n

\u2796 Two's Complement: Storing Negatives

\n
THE RECIPE
Computers have no minus sign. To negate a number: flip every bit, then add 1. The leftmost bit becomes the sign bit: 0 = positive, 1 = negative.
\n
WORKED EXAMPLE \u2014 build \u22125 in 8 bits
\n\n\n\n
StepBits
+500000101
Flip11111010
Add 111111011 = \u22125
\nWhy bother? 5 + (\u22125) with plain binary addition = 00000000 (the carry falls off the end) \u2014 zero, exactly right. The hardware never needs a separate subtract circuit.
\n\n\n
FactValue
8-bit signed range\u2212128 to +127
n-bit signed range\u22122\u207f\u207b\u00b9 to 2\u207f\u207b\u00b9 \u2212 1
\n
\u26a0\ufe0f TWO TRAPS
The negative range goes ONE further than the positive (\u2212128 but only +127) because zero eats a positive slot. And don't confuse two's complement (flip + add 1) with one's complement (just flip).
\n
\ud83c\udfaf OA-STYLE CHECK
How are signed integers represented in nearly every computer?\n
  1. Two's complement
  2. One's complement
  3. Sign-and-magnitude only
  4. BCD
\n
Show answer + steps
A. \"Invert the bits and add one\" \u2014 subtraction becomes addition, one representation of zero.
\n
\n
\ud83d\udcd6 Full lesson \u2014 every definition & detail (tap to collapse)

Two's complement: storing negatives

\n
\ud83d\udca1 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Computers have no minus sign \u2014 only 0s and 1s. So how do you store \u22125? The trick: give up the top bit to mean \u201cnegative,\u201d and store negatives so that subtraction just works as addition. That scheme is two's complement, and nearly every computer uses it.

\n
\u2699\ufe0f WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

To get the negative of a number: flip every bit, then add 1. In 8 bits: +5 is 00000101. Flip \u2192 11111010. Add 1 \u2192 11111011. That's \u22125.

Why bother? Because 5 + (\u22125) done with plain binary addition gives 00000000 (the carry falls off the end) \u2014 zero, exactly right. The hardware never needs a separate \u201csubtract\u201d circuit; it just adds the two's-complement form.

The leftmost bit is the sign bit: 0 means positive, 1 means negative.

\n
\ud83d\udcdd EXAM WORDING

\u201cTwo's complement\u201d is the standard answer for how signed integers are represented. The recipe \u201cinvert the bits and add one\u201d is common phrasing. An 8-bit signed range is \u2212128 to +127; n bits signed is \u22122\u207f\u207b\u00b9 to 2\u207f\u207b\u00b9\u22121.

\n
\u26a0\ufe0f WATCH OUT

The negative range goes one further than the positive (\u2212128 but only +127) because zero eats a positive slot. Don't confuse two's complement (flip + add 1) with one's complement (just flip).

\u2605 ON THE OA \u2014 WATCH FOR

Two's complement stores negatives so one circuit adds both signs. To negate: flip all bits, then add 1. The leftmost bit is the sign (1 = negative).

\u25b8 QUICK CHECK

In 8-bit two's complement, \u22121 = 11111111 and 0 = 00000000. The value \u22121 is always 'all ones'.

\ud83d\udcd6 More Gates (NAND, NOR, XOR) & Short-Circuit Evaluation

Two add-ons the test asks about beyond AND/OR/NOT: the combined gates, and how programming languages short-circuit Boolean expressions.

THE COMBINED GATES
\u2022 NAND = NOT-AND: output 0 only when both inputs are 1 (otherwise 1).
\u2022 NOR = NOT-OR: output 1 only when both inputs are 0.
\u2022 XOR (exclusive OR): output 1 when the inputs differ (exactly one is 1). 1\u22951 = 0!
NAND and NOR are universal gates \u2014 either one alone can build every other gate, which is why chips are full of them.
WORKED EXAMPLE 1 \u2014 XOR by table
aba XOR b
000
011
101
110
\u201cOne or the other but NOT both.\u201d XOR is used for parity checks and simple encryption (x \u2295 key \u2295 key = x).
SHORT-CIRCUIT EVALUATION
Languages evaluate Boolean expressions left to right and stop as soon as the answer is decided:
\u2022 In A AND B: if A is false, the whole thing is false \u2014 B is never evaluated.
\u2022 In A OR B: if A is true, the whole thing is true \u2014 B is skipped.
Programmers exploit this for safety: if (x != 0 AND 10/x > 2) never divides by zero, because when x is 0 the division is skipped.
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 \u2014 what gets evaluated?
With count = 0:  if (count > 0 AND total/count > 5).
count > 0 is false \u2192 AND short-circuits \u2192 total/count never runs \u2192 no crash. Reverse the order and it divides by zero. Order matters!
\u26a0\ufe0f XOR OF TWO TRUES IS FALSE
The most-missed row: 1 XOR 1 = 0. XOR means exclusively one. And in short-circuit questions, ask \u201ccan the left side alone decide?\u201d \u2014 if yes, the right side is skipped.
\ud83c\udfaf QUICK CHECK
In the expression (FALSE AND X), what happens to X under short-circuit evaluation?
  1. X is never evaluated \u2014 the result is already FALSE
  2. X is evaluated anyway
  3. The program crashes
Show answer
A. FALSE AND anything = FALSE, so evaluation stops at the left operand.
\n\n

Boolean logic & truth tables

\n
\ud83d\udca1 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Underneath every program is true/false logic. Boolean logic is just the rules for combining true/false values with three basic operations: AND, OR, and NOT. If you can read a truth table, you can predict what any combination does.

\n
\u2699\ufe0f WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

AND is true only when BOTH inputs are true. OR is true when AT LEAST ONE is true. NOT flips the value. XOR (exclusive or) is true when the inputs DIFFER.

These map directly to physical logic gates in the CPU \u2014 an AND gate outputs 1 only when both wires carry 1. Complex circuits (adders, memory) are built from thousands of these.

\n
\ud83d\udcdd EXAM WORDING

Know the truth tables cold. A AND B = A\u2227B; A OR B = A\u2228B; NOT A = \u00acA. De Morgan's laws appear constantly: NOT(A AND B) = (NOT A) OR (NOT B), and NOT(A OR B) = (NOT A) AND (NOT B).

\n
\u26a0\ufe0f WATCH OUT

The classic trap: OR in logic is inclusive \u2014 \u201cA or B\u201d is still true when BOTH are true. Everyday English often means \u201cone or the other but not both\u201d \u2014 that \u201cexactly one\u201d meaning is XOR.

\u2605 ON THE OA \u2014 WATCH FOR

Boolean logic: AND (true only if both), OR (true if at least one), NOT (invert). A truth table with n inputs has 2\u207f rows.

\u25b8 QUICK CHECK

3 inputs \u2192 2\u00b3 = 8 rows. NAND = NOT(AND); its output is 0 only when both inputs are 1.

\n
THE LOOP \u2014 billions of times a second
fetch \u2192 decode \u2192 execute

\nregisters \u2192 cache \u2192 RAM \u2192 disk
\nRegisters: tiny, ultra-fast slots INSIDE the CPU for values in use right now. RAM: larger but slower. CPU speed = the clock rate (GHz).

\u26a0\ufe0f MEMORY vs STORAGE
Memory (RAM) is temporary and clears on power-off (volatile). Storage (disk/SSD) persists. And registers live inside the CPU \u2014 they are NOT RAM.

How the CPU runs your program

\n
\ud83d\udca1 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A program is just a list of tiny instructions in memory. The CPU does one boringly simple loop, billions of times a second: get the next instruction, figure out what it means, do it, repeat. That loop is the whole show.

\n
\u2699\ufe0f WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

The loop is fetch\u2013decode\u2013execute. Fetch: copy the next instruction from memory (RAM) into the CPU. Decode: the control unit works out what it is. Execute: the ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit) does the math/logic and stores the result.

Registers are tiny, ultra-fast storage slots inside the CPU for the values in use right now. RAM is larger but slower. This is the memory hierarchy: registers \u2192 cache \u2192 RAM \u2192 disk, getting bigger and slower each step.

\n
\ud83d\udcdd EXAM WORDING

The \u201cfetch-decode-execute cycle\u201d is how a CPU processes instructions. The ALU does arithmetic/logic; the control unit directs traffic; registers hold operands. CPU speed is the clock rate (GHz).

\n
\u26a0\ufe0f WATCH OUT

Don't mix up memory (RAM) \u2014 temporary, clears on power-off (volatile) \u2014 with storage (disk/SSD), which persists. Registers are inside the CPU; they are not RAM.

\u2605 ON THE OA \u2014 WATCH FOR

The CPU runs the fetch\u2013decode\u2013execute cycle. The program counter (PC) holds the address of the NEXT instruction; the control unit directs, the ALU computes.

\u25b8 QUICK CHECK

Each cycle: fetch the instruction at the PC \u2192 decode it \u2192 execute it \u2192 advance the PC.

Compiled vs. interpreted

A compiler translates the whole program to machine code BEFORE it runs (fast execution, errors surface up front); an interpreter translates and runs line by line (slower, more flexible). Java does both: source compiles to bytecode, and the JVM runs that.

Abstraction = hiding unnecessary detail to reduce complexity, exposing only what's needed. You drive a car without knowing engine internals \u2014 same idea. Arguably the most important idea in all of CS.

Abstraction: hiding complexity

\n
\ud83d\udca1 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Nobody could build an app if they had to think about individual transistors. Computing is built in layers, where each layer hides the messy details of the one below and offers a simpler interface. You drive a car without knowing the engine internals \u2014 same idea. That hiding is abstraction, arguably the most important idea in all of CS.

\n
\u2699\ufe0f WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

From the bottom up: hardware (transistors, gates) \u2192 machine code (raw binary) \u2192 operating system (manages hardware, offers files/processes) \u2192 high-level languages (Java, Python) \u2192 applications. Each layer trusts the one below to \u201cjust work\u201d and exposes cleaner tools upward.

\n
\ud83d\udcdd EXAM WORDING

Abstraction = hiding unnecessary detail to reduce complexity, exposing only what's needed. An interface is the agreed set of operations a layer offers; encapsulation (you'll meet it in Java) is bundling data with the operations on it and hiding internals.

\n
\u26a0\ufe0f WATCH OUT

Abstraction is about hiding detail, not \u201cmaking something vague.\u201d On the exam it's a positive, deliberate design tool \u2014 the reason large systems are buildable at all.

\u2605 ON THE OA \u2014 WATCH FOR

Abstraction hides complexity behind a simple interface \u2014 you use what without knowing how. It's the key idea behind functions, ADTs, and layered systems.

\u25b8 QUICK CHECK

Calling sort(list) sorts without you knowing the algorithm inside \u2014 the implementation is abstracted away.

Functions, scope & recursion

A function hides its inner steps behind one name — abstraction in action. A variable declared inside a function has local scope (visible only there); one declared outside every function is global. A recursive function calls itself; each call stacks up memory, so a missing or unreachable base case overflows the call stack.

Big-O: how algorithms scale

\n
\ud83d\udca1 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Two programs can both be \u201ccorrect\u201d but one takes a second and the other a week on the same data. Big-O describes how an algorithm's work grows as the input gets bigger \u2014 not the exact time, just the shape of the growth. It answers: \u201cif I double the data, does the work double, quadruple, or barely change?\u201d

\n
\u2699\ufe0f WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

O(1) constant: same work regardless of size. O(log n) logarithmic: halves the problem each step (binary search); barely grows. O(n) linear: work grows in step with data.

O(n log n): good sorting. O(n\u00b2) quadratic: nested loops; doubling input quadruples work. O(2\u207f) exponential: explodes, usually impractical.

\n
\ud83d\udcdd EXAM WORDING

Big-O describes worst-case time (or space) complexity as n grows. Order best\u2192worst: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n\u00b2) < O(2\u207f). Binary search is O(log n); a simple nested loop is O(n\u00b2).

\n
\u26a0\ufe0f WATCH OUT

Big-O ignores constants and small terms \u2014 O(2n + 100) is just O(n). It's the growth trend for large inputs, not stopwatch time on small ones. Bigger-O = \u201cscales worse,\u201d not \u201cslower right now.\u201d

\u2605 ON THE OA \u2014 WATCH FOR

Big-O describes how work grows with input size. Ranking best\u2192worst: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n\u00b2) < O(2\u207f). Drop constants and lower-order terms.

\u25b8 QUICK CHECK

A loop inside a loop, each over n, is O(n\u00b2). Halving the input each step (binary search) is O(log n).

\ud83d\udcd6 Compression Techniques \u2014 Run-Length, Keyword & Huffman

Compression shrinks files. Lossless methods let you rebuild the original exactly (text, code, spreadsheets); lossy methods throw away detail people barely notice (JPEG photos, MP3 audio). Know the three named lossless techniques:

THE THREE LOSSLESS TECHNIQUES
\u2022 Run-length encoding (RLE): replace a repeated run of the same character with one copy + a count. Best when data has long runs.
\u2022 Keyword encoding: replace frequent whole words with short symbols (\u201cthe\u201d \u2192 ~, \u201cand\u201d \u2192 +). A lookup table maps symbols back.
\u2022 Huffman coding: give frequent characters short bit codes and rare characters longer codes. Frequency-based, provably efficient.
WORKED EXAMPLE 1 \u2014 run-length encoding
AAAAABBBCC \u2192 5A3B2C: 10 characters stored as 6. But on text with no runs (ABCABC), RLE saves nothing \u2014 technique must match the data.
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 \u2014 Huffman by hand
Codes: A = 0, B = 10, C = 110, D = 111 (A is most frequent, so shortest).
Encode \u201cABAD\u201d: 0\u00b710\u00b70\u00b7111 \u2192 0100111 = 7 bits, vs 32 bits in 8-bit ASCII.
Decode 010110: 0=A, 10=B, 110=C \u2192 \u201cABC.\u201d No code is a prefix of another, so decoding is never ambiguous.
COMPRESSION RATIO
Ratio = compressed size \u00f7 original size. A 500 KB file compressed to 100 KB has ratio 100/500 = 0.2 (or \u201c5:1\u201d). Smaller ratio = better squeeze. Lossless ratios are limited by the data\u2019s redundancy; lossy can go much smaller because it discards information permanently.
\u26a0\ufe0f MATCH TECHNIQUE TO CLUE WORDS
\u201cLong runs of repeated characters\u201d \u2192 RLE. \u201cCommon words replaced by symbols\u201d \u2192 keyword encoding. \u201cMost frequent characters get the shortest codes\u201d \u2192 Huffman. \u201cOpens identical to the original\u201d \u2192 lossless; \u201csome quality lost forever\u201d \u2192 lossy.
\ud83c\udfaf QUICK CHECK
Which technique assigns the SHORTEST bit patterns to the MOST frequent characters?
  1. Huffman coding
  2. Run-length encoding
  3. Lossy compression
Show answer
A \u2014 Huffman coding. It builds codes from character frequencies: common = short, rare = long.
\n\n

Data representation: text, floats & media

\n
\ud83d\udca1 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Binary integers are the easy case. But how does a computer store the letter 'A', the number 3.14, or a photo? The answer is always the same trick: agree on a code that maps the thing to a pattern of bits. Text uses a character-code table; decimals use a scientific-notation-in-binary scheme; images/sound are just huge grids of numbers.

\n
\u2699\ufe0f WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Text: each character maps to a number via a table. ASCII uses 7\u20138 bits (128\u2013256 characters, English + symbols); Unicode/UTF-8 extends this to every language and emoji. 'A' is 65, 'a' is 97, '0' the character is 48.

Floating point: decimals are stored like binary scientific notation \u2014 a sign, a mantissa (the digits), and an exponent (where the point goes). This is why 0.1 + 0.2 isn't exactly 0.3 \u2014 some decimals can't be represented exactly in binary.

Images/sound: an image is a grid of pixels, each a number for its color (RGB); sound is a stream of numbers sampling the wave. More bits = more detail = bigger files.

\n
\ud83d\udcdd EXAM WORDING

ASCII encodes characters in 7\u20138 bits; Unicode (often UTF-8) covers all languages. Floating-point numbers have a sign, mantissa, and exponent. Know that floats are approximate \u2014 rounding error is expected. Digital media is discrete samples of continuous signals.

\n
\u26a0\ufe0f WATCH OUT

The character '5' is not the number 5 \u2014 '5' is ASCII 53. And floating-point numbers can't represent every decimal exactly, so never test floats with ==; compare within a small tolerance.

\u2605 ON THE OA \u2014 WATCH FOR

Everything is bits: text via ASCII/Unicode code points, numbers via integer/floating-point (IEEE 754), images as pixels, sound as samples.

\u25b8 QUICK CHECK

If 'A' = 65 in ASCII, then 'C' = 67. More bits per sample/pixel = higher fidelity and larger files.

\ud83d\udcd6 Hash Tables & Recursion \u2014 two algorithm ideas that appear on the OA

HASH TABLES \u2014 jump straight to the data
A hash table stores key\u2192value pairs. A hash function converts the key into an array index, so lookup is (on average) O(1) \u2014 no searching at all.
\u2022 Collision = two keys hash to the same index. It\u2019s normal, and handled by chaining (keep a list at that slot) or probing (try the next open slot).
\u2022 A good hash function spreads keys evenly; a terrible one sends everything to one slot and lookups degrade toward O(n).
WORKED EXAMPLE 1 \u2014 a tiny hash table
Table size 10; hash(key) = key mod 10. Insert 27 \u2192 slot 7. Insert 42 \u2192 slot 2. Insert 37 \u2192 slot 7 \u2014 collision with 27! With chaining, slot 7 holds a small list [27, 37]. Lookup of 37: hash to 7, scan the 2-item list. Still nearly instant.
RECURSION \u2014 a function that calls itself
Recursion solves a problem by solving a smaller copy of itself. Every correct recursive function needs:
1. A base case \u2014 the smallest input, answered directly (no call). This stops the recursion.
2. A recursive case \u2014 do a step, then call yourself on a smaller input.
Miss the base case (or never shrink the input) and you recurse forever \u2192 stack overflow.
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 \u2014 factorial, traced
factorial(n): if n \u2264 1 return 1 (base); else return n \u00d7 factorial(n \u2212 1).
factorial(4) = 4 \u00d7 factorial(3) = 4 \u00d7 3 \u00d7 factorial(2) = 4 \u00d7 3 \u00d7 2 \u00d7 factorial(1) = 4\u00d73\u00d72\u00d71 = 24.
Each call waits on the smaller one; the base case ends the chain and the answers multiply on the way back up.
\u26a0\ufe0f THE BASE CASE IS NOT OPTIONAL
\u201cWhat is wrong with this recursive function?\u201d \u2014 the answer is nearly always missing/unreachable base case (infinite recursion \u2192 stack overflow). And any recursion can be rewritten as a loop (iteration); recursion trades memory (the call stack) for elegance.
\ud83c\udfaf QUICK CHECK
Two different keys hashing to the same table index is called:
  1. A collision
  2. An overflow
  3. A deadlock
Show answer
A \u2014 a collision. Handled by chaining (a list per slot) or probing (next free slot).
\n\n
\ud83d\udcd6 Full lesson \u2014 every definition & detail (tap to collapse)

Searching & sorting algorithms

\n
\ud83d\udca1 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Two everyday jobs: find something in a list, and put a list in order. There are simple, slow ways and clever, fast ways. The exam wants you to know which is which and roughly how fast each is \u2014 this is where Big-O becomes concrete.

\n
\u2699\ufe0f WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Linear search checks each item one by one \u2014 works on any list, O(n). Binary search repeatedly halves a SORTED list \u2014 O(log n), much faster, but only works if the data is already sorted.

Simple sorts (bubble, selection, insertion) are easy but O(n\u00b2) \u2014 fine for small lists. Efficient sorts (merge sort, quicksort) are O(n log n) \u2014 the go-to for large data. Merge sort splits, sorts halves, and merges; quicksort partitions around a pivot.

\n
\ud83d\udcdd EXAM WORDING

Linear search = O(n), works unsorted; binary search = O(log n), requires a sorted list. Bubble/selection/insertion sort = O(n\u00b2); merge sort and quicksort = O(n log n). \u201cWhich sort is fastest for large data?\u201d \u2192 the O(n log n) ones.

\n
\u26a0\ufe0f WATCH OUT

Binary search ONLY works on sorted data \u2014 that's the #1 trap. And a sort being \u201csimple\u201d (bubble sort) does not make it efficient; simple usually means O(n\u00b2).

\u2605 ON THE OA \u2014 WATCH FOR

Linear search O(n) works on any list; binary search O(log n) requires a SORTED list. Sorts: bubble/selection/insertion O(n\u00b2); merge sort O(n log n).

\u25b8 QUICK CHECK

Binary search on 1000 sorted items needs \u2248 10 comparisons (log\u2082 1000 \u2248 10), vs up to 1000 for linear search.

\ud83d\udcda Extra review \u2014 1 alternate explanation & recall cards (tap to open)

\n

Binary search ONLY works on sorted data. And \"simple\" (bubble sort) does not mean efficient \u2014 simple usually means O(n\u00b2).

Queues

A queue is first-in-first-out (FIFO) — the opposite of a stack’s last-in-first-out (LIFO). Think checkout line vs. plate stack.

\ud83d\udcd6 The Network MODELS \u2014 OSI (7 layers) & TCP/IP (4 layers)

Exams love these. A network model is a layered blueprint of how data travels: each layer does ONE job and hands the data to the next layer. Two models to know: the 7-layer OSI model (the theory) and the 4-layer TCP/IP model (what the real Internet uses).

THE OSI MODEL \u2014 7 layers, top to bottom
#LayerJob (plain words)Examples
7ApplicationWhat the user\u2019s program seesHTTP, email
6PresentationFormat/translate data (encryption, compression)SSL, JPEG
5SessionOpen/manage/close conversationslogins, sessions
4TransportDeliver reliably end-to-end, in orderTCP, UDP
3NetworkRoute packets between networks (addresses)IP, routers
2Data LinkMove frames on one local linkEthernet, MAC, switches
1PhysicalRaw bits on the wire/aircables, radio, hubs
Memory hook (bottom-up): Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away.
THE TCP/IP MODEL \u2014 4 layers (the practical one)
TCP/IP layerCovers OSI layersKey players
Application7, 6, 5HTTP, DNS, email (SMTP)
Transport4TCP (reliable), UDP (fast)
Internet3IP addresses, routing
Network Interface (Link)2, 1Ethernet, Wi-Fi, MAC
Same ideas, fewer boxes. When a question says \u201cthe TCP/IP suite,\u201d think this 4-layer stack.
WORKED EXAMPLE \u2014 follow one web request down the stack
You load a page: the browser makes an HTTP request (Application) \u2192 TCP breaks it into ordered, tracked segments (Transport) \u2192 IP addresses each packet to the server and routers pick the path (Internet/Network) \u2192 Ethernet/Wi-Fi turns packets into frames and bits on your local link (Link/Physical). At the server, the layers unwrap in reverse.
TCP vs UDP (the transport-layer choice)
\u2022 TCP: connection-based, reliable \u2014 every packet acknowledged, lost ones resent, order guaranteed. Use for web pages, email, files.
\u2022 UDP: connectionless, fast but best-effort \u2014 no resends, no ordering. Use for live video, gaming, voice calls, where a late packet is worse than a lost one.
MAC ADDRESS vs IP ADDRESS
\u2022 MAC address = the hardware ID burned into a network card (like a serial number). Works at the Data Link layer, only on the local network. Format: six hex pairs, e.g. 3C:2A:F4:1B:9E:07.
\u2022 IP address = the logical, changeable address used to route between networks (Network/Internet layer), e.g. 192.168.1.10.
Analogy: MAC = your fingerprint (permanent, identifies the device); IP = your mailing address (changes when you move networks).
\u26a0\ufe0f MATCH THE JOB TO THE LAYER
Routing/IP \u2192 Network (Internet) layer. Reliability/ordering \u2192 Transport (TCP). MAC/frames/switches \u2192 Data Link. Cables and radio \u2192 Physical. If a question asks \u201cwhich layer\u2026,\u201d find the job word (route, deliver reliably, frame, transmit bits) and map it.
\ud83c\udfaf QUICK CHECK
Which layer of the TCP/IP model is responsible for reliable, in-order delivery?
  1. Transport (TCP)
  2. Internet (IP)
  3. Network Interface
Show answer
A \u2014 Transport. TCP acknowledges, resends, and orders packets. IP just routes; the link layer just moves frames locally.
\n\n
\ud83d\udcd6 Full lesson \u2014 every definition & detail (tap to collapse)

Networking & the internet

\n
\ud83d\udca1 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

The internet is just an enormous number of computers passing messages. To make that work, every machine needs an address, messages get broken into labeled chunks, and everyone agrees on rules (protocols) for how to talk. Most of it follows a \u201cclient asks, server answers\u201d pattern.

\n
\u2699\ufe0f WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

IP address = a computer's numeric address. DNS is the phonebook that turns a name (google.com) into an IP. Data travels in packets \u2014 small labeled chunks reassembled at the destination.

Protocols are agreed rules: HTTP/HTTPS for web pages, TCP/IP for reliable delivery, DNS for name lookup. The client\u2013server model: your browser (client) requests, a server responds.

\n
\ud83d\udcdd EXAM WORDING

IP address identifies a device; DNS maps names \u2192 IP addresses; data moves in packets. HTTP/HTTPS = web, TCP = reliable transport. The client\u2013server model = requester and responder. HTTPS adds encryption.

\n
\u26a0\ufe0f WATCH OUT

DNS resolves names to addresses \u2014 it is not where the webpage lives. And a URL, a domain name, and an IP address are three different things that point at the same destination.

\u2605 ON THE OA \u2014 WATCH FOR

Data travels the Internet in packets, routed by shared protocols (TCP/IP, HTTP). An IP address identifies a device; DNS maps names to IPs.

\u25b8 QUICK CHECK

Typing a URL: DNS translates the domain name \u2192 IP address, then packets route to that address and reassemble.

\ud83d\udcda Extra review \u2014 1 alternate explanation & recall cards (tap to open)
\n

\ud83c\udf10 Networking & the Internet

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
TermDefinition
IP addressA computer's numeric address \u2014 identifies a device
DNSThe \"phonebook\" that turns a name (google.com) into an IP
PacketsSmall labeled chunks of data, reassembled at the destination
HTTP/HTTPSProtocol for web pages \u2014 HTTPS adds encryption
TCP/IPReliable delivery/transport rules
Client\u2013server modelYour browser (client) requests; a server responds
\n
WORKED EXAMPLE \u2014 loading a page
\nBrowser asks DNS for the IP of the name \u2192 sends an HTTP(S) request to that server \u2192 the response comes back in packets \u2192 reassembled into the page.
\n
\u26a0\ufe0f DNS RESOLVES, IT DOESN'T HOST
DNS maps names to addresses \u2014 it is NOT where the webpage lives. A URL, a domain name, and an IP address are three different things pointing at the same destination.
\n
\ud83c\udfaf OA-STYLE CHECK
What does DNS do?\n
  1. Maps domain names to IP addresses
  2. Hosts webpages
  3. Encrypts traffic
  4. Splits data into packets
\n
Show answer + steps
A. It's the internet's phonebook \u2014 lookup only.
\n

Latency, bandwidth & status codes

Latency is the DELAY of one round trip (ms); bandwidth is CAPACITY per second (Mbps). A wider pipe doesn’t make a single drop arrive sooner. HTTP status codes worth knowing: 200 OK · 404 not found · 500 server error.

"}, "D684/concepts/s10": {"body": "

\ud83d\udcd6 The SDLC Process MODELS \u2014 Waterfall, Agile, Iterative, Spiral, Prototyping

Knowing the SDLC steps isn\u2019t enough \u2014 exams also ask about the models: different strategies for moving through those steps. Each model answers \u201chow do we organize the work?\u201d differently.

THE FIVE MODELS TO KNOW
ModelHow it worksBest whenWeakness
WaterfallFinish each phase completely, then flow down to the next \u2014 no going backRequirements are fixed & well understoodRigid; errors found late are costly
AgileShort cycles (sprints, ~2 weeks) each delivering working software; constant customer feedbackRequirements change oftenLess predictable schedule/docs
Iterative/IncrementalBuild a small working version, then repeatedly improve and add piecesYou want usable software earlyArchitecture may need rework
SpiralLoops of plan \u2192 assess risk \u2192 build \u2192 evaluate; each loop grows the productLarge, high-risk projectsComplex and costly to manage
PrototypingBuild a quick throwaway mock-up to nail down requirements before real developmentUsers aren\u2019t sure what they wantPrototype may get mistaken for the product
WORKED EXAMPLE \u2014 pick the model from the scenario
\u2022 \u201cA government contract with fully specified, unchanging requirements and formal sign-offs at each phase\u201d \u2192 Waterfall.
\u2022 \u201cA startup wants to ship features every two weeks and adjust to user feedback\u201d \u2192 Agile (sprints, stand-ups, Scrum).
\u2022 \u201cA huge banking system where failure is catastrophic; managers demand explicit risk analysis every cycle\u201d \u2192 Spiral (its signature = risk assessment each loop).
\u2022 \u201cUsers can\u2019t articulate what they need, so the team mocks up screens to explore\u201d \u2192 Prototyping.
AGILE VOCABULARY (Scrum terms)
\u2022 Sprint: a short fixed-length work cycle (usually 1\u20134 weeks) ending in working software.
\u2022 Scrum: the most popular Agile framework \u2014 daily stand-up meetings, a product backlog of features, a Scrum Master who clears blockers.
\u2022 User story: a requirement written from the user\u2019s view (\u201cAs a student, I want\u2026\u201d).
TESTING TYPES (the other exam favorite)
\u2022 Unit testing \u2014 test one small piece (a single function/module) in isolation. First and lowest level.
\u2022 Integration testing \u2014 test that modules work together (interfaces between units).
\u2022 System testing \u2014 test the complete assembled system against requirements.
\u2022 Acceptance testing \u2014 the customer/user verifies the software meets their needs (last gate before release).
\u2022 Black-box testing \u2014 tester sees only inputs and outputs, not the code (tests behavior/spec).
\u2022 White-box testing \u2014 tester sees the code and exercises specific paths/branches inside it.
\u2022 Regression testing \u2014 re-run old tests after a change to be sure nothing that used to work broke.
\u26a0\ufe0f THE TWO MOST-MISSED DISTINCTIONS
1) Waterfall vs Agile: waterfall = one pass, no revisiting; agile = many short cycles with feedback. If the scenario mentions changing requirements or sprints, it\u2019s Agile.
2) Black vs white box: the color says what the tester can SEE. Black = can\u2019t see inside (spec-based); white = can see the code (path-based). Unit tests are usually white-box; acceptance tests are black-box.
\ud83c\udfaf QUICK CHECK
Which SDLC model is defined by explicit risk analysis on every loop?
  1. Spiral
  2. Waterfall
  3. Prototyping
Show answer
A \u2014 Spiral. Its four repeating quadrants are plan, analyze risk, build, evaluate. Risk analysis every cycle is its fingerprint.
\n\n
\ud83d\udcd6 Full lesson \u2014 every definition & detail (tap to collapse)

The software development lifecycle

\n
\ud83d\udca1 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Software isn't just \u201csit down and code.\u201d Teams follow a lifecycle so they build the right thing without chaos: figure out what's needed, design it, build it, test it, ship it, and maintain it. Different methodologies (Waterfall, Agile) sequence these stages differently.

\n
\u2699\ufe0f WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Typical SDLC phases: requirements (what to build) \u2192 design (plan the logic) \u2192 implementation (code it) \u2192 testing (verify) \u2192 deployment (release) \u2192 maintenance (fix & improve).

Waterfall does these strictly in order, once. Agile repeats them in short cycles (sprints), delivering working pieces often and adapting to feedback.

\n
\ud83d\udcdd EXAM WORDING

The SDLC phases: requirements \u2192 design \u2192 implementation \u2192 testing \u2192 deployment \u2192 maintenance. Waterfall is sequential; Agile is iterative/incremental (sprints, adapting to change). \u201cPlan the logic\u201d = design; \u201ccode the program\u201d = implementation.

\n
\u26a0\ufe0f WATCH OUT

Requirements/planning is not \u201cpaperwork to skip\u201d \u2014 ambiguity caught early is cheap, caught late is expensive. And Agile isn't \u201cno planning\u201d; it's planning in small, repeated cycles.

\u2605 ON THE OA \u2014 WATCH FOR

The SDLC runs in order: requirements/analysis \u2192 design \u2192 implementation \u2192 testing \u2192 deployment \u2192 maintenance. Each phase feeds the next.

\u25b8 QUICK CHECK

Coding happens in implementation, AFTER design; you can't skip straight from requirements to deployment.

\ud83d\udcda Extra review \u2014 1 alternate explanation & recall cards (tap to open)
\n

\ud83d\udd01 The Software Development Lifecycle

\n
THE SIX PHASES, IN ORDER
requirements \u2192 design \u2192 implementation \u2192 testing \u2192 deployment \u2192 maintenance
\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
PhaseWhat it delivers
RequirementsWHAT to build
DesignPlan the logic
ImplementationCode it
TestingVerify it works
DeploymentRelease it
MaintenanceFix & improve
\n
WATERFALL vs AGILE
\n\n
WaterfallAgile
Strictly in order, ONCE (sequential)Repeats phases in short cycles (sprints), delivering working pieces often, adapting to feedback (iterative/incremental)
\n\"Plan the logic\" = design \u00b7 \"code the program\" = implementation.
\n
\u26a0\ufe0f TWO MYTHS
Requirements/planning isn't paperwork to skip \u2014 ambiguity caught EARLY is cheap; caught LATE is expensive. And Agile isn't \"no planning\" \u2014 it's planning in small, repeated cycles.
\n
\ud83c\udfaf OA-STYLE CHECK
Which methodology repeats the phases in short sprints?\n
  1. Agile
  2. Waterfall
  3. Neither
  4. Both equally
\n
Show answer + steps
A. Agile is iterative/incremental; Waterfall runs the phases once, in strict order.
\n
