\ud83c\udfad Programming Paradigms

\n\n\n\n\n
ParadigmPhilosophyLanguages
Procedural (imperative)Step-by-step instructions, procedures/functionsC
Object-orientedOrganize around objects bundling data + behaviorJava
FunctionalPure functions, avoiding shared state / side effectsScheme, Haskell
DeclarativeDescribe the desired RESULT, not the steps \u2014 WHAT, not HOWSQL, HTML
\n
WORKED EXAMPLE \u2014 the exam's key contrast
\nDeclarative (SQL): \"give me these rows.\" Imperative: \"loop and check each row.\" Same goal, different philosophy. The same problem can be solved in multiple paradigms; many modern languages mix them.
\n
\u26a0\ufe0f NOTES TO KEEP STRAIGHT
Scheme is a common exam example of a declarative/functional language. Java is object-oriented \u2014 but also imperative under the hood.
\n
\ud83c\udfaf OA-STYLE CHECK
SQL, which describes WHAT data you want rather than HOW to fetch it, is:\n
  1. Declarative
  2. Procedural
  3. Object-oriented
  4. Assembly
\n
Show answer + steps
A. Describing the result, not the steps, is the definition of declarative.
\n
\n
\ud83d\udcd6 Full lesson \u2014 every definition & detail (tap to collapse)

Programming paradigms

\n
\ud83d\udca1 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

There's more than one philosophy for structuring code. Some styles give step-by-step commands; some organize around objects; some describe WHAT you want rather than HOW. Knowing the paradigms helps you recognize why languages feel different.

\n
\u2699\ufe0f WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Procedural (imperative): step-by-step instructions and procedures/functions (C). Object-oriented: organize around objects bundling data + behavior (Java). Functional: build programs from pure functions, avoiding shared state (Scheme, Haskell).

Declarative: describe the desired result, not the steps (SQL, HTML). The same problem can be solved in multiple paradigms; many modern languages mix them.

\n
\ud83d\udcdd EXAM WORDING

Procedural/imperative = step-by-step commands; object-oriented = objects with data + methods; functional = pure functions, no side effects; declarative = describe WHAT, not HOW (SQL is the classic example). Scheme is a common example of a declarative/functional language.

\n
\u26a0\ufe0f WATCH OUT

Declarative (SQL: \u201cgive me these rows\u201d) vs imperative (\u201cloop and check each row\u201d) is the key contrast the exam draws. Java is object-oriented but also imperative under the hood.

\u2605 ON THE OA \u2014 WATCH FOR

Major paradigms: procedural (steps/functions), object-oriented (objects + classes), functional (pure functions, no side effects), declarative (describe the what, e.g., SQL).

\u25b8 QUICK CHECK

Java/C++ lean object-oriented; SQL is declarative; Haskell is functional. Many languages are multi-paradigm.

Encapsulation — an object bundles its data with the methods that use it and hides the internals behind a public interface — is a defining trait of the object-oriented paradigm.

Section 2 Cheat Sheet \u2014 Computational Thinking & Professional Practice

\n

Lessons 1.1\u20132.1: the problem-solving phases, the SDLC, and the ACM/IEEE codes of ethics.

\n\n

\u2460 Computational thinking \u2014 the phases

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
PhaseWhat you do
AnalysisUnderstand the problem: requirements, constraints, objectives.
DesignPlan the solution \u2014 algorithms, flowcharts, pseudocode, data structures.
ImplementationWrite the actual code.
TestingRun with many inputs to confirm correct behavior.
MaintenanceKeep it working over time \u2014 fixes, updates, new features.
\n

An algorithm is the step-by-step procedure at the heart of all of this.

\n\n

\u2461 Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC)

\n

The SDLC is the organized, phased process for producing quality software: plan \u2192 analyze \u2192 design \u2192 implement \u2192 test \u2192 deploy \u2192 maintain.

\n
Vocabulary that maps to phases
\n\"Plan the logic\" = design \u00b7 \"Code the program\" = implementation \u00b7 \"Translate the code\" = compiler or interpreter
\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
TermMeaning
End userThe person who actually uses the software (e.g. a cashier on a POS system).
DocumentationWritten material to use/understand/maintain a program (manuals, comments).
DebuggingFinding and fixing errors (\"bugs\") in code.
High-level languageHuman-readable: Java, Python, Visual Basic.
Low-level languageClose to hardware: assembly, machine code.
\n\n

\u2462 Codes of ethics \u2014 ACM vs IEEE

\n\n\n\n\n\n
 ACMIEEE
FocusSoftware & computingHardware & engineering
Top priorityContribute to society, avoid harmPublic welfare first (safety/health)
Structure4 categories (below)~10 commitments
StandoutDetailed leadership principlesSustainable design + educating society
\n\n\n\n\n\n
ACM categoryCovers
1.x GeneralContribute to society, avoid harm, be honest, be fair, respect IP/privacy/confidentiality.
2.x ProfessionalHigh-quality work, competence, follow laws, peer review, evaluate risks, secure systems.
3.x LeadershipPublic good first, promote responsibility, support colleagues' growth, careful system changes.
4.x ComplianceUphold the code; treat violations seriously.
\n

IEEE commitments (key ones): public welfare first \u00b7 sustainable/ethical design \u00b7 disclose conflicts of interest \u00b7 honest & realistic claims \u00b7 reject bribery \u00b7 educate society \u00b7 maintain competence (only work you're qualified for) \u00b7 accept criticism & give credit \u00b7 non-discrimination \u00b7 prevent harm \u00b7 support colleagues.

\n\n
\u26a0 ETHICS TRAPS
    \n
  • \"Maximize profits\" is NOT an ACM principle.
    • \n
  • Hiding system limitations violates IEEE (honest claims).
    • \n
  • Eliminating/blocking professional development violates both codes.
    • \n
  • Disclosing a design flaw that could endanger users \u2192 satisfies both ACM and IEEE.
    • \n
  • An untrained engineer asked to do security work should disclose their limitations first.
    • \n
\n\n

\u2463 Computer crime (from the practice test)

\n\n\n\n\n
CrimeWhat it is
Identity theftStealing personal info (e.g. SSN) to impersonate someone.
Data breachUnauthorized access to protected/confidential data.
CyberbullyingUsing digital tools to harass or intimidate.
\n\n
\u2713 SECTION 2 MUST-KNOWS
    \n
  • Phases: analysis \u2192 design \u2192 implementation \u2192 testing \u2192 maintenance.
    • \n
  • SDLC vocab: \"plan the logic\" = design; \"code\" = implementation.
    • \n
  • ACM = software, IEEE = hardware. Both put the public good first.
    • \n
  • ACM 4 categories: general, professional, leadership, compliance.
    • \n
  • \"Maximize profits\" is not in any code; honesty about limitations is required by both.
    • \n
\n

Cybercrime quick hits: report to FBI IC3 \u2022 FBI = major intrusions, Secret Service = financial crimes, local police = small cases \u2022 IP theft = file sharing, password sharing, nation-state theft \u2022 real prison time applies (Hammond: 10 years).

Section 3 Cheat Sheet \u2014 Algorithms & Programming

\n

Lessons 1.1\u20133.1: loops & steps, searching, sorting, flowcharts, pseudocode arithmetic, and program structures.

\n\n

\u2460 Loops, steps & data terms

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
TermMeaning
Count-controlled loopRepeats a set number of times (for i = 1 to 10).
Event-controlled loopRepeats until an event/condition occurs (until user types \"quit\").
Desk checkingTracing an algorithm by hand (pencil/paper), not on a computer.
Concrete vs abstract stepExact \"how\" instruction vs high-level \"what\".
ProcessingPerforming operations on data (vs just storing it).
Homogeneous vs heterogeneousAll same type [1,2,3] vs mixed types [\"apple\", 5, true].
IndexAn element's numeric position (starts at 0): \"blue\" is index 2 in [red, green, blue].
\n\n

\u2461 Searching

\n\n\n\n
SearchHowUse when
Sequential / linearCheck each item one by oneList is small or unsorted
BinaryJump to middle, halve each timeList is sorted (required!)
\n
Binary search middle index: mid = (low + high) // 2
\n
while low <= high:\n    mid = (low + high) // 2\n    if array[mid] == target: return mid\n    elif array[mid] < target: low = mid + 1\n    else: high = mid - 1
\n\n

\u2462 Sorting

\n\n\n\n\n
SortHow it works
Selection sortFind the minimum, move it to the front; repeat.
Bubble sortCompare adjacent pairs and swap if out of order; repeat.
Insertion sortBuild a sorted section one item at a time, inserting each where it belongs.
\n\n

\u2463 Flowchart symbols

\n\n\n\n\n\n
SymbolShapeMeans
TerminalOvalStart / end
Input/Output (I/O)ParallelogramRead input / show output
ProcessingRectangleA step / calculation
FlowlineArrowDirection of flow
\n\n

\u2464 Pseudocode arithmetic templates

\n
\nPerimeter of rectangle: perimeter = 2 * (length + width)
\nTotal cost: total = price_per_item * quantity
\nSimple interest: interest = principal * rate * time
\nAverage of two: average = (a + b) / 2
\n\"d subtracted from f\" \u2192 f \u2212 d
\n
START\n    INPUT length\n    INPUT width\n    perimeter = 2 * (length + width)\n    OUTPUT perimeter\nEND
\n\n

\u2465 Program structures

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
StructureMeaning
SequenceSteps run one after another in order.
SelectionChoose a path based on a Boolean condition.
LoopRepeat a block while a condition holds.
Single-alternative ifActs only when true; does nothing if false.
Dual-alternative ifTwo paths \u2014 true and false (if-else).
Null caseA path where no action is taken (often the default).
End-structure statementMarks the end of a block (END IF).
Loop bodyThe statements that run each iteration.
Stacking structuresPlace one after another \u2014 connect only at entry/exit points.
Nesting structuresPlace one structure inside another.
BlockA group of statements executed together (braces or indentation).
\n\n
\u26a0 TRAPS
    \n
  • Binary search only works on a sorted list \u2014 on an unsorted list use sequential search.
    • \n
  • Selection = pick the min to the front; Bubble = swap neighbors; Insertion = one at a time.
    • \n
  • Count-controlled = fixed number of times; event-controlled = until something happens.
    • \n
\n
\u2713 SECTION 3 MUST-KNOWS
    \n
  • mid = (low + high) // 2; binary search needs a sorted list.
    • \n
  • Three sorts: selection (min\u2192front), bubble (adjacent swaps), insertion (one at a time).
    • \n
  • Flowchart: oval = start/end, parallelogram = I/O, rectangle = process, arrow = flowline.
    • \n
  • Dual-alternative if = if-else; single-alternative does nothing on false; null case = no action.
    • \n
\n

FactValue

Section 4 Cheat Sheet \u2014 Operating Systems & File Systems

\n

Lessons 1.1\u20132.1: OS basics, memory management, process scheduling, and file systems.

\n\n

\u2460 OS basics

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
TermMeaning
Operating systemMain software managing hardware/software: Windows, Linux, macOS, Unix, Android, iOS.
System vs application softwarePlatform/OS & utilities vs user task programs (Word, Chrome).
ProcessA running instance of a program.
MultiprogrammingSeveral programs loaded at once \u2192 raises CPU utilization.
Batch processingRuns jobs with no user interaction (payroll).
TimesharingMany users share one system by splitting CPU time.
Mainframe / dumb terminalLarge enterprise computer / input-output device with no processing power.
Virtual machineSoftware emulation of a computer (Ubuntu in VMware).
Real-time systemMust respond within a strict time frame (airbag controller).
Response timeFrom request submission to the start of the response.
\n\n

\u2461 Memory management

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
TermMeaning
Logical (virtual) addressAddress the CPU generates for code/data; not the real RAM location.
Physical addressThe actual RAM location. The MMU translates logical \u2192 physical.
Address bindingMapping symbolic/logical addresses to physical ones (compile/load/run time).
Single contiguousOne program loaded into one block \u2014 single-task systems.
Fixed vs dynamic partitionEqual preset blocks (wastes space) vs sized to each program's need.
Base + bounds registerStart address + highest allowed address \u2192 keeps a process inside its memory.
Page vs frameFixed block of virtual memory vs fixed block of RAM. \"Pages = cars, frames = parking spots.\"
Page Map Table (PMT)Maps each virtual page \u2192 its physical frame.
Demand pagingLoad a page only when needed.
Page swapMove pages between RAM and disk to free space.
Virtual memoryRAM + disk gives the illusion of more memory; lets programs > RAM run (pagefile.sys).
ThrashingExcessive paging kills performance (system swaps more than it works).
\n
\u26a0 MEMORY TRAPS
    \n
  • Fixed partitions waste memory inside a partition (internal fragmentation).
    • \n
  • Page = virtual; frame = physical RAM. The MMU does logical\u2192physical translation.
    • \n
  • Thrashing = too many processes causing constant paging \u2014 not idle CPU, not full disk.
    • \n
\n\n

\u2462 Processes & CPU scheduling

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
TermMeaning
Process statesNew \u2192 Ready \u2192 Running \u2192 Waiting (blocked) \u2192 Terminated.
Process Control Block (PCB)Stores all process info: PID, state, registers, memory pointers.
Context switchSave current process state, load the next \u2014 lets processes share the CPU.
Non-preemptive vs preemptiveRuns to completion vs can be interrupted for another process.
Turnaround timeSubmission \u2192 full completion (vs response time = submission \u2192 first response).
Time sliceFixed CPU time each process gets (used by round-robin).
\n\n\n\n\n
AlgorithmPicks\u2026Type
FCFS (First-Come First-Served)Arrival order (like a ticket line)Non-preemptive
SJN (Shortest Job Next)Shortest job firstNon-preemptive
Round-robinEach gets a time slice in turn (fairness)Preemptive
\n\n

\u2463 File systems

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
TermMeaning
File / file systemNamed data collection / how the OS organizes files: NTFS, FAT32, ext4.
Directory / directory treeA folder / the hierarchy of folders and subfolders.
Text vs binary fileHuman-readable (notes.txt) vs not (program.exe, vacation.jpg).
File type / file extensionCategory of file / suffix showing the format (.txt, .pdf, .exe).
Sequential vs direct accessRead start\u2192end vs jump straight to any record.
Root directoryTop of the tree: / (Linux) or C:\\ (Windows).
Working directoryThe folder you're currently operating in.
Absolute vs relative pathFrom the root (/home/user/x) vs from the current folder (../images/x).
Disk scheduling / seek timeOrdering disk access (SSTF = Shortest Seek Time First) / time to move the head to the track.
\n\n
\u2713 SECTION 4 MUST-KNOWS
    \n
  • MMU translates logical\u2192physical. Page = virtual block, frame = RAM block.
    • \n
  • Virtual memory (RAM + disk) lets programs bigger than RAM run; thrashing = too much paging.
    • \n
  • FCFS & SJN are non-preemptive; round-robin is preemptive (time slice = fairness).
    • \n
  • Turnaround = submission\u2192completion; response = submission\u2192first response.
    • \n
  • Absolute path starts at root (/ or C:\\); relative path uses ../ from the current folder.
    • \n
\n

Von Neumann / stored-program: programs + data share one memory \u2022 parts: memory, ALU, control unit, I/O \u2022 control unit runs fetch\u2013decode\u2013execute \u2022 round robin scheduling = fixed time slice per process in turn.

\n

Section 5 Cheat Sheet \u2014 Computer Architecture & Networking

\n

Lessons 1.1\u20133.1: CPU/motherboard, disk geometry, device types, and the big networking glossary.

\n\n

\u2460 CPU & computing components

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
TermMeaning
CPUThe \"brain\" \u2014 executes instructions and processes data.
ALUArithmetic Logic Unit \u2014 does arithmetic + logic operations.
Control unitDirects operations and coordinates components.
RegisterSmall, very fast CPU storage for temporary data.
Instruction registerHolds the current instruction being executed.
Program counterHolds the address of the next instruction.
Cache memorySmall, fast, volatile memory for frequently used data.
Bus widthBits transferred at once \u2014 wider = more data per cycle.
PipeliningOverlaps instruction phases to boost performance.
AddressabilityNumber of bits stored at each addressable location in memory.
MotherboardMain board housing CPU, memory, and core components.
\n
\u26a0 CLASSIC TRAP
\nInstruction register = the instruction running now. Program counter = the address of the next instruction. Don't mix them up.
\n\n

\u2461 Disk geometry & timing

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
TermMeaning
TrackA circular path on a platter where data is stored.
SectorThe smallest unit of disk storage.
BlockA fixed-size unit of data stored/transferred.
CylinderThe same-position tracks stacked across all platters.
LatencyThe delay before data transfer starts.
Access timeTime to retrieve data from memory/storage.
Transfer rateSpeed at which data moves (bps).
\n
\u26a0 TRAP
\nLatency = the wait before transfer begins. Transfer rate = how fast data then moves. They are not the same.
\n\n

\u2462 Device types

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
DeviceBest for
ServerProvides resources/services to clients over a network.
Desktop / laptopStationary personal PC / portable personal PC.
Tablet / smartphoneLarger touchscreen for media/reading / phone + apps + internet.
MainframeLarge-scale transaction processing (banks, government).
SupercomputerMassive scientific calculations & simulations.
Server farmMany servers together for huge scale (Google, AWS).
Multicore processor2+ cores \u2192 run multiple tasks at once.
GPUGraphics + parallel processing (3D, machine learning).
Embedded computerBuilt into a device to control it (car, microwave).
IoTEveryday devices connected to the internet to share data (smart thermostat).
\n\n

\u2463 Networking \u2014 reach, models & topologies

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
TermMeaning
Computer networkDevices linked to communicate and share resources.
BandwidthMax capacity of a path \u2014 like lanes on a highway.
Data transfer rateHow fast data actually moves (bps).
ProtocolRules for how data is formatted/transmitted (HTTP, TCP/IP).
Client/server vs P2PCentral server serves clients vs peers act as both client and server.
LAN / MAN / WANBuilding/campus \u2192 city \u2192 country+ (the internet is the biggest WAN).
\n\n\n\n\n
TopologyLayoutWeak point
StarAll connect to a central hub/switchHub failure
RingCircular chainOne link break stops the loop
BusAll on one cableCable break disrupts all
\n\n

\u2464 Network devices & connections

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
TermMeaning
GatewayConnects two different networks and translates protocols.
RouterDirects packets between networks along the best path.
RepeaterAmplifies a signal to extend distance.
BluetoothShort-range wireless for peripherals.
Internet backbone / ISPHigh-speed core carrying long-distance traffic / your internet provider.
Phone modemConverts digital \u21c4 analog for phone lines (dial-up).
DSLHigh-speed internet over phone lines \u2014 voice + data at the same time.
Cable modem / broadbandInternet over cable-TV lines / high-speed, always-on connection.
Download vs uploadReceive from a server vs send to a server.
\n\n

\u2465 Packets & protocols

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
TermMeaning
Packet / packet switchingSmall data unit with routing info / packets take multiple paths, reassembled at the end.
Proprietary vs open systemVendor-controlled (Apple iOS) vs public standards (Linux).
InteroperabilityDifferent systems working together seamlessly.
OSI reference modelOrganizes networking into 7 layers; aids troubleshooting.
Ethernet / protocol stackWired LAN standard / layered set of protocols working together (TCP/IP).
TCPReliable, ordered, error-checked delivery.
IP / TCP/IPAddressing + routing of packets / the suite powering the internet.
UDPFast, connectionless, less reliable \u2014 gaming, streaming.
Ping / tracerouteTests reachability + round-trip time / shows each hop along the path.
Port / MIME typeVirtual endpoint for a service (HTTP = 80) / file format label (text/html).
Firewall / access control policyFilters traffic by security rules / rules for who can access what.
\n

High-level protocols: SMTP (email), FTP (file transfer), HTTP (web), Telnet.

\n
\u26a0 TCP vs UDP TRAP
\nTCP = reliable + ordered (files, web). UDP = fast + connectionless, may drop packets (live video, gaming). Pick UDP when speed beats reliability.
\n\n

\u2466 Naming & DNS

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
TermMeaning
HostnameHuman-readable device name. It's the part before the first dot \u2014 in jenkins.develocorp.org the hostname is jenkins.
IP addressNumeric device label for routing (192.168.1.10).
Domain nameHuman-readable web address (www.example.com).
Top-Level Domain (TLD)The last segment: .com, .org, .edu.
ICANNGlobally manages domain names + IP allocation.
Domain squattingRegistering domains (often trademarks) to resell for profit.
DNS / domain name serverTranslates a domain \u2192 IP / the server that answers DNS queries.
Network neutralityISPs must treat all traffic equally (no throttling/favoring).
\n\n
\u2713 SECTION 5 MUST-KNOWS
    \n
  • Instruction register = current instruction; program counter = next address.
    • \n
  • Latency = delay before transfer; transfer rate = speed of transfer. Sector = smallest disk unit.
    • \n
  • Topology weak points: star \u2192 hub, ring \u2192 one link, bus \u2192 the cable.
    • \n
  • Gateway translates between networks; router picks the best path; repeater amplifies.
    • \n
  • TCP = reliable/ordered; UDP = fast/connectionless (gaming, streaming). HTTP = port 80.
    • \n
  • Hostname = before the first dot. DNS converts domain \u2192 IP; ICANN governs domains + IPs.
    • \n
\n

\u2467 Input / output devices & touch screens

Input = data in (keyboard, mouse, scanner, mic, camera). Output = results out (monitor, printer, speakers). Both = touch screen, storage, network card.

Touch screenDetects byGloves?
Resistivepressure \u2014 two layers touchYes
Capacitivechange in electrical charge (needs conductive skin)No
SAW (surface acoustic wave)interruption of high-frequency sound wavesYes
Infraredbreaking a grid of light beamsYes

Only capacitive fails with an ordinary glove \u2014 it is the one that needs the touch to conduct electricity. Capacitive also gives multi-touch, which is why phones use it.

"}, "D684/oa/s1": {"body": "\n
\n

\ud83c\udf93 How to Pass Your WGU OA: Strategy & Mindset

\n\n\n\n\n\n
Exam factDetail
FormatMultiple-choice in a proctored, locked-down browser; each has one best answer (a few may say \"select all that apply\" \u2014 read carefully)
To passReach \"Competent\" \u2014 roughly 70%+. Pass/fail, no letter grade
No guessing penaltyA blank and a wrong answer score the SAME \u2014 never leave a question blank; always lock in your best guess
Flag & returnIf a question eats time, mark it, move on, circle back fresh
Retakes existIf you don't pass, you get feedback on weak areas and can retake after a short waiting period
\n
STUDY THE WAY MEMORY WORKS
\n\n\n\n\n\n
MethodWhat to do
Active recallClose the notes and retrieve the answer from memory
Spaced repetitionReview a topic today, in two days, then in a week
InterleavingMix topics in a session rather than drilling one to death
Practice testingTake the full exam simulator under timed, no-notes conditions
Teach it back (Feynman)Explain a concept out loud in plain words, as if teaching a friend
\n
THE TWO-WEEK PLAN
\nWeek 1 \u2014 Learn & recall: read each lesson once, then immediately quiz that section. Week 2 \u2014 Simulate & patch: take the full exam simulator, note the topics you miss, and spend your time ONLY on those.
\n
QUESTION TACTICS
\nRead every word \u2014 watch for NOT, EXCEPT, ALWAYS, NEVER (they flip the meaning). Eliminate first \u2014 cutting two options turns a hard question into a coin flip in your favor. Predict before you peek \u2014 answer in your head before reading choices so a tempting-but-wrong option can't anchor you. Trust your first instinct unless you find a concrete reason to change. Watch the clock \u2014 budget about a minute per question; flag anything slower. Answer everything.
\n
\ud83c\udfaf OA-STYLE CHECK
With no guessing penalty, an unanswered question should be:\n
  1. Given your best guess \u2014 always
  2. Left blank to be safe
  3. Skipped permanently

\u25c6 WHY THIS MATTERS

The Intro to Computer Science (D684) OA is a multiple-choice objective assessment, and you only need to reach \"Competent\" to pass \u2014 roughly 70% of the questions. It is pass/fail (no letter grade), you can retake it if needed, and you can flag questions and come back. Knowing how the exam works, and studying the way memory actually works, removes most of the fear.

How the objective assessment works

  • Format: a set of multiple-choice questions in a proctored, locked-down browser. Each has one best answer (a few may say \"select all that apply\" \u2014 read carefully).
  • To pass: reach the \"Competent\" cut (about 70%+). Aim higher in practice so test-day nerves still leave you a cushion.
  • No guessing penalty: a blank and a wrong answer score the same \u2014 so never leave a question blank. Always lock in your best guess.
  • You can flag & return: if a question is eating time, mark it, move on, and circle back with a fresh head.
  • Retakes exist: if you don\u2019t pass, you get feedback on weak areas and can retake after a short waiting period. One exam is not your only shot.

The five study techniques that actually work

Decades of learning research keep pointing to the same handful of methods. They feel harder than rereading \u2014 and that \"desirable difficulty\" is exactly why they work.

TechniqueWhat to do
Active recallClose the notes and retrieve the answer from memory. Use this app\u2019s quizzes and flashcards instead of rereading \u2014 testing yourself is the single most powerful technique there is.
Spaced repetitionReview a topic today, in two days, then in a week. Short sessions spread over time beat one long cram by a wide margin.
InterleavingMix topics in a session rather than drilling one to death. The mixed/interleaved quiz mode forces you to pick the right approach \u2014 which is what the exam demands.
Practice testingTake the full exam simulator under timed, no-notes conditions. Each attempt is both practice and a diagnostic of what to fix next.
Teach it back (Feynman)Explain a concept out loud in plain words, as if teaching a friend. Where you get stuck is exactly what you don\u2019t truly understand yet.
\u25b2 A SIMPLE 2-WEEK PLAN

Week 1 \u2014 Learn & recall: read each lesson once, then immediately quiz that section. End each day with a short mixed quiz over everything so far.
Week 2 \u2014 Simulate & patch: take the full exam simulator, note the topics you miss, and spend your time only on those. Re-simulate every couple of days until you\u2019re comfortably above the pass line.

Exam-day tactics for multiple choice

  • Read every word. Watch for NOT, EXCEPT, ALWAYS, NEVER \u2014 they flip the meaning of a question.
  • Eliminate first. Cross out the obviously wrong options; even cutting two turns a hard question into a coin flip in your favor.
  • Predict before you peek. Try to answer in your head before reading the choices, so a tempting-but-wrong option can\u2019t anchor you.
  • Trust your first instinct unless you find a concrete reason to change it \u2014 second-guessing flips more right answers to wrong than the reverse.
  • Watch the clock. Budget about a minute per question; flag anything slower and return to it.
  • Answer everything. With no penalty for wrong answers, an educated guess always beats a blank.

Calm nerves, clear head

Some adrenaline is normal and even helpful. If it tips into panic, slow your breathing \u2014 in for four counts, hold four, out for four \u2014 for a few cycles to reset your body. Reframe the moment: this is a checkpoint, not a verdict on you, and you can retake it. Sleep the night before matters more than one more hour of cramming; a rested brain recalls far better than a tired one. Eat something, arrive early, and remember how much you\u2019ve already prepared.

\u2713 KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • You need ~70% (\"Competent\") to pass; it\u2019s pass/fail and retakeable.
  • Never leave a blank \u2014 there\u2019s no penalty for guessing.
  • Quiz yourself (active recall) and space it out; don\u2019t just reread.
  • Take the exam simulator until you\u2019re comfortably above the pass line.
  • On test day: read carefully, eliminate, answer everything, breathe.

Before writing code, programmers plan the logic \u2014 and the two tools for that are a flowchart, which shows the flow as a diagram, and pseudocode, which writes it as plain steps that read like English but follow programming logic. Neither belongs to any language, which is the point: the logic can be checked before syntax gets in the way.

Flowchart shapes are standardised and the OA asks you to name them.

ShapeMeans
Ovalstart or end
Parallelograminput or output
Rectanglea process \u2014 a calculation or assignment
Diamonda decision \u2014 a condition with two exits
Arrowthe direction of flow

Reading WGU-style pseudocode

WGU uses a consistent style, and questions are usually \"what does this output\" rather than \"write this\". The keywords are INPUT, OUTPUT, IF/ELSE/ENDIF, WHILE/END WHILE and FOR, with assignment written as = or SET.

\u25b8 WORKED EXAMPLE \u2014 an average with validation
START\n  SET total = 0\n  SET count = 0\n  INPUT n\n  WHILE n != -1\n      SET total = total + n\n      SET count = count + 1\n      INPUT n\n  END WHILE\n  IF count > 0 THEN\n      OUTPUT total / count\n  ELSE\n      OUTPUT \"no values entered\"\n  ENDIF\nEND

Notice the guard on the last decision. Dividing by count when no values were entered would divide by zero, so the IF exists to prevent it \u2014 the same defensive habit that shows up as parameter checking later.

Arithmetic in pseudocode

The arithmetic operators are where the OA plants its errors, and the three division operators must be kept apart.

OperatorDoesExample
/true (floating-point) division7 / 2 = 3.5
//floor or integer division \u2014 truncates7 // 2 = 3
%modulo \u2014 the remainder7 % 2 = 1
*multiplication7 * 2 = 14
**exponent7 ** 2 = 49

WGU also words type conversion in a specific way that is worth recognising verbatim: float(age) converts an integer to a floating-point number, and int(num) converts a float to an integer by truncating \u2014 not rounding. To add ten to a variable the expression is value + 10, and to store it back, value = value + 10.

How to be graded on pseudocode

Pseudocode has no compiler, so the standard it is held to is whether another person could follow it unambiguously. That means three habits. Name variables meaningfully \u2014 totalScore, not t. Indent the body of every branch and loop, because indentation is how a reader sees the structure. And close what you open: ENDIF for every IF, END WHILE for every WHILE, so where a block stops is never a guess.

The other half of the skill is reading it, which is what the OA mostly asks. Given a fragment and a set of inputs, the reliable method is a trace table: one column for each variable, one row for each pass, filled in line by line rather than held in your head. It feels slow and it is the difference between an answer you can check and an answer you guessed.

Watch the boundaries when you trace. A loop written WHILE count < 5 starting at 0 runs five times and leaves count at 5 \u2014 the value that failed the test. Questions frequently ask for the value after the loop, which is one more than the last value used inside it.

Connecting the symbols

The arrows joining flowchart shapes are called flowlines, and they carry the direction of flow. Two conventions matter for reading: flow runs top to bottom and left to right unless an arrowhead says otherwise, and every decision diamond has exactly two flowlines leaving it, labelled Yes/No or True/False. A shape with no outgoing flowline other than the terminal oval is a sign the diagram is incomplete.

Flowchart symbols

A flowchart shows the same algorithm as a picture, and each shape has a fixed meaning that is asked directly.

ShapeMeans
Oval (terminal)start or end
Parallelograminput or output \u2014 READ, DISPLAY
Rectanglea process \u2014 a calculation or an assignment
Diamonda decision \u2014 one way in, a labelled branch for each answer
Arrowthe flow of control from one step to the next

The rectangle is the one people lose marks on: \"Multiply subtotal by taxRate\" is a process step, not a decision and not output.

The accumulator pattern

Totalling and averaging appear constantly, and both use the same shape: a running total and a count, each initialised to zero before the loop and updated inside it.

SET total TO 0            // accumulator\nSET count TO 0            // counter\nFOR each number IN list\n    SET total TO total + number\n    SET count TO count + 1\nEND FOR\nSET average TO total / count

Two things are tested. Initialising inside the loop resets the total every pass and the answer is always the last value. And an average needs both running values \u2014 a total alone cannot produce one.

Off-by-one

An array of length n has indices 0 to n \u2212 1. A loop written FOR i = 0 TO length inclusive runs one time too many and reads index n, which does not exist \u2014 an off-by-one error, and the crash is an index-out-of-bounds. The correct bound is length \u2212 1, or a loop that stops before length.

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION

Flowchart: a diagram of program flow using standard shapes

Pseudocode: algorithm steps in plain, language-neutral terms

INPUT / OUTPUT: the pseudocode keywords for reading data in and producing results

True division (/): produces a fractional result

Floor division (//): produces the whole part only, discarding the remainder

Modulo (%): produces the remainder of a division

float() / int(): conversion operations; int() truncates rather than rounds

\u2605 ON THE OA

Keep the three division operators apart: 7 / 2 = 3.5, 7 // 2 = 3, 7 % 2 = 1. In a language where / on two integers is itself integer division \u2014 Java, for instance \u2014 7 / 2 is 3. Read which convention the question is using.

\ud83c\udfaf EXAM TIP

For a \"what does this pseudocode print\" question, make a small table with one column per variable and one row per pass through the loop. It is slower than reading and it is right far more often.

An operating system is the software that manages a computer's hardware and provides services to every other program \u2014 Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS. The single sentence to hold on to is that the OS is the resource manager: it decides who gets the CPU, who gets memory, and who may touch a device, so that applications never have to negotiate with each other.

Four responsibilities cover almost every question, and they map onto four resources.

ResponsibilityWhat the OS doesWithout it
Process managementcreates processes, schedules the CPU between themone program would monopolise the machine
Memory managementallocates and reclaims RAM, provides virtual memoryprograms would overwrite each other
File managementorganises files and enforces permissionsno structure, no access control
Device managementtalks to hardware through driversevery program would need code for every device

Processes, threads and CPU scheduling

A process is a program in execution, with its own memory. A thread is a lighter unit inside a process: threads of one process share its memory, which makes switching between them cheap and makes it possible for them to corrupt each other's data \u2014 the trade that defines concurrent programming.

When many processes want the one CPU, the OS plays traffic cop. Each strategy has a name, and the OA asks you to match the name to its one-line behaviour.

AlgorithmPicksStrengthWeakness
FCFS (first-come, first-served)whoever arrived firstsimple and fair by arrivalone long job blocks everyone behind it
SJN / SJF (shortest job next / first)the shortest execution timeminimises average waiting timelong jobs can starve indefinitely
Round robineach in turn for a fixed time sliceresponsive and faircontext switching costs overhead
Prioritythe highest-priority jobimportant work goes firstlow-priority jobs can starve

WGU's phrasings are worth memorising as phrases: \"selects the process with the smallest execution time remaining\" is shortest job next; \"each process gets a fixed time slice in rotation\" is round robin.

Memory management

Memory techniques evolved to solve one problem \u2014 fitting several programs into one physical memory.

TechniqueHow it worksWeakness
Single contiguousone program plus the OS occupy all of memoryonly one program at a time
Fixed partitioningmemory split into fixed-size blocks set in advancewasted space inside each block
Dynamic partitioningblocks sized to each program as it loadsgaps build up between them \u2014 fragmentation
Paging / virtual memorymemory divided into fixed pages; unused pages held on diskdisk access is slow \u2014 thrashing if overused

Virtual memory is the one to understand rather than memorise. It gives every process its own large address space and keeps only the pages currently in use in real RAM, holding the rest on disk. That is why a machine can run programs whose combined size exceeds its physical memory, and why it slows dramatically when it runs out \u2014 it starts swapping pages to disk.

Deadlock

A deadlock is two or more processes each holding a resource the other needs, so neither can ever proceed \u2014 process A holds the printer and wants the scanner, process B holds the scanner and wants the printer. Nothing resolves it on its own; the OS must prevent, avoid or detect and break it.

What \"resource manager\" really means

The phrase is easy to repeat and worth unpacking, because it is what makes the OS necessary rather than merely convenient. Without one, every program would have to know which region of memory was free, take turns with the CPU voluntarily, and contain a driver for every model of printer. Programs would have to cooperate, and a single badly written one could take down the machine.

The OS solves that by standing between applications and hardware and refusing to let them talk directly. An application asks for memory and gets an address; it asks to write a file and the OS decides whether it is allowed. That indirection is also the security boundary \u2014 the reason one program cannot read another's memory, and the reason permissions can be enforced at all.

Multitasking is an illusion, mostly

A single-core CPU runs exactly one instruction stream at a time. What looks like several programs running at once is the scheduler switching between them thousands of times a second \u2014 concurrency, achieved by a context switch that saves one process's state and restores another's. Genuine simultaneity needs multiple cores, and that is parallelism. Questions that ask whether a single-core machine can truly run two programs at the same instant are testing exactly this distinction, and the answer is no.

How memory protection actually works

Saying the OS \"manages memory\" leaves out the mechanism the exam asks about. Each process is given a base register holding the starting address of its partition and a bounds (limit) register holding its length. Every address the process generates is checked against that pair, and an address outside the range is refused \u2014 which is precisely what stops one program reading another's memory.

That also explains logical versus physical addresses. A process works in logical (relative) addresses starting at 0, as though it owned the machine; the hardware adds the base register to produce the real physical address. The translation is invisible to the program and is what makes relocation possible.

Two kinds of fragmentation

KindWhere the waste isCaused by
Internal fragmentationinside an allocated blockfixed-size blocks larger than the program needs
External fragmentationbetween allocated blocksvariable-size blocks leaving gaps as processes come and go

The distinction is worth holding by where the unusable space sits. Fixed partitioning wastes space within each block, because a 10KB program in a 16KB partition leaves 6KB unusable inside it. Dynamic partitioning fits each program exactly and instead leaves scattered gaps between them, none individually large enough to be useful. Paging reduces external fragmentation by dividing memory into fixed frames and programs into equal-sized pages, so any page fits any free frame \u2014 leaving only a little internal fragmentation in the final page.

Pushing paging too far causes thrashing: so little real memory is available that the system spends more time swapping pages to disk than executing instructions, and throughput collapses.

Multiprogramming, multitasking and preemption

Three related terms describe how an OS keeps several programs going, and questions ask you to tell them apart.

TermMeans
Multiprogrammingseveral programs are loaded in memory at once, so the CPU switches to another when one waits for I/O
Multitaskingthe same idea with rapid switching, so the user perceives simultaneous execution
Multiprocessinggenuinely simultaneous execution on more than one processor or core
Multithreadingseveral threads of execution within one process

Scheduling is also either preemptive or non-preemptive. A preemptive scheduler can preempt a running process \u2014 take the CPU away when its time slice (quantum) expires \u2014 which is what round robin does. A non-preemptive scheduler waits for the process to yield, which is why one long job under FCFS blocks everything behind it.

The life of a process

When you launch a program the OS creates a process \u2014 an instance of that program actually running, with its own memory and its own place in the schedule. The program on disk is passive; the process is the live thing.

A process moves through a fixed set of states, and the order is asked directly:

NEW  ->  READY  ->  RUNNING  ->  TERMINATED\n            ^         |\n            |         v\n          WAITING (blocked, e.g. on input)

New \u2014 being created. Ready \u2014 able to run, waiting for a CPU. Running \u2014 on the CPU now. Waiting (or blocked) \u2014 cannot continue until something outside finishes, typically I/O; it returns to ready, never straight to running. Terminated \u2014 finished.

Where a job is placed in memory

With dynamic partitions, free memory is a set of holes of different sizes, and the OS must choose one for an arriving job. Three named strategies, and the OA gives you the numbers.

StrategyChoosesTrade-off
First fitthe first hole big enough, scanning from the startfastest \u2014 no full scan needed
Best fitthe smallest hole that still fitsleast waste in that hole; leaves slivers, and must scan all
Worst fitthe largest hole of allleaves a big usable remainder; must scan all
\u25b8 WORKED EXAMPLE \u2014 holes of 400 KB, 250 KB and 600 KB; a 200 KB job arrives
first fit -> 400 KB   (the first one large enough)\nbest  fit -> 250 KB   (the smallest that still fits)\nworst fit -> 600 KB   (the largest, whatever else is free)

Read the hole list in the order printed \u2014 \"first fit\" depends on that order, the other two do not.

How the machine is used, and how you talk to it

TermMeans
Batch processingjobs are collected and run as a group with no user interaction \u2014 the earliest style, still used for payroll and billing
Time sharingmany users interact at once, the CPU switching between them fast enough to feel simultaneous
CLIcommand-line interface \u2014 you type commands; scriptable and precise
GUIgraphical user interface \u2014 windows, icons and a pointer; easier to learn, harder to automate

When the power comes on, the CPU runs firmware from ROM which finds and loads the operating system into RAM \u2014 booting. The OS is not running before this; it is loaded from storage like anything else, which is why a corrupt boot sector stops the machine before any program can start.

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION

Operating system: system software that manages hardware and provides services to applications

Process: a program in execution, with its own memory space

Thread: a unit of execution inside a process, sharing that process's memory

Scheduler: the OS component deciding which process runs next

Context switch: saving one process's state and restoring another's

Virtual memory: giving each process a large address space by paging unused parts to disk

Fragmentation: unusable gaps left in memory by repeated allocation and release

Deadlock: processes permanently blocked, each holding what another needs

Kernel: the core of the OS, with direct hardware access

Device driver: software letting the OS communicate with a particular piece of hardware

\u2605 ON THE OA

The OS is the resource manager \u2014 it schedules the CPU, manages memory, controls files and devices. You never allocate RAM directly; the OS does. Learn the scheduling algorithms by their one-line behaviour: round robin = fixed time slice in rotation, SJF = shortest job first, FCFS = arrival order.

\ud83c\udfaf EXAM TIP

Round robin optimises responsiveness and fairness; SJF optimises average waiting time but can starve long jobs. If a question mentions starvation, the answer is SJF or priority \u2014 never round robin.

A file is a named collection of data on storage. A file system is the method an operating system uses to organise, name, store and retrieve those files \u2014 it is the part of file management from the previous lesson, in detail.

Files are organised into directories (folders), which contain files and further directories, forming a tree that starts at the root. A path is the route through that tree to a particular file, and the two kinds of path are asked about directly.

Path typeStarts fromExample
Absolutethe root \u2014 unambiguous from anywhere/home/user/notes/file.txt
Relativethe current working directorynotes/file.txt

A relative path is shorter and breaks the moment the working directory changes, which is the single most common cause of \"it worked in my editor and failed from the terminal\".

Metadata and permissions

Alongside the contents, the file system stores metadata \u2014 data about the data: name, size, type, creation and modification dates, owner, and permissions. Metadata is why a file listing can show sizes and dates without opening anything.

Permissions control who may do what, conventionally read, write and execute, granted separately to the owner, a group and everyone else. That three-by-three grid is the whole of the classic Unix permission model, and it is the file-level end of the access control that security depends on.

How data is actually stored

Files are stored in fixed-size blocks, and a file larger than one block occupies several. When those blocks end up scattered across the disk rather than adjacent, the file is fragmented \u2014 reading it means more seeking, so it is slower. Defragmentation rearranges blocks to make files contiguous again, which matters on spinning hard disks and much less on solid-state drives, where there is no physical seek.

Two more distinctions the OA uses. A text file stores characters in an encoding you can read; a binary file stores raw bytes meaningful only to the program that wrote it. And access can be sequential \u2014 read from the start through to what you want \u2014 or direct/random, jumping straight to a position.

The file system as an abstraction

A disk has no notion of files. It has numbered blocks, and that is all. \"File\", \"folder\" and \"path\" are inventions of the file system, which keeps its own index recording which blocks belong to which file and what each file is called. This is abstraction in the sense of the earlier section: you work with a name and the system deals in block numbers.

Recognising that explains behaviour that otherwise looks arbitrary. Deleting a large file is instant because normally only the index entry is removed and the blocks are marked free \u2014 the data is still physically there, which is precisely why deleted files can often be recovered forensically. Renaming is instant for the same reason. And copying is slow, because that genuinely moves every block.

It also explains why the file system is where permissions live. The index is the one place that knows who owns each file, so it is the natural place to record who may read or change it.

Names, extensions and what they really do

A file name usually ends in a file extension \u2014 the part after the final dot, as in report.pdf. The extension is a convention: it tells the operating system which application to open the file with, and it tells you what to expect. It does not create or change the contents.

That is why renaming report.docx to report.txt changes nothing but the name. The bytes are identical; the OS now offers the wrong program to open them, and the file appears broken. Format is decided by how the data was written, never by the label on the end.

Paths

A path is the route to a file through the directory tree, and it comes in two kinds.

KindStarts fromExample
Absolutethe root of the file system \u2014 same meaning from anywhere/home/nat/notes/d684.txt
Relativethe current working directorynotes/d684.txt
.     the current directory\n..    the PARENT directory \u2014 one level up\n../..  two levels up\n\nfrom /home/nat/notes :\n    ../photos/cat.png   ->  /home/nat/photos/cat.png

A relative path is shorter but only means what it says from where you are standing; an absolute path always resolves the same way.

Copying, moving, and surviving a crash

A copy creates a second independent file \u2014 two copies exist afterwards, and changing one leaves the other alone. A move relocates the single file \u2014 one copy exists afterwards. Within the same drive a move usually rewrites only the directory entry, which is why it is instant on a large file while a copy is not.

A journaling file system keeps a log of what it is about to do before it does it. If the power fails mid-write, the OS replays or discards the journal on restart and the file system is left consistent instead of half-updated. It exists to solve corruption from interrupted writes \u2014 not to save space and not to make writes faster.

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION

File: a named collection of data held on storage

File system: the structure and method an OS uses to organise and retrieve files

Directory / folder: a container organising files and other directories

Root: the top of the directory tree

Absolute path: a path from the root \u2014 valid from anywhere

Relative path: a path from the current working directory

Metadata: data about a file: size, dates, owner, permissions

Permissions: the read, write and execute rights granted to owner, group and others

Fragmentation: a file stored in non-adjacent blocks, slowing reads

Sequential vs direct access: reading from the start versus jumping straight to a position

\u2605 ON THE OA

A file is named data on disk; a directory organises files hierarchically; a path locates one. An absolute path starts from the root, a relative path from the current directory. Metadata records size, dates and permissions \u2014 not the contents.

\ud83d\udca1 WHY IT MATTERS

File systems are the reason anything survives a reboot. RAM is volatile and loses everything when power goes; a file is how a program's results outlive the process that produced them.

"}, "D684/s5/l1_1": {"body": "

The CPU \u2014 the central processing unit \u2014 executes instructions, and everything else on the motherboard exists to feed it. The model the OA tests is von Neumann architecture, and its defining claim is that program instructions and data share the same memory. That is why a computer is general-purpose: change the contents of memory and you change what the machine does.

Von Neumann architecture has five parts, and the grouping matters as much as the list.

PartJob
Control unitdirects the fetch-decode-execute cycle and tells everything else what to do
ALU (arithmetic logic unit)performs the arithmetic and the logical comparisons
Memoryholds both the instructions and the data
Inputbrings data in \u2014 keyboard, sensor, network
Outputsends results out \u2014 screen, file, network

The control unit and the ALU together are the CPU; memory, input and output sit outside it. Getting that grouping right answers a surprising share of architecture questions.

The fetch-decode-execute cycle

Every instruction goes through the same three steps, billions of times per second.

FETCH    the control unit gets the next instruction from memory\nDECODE   it works out what the instruction means\nEXECUTE  the ALU (or another unit) carries it out\n         ...store the result, then repeat

Registers are tiny storage locations inside the CPU itself, used to hold the values an instruction is working on right now. They are the fastest storage in the machine because they are physically closest \u2014 which is the whole idea behind the memory hierarchy.

The memory hierarchy

Speed and capacity trade against each other, and the machine resolves that by having several layers rather than one.

LevelSpeedSizeVolatile?
Registersfastesta few dozen valuesyes
Cache (L1, L2, L3)very fastkilobytes to megabytesyes
RAM (main memory)fastgigabytesyes \u2014 lost on power off
SSD / hard diskslowhundreds of gigabytes upno \u2014 survives power off

Cache exists because RAM is slower than the CPU. It holds recently and frequently used data close to the processor, so most requests never have to travel to main memory. And the volatility column is the reason files exist at all: everything in RAM disappears when the power goes, so anything that must survive has to be written to storage.

The rest of the board

The motherboard is the board connecting everything, and a bus is the set of wires carrying data between components \u2014 a data bus for the values, an address bus for locations, a control bus for signals. Clock speed, measured in gigahertz, is how many cycles the CPU performs per second, and cores are independent processing units on one chip, so a quad-core processor can genuinely execute four instruction streams at once.

Why the von Neumann design matters

The claim that instructions and data share one memory sounds like a technicality and is the reason computers are general-purpose machines rather than appliances. Because a program is just data in memory, a computer can load a different program and become a different tool \u2014 and it is also why a computer can compile, generate or modify programs at all. Earlier machines were wired for a specific calculation and had to be physically rewired to do something else.

The same design has a cost the exam sometimes names: the von Neumann bottleneck. Because instructions and data travel over the same path between the CPU and memory, that path limits how fast the processor can be fed, no matter how fast the processor is. Cache exists largely to soften that bottleneck, and it is why adding cache can speed up a machine more than raising its clock speed.

One clarification on clock speed: it counts cycles, not instructions, so a 3 GHz processor does not perform three billion instructions a second. Comparing chips by gigahertz alone is unreliable, which is why cores, cache and architecture appear alongside it in any real specification.

The registers that drive the cycle

The fetch-decode-execute cycle needs somewhere to keep track of where it is, and that is what the special-purpose registers do. Two are named directly in exam questions.

RegisterHolds
Program counter (PC)the address of the next instruction to fetch
Instruction register (IR)the instruction currently being executed
Accumulatorthe working value the ALU is operating on
Memory address register (MAR)the address currently being read from or written to
Memory data register (MDR)the data travelling to or from that address

The two that matter most are easy to confuse and easy to separate once stated side by side: the PC points at what comes next, the IR holds what is happening now. Each pass of the cycle fetches the instruction at the PC, copies it into the IR, advances the PC, then decodes and executes.

FETCH     read the instruction at the address in the PC\n          copy it into the IR,  then ADVANCE the PC\nDECODE    the control unit works out what the instruction means\nEXECUTE   the ALU (or another unit) carries it out, result to a register\n          ...repeat

Watching a tiny program run makes the division of labour concrete. For LOAD A, ADD B, STORE C with A = 4 and B = 3: the control unit fetches each instruction (the PC says where), decodes it, and the ALU does the addition, leaving 7 in a register until STORE C writes it back to memory.

Bus width and clock speed

Bus width is the number of bits the bus carries at once \u2014 the number of lanes on the highway. A wider bus moves more data per transfer, which is why 64-bit systems can move twice as much per cycle as 32-bit ones. Clock speed, in gigahertz, is how many cycles happen per second, and it counts cycles rather than instructions, so it is not on its own a measure of how fast a processor gets work done.

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION

CPU: the processor \u2014 control unit plus ALU \u2014 which executes instructions

Von Neumann architecture: a design in which instructions and data share the same memory

Control unit: directs the fetch-decode-execute cycle

ALU: performs arithmetic and logic operations

Register: a very small, very fast storage location inside the CPU

Cache: fast memory close to the CPU holding recently used data

RAM: volatile main memory \u2014 erased when power is lost

Motherboard: the board connecting CPU, memory and peripherals

Bus: the wires carrying data, addresses and control signals between components

Clock speed: cycles per second, measured in GHz

Core: an independent processing unit within a CPU

\u2605 ON THE OA

Von Neumann has five parts \u2014 control unit, ALU, memory, input, output \u2014 and CU + ALU = the CPU. Program and data share the same memory. The ALU does arithmetic and logic; the control unit directs the fetch-decode-execute flow. Do not swap those two.

\ud83d\udca1 WHY IT MATTERS

The memory hierarchy explains costs you meet everywhere else: why a variable is fast and a file is slow, why virtual memory hurts performance when it starts swapping, and why an algorithm that touches memory in order beats one that jumps around, even at the same Big-O.

"}, "D684/s5/l2_1": {"body": "

A network is a group of devices linked to communicate and share resources. The internet is the largest one \u2014 an enormous number of computers passing messages \u2014 and it works because every device follows the same agreed rules, called protocols.

Networks are classified first by how far they reach. A LAN (local area network) covers one building or site; a WAN (wide area network) spans cities or countries, and the internet is the largest WAN. A MAN covers a metropolitan area, and a PAN is personal-scale, like a phone and its headphones.

Topologies

Topology is the shape of the connections, and the OA asks what happens to each shape when something fails.

TopologyArrangementIf one part fails
Busall devices share one backbone cablea break in the backbone takes down the whole network
Ringeach device connects to two neighbours in a loopone break can split the ring unless it is dual-ring
Starevery device connects to a central hub or switchone device failing is fine; the hub failing drops everything
Meshmany devices interconnected with redundant pathstraffic routes around the failure \u2014 the most fault-tolerant

Packets, addresses and names

Data does not travel as a whole file. It is broken into packets, each carrying a piece of the data plus the source and destination addresses. Packets travel independently, may take different routes, and are reassembled in order at the far end \u2014 which is what makes the network resilient, since losing one packet means resending one packet.

Every device has two addresses and the difference is examined. A MAC address is burned into the network hardware and does not change \u2014 it identifies the device physically. An IP address is assigned by the network and identifies the device logically; it changes when the device joins a different network.

DNS, the domain name system, is the internet's phone book: it translates a human-readable name into an IP address. Typing a URL triggers a DNS lookup first, then packets route to the returned address.

ProtocolDoes
TCP/IPthe core suite \u2014 IP routes packets, TCP guarantees they arrive in order
HTTP / HTTPStransfers web pages; HTTPS adds encryption
DNStranslates domain names into IP addresses
DHCPautomatically assigns IP addresses to devices joining a network
FTPtransfers files
SMTPsends email

The layered models

A network model is a layered blueprint in which each layer does one job and hands the data to the next. Two are examined: the OSI model with seven layers \u2014 physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, application \u2014 and the TCP/IP model with four: link, internet, transport, application. OSI is the teaching model; TCP/IP is what the internet actually runs on.

Finally, the devices: a switch connects devices within one network and forwards frames to the right port; a router connects different networks and decides which path a packet takes; a firewall filters traffic against rules, allowing or blocking it at the boundary.

TCP, UDP and ports

IP routes packets to the right machine; a transport protocol decides what guarantees come with them, and the two choices are a genuine trade.

TCPUDP
Connectionestablishes one firstnone \u2014 just sends
Guaranteesdelivery, order, error checkingnone
Speedslower \u2014 acknowledgements and retriesfaster \u2014 no overhead
Used forweb pages, email, file transferlive video, voice, gaming

The rule of thumb is that TCP is right when a missing piece ruins the result, and UDP is right when a late piece is worse than a missing one \u2014 a dropped frame in a video call is better than a call that stalls to re-send it.

A port number identifies which application on the machine a packet is for, so the IP address finds the computer and the port finds the program. The ones asked about are 80 for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS, 25 for SMTP, 53 for DNS and 22 for SSH.

The client-server model and status codes

Most of the internet follows the client-server model: a client requests, a server responds. Your browser is the client, the machine holding the site is the server, and each request gets an HTTP status code saying what happened \u2014 200 OK, 301 moved permanently, 404 not found, 500 server error. The first digit gives the category: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx the client's fault, 5xx the server's.

The alternative arrangement is peer-to-peer, where every machine is both client and server \u2014 used for file sharing and some messaging, with no central server to fail or to control.

Connection types

Broadband means a high-capacity, always-on connection, as opposed to the dial-up it replaced. The common kinds are DSL over telephone lines, cable over the television network, fibre optic, and cellular. Bandwidth is measured in bits per second \u2014 Mbps, Gbps \u2014 and is the maximum rate rather than a guaranteed one, which is why latency, the delay before data starts arriving, is a separate measure that matters just as much for interactive use.

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION

Network: devices linked to communicate and share resources

LAN / WAN: a network covering one site; a network spanning large distances

Topology: the arrangement of connections \u2014 bus, ring, star, mesh

Packet: a unit of data plus addressing, routed independently and reassembled

Protocol: an agreed set of rules for communication

IP address: the logical address identifying a device on a network

MAC address: the permanent physical address of network hardware

DNS: the system translating domain names into IP addresses

Router / switch: connects different networks; connects devices within one network

Firewall: filters network traffic against a rule set

OSI model: the seven-layer reference model for network communication

\u2605 ON THE OA

Topologies by failure behaviour: in a star, the hub failing drops everything; a mesh routes around failures and is the most fault-tolerant; a bus dies with its backbone. Data travels in packets. An IP address identifies a device; DNS maps names to IPs.

\ud83c\udfaf EXAM TIP

For \"what happens when you type a URL\" \u2014 DNS translates the name to an IP address, packets route to that address, and the response is reassembled. That sequence answers several questions on its own.

"}, "D684/s5/l3_1": {"body": "

The architecture in 1.1 is the same whether it sits in a watch or a national laboratory. What changes is scale, and the OA asks you to match a described role to a category.

TypeBuilt forExample
Supercomputermaximum raw performance on one huge calculationclimate modelling, protein folding
Mainframeenormous transaction throughput and reliabilitya bank's transaction backbone
Serverproviding services to many clients over a networka web or database server
Personal computerone user at a time, general purposea laptop or desktop
Mobile deviceportability and battery lifea phone or tablet
Embedded systemone dedicated job inside a larger devicea car's engine controller, a thermostat

The pair most often confused is supercomputer and mainframe, and the distinction is what \"big\" means. A supercomputer is optimised for speed on a single enormous computation; a mainframe is optimised for throughput and uptime across millions of small transactions. A weather model wants a supercomputer; a bank wants a mainframe.

Embedded systems and the Internet of Things

An embedded system is a computer built into a larger device to do one dedicated job. It usually has limited memory and processing power, often runs a real-time operating system, and typically has no general-purpose interface \u2014 you never install software on your microwave.

The Internet of Things is what happens when those embedded devices get network connectivity: everyday objects that sense, report and can be controlled remotely. A smart thermostat, a fitness tracker, a connected doorbell and an industrial sensor are all IoT devices, and the pattern is always the same \u2014 sense, transmit, analyse, act.

Two consequences follow, and the exam asks about both. IoT generates enormous volumes of data from the edge of the network, which is why edge computing exists \u2014 process it near the device rather than shipping it all to a data centre. And these devices are a security problem out of proportion to their size: they are numerous, rarely updated, often shipped with default passwords, and physically accessible. A compromised sensor is a foothold on the network it sits in.

Why the categories exist

It would be reasonable to ask why the scale categories matter when every one of these devices has the same von Neumann parts inside. The answer is that each is optimised for a different constraint, and the constraint is what the question is really describing. A supercomputer optimises raw floating-point throughput and accepts enormous power and cooling costs. A mainframe optimises reliability and transaction volume \u2014 it is built to run for years without stopping. An embedded system optimises cost, size and power, because it may run on a battery for a decade.

So when a scenario mentions a requirement rather than a machine \u2014 \"must never go down\", \"must fit on a battery-powered sensor\", \"must model the atmosphere overnight\" \u2014 it is naming the constraint, and the constraint identifies the category.

Embedded systems bring one more idea worth holding: many are real-time systems, meaning a correct answer delivered too late counts as a failure. An airbag controller that computes the right response fifty milliseconds after the crash has not partly succeeded. That is a different standard from ordinary software, where slow is merely slow.

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION

Supercomputer: a machine built for maximum performance on large computations

Mainframe: a machine built for very high transaction throughput and reliability

Server: a computer providing services to clients over a network

Embedded system: a computer built into a device to perform one dedicated function

Real-time system: one that must respond within a guaranteed time limit

Internet of Things (IoT): networked everyday devices that sense, report and can be controlled remotely

Edge computing: processing data near where it is generated rather than centrally

Firmware: software stored in hardware, providing low-level control of a device

\u2605 ON THE OA

Match the scale to the role: supercomputer for maximum performance, mainframe for enterprise throughput, server for network services, embedded for one dedicated job inside a device. A car's engine controller is embedded; a bank's transaction backbone is a mainframe.

\ud83d\udca1 WHY IT MATTERS

IoT security is where this section meets the ethics of Section 2. A device that cannot be patched, shipped with a default password, is not only a technical weakness \u2014 deploying it knowingly is the kind of decision both professional codes address.
