Computational thinking is the structured thought process of framing a problem so that a computer \u2014 or anyone following instructions literally \u2014 could solve it. It is not programming, and that distinction is the point: you do it before any code exists, and it is what makes the code writeable.

Four pillars make it up, and the OA asks you to name the one a scenario describes, so learn them by what they do rather than as a list.

PillarWhat you actually doExample
Decompositionbreak a large problem into smaller sub-problems that can be solved separately\"build an online store\" becomes catalogue, cart, checkout, accounts
Pattern recognitionspot similarities between problems or within datanoticing every report page needs the same header and filter logic
Abstractionignore the detail that does not matter to the problema route planner treats a city as points and distances, not buildings
Algorithm designwrite the ordered steps that solve itthe numbered procedure for checking out a cart

Abstraction is the pillar most often misread, because \"ignoring detail\" sounds like carelessness. It is the opposite: it is deciding deliberately which details are irrelevant to this problem. A map that showed every brick would be useless for navigation. In computing the same move appears at every level \u2014 a programmer uses a sort function without knowing which algorithm it runs, and that function uses memory without knowing about voltages.

The four are also not a strict sequence. In practice you decompose, notice a pattern between two of the pieces, abstract away what they do not share, and design one algorithm that handles both. But an exam question describing a single activity has one right label, and the labels are the ones above.

Why it comes before code

The practical version of all this is the habit from problem solving generally: understand the problem, work one example by hand, write the steps in plain language, and only then translate them into a language. Working an example by hand is the step people skip and the one that catches the most errors \u2014 if you cannot compute the answer for one specific input on paper, no amount of syntax will get you there.

Telling the four pillars apart under pressure

Because all four pillars sound reasonable for any problem, exam scenarios are written so that exactly one is being described. The reliable test is to ask what the person in the scenario is actually doing to the problem. Breaking it into parts is decomposition. Noticing that two parts are the same shape is pattern recognition. Deciding what can be ignored is abstraction. Writing the ordered steps is algorithm design.

A worked case makes it concrete. Planning a system to grade thousands of exams: splitting it into scanning, marking and reporting is decomposition. Noticing that every multiple-choice question is marked the same way is pattern recognition. Deciding the marker does not need the student's name, only the answers, is abstraction. Writing \"for each answer, compare with the key, add one if it matches\" is algorithm design.

One more distinction the OA relies on: computational thinking is a way of thinking about problems, not a programming skill. It applies to organising a wedding as much as to writing software, and questions sometimes deliberately use a non-computing scenario to check you understood that.

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION

Computational thinking: framing a problem so that its solution can be carried out by a computer

Decomposition: breaking a problem into smaller sub-problems

Pattern recognition: identifying similarities between or within problems

Abstraction: deliberately ignoring detail that is irrelevant to the problem at hand

Algorithm design: specifying the ordered steps that solve the problem

Algorithm: a finite sequence of unambiguous steps producing a result

\u2605 ON THE OA

A memory hook for the four pillars in order \u2014 All Programmers Practise Algorithms: decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, algorithm design. Splitting a big problem into sub-problems is decomposition; focusing only on the essentials is abstraction. Those two are the pair the OA most often asks you to tell apart.

\ud83d\udca1 WHY IT MATTERS

Every later section is an application of this. The SDLC is decomposition applied to a whole project, subprograms are decomposition applied to code, and Big-O is what happens when you compare two algorithm designs for the same problem.

"}, "D684/s2/l1_2": {"body": "

The Software Development Life Cycle is the organised, multi-phase process a team follows to build and maintain software. The analogy that makes it stick is building a house: you do not start nailing boards before you know what the owner wants, and you do not move people in before an inspection.

The classic ordering has seven phases, and the OA asks two things about them \u2014 the order, and what each one produces.

PhaseWhat happensWhat comes out
1. Planningdecide feasibility, scope, budget and schedulea project plan
2. Analysisgather requirements \u2014 what must it do?a requirements document
3. Designplan the logic and structureflowcharts, pseudocode, diagrams
4. Implementationwrite the code \u2014 \"translate the design\"working source code
5. Testingverify it does what the requirements saidtest results and defect reports
6. Deploymentrelease it to usersa live system
7. Maintenancefix, adapt and improve after releaseupdates and patches

Two of these carry more exam weight than the rest. Maintenance is where most of a system's total cost and time actually goes \u2014 it is the longest phase, not an afterthought, and questions about \"the majority of a program's lifetime\" point here. And design is the phase where flowcharts and pseudocode belong; if a question says \"plan the logic\", it is describing design, not implementation.

Models: waterfall and agile

The phases above describe what gets done. A model describes how they are sequenced. Waterfall runs them strictly once, in order, each phase finishing before the next begins \u2014 predictable and documented, but expensive to change once requirements are locked. Agile runs short iterations that each go through the whole cycle, delivering a working increment every few weeks \u2014 flexible and responsive to change, at the cost of less up-front certainty about the final scope.

The useful way to hold the difference: waterfall assumes you know the requirements at the start; agile assumes you will learn them as you go. Neither is the \"right\" one, and questions usually describe a situation and ask which fits.

Why the order is the question

Almost every SDLC question is really an ordering question in disguise. It describes an activity and asks which phase it belongs to, or asks what comes immediately before or after something. So it is worth being able to state not just the sequence but the reason for it: you cannot design what you have not specified, cannot code what you have not designed, cannot test what you have not built, and cannot deploy what has not passed testing. Each phase consumes the output of the one before.

The phase people place wrongly is design. Flowcharts, pseudocode and diagrams are design artefacts \u2014 planning the logic \u2014 not implementation. Implementation is writing the actual code, which WGU sometimes words as \"translate the design into code\". If a question mentions pseudocode, it is describing design.

Maintenance is the other one worth expecting. It is not a small tail on the end: most of a system's total cost and most of its calendar life happen after release, in fixing defects, adapting to new requirements and improving performance. A question about where the majority of effort goes over a program's lifetime is pointing at maintenance.

The other models, and what agile looks like in practice

Waterfall and agile are the two poles, and two more models appear in questions between them. The spiral model repeats the phases in cycles like agile, but adds an explicit risk analysis step to every cycle \u2014 so it suits large projects where the cost of getting it wrong is high. The iterative and incremental model builds the system in successive versions, each adding function to a working product.

Agile itself is a philosophy rather than a procedure, and Scrum is its most common concrete framework. Work happens in fixed-length sprints, usually two to four weeks, each ending in a potentially shippable increment. The vocabulary is examined: a product backlog is the prioritised list of everything wanted, a sprint backlog is what this sprint has committed to, the daily stand-up is a short synchronisation meeting, and the retrospective at the end asks how the team can work better next time.

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION

SDLC: the multi-phase process for developing and maintaining software

Requirements: the statement of what the software must do, produced in analysis

Design: planning the logic and structure \u2014 flowcharts and pseudocode live here

Implementation: writing the code that realises the design

Testing: verifying the software meets its requirements

Deployment: releasing the software to its users

Maintenance: fixing and improving software after release \u2014 the longest phase

Waterfall: a sequential model completing each phase before the next

Agile: an iterative model delivering working increments in short cycles

\u2605 ON THE OA

Know the phases in order and be able to name one from a scenario. \"The team is writing test cases\" is testing, which comes after implementation. \"Gathering requirements\" is analysis. \"Writing code\" is implementation. Order is what the question is testing.

\ud83c\udfaf EXAM TIP

When a scenario mentions changing requirements mid-project, the expected answer is agile. When it mentions fixed requirements, regulatory sign-off or heavy documentation, it is waterfall.

"}, "D684/s2/l2_1": {"body": "

A code of ethics is a set of professional guidelines governing how computing professionals should behave. It is not law and carries no criminal penalty \u2014 its force is professional: membership, reputation, and in some fields licensure. Two bodies publish the codes the OA cares about.

BodyFull nameCentre of gravity
ACMAssociation for Computing Machinerycomputing broadly \u2014 software, research, data
IEEEInstitute of Electrical and Electronics Engineershardware and electrical engineering

Both codes share the same themes, and the shared themes are what most questions test rather than the differences: protect the public \u2014 safety, health and welfare come first, ahead of employer or client interest; be honest and avoid conflicts of interest; respect privacy and confidentiality; credit others' work; and maintain and improve technical competence. That last phrase is WGU's own wording for what adopting the IEEE code commits a company to.

When a scenario violates both codes, it is typically one that puts people at risk while also concealing something \u2014 shipping a component known to be unsafe, or hiding a breach from the users it affects.

Intellectual property and licensing

Copyright protects a creative work automatically from the moment it is made. A licence is the creator saying what others may do with it \u2014 so a licence does not remove copyright, it grants permissions under it.

Licence typeWhat you may doExample
Proprietary (closed)use it under the terms you bought; you cannot see or change the sourcemost commercial software
Copyleft open sourceuse, modify and redistribute \u2014 but derivatives must stay open under the same licenceGPL
Permissive open sourceuse, modify and redistribute with few restrictions, including in closed productsMIT, Apache
Public domainanything \u2014 no rights reserved at allexpired copyright, or a deliberate release

The distinction that decides questions is copyleft versus permissive. Ship a commercial product built on GPL code and you must release your own source under the GPL; build the same product on MIT code and you need not. \"Open source\" alone does not tell you which \u2014 you have to read which family the licence is in.

Fair use is a separate idea and a narrow one: it is a legal doctrine permitting limited use of copyrighted material without permission for purposes such as criticism, comment, news reporting, teaching and research. It is a defence judged case by case on factors including how much was used and whether the use harms the market for the original \u2014 not a blanket permission.

System versus application software

One more classification the OA asks for directly. System software manages the machine itself \u2014 the operating system, device drivers, utilities. Application software does a task for the user \u2014 a spreadsheet, a browser, a game. An OS is system software; a word processor is application software.

Software piracy

Piracy is the unauthorised copying, distribution or use of software or media \u2014 downloading a paid application without paying, sharing a licence key, or distributing copyrighted films. It is a copyright violation rather than a licensing subtlety, and it is distinct from the open-source questions above: an open licence grants permissions, while piracy is use with no permission at all.

Cybercrime, and who investigates it

Ethics is what you should do; cybercrime is what the law forbids. A cybercrime is any crime committed using a computer or network \u2014 unauthorised access, identity theft, ransomware, phishing, denial-of-service, online fraud, and the distribution of copyrighted material. The exam asks you to recognise one from a scenario and to know where it is reported.

BodyWhat it isHandles
IC3Internet Crime Complaint Center, run by the FBIthe place U.S. victims file a cybercrime complaint
FBIFederal Bureau of Investigationcybercrime generally \u2014 intrusion, fraud, IP theft
U.S. Secret Servicea Treasury-founded agency, now Homeland Securityfinancial and payment-system crime \u2014 card fraud, counterfeiting

The distinction that gets tested: a victim reports to IC3; a payment-system or financial crime is investigated by the Secret Service. Complaints and reported losses to the FBI have risen year on year, not fallen. Penalties scale with harm and can include fines, restitution to victims, and imprisonment \u2014 a cybercrime is not a civil matter that ends with a payment.

The two professional bodies, and what each is for

BodyStands forIts focus
ACMAssociation for Computing Machinerythe Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct \u2014 how a computing professional must behave
IEEEInstitute of Electrical and Electronics Engineerstechnical standards for computing and electronics (Wi-Fi 802.11, Ethernet 802.3)

They also publish a joint Software Engineering Code of Ethics. The ACM code turns on one idea the OA tests repeatedly: the public good comes first. When a scenario pits your employer's reputation against user safety or honesty, the ethical answer is the one that protects the user \u2014 disclose the flaw, refuse to stay silent, report it up and then out if nothing is done.

The second recurring idea is that being able to is not being allowed to. Deploying employee surveillance simply because the technology makes it possible fails the code: capability is not justification.

Privacy principles

Privacy questions are scenario-shaped and resolve to a small number of named principles.

PrincipleMeansViolated by
Data minimisationcollect only what the stated purpose needsgathering extra personal data \"just in case\"
Purpose limitationuse data only for the purpose it was collected forselling analytics data collected for delivery tracking
Authorised accessonly people with a legitimate need may see itusing a coworker's login to read personnel records
Consentthe person knows and agreestracking location with no disclosure

Continuous monitoring of users' network activity and communications is surveillance, and it is a privacy concern whether or not it is legal where you are.

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION

Code of ethics: professional guidelines for how computing professionals should behave

ACM: Association for Computing Machinery \u2014 its code covers computing broadly

IEEE: Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers \u2014 hardware and electrical focus

Copyright: automatic legal protection for an original creative work

Licence: the permissions a creator grants others under copyright

Copyleft (GPL): open-source licensing requiring derivatives to stay open

Permissive (MIT, Apache): open-source licensing with few restrictions on reuse

Public domain: no rights reserved; free for any use

Fair use: limited use of copyrighted work without permission for purposes such as teaching or criticism

System software: software that manages the computer \u2014 OS, drivers, utilities

Application software: software that performs tasks for the user

\u2605 ON THE OA

A question about a code focused on hardware or electronics points to IEEE; a general computing-professional code points to ACM. Both prioritise the public interest above employer or client. For licences: GPL forces your derivative open, MIT does not, public domain reserves nothing.

\u26a0 COMMON MISTAKE

\"Open source\" and \"free\" are not the same claim, and neither means \"public domain\". Open source describes access to the source under a licence with terms; public domain means no rights are reserved at all.

"}, "D684/s1/l1_1": {"body": "

A data type is not a label stuck on a value. It is a contract with the machine that answers three questions at once: how many bytes to reserve, how to interpret the bits in them, and which operations are legal. The same 32 bits in memory are the integer 1078530011 or the decimal 3.14159 depending on nothing but the declared type. Memory holds no meaning; the type supplies it.

Five core types cover almost everything the OA asks about, and the exam tests whether you can pick the right one for a described value rather than recite the list.

TypeHoldsExampleChoose it when
Integerwhole numbers, no fractional part42, \u22127, 0you are counting, indexing or storing an ID
Real / floatnumbers with a fractional part3.14, \u22120.5you are measuring \u2014 money is the exception
Characterexactly one symbol'A', '7', '$'a single letter, digit or punctuation mark
Stringtext of any length\"hello\"anything you will never do arithmetic on
Booleantrue or false, nothing elsetruea yes/no state \u2014 a checkbox, a flag

The line between these is sharper than it looks, and two distinctions carry most of the marks. The character '7' is a symbol; the integer 7 is a number you can do arithmetic on. And the two numeric types behave differently even when they hold the same value: as integers, 7 / 2 is 3, because integer division keeps only the whole part and throws the remainder away. As reals, 7.0 / 2.0 is 3.5. Same symbols, different type, different answer.

That is also why the difference between exact and approximate matters. Integers are exact but bounded \u2014 an unsigned 8-bit integer holds 0 to 255 and nothing more. Floating point buys an enormous range by storing a number as mantissa \u00d7 baseexponent, which is scientific notation in binary, and pays for it with precision: any fraction whose denominator is not a power of two cannot be stored exactly, so 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3. Counting uses integers. Measuring uses floats. Money uses neither \u2014 it uses whole cents in an integer, because a rounding error in a float is a rounding error in someone's balance.

Strong typing and type mismatch

A strongly typed language enforces the declared type and refuses to silently mix incompatible ones. Storing \"abc\" into an integer variable is a type mismatch \u2014 the language stops you rather than guessing. Python is strongly typed: \"Hello\" + 5 raises a TypeError, while \"Hello\" + str(5) works because you converted deliberately.

The version of this the OA loves is the concatenation trap. If finalScore holds the string '95' and you compute finalScore + 5, many languages join them as text and give '955', not 100. The + did text-joining because the operand was text. When you expected a number and got text, that is a type mismatch caused by mixing types.

Converting between types

An implicit conversion happens automatically when a value is promoted to a compatible type \u2014 an integer used inside a floating-point expression becomes a float. This is widening, and it is safe, because the target can hold everything the source could. An explicit conversion, or cast, is one you request: converting a float to an integer truncates toward zero rather than rounding, so int(3.9) is 3 and int(\u22123.9) is \u22123. That is narrowing, it loses information, and that is exactly why the language makes you ask for it.

How text, images and sound become numbers

Every type in the table above is ultimately bits, and the encodings that make that possible are examined by name. ASCII covers 128 characters in 7 bits, so 'A' is 65. Unicode extends that to every writing system, and UTF-8 is the encoding that stores it using 1 to 4 bytes per character \u2014 which is why in Unicode text the byte count and the character count are not the same number.

Images work the same way with a different table: each pixel stores an RGB triple, one value each for red, green and blue, so a colour is three numbers. Sound is analog \u2014 a continuous wave \u2014 and becomes digital through sampling: pulse-code modulation (PCM) measures the wave many times a second and stores each measurement as a number. Bandwidth is the maximum rate a path can carry those bits, in bits per second.

Compression

Storing every byte is often wasteful, and compression divides into two kinds with a hard difference between them.

KindKeeps every bit?Used for
LosslessYes \u2014 the original is perfectly recoverableZIP, PNG, all text encoding
LossyNo \u2014 some detail is discarded permanentlyJPEG, MP3

Three classic text techniques are all lossless and all named in questions. Run-length encoding replaces repeats with a count plus the symbol, so AAAABBBCC becomes 4A3B2C. Keyword encoding replaces common words with short codes, so \"and\" might become &. Huffman encoding gives the most frequent characters the shortest codes.

Compression ratio is asked in two conventions and you must read which the question uses. As compressed \u00f7 original, a 200KB file reduced to 50KB gives 0.25 and smaller is better. As original \u00f7 compressed \u2014 the wording in the WGU glossary \u2014 the same file gives 4, or 4:1, and larger is better. They describe identical compression with the direction flipped.

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION

Data type: a contract fixing how many bytes a value takes, how the bits are interpreted, and what operations are legal

Strong typing: the language enforces types and refuses to mix them without an explicit conversion

Type mismatch: assigning a value of the wrong type to a variable, or an operator receiving a type it cannot handle

Implicit conversion: automatic promotion to a compatible type \u2014 safe, widening

Explicit conversion (cast): a conversion you request; may lose data, e.g. float to int truncates

Declaration: a statement that defines a variable and its type \u2014 float price = 19.99;

Boolean expression: a statement that is either true or false, such as 4 > 3

\u2605 ON THE OA

Match the value to the type: a checkbox is boolean, a price is float, a name is string, a count is integer. Phone numbers, ZIP codes and student IDs are strings \u2014 you never add two of them, and a numeric type destroys the leading zero in 007. And remember that \"strongly typed\" means the language enforces types, not that it has a lot of them.

\u26a0 COMMON MISTAKE

Integer division is the single most common arithmetic bug in this section. 9 / 4 with two integers is 2, not 2.25 \u2014 the remainder 1 is what 9 mod 4 would give you. If a calculation needs a decimal answer, at least one operand must be a real number.

"}, "D684/s1/l1_2": {"body": "

A variable is a named storage location whose value can change while the program runs. It has five properties, and the two that exams probe are the last two: a name, a type, a value, an address in memory, a scope \u2014 where the name is visible \u2014 and a lifetime \u2014 how long the storage exists. Scope is about the source code; lifetime is about runtime. They are related and not the same thing.

Three separate events happen to a variable and keeping them apart explains most beginner confusion. Declaring reserves storage and fixes the type. Initializing gives it its first value. Assigning replaces that value later. Reading a variable that was declared but never initialized is a genuine hazard: some languages refuse to compile, and others hand you garbage \u2014 whatever bytes happened to already be at that address \u2014 producing bugs that appear on one machine and not another.

Constants

A constant is a value that cannot change during execution. An unnamed constant is a literal written straight into the code, like 3.14 \u2014 considered poor practice, and known as a magic number because nobody reading it can tell what it means. A named constant gives it a meaningful name: final double PI = 3.14159;. That buys three things \u2014 it documents intent, it centralises change so one edit updates all twelve uses, and it turns an accidental modification into a compile error.

Identifiers and naming

An identifier is the name of a variable, method or class. The rules are enforced by the language: it must start with a letter or underscore (never a digit), it must be a single word with no spaces, and it must not be a reserved keyword such as int, while or class. So total and _count are valid and 2nd is not.

Conventions, by contrast, are agreements between programmers that the compiler ignores entirely \u2014 and the OA tests whether you can name them.

ConventionLooks likeTypically used for
camelCasemyVariableNamevariables and methods in Java
PascalCaseMyVariableNameclass names
snake_casemy_variable_namePython variables, constants, config
kebab-casemy-variable-nameURLs and CSS \u2014 not valid in Java
Hungarian notationstrNamea type prefix on the name
Mixed case with underscoresMy_Variable_Namereadability in some house styles

Scope, and why global variables are discouraged

A local variable is declared inside a function and visible only there \u2014 created when the function starts, destroyed when it returns. A global variable is declared outside all functions, visible everywhere, and alive for the whole run. When a local shares a name with a global, the local shadows it: every assignment inside the function hits the local copy, and the global is untouched.

\u25b8 WORKED EXAMPLE \u2014 shadowing
global total = 100\n\nfunction f():\n    total = 5           # a NEW local, not the global\n    print(total)        # 5\n\nf()\nprint(total)            # 100 \u2014 the global was never changed

Globals are readable from anywhere, which sounds convenient and is precisely the problem: any function may change one, so behaviour depends on execution order and bugs become impossible to trace. That is coupling, the thing modular design exists to reduce. The exam phrasing to recognise is that locals promote encapsulation and modularity while globals create hidden dependencies.

Lifetime explains the rest. Locals live in a stack frame created when a function is called and destroyed when it returns \u2014 which is why a local cannot be read after the function ends, why a value must be returned to survive, and why runaway recursion overflows the stack.

Literals, and naming conventions

A literal is a fixed value written directly in the code \u2014 42, \"dog\", true. It is the value itself, not a name for one, which is exactly what makes an unexplained literal a magic number.

Identifiers follow conventions rather than rules, and the exam asks you to recognise them by name.

ConventionLooks likeConventionally used for
camelCasefinalScore, totalPricevariables and methods
PascalCaseMyClass, BankAccountclass and type names
snake_casefinal_scorevariables in Python and C
UPPER_SNAKELEGAL_AGE, TAX_RATEnamed constants

camelCase starts lower and capitalises each later word; PascalCase capitalises the first as well. That single difference is the whole question.

Mutability, and two names for one thing

Assigning one variable to another does not always copy. For a simple number it does. For a mutable object \u2014 a list, an array, a dictionary \u2014 the variable holds a reference to it, and assigning copies the reference, not the contents.

a = [1, 2, 3]\nb = a            // b now refers to the SAME list\nb.append(9)\n\na is [1, 2, 3, 9]    <- changed too; there is only one list

Both names point at one object, so a change through either is visible through both. To get an independent list you must copy it explicitly. Reading a variable before assigning it anything is the related trap: it holds either nothing or leftover memory, and the result is a crash or a silently wrong answer.

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION

Variable: a named storage location whose value can change

Constant: a named value that cannot change during execution

Identifier: the name of a variable, method or class

Keyword: a reserved word with built-in meaning that cannot be used as an identifier

Scope: the region of the program where a name is visible

Lifetime: how long the storage for a variable exists at runtime

Garbage: the unpredictable leftover value in an uninitialized variable

Type safety: using a variable only in ways consistent with its type

Lvalue: something that can appear on the left of = \u2014 a memory location such as x

\u2605 ON THE OA

A variable can change, a constant cannot, and a keyword is reserved by the language \u2014 an identifier is just a name, which both variables and constants have. Identifiers cannot start with a digit. Assignment is right-to-left associative, so a = b = c = 5 sets all three to 5.

\ud83d\udca1 WHY IT MATTERS

Scope is the idea that makes everything later in this course possible: it is what encapsulation in object-oriented programming is built on, and the stack that holds local variables is the same stack the operating system allocates per thread in Section 4.

An algorithm is a step-by-step set of instructions for solving a problem, and pseudocode writes that logic in plain language without any real language's punctuation. What makes both tractable is a result worth stating outright: every algorithm ever written, however complex, can be expressed with exactly three control structures. This is the structured programming theorem, and it is a favourite exam idea because it means identifying which of the three a piece of logic uses answers most construct questions on its own.

ConstructWhat it doesLooks like
Sequencesteps run in order, top to bottom, once eachplain ordered statements
Selection (branch)chooses a path based on a conditionIF / IF-ELSE / SWITCH
Repetition (iteration)repeats a block while a condition holdsWHILE / FOR / DO-WHILE

Selection comes in two named forms the OA distinguishes: a single-alternative if does something only when a condition is true, while a dual-alternative if/else picks one of two paths. In a chain of conditions they are tested top to bottom and the first true branch wins \u2014 the rest are skipped even if they would also be true, which is the entire answer to grade-boundary trace questions.

\u25b8 WORKED EXAMPLE \u2014 selection in pseudocode
START\n  INPUT number\n  IF number > 0 THEN\n      PRINT \"The number is positive.\"\n  ELSE IF number < 0 THEN\n      PRINT \"The number is negative.\"\n  ELSE\n      PRINT \"The number is zero.\"\n  ENDIF\nEND

The four loops

Loops are where the distinctions get tested hardest, and the one that decides the most questions is when the condition is checked.

LoopTests the conditionRuns at least once?Use it when
Pretest (while)before each passNo \u2014 can run zero timesthe data might be empty
Posttest (do-while)after each passYes \u2014 always onceyou must prompt before you can judge the answer
Forbefore each pass, with a counternothe number of repetitions is known up front
Infinitea condition that never goes falseforevera background worker \u2014 otherwise a bug

Two more names for the same idea appear in WGU wording. A count-controlled loop repeats a known number of times: start a counter, test it against a limit, update it. An event-controlled loop keeps going until something happens, and the number of passes is not known in advance. The loop control variable is whichever variable the condition tests, and an infinite loop is almost always caused by forgetting to update it.

Nesting

A nested structure is simply one control structure placed inside another, and reading nested logic is what harder questions test.

\u25b8 WORKED EXAMPLE \u2014 reading nested logic
WHILE (more students)\n    IF (score >= 60)\n        PRINT \"Pass\"\n    ELSE\n        PRINT \"Fail\"\n    ENDIF\nEND WHILE

A loop around a decision: each pass makes one pass/fail judgement. If a question asks how many constructs are used, the answer is two \u2014 repetition and selection.

Nesting also has a cost you will meet again. Two nested loops each running n times execute the body n \u00d7 n times, and that is precisely where O(n\u00b2) comes from in Section 3 \u2014 and why sorting algorithms built on nested loops collapse on large inputs.

Why the three-construct claim matters

It is tempting to treat \"every program is sequence, selection and repetition\" as a slogan. It is not \u2014 it is a statement about what you have to be able to read. When you meet unfamiliar code in an exam, you are never looking at something new; you are looking at those three shapes nested inside each other. The skill being tested is decomposing what you see back into them.

That is also why the goto statement disappeared from modern practice. Before structured programming, a program could jump anywhere, which made control flow impossible to follow \u2014 the famous \"spaghetti code\". The three constructs are sufficient, so the jump was unnecessary, and removing it made programs readable. If a question asks whether goto is needed for some piece of logic, the answer is always no.

One practical consequence for tracing: because a loop repeats and a branch chooses, the two nest in opposite ways with very different results. A branch inside a loop makes a decision on every pass. A loop inside a branch runs the whole loop, or does not run it at all. Reading which is on the outside is the first thing to establish before counting anything.

Input, processing and output

Before the three constructs there are the three stages every program has. Input is data coming in from outside \u2014 typed at a keyboard, read from a file, sampled from a sensor. Processing is the work done on it. Output is the result sent out \u2014 printed to the screen, written to a file, sent to a device.

The exam tests the direction: a keyboard, a mouse, a scanner and a sensor are input; a screen, a printer and a speaker are output. Printing a result to the screen is output even though it happens at the end of a calculation.

Choosing the loop from the description

The description saysUseBecause
exactly 50 items, 10 times, once per recorda count-controlled loop (FOR)the number of repeats is known before it starts
until the user types quit, until end of filean event-controlled loop (WHILE)the number of repeats depends on something that happens

Read for the phrase that fixes the count. \"The 50 items in an array\" fixes it; \"until the correct password is entered\" does not \u2014 you cannot know in advance how many attempts there will be.

Nested conditionals

When one of several ranges must be chosen, the constructs chain: IF \u2026 ELSE IF \u2026 ELSE IF \u2026 ELSE. Order matters, because the first true test wins and the rest are skipped.

IF   score >= 90 THEN grade = \"A\"\nELSE IF score >= 80 THEN grade = \"B\"\nELSE IF score >= 70 THEN grade = \"C\"\nELSE                      grade = \"F\"

Written descending as above, a score of 85 fails the first test and passes the second \u2014 correct. Written ascending, 85 would match >= 70 first and be graded C. The tests do not need an upper bound because everything higher was already caught.

Short-circuit evaluation

In most languages AND stops as soon as it meets a false operand, and OR stops as soon as it meets a true one \u2014 there is no point evaluating the rest. This is short-circuit evaluation, and it makes the order of the conditions part of the logic.

IF (x != 0 AND 10 / x > 2)     // SAFE\n    x = 0 makes the first test false, so 10 / x is never evaluated\n\nIF (10 / x > 2 AND x != 0)     // CRASHES\n    the division runs first, and divides by zero

The guard must come first. Whenever a condition protects the one after it \u2014 a non-zero check before a division, a not-null check before a field access \u2014 reversing the two turns working code into a crash.

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION

Algorithm: a step-by-step set of instructions that solves a problem

Pseudocode: the logic written in plain language, without a real language's syntax

Sequence: statements executed in order, one after another

Selection / branch: the decision point where the path splits

Repetition / iteration: running instructions multiple times with a loop

Loop control variable: the variable the loop condition tests

Nested structure: one control structure placed inside another

Abstract step: a high-level \"what to do\" step that does not yet say how \u2014 e.g. \"validate the username\"

\u2605 ON THE OA

Structured programming uses exactly three control structures and needs no goto. Map the keywords: IF/ELSE \u2192 selection, WHILE/FOR \u2192 repetition, plain ordered steps \u2192 sequence. If a question asks which loop is guaranteed to execute its body, the answer is the posttest do-while.

\u26a0 COMMON MISTAKE

Off-by-one is the standard loop error: valid indexes run 0 to n\u22121, so the test is i < n. Writing i <= n reads one position past the end of the data.

When an expression mixes operators, two rules decide the answer before any arithmetic happens: precedence settles which operator goes first, and associativity settles which way to work when two operators tie.

The precedence ladder is short enough to memorise, and the OA expects you to have done so.

1.  ( )                      parentheses \u2014 always first\n2.  exponents\n3.  *  /  mod                multiplicative   (left to right)\n4.  +  \u2212                     additive         (left to right)\n5.  <  <=  >  >=  ==  !=     comparison\n6.  AND, OR, NOT             logic\n7.  =                        assignment       (RIGHT to left)

The consequence that catches people is that arithmetic always finishes before comparison, and comparison always finishes before logic. So a + b > c means (a + b) > c, and no inner parentheses are needed in x > 0 AND y > 0.

\u25b8 WORKED EXAMPLE \u2014 evaluate 2 + 3 * 4 \u2212 6 / 2

Multiplication and division first, left to right, then the additions.

2 + 3 * 4 \u2212 6 / 2\n2 +  12  \u2212  3            <- * and / resolved first\n        11               <- then + and \u2212, left to right\n\nwith parentheses: (2 + 3) * 4 \u2212 6 / 2  =  5 * 4 \u2212 3  =  17

Associativity decides ties. Most arithmetic operators are left-to-right, so 10 \u2212 3 \u2212 2 is (10 \u2212 3) \u2212 2 = 5, not 10 \u2212 (3 \u2212 2) = 9. Assignment is the exception and runs right-to-left, which is why a = b = c = 5 works and sets all three.

The modulo operator

mod returns the remainder of a division, not the quotient, and it is worth being fluent with because it powers a surprising number of exam questions. 10 mod 3 is 1; 10 mod 4 is 2, because 4 goes into 10 twice with 2 left over. Two idioms follow: n mod 2 == 0 tests whether n is even, and n mod 10 extracts the last digit of n.

Magic numbers

A magic number is a bare literal dropped into code with no explanation \u2014 if (age > 18) or a tax rate of 0.0825 repeated in four places. Nobody reading it can tell what it means, and nobody changing it can be sure they found all of them. The fix is the named constant from 1.2: final int LEGAL_AGE = 18; and then if (age > LEGAL_AGE).

Where precedence actually bites

Precedence questions rarely look like precedence questions. They look like a formula that produced the wrong number. The classic is an average: a + b + c / 3 divides only c by three, because division binds tighter than addition. The fix is parentheses \u2014 (a + b + c) / 3 \u2014 and the reason people miss it is that the written formula has a division bar, which is a parenthesis you cannot see.

The comparison and logic levels matter for the same reason one step later. Because arithmetic resolves before comparison, total + tax > limit compares the sum, which is what you meant. But because comparison resolves before logic, a > b AND c is not asking what an English reader thinks \u2014 it compares a with b, then combines that with c, which is only meaningful if c is itself a Boolean.

Unary operators and increment

A unary operator takes one operand rather than two: negation in \u2212x, logical NOT in !flag. They sit near the top of the ladder, just under parentheses, so \u22122 ** 2 and (\u22122) ** 2 can differ depending on the language's convention. Increment and decrement, written ++ and \u2212\u2212, are unary shorthand for adding or subtracting one, and they are worth recognising in pseudocode even where the exam does not require you to write them.

= and == are different operators

One equals sign assigns; two equals signs compare. x = 5 stores 5 in x and is a statement; x == 5 asks whether x holds 5 and produces true or false.

x = 5        // assignment  \u2014 x now holds 5\nx == 5       // comparison  \u2014 evaluates to true\nx != 5       // comparison  \u2014 evaluates to false\n\nIF (x = 5)   // a classic bug: assigns, then tests the result

They sit at opposite ends of the precedence ladder \u2014 comparison at level 5, assignment at level 7, last of all \u2014 which is why an assignment inside a condition binds after everything else and quietly succeeds instead of testing anything.

Division depends on the operand types

The division operator behaves differently depending on what it is dividing, and this produces more wrong answers than any other single rule.

ExpressionResultWhy
7 / 2 (both integers)3integer division truncates \u2014 the remainder is discarded
7 / 2.0 (one is real)3.5the integer is promoted, so real division happens
7 mod 21mod gives exactly the remainder integer division threw away

So total / count with total = 7 and count = 2 gives 2, not 3.5 \u2014 an average computed in integer arithmetic is silently wrong. The fix is to make one operand real. Together, / and mod recover the whole division: 7 / 2 is 3 remainder 1.

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION

Precedence: which operator is applied first when several appear in one expression

Associativity: the direction operators of equal precedence group in \u2014 left-to-right for arithmetic, right-to-left for assignment

Operand: a value an operator acts on \u2014 3 and 5 in 3 + 5

Binary operator: one that works on two operands

Modulo (mod): the remainder after division

Magic number: an unexplained hard-coded literal; replace it with a named constant

Overhead: extra time, memory or resources used beyond a program's core task

\u2605 ON THE OA

Multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction: 5 + 2 \u00d7 3 is 11, not 21. When operators tie, go left to right. And mod gives the remainder \u2014 10 mod 4 is 2, never 2.5.

\ud83c\udfaf EXAM TIP

When an expression looks ambiguous, add the parentheses even if precedence already gives the answer you want. It costs nothing at runtime and removes the reader's doubt \u2014 which includes yours, three weeks later.

\ud83d\udcd6 Worked example \u2014 a full challenge-style problem

WORKED EXAMPLE \u2014 bits, bytes, and cost together
Problem: An image is 2,000 × 1,000 pixels, 3 bytes per pixel. (a) Raw size? (b) After 4:1 compression? (c) How many compressed images fit in 3 GB?

(a) 2,000 × 1,000 = 2,000,000 pixels × 3 bytes = 6,000,000 bytes = 6 MB.
(b) 4:1 means one quarter the size: 6 MB ÷ 4 = 1.5 MB.
(c) 3 GB = 3,000 MB; 3,000 ÷ 1.5 = 2,000 images.

Every “cost” question is this pattern: count the units, multiply by size-per-unit, then divide into the budget.

Numbers, Bits, and Cost

Everything a computer does reduces to bit patterns and the operations over them, so fluency here is non-negotiable. To read an unsigned binary number, add the place values of the set bits: 10110110 is 128+32+16+4+2 = 182. Grouping bits by fours converts to hex instantly: 1011 0110 is B6.

Two's Complement

In n-bit two's complement the most significant bit has weight -2^(n-1). So 8-bit 11010110 is 214 - 256 = -42, and the representable range is -2^(n-1) to 2^(n-1)-1, i.e. -128..127 for 8 bits. Signed overflow happens when two same-signed operands produce a result whose sign flips: 79 + 49 = 128 cannot fit in signed 8 bits, so the pattern 10000000 reads as -128.

Bitwise and Boolean

AND/OR/XOR act per bit; XOR flips where bits differ. A left shift by k multiplies by 2^k (dropping high bits); a right shift divides. Truth tables let you verify logical equivalences such as De Morgan's laws.

Algorithm Cost

Rank growth as O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n^2) < O(2^n). Binary search does about ceil(log2(n+1)) comparisons worst case; naive recursive Fibonacci makes an exponential number of calls because it recomputes subproblems. When a problem says compute or trace, walk the steps literally rather than guessing.

\ud83d\udcd6 Worked example \u2014 reasoning about a system end-to-end

WORKED EXAMPLE \u2014 one page load, every layer
Problem: You tap a link on Wi-Fi. List what happens, in order, naming each responsible part.

1. Browser (application) asks DNS to turn the name into an IP address.
2. TCP opens a reliable connection to that IP; the HTTP request is split into packets.
3. IP/routers forward each packet hop by hop (packets may take different routes).
4. On your local network, Wi-Fi (link layer) carries frames between your device and the router using MAC addresses.
5. The server’s OS schedules the web-server process; it reads files via the file system and replies.
6. TCP reassembles packets in order; the browser renders the page.

Exam skill: match each behavior to its layer/component \u2014 naming (DNS), reliability (TCP), routing (IP), local delivery (MAC/link), execution (OS/process).

How Systems Are Built and Connected

SDLC: Waterfall runs fixed phases (requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment, maintenance) in sequence and suits stable, well-understood requirements; agile delivers in short iterations and adapts when requirements change often. Neither is universally 'better' \u2014 the trade-off is predictability versus flexibility.

Operating Systems

A process has its own memory space; threads within a process share that memory, which makes them lighter to create but prone to race conditions. The scheduler multiplexes the CPU among ready threads. The memory hierarchy trades speed for capacity: CPU registers < L1/L2 cache < RAM < SSD < hard disk, from fastest/smallest to slowest/largest.

Networking

Match functions to layers: HTTP and DNS are application-layer; TCP/UDP are transport; IP addressing and routing are the network layer. TCP is connection-oriented and reliable (handshake, ordering, retransmission); UDP is connectionless and low-latency, good for streaming or DNS lookups. A subnet with h host bits supports 2^h - 2 usable hosts (subtracting the network and broadcast addresses).

Data Structures & Thinking

A stack is LIFO; a queue is FIFO. Arrays give O(1) indexed access but costly insertion; linked lists give O(1) insertion at a known node but O(n) access. Computational thinking combines decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, and algorithm design \u2014 and professionals apply it under ethical duties like honesty and protecting user data.

Everything in the previous section assumed the computer can store a number at all. Underneath, it cannot \u2014 it has only switches that are on or off. Binary is how those switches become numbers, and every representation question on the OA comes back to it.

Any number system works by place value: each column is worth the base raised to a power, counting from zero on the right. Decimal columns are powers of ten. Binary columns are powers of two, doubling leftward \u2014 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. Memorise those eight numbers and you can read any byte.

\u25b8 WORKED EXAMPLE \u2014 binary \u2192 decimal

Add the columns that are switched on.

  1     1     0     1\n128  64  32  16   8   4   2   1     <- place values\n              1   1   0   1         <- the number 1101\n\n8 + 4 + 0 + 1 = 13
\u25b8 WORKED EXAMPLE \u2014 decimal \u2192 binary

Divide by 2 repeatedly, keep the remainders, then read them bottom to top.

27 \u00f7 2 = 13  r1   <- last digit\n13 \u00f7 2 =  6  r1\n 6 \u00f7 2 =  3  r0\n 3 \u00f7 2 =  1  r1\n 1 \u00f7 2 =  0  r1   <- first digit\n\nread upward: 11011      check: 16 + 8 + 2 + 1 = 27

The faster method for small numbers is subtraction: take the biggest place value that fits, mark a 1, and repeat with what is left. For 13 \u2014 8 fits (mark 1, 5 left), 4 fits (mark 1, 1 left), 2 does not (mark 0), 1 fits (mark 1) \u2014 giving 1101.

Hexadecimal

Binary is correct and unreadable, so people write it in hexadecimal \u2014 base 16, using 0\u20139 then A\u2013F for 10\u201315. Its usefulness is a coincidence of arithmetic: 16 is 24, so one hex digit is exactly four bits, and converting needs no division at all. Split the binary into groups of four from the right and translate each group.

1101 1010  ->  D    A    ->  0xDA   (13 and 10)\n0xFF = 1111 1111 = 255 = the largest unsigned byte

Negative numbers: two's complement

Computers have no minus sign, only bits, so a negative number has to be encoded. The obvious scheme is signed magnitude: use the leftmost bit as the sign, 0 for positive and 1 for negative, and the rest for the value. It is easy to read and bad to compute with, because it needs separate circuitry for addition and subtraction and it produces two different zeros.

Two's complement is what real machines use, and the reason is elegant: it makes subtraction into addition, so one adder circuit handles both signs. To negate a number, flip every bit, then add 1.

\u25b8 WORKED EXAMPLE \u2014 representing \u22125 in 8-bit two's complement
 5  = 0000 0101\nflip  = 1111 1010\nadd 1 = 1111 1011   ->  \u22125\n\ncheck: 5 + (\u22125)  ->  0000 0101 + 1111 1011 = 1 0000 0000\n       the carry out of the top bit is dropped, leaving 0000 0000 = 0  \u2713

Two facts follow that the OA asks for directly. \u22121 is always all ones (11111111 in 8 bits) and 0 is all zeros. And the range is asymmetric \u2014 8 bits span \u2212128 to +127, one more negative than positive \u2014 because there is only one zero, so the spare pattern goes to the negative side.

Overflow

Overflow is what happens when a result needs more bits than the type has. It is not an error the machine reports; the carry bit is simply dropped and the stored answer is wrong.

CalculationResultFits in unsigned 8-bit (max 255)?
200 + 70270No \u2014 overflow, carry dropped, stored value is wrong
100 + 50150Yes
254 + 1255Yes \u2014 exactly the maximum, still fine

The other signed representations

Two's complement is what machines use, and two earlier schemes are still examined because they show why it won. In all three the leftmost bit is the sign bit: 0 means positive, 1 means negative.

SchemeTo negate\u22125 in 8 bitsProblem
Signed magnitudeflip the sign bit only1000 0101two zeros (+0 and \u22120); addition needs separate circuitry
One's complementflip every bit1111 1010still two zeros; needs an end-around carry
Two's complementflip every bit, then add 11111 1011none \u2014 one zero, one adder for both signs

Reading down the \"to negate\" column shows the progression, and it is the cleanest way to remember which is which: signed magnitude flips one bit, one's complement flips them all, two's complement flips them all and adds one. That final +1 is what removes the duplicate zero and makes a single adder circuit work for both positive and negative values.

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION

Place value: each column is worth the base raised to a power, counting from 0 at the right

Binary (base 2): the two-symbol system a computer actually stores; columns double leftward

Hexadecimal (base 16): shorthand for binary; one hex digit is exactly four bits

Signed magnitude: leftmost bit is the sign, the rest is the value; produces two zeros

Two's complement: the standard encoding for negatives \u2014 flip all bits and add 1

Overflow: a result too large for the available bits; the carry is dropped and the value is wrong

Radix point: the \"decimal point\" in any base \u2014 binary 101.11 uses one

Bit / byte: a single 0 or 1; eight bits, enough for one character

\u2605 ON THE OA

Storage units in order, each roughly a thousand of the last: bit \u2192 byte \u2192 KB \u2192 MB \u2192 GB \u2192 TB. Unsigned 8-bit range is 0\u2013255; signed two's complement 8-bit is \u2212128 to +127. To negate: flip every bit, add 1. One hex digit = four bits.

\ud83c\udfaf EXAM TIP

Check every conversion by converting back. It takes five seconds and it catches the reading-the-remainders-downward error, which is the one people actually make under time pressure.

"}, "D684/s2/l3_1": {"body": "

Ethics says what a professional should do. Security is the set of techniques for making the wrong thing hard to do, and forensics is what happens after someone does it anyway. All three appear on the OA as concepts rather than as anything you implement.

The frame everything else hangs on is the CIA triad \u2014 the three properties security is trying to preserve.

PropertyMeansBroken when
Confidentialityonly authorised parties can read the dataa database of customer records leaks
Integritythe data has not been altered without authorisationa transaction amount is silently changed
Availabilityauthorised users can reach it when neededa denial-of-service attack takes the site down

Encryption

Encryption scrambles readable plaintext into unreadable ciphertext using a key; decryption reverses it. The oldest form is a cipher such as the Caesar shift, which moves every letter a fixed number of places \u2014 trivially breakable, but it demonstrates the shape: an algorithm plus a key.

Modern encryption divides into two families, and the difference is which keys are involved.

TypeKeysTrade-offUsed for
Symmetricone shared key encrypts and decryptsfast, but both sides must already share the key secretlyencrypting stored files, bulk data
Asymmetrica public key encrypts, a private key decryptsslower, but no secret needs to be shared in advanceestablishing secure connections, digital signatures

Asymmetric encryption solves the problem symmetric encryption creates: how do two parties agree a shared secret over a channel someone may be listening to? You publish your public key freely, anyone can encrypt with it, and only your private key can undo it. In practice the two are combined \u2014 asymmetric to exchange a symmetric key, then symmetric for the actual traffic, because it is much faster.

Hashing is often grouped with these and is a different thing: a hash is one-way. It turns any input into a fixed-length value that cannot be reversed, which is why passwords are stored as hashes and why a matching hash proves a file has not been altered.

Digital forensics

Digital forensics is the disciplined recovery and analysis of digital evidence, and its governing idea is the chain of custody: a documented record of who handled the evidence, when, and what they did with it. Break the chain and the evidence may be inadmissible however incriminating it is.

That is why investigators never work on the original. They take a verified copy \u2014 verified by hashing the original and the copy and confirming the hashes match \u2014 and analyse that, leaving the original untouched. Altering the original breaks the chain of custody, and no result obtained afterwards can repair it.

Lawful surveillance and decryption follow the same logic in a different arena: they generally require a warrant or comparable legal authority. The technical ability to decrypt something is not the question the exam is asking \u2014 the authorisation is.

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION

CIA triad: confidentiality, integrity and availability \u2014 the three goals of information security

Plaintext / ciphertext: readable data before encryption; scrambled data after

Cipher: an algorithm for encrypting, such as the Caesar shift

Symmetric encryption: one shared key both encrypts and decrypts \u2014 fast, but the key must be shared securely

Asymmetric encryption: a public key encrypts and a private key decrypts; no shared secret needed

Hashing: a one-way function producing a fixed-length value, used for passwords and integrity checks

Digital forensics: the recovery and analysis of digital evidence for investigation

Chain of custody: the documented record of everyone who handled evidence and what they did

\u2605 ON THE OA

Digital forensics preserves evidence through a documented chain of custody, and lawful decryption or surveillance normally requires a warrant. Symmetric = one shared key; asymmetric = public key encrypts, private key decrypts. Hashing is one-way and is not encryption.

\u26a0 COMMON MISTAKE

Altering the original evidence breaks the chain of custody. Investigators work on a copy whose hash matches the original \u2014 that hash match is the proof nothing changed.

"}, "D684/s4/l3_1": {"body": "

Everything so far assumed one operating system running on one machine. Virtualization breaks that assumption: it lets one physical computer run several complete operating systems at once, each believing it has the machine to itself.

The component that makes it work is the hypervisor, a layer that sits between the hardware and the virtual machines and hands each one a slice of the real CPU, memory and storage. A virtual machine is one of those guests \u2014 a full operating system with its own kernel, isolated from its neighbours.

TypeRuns onUsed for
Type 1 (bare metal)directly on the hardwaredata centres and servers \u2014 faster, no host OS in the way
Type 2 (hosted)as an application on a normal OSa desktop running Linux inside Windows for testing

The payoff is consolidation. A physical server running one application typically wastes most of its capacity; running ten virtual machines on it uses hardware that was already paid for, and each one can be snapshotted, copied or moved to another host. That efficiency is exactly what makes cloud computing economically possible \u2014 a cloud provider is running virtualization at enormous scale.

Containers are the lighter relative worth knowing about. A container packages an application with its dependencies but shares the host's kernel rather than running a whole operating system, so it starts in seconds instead of minutes and uses far less memory. A VM virtualises the machine; a container virtualises the application's environment.

Cloud computing

Cloud computing means renting computing over the internet instead of owning hardware. Rather than buying servers, you use someone else's and pay for what you consume. The three service models are asked about constantly, and the way to keep them straight is to ask how much of the stack you still manage.

ModelYou getYou manageExample
IaaS \u2014 Infrastructure as a Serviceraw compute, storage and networkthe OS, runtime and your applicationrenting virtual machines
PaaS \u2014 Platform as a Servicea platform to build and deploy ononly your application and dataa managed app hosting platform
SaaS \u2014 Software as a Servicefinished software, ready to usenothing but your own data and settingsGmail, Office 365

Read the table downward and the pattern is a trade: the further down, the less you manage and the less control you have. IaaS gives you the most control and the most responsibility; SaaS gives you the least of both.

Beyond the service models, the OA also asks about deployment models \u2014 public cloud (shared infrastructure from a provider), private cloud (dedicated to one organisation), and hybrid (a mix, often keeping sensitive data private while using public capacity for the rest). And edge computing is the counter-move: processing data on or near the device that generated it rather than shipping it to a distant data centre, which cuts latency and bandwidth \u2014 the reason a self-driving car does not ask the cloud whether to brake.

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION

Virtualization: running several complete operating systems on one physical machine

Hypervisor: the layer allocating real hardware to virtual machines

Virtual machine: a complete guest operating system running on virtualised hardware

Container: an application packaged with its dependencies, sharing the host kernel

Cloud computing: renting computing resources over the internet instead of owning them

IaaS: raw infrastructure \u2014 you manage the OS and everything above it

PaaS: a platform to deploy onto \u2014 you manage only your application

SaaS: finished software delivered over the internet

Edge computing: processing data near where it is generated instead of in a distant data centre

Scalability / elasticity: adding or removing capacity as demand changes

\u2605 ON THE OA

Learn the three service models by an example each: Gmail = SaaS, a managed app platform = PaaS, renting virtual machines = IaaS. More control means further up the stack toward IaaS. A hypervisor is what makes virtual machines possible.

\u26a0 COMMON MISTAKE

A virtual machine and a container are not the same thing. A VM includes a whole guest operating system; a container shares the host kernel and packages only the application and its dependencies.

"}, "D684/g1/x3_1": {"body": "
\ud83c\udfaf LEARNING OBJECTIVES

after this section you will be able to\u2026

\u2022 Distinguish data from information and explain why the difference matters in computing.

\u2022 Explain why computers store everything in binary, and why binary is more reliable than analog.

\u2022 Contrast analog and digital data, and describe how reclocking and PCM protect digital signals from degradation.

\u2022 Calculate how many bits are needed to represent N distinct things using the rule 2\u207f.

\u2022 Define data compression, compute a compression ratio, and tell lossless from lossy.

\u2022 \ud83d\udd0e Convert whole numbers between decimal, binary, and hexadecimal (the number-systems skill this unit is built on).

Plain-English First

Imagine a shoebox full of loose receipts. That pile is data \u2014 raw facts with no order. Now imagine you sort those receipts by month and add up each month's spending. The tidy summary that answers \"how much did I spend in March?\" is information. Same raw material; one is organized so it informs a decision. That single idea \u2014 that a computer's whole job is turning data into information \u2014 is the theme of this entire unit.

Here's the second big idea. The real world is continuous: a dimmer switch can be at any brightness, a thermometer can read 74.568\u00b0, and there are infinitely many numbers between 1 and 2. Computers are finite machines \u2014 they only have so many switches. So a computer has to digitize: chop the smooth, infinite world into separate, countable pieces and store each piece as a string of 1s and 0s. Everything \u2014 a photo, a song, this sentence \u2014 ultimately becomes binary digits (bits).

Going Deeper \u2014 The Technical Detail

Data is basic values or facts that can lack context. Information is data that has been organized or processed to be useful in solving a problem. The distinction is relative to the user's needs, but it captures the essence of what computers do for us.

Analog data is a continuous representation, analogous to the actual thing it represents \u2014 like mercury rising smoothly in a thermometer. Digital data is a discrete representation that breaks information into separate elements. Computers digitize continuous entities and then represent each discrete element in binary.

Why binary and not decimal? Computers could use other number systems (some early machines did), but the hardware that stores and moves data is far cheaper and far more reliable when each device only has to be one of two states. An analog signal fluctuates continuously in voltage; a digital signal holds only a high or low state \u2014 the two binary digits.

Every electronic signal degrades as it travels down a line because voltage fluctuates from environmental effects. This is where digital wins decisively:

When an analog signal degrades, information is lost immediately \u2014 because any voltage in the range is \"valid,\" you can't tell what the original was.

A digital signal jumps sharply between two extremes \u2014 a behavior called pulse-code modulation (PCM). It can degrade quite a lot before any information is lost, because any voltage above a threshold reads as \"high\" and any below reads as \"low.\" Periodically the signal is reclocked \u2014 refreshed to its original crisp shape. Reclock before too much degradation and no information is lost.

Bits and how many things they can represent

One bit is either 0 or 1 \u2014 so one bit represents exactly two things (e.g., sweet=0, sour=1). To represent more, use more bits. Two bits give four combinations (00, 01, 10, 11); three bits give eight; and so on. The master rule:

\ud83d\udccc MUST-KNOW FORMULA

n bits can represent 2\u207f things. Each extra bit doubles what you can represent. Turned around: to represent N distinct things you need the smallest n where 2\u207f \u2265 N.

Example of the \"turned-around\" version: to represent 25 unique things, 4 bits (16) is too few, so you need 5 bits (32) \u2014 and 32 \u2212 25 = 7 bit combinations simply go unused. Note also that even when you only need a few bits, hardware allocates storage in fixed chunks (a power of 2 such as 8, 16, or 32 bits), so real storage is given in multiples of that.

Data compression and the compression ratio

Data compression reduces the amount of space needed to store data. We care today less because of storage cost and more because of bandwidth \u2014 the maximum number of bits that can travel across a network in a fixed time (think streaming video). The compression ratio measures how much shrinking happened:

\ud83d\udccc MUST-KNOW FORMULA

Compression ratio = (size of compressed data) \u00f7 (size of original data). Both values must measure the same thing (bits, or characters). The result falls between 0 and 1 \u2014 the closer to 0, the tighter the compression.

A technique is lossless if the original data can be perfectly reconstructed (nothing lost), or lossy if some information is permanently discarded to save space. We never want to lose information, but sometimes the loss is acceptable \u2014 we always face a tradeoff between accuracy and size.

\ud83d\udd0e ADDED FOR COMPLETENESS

Number Systems (binary & hex)

The notes lean on base conversion from \"Chapter 2\" but don't restate it, and this WGU unit tests binary/hex directly, so here is the essential primer.

Positional value. In any base, a digit's worth = digit \u00d7 (base^position), counting positions from 0 at the right. Binary (base 2) uses digits 0\u20131; each position is a power of 2: \u202616, 8, 4, 2, 1. Hexadecimal (base 16) uses 0\u20139 then A\u2013F (A=10, B=11, C=12, D=13, E=14, F=15).

Binary \u2192 decimal: add the place values where a 1 sits. 1011 = 8+0+2+1 = 11.

Decimal \u2192 binary: repeatedly divide by 2, writing remainders bottom-up. 13 \u2192 13/2=6 r1, 6/2=3 r0, 3/2=1 r1, 1/2=0 r1 \u2192 read up \u2192 1101.

Hex \u2194 binary (the shortcut): each hex digit = exactly 4 bits. So 0xB=1011, 0x2F=0010 1111. Group binary in 4s from the right to go back. This is why hex is popular \u2014 it's a compact human-readable stand-in for binary.

Key Terms

TermDefinitionWhy it matters
DataRaw values or facts that can be processed.The raw material every computer manipulates.
InformationData organized/processed to be useful in solving a problem.The useful output \u2014 the point of computing.
Analog dataA continuous representation of information.Matches the real world but degrades poorly.
Digital dataA discrete representation using separate binary elements.What computers actually store; robust to noise.
BinaryBase-2 number system using only 0 and 1.Cheap, reliable hardware needs only two states.
BitA single binary digit (0 or 1).The atomic unit of all digital data.
Pulse-code modulation (PCM)Digital signaling that jumps between two extreme states.Lets digital signals resist degradation.
ReclockingRefreshing a digital signal to its original crisp shape.Restores the signal before information is lost.
BandwidthMax bits transferable across a channel per unit time.The modern reason compression matters.
Data compressionReducing the space needed to store data.Saves storage and fits data through bandwidth.
Compression ratioCompressed size \u00f7 original size (0\u20131).Quantifies how tight the compression is.
LosslessCompression with perfect reconstruction.Required when every detail must survive (text, code).
LossyCompression that permanently discards some data.Acceptable for media where small losses aren't noticed.
HexadecimalBase-16 system; digits 0\u20139 and A\u2013F.Compact, readable shorthand for binary (4 bits/digit).

PropertyAnalogDigital

LosslessLossy
ReconstructionPerfect \u2014 original fully recoveredApproximate \u2014 some data gone forever
Best forText, program code, spreadsheetsPhotos, music, streaming video
Example schemesHuffman, run-length, ZIP, PNGJPEG, MP3, MP4

Bits \u2192 things they represent

Bits (n)Combinations (2\u207f)Example use
12sweet/sour, on/off
24car gears: P, D, R, N
388 compass directions
416one hex digit
532enough for 25 things (7 unused)
8256one byte / extended ASCII

\ud83d\udca1 Tips, Tricks & Mnemonics

\"Data is dirt, information is a sandcastle.\" Same sand (facts); only one is shaped to be useful.

Powers of two to memorize cold: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024. The OA loves \"how many bits for N things?\" \u2014 just climb this ladder until you pass N.

Compression ratio direction: lower = better. Ratio near 0 means tiny file; ratio near 1 means barely compressed. (A ratio above 1 would mean it got bigger.)

\"Digital Doesn't Degrade (much)\" \u2014 three D's remind you digital tolerates noise and can be reclocked.

Hex = 4 bits each. One hex digit \u2194 one \"nibble\" (4 bits). Two hex digits \u2194 one byte.

\u26a0\ufe0f COMMON EXAM MISTAKES

Mixing up the compression-ratio direction. Compressed \u00f7 original, and smaller is tighter. Don't invert it.

Answering the \"how many bits?\" question with the exact count instead of the next power of two. 25 things needs 5 bits, not \"about 4.6.\"

Claiming digital signals never degrade. They do degrade \u2014 they just tolerate it until reclocked.

Saying computers use binary because it's the only possible system. Other bases work; binary is chosen for cheap, reliable two-state hardware.

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 \u2014 How many bits, and a compression ratio

Problem: (a) A vending machine sells 40 distinct products; each needs a unique binary code. How many bits minimum? (b) A 352-character message compresses to 317 characters. Give the compression ratio.

Part (a) \u2014 climb the powers of two. Need 2\u207f \u2265 40.

2\u2075 = 32 \u2192 too small (only 32 codes).

2\u2076 = 64 \u2192 64 \u2265 40 \u2714.

Answer (a): 6 bits. (64 \u2212 40 = 24 codes go unused.)

Part (b) \u2014 apply the formula. Ratio = compressed \u00f7 original = 317 \u00f7 352.

317 \u00f7 352 = 0.90 (about). Close to 1 \u2192 only mild compression.

Worked Example 2 \u2014 Decimal \u2192 binary \u2192 hex (the \ud83d\udd0e skill)

Problem: Convert decimal 206 to binary, then to hexadecimal.

Decimal \u2192 binary by repeated division by 2 (remainders read bottom-up):

206 \u00f7 2 = 103 r 0

103 \u00f7 2 = 51 r 1

51 \u00f7 2 = 25 r 1

25 \u00f7 2 = 12 r 1

12 \u00f7 2 = 6 r 0

6 \u00f7 2 = 3 r 0

3 \u00f7 2 = 1 r 1

1 \u00f7 2 = 0 r 1

Read remainders bottom-to-top: 11001110. Check: 128+64+8+4+2 = 206 \u2714.

Binary \u2192 hex: group into 4-bit nibbles from the right: 1100 1110.

1100 = 12 = C; 1110 = 14 = E.

Answer: 206 = 11001110\u2082 = 0xCE.

Wrong way \u2192 why \u2192 right way: A common error is reading the division remainders top-to-bottom, giving 01110011. That's wrong because the first remainder is the least-significant (rightmost) bit. Right way: always read remainders from the last division up to the first.

\ud83d\udcca FIGURE \u2014 one byte in decimal, binary and hex \u2014 where every digit\u2019s value comes from
\ud83c\udfaf EXAM TIP

Number-base questions are the highest-volume, most predictable points on this OA, and they are pure procedure \u2014 no reasoning required if you drill the two directions.

Binary \u2192 decimal: write 128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1 above the bits and add the columns with a 1. Decimal \u2192 binary: go the other way \u2014 subtract the biggest place value that fits, mark a 1, repeat. For 206: 128 fits (78 left), 64 fits (14 left), 32 no, 16 no, 8 fits (6), 4 fits (2), 2 fits (0), 1 no \u2192 11001110. That subtraction method is faster and less error-prone under time pressure than repeated division, because there are no remainders to read in the wrong order.

Anything to hex: never convert through decimal. Go to binary, split into nibbles of four from the right, and read each nibble off the 8-4-2-1 ladder. And when a question asks \u201chow many bits for N things?\u201d, do not compute a logarithm \u2014 climb 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256 until you pass N and count the rungs.

Choosing the right data type

A large share of the questions here give a scenario and ask which type fits. The reasoning is always the same: what operations must this value support, and what must not be lost?

The valueRight typeWhy
Student ID \"00427\", ZIP \"02139\"Stringthe leading zero is part of it; store as a number and 00427 becomes 427. It is never used in arithmetic.
Money \u2014 1042.75, exact to the centDecimal / fixed-point (BigDecimal, currency)binary floating point cannot hold 0.10 exactly, so cents drift over many additions
A count of itemsIntegerwhole, exact, no fraction possible
A measurement \u2014 6.4 kgFloat / doublefractional, and tiny rounding is acceptable
Yes / no, on / offBooleanexactly two states
\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION
An integer is a whole number with no fractional part \u2014 42, 0, \u22127. 3.0 is not an integer value in type terms: it is a float that happens to be whole.
\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION
A Boolean holds only true or false. A comparison such as x > 3 is guaranteed to produce one, which is why comparisons are what appear inside if-conditions.

Strong typing, and type mismatch

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION
Strong typing means the language enforces types: a value of one type cannot silently be used as another, and mixing them is reported rather than guessed at.

So in a strongly typed language, adding the integer 200 directly to the string \"Total: \" raises a type error unless you explicitly convert the number to text first.

\u26a0\ufe0f COMMON MISTAKE
number = \"10\" for something you intend to count with is a type mismatch. The quotes make it text. Then finalScore = \"95\" followed by finalScore + 5 does not give 100 \u2014 depending on the language it either errors, or concatenates to \"955\". Neither is the answer expected.

Implicit and explicit conversion

TermMeaningExample
Implicit (coercion, widening)the language converts automatically, safelyan int is promoted to a float in 3 + 2.5
Explicit (casting)you demand the conversion, and may lose data(int) 9.87 gives 9 \u2014 the fraction is truncated, not rounded
\u25b8 WORKED EXAMPLE \u2014 Trace it: integer division versus real division

int a = 7 / 2; and double b = 7 / 2.0;

  1. 7 / 2 \u2014 both operands are integers, so the division is integer division: it discards the remainder. a = 3.
  2. 7 / 2.0 \u2014 one operand is a float, so the int is promoted and real division happens. b = 3.5.

One character decides it. Whenever a question shows a division, check the types of both sides first.

Precision \u2014 why 0.1 ten times is not 1.0

Adding 0.1 ten times can give 0.9999999999999999. Nothing is broken: 0.1 has no exact representation in binary, in the same way 1/3 has no exact decimal representation. Each stored 0.1 is a hair off, and ten additions accumulate the error. This is why money is never stored in a binary float, and why floats are compared with a tolerance rather than with ==.
