\ud83c\udfaf LEARNING OBJECTIVES

after this section you will be able to\u2026

\u2022 Explain why signed-magnitude representation is intuitive but creates the \"two zeros\" problem.

\u2022 Compute the ten's complement and two's complement of a number, and use the invert-and-add-1 shortcut.

\u2022 Perform binary addition and subtraction using two's complement, and read the sign bit.

\u2022 Recognize overflow and explain why it happens on a finite machine.

\u2022 Convert a real number to floating-point form (sign, mantissa, exponent) and back, and convert a fractional decimal to binary.

Plain-English First

A computer has a fixed number of switches for each number \u2014 say 8 bits. That's like an odometer with only so many wheels: it can't grow, and it wraps around when it runs out of room. Two puzzles fall out of that: how do you write a negative number when all you have is 0s and 1s (no minus sign)? and how do you write a number with a fractional part like 3.75? This section solves both.

The clever trick for negatives is the complement. Think of a 12-hour clock: moving back 3 hours lands on the same spot as moving forward 9 hours. So on a clock, \"9\" can stand in for \"\u22123.\" Computers do exactly this with binary \u2014 that stand-in is called the two's complement, and it lets the same simple \"add\" circuitry do subtraction too.

Going Deeper \u2014 The Technical Detail

Signed-magnitude

Signed-magnitude representation is what you learned in grade school: a sign (+/\u2212) shows ordering and the digits show the magnitude. It's intuitive, but it has a flaw \u2014 there are two representations of zero (+0 and \u22120). Two zeros inside a computer cause needless complexity, so designers prefer complement schemes.

Fixed-size numbers & ten's complement

If we fix the number of digits, we can let the upper half of the values stand for negatives. With two decimal digits (100 values), let 1\u201349 be +1\u2026+49 and let 50\u201399 represent \u221250\u2026\u22121. Then addition just works (add and discard the carry), and subtraction becomes addition of a negative: A \u2212 B = A + (\u2212B). The negative of a value is found with:

\ud83d\udccc MUST-KNOW FORMULA

Ten's complement: Negative(I) = 10\u1d4f \u2212 I, where k = number of digits. Example (k=2): \u22123 \u2192 10\u00b2 \u2212 3 = 100 \u2212 3 = 97. So 97 \"means\" \u22123 in a two-digit fixed scheme.

Two's complement (the binary version)

Store everything in binary and the ten's complement becomes the two's complement: negative(I) = 2\u1d4f \u2212 I. The easy shortcut you'll actually use on the OA:

\ud83d\udccc MUST-KNOW SHORTCUT

Two's complement = invert all the bits, then add 1. The leftmost bit is the sign bit: 0 = positive, 1 = negative. Example (8-bit): +2 = 00000010 \u2192 invert \u2192 11111101 \u2192 +1 \u2192 11111110 = \u22122.

Addition and subtraction work exactly as in ten's complement \u2014 add the binary numbers and discard any carry out of the leftmost position. Because a negative number always starts with a 1, you can tell a number's sign at a glance.

Number overflow

Overflow happens when a computed value won't fit in the allocated bits. In 8-bit signed storage, 127 + 3 = 10000010, which our scheme reads as \u2212126, not +130 \u2014 the result wrapped past the top of the range. Overflow is the classic symptom of forcing an infinite world onto a finite machine; no matter how many bits you allocate, some number won't fit. How it's handled varies by hardware and programming language.

Representing real numbers (floating point)

A real number has a whole part and a fractional part (either may be zero). In binary the \"decimal point\" is called the radix point; positions to its right are halves (2\u207b\u00b9), quarters (2\u207b\u00b2), and so on. Computers store a real value using three properties:

\ud83d\udccc MUST-KNOW

A real value = sign \u00d7 mantissa \u00d7 base^exponent. The mantissa is the significant digits (radix point assumed at the far right); the exponent says how far to shift the radix point. This is called floating point because the digit count is fixed but the radix point \"floats.\" One common 64-bit standard uses 1 bit sign + 11 bits exponent + 52 bits mantissa.

To convert to floating point: the sign is obvious, the mantissa is the digits with the point removed, and the exponent is how many places the point moved. Example: 148.69 \u2192 sign +, mantissa 14869, exponent \u22122 \u2192 14869 \u00d7 10\u207b\u00b2. If only five mantissa digits are allowed, large values lose information (e.g., 155555000 \u2192 15555 \u00d7 10\u2074 drops the trailing detail).

Converting a fraction to binary: multiply the fractional part by 2 repeatedly; each whole-number carry is the next bit to the right. Stop when the fraction hits 0 (or you have enough bits). Scientific notation is a floating-point form with exactly one digit left of the point (printed with \"E\", e.g., 1.200132708E+4).

Key Terms

TermDefinitionWhy it matters
Signed-magnitudeSign bit + magnitude digits.Intuitive, but has two zeros \u2192 avoided.
Ten's complementNegative(I)=10\u1d4f\u2212I in decimal.Decimal model behind two's complement.
Two's complementBinary negative = invert bits + 1.Standard for signed integers; one zero; easy arithmetic.
Sign bitLeftmost bit: 0=positive, 1=negative.Instantly reveals a number's sign.
OverflowResult exceeds the allocated bits.Causes wrong/wrapped answers; finite-machine limit.
Real numberA value with a potential fractional part.Needed for measurements, money, science.
Radix pointThe \"decimal point\" in any base.Separates whole and fractional parts in binary.
Floating pointsign \u00d7 mantissa \u00d7 base^exponent.How computers store reals in fixed space.
MantissaThe significant digits of a float.Holds precision; too few digits \u2192 lost info.
ExponentShifts the radix point.Sets the number's scale/magnitude.
Scientific notationFloat with one digit left of the point.Compact form for very large/small reals.

Diagram \u2014 Finding a two's complement (invert & add 1)

Comparison / Reference Tables

Signed-magnitude vs. two's complement

Signed-magnitudeTwo's complement
How negatives are formedFlip the sign bit onlyInvert all bits, add 1
Representations of zeroTwo (+0 and \u22120)One
Arithmetic circuitryNeeds special handlingSame adder does subtraction
Used in modern CPUs?RarelyYes \u2014 the standard

Real value \u2192 five-digit floating point (from the source notes)

Real valueFloating-point valueNote
12001.0012001 \u00d7 10\u2070Exponent 0
\u2212120.01\u221212001 \u00d7 10\u207b\u00b2Negative sign kept
0.1200012000 \u00d7 10\u207b\u2075Small value, negative exponent
\u2212123.10\u221212310 \u00d7 10\u207b\u00b2
155555000.0015555 \u00d7 10\u2074Information lost (only 5 digits)

\ud83d\udca1 Tips, Tricks & Mnemonics

\"Flip, then plus one.\" That's the whole two's-complement recipe. Invert every bit, add 1.

Clock analogy for complements: \u22123 \u2261 +9 on a 12-clock because 12\u22123=9. In binary, \u2212I \u2261 2\u1d4f\u2212I.

Sign bit tells all: leftmost bit 1 \u2192 negative, 0 \u2192 positive. Check it first.

Overflow smell test: if you add two positives and get a negative (or two negatives and get a positive), you overflowed.

Fraction \u2192 binary = MULTIPLY by 2 (whole \u2192 binary = DIVIDE by 2). Opposite operations for the two halves of the number.

\"Float = point that floats\" \u2014 the digits are fixed, the radix point moves via the exponent.

\u26a0\ufe0f COMMON EXAM MISTAKES

Forgetting the \"+1\" after inverting. Inverting alone gives one's complement, not two's.

Keeping the final carry in two's-complement addition. Discard the carry out of the sign column.

Thinking two's complement has two zeros. That's signed-magnitude. Two's complement has exactly one zero.

Dividing (instead of multiplying) when converting a fraction to binary.

Reporting +130 for an 8-bit 127+3 \u2014 the real machine result is the wrapped value \u2212126 (overflow).

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 \u2014 Subtract using 8-bit two's complement: 5 \u2212 3

Rewrite as addition: 5 \u2212 3 = 5 + (\u22123).

Write +5 in 8 bits: 00000101.

Find \u22123: start with +3 = 00000011.

Invert the bits: 11111100.

Add 1: 11111101 = \u22123. \u2714

Add the two: 00000101 + 11111101.

The sum is 1\u00a000000010 (9 bits) \u2014 a carry pops out of the sign column.

Discard the carry \u2192 00000010.

Leftmost bit is 0 \u2192 positive \u2192 value = 2. Correct (5 \u2212 3 = 2). \u2714

Wrong way \u2192 why \u2192 right way: Keeping the carry gives 100000010 and a confused answer. Why wrong: the result must fit the fixed 8 bits; the carry out of the top is meant to be dropped. Right way: discard the final carry and read the low 8 bits.

Worked Example 2 \u2014 Convert 20.25 (decimal) to binary, then to floating-point notation

Whole part 20 \u2192 binary by dividing by 2: 20\u219210 r0, 10\u21925 r0, 5\u21922 r1, 2\u21921 r0, 1\u21920 r1. Read up: 10100.

Fractional part .25 \u2192 binary by multiplying by 2: .25 \u00d7 2 = 0.5 \u2192 carry 0; .5 \u00d7 2 = 1.0 \u2192 carry 1; fraction now 0 \u2192 stop. Bits (top-down): .01.

Combine: 20.25\u2081\u2080 = 10100.01\u2082.

Now express as floating point (base 2): mantissa = the digits with the radix point pushed to the right = 1010001; the point moved 2 places left of where it \"belongs,\" so exponent = \u22122.

Result: 1010001 \u00d7 2\u207b\u00b2. (Sign +, mantissa 1010001, exponent \u22122.)

\ud83d\udcca FIGURE \u2014 the 8-bit signed wheel \u2014 why 127 + 3 comes out negative
\ud83c\udfaf EXAM TIP

Two\u2019s complement is tested three ways, and each has a two-second check.

1. \u201cWhat is \u2212N in 8 bits?\u201d Write +N, invert, add 1. Then verify without redoing it: add your answer to +N and you must get 00000000 with a carry falling off the end. 00000011 + 11111101 = 1 00000000 \u2713. That check catches the missing +1 every time.

2. \u201cWhat value is this bit pattern?\u201d Look at the leftmost bit first. If it is 0, read it as plain binary and stop. If it is 1, the number is negative \u2014 invert, add 1, read the magnitude, and put the minus sign back. Students lose this one by reading 11111101 as 253.

3. \u201cDid it overflow?\u201d Only look at signs, never at magnitudes: positive + positive giving a negative, or negative + negative giving a positive, is overflow. A positive plus a negative can never overflow, so if the question mixes signs the answer is \u201cno overflow\u201d before you compute anything. And the carry that drops off the left end is not overflow \u2014 it is discarded on purpose.

Data type selection \u2014 picking the type for a stored value

Two cases come up repeatedly:

  • A customer balance such as 1042.75 needs a fractional type. For money the correct choice is a decimal / fixed-point type, because binary floating point cannot represent 0.10 exactly and rounding errors accumulate on repeated arithmetic.
  • A ZIP code such as 02139 must be a string. Stored as a number the leading zero is lost and it becomes 2139. It is an identifier, never arithmetic \u2014 you would never add two ZIP codes.
\ud83c\udfaf EXAM TIP
The test is not \"does it look like a number\" but \"will I ever do arithmetic on it, and does every character matter\". IDs, phone numbers and ZIP codes are text.

\ud83c\udfaf LEARNING OBJECTIVES

after this section you will be able to\u2026

\u2022 Define a character set and explain why standardizing one made text processing easier.

\u2022 Describe the ASCII character set: 7-bit origin, 128 vs. 256 characters, the check bit, and Latin-1 Extended ASCII.

\u2022 Explain why ASCII's ordering lets computers alphabetize, and why the first 32 codes are non-printing control characters.

\u2022 Describe Unicode, its goal, its typical 16-bit encoding, and why it is a superset of ASCII.

\u2022 Convert a character to its numeric/binary code and reason about uppercase vs. lowercase.

Plain-English First

A computer can't store the letter \"A.\" It can only store numbers. So the whole world agreed on a giant lookup table \u2014 \"let 65 mean A, 66 mean B\u2026\" \u2014 the way Morse code agrees that \"dot-dash\" means A. That agreed-upon table is a character set. Once everyone uses the same table, a message typed on one machine reads correctly on another. This section covers the two tables that won: ASCII (great for English) and Unicode (built for every language on Earth).

Going Deeper \u2014 The Technical Detail

A text document decomposes into paragraphs \u2192 sentences \u2192 words \u2192 individual characters. The document is the continuous (analog) whole; the characters are the discrete (digital) pieces we actually store. Because there are a finite number of characters, we simply list them all and assign each a binary string. (Note: this is separate from word processing, which also stores fonts, margins, and color \u2014 here we care only about the characters themselves.)

How many characters must we handle? English has 26 letters, but upper- and lowercase are separate \u2192 52. Add digits ('0'\u2013'9'), punctuation, the space, and other languages, and the list grows fast. A character set is a list of characters and the code for each. Standardizing one let manufacturers make text processing interoperable.

ASCII

ASCII = American Standard Code for Information Interchange. Originally 7 bits per character \u2192 128 unique characters. The 8th bit of the byte was a check bit (error detection during transmission). Later all 8 bits were used for characters, formally the Latin-1 Extended ASCII set \u2192 256 characters (adding accented letters and special symbols).

Two crucial properties:

Ordering. ASCII codes put characters in a definite order \u2014 uppercase letters are in sequence, and so are lowercase. Because the codes are ordered, a computer can compare codes to alphabetize a word list.

Control characters. The first 32 ASCII codes are non-printing \u2014 reserved for special functions like carriage return and tab. They're interpreted specially by whatever program processes the text.

Unicode

256 characters is enough for English but not the world. Unicode was created with the goal of representing every character in every language, including Asian ideograms and many special-purpose (e.g., scientific) symbols. It generally uses 16 bits per character but is flexible enough to use more space when needed.

\ud83d\udccc MUST-KNOW

Unicode is a superset of ASCII: its first 256 characters correspond exactly to Extended ASCII, using the same codes. So programs written assuming ASCII still work on Unicode systems. A related idea from Bob Bemer is the escape character, which signals that the following character(s) change the standard meaning of the characters that follow.

Key Terms

TermDefinitionWhy it matters
CharacterA single letter, digit, or symbol.The discrete unit of stored text.
Character setA list of characters and their codes.Lets machines agree on what each code means.
ASCIIAmerican Standard Code for Info Interchange; 7-bit \u2192 128 chars.The dominant early English text standard.
Check bitOriginal 8th ASCII bit for error detection.Helped ensure correct transmission.
Extended ASCII (Latin-1)8-bit ASCII \u2192 256 characters.Adds accented/special symbols.
Control characterNon-printing code (first 32 in ASCII).Tab, carriage return, etc. \u2014 actions, not glyphs.
UnicodeUniversal set, usually 16-bit, all languages.Enables truly international text.
SupersetA set containing all of another set.Unicode's first 256 = Extended ASCII exactly.
Escape characterSignals a change to following chars' meaning.Bemer's idea; extends limited character sets.

Diagram \u2014 ASCII & Unicode relationship

Comparison / Reference Tables

ASCII vs. Unicode

ASCII (original)Extended ASCIIUnicode
Bits per char78~16 (flexible)
Characters128256Tens of thousands+
ScopeEnglish basics+ accents/symbolsAll world languages
RelationshipSubset of Unicode= Unicode's first 256Superset of ASCII

Handy ASCII reference values

CharacterDecimal code8-bit binary
Space3200100000
'0' (digit zero)4800110000
'A'6501000001
'a'9701100001

\ud83d\udca1 Tips, Tricks & Mnemonics

\"A is 65, a is 97\" \u2014 memorize these two anchors. Lowercase = uppercase + 32. So 'C'(67) \u2192 'c'(99).

\"Digits start at 48.\" The character '0' is code 48, not 0 \u2014 a favorite exam trap (the glyph vs. the number).

First 32 = \"invisible commands\" (tab, carriage return). If a code is under 32, it's a control character.

ASCII \u2282 Unicode. Unicode is the big umbrella; ASCII lives inside it unchanged. That's why old ASCII programs still run.

7 bits \u2192 128, 8 bits \u2192 256, 16 bits \u2192 65,536. Match bit-width to character count.

\u26a0\ufe0f COMMON EXAM MISTAKES

Confusing the character '0' (code 48) with the number 0. They are different things in memory.

Treating 'A' and 'a' as the same character \u2014 they have different codes and sort/compare differently.

Saying Unicode replaced ASCII. Unicode includes ASCII as its first 256 codes.

Forgetting the original 8th bit was a check bit (error detection), not a character bit.

Assuming all 128 ASCII codes are printable \u2014 the first 32 are non-printing control characters.

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 \u2014 Encode \"Hi\" in ASCII (decimal and binary)

Look up each character. 'H' is an uppercase letter. Uppercase 'A' = 65, and H is the 8th letter (A=1\u2026H=8), so 'H' = 65 + 7 = 72.

'i' is lowercase. 'a' = 97, and i is the 9th letter, so 'i' = 97 + 8 = 105.

Convert 72 to 8-bit binary: 64+8 = 72 \u2192 01001000.

Convert 105 to 8-bit binary: 64+32+8+1 = 105 \u2192 01101001.

\"Hi\" = 72 105 (decimal) = 01001000 01101001 (binary).

Worked Example 2 \u2014 Why alphabetizing works, and an uppercase\u2194lowercase shift

Question: A program sorts \"Cat\", \"Apple\", \"Banana\" by comparing first-letter ASCII codes. In what order do they end up?

First letters: 'A' = 65, 'B' = 66, 'C' = 67.

Sorting ascending by code: 65 < 66 < 67 \u2192 Apple, Banana, Cat. The built-in ordering of ASCII is alphabetical for same-case letters.

Follow-up: What is the lowercase of 'C'?

Lowercase = uppercase + 32 \u2192 'C'(67) + 32 = 99 \u2192 'c' = 99.

Wrong way \u2192 why \u2192 right way: Sorting a mixed-case list like \"apple\", \"Banana\" naively by code puts \"Banana\" before \"apple\" \u2014 because uppercase codes (65\u201390) all come before lowercase codes (97\u2013122). Why: ASCII orders all capitals ahead of all lowercase. Right way: to sort case-insensitively, convert everything to one case first.

\ud83d\udcca FIGURE \u2014 the ASCII number line \u2014 the four blocks and the 32 between them
\ud83c\udfaf EXAM TIP

You are not asked to recite the table. You are asked to reason from four anchors, so memorise only these: space 32, \u20180\u2019 48, \u2018A\u2019 65, \u2018a\u2019 97. Everything else is arithmetic from an anchor \u2014 \u2018H\u2019 is the 8th letter, so 65 + 7 = 72; \u2018e\u2019 is the 5th, so 97 + 4 = 101.

Two question shapes recur. \u201cWhat order does this list sort into?\u201d \u2014 compare first characters by code, and remember every uppercase letter (65\u201390) sorts before every lowercase letter (97\u2013122), so \u201cZebra\u201d comes before \u201capple\u201d in a raw code sort. \u201cHow many bits/bytes for this text?\u201d \u2014 original ASCII is 7 bits but is stored in a byte, so an n-character ASCII string takes n bytes; the same string in a 16-bit Unicode encoding takes 2n.

If an answer choice says Unicode \u201creplaced\u201d or \u201cconflicts with\u201d ASCII, eliminate it \u2014 Unicode\u2019s first 256 codes are Extended ASCII, which is the whole reason old programs still work.

How floating point stores a real number

A floating-point value is stored in three parts, the same idea as scientific notation:

PartRoleIn 6.02 \u00d7 10\u00b2\u00b3
Signpositive or negative+
Mantissa (significand)the significant digits6.02
Exponentwhere the point sits \u2014 how far to shift it23

Because the mantissa has a fixed number of bits, only a fixed number of significant digits survive: that is the source of floating-point precision limits.

\ud83c\udfaf LEARNING OBJECTIVES

after this section you will be able to\u2026

\u2022 Explain and apply keyword encoding, and state its limitations.

\u2022 Encode and decode with run-length encoding, and explain why only runs of 4+ are worth it.

\u2022 Explain Huffman encoding, the prefix property, and why frequent characters get short codes.

\u2022 Compute a compression ratio for each technique.

\u2022 \ud83d\udd0e Build a Huffman tree from character frequencies and read off the binary codes.

Plain-English First

Compression is like packing a suitcase smarter. Three tricks appear here, each exploiting a different kind of \"waste\" in text. Keyword encoding is speed-dial: replace a whole common word (\"the\") with one short symbol. Run-length encoding handles the case where the same thing repeats over and over (\"AAAAAAA\") \u2014 instead of writing it out, you write \"A, seven times.\" Huffman encoding is the cleverest: it notices that some letters (like E and space) appear constantly while others (like X, Z) are rare, so it gives the common ones tiny codes and the rare ones longer codes \u2014 like abbreviating the words you say most.

Going Deeper \u2014 The Technical Detail

Keyword encoding

Replace frequently used words with a single character; reverse it to decompress. In the source example, encoding a 352-character paragraph down to 317 characters gives a ratio of 317/352 \u2248 0.90 (modest). Key limitations: (1) the symbols used cannot appear in the original text or decoding is ambiguous; (2) case matters \u2014 \"The\" and \"the\" are different, needing separate symbols; (3) no gain from encoding one-character words like \"a\" or \"I\"; longer words yield more savings, yet the most frequent words are often short.

Run-length encoding (recurrence coding)

Replace a run of one repeated character with: flag character + repeated character + count. With '*' as the flag, AAAAAAA \u2192 *A7. So *n5*x9ccc*h6 some other text *k8eee decodes to nnnnnxxxxxxxxxccchhhhhh some other text kkkkkkkkeee (ratio 35/51 \u2248 0.68).

\ud83d\udccc MUST-KNOW

Because each encoded run costs 3 characters, encoding runs of 3 or fewer is pointless (and encoding a run of 2 would make it longer). It only pays off for runs of 4 or more. If the count is read as an 8-bit binary number instead of a single ASCII digit, runs can be counted up to 255 (or 4\u2013259, since runs \u22643 aren't encoded).

Huffman encoding

Named for Dr. David Huffman. It uses variable-length bit strings: frequent characters get few bits, rare characters get more. That's the opposite of a fixed character set (where every character is, say, 8 or 16 bits). Using the source's sample codes, \"DOORBELL\" encodes to 1011110110111101001100100 \u2014 25 bits versus 8\u00d78 = 64 bits fixed, a ratio of 25/64 \u2248 0.39.

\ud83d\udccc MUST-KNOW

the Prefix Property

In any Huffman code, no character's bit string is a prefix of another's. That's what makes decoding unambiguous: scanning left to right, the moment the bits match a code, that must be the character. This is why 1010110001111011 can only decode to \"BOARD.\"

\ud83d\udd0e ADDED FOR COMPLETENESS

Building a Huffman tree

The source says the construction is \"beyond scope,\" but WGU tests it, so here's the algorithm:

List each character with its frequency.

Repeatedly take the two lowest-frequency nodes, combine them into a new parent whose frequency is their sum.

Repeat until one node (the root) remains.

Label every left branch 0 and every right branch 1 (a consistent choice).

A character's code is the sequence of branch labels from the root down to it.

The two-lowest rule automatically pushes frequent characters near the top (short codes) and rare ones deep (long codes), and it guarantees the prefix property.

Key Terms

TermDefinitionWhy it matters

Run-length encodingFlag + character + count for repeated runs.Great for long repeats (images, DNA).
Flag characterMarker that begins an RLE triple.Tells the decoder \"expand this run.\"
Huffman encodingVariable-length codes by frequency.Strong lossless compression of text.
Prefix propertyNo code is a prefix of another.Makes variable-length decoding unambiguous.
Frequency tableCounts of how often each character occurs.Drives which characters get short codes.
Variable-length codeCodes of differing bit lengths.Lets common characters be cheaper.

Diagram \u2014 A Huffman tree (frequencies A:5, B:2, C:1, D:1)

Read each code by walking root\u2192leaf: A=0, B=10, C=110, D=111. Notice no code is a prefix of another (prefix property \u2714), and the most frequent letter (A) got the shortest code.

Comparison / Reference Tables

The three text-compression techniques

KeywordRun-lengthHuffman
Core ideaWord \u2192 single symbolRepeat run \u2192 flag+char+countFrequency \u2192 variable-length code
Best onText with common wordsLong identical runsText with skewed letter frequencies

\ud83d\udca1 Tips, Tricks & Mnemonics

\"KRH: Keyword=words, Run-length=repeats, Huffman=frequency.\" Match the technique to the kind of redundancy.

RLE break-even = 4. Three characters to encode a run, so you need a run of 4+ to actually save. Runs of 2 get bigger.

Huffman rule of thumb: shortest codes go to the most frequent characters. If a rare letter has a short code, something's wrong.

Prefix property test: pick any code; make sure it doesn't \"start\" any other code. Build via the two-lowest merge and you get this free.

All three are lossless \u2014 you can perfectly rebuild the original. (Compression can be lossy, but these text methods are lossless.)

Lower ratio = better, so Huffman's 0.39 beats keyword's 0.90 here.

\u26a0\ufe0f COMMON EXAM MISTAKES

Encoding short RLE runs. A run of 2 or 3 should be left alone; encoding it wastes space.

Giving a frequent character a long Huffman code. It's backwards \u2014 frequent = short.

Forgetting the prefix property, then claiming a code stream is \"ambiguous.\" Proper Huffman codes are never ambiguous.

Using a keyword symbol that also appears in the text \u2014 that makes decoding ambiguous.

Assuming \"The\" and \"the\" share a keyword symbol. Different case = different characters = different symbol needed.

Calling any of these \"lossy.\" All three are lossless.

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 \u2014 Run-length encode and find the ratio

Problem: Encode WWWWWWWWWWKKKAAAAAA using '*' as the flag, then give the compression ratio.

Identify runs: W \u00d710, K \u00d73, A \u00d76.

W \u00d710 is a long run (\u22654) \u2192 encode as *W10... but the count must fit the scheme. Reading the count as a binary number allows up to 255, so *W + count(10) is fine \u2192 write *W10 conceptually (3 code positions: flag, char, count).

K \u00d73 \u2192 run of 3, not worth encoding (would take 3 chars to save 0). Leave as KKK.

A \u00d76 \u2192 long run \u2192 *A6.

Encoded stream: *W10 KKK *A6 \u2192 treating each triple as 3 character-positions: 3 + 3 + 3 = 9 characters.

Original length = 10 + 3 + 6 = 19 characters.

Compression ratio = 9 \u00f7 19 \u2248 0.47.

Wrong way \u2192 why \u2192 right way: Encoding the K run as *K3 gives no savings (3 chars \u2192 3 chars) and adds decoding overhead. Right way: leave runs of 3 or fewer as-is; only encode runs of 4+.

Worked Example 2 \u2014 \ud83d\udd0e Build a Huffman tree and encode a word

Problem: Characters and frequencies: A:5, B:2, C:1, D:1. Build the tree, list codes, then encode \"BAD\" and give its bit length vs. a fixed 2-bit code.

Start with four nodes: A(5), B(2), C(1), D(1).

Combine the two lowest: C(1) + D(1) \u2192 node \"CD\"(2).

Now: A(5), B(2), CD(2). Two lowest are B(2) and CD(2) \u2192 node \"BCD\"(4).

Now: A(5), BCD(4). Combine \u2192 root(9).

Label branches (left=0, right=1) from the diagram above: A=0, B=10, C=110, D=111.

Verify prefix property: 0, 10, 110, 111 \u2014 none begins another. \u2714

Encode \"BAD\": concatenate B + A + D = 10 + 0 + 111 = 100111. Length = 2+1+3 = 6 bits.

Fixed 2-bit code (4 symbols \u2192 2 bits each): 3 chars \u00d7 2 = 6 bits. Here they tie because \"BAD\" happens to use a rare letter (D). Over a whole document dominated by A's, Huffman wins big (each A costs 1 bit instead of 2).

\ud83d\udcca FIGURE \u2014 run-length encoding on a real string \u2014 and the runs it is not worth using on
\ud83c\udfaf EXAM TIP

Compression questions come in two flavours and both are arithmetic, not theory.

\u201cEncode this / decode this.\u201d For RLE, count each run before you write anything, and only encode runs of 4 or more \u2014 the encoded form always costs exactly 3 character positions, so a run of 3 is a tie and a run of 2 makes the file bigger. Decoding is the same rule backwards: every time you meet the flag character, take the next two positions as \u201cwhich character\u201d and \u201chow many\u201d.

\u201cGive the compression ratio.\u201d Compressed \u00f7 original, always in that order, always in the same unit. Sanity-check the direction: your answer should be below 1, and the smaller it is the better the compression. If you get 2.1, you inverted the fraction.

For Huffman, the fastest way to check a code set is offered as correct is the prefix test \u2014 read the codes and make sure none of them is the opening of another. And if a frequent letter has been given a long code, the tree was built wrong; the two-lowest merge rule always pushes frequent characters near the root.

Explicit conversion

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION
Converting a float to an integer so the fraction is truncated is an explicit conversion \u2014 a cast. You are asking for it, and accepting the data loss: (int) 9.87 gives 9. It truncates towards zero rather than rounding.

The opposite is an implicit conversion, which the language performs by itself and only where nothing is lost, such as promoting an int to a float.

\ud83c\udfaf LEARNING OBJECTIVES

after this section you will be able to\u2026

\u2022 Define an algorithm and pseudocode, and explain why we plan before we code.

\u2022 Use the foundational pseudocode elements: variables, constants, assignment, and input/output.

\u2022 Apply the order of operations and associativity when evaluating expressions.

\u2022 Write and read the three control structures: sequence, selection (if/if-else), and repetition (while).

\u2022 Trace an algorithm by hand using desk checking to verify it before implementation.

Plain-English First

Before a builder pours concrete, they draw a blueprint. An algorithm is the blueprint for a program \u2014 a step-by-step plan to solve a problem in a finite number of unambiguous steps. Pseudocode is how we sketch that blueprint in plain, structured English before translating it into a real programming language. The beauty is that pseudocode has no rigid grammar \u2014 it's for humans \u2014 so you can focus on logic first and syntax later.

Think of a variable as a labeled box in memory: you can put a value in it, look at what's inside, and swap the contents anytime. That \"swappability\" is the whole reason computers are useful \u2014 write payroll instructions once, then run them with a different employee's numbers in the boxes thousands of times.

Going Deeper \u2014 Foundations: Variables, Constants & Operators

A data type classifies a data item by (1) what values it can hold, (2) how it's stored, and (3) what operations are allowed on it. The two broadest types are numeric (numbers usable in arithmetic) and string (nonnumeric text, which cannot be used in arithmetic). A fixed value written directly in code is a constant/literal: a numeric constant like 43, or a string constant in quotes like \"Amanda\" (strings are also called alphanumeric because they may mix letters, digits, and symbols).

A variable is a named memory location whose contents can change. Before using one, most languages require a declaration providing a data type, an identifier (name), and optionally an initial value (initializing). An uninitialized variable holds garbage (an unknown value) \u2014 using it is a logic error.

\ud83d\udccc MUST-KNOW

Assignment

The assignment operator = (or \u2190 / \"Set \u2026 to \u2026\" in pseudocode) is a binary operator that works right-to-left: the expression on the right is evaluated first, then stored into the memory location on the left. The left side must be an lvalue (a name for a memory address); 5 = x is invalid because 5 is not a memory location.

Naming conventions you may see: camelCase (myVariableName), PascalCase (MyVariableName), snake_case (my_variable_name), and kebab-case (my-variable-name). A named constant gives a meaningful name to a fixed value set once (avoiding \"magic numbers\" \u2014 unexplained hard-coded values like 3.14). Rules of precedence (order of operations) decide which operators run first (multiplication/division before addition/subtraction); operators of equal precedence use left-to-right associativity (except assignment, which is right-to-left).

Going Deeper \u2014 Pseudocode & the Three Control Structures

To express any algorithm, pseudocode needs just a few concepts: variables, assignment (Set sum to 0), and input/output (Read num / Write \"\u2026\"; synonyms: Get/Input, Display/Print). Everything else is built from three control structures:

Sequence \u2014 statements executed in order, top to bottom.

Selection (branch) \u2014 choose an action based on a Boolean expression (true/false). The if-then form does an action or skips it; the if-then-else form chooses between two actions.

Repetition (iteration/looping) \u2014 a WHILE loop repeats the indented body as long as its Boolean test is true. Because the test runs before the body, it's a pretest loop; if the test starts false, the body never runs.

\ud83d\udccc MUST-KNOW

A loop needs three things or it breaks: initialize a loop control variable, test it in the condition, and update/increment it in the body. Forget the increment and the condition never changes \u2192 an infinite loop.

Key Terms

TermDefinitionWhy it matters
AlgorithmFinite set of unambiguous steps to solve a problem.The plan behind every program.
PseudocodeStructured plain-language sketch of an algorithm.Plan logic before worrying about syntax.
VariableNamed memory location whose value can change.Lets one instruction serve many values.
DeclarationStates a variable's type, name, (optional) initial value.Required before first use in most languages.
Data typeClassifies values, storage, and allowed operations.Numeric vs. string changes what's legal.
Constant / literalA fixed value written in code (43, \"Amanda\").Unchanging data; named constants add meaning.
Assignment operatorStores the right-side value into the left-side lvalue.Right-to-left; core of every computation.
lvalueAn expression naming a memory address.Only lvalues may sit left of =.
GarbageUnknown value in an uninitialized variable.Using it is a logic error.
Rules of precedenceOrder operations are evaluated in.Determines an expression's result.
SelectionChoose actions via a Boolean test (if/if-else).Gives programs decision-making.
RepetitionRepeat statements while a condition holds.Automates repeated work.
Pretest loopTests the condition before the body (while).May execute zero times.
Infinite loopLoop whose condition never becomes false.Common bug; usually a missing increment.
Desk checkingTracing an algorithm by hand on paper.Catches logic errors before coding.

Diagram \u2014 The three control structures

Comparison / Reference Tables

The three control structures

Selection: if-then-elseChoose between two actionsIF \u2026 ELSE

Numeric vs. String data

\ud83d\udca1 Tips, Tricks & Mnemonics

\"Plan, then program.\" Always write the algorithm/pseudocode before code. An algorithm must exist before coding can begin.

Loop = I-T-U: Initialize, Test, Update. Miss the U and you loop forever.

Assignment reads right-to-left: x = y + 2 means \"compute y+2, put it in x.\" The name always sits on the left.

\"PEMDAS-ish\": multiply/divide before add/subtract; same-level ties go left-to-right (except =, which is right-to-left).

Pretest = maybe zero. A WHILE loop can run zero times if its condition is false at the start.

Desk check with real numbers. Pick sample inputs and trace every variable in a table \u2014 it's \"simple but amazingly effective.\"

\u26a0\ufe0f COMMON EXAM MISTAKES

Putting a constant or expression on the left of =. Only an lvalue (a variable/memory name) may be there.

Forgetting to increment the loop control variable \u2192 infinite loop.

Assuming a pretest (while) loop always runs at least once. It may run zero times.

Treating \"43\" (string) as a number. A quoted value is a string and can't do arithmetic.

Using an uninitialized variable and expecting 0 \u2014 assume it holds garbage.

Ignoring precedence: 2 + 3 * 4 is 14, not 20.

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 \u2014 Desk-check a summing loop

Algorithm: Set sum to 0; Set counter to 0; Read limit; WHILE (counter < limit){ Read num; Set sum to sum+num; Set counter to counter+1 } Print sum. Inputs: limit=3, then nums 5, 10, 2.

Initialize: sum=0, counter=0. Read limit=3.

Test counter(0) < 3 \u2192 true. Read num=5 \u2192 sum=0+5=5, counter=1.

Test 1 < 3 \u2192 true. Read num=10 \u2192 sum=5+10=15, counter=2.

Test 2 < 3 \u2192 true. Read num=2 \u2192 sum=15+2=17, counter=3.

Test 3 < 3 \u2192 false. Exit loop.

Print sum = 17. Loop ran exactly limit = 3 times (counter 0,1,2). \u2714

Worked Example 2 \u2014 Evaluate an expression with precedence & associativity

Problem: Evaluate result = 2 + 3 * 4 - 10 / 2.

Apply higher precedence first (\u00d7 and \u00f7, left to right): 3 * 4 = 12.

10 / 2 = 5.

Now left-to-right for + and \u2212: 2 + 12 = 14.

14 - 5 = 9.

Assignment stores the right side into result \u2192 result = 9.

Wrong way \u2192 why \u2192 right way: Reading strictly left-to-right gives 2+3=5, \u00d74=20, \u221210=10, \u00f72=5. Why wrong: it ignores that \u00d7 and \u00f7 bind tighter than + and \u2212. Right way: do all \u00d7 and \u00f7 first, then + and \u2212.

\ud83d\udcca FIGURE \u2014 one while loop, drawn and desk-checked side by side
\ud83c\udfaf EXAM TIP

Almost every pseudocode question on this OA is answered the same way: build the trace table. One column per variable, one row per pass. It takes ninety seconds and it is the only method that does not lie to you \u2014 reading a loop \u201cin your head\u201d is exactly where the marks are lost.

The three things they test with it: how many times does this loop run? (a counter starting at 0 with test counter < limit runs limit times, values 0\u2026limit\u22121 \u2014 write the values out rather than reasoning about them); what is printed? (watch whether the print sits inside or outside the loop body); and what if the condition is false at the start? (a pretest WHILE runs zero times, which is a favourite distractor).

For expression questions, evaluate strictly by precedence \u2014 \u00d7 and \u00f7 before + and \u2212, ties left to right \u2014 and remember assignment is the one that works right to left. If an answer choice matches a pure left-to-right reading, it is the trap answer, not the answer.

Reading an algorithm line by line

Most questions on this section do not ask you to write an algorithm. They hand you one and ask what it produces. That skill is tracing: walking the steps with a table of the variables, writing each new value down rather than holding it in your head.

\u25b8 WORKED EXAMPLE \u2014 Tracing nested loops \u2014 how many times does the inside run?

An outer loop runs 3 times. Inside it, an inner loop runs 4 times.

  1. The inner loop completes a full set of 4 passes for each single pass of the outer loop.
  2. The outer loop makes 3 passes.
  3. So the innermost statement runs 3 \u00d7 4 = 12 times.

Nested loops multiply. Loops one after another add.

\u25b8 WORKED EXAMPLE \u2014 Tracing a running total

SET total = 0; SET count = 0; WHILE count < 3: total = total + count; count = count + 1

passcount at testtotal aftercount after
10 < 3 \u27130 + 0 = 01
21 < 3 \u27130 + 1 = 12
32 < 3 \u27131 + 2 = 33
\u20143 < 3 \u2717 stop33

The loop ends with total = 3 and count = 3. Note the body never ran with count = 3, because the test is checked before each pass.

Building a result up inside a loop like this \u2014 a variable that starts at zero and grows each pass \u2014 is the accumulator pattern, and total is the accumulator. Initialization matters: had total not been set to 0 first, every addition would build on a meaningless value.

The three control structures

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION
Every algorithm, in any language, is built from just three: sequence (steps in order), selection (choose a path \u2014 if), and repetition (do something again \u2014 loops, also called iteration).

Selection comes in three shapes, and the exam names them:

ShapeWhat it doesForm
Single-alternativeruns a block only when the condition is trueif \u2026 (no else)
Dual-alternativeone action if true, a different one if falseif \u2026 else
Multi-way / nesteda chain of tests, first match winsif \u2026 else if \u2026 else

In a chain like if score \u2265 90 \u2192 A; else if score \u2265 80 \u2192 B; else if score \u2265 70 \u2192 C, a score of 95 takes the first branch and stops. The later tests are never reached, even though 95 is also \u2265 80. That \"first match wins, then exit\" behavior is the whole point of the chain and a favorite exam trap.

Loops that count, and loops that wait

KindRunsUse when
Count-controlled (for)a number of times known in advanceyou know the count up front
Condition-controlled (while)until a condition goes falsethe count depends on the data

A count-controlled loop FOR i = 1 TO 5 runs exactly 5 times. A loop that keeps going until something happens rather than a set number of times is an event-controlled loop.

Sequence, selection and repetition are also called the three constructs. Putting one inside another is nesting, and choosing a construct is simply asking: one path or two (selection), or the same work repeated (repetition)? Every construct carries a small overhead \u2014 a loop must test its condition each pass, a call must set up a frame \u2014 which is why the cheapest correct construct is preferred.

Modulo \u2014 the remainder operator

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION
% (modulo) gives the remainder after division. 17 % 5 = 2, because 5 goes into 17 three times with 2 left over.

Its two standard uses are worth memorizing:

  • Even or odd: n % 2 == 0 means n is even.
  • Divisible by / wrapping: n % 12 keeps a value inside 0\u201311, which is how clocks and circular buffers work.

Operands and operators

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION
In the expression 3 + 5, the + is the operator and the values 3 and 5 are the operands \u2014 the things being operated on.

Operator precedence

Operators are not applied left to right; they have a fixed order, the same one as in arithmetic. 2 + 3 * 4 is 14, not 20, because * binds tighter than +. Brackets override it: (2 + 3) * 4 = 20. When a question shows an expression with mixed operators, that is almost always what it is testing.

Rough order, tightest first: brackets \u2192 unary NOT \u2192 * / % \u2192 + - \u2192 comparisons \u2192 AND \u2192 OR.

Short-circuit evaluation

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION
With AND, if the left side is false the whole thing must be false, so the right side is never evaluated. With OR, if the left side is true the right side is skipped. This is called short-circuiting.
\u25b8 WORKED EXAMPLE \u2014 Why the order of the conditions matters

if (count != 0 AND total / count > 5)

  1. Suppose count is 0.
  2. The left test count != 0 is false.
  3. Because AND short-circuits, total / count is never run \u2014 so the division by zero never happens.
  4. Reverse the two conditions and the program crashes.

The left condition is deliberately acting as a guard for the right one.

Scope, shadowing and lifetime

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION
Scope is the region of a program where a name is visible. A variable declared inside a function is local \u2014 visible only in that function. One declared outside all functions is global \u2014 visible throughout the program.

Three consequences the questions lean on:

  • Out of scope is an error. Using a variable declared inside one function from a different function fails, because the name does not exist there. Pass it as a parameter or return it.
  • Shadowing. If a global total exists and a function declares its own local total, the local one hides the global inside that function. Assigning to it changes only the local copy \u2014 the global is unchanged.
  • Lifetime. A local variable exists only while its function is running. When the function returns, its memory is released and the value is gone.

Initialization

Reading a variable before assigning it a value is dangerous because it holds no meaningful value yet \u2014 depending on the language it is a compile error, a default like 0, or whatever happened to be in that memory. The last case is the worst: the program runs and produces a different wrong answer each time, which is far harder to find than a crash.

Mutability

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION
A mutable object can be changed in place. If a and b both refer to the same mutable list and you call b.append(9), there is only one list \u2014 so a shows the 9 too. They are two names for one object, not two copies.
\u26a0\ufe0f COMMON MISTAKE
Reading = as \"equals\". In nearly every language = assigns and == compares. if (x = 5) assigns 5 to x rather than testing it.

Flowchart shapes

ShapeMeans
Ovalstart or end (terminator)
Rectanglea process \u2014 a step being carried out
Diamonda decision \u2014 two or more ways out
Parallelograminput or output
Flowline (arrow)the order \u2014 which step comes next, the flow of control

The flowline is the arrow itself. It carries no processing; it shows the sequence.

Identifying the right pseudocode

One question type accounts for a lot of the pseudocode domain: you are given a formula or a described task, and four pseudocode snippets that all look plausible. You are not being asked to write code \u2014 you are being asked to spot the one snippet that does exactly what was described. That is a checking skill, and it is quicker and more reliable than reading each option as a whole.

The method \u2014 four checks, in this order

Before looking at the options, read the task and write down what the answer must contain. Then test each option against these, stopping the moment one fails:

  1. The operation. Is it adding when the task says add, dividing when the task says divide? Wrong-operator options are the easiest to bin.
  2. The order. Subtraction and division are not reversible. \u201cSubtract d from f\u201d is f \u2212 d, never d \u2212 f.
  3. The grouping. Does it need parentheses to force the order? x + y / 2 is not the average \u2014 division happens first. The average needs (x + y) / 2.
  4. The result. Is the value stored in the right variable, and is it actually displayed or returned if the task asked for that? A snippet that computes correctly and never outputs is still wrong.

The five wrong-answer patterns

Distractors are built from a small set of predictable errors. Once you can name them you stop being fooled by them:

PatternLooks like
Operands swappedd \u2212 f where the task said subtract d from f
Parentheses droppedx + y / 2 instead of (x + y) / 2
Assignment reversedSET x + y TO total \u2014 you assign TO a variable, never to an expression
Accumulator not initialiseda loop adds to total with no SET total TO 0 before it
Off-by-one boundsFOR i FROM 1 TO N\u22121 when all N values are needed

Worked example

Which pseudocode calculates the average of val_1 and val_2?

A) SET average TO val_1 + val_2 / 2\nB) SET average TO (val_1 + val_2) / 2\nC) SET val_1 + val_2 TO average / 2\nD) SET average TO (val_1 \u2212 val_2) / 2

Check 1, the operation: an average adds, so D is out \u2014 it subtracts. Check 3, the grouping: A divides val_2 by 2 before adding, so it is not the average. Check 4, the result: C assigns to an expression, which is not a legal assignment at all. B survives every check.

Notice you never had to \u201csolve\u201d anything. Each wrong option died on a single named check.

\ud83d\udca1 The habit to build

Read the task, say out loud what the correct line must look like, then read the options. If you read the options first you will find yourself talking yourself into the plausible-looking one, which is exactly what the distractors are designed for.

\ud83e\udde0 Memory hooks \u2014 reading and picking pseudocode

HookWhat it unlocks
\u201cOld Owls Get Results\u201dThe four checks for \u201cwhich pseudocode is right\u201d: Operation \u00b7 Order \u00b7 Grouping \u00b7 Result. Run them in that order and each wrong option dies on one.

\ud83c\udfaf LEARNING OBJECTIVES

after this section you will be able to\u2026

\u2022 Distinguish application software from system software, and place the operating system among them.

\u2022 Explain booting, multiprogramming, and the three resources an OS manages (memory, process, CPU).

\u2022 Contrast batch processing and timesharing, and define a virtual machine.

\u2022 Describe the role of device drivers and real-time systems.

\u2022 Recognize common operating systems and the idea of a dual-boot setup.

Plain-English First

An operating system is the playground monitor of a computer. Dozens of programs all want the same toys \u2014 memory, the CPU, the printer \u2014 at the same time. The OS makes sure everyone \"shares nicely,\" takes turns, and doesn't grab someone else's stuff. It's also the front desk: it gives you (the human) a way to interact with the machine, and it gives application programs a way to reach the hardware without each one needing to know the hardware's every detail.

Going Deeper \u2014 The Technical Detail

Software splits into two categories. Application software solves real-world problems (word processors, games, inventory systems). System software manages the computer at a fundamental level and provides the environment in which applications run. The operating system (OS) is the core of system software: it manages resources (memory, I/O devices), provides a user interface, and lets applications reach other system resources.

When you power on, hardware loads a tiny set of instructions from permanent memory (ROM); those load the larger OS from secondary memory (disk) until the system is ready \u2014 this is booting (\"pull yourself up by your bootstraps\"). A machine may offer a dual-boot / multi-boot choice, but only one OS controls the computer at a time. Common OSes: Windows, macOS, UNIX/Linux, and mobile iOS and Android.

\ud83d\udccc MUST-KNOW

the OS's three big jobs

Multiprogramming keeps multiple programs in main memory at once, competing for the CPU. That forces the OS to do (1) memory management \u2014 track which programs are where in memory; (2) process management \u2014 track each running program's progress and states; (3) CPU scheduling \u2014 decide which process gets the CPU next. The OS is itself a program that must take its turn on the CPU too.

Historical/organizational concepts:

Batch processing \u2014 jobs (program + system instructions) grouped into batches needing similar resources, run without user interaction. Modern echo: .bat command files; payroll runs.

Timesharing \u2014 many users interact at once, each getting a slice of CPU time; it creates the illusion each user has the whole machine. Each user effectively gets a virtual machine (\"in effect, though not in essence\"). Classic setup: a mainframe with dumb terminals (just a monitor + keyboard).

Device driver \u2014 a small program that \"knows\" how a specific device communicates, so the OS doesn't need built-in knowledge of every device (an example of abstraction).

Real-time system \u2014 must guarantee a minimum response time (robots, reactors, missiles).

Key Terms

TermDefinitionWhy it matters
Operating system (OS)Core system software managing hardware/software resources.Runs the whole machine.
Application softwarePrograms solving real-world tasks.What users actually use.
System softwareSoftware providing a platform for other software.Includes the OS and utilities.
BootingLoading the OS at startup from ROM then disk.Gets the machine ready to use.
MultiprogrammingMultiple programs in memory competing for the CPU.Maximizes resource use.
Memory managementTracking/allocating memory to programs.One of the OS's three core jobs.
Batch processingRunning grouped jobs without user interaction.Efficient for large, hands-off jobs.
TimesharingMany users sharing CPU time slices concurrently.Illusion of a private machine each.
Virtual machineSoftware emulation of a full computer.Each user \"gets\" the whole system.
Mainframe / dumb terminalCentral computer + display-only terminals.Classic timesharing hardware.
Device driverSmall program that interfaces with a device.Abstraction; OS need not know every device.
Real-time systemGuarantees a minimum response time.Critical for control systems.

Diagram \u2014 Where the OS sits

Comparison / Reference Tables

Application vs. System software

Application softwareSystem software
PurposeSolve real-world tasksProvide a platform/environment
ExamplesWord, games, browsersOS, utilities, drivers
Talks to hardwareThrough the OSOften directly

Batch vs. Timesharing

Batch processingTimesharing
User interactionNone (hands-off)Interactive, concurrent
FeelSubmit & wait for resultsIllusion of a private machine
ExampleMonthly payroll, .bat filesMainframe + terminals; multiuser desktops

\ud83d\udca1 Tips, Tricks & Mnemonics

OS = \"sharing nicely.\" Its whole job is coordinating shared resources fairly.

Three OS jobs = M-P-C: Memory management, Process management, CPU scheduling.

Boot = bootstraps. ROM loads a little, which loads the rest of the OS from disk.

Batch = no human; Timesharing = many humans.

Driver = translator. The OS speaks to any device through its driver (abstraction).

Real-time = guaranteed response time (missile/reactor/robot), not \"fast\" in general.

\u26a0\ufe0f COMMON EXAM MISTAKES

Calling a game or word processor \"system software.\" Those are application software.

Thinking a dual-boot machine runs two OSes at once. Only one controls the computer at a time.

Confusing multiprogramming (multiple programs in memory) with timesharing (multiple users).

Believing the OS doesn't use the CPU. The OS is itself a program that takes its turn.

Thinking \"real-time\" just means fast \u2014 it means a guaranteed response time.

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 \u2014 Classify the software and the OS job

Problem: For each, name application vs. system software, and (if OS) which of the three jobs applies: (a) Microsoft Word, (b) the part of the OS deciding which process runs next, (c) a device driver for a printer.

(a) Word solves a real-world task \u2192 application software.

(b) Deciding which process runs next is CPU scheduling (a core OS job / system software).

(c) A printer driver is system software that interfaces the OS to the device.

Result: (a) application, (b) CPU scheduling, (c) system/driver. \u2714

Worked Example 2 \u2014 Why timesharing feels private (wrong way \u2192 right way)

Scenario: A student claims \"on a timesharing system each user truly has the whole CPU to themselves.\"

Wrong statement: each user literally owns the CPU.

Why it's wrong: the CPU is shared \u2014 each process gets small turns; it only seems private.

Right way: each user gets a virtual machine \u2014 \"in effect, though not in essence\" \u2014 the OS juggles turns so fast that delays are usually unnoticeable.

Caveat: with too many users, response can visibly degrade. \u2714

\ud83d\udcca FIGURE \u2014 the three resources the operating system hands out
\ud83c\udfaf EXAM TIP

Two classification questions carry most of the marks here, and both are decided by one word.

Application or system software? Does it solve a real-world problem for a person (word processor, game, browser, payroll) \u2192 application. Does it provide the environment other software runs in (the OS, utilities, device drivers) \u2192 system. A driver is always system software, no matter what device it drives.

Which of the three OS jobs? Memory management = where a program sits. Process management = what state each program is in. CPU scheduling = whose turn is next. Read the verb in the question and match it.

Then guard the four wordings they build distractors from: multiprogramming means several programs are in memory; timesharing means several users are interacting; a dual-boot machine has two operating systems installed but only one running at a time; and \u201creal-time\u201d means a guaranteed response time, not merely a fast one.

Multitasking, and keeping programs apart

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION
Multitasking (multiprogramming) is the OS keeping several programs in memory and switching the CPU between them fast enough that a browser, a music player and a word processor all appear to run at once.

Sharing memory between programs needs two registers per partition:

RegisterHoldsGives you
Base registerthe starting address of the program's partitionaddress binding \u2014 a logical address is turned into a real one by adding the base
Bounds registerthe size / limit of that partitionprotection \u2014 an address beyond the limit is refused

Together they provide address binding and protection: one program cannot read or corrupt another's memory, because every address it produces is checked against its own limit.

\ud83e\udde0 Memory hooks \u2014 what an OS actually does

HookWhat it unlocks
\u201cMy PC Files Down\u201dMemory, Processor (CPU), Files, Devices \u2014 the four things an operating system manages. Almost any \u201cwhat does the OS do?\u201d question is one of these four.
Referee, not playerThe OS never does your work \u2014 it decides who gets the CPU, the memory and the disk, and when. If an answer describes doing the work itself, it is describing an application.

Going Deeper \u2014 how memory is actually allocated

Base and bounds registers say where a program sits and how far it may reach. This is the other half of memory management: deciding which free space a new program gets, and what to do when there is not enough memory at all.

Fixed partitions vs dynamic partitions

SchemeHow memory is dividedThe waste it causes
Fixed partitionsa preset number of blocks of a fixed size, decided in advanceinternal fragmentation \u2014 a small program in a big block wastes the leftover inside its own block
Dynamic partitionseach partition is created to fit the program exactlyexternal fragmentation \u2014 as programs come and go, the free space breaks into scattered holes too small to use
\ud83d\udccc MUST-KNOW

first fit, best fit, worst fit

With dynamic partitions the OS must pick one of the free holes. Three strategies, and the exam wants you to apply them to a list:

\u2022 First fit \u2014 the first hole big enough, scanning from the start. Fastest to decide.

\u2022 Best fit \u2014 the smallest hole that still fits. Wastes least now, but leaves slivers.

\u2022 Worst fit \u2014 the largest hole. The leftover is big enough to be useful to somebody else.

Worked example. Free holes of 400 KB, 250 KB and 600 KB, in that order. A 200 KB job arrives.

StrategyWhich holeWhy
First fit400 KBthe first one scanned that is at least 200 KB
Best fit250 KBthe smallest hole that still fits \u2014 only 50 KB left over
Worst fit600 KBthe largest hole \u2014 400 KB left, still usable by another job

Read the strategy name first, then scan the list once: first = earliest, best = smallest that fits, worst = biggest. Nearly every mark lost here comes from answering with the wrong one of the three.

Paging and virtual memory

Paging divides physical memory into equal frames and each program into equal pages of the same size. A page can then be loaded into any free frame \u2014 the program no longer needs one continuous run of memory, which kills external fragmentation.

Virtual memory takes the next step: only the pages actually in use need to be in RAM, and the rest live on disk. That is how a machine runs a program larger than its physical RAM. When the program touches a page that is not resident, the hardware raises a page fault, the OS fetches that page from disk (evicting another if needed) and the instruction resumes.

The cost is speed: disk is far slower than RAM. If a system spends more time moving pages than running programs it is thrashing, and the fix is more RAM or fewer concurrent programs.

\ud83e\udde0 Memory hooks \u2014 allocation & virtual memory

HookWhat it unlocks
First = first, Best = biggest\u2026 no, smallestThe trap is the word \"best\". Best fit picks the smallest hole that fits, worst fit picks the largest. Say it out loud once and the pairing sticks.
Fixed \u2192 internal, Dynamic \u2192 externalFixed blocks waste space inside a block. Dynamic partitions leave unusable gaps between them.
Bigger than RAM = virtual memoryAny question where a program is larger than physical memory, or inactive parts move to disk, is virtual memory with paging.
Page fault = not residentA page fault is not an error. It just means the page needed is on disk, so the OS must fetch it.

\ud83c\udfaf LEARNING OBJECTIVES

after this section you will be able to\u2026

\u2022 Name and describe the five process states and the transitions between them.

\u2022 Explain what a process is versus a program.

\u2022 Describe the process control block (PCB) and what it stores.

\u2022 Define a context switch and why the program counter must be saved.

\u2022 Recognize that only one process runs at a time, while many may be ready or waiting.

Plain-English First

A program is a recipe sitting in a cookbook \u2014 static text. A process is what happens when a cook actually starts making the dish: ingredients out, a specific step in progress, timers running. The OS is the head chef tracking many dishes at once, but there's only one stove burner (the CPU), so it constantly notes exactly where each dish is, pauses some, and resumes others without losing anyone's place.

Going Deeper \u2014 The Technical Detail

A process is a program in execution \u2014 the dynamic entity representing a program while it runs. Through multiprogramming, many processes exist at once, so the OS does process management: tracking each process's progress and intermediate state. Processes move through five process states:

New \u2014 the process is being created.

Ready \u2014 no barriers; waiting only for a turn on the CPU.

Running \u2014 currently executing in the fetch\u2013execute cycle.

Waiting \u2014 waiting for a resource other than the CPU (e.g., I/O, a signal).

Terminated \u2014 finished; the OS no longer needs its info.

\ud83d\udccc MUST-KNOW

transitions & the one-at-a-time rule

After creation the OS admits a process to ready; the scheduler dispatches it to running. A running process may be interrupted back to ready, may request a resource and go to waiting, or may terminate. A waiting process, once it gets its resource, returns to ready (not directly to running). Many processes can be ready or waiting at once, but only ONE can be running.

The OS stores each process's data in a process control block (PCB). Each state is a list of PCBs; a process's PCB moves between lists as it changes state. The PCB holds the program counter (which instruction is next), all other CPU register values, CPU-scheduling info (like priority), memory-management info (base/bounds or page tables), and accounting info. Because there's only one set of CPU registers, switching processes means saving the current process's registers into its PCB and loading the next process's registers \u2014 this exchange is a context switch.

Key Terms

TermDefinitionWhy it matters
ProgramA static set of instructions.The recipe, not the cooking.
ProcessA program in execution (dynamic).What the OS actually manages.
Process statesNew, ready, running, waiting, terminated.The lifecycle the OS tracks.
Ready stateWaiting only for the CPU.Eligible to be dispatched.
Waiting stateWaiting for a non-CPU resource.Blocked until I/O/signal arrives.
PCBData structure holding all process info.Lets a process resume correctly.
Program counterAddress of the next instruction.Saved so a process resumes in place.
Context switchSaving one process's registers, loading another's.Enables CPU sharing.

Diagram \u2014 The process life cycle

Comparison / Reference Tables

Program vs. Process

ProgramProcess
NatureStatic instructionsDynamic, executing
Exists whereOn disk / in a fileIn memory, actively running
CountOne filePossibly many active at once

The five states at a glance

StateWhat's happeningHow many at once
NewBeing createdSeveral possible
ReadyWaiting for the CPUMany
RunningExecuting on the CPUExactly one
WaitingWaiting for I/O/resourceMany
TerminatedFinishedSeveral possible

\ud83d\udca1 Tips, Tricks & Mnemonics

States \"NRRWT\": New, Ready, Running, Waiting, Terminated.

Only ONE runs. Many ready, many waiting, exactly one running (single CPU).

Waiting \u2192 Ready, never straight to Running. After getting its resource, a process rejoins the ready line.

PCB = the process's \"save file.\" Program counter + registers let it resume exactly where it left off.

Context switch = swap the save files. Store current registers to PCB, load the next process's.

\u26a0\ufe0f COMMON EXAM MISTAKES

Saying a process goes from waiting directly to running. It returns to ready first.

Thinking multiple processes can be \"running\" simultaneously on one CPU. Only one runs at a time.

Confusing \"ready\" (needs only the CPU) with \"waiting\" (needs I/O/another resource).

Forgetting the program counter must be saved on a context switch, or the process loses its place.

Treating a program and a process as the same thing.

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 \u2014 Trace a process through the states

Scenario: A newly launched app needs to read a file partway through execution.

The app is created \u2192 New.

OS admits it \u2192 Ready (waiting for a CPU turn).

Scheduler dispatches it \u2192 Running.

It requests a file read (I/O) \u2192 moves to Waiting.

File data arrives \u2192 back to Ready (not straight to running).

Dispatched again \u2192 Running \u2192 finishes \u2192 Terminated. \u2714

Worked Example 2 \u2014 Why a context switch needs the PCB

Problem: Process A is interrupted at instruction 5000 so Process B can run. What must happen so A resumes correctly?

Save A's program counter (5000) and all CPU register values into A's PCB.

Load B's saved registers/program counter from B's PCB into the CPU.

B runs; later, reverse the process to bring A back.

Because A's state was saved, A resumes at instruction 5000 as if never interrupted \u2014 that swap is the context switch. \u2714

Wrong way \u2192 why \u2192 right way: Skipping the save and just loading B would lose A's place (its registers get overwritten). Right way: always store the outgoing process's registers to its PCB first.

\ud83d\udcca FIGURE \u2014 one context switch \u2014 what is saved, and why the program counter matters most
\ud83c\udfaf EXAM TIP

The five states are asked as a sequence question: \u201ca running process requests a file \u2014 what happens?\u201d Answer with the transition, not the state: running \u2192 waiting (it needs something other than the CPU), then when the data arrives waiting \u2192 ready, and only later ready \u2192 running when the scheduler picks it.

The single most-tested fact is that waiting never goes straight to running. It rejoins the ready queue and waits its turn. Any answer choice with \u201cwaiting \u2192 running\u201d in it is the trap.

The counting question is just as reliable: on one CPU there is exactly one running process, and any number of ready and waiting ones. If a question says two processes are running simultaneously on a single processor, it is wrong.

And keep program and process apart in the wording: a program is the static file on disk; a process is that program in execution, with its own memory and its own PCB. One program can have many processes running at once.

Deadlock

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION
Deadlock is a standstill in which each process holds a resource the other needs and waits for one the other holds, so none can ever proceed.
\u25b8 WORKED EXAMPLE \u2014 The classic two-process deadlock

Process A holds resource 1 and waits for resource 2. Process B holds resource 2 and waits for resource 1.

  1. A will not release resource 1 until it gets resource 2.
  2. B will not release resource 2 until it gets resource 1.
  3. Neither condition can ever become true. Both wait for ever: this is deadlock.

Note what it is not: not starvation (where a process is repeatedly passed over but could still run), and not an infinite loop (where a process is busy, not blocked).

Four conditions must all hold for deadlock, so breaking any one prevents it:

ConditionMeaning
Mutual exclusiona resource can be held by only one process at a time
Hold and waita process holds one resource while waiting for another
No pre-emptiona resource cannot be forcibly taken back
Circular waita closed chain of processes, each waiting on the next
\ud83c\udfaf EXAM TIP
The usual practical cure is to break circular wait by requiring every process to request resources in the same fixed order.

\ud83e\udde0 Memory hooks \u2014 the five process states

HookWhat it unlocks
\u201cNew Ready Runs, Waiting Terminates\u201dThe five states in order: New \u2192 Ready \u2192 Running \u2192 Waiting \u2192 Terminated. Read it as a sentence and the order comes back.
Only ONE runsOn a single core exactly one process is Running; every other ready process is queued. That single fact answers most state questions.
Waiting = blocked on I/OA process that asks the disk or the network for something goes to Waiting, not Ready \u2014 it cannot use the CPU until the data arrives. Ready means \u201conly needs the CPU\u201d.
Deadlock: \u201cMy Hands Need Cuffs\u201dMutual exclusion, Hold and wait, No preemption, Circular wait \u2014 all four must hold at once, so breaking any one prevents deadlock.

\ud83c\udfaf LEARNING OBJECTIVES

after this section you will be able to\u2026

\u2022 Define CPU scheduling and distinguish preemptive from nonpreemptive.

\u2022 Compute turnaround time and average turnaround time from a Gantt chart.

\u2022 Apply FCFS, SJN, and round-robin to a set of processes.

\u2022 Explain the trade-offs of each algorithm (fairness, efficiency, knowledge of the future).

\u2022 Read a Gantt chart and identify completion/turnaround times.

Plain-English First

Only one process can use the CPU at a time, so the OS is like a checkout clerk deciding who goes next in line. Do you serve people in arrival order (fair but slow if a big cart is first)? Serve the smallest cart first (fast average, but you must guess cart sizes)? Or give everyone a fixed 2 minutes and rotate (nobody waits forever)? Those three policies are FCFS, SJN, and round-robin.

Going Deeper \u2014 The Technical Detail

CPU scheduling decides which ready process moves to running. Scheduling can be nonpreemptive (a new choice happens only when the running process voluntarily leaves \u2014 it waits or terminates) or preemptive (the OS can interrupt a running process \u2014 e.g., on a timeout or when a higher-priority process becomes ready). A key metric is turnaround time: the time from when a process arrives in ready until it leaves running for the last time. Lower average turnaround is better. (When all arrive at time 0, turnaround = completion time.)

\ud83d\udccc MUST-KNOW

the three algorithms (all arrive at t=0)

Using service times p1=140, p2=75, p3=320, p4=280, p5=125:

FCFS (arrival order p1..p5, nonpreemptive): completions 140, 215, 535, 815, 940 \u2192 avg = 529.

SJN (shortest first: p2,p5,p1,p4,p3, nonpreemptive): completions 75, 200, 340, 620, 940 \u2192 avg = 435 (provably optimal if service times are known).

Round-robin (time slice 50, preemptive): completions p1=515, p2=325, p3=940, p4=920, p5=640 \u2192 avg = 668 (most fair, most widely used).

Notes on each: FCFS is easy but ignores service times, so a long job first delays everyone. SJN gives the smallest average turnaround if you know each job's length \u2014 but you can't know the future, so the OS estimates; bad estimates hurt it. Round-robin gives each process a time slice (quantum); when it expires the process is preempted back to ready. Its average turnaround here is highest, but you can't judge an algorithm from one example \u2014 round-robin is the most widely used and considered the fairest.

Key Terms

TermDefinitionWhy it matters
CPU schedulingChoosing which ready process runs next.Determines efficiency and fairness.
NonpreemptiveRunning process isn't interrupted; it finishes/waits.FCFS and SJN are nonpreemptive.
PreemptiveOS can interrupt a running process.Round-robin is preemptive.
Turnaround timeReady-arrival \u2192 last exit from running.The key performance metric.
FCFSRun in arrival order.Simple; can delay everyone.
SJN (shortest job next)Run the shortest service time next.Optimal avg turnaround if times known.
Round-robinFixed time slice, rotate.Fair; most widely used.
Time slice (quantum)CPU time each process gets before preemption.Defines round-robin behavior.

Diagram \u2014 Scheduling decision points

Comparison / Reference Tables

The three CPU-scheduling algorithms (this example)

FCFSSJNRound-robin (q=50)
TypeNonpreemptiveNonpreemptivePreemptive
Order/basisArrival orderShortest service timeRotate by time slice
Avg turnaround529435668
StrengthSimple, no starvationOptimal avg (if known)Fair, most used
WeaknessIgnores job lengthNeeds future knowledgeOverhead of switching

\ud83d\udca1 Tips, Tricks & Mnemonics

FCFS = fair-to-arrival; SJN = fast-but-psychic; RR = everyone-gets-a-turn.

Turnaround (all arrive at 0) = completion time. Just read the finish time off the Gantt chart.

SJN is provably optimal for average turnaround \u2014 but only if you truly know each job's length.

Round-robin is preemptive; FCFS and SJN are nonpreemptive.

Don't rank algorithms from one dataset. RR's higher average here doesn't make it \"worse.\"

Average = sum of completions \u00f7 number of processes.

\u26a0\ufe0f COMMON EXAM MISTAKES

Calling round-robin nonpreemptive. It is preemptive (time slice expiry).

Forgetting SJN needs the service times, which usually must be estimated.

Miscomputing average turnaround \u2014 sum the completion times, then divide by the count.

Assuming FCFS can starve a process. It can't; SSTF-style greediness (disk) can \u2014 not FCFS.

Declaring one algorithm universally best from a single example.

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 \u2014 FCFS vs. SJN average turnaround

Processes (arrive at t=0): p1=140, p2=75, p3=320, p4=280, p5=125.

FCFS order p1,p2,p3,p4,p5. Completions: 140; 140+75=215; 215+320=535; 535+280=815; 815+125=940.

Average = (140+215+535+815+940)/5 = 2645/5 = 529.

SJN order (shortest first): p2(75), p5(125), p1(140), p4(280), p3(320). Completions: 75; 200; 340; 620; 940.

Average = (75+200+340+620+940)/5 = 2175/5 = 435.

SJN's average (435) beats FCFS (529) \u2014 it front-loads short jobs. \u2714

Worked Example 2 \u2014 Round-robin with time slice 50

Same processes, quantum = 50, order p1..p5, preemptive.

Give each 50 units in turn, subtracting from remaining time, until each hits 0.

p2 needed 75: after two visits (50 + 25) it finishes at time 325.

Working through all rounds, completion times are p1=515, p2=325, p3=940, p4=920, p5=640.

Average = (515+325+940+920+640)/5 = 3340/5 = 668.

Higher average than FCFS/SJN here \u2014 but round-robin is the fairest and most widely used; one example doesn't crown a winner. \u2714

\ud83d\udcca FIGURE \u2014 FCFS, SJN and round robin drawn on the same time axis
\ud83c\udfaf EXAM TIP

These questions are arithmetic, and the arithmetic is short if you write the Gantt chart first. With every process arriving at time 0 \u2014 which is how this OA words it \u2014 turnaround time = completion time, so there is no subtraction to do.

The method: put the jobs in the order the algorithm dictates (arrival order for FCFS, shortest-first for SJN), write a running total across the row, and those running totals are the completion times. Add them, divide by the number of processes, done. For round robin, subtract the quantum from each job in rotation and note the time at which each one hits zero.

The three facts they ask directly: round robin is preemptive, FCFS and SJN are nonpreemptive; SJN gives the provably lowest average turnaround but requires knowing each job\u2019s length in advance, which is its whole weakness; and FCFS cannot starve anything, because everybody eventually reaches the front of the line.

Do not rank the algorithms from one data set. Round robin\u2019s higher average here does not make it worse \u2014 it is the most widely used one precisely because it is fair and responsive.

Round robin against first-come first-served

FCFSRound robin
Orderwhoever arrived first runs to completioneach process gets a fixed time quantum in turn
Pre-emptive?No \u2014 it keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocksYes \u2014 it is interrupted when its slice expires and moves to the back of the queue
Weaknessone long job makes everyone wait (the convoy effect)more context switching

So round robin differs from FCFS in that it pre-empts: it cycles a fixed time quantum among the processes rather than letting one run to completion.

\ud83e\udde0 Memory hooks \u2014 CPU scheduling

HookWhat it unlocks
\u201cFirst Short Priority Round\u201dThe four classics in the order they are usually taught: FCFS, SJF, Priority, Round Robin.
Each name IS its ruleFirst-Come First-Served takes the earliest arrival. Shortest Job First takes the smallest burst. Priority takes the highest rank. Round Robin gives everyone a fixed time slice in turn. You never have to memorise behaviour separately from the name.
Starvation lives with Priority and SJFA long or low-priority job can wait forever under those two. Round Robin cannot starve anyone, because the turn always comes back around.
