\ud83c\udfaf LEARNING OBJECTIVES

after this section you will be able to\u2026

\u2022 Define a file, a file system, and the difference between text and binary files.

\u2022 Explain file types/extensions and why an extension doesn't change a file's actual contents.

\u2022 List the standard file operations and the role of the file pointer.

\u2022 Contrast sequential and direct file access, and describe file protection (owner/group/world).

\u2022 Navigate a directory tree and write absolute and relative paths (including ..).

Plain-English First

Your computer's disk is a giant filing cabinet. A file is one labeled folder of related data; the file system is the whole organized cabinet plus the rules for finding things. Directories (folders) are drawers that hold files and even other drawers, forming a tree. To tell someone exactly where a document lives, you either give directions from the very top of the cabinet (absolute path) or from where you're currently standing (relative path).

Going Deeper \u2014 Files, Types & Operations

Recall main memory is volatile (lost without power) while secondary memory (disk) is nonvolatile \u2014 used for permanent storage. A file is a named collection of related data \u2014 the smallest unit a user writes to secondary memory. A file system is the logical view the OS provides for managing data as files, usually grouped into directories.

All files are ultimately binary, but we classify them as:

Text file \u2014 bytes organized as ASCII/Unicode characters (human-readable; e.g., source code, config).

Binary file \u2014 bits interpreted in a specific non-character format (images, executables, Word docs). Only a program built for that format can read it. (A word-processor document is actually binary because it stores formatting, fonts, etc.)

\ud83d\udccc MUST-KNOW

extensions don't define contents

The file extension (after the dot, e.g., .java, .jpg) tells the OS the likely file type so it can pick an application/icon. But an extension is only an indication: renaming photo.txt to photo.gif does not change the file's actual data or make it a real GIF \u2014 opening it in a GIF program gives an error.

File operations (via the OS): create, delete, open, close, read, write, reposition the file pointer, append, truncate (erase contents, keep the entry), rename, copy. An open file has a current file pointer marking where the next read/write happens; it advances as you read/write. Truncating deletes contents without removing the file's table entry.

Going Deeper \u2014 Access, Protection, Directories & Paths

File access methods:

Sequential access \u2014 process the file in order from start to end (simplest, most common).

Direct access \u2014 file is numbered logical records; jump to any record by number (great for databases where specific data must be reached fast).

File protection (multiuser systems): UNIX uses three categories \u2014 Owner, Group, World \u2014 each with read / write / execute permissions (shown as a 3\u00d73 grid). If you can write to a file you can also delete it. World permissions reach the most users, so they're usually the most restricted.

\ud83d\udccc MUST-KNOW

directory trees & paths

A directory can contain files and subdirectories; the top is the root (Windows C:\\, UNIX /), forming a directory tree. Your current location is the working directory. An absolute path starts at the root (C:\\Program Files\\MS Office\\WinWord.exe). A relative path starts at the working directory (applications\\calState.doc); .. means the parent directory and a single . means the current directory. Files in different directories may share a name; files in the same directory cannot.

Key Terms

TermDefinitionWhy it matters

File systemOS's logical view for managing files.Organizes secondary storage.
Text fileBytes as ASCII/Unicode characters.Human-readable; source/config.
Binary fileBits in a specific non-character format.Images, executables, Word docs.
File extensionSuffix indicating file type.OS picks app/icon; only an indication.
File pointerMarks next read/write location.Tracks position in an open file.
Sequential accessRead/write in order.Simple, common.
Direct accessJump to any numbered record.Fast for databases.
DirectoryNamed collection of files (a folder).Organizes files hierarchically.
Root directoryTop of the directory tree.Start of every absolute path.
Working directoryYour current location.Start of every relative path.
Absolute pathFull path from the root.Unambiguous location.
Relative pathPath from the working directory.Shorter; .. = parent.

Diagram \u2014 A directory tree with paths

Comparison / Reference Tables

Text vs. Binary files

Text fileBinary file
Bytes representASCII/Unicode charactersA specific custom format
Human-readable?Yes (any text editor)No (needs a specific program)
ExamplesSource code, .txt, configJPEG, EXE, Word .docx

Sequential vs. Direct access

OrderStart to end, in orderJump to any record by number
ComplexitySimpleMore complex

Starts atThe root (C:\\ or /)The working directory

\ud83d\udca1 Tips, Tricks & Mnemonics

Extension = label, not contents. Renaming .txt\u2192.gif doesn't make it a GIF.

Text = characters; Binary = special format. A Word doc is binary (it stores formatting).

Absolute starts at the top (root); Relative starts where you stand (working dir).

.. = up one level (parent); . = right here.

Owner > Group > World. World reaches everyone, so it's usually the most restricted.

Truncate keeps the file, empties it; delete removes the entry entirely.

\u26a0\ufe0f COMMON EXAM MISTAKES

Believing changing a file's extension changes its data/format. It doesn't.

Calling a Word document a text file \u2014 it's binary.

Starting a relative path at the root, or forgetting .. to go up a level.

Thinking two files in the same directory can share a name (they can't; different directories can).

Mixing up sequential (in order) and direct (jump to any record) access.

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 \u2014 Absolute vs. relative path

Tree: working directory is C:\\My Documents\\letters. Target file calState.doc is in C:\\My Documents\\letters\\applications. Give both an absolute and a relative path; then reach landscape.jpg in C:\\My Documents.

Absolute to calState.doc: start at root \u2192 C:\\My Documents\\letters\\applications\\calState.doc.

Relative (from letters): the file is one level down in applications \u2192 applications\\calState.doc.

To reach landscape.jpg in the parent My Documents: go up one level with .. \u2192 ..\\landscape.jpg.

Check: .. moves from letters up to My Documents, where landscape.jpg lives. \u2714

Worked Example 2 \u2014 Classify files & the extension trap (wrong way \u2192 right way)

Classify: report.docx \u2192 binary (stores formatting); notes.txt \u2192 text; Game.exe \u2192 binary.

Wrong way: a user renames song.mp3 to song.txt expecting to read lyrics in Notepad.

Why it's wrong: the bytes are still MP3 audio; the extension is just a label \u2014 the data is unchanged.

Right way: open it with a program that matches the real format; renaming can't convert a file. \u2714

\ud83d\udcca FIGURE \u2014 UNIX permissions, and sequential versus direct access
\ud83c\udfaf EXAM TIP

The highest-frequency item here is the extension trap, and it has a one-sentence answer: the extension is a label, not the contents. Renaming song.mp3 to song.txt changes nothing about the bytes \u2014 it only changes which application the OS offers to open it with.

Path questions are mechanical if you say where you are standing first. An absolute path starts at the root (C:\\ or /) and reads the same from anywhere. A relative path starts at the working directory, and .. means \u201cup one level to the parent\u201d. Write out the walk step by step rather than pattern-matching the answer choices.

For permissions, read the nine bits in three groups of three \u2014 owner, group, world, each with read, write, execute. World is the broadest audience, so it is normally the most restricted set.

Two more one-mark facts: a text file is bytes interpreted as ASCII/Unicode characters, so a Word document is a binary file (it stores formatting); and truncate empties a file but keeps it, while delete removes the entry altogether.

How a file system is organized, and two failure modes

A file system organizes directories and files into a hierarchical structure \u2014 a tree: one root, directories containing files and further directories, each file reached by a path from the root.

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION
Journaling. A journaling file system writes what it is about to do into a log before doing it. If power is lost mid-write, it replays or discards the log on restart and the file system is consistent again \u2014 solving the corruption that an interrupted write used to cause, without a long whole-disk check.
\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION
Thrashing. When too many large programs are open, memory is oversubscribed and the OS spends nearly all its time swapping pages between RAM and disk instead of running programs. The machine slows to a crawl while the disk runs constantly \u2014 that symptom is thrashing, and the fix is more RAM or fewer running programs.

\ud83e\udde0 Memory hooks \u2014 file systems

HookWhat it unlocks
Path = directions, not the fileAn absolute path starts at the root and works anywhere; a relative path starts where you are and breaks if you move. \u201cAbsolute = from the top.\u201d
Extension is a hint, not a factThe extension tells the OS which program to open a file with. Renaming it does not change what is inside \u2014 a classic trap answer.

\ud83c\udfaf LEARNING OBJECTIVES

after this section you will be able to\u2026

\u2022 Explain why disk I/O is the system's bottleneck and define seek time vs. latency.

\u2022 Apply FCFS, SSTF, and SCAN disk scheduling to a request list.

\u2022 Define starvation and identify which algorithm risks it.

\u2022 Describe the SCAN (elevator), LOOK, and Circular SCAN variations.

\u2022 Order cylinder visits and reason about head movement.

Plain-English First

Reading from a spinning disk is the slowest thing a computer does, so the order in which the read/write head visits requested tracks really matters. Picture an elevator with people waiting on many floors. Do you answer call buttons in the exact order they were pressed (fair but lots of zig-zagging)? Always go to the nearest floor next (efficient, but someone far away might wait forever)? Or sweep smoothly top-to-bottom then bottom-to-top (the elevator strategy)? Those are FCFS, SSTF, and SCAN.

Going Deeper \u2014 The Technical Detail

A disk is a stack of platters, each with tracks divided into sectors; the aligned tracks across platters form a cylinder. The heads sit over one cylinder at a time. Seek time is the time to move the heads to the right cylinder; latency is the extra time for the platter to rotate into position. Seek time is the bigger cost, so disk-scheduling algorithms focus on minimizing head movement. Transferring to/from disk is the system's worst bottleneck (far slower than CPU or main memory).

Example request queue (in arrival order): 49, 91, 22, 61, 7, 62, 33, 35; heads start at cylinder 26.

\ud83d\udccc MUST-KNOW

the three algorithms on this example

FCFS: visit in arrival order \u2192 49, 91, 22, 61, 7, 62, 33, 35 (lots of back-and-forth; simple, never starves).

SSTF (shortest seek time first): always go to the nearest pending request \u2192 22, 33, 35, 49, 61, 62, 91, 7 (efficient, but can cause starvation).

SCAN (elevator), moving toward lower cylinders first: sweep down servicing 22, 7, reach the low end, reverse, then service 33, 35, 49, 61, 62, 91. No starvation.

Starvation: under SSTF, if nearby requests keep arriving, a far-away request might never be served. FCFS can't starve (it honors order). SCAN sweeps to each extreme like an elevator; LOOK is a smarter SCAN that only goes as far as the outermost/innermost actual request (it \"looks ahead\"), and Circular SCAN (C-SCAN) treats the disk as a ring, jumping back to the start without servicing on the return to improve fairness of wait times.

Key Terms

TermDefinitionWhy it matters
Seek timeTime to move heads to the right cylinder.The dominant disk cost to minimize.
LatencyTime for platter rotation into position.Secondary cost after seek time.
CylinderAligned tracks across all platters.The unit disk scheduling targets.
Disk schedulingDeciding the order to serve disk requests.Reduces seek time; speeds I/O.
FCFS (disk)Serve requests in arrival order.Simple; no starvation; inefficient.
SSTFServe the nearest pending request next.Efficient but risks starvation.
StarvationA request never served due to closer ones.SSTF's main flaw.
SCAN (elevator)Sweep to one extreme, then reverse.Fair; no starvation.
LOOKSCAN that reverses at the last request.Avoids needless travel to the edge.
Circular SCANTreats disk as a ring; returns without servicing.Evens out wait times.

Diagram \u2014 Head movement for the example (start = 26)

Comparison / Reference Tables

Disk-scheduling algorithms

FCFSSSTFSCAN (elevator)
BasisArrival orderNearest requestSweep to extremes
EfficiencyLow (zig-zags)HigherGood, steady
Starvation?NoPossibleNo
Order (example)49,91,22,61,7,62,33,3522,33,35,49,61,62,91,722,7,then 33,35,49,61,62,91

SCAN vs. LOOK vs. C-SCAN

SCANLOOKCircular SCAN
Travels toThe physical edge/spindleOnly the last requestEdge, then jumps back
Services on return?YesYesNo (ring behavior)

\ud83d\udca1 Tips, Tricks & Mnemonics

Seek time > latency. Head movement (seek) is the main cost the algorithms attack.

FCFS = order; SSTF = nearest; SCAN = elevator.

Only SSTF starves. FCFS and SCAN cannot starve a request.

LOOK \"looks ahead\" and turns around at the last request instead of the physical edge.

C-SCAN = ring. It returns to the start without servicing on the way back.

SSTF \u2260 least total movement guaranteed \u2014 it's greedy, not globally optimal.

\u26a0\ufe0f COMMON EXAM MISTAKES

Saying FCFS or SCAN can starve. Only SSTF risks starvation.

Claiming SSTF always gives the least total head movement \u2014 it's greedy, not optimal.

Confusing seek time (head movement) with latency (rotation). Seek time dominates.

Forgetting SCAN needs an initial direction to compute the order.

Mixing up SCAN (goes to the edge) and LOOK (turns at the last request).

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 \u2014 SSTF order and starvation

Requests: 49, 91, 22, 61, 7, 62, 33, 35; head at 26.

From 26, nearest pending is 22 (distance 4) \u2192 go to 22.

From 22, nearest is 33 \u2192 then 35 \u2192 then 49 (49 now closest).

Continue nearest-first: 61, 62, 91, and finally the far-off 7.

Order: 22, 33, 35, 49, 61, 62, 91, 7.

Starvation note: if new nearby requests kept arriving, cylinder 7 (far away) might be postponed indefinitely \u2014 that's SSTF starvation. \u2714

Worked Example 2 \u2014 SCAN (elevator) going low first (wrong way \u2192 right way)

Head at 26 moving toward lower cylinders: service 22, then 7 on the way down.

Reach the low extreme, then reverse and sweep upward.

Going up, service 33, 35, 49, 61, 62, 91 in order.

Full order: 22, 7, (reverse) 33, 35, 49, 61, 62, 91.

Wrong way \u2192 why \u2192 right way: jumping straight from 26 up to 33 first ignores SCAN's rule to finish the current direction. Right way: service everything in the current direction (down to 22, 7) before reversing. \u2714

\ud83d\udcca FIGURE \u2014 track, sector and cylinder \u2014 and where seek time and latency come from
\ud83c\udfaf EXAM TIP

Ordering questions are answered by the algorithm\u2019s one rule, applied literally from the starting cylinder. FCFS: arrival order, ignore the head position entirely. SSTF: repeatedly take the nearest pending request \u2014 recompute the distances after every move, which is the step people skip. SCAN: keep going in the current direction to the end, servicing on the way, then reverse \u2014 so you must be told or must state the initial direction.

The conceptual mark is always starvation: only SSTF can starve a request, because a steady stream of nearby requests can postpone a far-away one indefinitely. FCFS and SCAN both guarantee everyone is eventually served.

Keep the two delays apart \u2014 seek time is the arm moving between cylinders, latency is the platter rotating the sector under the head, and access time is the two added together. Seek is the one worth optimising, which is why every algorithm here is about the order of cylinder visits.

Finally, do not upgrade SSTF to \u201coptimal\u201d. It is greedy \u2014 nearest next \u2014 and greedy is not the same as least total head movement over the whole queue.

Fragmentation

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION
Fragmentation is a file ending up stored in blocks scattered across the disk rather than in one run.

On a magnetic hard drive the effect is slower reads: the head must physically seek to each separate location instead of streaming one continuous stretch, so seek time dominates. No data is lost \u2014 it is purely a performance cost, which is what defragmenting addresses.

It barely matters on an SSD, which has no moving head and reaches any block in the same time.

\ud83e\udde0 Memory hooks \u2014 disk scheduling

HookWhat it unlocks
\u201cFast Seeks Scan Clean Looks\u201dFCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK.
SCAN is the liftSCAN sweeps to the end and back like a lift; LOOK is the polite lift that turns round as soon as there are no more requests ahead. C-SCAN always returns the same way, so waiting is fairer.

\ud83c\udfaf LEARNING OBJECTIVES

after this section you will be able to\u2026

\u2022 Decode a real laptop spec: CPU/clock speed, cache, RAM, SSD, GPU, ports.

\u2022 Explain the clock and what GHz/hertz measure.

\u2022 Distinguish RAM (main memory) from SSD (secondary storage).

\u2022 Use the computing size prefixes and the powers-of-10 vs. powers-of-2 rule.

\u2022 Identify common ports (USB, HDMI) and their uses.

Plain-English First

A computer ad is just a car sticker for a machine \u2014 horsepower, fuel tank, trunk space \u2014 written in acronyms. The CPU is the engine, its GHz is the RPM, RAM is the desk you spread your work on right now, the SSD is the filing cabinet that keeps everything when you go home, and ports are the plugs on the side. Learn to read the sticker and no spec sheet can intimidate you.

Going Deeper \u2014 The Technical Detail

Walking a real spec: Intel Core i7 (2.8 GHz Quad-Core), 12 MB cache, 20 GB SDRAM, 1 TB SSD, GPU, USB & HDMI ports.

CPU + clock: The processor's speed (2.8 GHz) is set by the clock \u2014 a steady stream of electrical pulses that coordinates all actions (like a conductor's baton). Hz = hertz = cycles per second; G = giga = one billion.

Cache: small, very fast memory built into the processor holding frequently used data, so the CPU often avoids slower main-memory trips.

RAM (main memory): random access means any byte can be reached directly. SDRAM = synchronous dynamic RAM. It's where active programs/data live while in use.

SSD (secondary storage): like RAM technology but nonvolatile (keeps data with power off); no moving parts, so faster and lower-power than a spinning hard drive.

GPU: a separate graphics chip that offloads image work from the main CPU, with its own memory.

Ports: USB (universal serial bus) connects almost anything; HDMI sends digital video/audio to displays/TVs.

\ud83d\udccc MUST-KNOW

the prefix rule

Time uses powers of 10 (decimal); storage uses powers of 2 (binary). So K = 1000 for speed but 1024 (2\u00b9\u2070) for storage. A byte = 8 bits; KB \u2248 10\u00b3, MB \u2248 2\u00b2\u2070, GB \u2248 2\u00b3\u2070, TB \u2248 2\u2074\u2070 bytes. (Milli/micro/nano/pico measure small times in powers of 10.)

Key Terms

TermDefinitionWhy it matters
CPUMain chip executing instructions.The \"engine\" of the computer.
ClockPulses coordinating all actions.Sets the processing tempo (GHz).
Hertz (Hz)Cycles per second.Unit of clock frequency.
Cache memorySmall fast memory in the CPU.Speeds access to frequent data.
RAM (main memory)Directly addressable working memory.Holds active programs/data; volatile.
SSDNonvolatile solid-state secondary storage.Fast permanent storage, no moving parts.
GPUSeparate graphics processor.Offloads image work from the CPU.
USB / HDMIPorts for devices / video-audio.Connect peripherals and displays.
Byte8 bits.Basic unit of storage size.

Diagram \u2014 Reading a laptop spec

Comparison / Reference Tables

RAM vs. SSD

RAM (main memory)SSD (secondary storage)
RoleActive working memoryPermanent storage
Volatile?Yes (lost at power-off)No (kept at power-off)
SpeedVery fastSlower than RAM, faster than HDD
Typical sizeGBsHundreds of GB to TBs

Size prefixes (the powers rule)

PrefixSpeed/time (base 10)Storage (base 2)
K (kilo)1,000 (10\u00b3)1,024 (2\u00b9\u2070)
M (mega)10\u20762\u00b2\u2070
G (giga)10\u20792\u00b3\u2070
T (tera)10\u00b9\u00b22\u2074\u2070

\ud83d\udca1 Tips, Tricks & Mnemonics

Clock = conductor. GHz is how many billion \"beats\" per second the CPU marches to.

RAM = desk (temporary), SSD = filing cabinet (permanent).

Time = base 10, Storage = base 2. \"K is 1000 for speed, 1024 for storage.\"

Byte = 8 bits. Always.

Cache is closest & fastest; the CPU checks it before going to main memory.

\u26a0\ufe0f COMMON EXAM MISTAKES

Thinking RAM keeps data when powered off. It's volatile; the SSD is permanent.

Using 1024 for time or 1000 for storage. Time = base 10, storage = base 2.

Confusing cache (tiny, in-CPU) with main memory (larger, slower).

Calling GHz a storage measure. It's a speed (cycles per second).

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 \u2014 Decode a spec line

Problem: Explain \"2.8 GHz Quad-Core, 16 GB RAM, 512 GB SSD.\"

2.8 GHz = clock speed of 2.8 billion cycles/second (speed, base 10).

Quad-Core = four processing cores on the CPU.

16 GB RAM = main working memory, volatile (base 2 sizing).

512 GB SSD = nonvolatile secondary storage for permanent files.

Plain meaning: a fairly fast laptop with roomy working memory and solid permanent storage. \u2714

Worked Example 2 \u2014 The prefix rule (wrong way \u2192 right way)

Question: Is \"1 KB of storage\" 1000 or 1024 bytes?

Wrong way: assume 1000 because \"kilo means 1000.\"

Why it's wrong: storage is measured in powers of 2, so K = 2\u00b9\u2070.

Right way: 1 KB (storage) = 1024 bytes. (For a \"1 K\" data rate/speed, it would be 1000.) \u2714

\ud83d\udcca FIGURE \u2014 the memory hierarchy \u2014 what a spec sheet is really listing
\ud83c\udfaf EXAM TIP

Spec-decoding questions are answered from three separations. Speed versus storage: GHz is a rate (billions of clock pulses a second), GB is a quantity \u2014 if a choice calls GHz a storage measure it is wrong. RAM versus SSD: RAM is the working desk and is volatile; the SSD is the filing cabinet and is nonvolatile. Cache versus main memory: cache is tiny, inside the processor, and checked first.

The prefix rule is a guaranteed mark and is easy to get backwards: time and speed use powers of 10 (1 K = 1,000), storage uses powers of 2 (1 KB = 1,024 bytes = 2\u00b9\u2070). Memorise 2\u00b9\u2070 = 1,024, 2\u00b2\u2070 \u2248 1 million, 2\u00b3\u2070 \u2248 1 billion and you can convert any of them.

And a byte is always 8 bits, so a question giving you bits and asking for bytes (or the reverse) is a division or multiplication by 8 \u2014 check which way round before answering.

The pieces, and what each one is for

ComponentWhat it is
Motherboardthe main circuit board that houses the CPU, memory and core components and connects them
Registera very small, very fast storage location inside the CPU, holding the value being worked on right now
Cachesmall fast memory between CPU and RAM, holding recently used data
RAMmain memory \u2014 large, fast, and volatile
ROMread-only memory \u2014 non-volatile, written at manufacture, holds firmware and start-up instructions
SSD / hard disksecondary storage \u2014 slower, much larger, non-volatile
Busthe shared set of wires carrying data, addresses and control signals between components

The speed order, fastest and smallest first: register \u2192 cache \u2192 RAM \u2192 SSD/disk. Every step down is bigger and slower.

Machines have several buses \u2014 a data bus carrying the values, an address bus carrying the location, and a control bus carrying the timing and read/write signals. A wider bus moves more bits per transfer, which is a direct performance benefit.

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION
Volatility. RAM is volatile \u2014 its contents are lost when power is removed. An SSD is non-volatile \u2014 it keeps its contents with the power off. That, not speed or size, is the defining difference between the two.
\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION
Addressability is the number of bits stored in each addressable location in memory. If a machine is byte-addressable, every address names 8 bits.

Clock speed or more cores?

Given a workload of many independent tasks running at once, more cores helps more than a higher clock speed on a single core: the tasks genuinely run in parallel, one per core. A higher clock speed only helps a single task go faster, which is what matters for work that cannot be split.

Compiler and interpreter

CompilerInterpreter
When it translatesthe whole program, before it runsline by line, as it runs
Producesan executable fileno separate file \u2014 it executes directly
Speedfaster to run, slower to startslower to run, immediate to start
Errorsreported all together before runningfound only when that line is reached

Input and Output Devices \u2014 including touch screens

The parts above are what the computer thinks with. This is how it communicates. An input device carries data in to the computer (keyboard, mouse, scanner, microphone, camera, barcode reader). An output device carries results out to you (monitor, printer, speakers, projector). A few devices do both \u2014 and the exam's favourite example is the touch screen, which displays the picture (output) and accepts your tap (input) in the same surface. Storage devices such as an SSD or a USB drive also count as both, since data flows in and out of them.

The four touch-screen technologies

They differ in what physically detects the touch, and every other difference \u2014 gloves, clarity, durability \u2014 follows from that one fact. Learn the mechanism and you can derive the rest instead of memorising a table.

TypeHow it detects a touchWorks with a gloved hand?
ResistiveTwo flexible conductive layers with a tiny gap. Pressing pushes them together so they make contact at that point.Yes \u2014 it only needs pressure, so a glove, fingernail or any stylus works.
CapacitiveThe glass carries a small electrical charge. A conductive object (bare skin) changes the charge at that spot and the controller locates the change.No \u2014 an ordinary glove is not conductive, so no change is registered. Only special conductive \"touch-screen\" gloves work.
Surface acoustic wave (SAW)Transducers send high-frequency sound waves across the glass. A touch absorbs part of the wave, and the interruption gives the position.Yes \u2014 a gloved finger absorbs the wave just as skin does.
InfraredLEDs and sensors in the bezel cast an invisible grid of light beams just above the glass. A touch breaks beams, and which ones break gives the x and y position.Yes \u2014 anything opaque blocks a beam, glove included.

Why capacitive is the odd one out

This is the single most tested point. Resistive needs pressure, SAW needs something that absorbs sound, infrared needs something that blocks light \u2014 a gloved hand does all three. Capacitive is the only one that needs the touching object to conduct electricity, which skin does and a glove or a plastic stylus does not. So whenever a question asks which screen fails with gloves, the answer is capacitive.

The trade-off is worth it for phones: capacitive gives a bright, clear image and reliable multi-touch (pinch and zoom), which is why every modern smartphone uses it.

Clarity and durability, in one line each

  • Resistive \u2014 cheapest and resists dust and moisture well, but the extra layers dim the image and it is usually single-touch.
  • Capacitive \u2014 excellent clarity and multi-touch; needs bare skin.
  • SAW \u2014 very clear, since it is plain glass with nothing layered on top; but dirt or water on the surface absorbs the waves and causes misreads.
  • Infrared \u2014 nothing at all over the glass, so the clarity is the best and it scales to very large screens and kiosks; dirt on the bezel can block beams and cause false touches.

\ud83d\udca1 How to keep them straight

Match the technology to the word in the question: press \u2192 resistive \u00b7 charge / conductive / skin \u2192 capacitive \u00b7 sound wave \u2192 SAW \u00b7 light beam / grid \u2192 infrared. And remember one exception: only capacitive fails with gloves.

\ud83c\udfaf LEARNING OBJECTIVES

after this section you will be able to\u2026

\u2022 State the stored-program concept and why it was revolutionary.

\u2022 Name the five components of the von Neumann architecture and each one's job.

\u2022 Explain memory addressability and that a bit pattern needs interpretation.

\u2022 Describe the ALU, registers, the control unit (IR, PC), the CPU, and the bus.

\u2022 Contrast RAM vs. ROM and describe secondary storage (tape, disk) and disk timing.

Plain-English First

The single biggest idea in computing (1944\u201345): instructions and data can live in the same memory, treated the same way. Before that, \"programming\" often meant physically rewiring the machine. Once programs became just data you could store and load, the modern computer was born. That design \u2014 the von Neumann architecture \u2014 still describes essentially every computer today. Think of it as a kitchen: a pantry (memory) holds both recipes and ingredients, a chef's station (ALU) does the work, a door in and a door out (input/output), and a head chef (control unit) directing everything.

Going Deeper \u2014 The Five Components

The stored-program concept (von Neumann architecture, credited to von Neumann; ideas also from Eckert, Mauchly, and Atanasoff) separates the units that process information from those that store it, giving five components:

Memory unit \u2014 holds both data and instructions.

Arithmetic/logic unit (ALU) \u2014 does arithmetic (+, \u2212, \u00d7, \u00f7) and logic (AND, OR, NOT).

Input unit \u2014 moves data from the outside world in (keyboard, mouse, scanner).

Output unit \u2014 moves results out (monitor, printer).

Control unit \u2014 the \"stage manager\" coordinating everything (runs the fetch\u2013execute cycle).

The ALU and control unit together are the CPU.

\ud83d\udccc MUST-KNOW

memory, registers, and interpretation

Memory is a collection of cells, each with a unique address (numbered from 0). Addressability = bits per addressable cell; most machines are byte-addressable (8 bits). A stored bit pattern (e.g., 10101010) has no inherent meaning \u2014 it could be an instruction, an integer, part of an image \u2014 you must apply an interpretation. Registers are tiny, ultra-fast CPU storage (one word each) used to hold intermediate results; the control unit has two special ones: the instruction register (IR) (current instruction) and the program counter (PC) (address of the next instruction).

The components connect via a bus (a set of wires) carrying three kinds of information: address, data, and control. Bus width = bits transferable at once (wider = more at once). Speed helpers: cache (fast copy of frequent data, checked before main memory) and pipelining (overlapping instruction steps). All these components sit on the motherboard.

Going Deeper \u2014 RAM vs. ROM and Secondary Storage

RAM (random-access memory) is directly accessible and changeable, but volatile (lost at power-off). ROM (read-only memory) is nonvolatile and cannot be changed (its pattern is burned in) \u2014 used to store the instructions the computer needs to start. Main memory usually has some ROM plus general RAM.

Secondary (auxiliary/mass) storage keeps programs/data when not in use or when powered off; each device is both input and output. Magnetic tape is sequential (must pass earlier data to reach the middle) \u2014 good for backup. Magnetic disks use tracks (concentric circles) divided into sectors (each holding a block). Four disk-efficiency measures: seek time (head to the track), latency (sector spins to the head; avg = \u00bd rotation \u2014 a.k.a. rotation delay), access time (seek + latency), and transfer rate (data speed disk\u2192memory).

Key Terms

TermDefinitionWhy it matters
Stored-program conceptData & instructions share memory, treated alike.Foundation of all modern computers.
von Neumann architectureFive-component design separating processing from storage.The universal computer blueprint.
ALUDoes arithmetic and logic.The computation engine.
Control unitCoordinates components; runs fetch\u2013execute.The \"stage manager.\"
CPUALU + control unit.Executes instructions.
RegisterTiny, fast CPU storage (one word).Holds intermediate results fast.
Instruction register (IR)Holds the current instruction.What's being executed now.
Program counter (PC)Address of the next instruction.Drives the cycle forward.
AddressabilityBits per addressable memory cell.Usually 8 (byte-addressable).
BusWires carrying address/data/control.Connects CPU, memory, I/O.
RAMVolatile, changeable main memory.Working memory.
ROMNonvolatile, unchangeable memory (burned).Stores startup instructions.
Seek time / latencyHead-to-track time / sector-rotation time.Disk performance measures.

Diagram \u2014 The von Neumann architecture

Comparison / Reference Tables

RAMROM
Changeable?YesNo (burned)
Volatile?Yes (lost at power-off)No (permanent)
Typical useActive programs/dataStartup instructions

The five components at a glance

ALUArithmetic & logic operations

\ud83d\udca1 Tips, Tricks & Mnemonics

Five components = \"MAIOC\": Memory, ALU, Input, Output, Control.

CPU = ALU + Control unit.

IR = \"what now\", PC = \"what next\". Instruction Register holds the current instruction; Program Counter points to the next.

Bus carries A-D-C: Address, Data, Control.

RAM = changeable + volatile; ROM = fixed + permanent (burned).

Access time = Seek + Latency. Average latency = half a rotation.

A bit pattern means nothing without an interpretation.

\u26a0\ufe0f COMMON EXAM MISTAKES

Swapping IR and PC. IR = current instruction; PC = address of the next.

Calling ROM volatile or changeable \u2014 it's neither.

Forgetting the control unit is part of the CPU (CPU = ALU + control unit).

Thinking a bit pattern has a fixed meaning. Its meaning depends on interpretation.

Miscomputing access time \u2014 it's seek time plus latency, not either alone.

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 \u2014 Map jobs to components

Problem: Which von Neumann component handles each: (a) adding two numbers, (b) holding a program while it runs, (c) coordinating the fetch\u2013execute cycle, (d) a keyboard press, (e) printing a result?

(a) Add \u2192 ALU.

(b) Hold program \u2192 Memory unit.

(c) Coordinate cycle \u2192 Control unit.

(d) Keyboard \u2192 Input unit.

(e) Print \u2192 Output unit. \u2714

Worked Example 2 \u2014 Interpret a bit pattern (wrong way \u2192 right way)

Question: Memory address 11111110 holds 10101010. What does it mean?

Wrong way: declare it \"equals 170\" as if that's the only truth.

Why it's incomplete: the same bits could be an instruction, a signed value, part of an image, etc.

Right way: you must know the intended interpretation first; without it, 10101010 is just a bit pattern. (As an unsigned integer it is 170, but that's only one interpretation.) \u2714

\ud83d\udcca FIGURE \u2014 memory as numbered cells, and the three buses that reach it
\ud83c\udfaf EXAM TIP

Name-the-component questions are free marks if you keep the five straight: memory stores data and instructions, the ALU does arithmetic and logic, input brings data in, output sends results out, and the control unit coordinates. Then the fact they ask straight after: CPU = ALU + control unit, and memory is not part of the CPU.

The pair most often swapped is PC and IR. The Instruction Register holds the instruction being executed now; the Program Counter holds the address of what comes next. \u201cIR = now, PC = next\u201d is worth writing on your scratch paper.

The stored-program concept itself gets a conceptual question: instructions and data live in the same memory, in the same binary form, which is what makes a general-purpose computer possible. That is also why \u201cwhat does 10101010 mean?\u201d has no answer without knowing the intended interpretation.

RAM versus ROM: RAM is changeable and volatile; ROM is fixed and permanent. If a choice calls ROM volatile, or says it can be rewritten in normal use, it is wrong.

The four parts of a von Neumann machine

PartJob
Memoryholds both instructions and data
Arithmetic/Logic Unit (ALU)performs the calculations and comparisons
Control unitfetches and decodes instructions, and directs the rest
Input/Outputmoves data in and out

The fourth, and the one usually left blank in the question, is the control unit. The ALU and control unit together make up the CPU.

Storing instructions as data in the same memory is the stored-program concept, and its benefit is that a computer can run different programs without being physically rewired \u2014 you load new instructions the same way you load new data.

"}, "D684/g4/x5_2b": {"body": "
\ud83c\udfaf LEARNING OBJECTIVES

after this section you will be able to\u2026

\u2022 List the four steps of the fetch\u2013execute (fetch\u2013decode\u2013execute) cycle in order.

\u2022 Explain the roles of the PC and IR during the cycle.

\u2022 Describe how the PC is incremented and when it might change.

\u2022 Explain why a computer can only run instructions in its own machine language.

\u2022 Connect cache and pipelining to speeding up the cycle.

Plain-English First

Everything a computer does boils down to one endlessly repeating loop: get the next instruction, figure out what it means, grab any data it needs, do it \u2014 then repeat. As computer scientist Alan Perlis quipped, \"the only universal in the computing field is the fetch\u2013execute cycle.\" Master these four steps and you understand, at heart, how every program runs.

Going Deeper \u2014 The Four Steps

Because instructions and data both live in addressable memory (instructions stored contiguously), the cycle begins by loading the address of the first instruction into the program counter (PC). Then it repeats four steps:

\ud83d\udccc MUST-KNOW

the four steps

1. Fetch the next instruction: the control unit reads the address in the PC, copies that memory's contents into the instruction register (IR), and increments the PC to point to the following instruction.

2. Decode the instruction: the control unit determines which operation it is, turning it into control signals (this is why a CPU only runs its own machine language \u2014 the operations are built into the circuits).

3. Get data if needed: if the instruction references memory, the control unit fetches that data.

4. Execute: the control unit signals the ALU (or I/O) to carry out the operation; results go to registers or memory. Then the cycle repeats.

Normally the PC just increments by the instruction's size (next contiguous instruction), but a control instruction can change the PC (e.g., a branch/jump based on a result), which is how loops and decisions work. Cache and pipelining both speed the cycle up \u2014 cache by avoiding slow memory trips, pipelining by overlapping the steps of successive instructions.

Key Terms

TermDefinitionWhy it matters
Fetch\u2013execute cycleThe four-step loop every instruction follows.How all programs actually run.
FetchCopy the next instruction into the IR.Step 1; also increments the PC.
DecodeDetermine the operation (control signals).Step 2; ties CPU to machine language.
ExecuteCarry out the operation (often via ALU).Step 4; produces the result.
Program counter (PC)Address of the next instruction.Incremented each fetch; can be changed.
Instruction register (IR)The instruction being executed.Holds what's decoded/executed.
Machine languageThe only instructions a CPU can run.Operations are built into circuits.
PipeliningOverlapping instruction steps.Speeds up throughput.

Diagram \u2014 The fetch\u2013execute cycle

Comparison / Reference Tables

The four steps and who does what

StepActionKey part
1. FetchCopy next instruction to IR; increment PCControl unit, PC, IR
2. DecodeIdentify the operationControl unit
3. Get dataFetch needed operandsControl unit, memory/bus
4. ExecutePerform op; store resultALU / registers / memory

\ud83d\udca1 Tips, Tricks & Mnemonics

\"Fetch, Decode, Get, Execute\" \u2014 or simply fetch\u2013decode\u2013execute (the \"get data\" step folds into it).

PC points to next; IR holds current. Fetch copies PC's target into the IR, then bumps the PC.

Loops/branches = changing the PC. A control instruction rewrites the PC instead of just +1.

CPU only speaks machine language \u2014 the operations are literally wired in.

\"The only universal is the fetch\u2013execute cycle.\"

\u26a0\ufe0f COMMON EXAM MISTAKES

Putting the steps out of order. It's fetch \u2192 decode \u2192 (get data) \u2192 execute.

Saying the IR is incremented. The PC is incremented; the IR holds the current instruction.

Forgetting the PC can be changed by a control instruction (that's how branching works).

Thinking a CPU can directly run high-level code. It runs only its own machine language.

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 \u2014 Trace one pass of the cycle

Scenario: PC = 100, and the instruction at 100 says \"add memory[200] to a register.\" Each instruction is 4 bytes.

Fetch: control unit reads address 100, copies that instruction into the IR, and increments PC \u2192 104.

Decode: control unit recognizes it as an \"add from memory\" operation.

Get data: fetch the value at memory[200].

Execute: ALU adds that value to the register; result stays in the register.

Cycle repeats using PC = 104 for the next instruction. \u2714

Worked Example 2 \u2014 Why a branch changes the PC (wrong way \u2192 right way)

Question: After a comparison, a program must jump to instruction at address 300 instead of the next one.

Wrong assumption: the PC always just adds the instruction size, so it can't jump.

Why it's wrong: a control instruction can write a new value into the PC.

Right way: the execute step sets PC = 300, so the next fetch pulls the instruction at 300 \u2014 that's exactly how branches and loops work. \u2714

\ud83d\udcca FIGURE \u2014 fetch, decode, get data, execute \u2014 one instruction, step by step
\ud83c\udfaf EXAM TIP

The order is the question: fetch \u2192 decode \u2192 (get data) \u2192 execute. Any answer that decodes before fetching, or executes before decoding, is wrong. If only three steps are offered, \u201cget data\u201d has been folded into execute \u2014 fetch\u2013decode\u2013execute is the same cycle.

Two register facts settle most of the rest: the PC is incremented during the fetch (never the IR), and the IR holds the current instruction. A choice saying \u201cthe IR is incremented\u201d is a distractor built from exactly this confusion.

When a question asks how a loop or an if works at hardware level, the answer is that a control instruction writes a different address into the PC instead of letting it step to the next contiguous instruction. Branching is just PC assignment.

And the conceptual one: a CPU can only run instructions in its own machine language \u2014 the operations are physically wired in, which is why high-level source has to be translated first.

"}, "D684/g4/x5_3": {"body": "
\ud83c\udfaf LEARNING OBJECTIVES

after this section you will be able to\u2026

\u2022 Define an embedded system and give everyday examples.

\u2022 Explain why embedded programs are stored in ROM and often written in assembly language.

\u2022 Describe how embedded programs are developed (write on a PC, cross-compile).

\u2022 Define the Internet of Things (IoT) and its growth.

\u2022 Recognize the range of embedded processors (8-bit \u2192 64-bit RISC/DSP).

Plain-English First

Most computers aren't laptops \u2014 they're hidden inside other things. The chip running your microwave, your car's brakes, your smartwatch, a traffic light: those are embedded systems \u2014 small computers built to do one narrow job as part of a bigger device, usually with little or no user interaction. When millions of these gadgets also talk to each other over the internet, we call that the Internet of Things.

Going Deeper \u2014 The Technical Detail

An embedded system is a computer designed to perform a narrow range of functions as part of a larger system. Typically it lives on a single microprocessor chip with its programs stored in ROM. They're everywhere: watches, microwaves, cars, networking equipment, industrial controls. Some include an operating system; many are so specialized the whole logic is a single program. The term is broad \u2014 it covers essentially every computer except desktop PCs \u2014 and implies minimal user intervention.

\ud83d\udccc MUST-KNOW

development & language

You can't easily develop/test on the embedded chip itself, so programs are written on a PC and cross-compiled \u2014 the executable is generated for the target processor, then burned into its ROM. Because early embedded systems were tight on code size and speed, assembly language was used almost exclusively; even with C available, many stuck with assembly. C programs are about 25% larger and slower than assembly but easier to write; limited ROM size can still force assembly today.

Embedded processors range from 8-bit controllers to 32-bit DSPs (digital signal processors) to 64-bit RISC (reduced instruction set computer) chips, increasingly networked as distributed microprocessors. The Internet of Things (IoT) is the collection of internet-connected devices with embedded electronics/software \u2014 phones, vehicles, appliances, cameras, medical implants, animal transponders. Growth: 8.4 billion devices (2017), 13+ billion (2023), predicted 25+ billion by 2030.

Key Terms

TermDefinitionWhy it matters
Embedded systemComputer for a narrow function in a larger system.The most common kind of computer.
ROM (in embedded)Where the embedded program is stored/burned.Nonvolatile; runs on power-up.
Cross-compileCompile on a PC for a different target chip.How embedded code is built.
Assembly languageLow-level language close to machine code.Small/fast; common in embedded.
DSPDigital signal processor (often 32-bit).Specialized embedded processing.
RISCReduced instruction set computer.Efficient chips (up to 64-bit).
Internet of Things (IoT)Networked devices with embedded tech sharing data.Rapidly growing device ecosystem.

Diagram \u2014 Embedded systems & the IoT

Comparison / Reference Tables

Embedded system vs. desktop PC

Embedded systemDesktop PC
PurposeNarrow, dedicated functionGeneral-purpose
Program storageROM (burned)Disk/SSD, loaded to RAM
User interactionMinimal or noneExtensive
Typical languageOften assembly (size/speed)High-level languages

Assembly vs. C for embedded

AssemblyC
Code size/speedSmallest/fastest~25% larger & slower
Ease of writingHarderEasier
When forcedVery limited ROMMore ROM available

\ud83d\udca1 Tips, Tricks & Mnemonics

Embedded = \"everything but the desktop.\" A computer doing one dedicated job inside a bigger device.

Program lives in ROM \u2014 nonvolatile, ready the instant power is on.

Write on a PC, cross-compile to the chip. You don't code on the toaster.

Assembly = small & fast; C = easier but ~25% bigger/slower.

IoT = embedded + network. Connect the gadgets and you get the Internet of Things.

\u26a0\ufe0f COMMON EXAM MISTAKES

Thinking embedded systems are general-purpose. They do a narrow job.

Assuming every embedded system has a full OS. Many are a single program.

Believing you develop embedded code on the device itself \u2014 you cross-compile from a PC.

Saying C is smaller/faster than assembly \u2014 it's the reverse (~25% larger/slower, but easier).

Confusing IoT with a single device; it's the network of connected embedded devices.

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 \u2014 Is it an embedded system?

Problem: Classify each: (a) a smart thermostat chip, (b) a general gaming desktop, (c) a car's anti-lock brake controller, (d) a fitness tracker.

(a) Thermostat chip \u2192 narrow function in a device \u2192 embedded.

(b) Gaming desktop \u2192 general-purpose PC \u2192 not embedded.

(c) ABS controller \u2192 dedicated control task \u2192 embedded.

(d) Fitness tracker \u2192 dedicated, networked \u2192 embedded (and part of the IoT). \u2714

Worked Example 2 \u2014 Language choice (wrong way \u2192 right way)

Scenario: A tiny sensor has very limited ROM; a developer wants to use C for convenience.

Wrong assumption: \"C is smaller, so it'll fit fine.\"

Why it's wrong: C programs are about 25% larger and slower than assembly.

Right way: with severely limited ROM, choose assembly to keep the code small enough to fit; use C only when there's ROM headroom. \u2714

\ud83d\udcca FIGURE \u2014 cross-compiling onto a device, and what turns it into IoT
\ud83c\udfaf EXAM TIP

Classification questions here are one-word decisions: does the machine do a narrow, dedicated job inside a larger device (thermostat chip, ABS controller, fitness band, microwave) \u2192 embedded; is it general-purpose (a gaming desktop, a laptop) \u2192 not embedded, no matter how small it is.

Three facts are asked almost verbatim. The program is stored in ROM \u2014 nonvolatile, so it is there the moment power arrives. Development happens on a PC and is cross-compiled onto the chip, because you cannot practically develop on the device itself. And assembly is smaller and faster than C, with C running roughly 25 % larger and slower but far easier to write \u2014 so a severely ROM-limited device forces assembly.

Watch the direction of that last fact; the reversed version (\u201cC is smaller and faster\u201d) is the standard distractor. And IoT is not one device \u2014 it is the network of connected embedded devices.

Edge computing, sensors and constraints

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION
Edge computing processes data near where it is produced instead of sending it to a distant data center. A self-driving car analyzing its sensor feed on board is the standard example: the benefit is much lower latency (plus it keeps working without a network, and sends less data).
ComponentDirectionJob
Sensorinputmeasures the physical world \u2014 a thermistor reading temperature
Actuatoroutputacts on the physical world \u2014 the relay switching the boiler on

Battery-powered IoT sensors send small readings infrequently rather than streaming continuously because their binding constraints are power and bandwidth: the radio is the hungriest component, so every extra transmission costs battery life directly.

"}, "D684/g2/k_sub": {"body": "
\u2605 NOT IN YOUR COURSE GUIDE

This topic is not in the D684 guide you were given, but the OA asks about it. It sits here because this is the unit it belongs to \u2014 study it like the rest.

A subprogram \u2014 also called a function, method, procedure or subroutine depending on the language \u2014 is a named block of code you can call by name, hand values to, and get a value back from. It is the first tool for making a program out of parts instead of one long script, and the reasons for using one are worth stating precisely because the OA asks for them.

Reuse removes duplication, so a fix happens in one place rather than five. Abstraction lets you call calculateTax(salary) without holding the tax brackets in your head. Decomposition breaks a large problem into pieces small enough to test separately. Together these are why a well-organised program has a short main routine that calls small named things.

Parameters and arguments

The vocabulary here is tested directly, so keep the two words apart. A parameter is the variable named in the subprogram's definition. An argument is the actual value supplied at the call. The definition is written once; the call can happen many times, each with different arguments.

\u25b8 WORKED EXAMPLE \u2014 definition versus call
FUNCTION square(n)          <- n is the PARAMETER\n    RETURN n * n\nEND FUNCTION\n\nresult = square(6)          <- 6 is the ARGUMENT, result gets 36

Parameters are simply local variables initialised from the caller's arguments \u2014 which is why reassigning a parameter inside a subprogram never affects the caller's variable. The return value is the one channel back out. A subprogram that returns nothing is often called a procedure or declared void; one that returns a value can have its result stored, compared or passed straight into another call.

That distinction matters more than it first appears. A subprogram that prints its answer can only ever print it. One that returns its answer can be printed, stored, tested or reused \u2014 which is what makes it testable at all.

The call, mechanically

When a subprogram is called, execution jumps to it, a stack frame is created holding that call's parameters and local variables, the body runs, and on return the frame is destroyed and execution resumes at the line after the call. This is the same stack from 1.2, and it explains why locals vanish on return and why a value has to be returned to survive.

What makes a good subprogram

Beyond the definitions, the OA asks about the qualities of a well-designed subprogram, and they follow from one idea: it should do one clearly-named thing. That is cohesion. A subprogram called calculateTax that also prints a receipt and updates a database has low cohesion \u2014 nobody can reuse it, and its name lies about what it does.

The matching idea is coupling: how much a subprogram depends on the rest of the program. A subprogram that takes what it needs as parameters and returns its result is loosely coupled and can be moved, tested or replaced on its own. One that reads and writes global variables is tightly coupled \u2014 it only works in the exact context it was written for. High cohesion and low coupling is the phrase the exam uses, and it is simply the two habits stated together.

This is also why the number of parameters matters. A subprogram needing eight of them is usually doing more than one thing, and the fix is to split it rather than to add a ninth.

Recursion

A subprogram may call itself. That is recursion, and it is the natural shape for any problem that contains a smaller copy of itself \u2014 a factorial, a directory tree, a binary search.

Every correct recursive function has exactly two parts. The base case is the smallest input, answered directly with no further call \u2014 it is what stops the recursion. The recursive case calls the function again on a smaller input and builds the answer from the result.

FUNCTION factorial(n)\n    IF n <= 1 THEN            // BASE CASE \u2014 stops the recursion\n        RETURN 1\n    ELSE                        // RECURSIVE CASE \u2014 smaller input\n        RETURN n * factorial(n - 1)\n\nfactorial(4) = 4 * factorial(3)\n             = 4 * 3 * factorial(2)\n             = 4 * 3 * 2 * factorial(1)   <- base case reached\n             = 24

Leave the base case out \u2014 or write one the input never reaches \u2014 and the function calls itself for ever. Each call takes a frame of memory on the call stack, the stack fills, and the program crashes with a stack overflow. That is the single most tested consequence in this topic: no base case means infinite recursion and a stack-overflow crash, not a wrong answer.

RecursionIteration (a loop)
Repeats bycalling itselflooping
Stops onthe base casethe loop condition
Memorya stack frame per callconstant
Prefer whenthe data is nested \u2014 trees, divide and conquerthe depth is large or performance matters

Anything recursive can be written iteratively and the reverse is also true, so the question is never \"which works\" but which is clearer and which is safe. Choose iteration when the depth could be large, because a loop cannot overflow the stack.

How a parameter is passed

Two conventions decide whether a subprogram can change the caller's variable.

PassingThe subprogram receivesChanging it inside
By valuea copy of the valuedoes not affect the caller's variable
By referencethe address of the caller's variabledoes change the caller's variable

A reference parameter therefore passes the location, not the contents \u2014 which is how a subprogram returns more than one result, and also how it causes a side effect the caller did not expect.

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION

Subprogram: a named, reusable block of code \u2014 also function, method, procedure or subroutine

Parameter: a variable in the definition that receives a value

Argument: the actual value passed at the call site

Return value: the result handed back to the caller

Void / procedure: a subprogram that returns no value

Stack frame: the memory holding one call's parameters and locals; destroyed on return

Modularity: building a program from independent, replaceable parts

Decomposition: splitting a problem into smaller solvable pieces

\u2605 ON THE OA

Parameter is in the definition; argument is at the call. The benefits list is reuse, abstraction, modularity and easier testing \u2014 and \"reduces duplicated code\" is the phrasing that appears most often.

\u26a0 COMMON MISTAKE

Passing arguments in the wrong order is the error no compiler catches. divide(b, a) compiles perfectly when both parameters are the same type, and returns the wrong answer forever.

\ud83d\udcca FIGURE \u2014 the call stack for factorial(4) \u2014 every call keeps its own n
\u25b8 WORKED EXAMPLE \u2014 parameters passed by value versus by reference

Two subprograms, identical bodies, one difference in how the parameter arrives. Trace what the caller sees afterwards.

PROCEDURE bumpByValue(x)      // x arrives as a COPY\n    Set x to x + 10\nEND PROCEDURE\n\nPROCEDURE bumpByRef(ref x)    // x arrives as an ADDRESS\n    Set x to x + 10\nEND PROCEDURE\n\nSet total to 40\ncall bumpByValue(total)\nPrint total          \u2192  ?\ncall bumpByRef(total)\nPrint total          \u2192  ?

Step 1 \u2014 the by-value call. total holds 40. The call hands the subprogram a copy of the value 40, which lands in the local variable x. Inside, x becomes 50.

Step 2 \u2014 what happens on return. The frame is destroyed and x disappears with it. total was never touched, so the first print is 40.

Step 3 \u2014 the by-reference call. This time the subprogram receives the location of total, not its contents. Set x to x + 10 writes 50 into that location \u2014 which is total itself.

Step 4 \u2014 after return. The frame is gone but the write already happened in the caller\u2019s memory. The second print is 50.

Answer: 40, then 50. The rule to carry away: by value the subprogram can read the caller\u2019s data but not change it; by reference it can do both. That is exactly how a subprogram \u201creturns\u201d more than one result without a return value.

\u25b8 WORKED EXAMPLE \u2014 rewriting a loop as recursion, and reading the base case

Problem: this loop sums the numbers 1\u2026n. Write the recursive version and check it on n = 4.

FUNCTION sumTo(n)                FUNCTION sumTo(n)\n    Set total to 0                   IF n = 1 THEN\n    Set i to 1                           RETURN 1          // BASE CASE\n    WHILE i <= n                     ELSE\n        Set total to total + i           RETURN n + sumTo(n - 1)\n        Set i to i + 1               END IF\n    END WHILE                    END FUNCTION\n    RETURN total\nEND FUNCTION

Step 1 \u2014 find the smaller version of the same problem. The sum of 1\u2026n is n plus the sum of 1\u2026(n\u22121). That sentence is the recursive case, written directly.

Step 2 \u2014 find the smallest input you can answer outright. The sum of 1\u20261 is 1, and no call is needed. That is the base case, and it must be reachable: each call passes n \u2212 1, so any n \u2265 1 walks down to 1.

Step 3 \u2014 expand n = 4 on paper. sumTo(4) = 4 + sumTo(3) = 4 + 3 + sumTo(2) = 4 + 3 + 2 + sumTo(1) = 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10. Four frames existed at the deepest point; they then popped in reverse order carrying 1, 3, 6, 10.

Step 4 \u2014 compare the two. Identical answers. The loop uses one variable and constant memory; the recursion uses n stack frames. That is the real trade-off the exam asks about \u2014 not correctness, but memory and readability.

Break it deliberately: change the base case to IF n = 0 and call sumTo(4) \u2014 it still works, returning 0 at the bottom. Change it to IF n = 10 and call sumTo(4) and nothing stops it: n runs 4, 3, 2, 1, 0, \u22121 \u2026 for ever. A base case that the input never reaches is the same bug as having no base case at all.

\ud83c\udfaf EXAM TIP

Three things are tested here and each has a giveaway.

Vocabulary. Parameter is in the definition; argument is at the call. Remember it by position: the definition declares parameters. Any answer that swaps them is wrong regardless of how the rest reads.

\u201cWhat does this recursive function return?\u201d Do not reason about it \u2014 expand it on paper the way step 3 above does, down to the base case, then fold the answers back up. Four lines of writing beats any amount of staring.

\u201cWhy did this crash / never stop?\u201d Look for the base case first. Missing base case, or one the argument never reaches, means infinite recursion and stack overflow. If the base case is fine, check that the recursive call actually moves toward it \u2014 factorial(n) calling factorial(n) instead of factorial(n \u2212 1) is the other version of the same bug.

Why break a program into subprograms

The primary benefit is reuse and manageability: logic written once can be called from many places, so it is not duplicated, and a fix has to be made in only one spot. Each piece can also be understood, tested and replaced on its own.

Speed is not the reason \u2014 a function call carries a small overhead. The gain is in correctness and maintenance, which is what the exam is looking for.

\u2605 NOT IN YOUR COURSE GUIDE

This topic is not in the D684 guide you were given, but the OA asks about it. It sits here because this is the unit it belongs to \u2014 study it like the rest.

A single variable holds one value. A data structure organises many values so a program can find, add and remove them efficiently. Which structure you pick is a decision about which operation you want to be fast, because none of them is fast at everything \u2014 and that trade-off is what the OA actually tests.

StructureOrganisationFast atSlow at
Arrayfixed number of same-type items in contiguous memoryreading item i directlyinserting, deleting, growing
Listordered, dynamic, grows and shrinksadding and removingjumping to position i
Recorda group of named fields of mixed typesholding one entity togethernot a collection at all
Stacklast in, first out (LIFO)push and pop at the topreaching anything but the top
Queuefirst in, first out (FIFO)enqueue at the back, dequeue at the frontreaching the middle
Treehierarchical \u2014 parent and child nodesordered search, hierarchyunordered bulk access
Hash tablekey mapped to a slot by a hash functionlookup by key, near-instantordered traversal

The array deserves the most attention because everything else is defined against it. Its items are the same type and physically adjacent in memory, which is what makes arr[i] instant \u2014 the machine computes the address arithmetically instead of searching. The price is that its size is fixed at creation, so inserting in the middle means shifting everything after it. A list makes the opposite trade: it grows freely and inserts cheaply, but has no direct index arithmetic.

A record is a different kind of thing from all of these \u2014 not a collection of similar items but a group of differently-typed fields describing one entity, like a single row in a table. A CustomerRecord with Name, Address and PhoneNumber is one record; an array of those records is the collection.

Stacks and queues by their discipline

Stacks and queues are defined not by how they store things but by which end you are allowed to touch. A stack is last-in-first-out: the last thing pushed is the first thing popped, like a stack of plates. It is the natural structure for anything nested \u2014 undo history, matching brackets, and the call stack that holds function frames. A queue is first-in-first-out: the first thing enqueued is the first dequeued, like a printer queue or a checkout line.

Searching \u2014 why the structure matters

The reason to care about all this is what it costs to find something. A linear search checks each item in turn and works on anything, sorted or not, taking up to n comparisons. A binary search repeatedly halves a sorted range and takes about log\u2082n. On a million items that is a million comparisons against roughly twenty \u2014 and it is why a hash table, which computes the location directly from the key, is faster still.

Choosing a structure from a description

Exam questions in this area almost never name the structure. They describe a requirement and expect you to pick. The translation is mechanical once you know it: \"must be processed in the order received\" is a queue; \"the most recent must be handled first\" or \"undo\" is a stack; \"look it up instantly by a unique key\" is a hash table; \"fixed number of same-type items, accessed by position\" is an array; \"grows and shrinks as items are added\" is a list; \"organised into a hierarchy\" is a tree.

The reason a structure can be fast at one thing and slow at another comes down to whether the machine can compute where something is or has to look for it. An array element's address is the start address plus the index times the item size \u2014 one calculation, no searching, which is why it is instant. A linked list has no such formula, so reaching the tenth item means following nine links. A hash table gets back the arithmetic by computing the location from the key itself, which is why it is nearly as fast as an array while still accepting any key you like.

What makes a hash table fast, and where it breaks

A hash table computes the storage slot directly from the key with a hash function, which is why lookup does not depend on the number of items. A good hash function distributes keys uniformly across the available slots, so no slot becomes crowded.

When two keys hash to the same slot that is a collision, and every real hash table needs a plan for it. Chaining keeps a list of entries at each slot; open addressing probes for the next free slot instead. Collisions are why the O(1) lookup is an average rather than a guarantee \u2014 if every key collided, the table would degrade to a linear search.

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION

Data structure: an organised collection of values, chosen for which operations it makes fast

Array: a fixed-size collection of same-type items in contiguous memory, accessed by index

List: an ordered, dynamically sized collection that is easy to add to and remove from

Record: a group of named fields of mixed types describing one entity

Stack: a last-in-first-out collection \u2014 push, pop, peek

Queue: a first-in-first-out collection \u2014 enqueue, dequeue

Tree: a hierarchical structure of parent and child nodes

Hash table: a structure mapping a key to a storage slot with a hash function, for near-instant lookup

Index: the position of an element, counting from 0

\u2605 ON THE OA

Match the discipline to the name: LIFO is a stack, FIFO is a queue. An array is fixed-size and same-type with instant indexing; a list is flexible; a record groups fields of different types. Binary search requires sorted data \u2014 on unsorted data you must use linear search.

\ud83d\udca1 WHY IT MATTERS

This is the same trade-off you will meet again as Big-O later in this unit. \"Which structure should I use\" and \"how does this algorithm scale\" are the same question asked from two directions.

\ud83d\udcca FIGURE \u2014 stack and queue \u2014 the same items, different ends
\ud83d\udcca FIGURE \u2014 an array and a linked list holding the same five salaries
\ud83d\udcca FIGURE \u2014 a hash table, a hash function and a collision
\u25b8 WORKED EXAMPLE \u2014 a stack and a queue fed exactly the same input

Problem: three print jobs arrive \u2014 J1, J2, J3, in that order. Push them onto a stack, and separately enqueue them onto a queue. Then remove everything from each. In what order does each hand the jobs back, and which structure should a printer actually use?

Step 1 \u2014 the stack, filling. push J1 \u2192 [J1]. push J2 \u2192 [J1, J2], top is J2. push J3 \u2192 [J1, J2, J3], top is J3. Only the top is reachable.

Step 2 \u2014 the stack, emptying. pop returns the top: J3, then J2, then J1. Output order J3, J2, J1 \u2014 the reverse of arrival. That is LIFO.

Step 3 \u2014 the queue, filling. enqueue J1 \u2192 front J1. enqueue J2 \u2192 [J1, J2]. enqueue J3 \u2192 [J1, J2, J3]. Items join at the back; the front never moves except by dequeueing.

Step 4 \u2014 the queue, emptying. dequeue returns the front: J1, then J2, then J3 \u2014 arrival order preserved. That is FIFO.

Step 5 \u2014 choose. A printer must be fair to whoever submitted first, so it needs FIFO: a queue. A stack would print the newest job first and leave the person who queued at 9 a.m. waiting all day. Note also what a stack is right for \u2014 the call stack in the recursion section, and \u201cundo\u201d, both of which genuinely want the most recent thing first.

\u25b8 WORKED EXAMPLE \u2014 choosing a structure from a description, four times

Exam questions almost never name the structure; they describe a requirement. Work each one from the operation that must be fast.

(a) \u201cLook up a customer by their account number, instantly, out of two million records.\u201d The access is by key, not by position, and it must not slow down as the data grows. Computing a slot from the key does exactly that \u2192 hash table. (An array would need the account number to be the index; a list would need a walk.)

(b) \u201cHold one student\u2019s name, ID and GPA together.\u201d Three values of different types describing one entity, reached by name rather than by number \u2192 record. This is the one that is not a collection at all, which is why it is the answer whenever \u201cdifferent types\u201d appears.

(c) \u201cStore 500 exam scores and read the 200th directly.\u201d Same type, fixed count, access by position \u2192 array. The index arithmetic in the figure is precisely the property being asked for.

(d) \u201cItems are added and removed constantly and the count is unknown up front.\u201d Growth and cheap insertion matter; position does not \u2192 list. Choosing an array here is the classic wrong answer, because a fixed contiguous block cannot grow and every insertion shifts everything after it.

The method: read the sentence for which operation must be fast \u2014 by key \u2192 hash table, by position \u2192 array, constant change \u2192 list, newest first \u2192 stack, oldest first \u2192 queue, hierarchy \u2192 tree. Then check the second half of the sentence for the thing that structure is bad at, which is usually where the distractor lives.

\u26a0\ufe0f COMMON MISTAKE

The error is assuming a structure\u2019s strength applies to every operation. Every structure in the table is fast at one thing because it is slow at another, and the exam builds its distractors out of exactly that trade.

The three specific slips: saying a linked list can jump straight to element 7 (it cannot \u2014 there is no address to compute, so you walk); saying an array is a good choice when items are constantly inserted and removed (it is not \u2014 it is a fixed block, so every insertion shifts the rest); and saying a hash table can list keys in order (it cannot \u2014 the hash scatters them deliberately, so ordered traversal is the one thing it is bad at).

How to notice: after you pick a structure, say out loud what it is bad at and re-read the question for that word. If the question contains \u201cin order\u201d, \u201csorted\u201d, \u201cposition\u201d or \u201cgrows\u201d, and your structure is bad at that word, you picked the distractor.

\ud83c\udfaf EXAM TIP

Answer the discipline questions from the acronym and stop: LIFO is a stack, FIFO is a queue. If the scenario says \u201cmost recent first\u201d, \u201cundo\u201d, \u201cback button\u201d or \u201cnested\u201d, it is a stack; if it says \u201cfair\u201d, \u201cin the order received\u201d, \u201cprint jobs\u201d, \u201cwaiting line\u201d, it is a queue.

For the array questions, two facts carry nearly all the marks: indexing starts at 0 (so the last element of an array of size n is at n \u2212 1, and asking for index n is the off-by-one they are testing), and an array is fixed size and one type while a record is mixed types reached by field name.

Where a question asks about speed, the one-line answer is: array index and hash lookup do not depend on how much data there is; searching a list one item at a time does. That sentence answers most of the \u201cwhich is faster and why\u201d items without any calculation.

The vocabulary of data storage

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION
An Abstract Data Type (ADT) specifies what operations exist and how they behave \u2014 not how they are built. \"A stack offers push and pop, last in first out\" is an ADT. Whether it is implemented with an array or a linked list is a separate choice, hidden behind that interface.
TermMeansExample
Scalarholds a single valuean int, a char, a Boolean
Compositeholds several values as one unitan array, a record, an object
Containeran object whose job is to hold other objectsArrayList, HashMap, a set
Homogeneousevery element is of the same typean array of int \u2014 the rule for arrays
Heterogeneouselements may be of differing typesa record/struct with a name and an age

Why array access is O(1) but searching is O(n)

Big-O describes the complexity of an operation \u2014 how its cost grows as the data grows. Both of these touch the same array, so the difference is worth understanding rather than memorizing.

  • arr[7] is O(1) because the position is calculated: start address + 7 \u00d7 element size. One arithmetic step, whatever the array's size.
  • Searching an unsorted array for a value is O(n) because nothing tells you where it might be. You must check elements one by one, and the value could be the last one you look at.

Sort the array and search becomes O(log n) with binary search \u2014 the order is what buys the speed.
