\ud83c\udfaf LEARNING OBJECTIVES

after this section you will be able to\u2026

\u2022 Identify the ACM and IEEE and what each traditionally represents.

\u2022 State the purpose of a code of ethics and the four categories of the ACM Code.

\u2022 Recognize the core general ethical principles (avoid harm, be honest, be fair, respect privacy, honor confidentiality).

\u2022 Apply ethical principles to real-world scenarios (privacy, security, public interest, professionalism).

\u2022 Distinguish key IEEE commitments (safety paramount, reject bribery, honest claims, no discrimination).

Plain-English First

A code of ethics is a profession's shared promise about how to behave \u2014 like the doctor's \"do no harm,\" but for people who build software and hardware. Because computing touches money, privacy, safety, and infrastructure, the two big professional bodies wrote down principles their members agree to follow. You don't memorize all of them word-for-word; you learn the themes so you can recognize the right choice in a scenario question, which is exactly how the OA tests this.

Going Deeper \u2014 The Two Organizations & the ACM Code

There are two major computing organizations: the Association for Computing Machinery (ACM), traditionally the software side, and the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), traditionally the hardware side. A code of ethics is a professional code of conduct governing the behavior of computing professionals.

The ACM Code of Ethics has four categories:

General Ethical Principles (1.x): contribute to society and human well-being; avoid harm; be honest and trustworthy; be fair and don't discriminate; respect the work required to produce ideas/IP; respect privacy; honor confidentiality.

Professional Responsibilities (2.x): strive for high quality; maintain competence; know and respect existing rules; accept/provide review; give thorough evaluations including risks; work only in areas of competence; foster public awareness; access resources only when authorized; design systems that are robustly and usably secure.

Professional Leadership Principles (3.x): keep the public good central; support social responsibility; enhance quality of working life; apply the Code's policies; grow others professionally; use care when modifying/retiring systems; take special care of systems integrated into society's infrastructure.

Compliance (4.x): uphold and promote the Code; treat violations as inconsistent with ACM membership.

\ud83d\udccc MUST-KNOW

IEEE highlights

The IEEE Code commits members to hold paramount the safety, health, and welfare of the public; avoid/disclose conflicts of interest; be honest and realistic in claims; reject bribery; maintain and improve technical competence; offer/accept honest criticism and credit others; treat all people fairly with no discrimination; avoid injuring others' person, property, reputation, or employment; and help colleagues follow the code.

Key Terms

TermDefinitionWhy it matters
ACMAssociation for Computing Machinery (software side).Authors a major computing code of ethics.
IEEEInstitute of Electrical & Electronics Engineers (hardware side).Authors the other major code.
Code of ethicsProfessional conduct/ethical guidelines.Governs professional behavior.
PrivacyProtecting individuals' personal data.Core ethical duty in data handling.
ProfessionalismCompetence, responsibility, accountability.Standard for professional work.
Public interestPrioritizing public well-being and safety.Central to leadership principles.
SecurityProtecting systems/data from unauthorized access/harm.Systems must be robustly, usably secure.

Diagram \u2014 Structure of the ACM Code

Comparison / Reference Tables

ACM vs. IEEE

ACMIEEE
Traditional focusSoftwareHardware
Signature emphasis4 categories of principlesPublic safety paramount; reject bribery
Shared themesHonesty, avoid harm, fairness/no discrimination, competence, credit others, privacy

Principle \u2192 everyday application

PrincipleWhat it looks like on the job
Avoid harmDon't ship code you know can hurt users or data
Respect privacyCollect/store only necessary personal data, protect it
Honor confidentialityDon't leak information entrusted to you
Be honestDon't overstate what a system can do
CompetenceTake on work only where you're qualified
Public goodWeigh society's welfare in design decisions

\ud83d\udca1 Tips, Tricks & Mnemonics

ACM = softwAre-ish \"M\" for Machinery; IEEE = \"E\" for Electronics/hardware. ACM\u2192software, IEEE\u2192hardware.

General principles = \"HARP-CP\": Harm-avoid, honest, fair, Respect-IP, Privacy, Confidentiality, Contribute to society \u2014 the human-decency core.

IEEE's first commandment: public safety, health, welfare paramount. If a scenario risks the public, that principle wins.

Scenario tip: pick the answer that protects people, tells the truth, and stays within your competence/authorization.

Reject bribery & disclose conflicts \u2014 classic IEEE test triggers.

\u26a0\ufe0f COMMON EXAM MISTAKES

Swapping ACM and IEEE \u2014 ACM is software, IEEE is hardware (though the line blurs in practice).

Choosing a \"profitable but harmful\" option. Codes put public welfare and honesty above convenience.

Thinking accessing any system you can reach is fine. You must be authorized.

Ignoring \"credit others\" \u2014 using someone's work without attribution violates the codes.

Assuming ethics are optional guidelines with no membership consequences \u2014 violations conflict with ACM membership.

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 \u2014 Map a scenario to the right principle

Scenario: A developer discovers the app stores users' full credit-card numbers in plain text. What does the Code require, and which principles apply?

Identify the risk: exposed personal/financial data \u2192 potential harm and a privacy/security failure.

Applicable ACM principles: Avoid harm (1.2), Respect privacy (1.6), and design robustly and usably secure systems (2.9).

Required action: report the flaw and fix it (encrypt/limit data), not hide it \u2014 being honest and trustworthy (1.3).

Correct ethical choice: remediate and disclose responsibly. \u2714

Worked Example 2 \u2014 Competence & honesty (wrong way \u2192 right way)

Scenario: You're offered a contract to build medical-device firmware, an area you've never worked in, on a tight deadline.

Wrong way: accept quietly and figure it out, overstating your experience to win the job.

Why it's wrong: violates \"perform work only in areas of competence,\" \"be honest,\" and risks public safety (IEEE paramount clause).

Right way: disclose your limitations, decline or bring in qualified help, and be honest about timelines.

Outcome: protects users and your integrity \u2014 the codes value honesty and competence over the paycheck. \u2714

\ud83d\udcca FIGURE \u2014 the order to apply the principles in when a scenario gives you two bad options
\ud83c\udfaf EXAM TIP

Nearly every ethics item is a scenario with four plausible-sounding actions, and they are answered by ranking, not by recall. Apply the ladder in the figure and take the first rule that fires: harm to people beats honesty beats competence beats credit and privacy beats convenience and profit.

Eliminate first \u2014 it is faster than choosing. Strike any option that conceals a defect, that proceeds without authorisation, that takes on work outside your competence, or that puts cost or schedule above someone\u2019s safety. That usually leaves one answer standing before you have thought about it properly.

Know the two organisations apart, because a question will simply ask: ACM is the software body, and its Code has four categories \u2014 general principles, professional responsibilities, leadership principles, compliance. IEEE is the hardware/electronics body, and its signature commitments are hold paramount the safety, health and welfare of the public and reject bribery in all its forms.

Finally, keep certification and licensing straight \u2014 they appear as a one-mark freebie. Certification is voluntary and granted by a non-governmental body; licensing is mandatory and granted by government. Computing professionals are commonly certified and rarely licensed.

Intellectual property theft at national scale

IP theft is not only an individual act. Governments have publicly accused state-backed actors of large-scale commercial espionage \u2014 most prominently, US and European accusations against China over the theft of trade secrets and industrial designs, which both the ACM and IEEE codes treat as a professional and societal harm rather than a merely legal one.

The point the codes make is one of scale: the same principle that forbids copying a colleague's work forbids it when the actor is an organization or a state.

\ud83c\udfaf LEARNING OBJECTIVES

after this section you will be able to\u2026

\u2022 Define intellectual property and distinguish copyright, patent, trademark, fair use, and public domain.

\u2022 Compare common software licenses: GNU GPL (copyleft), Creative Commons, MIT, and public domain.

\u2022 Explain piracy, file sharing, P2P networks, and the malware risk of piracy.

\u2022 Identify major cybercrime types, who investigates them, and how they're punished.

\u2022 Define cyberbullying, why it can be worse than in-person bullying, and the correct responses.

Plain-English First

Ideas can be owned. Intellectual property (IP) is \"creations of the mind\" \u2014 songs, code, inventions, logos \u2014 and the law gives creators certain rights over them. Different protections cover different things: copyright for creative works, patents for inventions, trademarks for brand identifiers. When people copy or share protected work without permission, that's piracy. Two darker corners of the online world round out this section: cybercrime (crimes committed with computers) and cyberbullying (online harassment). The OA tests whether you can classify a scenario and pick the responsible action.

Going Deeper \u2014 Intellectual Property & Licensing

Intellectual property = creations of the mind (inventions, works, designs, symbols, names, images). The main protections:

Copyright \u2014 protects original creative works (literature, music, art) from use without permission.

Patent \u2014 gives an inventor exclusive control over an invention for a limited period.

Trademark \u2014 a symbol, word, or phrase representing a company or product.

Fair use \u2014 a legal doctrine allowing limited use of copyrighted material (e.g., commentary, education).

Public domain \u2014 works not (or no longer) copyrighted, free for anyone. \ud83d\udd0e Per the source, works published before 1923 are treated as public domain.

\ud83d\udccc MUST-KNOW

License types

GNU GPL \u2014 free software license; copyleft means any derivative must use the same license (ex: Linux kernel, Ubuntu, MySQL). Creative Commons (CC) \u2014 variations include CC0 (no restrictions), CC BY (credit the author), CC BY-SA (credit + share-alike license), CC BY-NC (credit + non-commercial). MIT license \u2014 reuse freely as long as the license and copyright notice are included (ex: Bitcoin Core, jQuery, Ruby on Rails). Public domain \u2014 no license needed.

Going Deeper \u2014 Piracy, Cybercrime & Cyberbullying

Piracy is the unauthorized copy, distribution, or sale of copyrighted work. File sharing and the Internet make it easy; a common method is a peer-to-peer (P2P) network, where peers share files directly with no central server (Napster, Kazaa, LimeWire \u2014 Napster was shut down in 2001 for copyright infringement). Piracy also spreads malware (malicious software) because pirated files are unregulated \u2014 piracy-site visitors are far more likely to be infected.

Cybercrime is any crime involving a computer and network \u2014 the computer can be the target, the tool, or both. Common types: identity theft, fraud, data breaches, trafficking, extortion (e.g., ransomware), malware, and harassment. Investigators use digital forensics (recovering data as evidence), decryption, and surveillance. Local police handle individual crimes (harassment, identity theft); the FBI and Secret Service handle larger cases (extortion, trafficking); Interpol handles international ones. Crimes are reported to the FBI's IC3. Punishment (fines, jail, loss of computer-use rights) depends on severity, monetary damage, and jurisdiction; offenders may be extradited to where the crime occurred.

\ud83d\udccc MUST-KNOW

Cyberbullying

Cyberbullying is the willful use of electronic technology to repeatedly threaten, abuse, or dominate others, often anonymously \u2014 a form of harassment. It can be worse than face-to-face bullying because the victim can't easily escape it, it reaches more people, and anonymity makes the bully hard to trace. Effects include lower academic performance, low self-esteem, depression, anxiety, and suicidal thoughts.

Correct responses to cyberbullying: tell someone (parent, teacher, friend), block the abuser, keep evidence, and never retaliate; notify the school principal for student-on-student cases. Contact law enforcement if there are threats of violence/death, physical stalking or attack, prolonged harassment based on protected traits (race, religion, sexuality, disability), or explicit images of a minor. Parents should not remove a child's technology (it increases isolation) \u2014 instead encourage behavior changes like spending less time online.

Key Terms

When to contact law enforcement about cyberbullying

Contact police if\u2026Handle at school/home if\u2026
Threats of violence or deathRumors or mean messages (no threats)

Prolonged harassment on protected traitsBlock abuser, keep evidence, don't retaliate

\ud83d\udca1 Tips, Tricks & Mnemonics

C-P-T: Copyright = Creative works; Patent = Products/inventions; Trademark = Trade/brand identity.

Copyleft = \"share-alike.\" GPL forces derivatives to keep the same free license.

Piracy = unauthorized copy/distribute/sell. If there's no permission, it's piracy.

Cybercrime roles: computer can be the target, the tool, or both.

Who investigates? Local (personal crimes) \u2192 FBI/Secret Service (big/national) \u2192 Interpol (international).

Cyberbully response = \"Tell, Block, Save, Don't retaliate.\" And never take away a kid's tech \u2014 it isolates them.

\u26a0\ufe0f COMMON EXAM MISTAKES

Mixing up copyright/patent/trademark \u2014 creative work vs. invention vs. brand.

Thinking fair use means \"any use is fine.\" It's limited use only.

Forgetting GPL is copyleft (derivatives must stay under GPL), unlike permissive MIT.

Choosing \"remove the child's phone\" for cyberbullying \u2014 the source says don't, as it increases isolation.

Assuming all cyberbullying is a crime \u2014 only when it involves threats, stalking, protected-trait harassment, or minor's explicit images does it clearly trigger law enforcement.

Retaliating against a bully \u2014 victims should never retaliate.

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 \u2014 Classify the IP protection

Problem: Match each to copyright, patent, or trademark: (a) a startup's swirl logo, (b) a novel algorithm-driven engine part, (c) a mobile game's source code.

(a) A logo identifies a brand \u2192 trademark.

(b) A new physical invention \u2192 patent (exclusive control for a period).

(c) Source code is an original creative/authored work \u2192 copyright.

Result: logo=trademark, invention=patent, code=copyright. \u2714

Wrong way \u2192 why \u2192 right way: Calling the logo a \"copyright\" is a common slip. Why wrong: copyright covers creative works, but brand identifiers are protected by trademark. Right way: match brand identity \u2192 trademark.

Worked Example 2 \u2014 Decide the cyberbullying response

Scenario: A teen is receiving repeated anonymous messages that now include a threat of physical violence.

Identify severity: it escalated to a threat of violence.

Standard first steps still apply: tell a trusted adult, block the sender, and save evidence (don't delete the threatening messages before documenting).

Because there's a violent threat, this crosses into contact law enforcement territory.

Do not retaliate, and parents should not confiscate the teen's technology (it increases isolation).

Correct response: preserve evidence + involve police. \u2714

\ud83d\udcca FIGURE \u2014 the three IP protections, and the licence spectrum from permissive to copyleft
\ud83c\udfaf EXAM TIP

Classification questions here are decided by a single word in the stem, so read for the noun: a work (song, book, code, photo) \u2192 copyright; an invention or process \u2192 patent; a name, logo or slogan \u2192 trademark. Source code trips people up \u2014 it is an authored work, so it is copyright, even though it is technical.

For licences, only one distinction is really tested: copyleft versus permissive. GPL is copyleft \u2014 anything derived from it must carry the same licence. MIT is permissive \u2014 reuse it almost anywhere, just keep the notice. If a question describes a company building a closed product on top of GPL code, the answer involves the copyleft obligation.

Cybercrime items usually ask who investigates: local police for personal crimes, the FBI or Secret Service for large or national ones, Interpol when it crosses borders. And remember the framing that the answer choices are built from: the computer can be the target, the tool, or both.

Cyberbullying scenarios have four fixed correct actions \u2014 tell someone, block the abuser, keep the evidence, never retaliate \u2014 and two fixed wrong ones: taking the child\u2019s technology away (it isolates them) and deleting the messages (it destroys the evidence). Escalate to police only for threats of violence, stalking, harassment on protected traits, or explicit images of a minor.

Protecting data: encryption and hashing

Symmetric encryptionAsymmetric (public-key)
Keysone shared key encrypts and decryptsa pair \u2014 public key encrypts, private key decrypts
Speedfastslower
Problem it hasboth sides must exchange the secret key safelysolves that: the public key can be published
Typical usebulk dataexchanging a symmetric key, and digital signatures

So asymmetric encryption works by publishing one key that anyone may use to encrypt, while only the matching private key can decrypt.

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION
Hashing is one-way. It turns any input into a fixed-length value that cannot be reversed back into the original. Encryption is two-way by design \u2014 the whole point is to get the data back. That is why passwords are hashed, not encrypted: a stolen database of hashes does not hand over the passwords.
\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION
Decryption is converting unreadable ciphertext back into readable plaintext.

Who investigates, and the trend

In the United States, financial and payment-system cybercrime falls to the Secret Service, whose original remit was currency counterfeiting. The FBI leads on computer intrusion, espionage and terrorism, and runs the IC3 complaint center.

Digital forensics is the investigation itself: recovering deleted files and analyzing storage and logs to reconstruct what happened, in a way that holds up as evidence.

Cybercrime complaints and reported dollar losses to the FBI have been rising steadily year on year.

\ud83c\udfaf LEARNING OBJECTIVES

after this section you will be able to\u2026

\u2022 Define a computer network, node/host, and data transfer rate/bandwidth.

\u2022 Contrast the client/server and peer-to-peer (P2P) models.

\u2022 Distinguish LAN, WAN, and MAN, and the ring / star / bus topologies.

\u2022 Compare Internet connection types (phone modem, DSL, cable, broadband) and the roles of ISP, backbone, router, repeater.

\u2022 Explain packet switching and why packets may arrive out of order.

Plain-English First

A network is just computers that can talk to each other and share stuff \u2014 files, printers, web pages. The magic trick that makes the whole internet work is packet switching: instead of sending a message as one big stream, your computer chops it into little numbered envelopes (packets), fires them off \u2014 possibly by different routes \u2014 and the far end reassembles them in order. Think of mailing a book one page at a time in separate envelopes; even if they arrive scrambled, the page numbers let the recipient rebuild it.

Going Deeper \u2014 Models & Network Types

A computer network is a collection of computing devices connected to communicate and share resources. Any device on it is a node (or host) \u2014 computers, printers, traffic-handling devices. Key metric: the data transfer rate (a.k.a. bandwidth) \u2014 how fast data moves, in bits per second. Communication follows protocols (rules for formatting/processing data).

Two interaction models:

Client/server \u2014 a client requests; a server responds (e.g., a web server answering a browser, a file server storing shared files). Can support parallel processing.

Peer-to-peer (P2P) \u2014 decentralized; each node can act as client or server, sharing resources directly. No single server, but harder to administer and more prone to security problems.

\ud83d\udccc MUST-KNOW

LAN / WAN / MAN & topologies

LAN = small area (room/building). WAN = connects LANs over large distances (the Internet is the ultimate WAN). MAN = city/campus scale. A LAN node set up to link a LAN to other networks is a gateway. LAN topologies: ring (closed loop, messages travel one direction), star (all nodes connect to one central node \u2014 huge burden; if it fails, no communication), bus (all nodes on one shared line carrying messages both directions; nodes ignore messages not addressed to them).

Going Deeper \u2014 Wireless, Internet Connections & Packet Switching

Wireless networks use a wireless access point (usually wired to the rest) so devices connect via radio waves \u2014 flexible and cheap to install, but more prone to interference and access-control issues. Bluetooth is short-range wireless for peripherals.

No one owns the Internet. Latency (delay between request and receipt) defines speed; the goal is to minimize it. The Internet backbone is a set of high-capacity routes (with heavy redundancy \u2014 no true center). An ISP (Internet service provider) connects you to the backbone. Connection types: phone modem (modulator/demodulator; converts data to analog audio over phone lines, ~64 kbps max), DSL (digital over copper phone lines, always-on, distance-limited), and cable modem (over TV cable). DSL and cable are broadband (generally \u226525 Mbps download; always on). For both, download (data to you) is usually faster than upload (data from you), since download traffic dominates.

Packet switching: messages are split into fixed-size numbered packets sent individually, possibly by different routes, then reassembled in order at the destination. Routers direct packets between networks (each knows only the best next hop, not the whole route, and can reroute around congestion/failures). Repeaters strengthen a signal over long distances so it doesn't degrade too much.

Key Terms

TermDefinitionWhy it matters
Computer networkConnected devices sharing data/resources.The basis of all internet activity.
Node / hostAny device on a network.Generic term for a network member.
Data transfer rate / bandwidthSpeed data moves (bits/second).Determines network performance.
Client/serverClient requests; server responds.Dominant web architecture.
P2PDecentralized; peers are client & server.No central server; harder to secure.
LAN / WAN / MANLocal / wide / metropolitan networks.Classify networks by geographic size.
GatewayNode linking a LAN to other networks.Handles cross-network traffic.
Ring/Star/Bus topologyLoop / central-hub / shared-line layouts.How LAN nodes are arranged.
ISPProvides Internet access.Your on-ramp to the backbone.
BroadbandAlways-on, high-speed (\u226525 Mbps down).DSL/cable replaced dial-up.
Packet switchingSplit into numbered packets, reassemble.How data efficiently shares lines.
RouterDirects packets between networks.Knows the best next hop.
RepeaterStrengthens a signal over distance.Prevents signal degradation.

Diagram \u2014 LAN topologies

Comparison / Reference Tables

StructureCentral server responds to clientsDecentralized; peers share directly
RolesFixed (client or server)A peer can be either
Admin/securityEasier to administer/secureHarder; more security risk

Network topologies

StarAll to a central nodeCentral node fails \u2192 all down
BusSingle shared line, both waysShared line contention

LANRoom/buildingOffice network
MANCity/campusUniversity-wide network
WANLarge distanceThe Internet

\ud83d\udca1 Tips, Tricks & Mnemonics

Node = any device; \"host\" is the same idea.

Star = single point of failure. Kill the hub, kill the network.

LAN < MAN < WAN by geographic size; the Internet is the biggest WAN.

Packets are numbered so out-of-order arrival can be reassembled.

Router = next hop; Repeater = signal booster.

Download > upload speed on most home broadband (download traffic dominates).

\u26a0\ufe0f COMMON EXAM MISTAKES

Confusing LAN and WAN \u2014 LAN is local (building), WAN spans large distances.

Thinking a router knows the entire path. It only knows the best next hop.

Saying packets always arrive in order. They may not; numbering fixes this.

Mixing up client/server (central) with P2P (decentralized).

Calling a repeater a router \u2014 a repeater just boosts the signal.

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 \u2014 Classify the network and model

Problem: A university links every building's LAN across campus; students' browsers request pages from a central library catalog computer. Identify the network scope and the interaction model.

Scope: connects many LANs across a campus/city area \u2192 MAN (a WAN if it spanned larger distances).

Browsers requesting from a central catalog computer = requests to a responder \u2192 client/server model (the catalog is the server).

If instead students shared files directly among their laptops with no central host, that would be P2P. \u2714

Worked Example 2 \u2014 Packet switching & a star weakness (wrong way \u2192 right way)

A 3-packet message is sent; packets take different routes and arrive as #2, #3, #1.

The destination uses the packet numbers to reorder them \u2192 #1, #2, #3 \u2192 original message. \u2714

Wrong way \u2192 why \u2192 right way (star topology): a team assumes a star network is the most fault-tolerant. Why wrong: the central node is a single point of failure \u2014 if it dies, no one can communicate. Right way: recognize the star's central-node risk when judging reliability. \u2714

\ud83d\udcca FIGURE \u2014 packet switching \u2014 why packets arrive out of order and why it does not matter
\ud83c\udfaf EXAM TIP

Two vocabulary pairs supply most of the questions. LAN / MAN / WAN is purely about geographic size \u2014 one building, one city or campus, one large distance \u2014 and the Internet is the biggest WAN. Client/server versus peer-to-peer is about whether there is a central responder: if one machine answers requests it is client/server; if every node can be both, it is P2P.

Topology questions almost always want a weakness. Star = a single point of failure at the hub. Ring = a break disrupts the loop. Bus = one shared line, so everybody contends for it. If the question asks which is most vulnerable to one device failing, it is the star.

The packet-switching item is worded as a puzzle: \u201cpackets arrived in the order 2, 3, 1 \u2014 what went wrong?\u201d Nothing. Packets are sent individually and may take different routes; the numbers let the destination reassemble them. Any answer implying the message is corrupted or must be resent is wrong.

Keep the devices apart, too: a router chooses the next hop toward a destination; a repeater only boosts a weakening signal. And a router never knows the whole path \u2014 only the best next step.

Reading a network complaint

When a call connects but voices arrive noticeably late, the metric to blame is latency \u2014 the delay in getting each packet there. Bandwidth is capacity, and a connection can have plenty of it while still being slow to respond.

"}, "D684/g4/x15_2": {"body": "
\ud83c\udfaf LEARNING OBJECTIVES

after this section you will be able to\u2026

\u2022 Contrast proprietary and open systems, and explain interoperability.

\u2022 Describe the OSI Reference Model (7 layers) and a protocol stack.

\u2022 Explain TCP/IP and how TCP and IP divide the work; contrast UDP.

\u2022 Identify the high-level protocols (SMTP, FTP, Telnet, HTTP) and the role of ports.

\u2022 Explain ping, traceroute, MIME types, and firewalls.

Plain-English First

For computers from different companies to talk, they need shared \"manners\" \u2014 protocols (rules of etiquette for communication). Early vendors built proprietary systems that couldn't talk to each other; the fix was open systems built on common standards so anything can interoperate. The most famous rulebook is TCP/IP, a team of two: IP is the mail carrier that routes packets, and TCP is the meticulous shipping clerk that numbers packets, checks nothing got lost, and reassembles them in order.

Going Deeper \u2014 Open Systems & the OSI Model

A proprietary system is privately controlled and often can't talk to other vendors' networks. As networking grew, the need for interoperability (different systems working together) drove open systems \u2014 based on common architecture and protocol suites. The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) created the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) Reference Model: seven layers, each handling one aspect of communication. The highest layer is closest to the application; the lowest handles the physical medium (wiring); the network layer, for example, handles routing/addressing of packets.

\ud83d\udccc MUST-KNOW

protocol stacks & TCP/IP

Protocols are layered \u2014 each relies on the ones beneath it \u2014 forming a protocol stack. This lets new protocols be added without disturbing lower layers. TCP/IP is the core Internet suite: IP (Internet Protocol) routes packets to their destination; TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) breaks messages into packets, hands them to IP, then orders/reassembles them and handles errors (very reliable, a bit slower). UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is TCP's alternative \u2014 connectionless, less reliable but faster. Ethernet spans the physical/data-link layers.

Going Deeper \u2014 Utilities, High-Level Protocols, Ports & Firewalls

Two TCP/IP utilities: ping tests whether a host is reachable (like a sonar \"ping\"/echo); traceroute lists the intermediate computers (hops) a packet passes through to a destination. High-level protocols build on TCP/IP:

SMTP \u2014 Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (sending email).

FTP \u2014 File Transfer Protocol (transferring files between computers).

Telnet \u2014 log into a remote computer.

HTTP \u2014 Hypertext Transfer Protocol (exchanging Web documents, usually HTML).

A port is a numeric designation for a particular high-level protocol; servers/routers use it to control traffic (HTTP has a default port; Telnet uses port 23). A MIME type (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extension) is a standard identifying a file's format so a program knows how to handle it (e.g., an email attachment). A firewall is a gateway machine/software that filters traffic and enforces an organization's access control policy \u2014 commonly by denying traffic on particular ports (e.g., blocking inbound Telnet on port 23).

Key Terms

TermDefinitionWhy it matters
ProtocolRules for formatting/transmitting data.Lets computers communicate.
Proprietary systemPrivately controlled; limited interop.The problem open systems solved.
Open systemBuilt on common standards.Maximizes interoperability.
InteroperabilityDifferent systems working together.Goal of open standards.
OSI Reference Model7-layer conceptual network framework.Standardizes network functions.
Protocol stackLayered set of protocols.Add protocols without breaking lower ones.
TCPSplits/orders/reassembles packets; reliable.Reliable delivery.
IPRoutes packets to destination.Delivery/addressing foundation.
UDPConnectionless; faster, less reliable.Speed over reliability.
ping / tracerouteReachability test / hop path.Network diagnostics.
PortNumber for a high-level protocol.Controls/identifies traffic.
FirewallFilters traffic per access policy.Protects a network.
MIME typeIdentifies a file's format.Tells programs how to handle data.

Diagram \u2014 TCP/IP protocol layering

Comparison / Reference Tables

TCP vs. UDP

TCPUDP
ReliabilityHigh (orders, reassembles, error-checks)Lower (connectionless)
SpeedSlowerFaster
Use whenAccuracy matters (web, email, files)Speed matters more than reliability

High-level protocols

ProtocolPurpose
SMTPSend email
FTPTransfer files
TelnetRemote login (port 23)
HTTPExchange Web documents (HTML)

Proprietary vs. Open

ProprietaryOpen
ControlPrivate vendorCommon standards
InteroperabilityLimitedMaximized

\ud83d\udca1 Tips, Tricks & Mnemonics

IP routes, TCP reassembles. IP = the road; TCP = the careful courier.

TCP = reliable/slower, UDP = fast/less reliable. \"U\" for \"Unreliable but fast.\"

OSI = 7 layers (physical at the bottom, application at the top).

Open beats proprietary for interoperability.

Ping = \"are you alive?\"; Traceroute = \"what path did you take?\"

Firewall = port bouncer. It commonly blocks traffic on specific ports.

\u26a0\ufe0f COMMON EXAM MISTAKES

Swapping TCP and IP jobs. IP routes; TCP splits/orders/reassembles and handles errors.

Calling UDP more reliable than TCP. UDP is faster but less reliable.

Thinking the OSI model has a different number of layers \u2014 it has 7.

Confusing ping (reachability) with traceroute (hop-by-hop path).

Believing a firewall stores files \u2014 it filters traffic.

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 \u2014 Who does what in TCP/IP?

Problem: A large file is emailed. Which protocol (a) breaks it into ordered packets and checks for loss, (b) routes each packet, (c) actually sends the email between mail servers?

(a) Break into packets, order, error-check \u2192 TCP.

(b) Route packets to destination \u2192 IP.

(c) Transfer the email between servers \u2192 SMTP (a high-level protocol built on TCP/IP). \u2714

Worked Example 2 \u2014 Choose the diagnostic / firewall action (wrong way \u2192 right way)

An admin wants to know whether a server is reachable \u2192 use ping.

To see which route packets take to it \u2192 use traceroute.

To block outside users from remotely logging in via Telnet \u2192 deny inbound traffic on port 23 at the firewall.

Wrong way \u2192 why \u2192 right way: using UDP for a banking transaction \"to be faster.\" Why wrong: UDP is unreliable; lost data could corrupt the transaction. Right way: use TCP for accuracy-critical transfers. \u2714

\ud83d\udcca FIGURE \u2014 a message going down the sending stack and back up the receiving one
\ud83c\udfaf EXAM TIP

The division of labour is the exam\u2019s favourite question, and one sentence settles it: IP routes, TCP reassembles. IP puts an address on each packet and gets it to the next hop; TCP splits the message, numbers the pieces, checks for loss and puts them back in order. If a choice gives TCP the routing job, it is wrong.

TCP versus UDP is a trade, not a ranking: TCP is reliable and slower, UDP is fast and connectionless with no guarantee of delivery or order. Money, mail and file transfers want TCP; live streaming and games can afford UDP.

Memorise the four high-level protocols by their verb: SMTP sends mail, FTP transfers files, Telnet logs in remotely (port 23), HTTP exchanges web documents. Ports are how a firewall filters \u2014 \u201cblock remote logins\u201d means deny inbound traffic on the Telnet port.

And two number facts they ask directly: the OSI model has seven layers, physical at the bottom and application at the top; and the reason layering exists at all is that a new protocol can be slotted in without rewriting the ones below it.

Naming, capacity and delay

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION
DNS (Domain Name System) translates a human-readable name such as wgu.edu into the numeric IP address a machine needs in order to connect. It is the internet's phone book.
TermMeansAnalogy
Bandwidthmaximum data capacity of a path \u2014 how much can flow at oncelanes on a motorway
Latencydelay \u2014 how long one piece takes to get therehow long the journey takes

They are independent, which is the point of the classic question: a connection can advertise very high bandwidth and still give a choppy video call, because the call is ruined by high latency (and jitter), not by lack of capacity. Equally, a call where voices arrive noticeably late is a latency problem.

Choosing a transport protocol

TCPUDP
Guaranteesevery byte arrives, in order, re-sending what is lostnone \u2014 best effort
Costslower, more overheadfast, minimal overhead
Use forfile transfer, web pages, emaillive video/voice, gaming, where late data is useless

An application that must have every byte arrive reliably and in the correct order uses TCP.

Client and server

The client requests; the server provides. A web browser asking for a page is the client, and the remote machine that sends the page back is the server.

HTTP status codes

CodeMeans
200OK \u2014 the request succeeded
404Not found \u2014 the server was reached, but has nothing at that address
403Forbidden \u2014 it exists, you may not have it
500Server error \u2014 the fault is at the server end

404 is the one to know: the server answered, so the network and the server are fine. The resource is what is missing.

\ud83c\udfaf LEARNING OBJECTIVES

after this section you will be able to\u2026

\u2022 Distinguish a hostname from an IP address.

\u2022 Compare IPv4 (32-bit) and IPv6 (128-bit) and know why IPv6 exists.

\u2022 Explain the domain name system (DNS) and how names resolve to IP addresses.

\u2022 Identify domain names, top-level domains (TLDs), and ICANN.

\u2022 Define domain squatting and network neutrality.

Plain-English First

Every computer on the Internet needs an address \u2014 but humans hate memorizing numbers. So we use friendly hostnames like villanova.edu, and a giant behind-the-scenes phone book called DNS translates them into the numeric IP addresses computers actually use. When you type a web address, DNS quietly looks up the number and connects you.

Going Deeper \u2014 Hostnames, IP Addresses, DNS

A hostname is a unique, human-readable name (e.g., matisse.csc.villanova.edu) \u2014 the computer name plus the domain name. Network software translates it to an IP address the computer uses.

\ud83d\udccc MUST-KNOW

IPv4 vs. IPv6

IPv4 stores addresses in 32 bits = four bytes shown as four decimal numbers 0\u2013255 separated by dots (e.g., 205.39.155.18), giving only about 4 billion addresses \u2014 which ran out (last block assigned in early 2011). IPv6 uses 128 bits = eight groups of 16, written in hexadecimal (e.g., FE80:0000:...:8329), giving vastly more addresses. The IPv4 scheme is hierarchical: first numbers = network, then subnetwork, then host.

The domain name system (DNS) translates hostnames into IP addresses. It's a distributed database (designed 1984) \u2014 no single organization holds all mappings. When you enter a hostname, your software asks a nearby domain name server; if it can't resolve the name, it asks another, propagating until the name resolves or the request expires. (Before DNS, a single Stanford-maintained host table was used \u2014 it didn't scale.)

Going Deeper \u2014 Domains, TLDs, ICANN & Neutrality

A domain name narrows to a particular organization's networks. Its last section is the top-level domain (TLD) \u2014 .com (commercial), .edu (universities; tightly controlled), .org, .net, or two-letter country codes. ICANN (Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers) is the international authority managing TLD names and IP assignments. Because early .com/.org/.net were unrestricted, people practiced domain squatting \u2014 registering names (often trademarks) hoping to resell them at a profit \u2014 generally considered unethical; more TLDs (now 1,500+) were added to relieve pressure. Finally, network neutrality is the principle that ISPs should treat all Internet traffic equally, without favoring or throttling based on user, content, or application.

Key Terms

TermDefinitionWhy it matters
HostnameHuman-readable name of a computer.Easy for people to use.
IP addressNumeric identifier for a device.What computers use to communicate.
IPv432-bit address; four 0\u2013255 numbers.~4 billion addresses (ran out).
IPv6128-bit address in hex.Vastly more addresses.
DNSTranslates hostnames to IP addresses.The Internet's phone book.
Domain name serverComputer that resolves hostnames.Performs the lookup.
Domain nameIdentifies an organization's networks.Groups hosts logically.
Top-level domain (TLD)Last part (.com, .edu, country codes).Highest-level grouping.
ICANNManages TLDs and IP assignment.Global naming/numbering authority.
Domain squattingRegistering names to resell for profit.Considered unethical.
Network neutralityTreat all traffic equally.Contested policy principle.

Diagram \u2014 Resolving a hostname via DNS

Comparison / Reference Tables

IPv4 vs. IPv6

IPv4IPv6
Bits32 (4 bytes)128 (8 groups of 16)
NotationFour decimals 0\u2013255Hexadecimal
Address count~4 billion (exhausted)Enormous

Common TLDs

TLDIntended use
.comCommercial (unrestricted)
.eduUniversities (controlled)
.org / .netOrganizations / networks
country codesTwo-letter (e.g., .uk, .ca)

\ud83d\udca1 Tips, Tricks & Mnemonics

Hostname = for humans; IP = for computers. DNS is the translator.

IPv4 = 4 numbers (32 bits); IPv6 = hex (128 bits). \"4 = four numbers.\"

Each IPv4 number is 0\u2013255 (one byte).

DNS is distributed \u2014 no single owner; requests propagate until resolved.

TLD = the last part (.com/.edu). ICANN runs the naming system.

Net neutrality = equal treatment of all traffic.

\u26a0\ufe0f COMMON EXAM MISTAKES

Saying an IPv4 number can exceed 255. Each byte maxes at 255.

Mixing up IPv4 (32-bit, decimal) and IPv6 (128-bit, hex).

Thinking DNS is one central server \u2014 it's a distributed database.

Confusing the hostname (human-readable) with the IP address (numeric).

Calling domain squatting ethical \u2014 it's generally considered unethical.

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 \u2014 Read an address and pick the version

Problem: Classify each: (a) 193.133.20.4, (b) FE80:0000:0000:0000:0202:B3FF:FE1E:8329. Is 256.10.10.1 a valid IPv4 address?

(a) Four decimal numbers separated by dots \u2192 IPv4 (32-bit).

(b) Eight hex groups separated by colons \u2192 IPv6 (128-bit).

(c) 256 exceeds the 0\u2013255 range of one byte \u2192 invalid IPv4 address. \u2714

Worked Example 2 \u2014 Trace a DNS lookup (wrong way \u2192 right way)

You type example.edu; the browser sends the name to a nearby domain name server.

If that server knows the mapping, it returns the IP address; if not, it asks another server, and the request propagates.

Once resolved, the browser connects to the returned IP.

Wrong way \u2192 why \u2192 right way: assuming one master DNS server holds every mapping. Why wrong: DNS is a distributed database; no single server has everything. Right way: understand requests hop between servers until resolved. \u2714

\ud83d\udcca FIGURE \u2014 an IPv4 address, an IPv6 address, and what DNS is for
\ud83c\udfaf EXAM TIP

Spot-the-invalid-address is the most common item, and it has one rule: each IPv4 number is one byte, so 0\u2013255. Anything with 256 or above in it is not a valid IPv4 address. Scan the four numbers before reading the answer choices.

Tell the versions apart by shape rather than by counting bits: four decimal numbers separated by dots \u2192 IPv4 (32 bits); hexadecimal groups separated by colons \u2192 IPv6 (128 bits). IPv6 exists because IPv4\u2019s roughly 4.3 billion addresses ran out.

DNS questions test one property: it is a distributed database, not a single master server. If your nearby name server does not know a mapping, the request propagates to others until it is resolved. Any choice describing \u201cthe DNS server that holds every mapping\u201d is wrong.

The last-mark facts: the TLD is the final part of a domain name (.com, .edu, a two-letter country code), ICANN administers the naming system, domain squatting \u2014 registering a name purely to resell it \u2014 is regarded as unethical, and network neutrality means all traffic is treated equally regardless of what it is or who sent it.

Two kinds of address, and the firewall

IP addressMAC address
What it identifiesa device's logical position on a networkthe physical network adapter itself
Assigned bythe network (often DHCP) \u2014 it changes when you move networksthe manufacturer, burned into the hardware
Scoperoutable across networks, worldwidethe local network segment only

Both are needed: IP gets a packet across the internet to the right network, MAC delivers it to the right machine on that final segment. That two-level addressing scheme is what lets one design scale from a home network to the whole internet.

\ud83d\udcd8 DEFINITION
A firewall filters network traffic against a set of rules, allowing or blocking it by address, port or protocol. It controls what may cross the boundary \u2014 it is not antivirus, and it does not encrypt.

\ud83c\udfaf LEARNING OBJECTIVES

after this section you will be able to\u2026

\u2022 Explain what cloud computing is and why organisations use it.

\u2022 Tell IaaS, PaaS and SaaS apart from a scenario, and say who manages what.

\u2022 Distinguish public, private and hybrid deployment.

\u2022 Say when edge computing beats sending data to the cloud.

\u2022 Identify the common attacks \u2014 DDoS, malware, phishing, man-in-the-middle, brute force \u2014 and the defence for each.

Plain-English First

The last section ended with server farms \u2014 warehouses of servers. Cloud computing is simply renting space on somebody else's server farm, over the internet, instead of buying and running your own. You pay for what you use and give it back when you are done.

The only real question is how much of the stack you rent. Rent bare machines and you still install everything yourself. Rent a ready-made platform and you supply only your code. Rent a finished application and you just log in. Those three levels are IaaS, PaaS and SaaS, and telling them apart from a short scenario is the single most commonly tested idea here.

Going Deeper \u2014 the three service models

ModelYou manageThe provider managesTypical example
IaaS
Infrastructure as a Service		the operating system, runtime and your applicationhardware, storage, network, virtualisationrenting virtual machines and disks
PaaS
Platform as a Service		your application code and data onlyeverything below your code \u2014 OS, runtime, scaling, patchingpush code, the platform runs it
SaaS
Software as a Service		nothing but your own data and settingsthe entire stack including the applicationweb email, online documents
\ud83d\udccc MUST-KNOW

reading the scenario

Every one of these questions is answered by finding the highest thing the customer still manages:

\u2022 They mention installing or patching an operating system, or renting virtual machines \u2192 IaaS.

\u2022 They deploy their own code but no OS is ever mentioned \u2192 PaaS.

\u2022 They just use a finished application in a browser \u2192 SaaS.

It is one sliding scale: from IaaS to SaaS, what the customer manages goes down and what the provider manages goes up.

Going Deeper \u2014 deployment models

DeploymentWho the infrastructure servesChosen when
Publicmany unrelated customers share the provider's hardwarecost and elasticity matter most
Privateone organisation only, dedicatedregulation or sensitivity demands isolation
Hybridboth, connected togethersensitive systems stay private while public services scale in the public cloud

Going Deeper \u2014 why it is worth it, and what it costs you

The gains. Elasticity \u2014 add capacity for the busy week and release it afterwards. Pay-as-you-go \u2014 an operating cost instead of buying hardware up front. No data centre to power, cool, secure or replace. Someone else handles hardware failure.

The costs. You now depend on the provider and on your own internet link: their outage is your outage. Data lives somewhere you do not own, which can matter legally. Heavy long-running workloads can end up dearer than owning. Moving to another provider later is rarely easy.

Going Deeper \u2014 edge computing

Edge computing processes data near where it is produced \u2014 on the device or a local gateway \u2014 instead of shipping everything to the cloud. A factory gateway that reads its own sensors, or a camera that recognises a face on-device, is doing edge computing.

\ud83d\udccc MUST-KNOW

edge or cloud?

\u2022 Edge when the answer is needed fast (low latency, milliseconds), when bandwidth is limited or costly, or when raw data should not leave the site.

\u2022 Cloud when the work needs heavy computation or must combine data from many places. One site's gateway cannot see the other thousand sites.

Going Deeper \u2014 network & IoT security

Connecting everything to the internet \u2014 including the billions of embedded and IoT devices from the previous unit \u2014 is what makes these attacks possible. Learn each one by what it targets.

AttackHow it worksWhat stops it
DoSone machine floods a server so real users cannot get througha firewall filtering and rate limiting at the boundary
DDoSthe same flood from many hijacked machines at once \u2014 a botnetupstream scrubbing; and securing the devices so they are never recruited
Malwarea virus needs a host file to be run; a worm spreads by itself; a trojan is disguised as something wanted; ransomware encrypts your files for paymentpatching, anti-malware, least privilege, backups
Phishinga message imitates someone trusted to get credentials \u2014 it attacks the persontraining, and 2FA so a stolen password is not enough
Man-in-the-middlethe attacker sits in the path and reads or alters traffic while both sides think they are talking directlyencryption in transit (HTTPS) makes what is intercepted useless
Brute forceguessing passwords over and over until one worksaccount lockout or rate limiting \u2014 it removes the unlimited guesses
\ud83d\udccc MUST-KNOW

why IoT devices end up in botnets

Not because they are powerful \u2014 because they are neglected. They ship with default passwords nobody changes and firmware nobody ever updates, and there are billions of them. Change the credentials and keep the firmware current and the whole attack falls apart.

Key Terms

TermDefinition
Cloud computingrenting computing resources over the internet instead of owning them
IaaSyou rent virtual machines, storage and networking; you manage the OS upward
PaaSyou rent a managed platform and supply only your application code
SaaSyou use a finished application; the provider manages everything

Elasticitycapacity can be added and released on demand

Botneta network of compromised machines controlled by an attacker

Man-in-the-middlean attacker secretly relaying traffic between two parties
Firewalla filter at the network boundary that allows or blocks traffic by rule
Two-factor authenticationproof from two different categories \u2014 knowledge, possession or biometrics

\ud83e\udde0 Memory hooks

HookWhat it unlocks
\u201cInfrastructure, Platform, Software\u201dIaaS \u2192 PaaS \u2192 SaaS is bottom to top of the stack. The further up you rent, the less you manage. Read the scenario for the highest layer the customer still touches.
OS mentioned = IaaSIf the customer installs, patches or chooses the operating system, it is IaaS. PaaS and SaaS both hide the OS completely.
Distributed = manyThe extra D in DDoS is the botnet. If the question says the traffic came from thousands of hijacked devices, it is a DDoS, not a DoS.

\u25c6 HOW TO TRACE THIS

Write the variable and its value in the margin. Read the condition out loud with the real number substituted in \u2014 \"is 65 greater than 65?\" \u2014 and answer it before you look at the options.

The one that decides these questions

> is strict. A value equal to the cut-off FAILS a > test and falls to ELSE. >= includes the cut-off. Most \"what prints\" items are built on exactly that difference, so the test writer will hand you the boundary value on purpose.

Two rules that never change

An IF/ELSE runs exactly one branch \u2014 never both, never neither. And quoted text prints literally: OUTPUT \"Continue\" prints Continue, it does not look up a variable called Continue.

"}, "D684/trace_drill/t2": {"body": "
\u25c6 HOW TO TRACE THIS

Test the branches top to bottom and stop at the first true one. Everything below it is skipped, even if it would also be true.

Why order matters

In a grade chain, 95 is greater than 90 AND 80 AND 70 \u2014 but only the first match runs. That is why the chain is written highest cut-off first. Reversed, every score would print the lowest grade.

Nested IFs

An inner IF is only reached if the outer condition passed. If the outer test fails, the whole inner block \u2014 both its branches \u2014 is skipped without being evaluated at all.

"}, "D684/trace_drill/t3": {"body": "
\u25c6 HOW TO TRACE THIS

Write out the values the loop variable actually takes: 1, 2, 3 \u2026 Do not divide the range and estimate. For short loops, tracing every pass is faster and safer than reasoning about it.

Inclusive ends

FOR i = 1 TO 10 runs 10 times \u2014 both endpoints are included. That is where off-by-one answers come from, and the wrong options are usually the count \u00b11.

Accumulators

A running total must be initialised before the loop. Set it inside and it resets on every pass, leaving only the last value.

Nested loops

The inner loop runs completely for each pass of the outer one, so the body runs outer \u00d7 inner times \u2014 nested loops multiply, they never add.

"}, "D684/trace_drill/t4": {"body": "
\u25c6 HOW TO TRACE THIS

Keep a two-column table: the variable, and whether the condition is still true. Stop the moment it turns false \u2014 the value it holds then is the answer.

The overshoot

A WHILE checks its condition before each pass, so it exits with the first value that fails the test. x = 4, x < 11, x = x + 3 ends at 13, not 11 \u2014 the limit itself is rarely the answer, which is why it is always offered as a distractor.

Infinite loops

If nothing inside the body changes the variable in the condition, the loop never ends. Every WHILE needs its own update line.

"}, "D684/trace_drill/t5": {"body": "
\u25c6 HOW TO TRACE THIS

Give each variable a column and cross out the old value on every assignment. Assignment replaces; it is not an equation that stays true.

Order is everything

SET x = x + 5 means \"take the current x, add 5, store it back\". The right-hand side is worked out first, using the values as they are at that moment.

The classic swap

Swapping needs a third variable: temp = a; a = b; b = temp. Without temp, the first line overwrites a and both variables end up holding b \u2014 a favourite exam trap.

"}, "D684/trace_drill/t6": {"body": "
\u25c6 HOW TO TRACE THIS

Work the expression in precedence order and write down each intermediate value rather than doing it in your head.

MOD is the remainder

17 MOD 5 = 2 (17 = 3\u00d75 + 2), not 3. The quotient is the distractor. MOD is the standard test for divisibility: n MOD 2 = 0 means n is even.

Division

In this course\u2019s pseudocode, / is ordinary division and keeps the fraction: 33 / 4 = 8.25. Some real languages truncate to 8 when both operands are integers \u2014 read which convention the question is using.

Precedence

Multiply and divide before add and subtract: 2 + 3 * 4 is 14, not 20. Brackets override it.

"}, "D684/trace_drill/t7": {"body": "
\u25c6 HOW TO TRACE THIS

For strings, copy the output character by character \u2014 including the spaces. For lists, write the index above each value before you answer.

Concatenation

first + \" \" + last joins in written order and the \" \" supplies the space. Drop it and the words run together.

Indexing starts at 0

In a list of 6 values the valid indexes are 0\u20135. nums[2] is the third value, and nums[6] is out of range. Off-by-one here is the single most common tracing error.

FOR EACH

FOR EACH visits every element once, in order, without you managing an index \u2014 useful when you need the values but not their positions.

"}, "D684/trace_drill/t8": {"body": "
\u25c6 HOW TO TRACE THIS

When a line contains a call, work out the call first, write its returned value above the line, then finish the expression.

RETURN hands a value back

doubleIt(5) + 3 is 10 + 3 = 13. The argument is not added first \u2014 the call completes, then the rest of the expression runs.

Scope

A variable created inside a function is local: it exists only during that call and disappears afterwards. Assigning to a local of the same name does not change the outer variable.

Loops with a condition inside

Every pass reaches the IF, but only the passes that satisfy it perform the action. Trace which values pass the test first, then apply the action only to those.

"}, "D684/write_drill/p1": {"body": "
\u25c6 HOW TO ANSWER THESE

The question gives you a goal in English and four candidate lines. Ask one thing first: does the option store its result? If it does not, it cannot be the answer.

A statement assigns; an expression does not

f - d works out a value and immediately loses it. set b = f - d keeps it. Options written as bare expressions are there to catch you.

Order matters for - and /

\"Subtract d from f\" is f - d, not d - f. Read which value is being taken FROM which. Addition and multiplication survive being reversed; subtraction and division do not.

Two other decoy shapes

Plain English (\"subtract d from f\") is not pseudocode, and function-call forms like sub(f, d) are not how this course writes arithmetic.

"}, "D684/write_drill/p2": {"body": "
\u25c6 HOW TO ANSWER THESE

Conversions are named after the type you WANT, and input/output questions are decided by direction.

Conversion is a function named for the target

float(a) turns the integer a into a floating-point number. int(num) goes the other way. Decoys invent methods (a.to_float()) or bolt on a decimal (a.0) \u2014 neither is how this course writes it.

int() truncates, it does not round

int(8.9) is 8. The decimal part is chopped off. This is a favourite one-mark question.

Direction decides input vs output

INPUT/read brings a value IN from the user. OUTPUT/print/DISPLAY sends one OUT to the screen. Decide which way the value is travelling before you read the options.

"}, "D684/write_drill/p3": {"body": "
\u25c6 HOW TO ANSWER THESE

A handful of routines come up again and again. Learn their SHAPE and you can recognise the right option instantly \u2014 and name what each wrong option actually does.

The four shapes

Average: add the values, then divide by how many. Max: compare with > and keep the winner. Swap: three lines using a temp. Accumulator: set the total to 0 before the loop, add inside it.

Name the decoys

Wrong options in these items are usually a DIFFERENT valid routine \u2014 a swap offered for an average, or a min offered for a max. Ask what the option really does rather than whether it looks plausible.

The precedence trap

val_1 + val_2 / 2 is not an average: division runs first, so only val_2 is halved. The average needs the sum computed first, or brackets around it.

"}, "D684/write_drill/p4": {"body": "
\u25c6 HOW TO ANSWER THESE

These are vocabulary questions: the exam gives the definition and wants the name, or gives the name and wants the shape. Precision matters more than intuition.

The two ifs

Single-alternative: if (condition) then \u2014 acts when true, does nothing when false (that empty path is the null case). Dual-alternative: if (condition) then \u2026 else \u2014 two paths.

Stacking vs nesting

Stacked structures run one AFTER another. Nested structures sit one INSIDE another, so the inner test is only reached when the outer one passed \u2014 that is how you express combined conditions without repeating tests.

The loop words

Loop control variable \u2014 tested in the condition and changed in the body. Counter \u2014 goes up by a fixed 1. Accumulator \u2014 adds a varying amount. Sentinel \u2014 a value that means STOP, never real data. Priming read \u2014 the input before the loop that gives the first test something to look at.

"}, "D684/write_drill/p5": {"body": "
\u25c6 HOW TO ANSWER THESE

Almost every question here is answered by knowing the order and being able to translate between two vocabularies.

The order

Understand the problem \u2192 Plan the logic \u2192 Code the program \u2192 Translate the code \u2192 Test the program \u2192 Put into production \u2192 Maintain. It always starts with understanding the problem, no matter how urgent the project sounds.

The same work, two vocabularies

\"Plan the logic\" = design (flowcharts and pseudocode live here). \"Code the program\" = implementation. \"Translate the code\" = the compiler or interpreter. Questions often switch vocabulary mid-sentence.

Which error, which step

A misspelled keyword is a syntax error and is caught at translation. A program that runs but gives wrong answers has a logic error and is caught by testing.

Maintenance is the long tail

Software spends far longer being maintained than being written, which is why changes to a live program belong to maintenance and why documentation pays off.

"}, "D684/write_drill/p6": {"body": "
\u25c6 HOW TO ANSWER THESE

Scenario questions give four situations and ask which breaches the codes. Read each one and ask: who could be harmed, was anyone deceived, and was anything taken that was not theirs?

What both codes demand

Put the public's safety and welfare first; be honest in claims and estimates; respect privacy and access only what you are authorised to; credit others' work; work only within your competence (or disclose the gap); accept and give honest review, and correct errors; treat people fairly; reject bribery and disclose conflicts of interest; and support colleagues' professional development.

The trap in these items

Options that sound corporate are often perfectly ethical \u2014 signing the code annually, halting production when harm is found, paying for training. The violation is usually the one that removes a protection, hides something, or takes credit.

Responsibility does not transfer

\"My manager told me to\" is not a defence in either code, and neither is handing the task to a colleague.

📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)

The three trees

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Git feels confusing until you see that your work lives in three places, and every command just moves changes between them. Think of packing a box to ship: your desk (where you edit), the box you're loading (what you've decided to send), and the shipped-and-logged shipment (the permanent record). See the three, and every Git command makes sense.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Working directory: your actual files as you edit them now. Changes here are “unstaged.”

Staging area (index): a holding zone for the exact changes you want in your next commit. git add moves changes from working → staging.

Repository (.git): the permanent, committed history. git commit moves what's staged → repository as a new snapshot.

So the flow is: edit (working) → git add (staging) → git commit (repository).

📝 EXAM WORDING

The working directory holds your edits; the staging area (index) holds changes queued for commit; the local repository holds committed history. git add = stage; git commit = record; git status shows staged vs unstaged vs untracked.

⚠️ WATCH OUT

A file you edited is NOT in your next commit until you git add it — editing alone doesn't stage it. And git add stages a snapshot at that moment; edit again afterward and you must add again.

The three areas, named exactly as the exam names them: the working directory (your files as they are now), the staging area — also called the index — (what will go into the next commit), and the repository (the committed history in .git). git add crosses the first boundary, git commit the second.

📸 What a Commit Really Is

A commit is a snapshot of your whole project at one moment, plus a note about who/when/why, plus a pointer back to the commit that came before it. String those pointers together and you get your project's history — like save points in a game you can always return to.

Branches are just pointers

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A branch sounds heavy, like copying your whole project. It isn't. A branch is just a lightweight sticky note pointing at one commit. Making a branch is instant — one tiny pointer. That's why Git encourages branching for every feature: it's basically free.

📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)

Merging vs rebasing

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

You've done work on a branch; now you want it back in main. Two ways: merge ties the two histories together with a joining commit (keeps true history, a bit messier). Rebase replays your commits on top of main as if you'd started there (clean, linear history, but rewrites your commits).

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Fast-forward merge: if main hasn't moved since you branched, Git just slides main's pointer forward to your latest commit — no extra commit.

Three-way (true) merge: if both branches advanced, Git creates a new merge commit with TWO parents, combining both lines of work.

Rebase: moves your branch's commits to begin at the tip of main, producing a straight line. Cleaner log, but it rewrites commit hashes — so avoid rebasing commits others already pulled.

📝 EXAM WORDING

Merge combines branches, creating a merge commit (two parents) unless a fast-forward is possible; it preserves history. Rebase replays commits onto a new base for a linear history but rewrites them.

⚠️ WATCH OUT

Golden rule: don't rebase commits you've already pushed/shared — rewriting shared history breaks others' repos. A fast-forward happens only when there's no divergent work; otherwise you get a merge commit.

Remotes: local vs the server

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Everything so far is on your own machine. A remote is a copy of the repo on a server (GitHub, GitLab) your team shares. You push your commits up to share them, and pull others' down. “origin” is just the default nickname for that server copy.

⚔️ Merge Conflicts

WHAT IT IS
Two branches changed the SAME LINES of the same file differently — Git can't know which you want. It's not an error; it's Git honestly asking you to decide. Changes to DIFFERENT parts merge automatically.
THE MARKERS & THE RESOLUTION RECIPE
MarkerMeans
<<<<<<<Start of YOUR branch's version
=======The divider — yours above, theirs below
>>>>>>>End of THEIR version
Recipe: edit the file to the content you want, DELETE the marker lines, then git add the resolved file ("I've handled it") and git commit to complete the merge. git status lists conflicted files.
⚠️ REMOVE THE MARKERS
You must delete the marker lines yourself — leaving <<<<<<< in the file will break your code.
🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
A merge conflict occurs when:
  1. The same lines were changed on both branches
  2. Any two branches are merged
  3. You forget to push
  4. The repo is too large
Show answer + steps
A. Only OVERLAPPING line changes conflict — different areas merge cleanly.
📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)

Merge conflicts

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A merge conflict happens when two branches changed the same lines of the same file differently, and Git can't know which you want. It's not an error — it's Git honestly asking you to decide. You edit the file to the version you want, then finish the merge.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Git marks the clash inside the file with <<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>>. Above the ======= is your branch's version; below is theirs. You edit the file to keep the right content and delete the marker lines.

Then git add the resolved file (telling Git “I've handled it”) and git commit to complete the merge. Git only flags conflicts on the same lines; changes to different parts merge automatically.

📝 EXAM WORDING

A merge conflict occurs when the same lines were changed on both branches. Git inserts conflict markers (<<<<<<< ======= >>>>>>>); you manually edit, then git add and git commit to resolve. git status lists conflicted files.

⚠️ WATCH OUT

Conflicts arise only from overlapping line changes — edits in different areas merge cleanly. You must remove the marker lines yourself; leaving <<<<<<< in the file will break your code.

📘 DEFINITION
A fast-forward merge happens when the branch you are merging into has not moved since you branched off. There is nothing to reconcile, so Git simply slides the pointer forward and creates no merge commit. Force a merge commit anyway with --no-ff when you want the branch to remain visible in the history.

Conflicts cannot occur in a fast-forward, precisely because only one side changed. When both sides have moved, Git must build a merge commit, and that is when conflicts become possible. If you check out a commit rather than a branch during any of this, you are in detached HEAD: commits made there belong to no branch.

Undoing: reset vs revert vs checkout

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Three different “undo” tools that people constantly mix up. checkout/restore = throw away un-committed edits in your working files. reset = move the branch pointer backward (rewrites history). revert = make a NEW commit that cancels out an old one (safe, keeps history). The safe one for shared work is revert.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

git checkout / git restore <file>: discards uncommitted changes to that file, restoring the last committed version.

git reset: moves the current branch pointer to an earlier commit. --soft keeps changes staged, --mixed (default) unstages them, --hard discards them entirely. Rewrites history — use on local, unshared commits.

git revert <commit>: creates a new commit that undoes a past commit's changes, without erasing history. The safe way to undo something already pushed.

📝 EXAM WORDING

revert = new commit that undoes a prior one (history-safe, use for pushed commits); reset = move the branch pointer back (rewrites history, local use); checkout/restore = discard working-directory changes. reset --hard also discards working changes — destructive.

⚠️ WATCH OUT

Use revert, not reset, on commits others already have — reset rewrites shared history and causes chaos. And git reset --hard permanently discards uncommitted work; there's often no undo.

Clone vs fork

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Both make a copy of a repo, but for different reasons. A clone is a local working copy on your machine, still linked to the original. A fork is your own server-side copy of someone else's project (on GitHub/GitLab), so you can change it freely without touching theirs.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

git clone <url> downloads a full copy to your computer and links it to the original as “origin.” You clone to work on a repo you have access to.

A fork (a platform feature, not a git command) copies the whole repo into YOUR account on the server. You then clone your fork, make changes, and propose them back to the original via a pull request. This is the standard open-source contribution flow.

📝 EXAM WORDING

clone = a local copy linked to the remote (a git command); fork = your own server-side copy of another's repo (a GitHub/GitLab feature). The open-source flow: fork → clone your fork → change → pull request back to the original.

⚠️ WATCH OUT

Clone is local and via git; fork is server-side and via the platform (GitHub/GitLab). You typically clone your fork — the two work together in the contribution workflow.

A clone can have multiple remotes. Cloning gives you one, named origin by default — that name is a convention Git applies, not a rule. When you fork a project, the usual arrangement is origin for your own fork and upstream for the project you forked from, added with git remote add upstream <url>, so you can pull in their changes while pushing to yours.

.gitignore & tracked vs untracked

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Not every file belongs in version control — build outputs, secrets, huge binaries, and IDE settings just clutter history. A .gitignore file lists patterns Git should pretend it doesn't see, so they never get committed by accident.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Important gotcha: .gitignore only affects untracked files. If a file is already tracked, adding it to .gitignore does nothing until you untrack it (git rm --cached).

📝 EXAM WORDING

A .gitignore file lists patterns Git should not track (build artifacts, secrets, dependencies). Files are tracked, untracked, or ignored. Common entries: *.log, node_modules/, .env. .gitignore only affects files not already tracked.

⚠️ WATCH OUT

Adding an already-committed file to .gitignore won't stop tracking it — you must git rm --cached it first. And never commit secrets (API keys, passwords); once pushed, they're in history.

git status is the command that reports which files are untracked, which are modified, and which are staged — it is the answer to nearly every "how do you check" question in this section.

Adding a file to .gitignore after it has already been committed does nothing: .gitignore only affects untracked files. Stop tracking it first with git rm --cached <file>, then commit that removal.

Stash, tags & cherry-pick

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Three useful power tools. Stash shelves unfinished work so you can switch tasks and come back. Tags put a permanent label on a commit (like a release version). Cherry-pick copies one specific commit from another branch without merging everything.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

git stash saves your uncommitted changes and reverts your working directory to clean; git stash pop brings them back. Great for “I need to switch branches but I'm mid-change.”

git tag v1.0 marks a commit permanently — used for releases. git cherry-pick <hash> applies the changes from one specific commit onto your current branch (handy for grabbing a single fix).

📝 EXAM WORDING

git stash shelves uncommitted changes (restore with stash pop); git tag labels a commit (releases like v1.0); git cherry-pick copies one specific commit onto the current branch. Tags are commonly annotated (with metadata) or lightweight.

⚠️ WATCH OUT

Stash is temporary and local — don't rely on it as long-term storage. Cherry-pick copies ONE commit's changes (creating a new commit), it doesn't merge the whole branch.

✅ Pull Requests, Review & CI/CD

THE TEAM FLOW
On a team you don't just push to main. You open a pull request (GitLab: merge request) proposing your branch, teammates REVIEW it, automated checks run — only then does it merge. This catches bugs before they hit the shared codebase.
TermDefinition

Pull requests, review & CI/CD

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

On a team you don't just push to main. You open a pull request (or merge request) proposing your branch be merged, teammates review it, automated checks run, and only then does it merge. This catches bugs before they hit the shared codebase.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

A pull request (PR) / merge request bundles your branch's changes for review and discussion. Reviewers comment, request changes, and approve. This is where code review happens.

CI/CD automation runs on each PR: Continuous Integration builds the code and runs tests automatically; Continuous Delivery/Deployment automatically ships passing code to staging/production. A failing CI check blocks the merge.

📝 EXAM WORDING

A pull request (GitLab: merge request) proposes merging a branch, enabling code review and discussion before merging. CI = automatically build + test on each change; CD = automatically deliver/deploy passing builds. A pipeline runs these automated stages; a red check blocks the merge.

⚠️ WATCH OUT

GitHub calls it a “pull request,” GitLab calls it a “merge request” — same idea. CI (integrate/test) and CD (deliver/deploy) are distinct stages; “the pipeline failed” means an automated check blocked the merge.

The purpose of a pull request (GitHub) or merge request (GitLab) — the two names describe the same thing — is review and traceability before code reaches a shared branch: a place to discuss the change, a record of who approved it, and a gate that automated checks must pass first.

CI/CD stands for Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery (or Continuous Deployment). CI builds and tests every push; Continuous Delivery keeps every passing build ready to release with a human approving the release itself, while Continuous Deployment releases automatically with no manual step.

🔬 GOING DEEPER — why Git is built the way it is

Centralized vs distributed

In a centralized system (SVN, CVS) there is one server holding the history; your machine has only a working copy. Lose the server and you lose the history; lose the network and you cannot commit or view the log.

Git is distributed: git clone copies the entire repository, with full history, to your machine. Three consequences follow, and they explain most of Git's behavior:

  • Committing and sharing are separate steps. This is the thing that confuses people coming from SVN: git commit saves to your repository, and only git push sends it anywhere.

The three trees

Git tracks three areas, and nearly every command is explained by which of them it moves data between:

  2. Staging area (index) — what you have marked to go into the next commit.

Many systems store a file plus a list of changes over time. Git stores a snapshot of the whole project at each commit. Files that did not change are not duplicated — the new snapshot simply points at the identical existing object, which is why full snapshots are not wasteful.

This is why checking out any commit is fast and exact: Git does not have to replay a chain of deltas, it just reads that snapshot.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Git's SHA-1 hashing is how it guarantees data integrity. Any bit flip, any corruption, any tampering produces a different hash — Git detects it immediately. Understanding Git objects explains what's really happening under the hood when you commit.

SHA-1 Integrity

Every file, tree, and commit in Git is identified by a SHA-1 hash — a 40-character hex string computed from the content. Any byte change produces a completely different hash. This makes Git a content-addressed storage system.

Commit A stores: content + author + timestamp + message + parent's hash
→ Parent's hash is embedded in child's hash
→ Changing any historical commit changes all subsequent hashes
→ History is immutable and tamper-evident

  • Blob: file content. Tree: directory. Commit: snapshot. Tag: named pointer.

- Same content → same hash (deduplication for free)
- Change ONE byte → totally different hash
- A commit's hash covers its tree AND its parent's hash
  → changing ANY historical file changes every later commit hash
  → history is TAMPER-EVIDENT. That's the integrity guarantee.

Git has 4 object types: blob (file content), tree (a directory), commit (snapshot + parent(s) + message), tag. Every object is named by the SHA-1 of its content (40 hex chars), so identical content is stored once and any change flips the hash.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
echo 'hi'  > f  -> blob hash X
