🔬 GOING DEEPER — the object model — and why hashes matter

Four object types

  • Blob — the contents of one file. No filename, no metadata; just bytes.
  • Tree — a directory listing: names, permissions, and the blob or tree each name points to.
  • Commit — one tree (the snapshot), one or more parent commits, author, committer, timestamps and the message.
  • Tag — an annotated tag object pointing at a commit.

Content addressing

Every object's name is the SHA-1 hash of its contents. Two files with identical content produce the same hash, so Git stores them once — the same mechanism that makes full snapshots cheap.

It also makes history tamper-evident. A commit's hash is computed over its tree, its parent hash, and its metadata — so changing anything about a commit changes its hash, and because the next commit records the old parent hash, every descendant hash changes too.

The consequence you must carry into every later unit

Git cannot edit a commit. Commands that appear to modify history — commit --amend, rebase, cherry-pick — actually create new commits with new hashes and move a pointer to them. The originals still exist, unreferenced, until garbage collection.

That single fact explains: why the reflog can recover "lost" work, why rebasing shared branches causes chaos (everyone else still has the old hashes), and why an amended commit cannot be pushed normally after it was already published.

Refs are just pointers

A branch is a tiny file containing one commit hash. That is the whole implementation. It is why creating a branch is instantaneous regardless of project size, and why deleting a branch destroys no commits — it only removes a label.

📊 FIGURE — the four object types, and what each one points at

A commit hash is 40 hexadecimal characters (Git will accept an unambiguous short prefix, usually 7). The hash is computed from the content, which is what gives Git its immutability: you cannot alter a commit. Commands that appear to edit history — amend, rebase — build new objects with new hashes and move the branch pointer to them. The originals sit untouched until garbage collection removes what nothing references.

Merge vs rebase is one of the most important decisions in team Git workflows. Merge preserves history accurately; rebase creates clean linear history but rewrites hashes. Misusing rebase on a shared branch is one of the most damaging things you can do to a team's repository.

Creates a merge commit combining two branch histories. Non-destructive — original commits unchanged. Shows exactly when branches diverged and were combined. Safe to use on shared branches.

Fast-forward merge: when the target branch has no new commits since the feature branched off, Git simply moves the pointer forward. No merge commit created.

Replays your commits on top of another branch, rewriting each commit's hash. Creates a clean linear history — looks as if you branched from the latest commit. Useful for cleaning up messy feature branch history before a PR.

Never rebase commits that have been pushed to a shared branch. Rebase rewrites hashes. Rebase is safe ONLY on commits that exist only in your local repo.

How a merge actually works

Git finds the merge base — the most recent commit both branches share — then performs a three-way merge: base versus yours versus theirs. Changes in different places combine automatically; changes to the same lines produce a conflict.

The result is a merge commit with two parents. Nothing is rewritten: both original histories remain intact, which is why merging is the safe, non-destructive option and why the graph shows what really happened.

How a rebase actually works

Rebase takes your commits, sets them aside, moves your branch to the tip of the target, and replays each change on top. Because a commit's hash covers its parent, every replayed commit is a brand-new commit with a new hash — the originals are orphaned.

You get a clean linear history with no merge commits, at the cost of a history that no longer reflects the real sequence of events.

The golden rule

Never rebase commits that other people already have. Their repositories still reference the old hashes; your rewritten branch has different ones, so Git sees two divergent histories and every collaborator gets conflicts and duplicate commits. Rebase freely on your own unpublished work; merge when the branch is shared.

Resolving a conflict

Git marks the file with <<<<<<< HEAD, your version, =======, their version, >>>>>>>. You edit the file to the intended final state — deleting the markers — then git add it to mark it resolved, then git commit (merge) or git rebase --continue.

Two escapes worth knowing: git merge --abort and git rebase --abort return you to exactly where you started. Conflicts are never a point of no return.

Choosing

Scenario questions turn on one thing: has this branch been shared? Shared → merge. Private cleanup before a pull request → rebase.

🔬 GOING DEEPER — cherry-pick, interactive rebase and team workflows

Cherry-pick

git cherry-pick <hash> applies the changes introduced by one commit onto your current branch as a new commit with a new hash. Use it for a hotfix that must land on both a release branch and main, or to rescue one useful commit from an abandoned branch.

The cost is duplication: the same change now exists as two distinct commits, which can cause conflicts if those branches are later merged. Cherry-pick deliberately, not as a substitute for merging.

Interactive rebase — history as a draft

git rebase -i HEAD~5 opens the last five commits with an action for each:

  • pick — keep as is
  • reword — change the message
  • squash / fixup — fold into the previous commit (fixup discards the message)
  • drop — remove the commit
  • reorder by moving the lines

The purpose is to turn a messy working sequence — "wip", "fix typo", "actually fix it" — into a few clean, reviewable commits before anyone sees them. Same golden rule: only on unpublished history.

Workflows, and what each optimizes for

  • Centralized — everyone commits to main. Simple, but no isolation; suits tiny teams.
  • Feature branch / GitHub flow — a short-lived branch per change, merged via pull request. The common default: isolation plus review, with little ceremony.
  • GitFlow — long-lived develop, release and hotfix branches alongside main. Powerful for scheduled versioned releases; heavy for continuous delivery.
  • Trunk-based — very short branches merged to main daily, behind feature flags. Optimizes for continuous integration and fast feedback.

Scenario questions describe the release cadence and team size; match the workflow to that rather than to a favourite.

git cherry-pick <hash> applies the change from one commit onto the branch you are on now, as a new commit. Use it to take a single fix from a branch you do not want to merge in full.

The copy normally gets a different hash, because the hash covers the parent as well as the change — and the parent is different. Worth knowing precisely: if you cherry-pick onto a commit that is the original's parent, everything hashed is identical and you get the same hash back. The change of hash is a consequence, not a rule.

Remote-tracking branches

🔬 GOING DEEPER — fetch, pull, push — and why a push gets rejected

fetch vs pull

git fetch downloads new commits and updates your remote-tracking branches only. Your working branch and files are untouched — it is always safe. git pull is fetch plus an immediate merge (or rebase with --rebase) into your current branch.

The professional habit is fetch first, look, then integrate: git fetch then git log --oneline HEAD..origin/main shows exactly what arrived before you let it touch your work.

Why a push is rejected

Git refuses a push when the remote branch has commits you do not have — accepting it would discard someone else's work. That is the entire meaning of "non-fast-forward" and "fetch first."

The correct fix is to integrate first: git pull (merge or rebase), resolve anything that conflicts, then push. The dangerous "fix" is --force, which overwrites the remote branch and deletes whatever was there. If you must, --force-with-lease refuses to overwrite when the remote moved since your last fetch — it is the seatbelt version, and knowing the difference is exam-worthy.

Tracking branches

git push -u origin feature sets the upstream for that branch. After that, bare git push and git pull know where to go, and git status can tell you how far ahead or behind you are. Without it Git asks you to name the remote and branch every time.

Deleting

git push origin --delete feature removes the branch on the server. Deleting your local branch does not remove the remote one, and vice versa — they are independent pointers, and stale remote-tracking refs are cleaned up with git fetch --prune.

📊 FIGURE — fetch updates origin/main; merge moves YOUR main
📘 DEFINITION
A remote-tracking branch such as origin/main is your local record of where that branch stood on the remote the last time you talked to it. It lives under refs/remotes/, and you never commit to it — it moves only when you fetch, pull or push. Its partner is the upstream: the remote branch your local branch is set to compare against, which is what lets Git say "your branch is ahead by 2 commits".

git pull is fetch followed by merge. git pull --rebase substitutes rebase for that second step, which is how you get linear integration — your local commits are replayed on top of what you fetched instead of being tied in with a merge commit.

🎯 EXAM TIP
Set the upstream the first time with git push -u origin <branch>; after that plain git push and git pull know where to go. If a question says "the branch has no upstream", -u is the answer.

WGU's Version Control course and its performance assessment use GitLab. On GitLab, a request to merge one branch into another is called a merge request (MR) — GitHub calls the exact same thing a pull request (PR). On the OA, if you see \"merge request,\" think GitLab; \"pull request,\" think GitHub — both mean review-then-merge.

DevOps & CI/CD

DevOps combines Development and Operations into one culture and toolchain so software is built, tested, and released quickly and reliably. CI (Continuous Integration) means every push is automatically built and tested; CD (Continuous Delivery/Deployment) means passing changes are automatically released. GitLab runs these through a pipeline defined in a .gitlab-ci.yml file, and a merge request typically must pass its pipeline (build + automated tests) before it can be merged.

🔬 GOING DEEPER — pull requests, review and CI/CD

What a pull request adds

A pull request (GitHub) or merge request (GitLab) is not a Git feature — it is a platform workflow around a merge. It proposes merging one branch into another and creates the place where review, automated checks and discussion happen before the merge is allowed.

The value is process: a second pair of eyes, an audit trail of why a change was made, and an automated gate that runs before anything reaches main.

Branch protection

Protected branches enforce the process technically rather than by good intentions: no direct pushes to main, at least one approving review, status checks must pass, and often no force-pushing. Scenario questions about "how do we stop unreviewed code reaching production" are answered by branch protection.

CI vs CD — keep them distinct

  • Continuous Integration — every push triggers an automated build and test run, so integration problems surface within minutes instead of at release.
  • Continuous Delivery — every change that passes CI is ready to deploy; the release itself is a manual decision.
  • Continuous Deployment — passing changes deploy to production automatically, with no human step.

Delivery vs deployment is exactly the presence or absence of that manual approval, and it is a favourite distinction to test.

The pipeline

A typical pipeline runs: build → unit tests → integration tests → security/lint scans → deploy to staging → deploy to production. It is triggered by a push or a PR, and a failure at any stage stops the pipeline and reports back on the request. Fast feedback is the whole point, which is why unit tests run first — the cheapest checks should fail earliest.

A pull request on GitHub and a merge request on GitLab are the same thing under different names: a request to merge one branch into another, with a place to discuss it, an automatic record of who approved it, and a gate that CI must pass first. 🔬 GOING DEEPER — the reflog — why nothing is really lost

What the reflog records

Every time HEAD moves — commit, checkout, merge, rebase, reset — Git appends an entry to the reflog. It is a local, private journal of where you have been, and it exists precisely because the commands that appear destructive only move pointers.

Remember the object model: commits are immutable and content-addressed, so a "deleted" commit is still in the object database — it has simply lost every reference pointing to it. The reflog is a reference that survives, which is what makes recovery possible.

The recovery procedure

  1. git reflog — read the list; each line shows a hash and what moved HEAD there (HEAD@{2}: reset: moving to HEAD~3).
  2. Identify the hash from before the mistake.
  3. git reset --hard <hash> to return the branch there, or git branch rescue <hash> to recover it under a new name without disturbing your current branch.

This recovers work lost to a bad hard reset, a botched rebase, a deleted branch, or commits stranded in a detached HEAD.

Its limits — worth knowing honestly

  • The reflog is local. It is not cloned or pushed, so it cannot recover someone else's lost work.
  • Entries expire (roughly 90 days by default) and unreachable objects are eventually garbage-collected.
  • It only tracks committed work. Uncommitted changes destroyed by reset --hard or checkout are genuinely gone — which is the real argument for committing or stashing often.
📊 FIGURE — reflog remembers where HEAD has been, even when nothing points there

Deleting a branch or resetting hard does not delete commits. It only removes the thing that pointed at them. The commits stay in the object database, and the reflog keeps a local record of every position HEAD has held — so they are still reachable through it.

Two limits matter. The reflog is local only: it is never cloned, fetched or pushed, so it cannot rescue anyone else. And entries expire — by default after 90 days for reachable entries and 30 for unreachable ones, after which garbage collection may remove the objects for good.

🎯 EXAM TIP
The syntax is HEAD@{n} — "where HEAD was n moves ago" — and it is a position in the reflog, not a commit ancestor. Do not confuse HEAD@{2} (two moves ago) with HEAD~2 (two commits back in the history).

commit --amend

🔬 GOING DEEPER — stash, bisect and revert — the situational tools

Stash

git stash takes your uncommitted changes, saves them aside, and returns the working directory to a clean state. It solves one specific problem: you need to switch branches right now but your work is not ready to commit.

Practicalities that get tested: git stash pop applies the most recent stash and removes it, while git stash apply keeps it in the list; the stash is a stack, so multiple stashes are addressed as stash@{0}, stash@{1}; and by default it does not include untracked files unless you pass -u.

Bisect — binary search over history

When a bug appeared somewhere in the last few hundred commits, git bisect finds the culprit in about log₂(n) steps — roughly 10 tests for 1,000 commits, versus checking them one by one.

The procedure: git bisect start, mark a known bad commit and a known good one, and Git checks out the midpoint. You test and answer git bisect good or bad; it halves the range each time until it names the first bad commit. Finish with git bisect reset. This is literally the binary search from your algorithms course applied to a commit graph — and it requires the same precondition, an ordered range with a single transition point.

Revert

git revert <hash> creates a new commit undoing that commit's changes. History is preserved and the record shows both the original change and its withdrawal — which is what makes it safe on shared branches and appropriate for production rollbacks.

Reverting a merge commit needs -m 1 to say which parent is the mainline, since Git otherwise cannot tell which side to keep.

📊 FIGURE — bisect halves the search every time

git bisect is a binary search over history. You mark a known good commit and a known bad one; Git checks out the midpoint, you test and say git bisect good or git bisect bad, and it halves the range each time until one commit is left. Finish with git bisect reset to return to where you were.

📘 DEFINITION
Stash puts uncommitted work aside so you can switch branches with a clean tree. git stash pop reapplies the most recent entry and deletes it from the stash list; git stash apply reapplies it but keeps it. Use apply when you want the same changes on more than one branch.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Match the tool to the situation: revert to undo something already pushed (it adds a commit and rewrites nothing), reset to undo local work not yet shared, reflog to recover from a reset you regret, and bisect to find which commit introduced a bug.

📖 Learn it step by step — Submodules (a repo pinned inside a repo)

A submodule embeds another Git repository inside yours at a fixed folder — and pins it to an exact commit, not a branch. Your repo stores just the pointer (URL + commit hash), never the library’s files themselves.

WORKED EXAMPLE — add, clone, and update a submodule
git submodule add https://example.com/lib.git lib
git commit -m "Add lib as submodule"
This creates the lib/ folder and a .gitmodules file recording the mapping. Your commit stores “lib = that repo AT commit abc123.”

A teammate clones and sees an EMPTY lib/ folder unless they run:
git clone --recurse-submodules https://example.com/app.git
# or, after a plain clone:
git submodule update --init
To move the pin to the library’s newest commit: git submodule update --remote, then commit the changed pointer in YOUR repo.
⚠️ THE PIN DOES NOT FOLLOW THE BRANCH
A submodule stays at its recorded commit even when the library’s remote moves ahead — that’s the point (reproducible builds). The classic exam facts: empty folder after a plain clone (needs --init), and updating the library = committing a new pointer in the outer repo.

Submodules — repos inside repos

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A submodule lets one Git repo contain another Git repo as a subdirectory, pinned to a specific commit. Think of it as a bookmark: your project doesn't copy the library's code into its own history — it records "use this exact commit of that other repo."

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

git submodule add <url> path/ clones the other repo into path/ and records the pointer in a .gitmodules file plus a special "gitlink" entry. The parent repo tracks only the submodule's commit hash, not its files.

After cloning a repo that HAS submodules, they start empty. You must run git submodule init then git submodule update (or clone with --recurse-submodules) to fill them.

THE PINNED-COMMIT MODEL
The parent repo points at ONE commit of the submodule. Updating the library is deliberate: you cd into the submodule, checkout a newer commit, then commit that pointer change in the parent. This keeps builds reproducible — everyone gets the exact same dependency commit.
📝 EXAM WORDING

.gitmodules stores each submodule's URL and path. A clone needs git submodule update --init (or clone --recurse-submodules) to populate them. The parent tracks the submodule's commit hash, not its contents. Submodules are for including a separate, independently-versioned repo — not for splitting your own project.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Cloning normally leaves submodule folders EMPTY. Forgetting git submodule update --init is the #1 submodule gotcha — the build fails because the dependency's files aren't there.

🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
After a plain `git clone` of a repo with submodules, the submodule folders are empty. Why?
  1. The clone failed
  2. Submodules must be initialized/updated separately
  3. Submodules are deprecated
  4. You need admin rights
Show answer
B. A normal clone records the submodule pointers but doesn't fetch their contents; run git submodule update --init (or clone with --recurse-submodules).
🔬 GOING DEEPER — submodules — repositories inside repositories

What a submodule stores

A submodule embeds another repository inside yours. The critical detail: your repository records only the URL and one specific commit hash of the submodule — not its files. Your project is pinned to that exact commit, which is the point: reproducible builds against a known version of a shared library.

Why cloning "loses" the files

A plain git clone leaves submodule directories empty, because the submodule's content is not part of your repository. You need git clone --recurse-submodules, or git submodule update --init --recursive afterwards. This is far and away the most common submodule question, and the most common real-world stumble.

Updating

The submodule does not follow its own branch automatically. To move to a newer version you enter the submodule, check out the commit you want, then commit that pointer change in the parent repository — the parent's commit records "now use this hash." Forgetting the second step means the update exists only on your machine.

When to use something else

Submodules are right for genuinely separate projects with independent release cycles. They add real friction to everyday work, so for shared code within one team a package manager (npm, Maven, pip) or a monorepo is usually the better answer. Recognizing that trade-off is what a scenario question is testing.

📊 FIGURE — a submodule is a pinned commit, not a copy of the code
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Reading a submodule change in a diff

A commit that updates a submodule shows only this:

-Subproject commit 9f2c4d1a…
+Subproject commit 3b7e88f2…
  1. No file contents appear, because none changed in the parent.
  2. The parent is simply now pinned to a different commit of the submodule.
  3. To see what actually changed, look at that range inside the submodule itself.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Why a fresh clone has empty submodule folders
  1. git clone alone creates the directories but does not fill them.
  2. The parent recorded a commit hash; nothing fetched that repository yet.
  3. git submodule update --init --recursive clones each one and checks out the exact recorded commit.
  4. That leaves the submodule in detached HEAD — it is on a commit, not a branch, which is exactly what pinning means.
🎯 EXAM TIP
The two facts that get tested: the parent stores one commit hash (so the dependency cannot drift), and a submodule checkout sits in detached HEAD. To move it, commit inside the submodule, then commit the new pointer in the parent.

📖 Learn it step by step — Git Hooks (scripts that fire on events)

WHAT HOOKS ARE
Executable scripts in .git/hooks/ that Git runs automatically at lifecycle moments:
• pre-commit — before a commit is created; a non-zero exit ABORTS the commit (lint/tests gate).
• commit-msg — validates/edits the message (enforce “starts with a ticket number”).
• pre-push — last check before upload.
• Server-side (pre-receive) hooks enforce team policy centrally.
WORKED EXAMPLE — a pre-commit hook that blocks debug prints
# .git/hooks/pre-commit   (make it executable!)
#!/bin/sh
if git diff --cached | grep -q "console.log"; then
    echo "Remove console.log before committing."
    exit 1        # non-zero = commit REFUSED
fi
exit 0
Stage a file containing console.log and try to commit: the hook prints the warning and the commit never happens. Fix the file, commit again — clean. Automated discipline, no memory required.
⚠️ HOOKS DON’T TRAVEL
.git/hooks/ is NOT cloned or pushed — each developer’s hooks are local. Teams share them via a scripts/ folder + setup step, or enforce on the server side. “Why didn’t my teammate’s hook run for me?” — because hooks never left their machine.
🎯 QUICK CHECK
A pre-commit hook exiting with a non-zero status:
  1. Aborts the commit
  2. Commits anyway with a warning
  3. Deletes the hook
Show answer
A — the commit is refused until the script passes (or is bypassed with --no-verify).

Git hooks — automating your workflow

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A hook is a script Git runs automatically at a certain moment — before a commit, after a merge, before a push. They let you enforce rules (run tests, check formatting, block bad commit messages) without anyone remembering to do it manually.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Hooks live in the .git/hooks/ directory. Each is an executable script named for its trigger. Git ships .sample versions; remove the .sample suffix and make it executable to activate.

They split into client-side (run on your machine — commit, merge, push events) and server-side (run on the remote — pre-receive, update, post-receive — to accept/reject pushes centrally).

COMMON HOOKS
HookFiresTypical use
pre-commitBefore the commit is createdRun linters/tests; abort commit if they fail
commit-msgAfter the message is writtenEnforce a message format
pre-pushBefore a push runsRun the test suite before sharing
post-mergeAfter a successful mergeReinstall dependencies
pre-receive (server)When the remote receives a pushReject commits violating policy
EXIT CODE = ACCEPT OR REJECT
A hook that exits with 0 lets the action continue; a non-zero exit aborts it. That's how pre-commit can stop a commit when tests fail.
📝 EXAM WORDING

Hooks live in .git/hooks/ and are NOT copied by a clone or pushed to the remote (they're local by design). Client-side hooks (pre-commit, commit-msg, pre-push) run on your machine; server-side hooks (pre-receive, update, post-receive) run on the remote. Non-zero exit cancels the operation.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Because hooks aren't version-controlled or cloned, you can't rely on teammates having them. Teams use tools (or a tracked hooks folder + core.hooksPath) to share them. Don't assume a pre-commit check runs on everyone's machine.

🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
A pre-commit hook exits with code 1. What happens?
  1. The commit proceeds anyway
  2. The commit is aborted
  3. Git ignores the hook
  4. The repo is deleted
Show answer
B. A non-zero exit from pre-commit aborts the commit — the mechanism for blocking commits that fail checks.
🔬 GOING DEEPER — hooks — automation at the Git level

What hooks are

Hooks are scripts Git runs automatically at defined points. They live in .git/hooks/, must be executable, and — importantly — are not cloned, because .git/ is local. That is a deliberate security decision: cloning a repository must never execute someone else's code on your machine.

Because they are not shared, teams distribute them through a tracked directory plus a setup step, or a tool like Husky or pre-commit.

Client-side hooks

  • pre-commit — runs before the commit is created; exiting non-zero aborts it. The usual home for linting, formatting and fast tests.
  • commit-msg — validates the message, e.g. enforcing a ticket number or conventional-commit format.
  • pre-push — last check before code leaves your machine; a good place for the test suite.

Server-side hooks

pre-receive and update run on the server and can reject a push outright — the only way to truly enforce a policy, since client hooks can be skipped with --no-verify. That distinction is the exam point: client hooks are a convenience for the developer; server hooks are enforcement.

Using them sensibly

Keep pre-commit hooks fast. A hook that takes 30 seconds trains people to bypass it, and a bypassed hook enforces nothing. Slow, thorough checks belong in CI, where they do not block typing.

📊 FIGURE — where each hook fires
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A pre-commit hook that blocks a bad commit
  1. Create .git/hooks/pre-commit and make it executable (chmod +x) — Git ignores a hook it cannot execute.
  2. The script runs the linter over the staged files.
  3. It ends with exit 0 to allow the commit, or any non-zero exit to abort it.
  4. That exit status is the whole interface: non-zero stops the operation.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Sharing hooks with the team
  1. .git/hooks is not part of the repository, so a clone gets none of it.
  2. Commit the scripts to a tracked folder such as .githooks/.
  3. Point Git at it: git config core.hooksPath .githooks.
  4. Now the hooks are versioned and reviewed like any other file.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Two points carry most questions: hooks are local and not cloned, and a non-zero exit aborts the operation. Anything that must apply to everyone belongs in CI, not in a hook — a hook can always be bypassed with --no-verify.

📖 Learn it step by step — Worktrees (two checkouts, one repository)

A worktree gives you a SECOND working directory attached to the SAME repository — so you can have main checked out in one folder and a feature branch in another, without cloning twice or stashing anything.

WORKED EXAMPLE — hotfix while mid-feature
You’re knee-deep in messy changes on feature-x when an urgent bug report lands. Instead of stashing:
git worktree add ../hotfix main
Now ../hotfix is a real working directory with main checked out. Fix the bug there, commit, push — then just keep working in your original folder, untouched. When done:
git worktree remove ../hotfix
git worktree list      # see all attached worktrees
Both folders share ONE .git object store — commits made in either are instantly visible to both.
⚠️ ONE BRANCH PER WORKTREE
The same branch cannot be checked out in two worktrees at once (Git blocks it — two folders writing one branch would corrupt it). And prefer git worktree remove over deleting the folder by hand, so Git’s bookkeeping stays clean.

Worktrees — multiple working directories, one repo

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Normally a repo has ONE working directory, so switching branches means stashing or committing whatever you're in the middle of. A worktree lets you check out a second branch into a separate folder that shares the same repository — so you can work on two branches at once without stashing.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

git worktree add ../hotfix main creates a new folder ../hotfix with main checked out, linked to the same .git database. Commits you make there go into the same repo. git worktree list shows all worktrees; git worktree remove <path> cleans one up.

ONE BRANCH PER WORKTREE
A branch can be checked out in only ONE worktree at a time. Try to check out a branch that's already active in another worktree and Git refuses — this prevents two folders from fighting over the same branch pointer.
📝 EXAM WORDING

git worktree add <path> <branch> checks a branch out into a new linked folder sharing one .git. Use it to fix an urgent bug on main while a big feature stays checked out elsewhere — no stashing, no second clone. Each branch can be active in only one worktree at a time.

🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
Why use a worktree instead of stashing to fix an urgent bug?
  1. It compresses history
  2. You can work on a second branch in a separate folder without disturbing your current work
  3. It deletes the other branch
  4. It is required for pushing
Show answer
B. A worktree checks out another branch into its own folder sharing the same repo, so your in-progress work stays untouched — no stash needed.
🔬 GOING DEEPER — worktrees — several branches checked out at once

The problem they solve

Normally one repository has one working directory, so viewing another branch means switching — which forces you to commit or stash whatever you are in the middle of. git worktree add ../hotfix main creates a second working directory for the same repository, checked out to a different branch.

The classic use: an urgent hotfix arrives while your feature is half-finished. Instead of stashing, you open a second directory, fix and push from there, and return to your untouched feature work.

Why this is better than a second clone

Worktrees share one object database. A second clone duplicates the entire history on disk and keeps its own remotes and branches to synchronize. Worktrees cost only the checked-out files, and every branch, commit and stash is immediately visible from all of them.

The rules

  • A branch can be checked out in only one worktree at a time — Git refuses a duplicate checkout, which prevents two directories writing the same branch.
  • Remove a worktree with git worktree remove, and clean stale entries with git worktree prune. Deleting the folder by hand leaves the registration behind.
📊 FIGURE — one repository, several working directories
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Fixing an urgent bug without disturbing what you are doing
  1. You are mid-change with a dirty working tree; switching branches would mean stashing.
  2. git worktree add ../app-hotfix hotfix creates a second directory checked out on hotfix.
  3. Your original directory is untouched — edits, build output and all.
  4. Fix, commit and push from the new directory, then come back.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Adding a worktree with no branch name
  1. git worktree add ../review — no branch given.
  2. Git creates a branch implicitly, named after the directory (review), and checks it out there.
  3. To remove it cleanly, use git worktree remove ../review rather than deleting the folder: that unregisters it as well as deleting it.
  4. If a folder was already deleted by hand, git worktree prune clears the stale registration.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Deleting a worktree folder with rm -rf. Git still lists it and still considers its branch checked out, so you cannot check that branch out elsewhere until you run git worktree prune.
🎯 EXAM TIP
The rule that gets tested: the same branch cannot be checked out in two worktrees at once. Git refuses, because two directories moving one branch pointer would be incoherent.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
git worktree remove refuses when the worktree still holds modified or untracked files — "use --force to delete it". That refusal is Git protecting unsaved work, so the fix is to deal with the work first: commit it, stash it, or deliberately discard it, then remove again. Reach for --force only when you actually mean to throw the changes away. Never delete the folder by hand — that leaves stale bookkeeping behind, which git worktree prune then has to clean up.

WORKED EXAMPLE — “who changed this line, and why?”
git blame config.yml
# ^a1b2c3 (Maria 2026-05-02) timeout: 30
#  d4e5f6 (Jon   2026-07-11) timeout: 5     ← the suspicious change

git show d4e5f6          # the full commit: diff + message ("Speed up tests")
git log -S "timeout" --oneline    # every commit that ADDED/REMOVED that text
blame answers WHO+WHEN per line; show reveals the WHY (message + full diff); log -S (“pickaxe”) traces a string’s whole life across history. Together they turn “the config broke” into “Jon lowered the timeout on July 11 to speed up tests.”
THE DETECTIVE TOOLKIT
• git log --oneline --graph --all — the shape of history.
• git log -- file.txt — commits touching one file.
• git log --author=Maria --since="2 weeks ago" — filter by who/when.
• git grep "TODO" — search the CURRENT tree; git grep "TODO" v1.0 — search an OLD version without checking it out.
⚠️ BLAME ISN’T ABOUT BLAME
git blame shows the LAST commit to touch each line — which may be a trivial reformat. Follow up with git show / log -S to find the meaningful change. (And use it to find context, not culprits.)

History forensics — blame, log detective work & grep

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

When something breaks, Git's history is a crime scene. A handful of read-only commands let you find who changed a line, when a bug appeared, and which commits touched a piece of code — without changing anything.

THE FORENSICS TOOLKIT
CommandAnswers
git blame <file>Who last changed each LINE, and in which commit
git log -pFull history WITH the diff of each commit
git log --oneline --graphCompact, visual branch/merge history
git log -S"text"Commits that ADDED or REMOVED that text (the "pickaxe")
git log -- <file>Only commits that touched that file
git show <hash>One commit's metadata AND its diff
git grep "text"Search the tracked files (current or any commit)
git bisectBinary-search commits to find the one that introduced a bug
⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

blame is per-line authorship: it prints each line prefixed with the commit, author, and date that last touched it — the fastest way to answer "who wrote this and why." Follow up with git show <that hash> to read the full commit.

bisect automates the hunt: mark a known-good and known-bad commit, and Git checks out the midpoint repeatedly (binary search) until it names the first bad commit — log n steps instead of checking every commit.

📝 EXAM WORDING

git blame = per-line last-change author/commit. git log -p = history with diffs; -S/--graph/-- file filter it. git show = one commit's details+diff. git bisect = binary search for the bug-introducing commit. All are read-only — they don't change your files.

🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
You need to know who last edited line 42 of App.java and in which commit. Best command?
  1. git log
  2. git blame App.java
  3. git status
  4. git diff
Show answer
B. git blame annotates every line with the commit, author, and date that last changed it — exactly per-line authorship.
🔬 GOING DEEPER — history forensics — finding when and why

blame — who last touched each line

git blame <file> annotates every line with the commit, author and date that last changed it. Its real value is not attribution but context: from the commit hash you reach the message, the rest of the change, and often the ticket explaining why.

The caveat worth knowing: reformatting or moving a file rewrites blame for every line touched, which is why cosmetic changes belong in their own commit — and why -w (ignore whitespace) exists.

Searching history

  • git log -S"functionName" — the pickaxe: finds commits where the number of occurrences of that string changed. This is how you find when a function was introduced or deleted.
  • git log -p <file> — the full change history of one file, with diffs.
  • git log --follow <file> — keeps tracking across renames.
  • git log --since / --author / --grep — narrow by time, person, or message text.
  • git grep <pattern> — search the working tree fast; add a commit to search that snapshot instead.

Choosing the right tool

The three techniques answer different questions, and matching them is the exam skill: blame = "who changed this line and why"; pickaxe log -S = "when did this code appear or vanish"; bisect = "which commit broke the behavior". Bisect is for behavior you can test; the others are for code you can read.

Why commit messages matter

All of this forensics depends on messages that explain intent. "fix" tells a future reader nothing; a subject line plus a short body explaining why the change was needed turns your history into documentation that never goes stale.

📊 FIGURE — four questions, four tools
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Reading blame output
3f06762f (Priya Raman 2025-03-14 12:04:51 +0000 42) return total * TAX_RATE;

  2. Priya Raman, and the date it landed.
  3. 42 — the line number in the current file.
  4. Then the line itself.

Blame answers "which commit last touched this line" — not "who wrote the logic". A reformat or a rename will make the whole file appear to be yours.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Blaming just the lines you care about

  4. Together these skip the reformat commits and reach the change that actually matters.
🎯 EXAM TIP
git log -S"someText" — the "pickaxe" — finds the commits where the number of occurrences of that string changed, which is how you locate where a function was introduced or deleted. Distinguish it from git log --grep, which searches commit messages rather than the code.

THE MOVING PARTS
• Project = repo + issues + MRs + pipeline, in one page.
• Roles: Guest < Reporter < Developer (push branches, open MRs) < Maintainer (merge to protected branches, settings) < Owner.
• Protected branch: main typically blocks direct pushes — changes arrive ONLY through merge requests. That’s policy, not a Git limitation.

1. Issue #42 “Fix login” is assigned to you.

4. Pipeline runs; reviewer comments; you push fixes (the MR updates automatically).
5. Maintainer merges. Issue closes. Branch deleted. The MR remains the permanent record.

  2. Delete branch 42

Collaborating on GitLab

📝 COURSE & PROJECT NOTE

D197 is built around GitLab and is assessed by a hands-on project (performance assessment) — you create a repo, branch, commit, merge, and set up a pipeline in GitLab, then submit it. There is no proctored multiple-choice OA; these checks build the concepts your project needs.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

GitLab is a web platform that hosts your Git repositories and adds team features on top: code review, issue tracking, and automated pipelines. It plays the same role GitHub does, but GitLab is the tool this course uses. The centerpiece of collaboration is the merge request.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

A merge request (MR) is GitLab's name for what GitHub calls a pull request: you push a feature branch and open an MR proposing to merge it into main. Teammates review the diff, comment, and the MR shows whether the pipeline passed. Only after review + green pipeline is it merged.

Protected branches (usually main) block direct pushes, forcing changes to go through an MR. GitLab member roles — Guest, Reporter, Developer, Maintainer, Owner — control who can push, merge, or administer the project.

GITHUB → GITLAB VOCABULARY
ConceptGitHub termGitLab term
Propose merging a branchPull Request (PR)Merge Request (MR)
Automated build/test configGitHub Actions (workflow).gitlab-ci.yml (pipeline)
Task/bug trackingIssuesIssues
THE TEAM FLOW
Clone → create a feature branch → commit → push → open a merge request → review + passing pipeline → merge to main → delete the branch. Protected main ensures nothing lands unreviewed.
🎯 CONCEPT CHECK
In GitLab, what is the equivalent of a GitHub pull request?
  1. A commit
  2. A merge request
  3. A runner
  4. A stage
Show answer
B. GitLab calls the propose-and-review-a-branch-merge feature a merge request (MR); GitHub calls it a pull request.
🔬 GOING DEEPER — collaborating on GitLab — roles and merge requests

The merge request as a control point

A GitLab merge request is the same idea as a GitHub pull request: a proposal to merge one branch into another, with review, discussion and automated checks attached. Nothing about Git requires it — it is the platform layer where a team's policy lives.

Useful mechanics: draft status signals work in progress and blocks merging; approvals can be required by count or by specific reviewers; squash on merge collapses a messy branch into one commit on the target; and delete source branch keeps the branch list from rotting.

Permission levels

GitLab grants access by role, and the exam expects you to match a role to a task:

  • Guest — view issues; no repository access.
  • Reporter — read the code; cannot push.
  • Developer — push to non-protected branches, open merge requests. The normal contributor role.
  • Maintainer — push to protected branches, manage settings, merge to main.
  • Owner — full control, including deleting the project.

The principle underneath is least privilege: give the minimum that lets someone do their job. A contributor who only needs to propose changes is a Developer, not a Maintainer.

Reviewing well

Small merge requests get real review; large ones get rubber-stamped. Comments should target correctness, clarity and tests — and a review that blocks a merge should say specifically what must change. This is the human half of the quality gate that CI automates.

📊 FIGURE — GitLab roles — what each level may do
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Why a Developer cannot merge their own merge request
  1. A protected branch (typically main) allows merges only from Maintainer and above.
  2. A Developer can push their feature branch and open the MR.
  3. The merge itself waits for someone with the right role to approve it.
  4. That is deliberate: it enforces review rather than trusting everyone to self-merge.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The traceability an MR leaves behind
  1. The MR records who wrote the change and who approved it.
  2. It links the discussion and the CI result to the exact commits.
  3. Six months later, git log gives the change, and the MR gives the reason — which is the part code cannot tell you.

That audit trail is the collaborative benefit the rubric asks about: shared review, a record of the decision, and no single person able to change main unseen.

🎯 EXAM TIP
Learn the boundary that matters: Developer pushes and proposes, Maintainer merges. Most role questions turn on exactly that line.

📖 Learn it step by step — Building a CI/CD Pipeline

WORKED EXAMPLE — a minimal .gitlab-ci.yml, line by line
stages:
  - build
  - test

build-job:
  stage: build
  script:
    - echo "Compiling..."
    - mvn compile

test-job:
  stage: test
  script:
    - mvn test
Push this file to the repo root and every push now triggers: a runner picks up the pipeline → build stage runs → if it succeeds, test stage runs → the MR shows ✅ or ❌. Stages run in order; jobs within a stage run in parallel.
THE VOCABULARY
• Pipeline — the whole run for one push/MR.
• Stage — an ordered phase (build → test → deploy).
• Job — one script in a stage, executed by a runner (the worker machine).
• A failing job stops later stages and marks the pipeline red — protecting main from broken code.
⚠️ THE PIPELINE GUARDS THE MERGE
The point of CI here isn’t ceremony: with “pipeline must succeed” enabled, red builds physically cannot merge. “What prevents broken code reaching main?” → the pipeline gate on the MR.
🎯 QUICK CHECK
In GitLab CI, the machine that executes your jobs is called a:
  1. Runner
  2. Stage
  3. Blob
Show answer
A — runner. Pipelines contain stages, stages contain jobs, runners execute jobs.

Building a CI/CD pipeline & DevOps foundation

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A pipeline automatically builds and tests your code every time you push, so problems are caught immediately instead of at merge time. In GitLab you describe the pipeline in a file named .gitlab-ci.yml at the repo root — GitLab reads it and runs the steps for you.

THE VOCABULARY
CI = Continuous Integration (merge small changes often; auto-build and auto-test each one). CD = Continuous Delivery/Deployment (automatically make the build ready to release, or deploy it). A pipeline is made of stages; each stage contains jobs; jobs are executed by GitLab Runners.
⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Stages run in order (e.g., build → test → deploy). Jobs within the same stage run in parallel. If any job in a stage fails, the pipeline stops — later stages don't run — so broken code can't move forward.

Pipelines are triggered by events: a push, a merge request, a tag, or a schedule. A Runner is the agent (a machine/container) that actually executes each job.

A MINIMAL .gitlab-ci.yml
stages:
  - build
  - test

build-job:
  stage: build
  script:
    - echo "Compiling..."

test-job:
  stage: test
  script:
    - echo "Running tests..."

Two stages; each has one job with a script. GitLab runs build first, then test, on a Runner.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

DevOps is the practice/culture of uniting software development and IT operations to deliver software faster and more reliably. CI/CD pipelines are the automation backbone of DevOps — they turn "build, test, deploy" from manual steps into an automatic, repeatable flow.

📝 COURSE & PROJECT NOTE

For the D197 project you'll add a .gitlab-ci.yml so a pipeline runs on your pushes. Know: stages run sequentially, jobs run in parallel, runners execute jobs, a failed job fails the pipeline, and CI/CD is the automation layer of DevOps.

🎯 CONCEPT CHECK
Where is a GitLab pipeline defined?
  1. In README.md
  2. In a .gitlab-ci.yml file at the repo root
  3. In the commit message
  4. In the runner
Show answer
B. GitLab reads the pipeline configuration from .gitlab-ci.yml at the repository root.
🔬 GOING DEEPER — pipelines and the DevOps loop

What a pipeline is made of

A pipeline is defined in the repository (GitLab reads .gitlab-ci.yml, GitHub reads workflow files under .github/workflows/). That matters: the build process is versioned alongside the code, so a change to the pipeline is reviewed like any other change.

Structure: a pipeline contains stages that run in order, and each stage contains jobs that run in parallel. Jobs execute on runners — the machines or containers that do the work. If any job in a stage fails, the pipeline stops and the following stages do not run.

Ordering jobs by cost

Put the fastest, cheapest checks first — lint and unit tests before integration tests before deployment. The goal is failing early: a developer should learn about a broken build in minutes, not after a half-hour deploy stage. This is the same "cheapest test first" reasoning behind short-circuit evaluation and the cost-of-change curve.

Artifacts, caches and secrets

  • Artifacts — files a job produces (a built binary, a test report) passed to later stages or downloaded.
  • Cache — dependencies reused between runs so you do not re-download them every time.
  • Secrets / CI variables — credentials injected at run time and masked in logs. They must never be committed to the repository; a token in git history is compromised permanently and must be rotated, not deleted.

DevOps as a loop

Plan → code → build → test → release → deploy → operate → monitor, feeding back into plan. The reason version control sits at the centre is that every stage is triggered by, and traceable to, a commit. Monitoring closes the loop: production behavior informs the next change.

📊 FIGURE — a pipeline: stages run in order, jobs inside a stage run together
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — What happens on a push
  1. You push a branch. The runner picks up .gitlab-ci.yml.
  2. build compiles and packages. If it fails, the pipeline stops here.
  3. test runs the unit tests. A single failing test fails the stage.
  4. deploy runs only if everything before it passed.
  5. The MR shows the result, and a protected branch can refuse the merge until it is green.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Why the pipeline lives in the repository
  1. .gitlab-ci.yml is committed alongside the code.
  2. So the pipeline is versioned with the thing it builds: an old commit still builds the way it did then.
  3. And a change to the build is reviewed like any other change, through an MR.
🎯 EXAM TIP
CI = Continuous Integration, merging and testing constantly. CD = Continuous Delivery (ready to ship, human approves) or Continuous Deployment (ships automatically). DevOps is the wider practice; CI/CD is the automation inside it.

📖 Learn it step by step — Automated Unit Tests in the Pipeline

WORKED EXAMPLE — one test, wired into CI
// src/test/java/CalcTest.java
@Test
void addsTwoNumbers() {
    assertEquals(5, Calc.add(2, 3));   // expected, actual
}
Locally: mvn test runs it. In CI, the test job from the pipeline file runs the SAME command on every push. Now break add() and push: the pipeline turns red, the MR is blocked, and the diff that broke it is one click away. That loop — write test → push → machine re-checks forever — is the whole point of automated testing.
WHAT MAKES A GOOD UNIT TEST
• Tests ONE unit (a method/class) in isolation — fast, no network/database.
• Asserts a specific expected outcome (assertEquals, assertThrows).
• Independent: any order, any subset, same result.
• Covers the edges: zero, negative, empty, boundary values — where real bugs live.
⚠️ TESTS IN CI ≥ TESTS ON YOUR MACHINE
“Works on my machine” dies here: the runner is a fresh environment, so passing in CI proves the repo itself is complete and correct. If it passes locally but fails in CI, something (a file, a dependency) never got committed.
🎯 QUICK CHECK
A unit test verifies:
  1. One small unit of code in isolation
  2. The whole deployed system
  3. The GitLab UI
Show answer
A. Unit = smallest testable piece; integration/system tests cover the bigger assemblies.

Establishing automated unit tests

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A unit test checks one small piece of code — a single function or method — in isolation, verifying it returns the right result for given inputs. Automating them means the pipeline runs the whole test suite on every push, so a change that breaks something is caught within minutes.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

In GitLab, unit tests live in a test stage/job in .gitlab-ci.yml. On each push the runner installs dependencies and runs the test command (e.g., pytest, mvn test, npm test). If any test fails, the job fails → the pipeline fails → the merge request is blocked from merging. Green tests are the gate that protects main.

A test job in .gitlab-ci.yml
test-job:
  stage: test
  script:
    - pip install -r requirements.txt
    - pytest

Every push triggers this; a failing pytest run fails the pipeline and blocks the MR.

WHY AUTOMATE TESTS
Manual testing is skipped under deadline pressure. Automated tests in CI run every time, catch regressions (something that used to work and now doesn't) immediately, and give reviewers confidence that an MR is safe to merge.
📝 COURSE & PROJECT NOTE

Common frameworks: JUnit (Java), pytest/unittest (Python), Jest (JavaScript). In the D197 project you add a test job so tests run automatically; a failing test fails the pipeline and blocks the merge.

🎯 CONCEPT CHECK
What happens when an automated unit test fails in the CI pipeline?
  1. The commit is deleted
  2. The pipeline fails and the merge request is blocked
  3. Tests are skipped next time
  4. The branch auto-merges
Show answer
B. A failing test fails its job and the pipeline, which blocks the merge request — protecting main from broken code.
🔬 GOING DEEPER — automated tests as the gate

Why the pipeline needs tests to mean anything

A pipeline that only compiles proves the code is syntactically valid, not correct. Automated tests are what turn CI into a safety net — they let you merge frequently because a regression is caught by the machine rather than by a user.

The levels, and what each is for

  • Unit — one function or class in isolation, dependencies replaced by stubs. Fast (milliseconds) and precise about where the fault is. Should be the bulk of your tests.
  • Integration — several components together, including real databases or services. Slower, catches wiring problems unit tests cannot.
  • System / end-to-end — the whole application through its real interface. Slowest and most brittle; keep few.
  • Acceptance — does it satisfy the customer's requirement?

That shape is the test pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, very few end-to-end. Inverting it produces a suite that is slow and flaky, which teams then start ignoring.

What makes a good test

The arrange–act–assert shape, one behavior per test, a name that states the expectation, and independence — tests must not depend on execution order or on each other's leftovers. A test that fails intermittently ("flaky") is worse than no test, because it teaches the team to ignore red builds.

Coverage, honestly

Coverage measures which lines ran during the suite — not whether the assertions were meaningful. 100% coverage with weak assertions proves very little, and chasing a coverage number is a classic way to write tests that do not catch bugs. Treat it as a signal for finding untested areas, not as a goal.

📊 FIGURE — where the tests sit in the loop
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — What makes a unit test a unit test
  1. It exercises one unit — a single method or class.
  2. It does not need a database, a network or a file, so it runs in milliseconds.
  3. It is deterministic: same input, same result, every run.
  4. It asserts a specific expected value rather than merely running without error.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Automating them so they actually get run
  1. Tests live in the repository next to the code.
  2. The pipeline runs the whole suite on every push, on a clean machine.
  3. The MR shows pass or fail, and a protected branch blocks the merge on failure.
  4. Nobody has to remember to run them, which is the entire point of automating.
🎯 EXAM TIP
For the PA, say what the test proves, not that it exists: name the method under test, the input, and the expected output. "Tests the calculator" scores nothing; "asserts that divide(10, 0) throws ArithmeticException" scores.

📖 Worked example — why PAs come back, and the 5-minute pre-submit check

WORKED EXAMPLE — a returned PA, diagnosed and fixed
Case: a submission comes back “conflict resolution not evident.” The student DID resolve a conflict — but squashed everything into one final commit, so the history shows a single commit and no merge.

Diagnosis: the rubric grades the history, and the history was erased. Fix: redo the branch work with commits per step, keep the real merge commit, re-push, resubmit.

The pre-submit check (run these and screenshot):
git log --oneline --graph --all   # several commits? branch structure? merge visible?
git branch -a                     # required branches exist (locally AND origin)?
git status                        # clean — nothing uncommitted
grep -r "<<<<<<<" .              # no conflict markers left behind
Top return reasons, in order: single-commit history, missing/never-pushed branch, no visible merge commit, conflict markers committed, and submitting the wrong repo URL. Every one is caught by the four commands above.

Build in this order, then verify before submitting

  1. Create the GitLab project and git init locally; add the origin remote.
  2. Add .gitignore first (language-appropriate) so secrets, node_modules/venv, and large binaries never get committed.
  3. Commit a small working app with a real unit test, using a descriptive first message.
  4. Add .gitlab-ci.yml defining a test stage that installs dependencies and runs the suite; push and confirm the pipeline is green.
  5. Create a feature branch, make commits, and merge back to main.
  6. Deliberately create a merge conflict (edit the same line on two branches) and resolve it; the resolution commit is your evidence.
  7. Tag a release (git tag -a) and push tags.
  8. git push everything; open the GitLab Pipelines and Tags pages to confirm all artifacts are visible.
  9. Record the video showing the pipeline running and touring the repo; write the reflection referencing real commits/branches.

Why PAs get returned

  • Committed secrets or large binaries because .gitignore was missing or added too late.
  • No real conflict resolution shown, only a description of one.
  • Pipeline that does not actually run tests, or is red/failing at submission.
  • Commit messages that do not explain the why ("update", "fix", "asdf").
  • Video that never shows the pipeline running, so the CI claim is unverifiable.
  • Missing tags, or a remote that is out of sync with local work.

If .gitignore was added late and a secret is already in history, removing the file in a new commit is not enough; the secret remains in prior commits. Rewrite history (or start clean) and rotate the secret.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Commit messages like "update" or "fix". The evaluator reads the log as the record of your process; a message that does not say what changed is treated as no evidence at all. Write "Add tax calculation to Invoice.total()" instead.

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its "J-Method"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
THE 3-STEP LOOP
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
Start the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers "learn it in 25 minutes" instead of hours.

Printing is a separate action \u2014 a module can return a value without displaying anything.", "topic": "Modularity", "id": "wr_p4_16", "difficulty": "medium"}, {"text": "What is the scope of a variable?", "options": ["The part of the program in which that variable can be accessed", "The number of times the variable is used", "The range of values the variable can hold", "The amount of memory the variable occupies"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Scope is about WHERE a name is visible. These four cover almost every flowchart question.", "topic": "Flowcharts", "id": "wr_p4_19", "difficulty": "medium"}, {"text": "In a flowchart, which symbol represents input or output?", "options": ["A parallelogram", "An oval", "A rectangle", "A diamond"], "correct": 0, "explain": "A parallelogram is input/output \u2014 reading a value or displaying one. A rectangle is a processing step such as a calculation.", "topic": "Flowcharts", "id": "wr_p4_20", "difficulty": "medium"}, {"text": "What does an end-structure statement (such as END IF or END WHILE) do?", "options": ["It resets the loop control variable", "It marks where a structure finishes, so the reader knows which statements belong to it", "It stops the program from running", "It converts pseudocode into a programming language"], "correct": 1, "explain": "End-structure statements delimit a block. Without them \u2014 or without indentation \u2014 it is ambiguous which statements sit inside the if or the loop.", "topic": "Program structures", "id": "wr_p4_21", "difficulty": "medium"}, {"text": "What is an abstract (high-level) step in a design?", "options": ["A comment ignored by the computer", "A step written in a real programming language", "A step that states WHAT must happen without yet saying HOW", "A step that cannot be implemented"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Top-down design starts with abstract steps and refines each into concrete ones. \"Calculate the payroll\" is abstract; the arithmetic that does it is the concrete refinement.", "topic": "Modularity", "id": "wr_p4_22", "difficulty": "medium"}, {"text": "Which is the best reason to use a named constant instead of a literal value?", "options": ["Constants prevent all logic errors", "Constants use less memory than variables", "One meaningful name documents the value and it can be changed in a single place", "Constants make the program run faster"], "correct": 2, "explain": "A named constant such as TAX_RATE explains what the number means and is changed in one place instead of hunting for every 0.07. Logic errors are grammatically valid but do the wrong thing.", "topic": "Errors", "id": "wr_p5_8", "difficulty": "medium"}, {"text": "In the analysis phase, what is the programmer mainly producing?", "options": ["A maintenance schedule", "Working source code", "A compiled executable", "A clear statement of the requirements and constraints"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Analysis is about understanding: what the program must do, what data it needs, and what limits apply. Which approach is this?", "options": ["Regression testing", "Prototyping", "Waterfall", "Maintenance"], "correct": 1, "explain": "A prototype is a throwaway or partial build made to gather feedback early, when changes are still cheap.", "topic": "SDLC models", "id": "wr_p5_14", "difficulty": "medium"}, {"text": "Which SDLC model is organised around repeated cycles that each include a risk analysis?", "options": ["Waterfall", "Spiral", "Prototyping", "Agile"], "correct": 1, "explain": "The spiral model repeats a loop of planning, risk analysis, engineering and evaluation \u2014 its distinguishing feature is that explicit risk assessment on every pass.", "topic": "SDLC models", "id": "wr_p5_15", "difficulty": "medium"}, {"text": "Why is documentation produced throughout the lifecycle rather than only at the end?", "options": ["It replaces the need for testing", "Later maintainers need to understand the decisions, and the details are forgotten quickly", "It makes the program run faster", "It is required before a program can be compiled"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Most of a program's life is maintenance, often by someone who did not write it. They are the yardstick that acceptance testing measures the finished product against.", "topic": "SDLC phases", "id": "wr_p5_17", "difficulty": "medium"}, {"text": "Which step comes immediately BEFORE coding the program?", "options": ["Test the program", "Plan the logic", "Put the program into production", "Translate the code"], "correct": 1, "explain": "The order is understand the problem, plan the logic, code the program, translate, test, put into production, maintain.
